en: The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll One. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter One: The Introduction. **Chapter One: The Introduction** At that time, the Bhagavat was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of five thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge had become liberated. Among them were the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the venerable Aśvajit, the venerable Vāṣpa, the venerable Mahānāman, the venerable Bāṣpa, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, the venerable Gayākāśyapa, the venerable Nadīkāśyapa, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Mahākapphiṇa, the venerable Bakkula, the venerable Aniruddha, the venerable Revata, the venerable Khadiravaniya-Śāriputra, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Nanda, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, the venerable Gavāmpati, the venerable Pilindavatsa, the venerable Svāgata, the venerable Upāli, the venerable Rāhula, and others such as these, numbering five thousand in all. Also present were twelve hundred bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-regressive, possessed of the power of the dhāraṇīs, skilled in the profound gates of dharma, and endowed with the unhindered wisdom of eloquence. Among them were the bodhisattva mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Anantamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vidyuddeva, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vajradatta, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Padmaśrīgarbha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya, and others such as these, numbering twelve hundred in all. Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, including Śakra Devendra; thirty-two thousand Cāturmahārājika devas, including Vaiśravaṇa; twenty thousand devas of the Yāma heaven, including Suyāma; ten thousand devas of the Tuṣita heaven, including Sunirmita; ten thousand devas of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, including Vasavartin; and ten thousand devas of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, including Vaśavartin. There were also five hundred Brahmās, including Śikhin and Sahāmpati. Furthermore, there were the four great kings of the dragon kings, including Sāgara; eight thousand yakṣa generals, including Vajrapāṇi; and eight thousand gandharva kings, including Druma. There were also eight thousand kinnara kings, including Druma; eight thousand mahoraga kings, including Elapatra; and eight thousand garuḍa kings, including Vejayanta. There were also eight thousand asura kings, including Vemacitrin; eight thousand rākṣasa kings, including Pāñcika; and eight thousand piśāca kings, including Kuntī. There were also eight thousand mahāpiśāca kings, including Kumbhīra; eight thousand kumbhāṇḍa kings, including Pāñcika; and eight thousand nāga kings, including Manasvin. There were also eight thousand kimnara kings, including Druma; eight thousand mahoraga kings, including Elapatra; and eight thousand garuḍa kings, including Vejayanta. There were also eight thousand asura kings, including Vemacitrin; eight thousand rākṣasa kings, including Pāñcika; and eight thousand piśāca kings, including Kuntī. There were also eight thousand mahāpiśāca kings, including Kumbhīra; eight thousand kumbhāṇḍa kings, including Pāñcika; and eight thousand nāga kings, including Manasvin. There were also the four great kings of the world, including Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa; the four great queens of the nagas, including Sāgara, Valguka, Mucilinda, and Elapatra; the four great queens of the asuras, including Śacī, Hāritī, Māyā, and Vemacitrin; and the four great queens of the rākṣasas, including Caturmahārājika, Piṅgalā, Kuntī, and Kumbhīra. There were also the four great queens of the piśācas, including Kumbhīra, Kumbhāṇḍa, Piśāca, and Mahāpiśāca; the four great queens of the kumbhāṇḍas, including Kumbhāṇḍa, Piśāca, Mahāpiśāca, and Kumbhīra; the four great queens of the nāgas, including Manasvin, Sāgara, Valguka, and Mucilinda; the four great queens of the kimnaras, including Druma, Elapatra, Vejayanta, and Vemacitrin; the four great queens of the mahoragas, including Elapatra, Vejayanta, Vemacitrin, and Manasvin; the four great queens of the garuḍas, including Vejayanta, Vemacitrin, Manasvin, and Sāgara; the four great queens of the asuras, including Vemacitrin, Manasvin, Sāgara, and Valguka; the four great queens of the rākṣasas, including Pāñcika, Kuntī, Kumbhīra, and Kumbhāṇḍa; and the four great queens of the piśācas, including Kumbhīra, Kumbhāṇḍa, Piśāca, and Mahāpiśāca. In addition, there were the four great kings of the earth, including Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa; the four great queens of the nagas, including Sāgara, Valguka, Mucilinda, and Elapatra; the four great queens of the asuras, including Śacī, Hāritī, Māyā, and Vemacitrin; and the four great queens of the rākṣasas, including Caturmahārājika, Piṅgalā, Kuntī, and Kumbhīra. There were also the four great queens of the piśācas, including Kumbhīra, Kumbhāṇḍa, Piśāca, and Mahāpiśāca; the four great queens of the kumbhāṇḍas, including Kumbhāṇḍa, Piśāca, Mahāpiśāca, and Kumbhīra; the four great queens of the nāgas, including Manasvin, Sāgara, Valguka, and Mucilinda; the four great queens of the kimnaras, including Druma, Elapatra, Vejayanta, and Vemacitrin; the four great queens of the mahoragas, including Elapatra, Vejayanta, Vemacitrin, and Manasvin; the four great queens of the garuḍas, including Vejayanta, Vemacitrin, Manasvin, and Sāgara; the four great queens of the asuras, including Vemacitrin, Manasvin, Sāgara, and Valguka; the four great queens of the rākṣasas, including Pāñcika, Kuntī, Kumbhīra, and Kumbhāṇḍa; and
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great community of monks numbering five thousand, all of whom were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated; whose hearts were as supple and gentle as great elephants (mahānāga); who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge had realized liberation—with the sole exception of Ānanda, who remained in the stage of training and had attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
Furthermore, there were five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and others, all of whom had attained the Noble Truths.

There were also bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—all of whom had attained dhāraṇīs and the practices of various samādhis; who had realized emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; who had already attained equal patience (samartha-kṣānti) and unimpeded dhāraṇīs; who possessed all five supernormal powers; whose words were always received with faith and trust and who were free from indolence; who had already renounced gain, offerings, and fame; who preached the Dharma without expectation of reward; who had crossed over to profound dharma-patience and attained the power of fearlessness; who had transcended all demonic activities; and who were entirely liberated from all karmic obstructions.
He skillfully expounds the Dharma of causes and conditions.

Having made great vows since incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), his countenance is harmonious and joyful; he always greets others first, and his speech is never coarse. Amidst the great assembly, he is without fear.

For countless billions of kalpas, they have skillfully expounded the Dharma, understanding that all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, like space, like echoes, like a city of the Gandharvas, like dreams, like shadows, like images in a mirror, and like transformations; thus they have attained unimpeded eloquence and fearlessness.
They fully know the mental activities and inclinations of sentient beings, delivering and liberating them through subtle and wondrous wisdom.
Their minds are without obstruction; having accomplished great patience, they skillfully deliver others in accordance with reality.
May I vow to receive immeasurable Buddha-lands; may the samādhi of recollecting the Buddhas of immeasurable lands be ever present before me; and may I be able to invite immeasurable Buddhas.
They are able to sever the various fetters of views and all afflictions, and they sport in the arising of hundreds of thousands of samādhis—
bodhisattvas who have thus accomplished such various and immeasurable merits,
whose names are: Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Bodhisattva Keṅanajia, Bodhisattva Daoshi, and Bodhisattva Nara...
The Bodhisattva Prāpta, the Bodhisattva Tārakajita, the Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva, the Bodhisattva Indradeva, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati,
the Bodhisattva Upakāramati, the Bodhisattva Vardhamānamati, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin,
the Bodhisattva Suvikrānta, the Bodhisattva Vegavasu, the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, and the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura.
Sākyamuni, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sun-Store (Dīpaṅkara), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Defectless-Mind (Anikṣiptadhura), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Holder-of-the-Jewel-Seal (Ratnamudrādhara), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Constantly-Raised-Hand (Nityotkṣiptahasta),
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, and so forth— immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
"Oṃ! All Bodhisattvas are those in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), destined to succeed to the position of the Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One personally prepared a lion throne, sat upon it in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), straightened his body, and fixed his mindfulness before him. He entered the Samādhirāja-samādhi, into which all other samādhis are subsumed."

At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi and surveyed the world with his divine eye. He smiled with his entire body, emitting six hundred trillion rays of light from the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of his feet. From each of his ten toes, both ankles, both calves, both knees, both thighs, waist, spine, abdomen, ribs, back, navel, the "virtue" (*śrīvatsa*) mark on his chest, shoulders, arms, ten fingers of the hands, neck, forty teeth in his mouth, two nostrils, two eyes, two ears, the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft between his brows, and the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of his head, he likewise emitted six hundred trillion rays of light.
From these various lights, a great radiance issued forth, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm;

from that trichiliocosm, it illuminated as many Buddha-lands in the eastern direction as there are sands in the Ganges River, and likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This radiance extends beyond Buddha-lands in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; it is likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

At that time, the World-Honored One’s pores all smiled and emitted rays of light that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm, extending further to Buddha-lands in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his constant radiance, illumined the trichiliocosm, and it likewise reached the Buddha-lands in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and so it was throughout the ten directions.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue, covering the entire trichiliocosm.

With a joyful and smiling countenance, he emitted immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of rays of light from the root of his tongue; each individual ray transformed into a golden precious flower with a thousand petals.
Upon each of these flowers there is a transformed Buddha, sitting in the full lotus posture and preaching the six pāramitās.
Any sentient being who hears this will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, this was likewise the case in all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

At that time, the World-Honored One remained upon his lion throne and entered the Lion’s Play Samādhi (*siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*). By means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*), he caused the trichiliocosm to tremble in six ways: it surged in the east and subsided in the west; surged in the west and subsided in the east; surged in the south and subsided in the north; surged in the north and subsided in the south; surged at the periphery and subsided in the center; and surged in the center and subsided at the periphery. The earth became entirely supple, causing all sentient beings to feel harmony and joy.
The hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and the eight states of woe within this trichiliocosm were immediately liberated, and they attained rebirth in the heavens.

From the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, these devas, having personally realized their own past lives, all came to the place where the Buddha was with great joy.
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

In this manner, the lands of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions all shook in six ways; all those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and the eight difficult states were immediately liberated and attained rebirth in the heavens, reaching as far as the sixth heaven.

At that time, throughout the trichiliocosm, sentient beings who were blind regained their sight; those who were deaf regained their hearing; those who were mute were able to speak; those who were insane regained their sanity; those who were distracted attained concentration; those who were naked obtained clothing; those who were hungry and thirsty became satiated; the sick were healed; and those with physical impairments became whole.

All sentient beings shall attain a mind of equality, regarding one another as father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, elder sister, or younger sister, as well as kinsmen and spiritual friends.

At that time, sentient beings equally practiced the ten paths of wholesome action and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring; free from all blemishes and impurities, they were tranquil and happy, just as bhikṣus who have entered the third dhyāna attain excellent wisdom, maintaining their precepts and self-restraint without harming any living being.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne; within the trichiliocosm, his virtue was preeminent and supreme, and his radiance, physical form, and majestic power were so sublime that they pervaded the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
For example, the light and color of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, are so exceptionally sublime that no other mountains can equal them.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested his ordinary body to all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm.

At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, as well as humans and non-humans from the trichiliocosm, took various celestial flowers, celestial garlands, celestial unguents, celestial powdered incense, celestial blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, pink lotuses, and celestial tree-leaf incense, and went to where the Buddha was. They scattered these celestial flowers, up to the celestial tree-leaf incense, over the Buddha; the precious flowers thus scattered formed a great platform in the void above this trichiliocosm.

From the edges of these flower pedestals hung various necklaces, and canopies of variegated flowers displayed a profusion of five colors; these flower canopies and necklaces filled the entire trichiliocosm.

Because these flower canopies and necklaces were so exquisitely adorned, this trichiliocosm became entirely golden in color, and all the Buddha-lands in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, became likewise so.

At that time, the sentient beings of the three-thousandfold world system and throughout the ten directions each thought to themselves, "The Buddha is preaching the Dharma for me alone, and not for others.
Then, while the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne, he smiled with a serene and joyful countenance; light issued forth from his mouth, illuminating the entire three-thousandfold world system.
By means of this light, the sentient beings within this trichiliocosm all see the Buddhas and their Saṅghas in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
likewise, the sentient beings in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in that direction also see Śākyamuni Buddha and his great assembly within this trichiliocosm.
It was likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
At that time, in the eastern direction, beyond as many worlds as there are sands in the Ganges, there was a bodhisattva named Samantaprabhāsa.
Seeing the great radiance, seeing the great trembling of the earth, and seeing the body of the Buddha, he went to the place where the Buddha Ratnākara was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions does this radiance now illuminate the world, while the great earth trembles and the body of the Buddha is seen?
The Buddha Ratnākara replied to Samantaprabha:

“Good son! To the west, passing through as many lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a world named Sahā. The Buddha there is named Śākyamuni, who is currently present, desiring to preach the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
"This is due to his spiritual power.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi addressed the Buddha Ratnākara, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

I shall now go to see Śākyamuni Buddha to pay homage and make offerings, and to see those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have succeeded to the position of the Honored One—all of whom have attained dhāraṇīs and various samādhis, and have attained mastery over all samādhis.
The Buddha told Puming:
"If you wish to go, do as you please; you should know that now is the time.
At that moment, the Buddha Ratnākara gave a thousand-petaled golden lotus to the Bodhisattva Puming and addressed him, saying:
“Good son! Scatter these flowers over Śākyamuni Buddha.
The bodhisattvas born in that Sahā world-system are difficult to surpass and difficult to equal; you should travel to that land with single-minded devotion.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi received from the Buddha Ratnākara a thousand-petaled lotus of golden radiance. Together with countless bodhisattvas—both monastics and laypeople—as well as boys and girls, they set out as a company, all making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, and praising the Buddhas of the eastern direction. Carrying various flowers, incense, necklaces, fragrant ointments, powdered incense, unguents, robes, banners, and parasols, they proceeded toward the dwelling of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata Ratnākara sends his greetings:”
“World-Honored One!
Are you free from affliction and illness? Are your daily activities light and easy, and is your physical strength at ease and in comfort?
He then offered these thousand-petaled golden lotuses to the World-Honored One as an act of worship.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha accepted these thousand-petaled golden lotuses and scattered them throughout as many lands in the eastern direction as there are sands in the Ganges River.

The precious flowers scattered by the Buddha filled as many Buddha-lands in the eastern direction as there are sands in the Ganges River; upon each flower sat a bodhisattva in the full lotus posture preaching the six pāramitās, and those who heard this Dharma would certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

All the monastic and lay bodhisattvas, as well as the boys and girls, prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha, each offering articles of worship to honor, revere, respect, and praise Śākyamuni Buddha.

These bodhisattvas, both monastic and lay, as well as the boys and girls, each by the power of their own roots of goodness and merit, were able to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

To the south, beyond as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a land situated at the very edge called Free from All Sorrow; the Buddha there is named Virtue of Freedom from Sorrow, and the Bodhisattva is named Free from Sorrow.

To the west, beyond as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a land situated at the very edge called Extinction of Evil; the Buddha there is named Jewel Mountain, and the bodhisattva is named Ritual Mind.

To the north, passing through as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a land situated at the very edge called Vijaya; the Buddha there is named Vijayarāja, and the bodhisattva is named Guṇavijaya.

Below, passing through as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a land situated at the very edge called *Sādhu*; the Buddha there is named *Sādhugati*, and the bodhisattva is named *Puṣpadatta*.

Above, passing through as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a land at the very edge named *Priya*; the Buddha there is named *Priyaguna*, and the Bodhisattva is named *Gunapriya*.
In this way, everything was exactly as it was in the eastern direction.

At that time, this trichiliocosm became entirely covered with precious flowers; banners, streamers, and canopies were suspended from the ground, and fragrant trees and flowering trees were all magnificently adorned.

For example, it is like the world-system Puṣpasañcaya, the Buddha-field of the Buddha Samantakusuma, where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Susthitamati, and other bodhisattvas of great majestic power all reside.

At that time, the Buddha knew that all those in every world—whether in the world of devas, the world of Māras, or the world of Brahmās; whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or gods; whether gandharvas, humans, asuras, and so forth; as well as all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had succeeded to the position of the Honored One—had all assembled.
Knowing that the assembly had gathered, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know all phenomena through the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know all dharmas by means of the knowledge of all modes practice the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom by means of the dharma of non-dwelling; he should fulfill the perfection of giving by means of the dharma of non-renunciation, because the giver, the recipient, and the material gift cannot be apprehended;
and because neither transgression nor non-transgression can be apprehended, he should fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline.”
Because the mind is unmoving, one should fulfill the perfection of patience;
because body and mind are diligent and untiring, one should fulfill the perfection of vigor;
because there is neither distraction nor attachment to flavors, one should fulfill the perfection of meditation.
Because of non-attachment to all dharmas, one should fulfill the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom by means of the dharma of non-dwelling,
because of non-arising, should fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, and the five faculties.
The five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path; the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness;

the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, the ten totalities, and the nine perceptions—

The sign of bloating, the sign of decay, the sign of being smeared with blood, the sign of festering pus, the sign of bluish discoloration, the sign of being devoured, the sign of scattering, the sign of bones, and the sign of burning;

and the ten perceptions: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of virtue, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, and mindfulness of death.
The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of the impurity of food, the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds,
the perception of death, the perception of impurity, the perception of cessation, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of exhaustion— these constitute eleven knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

The knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of things as they truly are;

the three samādhis—samādhi with directed thought and sustained thought, samādhi without directed thought and with sustained thought, and samādhi without directed thought and without sustained thought;
and the three faculties—the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and [the faculty of one who has known].
The faculties and the faculty of having known. Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully know the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion, should practice the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the wisdom of the path should practice the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the wisdom of the aspects of the path through the wisdom of the path should practice the perfection of wisdom.
If one wishes to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) by means of the wisdom of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), one should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If one wishes to fulfill the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) by means of all-knowledge, one should practice the perfection of wisdom.
If one wishes to sever the habitual tendencies of afflictions by means of the knowledge of all modes, one should practice the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to ascend to the bodhisattva stage should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One who wishes to transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha and abide in the stage of *avaivartika* should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abide in the six supernormal powers should study the perfection of wisdom.
One who wishes to know the inclinations and mental dispositions of all sentient beings should study the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to surpass the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to attain the various dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
When all those seeking the state of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha practice giving, one who wishes to surpass them by means of a mind of sympathetic joy should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
When those who seek the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha observe the precepts, one who wishes to surpass them by means of a mind of sympathetic joy should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Those who seek the samādhis, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and who wish to surpass them with a mind of sympathetic joy, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who seek the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and who wish to surpass them with a mind of sympathetic joy, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices little giving, little morality, little patience, little diligence, little meditation, and little wisdom, yet wishes to attain immeasurable and boundless merit through the power of dedication by means of skillful means, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause his body in every lifetime to resemble that of a Buddha, and wishes to be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Those who wish to be born into the family of Bodhisattvas, who wish to attain the stage of the youthful (kumārabhūmi), and who wish never to be separated from the Buddhas, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who wish to offer all their roots of goodness to the Buddhas, and to achieve with ease the acts of honoring, respecting, and praising them, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings regarding food and drink, clothing, bedding, ointments, vehicles, dwellings, couches, lamps, and candles, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish sentient beings in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the perfection of dāna, and to establish them in the perfections of śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, and prajñā, should study the perfection of prajñā."

If one wishes to plant a single root of goodness within the field of merit of the Buddha so that it remains inexhaustible until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cause the Buddhas of the ten directions to praise his name should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach as many buddha-fields in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges by means of a single resolve should study the Prajñāpāramitā. "Furthermore, Śāriputra..."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to emit a single sound so that it may be heard in as many Buddha-fields in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who wishes to ensure that the buddha-fields are never interrupted should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra..."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence, should study the perfection of wisdom.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to know the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of all phenomena should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know the suchness (tathatā), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) of all dharmas should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know by calculation the number of atoms in the great earth and all its mountains within a trichiliocosm should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to split a single hair into a hundred parts and, with one such part, lift up all the waters of the great oceans, rivers, lakes, and springs within a trichiliocosm without disturbing the nature of water, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If all the fires within the trichiliocosm were to ignite simultaneously, like at the time of the conflagration at the end of an eon, and a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to extinguish them with a single breath, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If great winds should arise within the trichiliocosm, wishing to blow apart the trichiliocosm and all its Mount Sumerus as if crushing rotten grass, and if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to obstruct that wind-force with a single finger so that it does not arise, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to sit cross-legged once and fill the entire space of the trichiliocosm, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to lift all the Sumeru kings within a trichiliocosm with a single hair and cast them beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddha-fields in other directions without harming any sentient beings, and wishes to offer a single meal to as many Buddhas and their Saṅghas in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to offer a single garment, flowers, fragrant garlands, powdered incense, ointments, burning incense, lamps, candles, banners, pennants, flower canopies, and so forth, as offerings to the Buddhas and the Saṅgha, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause all sentient beings in as many lands in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River to be fully endowed with morality, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and to enable them to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, and the fruit of arhat, even unto the attainment of nirvāṇa without remainder, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom while giving, he should make such a distinction: "

"By giving such gifts, one obtains great rewards; by giving such gifts, one is born into the great clans of the Kṣatriyas, the great clans of the Brāhmaṇas, or the great households of householders; by giving such gifts, one is born in the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. Because of these gifts, one attains the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Because of these gifts, one attains the eight factors of the Noble Path; because of these gifts, one is able to attain the path of the Srotāpanna up to the path of Buddhahood. One should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom while giving, by means of the power of skillful means, they are able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing giving, fulfill the dānapāramitā through to the prajñāpāramitā by means of the power of wisdom and skillful means?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Because the giver, the receiver, and the material wealth cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the dānapāramitā;
because transgression and non-transgression cannot be apprehended, one fulfills the śīlapāramitā.”
Because the mind is unmoving, one fulfills the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
because body and mind are diligent and free from indolence, one fulfills the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā);
because there is neither distraction nor attachment to flavors, one fulfills the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
Because one knows that all dharmas are unattainable, one fulfills the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the merits of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach the further shore of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the suchness, the dharma-characteristic, and the limit of non-arising of all dharmas of the past, future, and present, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to stand before all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; wishes to serve and attend upon the Buddhas; wishes to become an inner retinue of the Buddhas; wishes to obtain a great retinue; wishes to obtain a retinue of bodhisattvas; and wishes to purify the retribution for great giving, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes not to give rise to a mind of stinginess, a mind of broken precepts, a mind of ill-will, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, or a mind of delusion, should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to establish all sentient beings in the merit of giving, the merit of ethical discipline, the merit of cultivating meditative concentration, and the merit of exhortation; and if he wishes to establish sentient beings in the merit of material wealth and the merit of the Dharma, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the five eyes should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
What are the five eyes?
The fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see with the divine eye all the Buddhas within lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions; wishes to hear with the divine ear the Dharma preached by those Buddhas of the ten directions; and wishes to know the minds of those Buddhas, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to hear the Dharma taught by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, and having heard it, not forget it until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to see the buddha-fields of the past and the future, as well as the buddha-fields of the present throughout the ten directions, should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear the twelvefold scriptures— sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas— as preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions, and wishes to recite, receive, and uphold them all, whether they have been heard by other śrāvakas or not, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

In as many worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, regarding all the dharmas taught by the Buddhas—those already taught, those currently being taught, and those yet to be taught—one who, having heard them, desires to believe and uphold them all, to practice them oneself, and also to explain them to others, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to hear what has been taught by the Buddhas of the past and will be taught by the Buddhas of the future— and having heard it, to benefit both themselves and others— should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

If one wishes to hold forth light to universally illuminate the dark spaces between the worlds of the ten directions—spaces as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River where neither the sun nor the moon shines—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

In as many worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, where there is no name for the Buddha, no name for the Dharma, and no name for the Saṅgha—if one wishes to cause all sentient beings to attain right view and hear the names of the Triple Gem, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cause the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions—by the power of my own strength—to have those who are blind regain their sight, those who are deaf regain their hearing, those who are insane regain their mindfulness, those who are naked obtain clothing, and those who are hungry and thirsty attain fullness, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions who are currently in the three evil destinies to obtain human bodies through the power of my [the Buddha's] might, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

If one wishes to cause the sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, by means of my power, to be established in morality, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and to enable them to attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to learn the majestic deportment of all Buddhas should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the gaze of an elephant king should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Bodhisattva makes this vow:

"When I walk, may I remain four finger-widths above the ground so that my feet do not touch the earth; surrounded and revered by immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of devas from the Four Great Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, may I proceed to the foot of the Bodhi tree."
"One should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
'I shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, with the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven providing celestial robes as my seat.'"
"One should study the Prajñāpāramitā with this thought:
'When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall cause every place where I walk, stand, sit, or lie down to become entirely composed of vajra.'"
"One should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* on the very day he leaves the household life, and on that same day turns the wheel of Dharma; and at the time of turning the wheel of Dharma, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings become free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, because they do not grasp at any phenomena, attain liberation of mind through the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*); and immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"When I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, I shall have an assembly of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya śrāvakas; when I preach the Dharma even once, they shall all attain arhatship while remaining on their seats—I should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"I shall take immeasurable, incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as my saṃgha; when I preach the Dharma once, immeasurable, incalculable bodhisattvas will all attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika). Those who wish to obtain an immeasurable lifespan and be endowed with immeasurable radiance should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"When I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there shall be no lust, anger, or delusion in my world, nor even the names of the three poisons. All sentient beings shall achieve such virtues as wisdom, generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and pure conduct, and shall not afflict other beings; for this purpose, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"May it be that after my parinirvāṇa, the Dharma shall neither perish nor even have the name 'perishing'; for this purpose, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, may all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions who hear my name necessarily attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Those who wish to attain such merits as these should study the Prajñāpāramitā. **Chapter Two:
The Offering of the Bowl** From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Two: The Offering of the Bowl. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā is able to perform such meritorious deeds, at that time the Four Heavenly Kings will all rejoice greatly and think to themselves:"
"We shall present four alms bowls to the Bodhisattva, just as the heavenly kings previously offered bowls to the former Buddhas.
The gods from the Heaven of the Thirty-three up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations were likewise filled with joy, thinking to themselves:
"We shall attend upon and make offerings to the Bodhisattva, thereby diminishing the race of the asuras and increasing the hosts of devas."
The gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven throughout the trichiliocosm were all greatly rejoiced, and they thought to themselves:
"We shall entreat this bodhisattva to turn the wheel of Dharma."
"Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom and cause the six perfections to increase, various sons and daughters of good family will each rejoice and think:
'We shall act as parents, wives, children, kinsmen, and friends for this person.'"
At that time, the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven were all greatly rejoiced, each thinking to themselves:

"We shall employ skillful means to cause this bodhisattva to remain free from sexual desire; from the first moment he resolved his mind, he shall always remain a celibate youth. Let him not encounter the pleasures of form and desire, for if he were to experience the five desires, it would obstruct his birth in the Brahma Heaven, let alone his attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"For this reason, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has renounced the world by severing sexual desire shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, whereas one who does not so sever it shall not."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Must a bodhisattva mahāsattva necessarily have parents, wife and children, kinsmen, and acquaintances?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There are some bodhisattvas who have parents, wives, children, relatives, and acquaintances.

There are also some bodhisattvas who, from the moment they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], sever sexual desire and cultivate the practice of celibacy, continuing until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without ever transgressing against sensual desire."
There may be bodhisattvas who, by the power of skillful means, experience the five desires and then leave the household life to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, being well-versed in the arts of illusion, conjures the five desires through magic and enjoys them together.
"What do you think? Does this person have any real experience of these five desires?
Śāriputra replied, "No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“It is likewise for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, by the power of skillful means, manifests the five desires and experiences pleasure therein to bring sentient beings to maturity.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is not defiled by desire; through various causes and conditions, he reviles the five desires, seeing that desire is a blazing fire, desire is foul and evil, desire is destructive, and desire is like an enemy.
"Therefore, Śāriputra, you should know that it is for the sake of sentient beings that a bodhisattva accepts the five desires.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the word ‘bodhisattva. He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive that ‘I am practicing the perfection of wisdom,’ nor does he perceive that ‘I am not practicing the perfection of wisdom.’”
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva and the nature of the word "Bodhisattva" are empty. Within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
yet apart from form there is no emptiness, and apart from sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is also no emptiness.
Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are emptiness, and emptiness is consciousness. Why is this so?

Śāriputra! It is only because of names that we speak of "enlightenment" (bodhi); it is only because of names that we speak of a "bodhisattva"; it is only because of names that we speak of "emptiness."
Why is this? Because the true nature of all phenomena is without arising and without cessation, and without defilement and without purity.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they neither perceive arising nor perceive cessation, and they neither perceive defilement nor perceive purity.
Why is this? Names are dharmas produced by the cooperation of causes and conditions; they are merely conventional designations spoken through conceptual discrimination and recollection.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive any names; because they do not perceive them, they do not cling to them.
Chapter 3: Practice and Correspondence (*Abhyāsa-saṃprayoga*) The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Three: Practice and Correspondence (in the Dan-zang edition, titled "Practice and Correspondence").
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he should reflect in this way:

'A bodhisattva exists only as a name; a Buddha also exists only as a name; the prajñāpāramitā also exists only as a name; form exists only as a name; and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also exist only as names.'"
"Śāriputra! Just as 'self' exists only as a mere name, and no permanent self can ever be found, so too all these— sentient beings,

life-spanners, living beings, those who are born, those who nourish and count as persons, agents, instigators of action, originators, instigators of origination, experiencers, instigators of experience, knowers, and seers— all of these are utterly unfindable."
Because they are empty of being unapprehendable, they are spoken of merely by means of names.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive sentient beings, nor even a knower or a perceiver; the names by which these are spoken are likewise unperceivable.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, with the exception of the Buddha’s wisdom, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by virtue of the emptiness of the unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because, Śāriputra, these dharmas of names and the objects to which names adhere are likewise unobtainable for this bodhisattva mahāsattva. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

For example, suppose Jambudvīpa were filled with bamboo, hemp, rice, and reeds, and there were as many bhikṣus as there are stalks therein, each possessing wisdom like that of Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana; yet, compared to the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, their wisdom would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth, nor one hundred-thousandth, nor one billionth part—and indeed, it could not be reached by any calculation or analogy.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas deliver all sentient beings by means of wisdom. Śāriputra!
Suppose there were as many [beings] throughout Jambudvīpa as there are such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana;
or suppose there were as many throughout the trichiliocosm as there are such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—let us set aside this matter.

If one were to take the wisdom of those such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana filling as many lands in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, and compare it to the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā, it would not equal even a hundredth part; nor a thousandth, nor a hundred-thousand-billionth part; indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy whatsoever.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, the wisdom cultivated by them in a single day surpasses that of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The wisdom possessed by śrāvakas—whether that of srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or the wisdom of a buddha—all these various forms of wisdom are without distinction; they do not contradict one another, for they are of the nature of non-arising and emptiness.”
If dharmas are non-contradictory, unarisen, and empty by nature, then these dharmas possess no distinction.
Why, then, does the World-Honored One say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* for a single day cultivates wisdom that surpasses that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “What do you think?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates wisdom for a single day, with the thought in mind:”
"I practice the wisdom of the path to benefit all sentient beings; I shall know all dharmas through the knowledge of all modes and deliver all sentient beings.
Do the wisdoms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess such a capacity?
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One. “Śāriputra! [the Buddha continued.]
What do you think? Do the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ever have this thought:
"We shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and deliver all sentient beings, causing them to attain nirvāṇa without remainder"?
Śāriputra replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"For this reason, you should know that if one were to compare the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas with the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, it would not equal even a hundredth part; nor a thousandth, a hundred-thousandth, a ten-millionth, or even any part reachable by calculation or analogy."
Śāriputra, what do you think? Do any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas ever have such a thought as this:

"By practicing the six pāramitās, do I bring sentient beings to maturity, adorn the buddha-fields, and fully realize the Buddha's ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and eighteen unique dharmas, so as to deliver immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings and cause them to attain nirvāṇa?"
Śāriputra replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva can form this thought:

‘I shall practice the six pāramitās, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; I shall realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and deliver immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, enabling them to attain nirvāṇa.’”
"Just as a firefly does not think,
'By my power I can illuminate Jambudvīpa and cause it to shine everywhere with great brilliance,' so too it is with all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; they do not think:"

"We shall practice the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and deliver immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, enabling them to attain nirvāṇa."
"Śāriputra! It is like when the sun rises, its radiance shines everywhere; there is no one in Jambudvīpa who does not receive its light.
So it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

Practicing the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and delivers immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, causing them to attain nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, abide in the stage of avaivartika, and purify the path of the buddhas?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the six pāramitās and dwells in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they are able to transcend all stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, abide in the stage of avaivartika, and purify the path to buddhahood.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what stage does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide so that he can serve as a field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, until they sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), throughout that interval, they constantly serve as a field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Why is this? It is because, due to the causal conditions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all wholesome dharmas arise in the world.
What are these wholesome dharmas?

What are known as the ten paths of wholesome action, the five precepts, the eightfold fast, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—all these appear in the world.

By reason of the Bodhisattva, the six pāramitās, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, great kindness and great compassion, and the knowledge of all modes appear fully in the world.

Because of the causes and conditions of bodhisattvas, there appear in the world the great clans of kṣatriyas, the great clans of brahmins, and the great households of householders, as well as all the heavens from the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
It is because of the Bodhisattvas that there are Srotāpannas, Sakṛdāgāmins, Anāgāmins, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas, all of whom appear in the world.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Does the bodhisattva mahāsattva completely purify the merit of giving?
The Buddha said:
"No. Why is this? Because it has already been fundamentally purified."
Śāriputra! The bodhisattva mahāsattva is a great donor.
What does he give?
He bestows all wholesome dharmas.
What are these wholesome dharmas?
They are the ten paths of wholesome action, the five precepts, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and all-knowledge; it is with these that he bestows.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice and respond to the prajñāpāramitā so as to be in union with the prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in accordance with the emptiness of form, this is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
When they practice in accordance with the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and accords with the emptiness of the eye, this is called being in correspondence with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
When they practice and accord with the emptiness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, this is called being in correspondence with the perfection of wisdom.
To practice and accord with the emptiness of form is called being in correspondence with the prajñāpāramitā.
To practice and accord with the emptiness of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena is called being in correspondence with the prajñāpāramitā.
To practice and accord with the emptiness of the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element is called being in correspondence with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

To practice and accord with the emptiness of the ear-sound-consciousness, nose-odor-consciousness, tongue-taste-consciousness, body-touch-consciousness, and mind-dharma-consciousness-elements is called being in correspondence with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
To practice and respond to the emptiness of suffering is called being in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā.
To practice and respond to the emptiness of origination, cessation, and the path is called being in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā.
To practice and respond to the emptiness of ignorance is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

To practice and respond to the emptiness of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom.
To practice and accord with the emptiness of all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned—is called being in correspondence with the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and accords with the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), this is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Thus, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice and accord with the seven kinds of emptiness, namely: the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence (*abhāvabhāva-śūnyatā*). This is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom.

The Buddha told Śāriputra: “When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and accords with the seven kinds of emptiness, he does not perceive form as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either conjoined or unconjoined. He does not perceive form as having the characteristic of arising or the characteristic of ceasing; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having the characteristic of arising or the characteristic of ceasing. He does not perceive form as having the characteristic of defilement or the characteristic of purity; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having the characteristic of defilement or the characteristic of purity. He does not perceive form as being united with feeling, nor feeling as being united with perception, nor perception as being united with mental formations, nor mental formations as being united with consciousness.”
Why is this? Because there is no dharma that can be conjoined with another dharma, for their nature is empty. Śāriputra!
In the emptiness of form, there is no form; in the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is no consciousness.

Śāriputra, because form is empty, it has no characteristic of affliction or destruction; because feeling is empty, it has no characteristic of feeling; because perception is empty, it has no characteristic of cognition; because mental formations are empty, they have no characteristic of volitional activity; because consciousness is empty, it has no characteristic of awareness.

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is not that form is different from emptiness, nor is emptiness different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Śāriputra! These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

This dharma of emptiness is neither past, nor future, nor present. Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; no眼界 (eye-element) up to and including no consciousness-element; furthermore, there is no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment; no stream-enterer and no fruit of stream-entry; no once-returner and no fruit of once-returning; no non-returner and no fruit of non-returning; no arhat and no fruit of arhatship; no pratyekabuddha and no pratyekabuddha-path; and no Buddha and no Buddha-path.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this manner, it is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Śāriputra!
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom as either associated or dissociated; nor do they perceive the perfection of generosity,
the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, or the perfection of meditative concentration.
Whether associated or dissociated, one does not perceive form as associated or dissociated;
one does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as associated or dissociated;
one does not perceive the eye up to the mind, nor forms up to phenomena, nor the eye-form-consciousness element up to the mind-phenomena-consciousness element, whether associated or dissociated.

They are not associated; one does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, nor the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-knowledge, as being either associated or dissociated.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
You should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is conjoined with the prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, emptiness does not unite with emptiness, signlessness does not unite with signlessness, and wishlessness does not unite with wishlessness.
Why is this? Śāriputra, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness have neither conjunction nor non-conjunction. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this way, it is called being in correspondence with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they enter into the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) of all phenomena. Having entered therein, they do not bring form (*rūpa*) into conjunction nor do they bring it into non-conjunction; they do not bring feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) into conjunction nor do they bring them into non-conjunction. Form does not conjoin with the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
Why is this? Because the prior limit is not perceived.
Form does not unite with the posterior limit.
Why is this? Because the future limit is not perceived.
Form does not conjoin with the present.
Why is this? Because the present is not perceived.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the past does not join with the future, the future does not join with the past, the present does not join with the past or the future, and the past and the future do not join with the present, because the three periods of time are empty by name."
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this way, it is called being in accord with the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, omniscience (sarvajñatā) does not conjoin with the past. Why is this?
Because the past cannot be perceived; how much less can omniscience conjoin with the past?
All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) does not conjoin with the future. Why is this?
Because the future cannot be seen; how much less can all-knowledge conjoin with the future?
All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) does not conjoin with the present time. Why is this?
Because the present time is unobservable; how much less could all-knowledge conjoin with the present time?
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this manner, it is called being in accord with the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, form does not unite with omniscience (*sarvajñā*), because form is invisible.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
The eye does not unite with omniscience (sarvajñā), because the eye is invisible.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Form does not unite with omniscience, because form is invisible.
Sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are also like this. Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this manner, it is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of giving does not unite with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), because the perfection of giving cannot be perceived."
This applies even up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The four foundations of mindfulness do not unite with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), because the four foundations of mindfulness are unobservable.
This applies even up to the eightfold noble path.

The ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities, are not conjoined with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), because the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities, are invisible.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this manner, it is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha does not unite with omniscience (sarvajñatā), nor does omniscience unite with the Buddha.
Awakening (bodhi) does not unite with omniscience, nor does omniscience unite with awakening.
Why is this? The Buddha is itself omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and omniscience is itself the Buddha.
Awakening (*bodhi*) is itself omniscience, and omniscience is itself awakening.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner of training and responding, this is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not cultivate the existence of form, nor do they cultivate the non-existence of form; it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

One does not practice with regard to form as being permanent, nor does one practice with regard to form as being impermanent; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

One does not practice with regard to form as being suffering, nor does one practice with regard to form as being pleasure; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One does not practice with regard to form as "I," nor does one practice with regard to form as "not-I"; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

One does not practice with regard to the cessation of form, nor does one practice with regard to the non-cessation of form; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One does not practice the emptiness of form, nor does one practice that form is not empty; it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One does not practice that form has marks, nor does one practice that form is markless; it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One does not practice with the notion that form exists, nor does one practice with the notion that form does not exist;
it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such thoughts:
"I am practicing the perfection of wisdom," "I am not practicing the perfection of wisdom," or "I am neither practicing nor not practicing the perfection of wisdom."
"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this way, it is called being in accord with the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of wisdom;
nor does he practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline,
the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, or the perfection of meditative concentration.
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the stage of an avaivartika;
one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of maturing sentient beings; one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of purifying buddha-fields;
nor for the sake of the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, or the ten...
One practices the perfection of wisdom because of the eight unique qualities of a Buddha; one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of internal emptiness,
nor for the sake of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness,
the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, or beginningless emptiness.
One practices the perfection of wisdom because of the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of all phenomena,
the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence;
one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of suchness, the dharma-nature, or the reality-limit.
Why is this? Because when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not destroy the characteristics of phenomena.
To train and respond in this manner is called being in correspondence with the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the supernormal power of psychic transformation; they do not practice it for the sake of the divine ear, nor for the knowledge of others' minds, nor for the knowledge of past lives, nor for the divine eye, nor for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows."

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not even perceive the perfection of wisdom, let alone perceive the supernatural powers (abhijñā) of a bodhisattva.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, it is called being in accord with the prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form this thought:
"By means of my supernormal power of psychic travel, I shall fly to the eastern direction and make offerings and show reverence to as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges."
The same applies to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions,
and the zenith and nadir. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such thoughts:
"I hear the Dharma preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions with my divine ear," yet he does not form this thought:
"I know the thoughts and mental activities of sentient beings in the ten directions with my knowledge of others' minds."
He does not form this thought:
"By means of my knowledge of past lives, I shall know the deeds performed in past lives by sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
He does not form this thought:
“With my divine eye, I see beings in the ten directions dying here and being born there.

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, it is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and he is also able to deliver immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, evil Māras cannot find an opportunity to harm them; all worldly affairs and desires are fulfilled according to their wishes; and all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will protect this bodhisattva, ensuring they do not fall into the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
The gods from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven shall all likewise protect this bodhisattva, ensuring that no obstacles arise.
All the grave offenses committed by this bodhisattva will be experienced as light in the present life.
