Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas bestow universal loving-kindness upon all sentient beings. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, it is called being in accord with the prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they swiftly attain all the gates of dhāraṇī and all the gates of samādhi; in whatever place they are born, they always encounter the Buddhas, and until they reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they never cease seeing the Buddhas.
"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this manner, it is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such a thought:
"There is a dharma that either conjoins with or does not conjoin with another dharma, or is equal to or unequal to it."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive this dharma as being either conjoined or unconjoined with other dharmas, nor as equal or unequal to them.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this way, it is called being in correspondence with the prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form the thought:
"I shall quickly attain the dharma-nature, or perhaps I shall not. Why is this?
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is characterized by non-attainment, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this manner, it is called being in correspondence with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any dharma that transcends the nature of dharmas (dharmatā)."
Practicing and responding in this manner is called being in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he does not form such a thought:"
"To discern all phenomena through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and to practice accordingly— this is called being in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form the thought:
"This dharma can attain the dharma-nature, or it cannot. Why is this?
This bodhisattva does not perceive that by means of this dharma one can either attain or fail to attain the nature of dharmas (dharmatā). Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and responds in this way, it is called being in accord with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the dharma-nature does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the dharma-nature."
Practicing and responding in this manner is called being in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, the eye-element does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the eye-element; the form-element does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the form-element; the eye-consciousness-element does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the eye-consciousness-element; and so on, up to the mind-element which does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the mind-element; the phenomena-element does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the phenomena-element; and the mind-consciousness-element does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the mind-consciousness-element."
Therefore, Śāriputra, this correspondence with emptiness is called the foremost correspondence. Śāriputra!

The bodhisattva mahāsattva Gaganagañja does not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; he is able to purify buddha-fields, bring sentient beings to maturity, and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! Among all associations, the association with the perfection of wisdom is the foremost; it is the most honored, the most excellent, the most sublime, and unsurpassed.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in accordance with the perfection of wisdom—namely, through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—it should be known that this bodhisattva is no different from one who has received the prediction, or is close to receiving it.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in such a manner is able to bring great benefit to immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form such a thought:

"I am in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā; the Buddhas shall bestow upon me the prediction [of enlightenment]; I shall soon receive that prediction; I shall purify a Buddha-field; and having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall turn the wheel of Dharma."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive any dharma that emerges from the dharma-nature; nor do they perceive any dharma that practices the prajñāpāramitā; nor do they perceive any dharma for which the Buddhas bestow a prediction; nor do they perceive any dharma that attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not give rise to the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, nor even the notions of a knower or a viewer.
Why is this? Because sentient beings are ultimately neither born nor extinguished; sentient beings have no birth and no extinction.
If a dharma has no characteristic of birth and no characteristic of extinction, how could there be a dharma that should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
In this way, Śāriputra,
because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive sentient beings, they practice the perfection of wisdom.

Because sentient beings are not received, because sentient beings are empty, because sentient beings are unapprehendable, and because sentient beings are detached, they practice the perfection of wisdom.

Śāriputra! Among all forms of mental application (*yoga*), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva possesses the foremost application, namely, the application of emptiness (*śūnyatā-yoga*). This application of emptiness is superior to all other applications.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice emptiness in this way, they are able to give rise to great loving-kindness and great compassion.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice in such correspondence, they do not give rise to a mind of stinginess, a mind of violating the precepts, a mind of anger, a mind of indolence, a mind of distraction, or a mind of ignorance.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll One;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Four: Rebirth in the Pure Land Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom can thus cultivate such correspondence, from where did they pass away to be born here?
And after passing away from this place, where will they be born?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom can cultivate such correspondence as this, they have either come from a buddha-field in another direction to be born here, or come from the Tuṣita heaven to be born here, or come from among human beings to be born here.”
Śāriputra! Those who have come from other Buddha-fields quickly become associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Because they are associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, they cast off their bodies and are reborn here; all profound and wondrous dharmas appear before them, and subsequently they again become associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In whatever place they are born, they always encounter the Buddhas.
Śāriputra! There is a bodhisattva in the stage of being bound to only one more birth who, having passed away from Tuṣita Heaven, comes to be born here in this world.
This bodhisattva does not lose the six pāramitās; in whatever place they are born, all the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi swiftly manifest before them.
Śāriputra! There are bodhisattvas who, at the end of their lives among humans, are reborn again among humans—excluding those who are *avaivartika*.
These bodhisattvas have dull faculties; they cannot quickly become associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can the various *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates quickly manifest before them.
Śāriputra! Regarding your question as to where a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is in accord with the prajñāpāramitā will be reborn after passing away from this world: [the answer is as follows].
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva travels from one buddha-field to another, constantly encountering all buddhas and never being separated from them.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, without employing skillful means, enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, and also practice the six pāramitās.

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained the dhyānas, he is reborn in the long-lived heavens; when his lifespan there comes to an end, he returns to this world, obtains a human body, and encounters the Buddhas.
Such a bodhisattva’s faculties are not sharp.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna and also practice the perfection of wisdom, yet because they lack skillful means, they abandon those dhyānas and are reborn in the desire realm.
The faculties of these bodhisattvas are also dull.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; they enter the mind of loving-kindness up to equanimity; they enter the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they practice the ten powers of a Buddha up to great loving-kindness and great compassion.

By the power of skillful means, this bodhisattva does not take birth in accordance with the dhyānas, nor in accordance with the immeasurables, nor in accordance with the four formless attainments; rather, they are born in all places where Buddhas reside, never being separated from the practice of the prajñāpāramitā.
In this way, such bodhisattvas shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the Bhadrakalpa.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; they enter loving-kindness up to equanimity; they enter the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Yet, by the power of skillful means, they do not take birth according to those meditative states, but instead return to birth in the desire realm—whether among the great clans of kṣatriyas, the great clans of brāhmaṇas, or the great households of householders—in order to bring sentient beings to maturity.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; they enter the mind of loving-kindness up to equanimity; they enter the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. By the power of skillful means, they do not take birth according to these meditative states. Instead, they may be born in the realm of the Four Great Kings, or they may be born among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods. While dwelling therein, they bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and constantly encounter the Buddhas.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā and, through the power of skillful means, enter the first dhyāna. Having ended their lives here, they are reborn in the Brahma-heaven as Great Brahmā Kings. From that Brahma-heaven, they travel from one buddha-field to another, and wherever there are Buddhas who have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi but have not yet turned the wheel of Dharma, they exhort them to turn it.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, being in their final birth before buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). By the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; they enter loving-kindness (*maitrī*) up to equanimity (*upekṣā*); they enter the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); and they enter the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the signless (*animitta-samādhi*), and the wishless (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). Yet, they do not take rebirth according to those dhyānas, but are born where there is a Buddha and cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

If they are born in the Tuṣita Heaven, at the end of their lifespan, they will possess perfected roots of goodness and, without losing right mindfulness, surrounded and honored by countless hundreds of thousands of billions of devas, they will come to be born here in this world and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers; they are not born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, but travel from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising the Buddhas."

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who sport with supernatural powers, traveling from one buddha-field to another; wherever they arrive, there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor even the names of the two vehicles.
Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who sport with supernatural powers, traveling from one buddha-field to another, and wherever they arrive, their lifespan is immeasurable.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who sport with supernatural powers, traveling from one land to another. Wherever they go, if there is no Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha, they praise the merits of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. Because sentient beings hear the name of the Buddha, the name of the Dharma, and the name of the Saṅgha, when their lives end here, they are reborn in the presence of the Buddhas.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, at the time they first resolve their minds, attain the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; they attain the four immeasurable minds and the four formless concentrations; and they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
This bodhisattva is not born within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, but is always born in places where they can benefit sentient beings.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from the moment they first resolve their minds, practice the six pāramitās, ascend to the stage of a bodhisattva, and attain the level of avaivartika.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, at the very moment they first resolve their minds [on awakening], attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the wheel of Dharma. Having brought immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings to great benefit, they enter nirvana without remainder. After these Buddhas have passed into parinirvāṇa, their remaining Dharma may abide for one kalpa or slightly less than one kalpa.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from the moment they first resolve their minds upon enlightenment, are in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*, and together with countless hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas, travel from one buddha-field to another for the sake of purifying the buddha-fields.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, attain the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; they sport within them, entering the first dhyāna, arising from the first dhyāna to enter the attainment of cessation, arising from the attainment of cessation to enter up to the fourth dhyāna, arising from the fourth dhyāna to enter the attainment of cessation, arising from the attainment of cessation to enter the sphere of infinite space, arising from the sphere of infinite space to enter the attainment of cessation, arising from the attainment of cessation to enter up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to enter the attainment of cessation.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
By means of the power of skillful means, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom enters the concentration of transcendence. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; yet, they do not grasp at the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha. By the power of skillful means, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they give rise to the eightfold noble path.
"By means of these eight branches of the noble path, one causes others to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the path of a pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The fruits and the wisdom of all arhats and pratyekabuddhas constitute the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, you should know that he dwells within the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, dwelling in the adornment of the six pāramitās, occupy the Tuṣita heaven; you should know that these are bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivate the four dhyānas up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, yet have not yet realized the four noble truths; you should know that such a bodhisattva is in his final birth before buddhahood.
Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having practiced for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Śāriputra!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the six pāramitās, constantly and diligently exerting themselves to benefit sentient beings, never speaking words that are without benefit. Śāriputra!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the six pāramitās, constantly and diligently exerting themselves to benefit sentient beings, traveling from one buddha-field to another to sever the three evil paths for those beings.
Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the six pāramitās, with dāna as their foremost practice, bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.

To those who need food and drink, they give food and drink; to those who need clothing, bedding, necklaces, flowers, incense, houses, or lamps and candles, they provide them all according to each person's needs.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, manifest bodies like those of Buddhas to preach the Dharma to sentient beings in the hells, and to preach the Dharma to sentient beings among animals and hungry ghosts.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while practicing the six pāramitās, manifest bodies like those of the Buddhas and travel throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. They also make offerings to the Buddhas and purify the Buddha-lands, and they hear the Buddhas preaching the Dharma.

One merely contemplates the signs of the pure and wondrous lands of the ten directions and then personally manifests a particularly sublime land, wherein all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are in their final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).
Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while practicing the six pāramitās, achieve the thirty-two marks and possess faculties that are pure and sharp.
Because their faculties are pure and sharp, they are loved and respected by all people; because they are loved and respected, they gradually deliver them through the Dharma of the three vehicles.
In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should train in the purity of body and the purity of speech. Śāriputra!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while practicing the six pāramitās, attain purity of the faculties; by means of these pure faculties, they neither exalt themselves nor disparage others.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment, abide in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), and so forth, up to the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika-bhūmi), and never fall into the three evil destinies.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until they reach the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika-bhūmi), never abandon the ten virtuous actions. Śāriputra!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, abiding in the perfection of giving and the perfection of ethical discipline, become wheel-turning sage-kings; they establish sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action and also bestow material wealth as gifts upon them.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, abiding in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) and the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), have for immeasurable tens of millions of lifetimes served as universal monarchs (cakravartin), encountering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, revering, and praising them.

Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who constantly illuminate sentient beings with the Dharma and also illuminate themselves; until they reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they never depart from such illumination.
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained reverence within the Buddha-dharma. Śāriputra!
"For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not allow impurities of body, speech, or mind to arise falsely.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s impurity of physical action, impurity of verbal action, and impurity of mental action?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought:”
"This is the body, this is speech, this is the mind.
Śāriputra, grasping at such characteristics and making them a condition is called the impurity of body, speech, and mind.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend the body, they do not apprehend speech, and they do not apprehend the mind. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they were to obtain a body, or obtain speech, or obtain a mind, then by virtue of obtaining such body, speech, and mind, they would be able to give rise to a mind of stinginess, a mind of violating the precepts, a mind of anger, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, and a mind of delusion.
"You should know that when this bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they are unable to eliminate the coarse karmas of body, speech, and mind.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva eliminate the coarse karma of body, speech, and mind?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend body, speech, or mind, then such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to eliminate the coarse karma of body, speech, and mind.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the ten paths of wholesome action and does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka nor the mind of a pratyekabuddha, such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to eliminate the coarse karma of body, speech, and mind.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and purifies the Buddha-way, they practice the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s elimination of coarse karma of body, speech, and mind.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the Buddha-way of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“As for the Way of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend body, does not apprehend speech, and does not apprehend mind; does not apprehend the dāna-pāramitā, does not apprehend the śīla-pāramitā, does not apprehend the kṣānti-pāramitā, does not apprehend the vīrya-pāramitā, does not apprehend the dhyāna-pāramitā, and does not apprehend the prajñā-pāramitā; does not apprehend śrāvaka, does not apprehend pratyekabuddha, does not apprehend bodhisattva, and does not apprehend buddha—Śāriputra! [This is the Way of the Buddha.]”
This is called the Buddha-way of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
that is to say, because all dharmas are unobtainable. Śāriputra!
“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, when practicing the six pāramitās, cannot be defeated by anyone.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

“How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, none are able to destroy them? The Buddha told Śāriputra: “When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, they do not conceive of the existence of form up to consciousness;

they do not conceive of the existence of the eye up to the mind; they do not conceive of the existence of forms up to dharmas; they do not conceive of the existence of the eye-element up to the mental-consciousness-element; they do not conceive of the existence of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they do not conceive of the existence of the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā; they do not conceive of the existence of the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities; they do not conceive of the existence of the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat; and they do not conceive of the existence of pratyekabuddhahood up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they augment the six pāramitās, and no one is able to destroy them. Śāriputra!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, dwelling within the perfection of wisdom, are fully endowed with wisdom. By means of this wisdom, they never fall into the evil realms, are never born among wicked people, and never become impoverished. Furthermore, the bodies they receive are never loathed by humans, devas, or asuras.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“By means of this accomplishment of wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; he hears the Dharma and sees the Saṃgha, and he also beholds the adorned and purified buddha-fields.”

By means of this wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form the notion of a Buddha, does not form the notion of a bodhisattva, does not form the notion of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, does not form the notion of a self, and does not form the notion of a buddha-field.

Using this wisdom, when practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one does not apprehend the perfection of giving; likewise, up to and including the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom. When practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one does not apprehend the four foundations of mindfulness; likewise, up to and including the practice of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), one does not apprehend the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Śāriputra! This is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
By means of this wisdom, they are able to fulfill all dharmas while also not apprehending any dharma.
Śāriputra! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, purify the five eyes:
the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the purity of the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”

The Buddha told Śāriputra: “There are bodhisattvas whose fleshly eye sees one hundred yojanas; there are bodhisattvas whose fleshly eye sees two hundred yojanas; there are bodhisattvas whose fleshly eye sees one Jambudvīpa; there are bodhisattvas whose fleshly eye sees two continents, three continents, or four continents; there are bodhisattvas whose fleshly eye sees a small thousandfold world system; there are bodhisattvas whose fleshly eye sees a medium thousandfold world system; and there are bodhisattvas whose fleshly eye sees a great trichiliocosm.”
“Śāriputra! This is the purification of the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the divine eye?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, with the divine eye, see all that is seen by the gods of the Four Great Kings; they see what is seen by the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens; they see what is seen by the Brahmā kings, up to and including what is seen by the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven.”
That which is seen by the divine eye of a bodhisattva is unknown and unseen by the gods from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Śāriputra, with this divine eye, the bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the deaths and rebirths of beings within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
“Śāriputra! This is called the pure divine eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the wisdom-eye of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is purified?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus does not form such thoughts:
'There are dharmas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether mundane or supramundane, whether with outflows or without outflows.'"

"Śāriputra, this Bodhisattva of the Wisdom-Eye likewise has no dharma that he does not see, no dharma that he does not hear, no dharma that he does not know, and no dharma that he does not recognize."
"This is called the purification of the wisdom-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is the pure Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? The Buddha told Śāriputra: “With the Dharma-eye, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows:

‘This person is a follower by faith; this person is a follower by dharma; this person practices the signless. He knows: ‘This person practices the gate of liberation of emptiness; this person practices the gate of liberation of the signless; this person practices the gate of liberation of the wishless and attains the five faculties. Because he attains the five faculties, he attains the uninterrupted samādhi (*ānantarya-samādhi*). Because he attains the uninterrupted samādhi, he attains the knowledge of liberation. Because he attains the knowledge of liberation, he severs the three fetters—view of self, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—and such a person is called a srotāpanna.”
If this person attains the path of contemplation and thins out lust, anger, and delusion, they shall become a Sakṛdāgāmin;
by further advancing in the path of contemplation and severing lust, anger, and delusion, they attain the state of an Anāgāmin;

by further advancing in the path of contemplation and severing attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness, they attain the state of an Arhat.

This person practices the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and attains the five faculties. Because they attain the five faculties, they attain the uninterrupted samādhi (*ānantarya-samādhi*). Because they attain the uninterrupted samādhi, they attain the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*). Because they attain the knowledge of liberation, they know that all phenomena that arise are phenomena that cease, and thus they become a pratyekabuddha.
This is the purification of the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that this bodhisattva has first resolved their mind and is practicing the dāna-pāramitā.
When practicing the perfection of wisdom, having accomplished the faculty of faith and the faculty of diligence,
and because their roots of goodness are pure and thick through the power of skillful means, they take on bodies for the sake of sentient beings—
whether being born into a great clan of Kṣatriyas, or a great clan of Brāhmaṇas, or a great household of lay devotees, or among the Four Heavenly Kings.
From the realm of the gods up to the realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, the bodhisattva dwells therein to bring sentient beings to maturity,
bestowing upon them whatever they desire; furthermore, he purifies buddha-fields,
encounters all Buddhas, and makes offerings to, reveres, honors, and praises them, until reaching *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Awakening (bodhi) likewise does not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
This is called the purification of the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows that this bodhisattva will regress from unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, and knows that this bodhisattva will not regress from unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment;

he knows that this bodhisattva has received the prediction of unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, and knows that this bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction of unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment;
he knows that this bodhisattva has reached the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), and knows that this bodhisattva has not yet reached the stage of non-retrogression.
They know which bodhisattvas are fully endowed with supernormal powers and which bodhisattvas are not yet fully endowed with supernormal powers;

they know which bodhisattvas, being fully endowed with supernormal powers, fly to worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to see the Buddhas, making offerings, paying respect, honoring, and praising them.
He knows that this bodhisattva has not yet attained supernormal powers but will attain them;
he knows that this bodhisattva will purify a buddha-field or will not purify a buddha-field;
and he knows that this bodhisattva has matured sentient beings or has not yet matured sentient beings.
This bodhisattva is praised by the Buddhas or not praised by the Buddhas;
this bodhisattva draws near to the Buddhas or does not draw near to the Buddhas;
this bodhisattva has a limited lifespan or an unlimited lifespan.
When this bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, the assembly of bhikṣus will be finite;
when this bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he will take bodhisattvas as his saṅgha, rather than taking bhikṣus as his saṅgha;
this bodhisattva will practice asceticism and difficult austerities, rather than practicing asceticism and difficult austerities.
This bodhisattva is one who is in his last birth before Buddhahood, yet not yet in his last birth;
this bodhisattva has received his final body, yet has not yet received his final body;

Subhūti! The perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva, and the word "bodhisattva" are also like this: they all exist through a combination of factors and are spoken of merely by way of names. These, too, are neither born nor extinguished; they are not within, not without, and not in between.

Subhūti! For example, external things such as grasses, trees, branches, leaves, stems, and nodes—all these are spoken of merely by way of names. These phenomena and their names are neither born nor extinguished; they do not abide internally, externally, or in between.

Subhūti! Prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva, and the name "bodhisattva" are also like this: they all exist through combination. These dharmas and their names are neither born nor extinguished; they do not abide internally, externally, or in between.

Subhūti! For example, the names of the Buddhas of the past exist because of the conjunction of designations; they, too, are neither born nor extinguished, being spoken of merely by way of names. Furthermore, they do not abide internally, externally, or in between.
The *prajñāpāramitā*, the bodhisattva, and even the word "bodhisattva" are likewise so.

Subhūti! For example, like a dream, an echo, a reflection, an illusion, a mirage, or a magical creation—they all exist because of a combination of conditions and are spoken of merely by means of names. These phenomena and their names are neither born nor extinguished; they do not abide internally, externally, or in between.
The perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva, and even the word "bodhisattva" are likewise so.

Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in this way: regarding the designation of names, the designation of acquisitions, and the designation of dharmas as mere conventional designations.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that the name 'form' is permanent, nor does he perceive that the names 'feeling,' 'perception,' 'volitional formations,' or 'consciousness' are permanent."
One does not perceive that the names of form are impermanent; one does not perceive that the names of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
One does not perceive that the names of form are pleasant; one does not perceive that the names of form are suffering.
One does not perceive form as being named "self," nor does one perceive form as being named "non-self.

One does not perceive form as being named "emptiness," nor does one perceive form as being named "signlessness," nor does one perceive form as being named "wishlessness," nor does one perceive form as being named "quiescence."
One does not perceive the name-and-form of form as defiled, nor does one perceive the name-and-form of form as pure.
One does not perceive the name-and-form of form as arising, nor does one perceive the name-and-form of form as ceasing.
One does not perceive the name-and-form of form within, nor does one perceive it without, nor does one perceive it abiding in between.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

The eye, forms, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact—and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition—up to and including the mind, mental phenomena, mind-consciousness, and mind-contact—and the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—are also like this.

Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, neither the word "perfection of wisdom" nor the word "bodhisattva" is perceived within the nature of the conditioned, nor is it perceived within the nature of the unconditioned.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not make any conceptual distinctions regarding these dharmas.

When this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom and dwells within the indestructible dharmas while cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they perceive the word "perfection of wisdom"; they do not perceive the bodhisattva, nor do they perceive the word "bodhisattva."

Even when practicing the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the word "perfection of wisdom"; one does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the word "bodhisattva."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they know only the true mark of all phenomena.
The true mark of all phenomena is neither defiled nor pure.
"So it is, Subhūti. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should understand that names are merely conventional designations."
Having understood that these are merely provisional names, one does not cling to form, nor to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one does not cling to the eye up to the mind; one does not cling to forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); one does not cling to eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness;
one does not cling to eye-contact up to mind-contact; and one does not cling to that which arises conditioned by eye-contact.
Regarding feeling— whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— even up to feeling born of the condition of mental contact—
whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— one does not cling to conditioned nature,
does not cling to unconditioned nature, and does not cling to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā);

they do not cling to the thirty-two marks, they do not cling to the body of a bodhisattva, and they do not cling to the bodhisattva’s fleshly eye, up to and including the Buddha-eye; they do not cling.
The perfection of wisdom, the perfection of non-attachment to supernormal powers, non-attachment to inner emptiness up to and including non-attachment to the emptiness of non-existence and existence,
non-attachment to the maturation of sentient beings, non-attachment to the purification of buddha-fields,
and non-attachment to skillful means.
Why is this? Because these dharmas have no one who clings, no clinging dharma, and no object of clinging;
all are non-existent. Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not cling to any dharmas; thus, they increase the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā. They enter the rank of bodhisattvas and attain the stage of avaivartika. Endowed with the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, they travel from one buddha-field to another to bring sentient beings to maturity, revering, honoring, and praising all buddhas, purifying buddha-fields, and making offerings to behold the buddhas.
Because their roots of goodness have been perfected, they obtain all requisites for making offerings according to their wishes.

They also hear the Dharma taught by all Buddhas; having heard it, they never forget it until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they attain the various *dhāraṇī* gates and the various *samādhi* gates.
Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
they should know that the names of all phenomena are merely provisional designations.
Subhūti, what do you think? Is form the bodhisattva? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the bodhisattva?
“No, World-Honored One! Are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the bodhisattva? “No, World-Honored One!”
“Are form, sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena the bodhisattva? “No, World-Honored One.
“Are visual consciousness up to mental consciousness the bodhisattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, what do you think? Is the earth element the bodhisattva?"
“No, World-Honored One! ‘Are the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness the bodhisattva?
‘No, World-Honored One!’”
“What do you think, Subhūti, is ignorance the bodhisattva? “No, World-Honored One.
“And so on, up to: is old age and death the bodhisattva?”
"No, World-Honored One. "What do you think, Subhūti?
Is one who is detached from form, detached from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and even detached from old age and death, a bodhisattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, what do you think:
is the mark of the suchness of form the bodhisattva?"
“No, World-Honored One! ‘...Is the suchness of everything up to old age and death the bodhisattva? ‘No, World-Honored One!’”
“Is it the case that the bodhisattva is [defined by] being detached from the suchness of form, up to and including being detached from the suchness of old age and death?
“No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What meaning do you perceive such that you say that form is not a bodhisattva, and so on, up to old age and death are not a bodhisattva?
Or that apart from form there is no bodhisattva, and so on, up to apart from old age and death there is no bodhisattva?”
Is the suchness of form not the bodhisattva, and so on, up to the suchness of old age and death not the bodhisattva?
Is it apart from the suchness of form that there is no bodhisattva, and so on, up to being apart from the suchness of old age and death that there is no bodhisattva?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
Sentient beings are ultimately unobtainable; how much more so, then, could there be such a thing as a bodhisattva?”

Form cannot be apprehended; how much less so can form be separated from form, or the suchness of form be separated from form—such is the bodhisattva. This applies even unto old age and death, which cannot be apprehended; how much less so can old age and death be separated from old age and death, or the suchness of old age and death be separated from old age and death—such is the bodhisattva.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent, excellent! It is so, Subhūti!”
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva and sentient beings cannot be apprehended, the prajñāpāramitā also cannot be apprehended.
One should train in this manner.
What do you think, Subhūti—is "form" the meaning of "bodhisattva"?
“No, World-Honored One! Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No, World-Honored One!”
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is ‘form is permanent’ the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?
“No, World-Honored One. “Are ‘feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent’ the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is it the meaning of 'bodhisattva' that form is impermanent? "No, World-Honored One!"
“Is it the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent? “No, World-Honored One.
“Is it the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ that form is pleasant?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is it the case that the bodhisattva's meaning consists in the pleasure of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? "No, World-Honored One!"
“Is ‘form is suffering’ the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?
“No, World-Honored One. “Are ‘feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering’ the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is 'form is self' the meaning of a bodhisattva? No, World-Honored One!"
“Is it the meaning of ‘I am a bodhisattva’ that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness [are the self]? “No, World-Honored One.
“Is it the meaning of ‘I am a bodhisattva’ that form is not the self?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is it not the meaning of 'Bodhisattva' that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the self? "No, World-Honored One!"
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is ‘the emptiness of form’ the meaning of a bodhisattva?
“No, World-Honored One. “Is ‘the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness’ the meaning of a bodhisattva?”
“No, World-Honored One! Is it not the case that form is not empty—that is the meaning of a bodhisattva? “No, World-Honored One!”
“Is it the case that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not empty—that this is the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No, World-Honored One.
“Is the characteristic of form the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?”
“No, World-Honored One! Is the characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No, World-Honored One!”
“Is ‘form is signless’ the meaning of a bodhisattva?
“No, World-Honored One. “Are ‘feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are signless’ the meaning of a bodhisattva?”
“No, World-Honored One! “Is ‘form-making’ the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No, World-Honored One!”
“Is it the case that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitute the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No, World-Honored One.
“Is it the case that form being without activity constitutes the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is it the case that the non-activity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitutes the meaning of 'bodhisattva'? "No, World-Honored One!"
"Even up to old age and death, it is likewise.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Based on what meaning do you say that form is not the meaning of a bodhisattva, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the meaning of a bodhisattva; even up to the fact that the non-activity of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not the meaning of a bodhisattva, and even up to old age and death, it is likewise?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Form is ultimately unobtainable; how much more so is the meaning of ‘form’ as a bodhisattva? It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”

"Bhagavān! Form (*rūpa*) is ultimately non-apprehendable; how much less so is 'the impermanence of form' the meaning of a bodhisattva? This applies likewise up to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Bhagavān!"

"Form-pleasure is ultimately unobtainable; how much more so is form-suffering? This is the meaning of 'bodhisattva. It is the same for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, up to and including consciousness itself.

World-Honored One! The self of form is ultimately unobtainable; how much more so is the non-self of form? This is the meaning of 'bodhisattva. It is the same for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, up to and including consciousness itself."
World-Honored One!

Form is ultimately unattainable; how much more so is the emptiness of form? This is the meaning of a bodhisattva. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including consciousness itself, World-Honored One.
The characteristic of form is ultimately unobtainable; how much more so is the meaning of "bodhisattva" as the signlessness of form? This applies likewise up to consciousness. World-Honored One!
The activity of form is ultimately unobtainable; how much more so is the meaning of "bodhisattva" as the non-activity of form? This applies likewise up to consciousness.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent, excellent! It is so, Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the meaning of form cannot be apprehended; the meanings of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, up to and including the meaning of non-action. In this manner, one should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti! As for what you said:
"I do not see any dharma that is called 'bodhisattva'."
"Subhūti! All dharmas do not perceive all dharmas.
All dharmas do not perceive the dharma-nature, and the dharma-nature does not perceive all dharmas."
The nature of phenomena does not perceive the element of earth, and the element of earth does not perceive the nature of phenomena.
This extends even to the element of consciousness, which does not perceive the nature of phenomena, nor does the nature of phenomena perceive the element of consciousness.

The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not perceive the nature of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness; the nature of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness does not perceive the nature of phenomena.

This extends up to the point where the nature of phenomena does not perceive the nature of the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness; the nature of the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness does not perceive the nature of phenomena.
Subhūti! The nature of the conditioned does not perceive the nature of the unconditioned, and the nature of the unconditioned does not perceive the nature of the conditioned. Why is this?
Apart from the conditioned, the unconditioned cannot be spoken of; apart from the unconditioned, the conditioned cannot be spoken of.

Thus, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they see nothing among all phenomena; at that time, they are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid, and their mind neither sinks nor regrets.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not perceive the eye up to the mind; they do not perceive forms up to phenomena (*dharma*); they do not perceive lust, anger, or delusion; they do not perceive ignorance up to old age and death; they do not perceive a self up to a knower or a seer; they do not perceive the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they do not perceive the mind of a śrāvaka or the mind of a pratyekabuddha; they do not perceive a bodhisattva nor the qualities of a bodhisattva; they do not perceive a Buddha, the qualities of a Buddha, or the path of a Buddha.
"Because this bodhisattva does not perceive any phenomena, they are not startled, not afraid, not terrified, do not sink into despondency, and have no regret.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason does this bodhisattva’s mind neither sink nor regret?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because all minds and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva are unobtainable and invisible; for this reason, the mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva neither sinks nor regrets."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva’s mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because this bodhisattva’s mind and mental consciousness are unobtainable and invisible, for this reason they are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid.
Thus it is, Subhūti!”
Because all dharmas are unattainable, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in all spheres of activity,

does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend the bodhisattva, does not apprehend the name "bodhisattva," and likewise does not apprehend the mind of a bodhisattva— this is the instruction for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Second;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Third.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: Encouraging Study At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the dānapāramitā should study the prajñāpāramitā; one who wishes to fulfill the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā should study the prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know form should study the perfection of wisdom; likewise, one who wishes to know consciousness should study the perfection of wisdom.

If one wishes to know the eye up to the mind; if one wishes to know forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); if one wishes to know eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; if one wishes to know eye-contact up to mind-contact; and if one wishes to know the feelings produced by conditions of eye-contact up to the feelings produced by conditions of mind-contact—one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Those who wish to sever lust, anger, and delusion should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire, ill will, craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), pride and conceit (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and all other fetters (*saṃyojana*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who wish to sever the four bonds, the four fetters, and the four inversions should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Those who wish to know the ten paths of wholesome action, those who wish to know the four dhyānas, those who wish to know the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to enter the samādhi of the awakening-mind (bodhicitta) should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

One who wishes to enter the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the transcending samādhi (vyutkrāntakasamādhi) should study the perfection of wisdom.
One who wishes to attain the Lion’s Play Samādhi should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to attain the Lion’s Unfurled Samādhi and wishes to attain all the gates of dhāraṇī should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Ratnamudrā Samādhi, the Suvimalacandra Samādhi, the Candradhvajaketu Samādhi, the Sarvadharmamudrā Samādhi, the Vipaśyanāmudrā Samādhi, the Dharmatāparyanta Samādhi, the Paryantasthiti-lakṣaṇa Samādhi, and the Vajropama Samādhi... [enter]... the [Samādhi].
The Samādhi of All Dharma-Gates, the Samādhi of the King of Samādhis, the Samādhi of the Royal Seal, the Samādhi of Pure Power,
the Samādhi of Exalted Emergence, the Samādhi of Entering All Eloquence, the Samādhi of Entering the Names of All Dharmas,
the Samādhi of Contemplating the Ten Directions, and the Samādhi of the Seal of the Gates of All Dhāraṇīs. One.
The Samādhi of Never Forgetting All Dharmas, the Samādhi of the Seal that Collects the Multitude of All Dharmas,
the Samādhi of Abiding in Space, the Samādhi of Triple Purity, the Samādhi of Non-retrogressive Supernatural Powers,
the Samādhi of Producing the Alms Bowl, and the Samādhi of the Banner-Marks of All Samādhis— one who wishes to attain such gateways of samādhi as these should...
One should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Those who wish to be fully endowed with such roots of goodness and never fall into the evil realms; those who wish not to be born into lowly or base families; those who wish not to dwell in the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and those who wish not to fall from the summit of the bodhisattva path—should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fall from the summit? Subhūti replied:

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās without skillful means, enters the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet neither falls into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas nor enters the bodhisattva stage, this is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva falling from the summit due to the arising of dharmas.”
Śāriputra asked Subhūti, “What is meant by the ‘birth’ of a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Birth is called 'attachment to dharmas'. Śāriputra asked:
"What is attachment to dharmas?"

Subhūti said: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they grasp at and become attached to form as empty; they grasp at and become attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty."
Śāriputra! This is called the arising of the love for the Dharma that accords with the path in a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas experience and become attached to form as being signless; they experience and become attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being signless.
They experience and become attached to form as being unconditioned; they experience and become attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being unconditioned.
One attends to and clings to form as being cessation; one attends to and clings to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being cessation.

One attends to and clings to form as impermanent, up to consciousness; one attends to and clings to form as suffering, up to consciousness; one attends to and clings to form as non-self, up to consciousness.

This is the arising of a Bodhisattva’s attachment to the Dharma that accords with the Path. [One thinks: "This is suffering and should be known; this is its origin and should be abandoned; this is its cessation and should be realized; this is the path and should be cultivated. [One thinks: "These are defiled dharmas; these are pure dharmas; these should be approached; these should not be approached. [One thinks: "This is what a Bodhisattva should practice; this is what a Bodhisattva should not practice. [One thinks: "This is the Bodhisattva path; this is not the Bodhisattva path. [One thinks: "This is the Bodhisattva training; this is not the Bodhisattva training. [One thinks: "This is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; this is not the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom. [One thinks: "This is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means; this is not the Bodhisattva’s skillful means. [One thinks: "This is the Bodhisattva’s maturation; this is not the Bodhisattva’s maturation."

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they experience, attend to, or become attached to these dharmas, this is called the arising of attachment to the Dharma that accords with the Path in a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti, "What is meant by the non-arising of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Subhūti replied:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, within internal emptiness he does not perceive external emptiness, and within external emptiness he does not perceive internal emptiness;
within external emptiness he does not perceive internal-and-external emptiness, and within internal-and-external emptiness he does not perceive external emptiness;
within internal-and-external emptiness he does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness, and within the emptiness of emptiness..."

One does not perceive internal-external emptiness within emptiness-of-emptiness; one does not perceive great emptiness within emptiness-of-emptiness, nor does one perceive emptiness-of-emptiness within great emptiness.
One does not perceive emptiness-of-the-ultimate-meaning within great emptiness, nor does one perceive great emptiness within emptiness-of-the-ultimate-meaning.
One does not perceive emptiness-of-the-conditioned within emptiness-of-the-ultimate-meaning, nor does one perceive the ultimate-meaning emptiness within emptiness-of-the-conditioned.
Regarding the emptiness of a single meaning: within the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), one does not perceive the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*);

within the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, one does not perceive the emptiness of conditioned phenomena. Within the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, one does not perceive ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*); within ultimate emptiness, one does not perceive the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena.
Within ultimate emptiness, one does not perceive the emptiness of the beginningless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*); within the emptiness of the beginningless, one does not perceive...
In ultimate emptiness, one does not perceive beginningless emptiness within beginningless emptiness; in beginningless emptiness, one does not perceive emptiness of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*);
in emptiness of dispersion, one does not perceive emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*);

in emptiness of nature, one does not perceive emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); and in emptiness of all phenomena, one does not perceive emptiness of nature. Within emptiness of all phenomena...

One does not perceive the emptiness of self-characteristics within the emptiness of self-characteristics; one does not perceive the emptiness of all phenomena within the emptiness of self-characteristics.

One does not perceive the emptiness of the unapprehendable within the emptiness of self-characteristics; one does not perceive the emptiness of self-characteristics within the emptiness of the unapprehendable.
One does not perceive the emptiness of non-existence within the emptiness of the unapprehendable; one does not perceive the emptiness of the unapprehendable within the emptiness of non-existence.
Within the emptiness of non-existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of existence; within the emptiness of existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of non-existence.

Within the emptiness of existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of both non-existence and existence; within the emptiness of both non-existence and existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of existence.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they attain entry into the bodhisattva stage.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should study it in this way:

they should not attend to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they should not attend to the eye up to the mind; they should not attend to forms up to phenomena (dharmas); and they should not attend to the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of wisdom, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon nor exalt this mind; they should not dwell upon nor exalt the unequaled mind; they should not dwell upon nor exalt the great mind.
"Why is this? Because this mind is no-mind, for the characteristic of the mind is eternally pure.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“What is meant by ‘the characteristic of the mind is eternally pure’? Subhūti replied:

“If a bodhisattva knows that this characteristic of the mind neither conjoins with nor separates from lust, anger, and delusion; neither conjoins with nor separates from any entanglements, outflows, fetters, or any of the underlying tendencies and all afflictions; and neither conjoins with nor separates from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
"Śāriputra! This is called the constant purity of the mental characteristics of a bodhisattva.
Śāriputra then said to Subhūti:
"Is there such a thing as a mind characterized by the absence of mind? Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Within the state of no-mind, can a mind characterized by existence or a mind characterized by non-existence be apprehended?"
Śāriputra said, “It cannot be apprehended. Subhūti said:
"If it cannot be apprehended, one should not ask:
'Is there this mind that has the characteristic of being without mind? Śāriputra asked again:
“What is the characteristic of being without mind? Subhūti replied:
“That all dharmas are neither destroyed nor differentiated—this is called the characteristic of being without mind.”
Śāriputra again asked Subhūti:

"Is it only the mind that is neither destroyed nor differentiated, and is form likewise neither destroyed nor differentiated, even up to the Buddha-way, which is also neither destroyed nor differentiated?"

Subhūti said: "If one can know that the characteristics of the mind are neither destroyed nor differentiated, then this bodhisattva can also know that everything from form up to the Buddha-way is neither destroyed nor differentiated."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

You are truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth, born from the vision of the Dharma, and born through transformation by the Dharma; you have taken a portion of the Dharma, not a portion of material wealth.”

Within the Dharma, you have gained personal realization with confidence, just as the Buddha has taught; that you are foremost among those who have attained the *araṇā-samādhi* is truly as the Buddha has proclaimed.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, and therein should also discern and know it.
If a bodhisattva practices as you have described, they will not be separated from the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti! A son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to train in the stage of a śrāvaka should likewise hear the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, recite it, read it, correctly attend to it, and practice according to its teaching;
one who wishes to train in the stage of a pratyekabuddha should likewise hear the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, recite it, read it, correctly attend to it, and practice according to its teaching.
Those who wish to study the bodhisattva stages should likewise hear the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, recite it, read it, correctly contemplate it, and practice according to its teachings. Why is this?
Because within this Prajñāpāramitā the three vehicles are explained in detail; herein, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should train.
Chapter Nine: Gathering and Dispersion. From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Nine, "Gathering and Dispersion. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I do not perceive, nor do I apprehend, this Bodhisattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā*; for whom, then, should I teach the *prajñāpāramitā*?
World-Honored One!
I do not apprehend the gathering or dispersing of any dharmas; if I were to assign a name to a bodhisattva and say 'bodhisattva,' there might well be cause for regret."
World-Honored One!
This word neither abides nor does it not abide. Why is this?
Because these syllables are non-existent,
for this reason, these syllables neither abide nor do they not abide.
World-Honored One!
"I do not apprehend the collection or dispersion of form, nor even the collection or dispersion of consciousness.
If these cannot be apprehended, how could they be given names?
World-Honored One!"
For this reason, this term neither abides nor does it not abide.
Why is that? Because this term has no existence.
World-Honored One!
I also do not apprehend the collection or dispersion of the eye, up to and including the collection or dispersion of the mind.
If these cannot be apprehended, how can one assign a name and say, "This is a bodhisattva"?
World-Honored One!
These names, from "eye" up to "mind," neither abide nor do they not abide. Why is this?
Because these names do not exist,
for this reason, these words neither abide nor do they not abide.
World-Honored One!
I do not apprehend the collection or dispersion of form, nor even the collection or dispersion of dharmas.
If these cannot be apprehended, how can one designate a name and say, "This is a bodhisattva"?
World-Honored One!
These characters, from the character for "form" (rūpa) up to the character for "dharmas," neither abide nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because these characters are non-existent.
For this reason, these names neither abide nor do they not abide.

This applies likewise to visual consciousness up to mental consciousness; to eye-contact up to mind-contact; and to the feelings produced by conditions of eye-contact up to the feelings produced by conditions of mind-contact.
“World-Honored One!
I do not apprehend the accumulation or dispersal of ignorance, nor do I apprehend the accumulation or dispersal of anything up to old age and death.
World-Honored One!”
“World-Honored One, I do not apprehend the accumulation or dispersal of the exhaustion of ignorance, nor even the accumulation or dispersal of the exhaustion of old age and death.
World-Honored One, I do not apprehend the accumulation or dispersal of lust, anger, and delusion; it is the same for all accumulations and dispersions of false views.”

"Bhagavān! I do not perceive the accumulation or dispersion of the six pāramitās; I do not perceive the accumulation or dispersion of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path; nor do I perceive the accumulation or dispersion of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor do I perceive the accumulation or dispersion of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; nor do I perceive the accumulation or dispersion of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of goodness, mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, mindfulness of the body, or mindfulness of death."
I also do not perceive the gathering or dispersal of the Buddha’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
World-Honored One!
If I do not perceive the gathering or dispersal of the six perfections, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities, how could I designate a name and say, "This is a bodhisattva"?
World-Honored One!
This word neither abides nor does it not abide. Why is this?
Because these syllables do not exist,
for this reason, these syllables neither abide nor do they not abide.
World-Honored One!

I do not perceive the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates as being like a dream; nor do I perceive the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging as being like an echo, a shadow, a flame, or a magical illusion, just as was explained above.
"Bhagavān! I do not apprehend a collection apart from dispersion; I do not apprehend a collection that is quiescent, unarisen, undestroyed, unmanifested, non-defiled, and non-pure. Bhagavān!

I do not apprehend the collection or dispersion of suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), or the established order of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*); it is as described above.

I do not apprehend the collection or dispersion of wholesome or unwholesome phenomena; I do not apprehend the collection or dispersion of conditioned or unconditioned phenomena, of tainted or untainted phenomena, of past, future, or present phenomena, nor of phenomena that are neither past, nor future, nor present.
"What is that which is neither past, nor future, nor present?
It is the unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛtadharma),
World-Honored One!"
"World-Honored One, I also do not apprehend the gathering or dispersing of unconditioned dharmas;
World-Honored One,
I also do not apprehend the gathering or dispersing of Buddhas."
“World-Honored One!
I also do not perceive the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas, or their gathering and dispersal, in the worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
World-Honored One!”
If I do not perceive the gathering or dispersing of the Buddhas, how could I teach the *prajñāpāramitā* to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
World-Honored One!
This designation "bodhisattva" neither abides nor does it not abide.
Why is this? Because these syllables do not exist.
For this reason, these syllables neither abide nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!
I do not perceive the gathering or dispersing of the true reality (dharmatā) of these dharmas; how then could I assign a name to a bodhisattva and say, ‘This is a bodhisattva’?
World-Honored One!”
This true reality of all phenomena (dharmas) neither abides in names nor does it not abide.
Why? Because these names have no intrinsic existence.
For this reason, World-Honored One, these names neither abide nor do they not abide.

All dharmas are provisionally designated through the conjunction of causes and conditions; that which is called "Bodhisattva" is a mere name. It cannot be spoken of within the five aggregates (*skandha*), nor can it be spoken of within the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), or even the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). Furthermore, it cannot be spoken of within the dharma of their conjunction.
World-Honored One!
For example, a dream cannot be described among all phenomena; likewise, echoes, shadows, mirages, and transformations also cannot be described among all phenomena.
Just as the name "space" exists, there is no phenomenon among which it can be described.
“World-Honored One!
Just as the names ‘earth,’ ‘water,’ ‘fire,’ and ‘wind’ cannot be found within the Dharma,
so too the names ‘precepts,’ ‘concentration,’ ‘wisdom,’ ‘liberation,’ and ‘knowledge and vision of liberation’ cannot be found within the Dharma.”
Just as the name "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna), up to the names "arhat" and "pratyekabuddha," cannot be spoken of within the Dharma,
so too the name of the Buddha and the name of the Dharma cannot be spoken of within the Dharma.
That is to say: whether wholesome or unwholesome, permanent or impermanent, suffering or happiness, self or non-self, cessation or detachment, existence or non-existence.
World-Honored One!

For this reason, my mind feels regret that the characteristics of accumulation and dispersal of all dharmas cannot be apprehended; how then can one assign a name to a bodhisattva and say, "This is a bodhisattva"?
World-Honored One!
This word neither abides nor does it not abide. Why is this?
Because this word has no existence,
for this reason, this word neither abides nor does it not abide.
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching on the characteristics and the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* as they are thus described, does not sink in spirit, does not regret, and is not startled, terrified, or frightened, one should know that this bodhisattva certainly dwells within the nature of *avaivartika*, because they dwell in the dharma of non-dwelling.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* should not abide in form; he should not abide in sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He should not abide in the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; he should not abide in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. He should not abide in eye-consciousness up to and including mind-consciousness; he should not abide in eye-contact up to and including mind-contact.
