He should not abide in the sensations produced by the conditions of eye-contact up to and including the sensations produced by the conditions of mind-contact. He should not abide in the element of earth, nor in the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness. He should not abide in ignorance up to and including old age and death."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Form is empty of the characteristic of form.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the characteristic of consciousness is empty.
World-Honored One!
That which is empty of form is not called 'form,' and apart from emptiness, there is no form."
Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—consciousness is emptiness and is not called "consciousness," and apart from emptiness there is no consciousness.
Consciousness is emptiness, and emptiness is consciousness.
Up to and including old age and death, old age and death are empty of the characteristics of old age and death.
World-Honored One!
The emptiness of old age and death is not called "old age and death," and apart from emptiness, there is no old age and death.
Old age and death are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself old age and death.
World-Honored One!
For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the prajñāpāramitā should not dwell within form, nor should they dwell within anything up to and including old age and death.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should not dwell within the four foundations of mindfulness. Why is this?
The four foundations of mindfulness, World-Honored One, are empty of the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness.
The emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness is not called "the four foundations of mindfulness," yet apart from emptiness, there are no four foundations of mindfulness.
The four foundations of mindfulness are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself the four foundations of mindfulness.
This applies likewise even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
World-Honored One!

For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should not dwell in anything from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not abide in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā); they should not abide in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
Why is this? The perfection of giving is empty of the mark of the perfection of giving, and so on, up to the perfection of wisdom, which is empty of the mark of the perfection of wisdom.
World-Honored One!
The emptiness of the dānapāramitā is not called the dānapāramitā, and apart from emptiness there is no dānapāramitā.
The dānapāramitā is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the dānapāramitā.
It is the same even for the *prajñāpāramitā*.
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* should not abide within the six *pāramitās*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* should not dwell upon syllables.
He should not dwell upon the gate of one syllable, the gate of two syllables, nor indeed upon any such various gates of syllables."
Why is this? Because all syllables and the characteristics of all syllables are empty.
It is also as explained above.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the prajñāpāramitā should not dwell in any of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Why is this? "
All supernormal powers (abhijñā) and the characteristics of all supernormal powers are empty.
That which is empty of supernormal powers is not called "supernormal powers," yet apart from emptiness there are no supernormal powers.
Supernormal powers are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself supernormal powers.
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should not dwell in any of the supernormal powers.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell on form as impermanent, nor should they dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as impermanent."
Why is this? Impermanence is empty of the characteristic of impermanence,
World-Honored One!
Impermanence and emptiness cannot be called impermanence; apart from emptiness, there is also no impermanence.
Impermanence is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself impermanence.
World-Honored One!

For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should not dwell on the idea that form is impermanent, nor should they dwell on the idea that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
One should not dwell on the notion that form is suffering; one should not dwell on the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering.
One should not dwell on the notion that form is non-self; one should not dwell on the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self.
One should not dwell on the emptiness of form; one should not dwell on the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One should not dwell on the cessation of form; one should not dwell on the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"One should not dwell on form as being detached; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being detached.
It is as explained above.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should not abide even in suchness.
Why is this? Suchness and the characteristic of suchness are empty.
World-Honored One!
The mark of suchness is empty and is not called "suchness"; apart from emptiness, there is no suchness.
Suchness is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself suchness.
World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should not dwell within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), the fixed position of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), or the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Why is this? Because the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is empty of the reality-limit.
World-Honored One!
The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is empty and is not called the reality-limit; apart from emptiness, there is no reality-limit.
The reality-limit is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the reality-limit.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should not dwell in any of the doors of dhāraṇī, nor should they dwell in any of the doors of samādhi.
Why is this? The gateways of dhāraṇī are empty of the characteristics of the gateways of dhāraṇī; the gateways of samādhi are empty of the characteristics of the gateways of samādhi.
World-Honored One!
The gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi are empty and thus are not called "gates of dhāraṇī" or "gates of samādhi"; yet apart from emptiness, there are no gates of dhāraṇī or samādhi.
Dhāraṇīs and the gates of samādhi are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself dhāraṇīs and the gates of samādhi.
World-Honored One,
for this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the prajñāpāramitā should not dwell even within dhāraṇīs and the gates of samādhi.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the prajñāpāramitā but lacks skillful means, they dwell within form with a mind of ‘self’ and ‘mine’; this bodhisattva performs the practice of form.”
If one dwells within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness with a self-centered mind, that bodhisattva is practicing the activity of consciousness.
If a bodhisattva practices such activity, they do not receive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
Because they are not fully endowed with the *prajñāpāramitā*, they cannot achieve the realization of *sarvajñā*.

World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* but lacks skillful means (*upāya*), they dwell within the twelve bases (*āyatana*) up to the doors of *dhāraṇī* and samādhi with a mind of "I" and "mine. Such a bodhisattva constructs the practice of the twelve bases up to the construction of the doors of *dhāraṇī* and samādhi.
If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, they do not receive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
Because they do not fulfill the perfection of wisdom, they cannot achieve the realization of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Why is this? Form is non-appropriation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-appropriation.
When form is non-appropriated, it is no longer form, because its nature is empty.
If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not grasped, they are not consciousness, because their nature is empty.

The twelve bases (*āyatana*) are not grasped, and so on up to the *dhāraṇīs* and the gates of samādhi; these are not grasped. If the twelve bases are not grasped, they are not the twelve bases; and so on up to the *dhāraṇīs* and the gates of samādhi—if they are not grasped, they are not *dhāraṇīs* or gates of samādhi, because their nature is empty.
The perfection of wisdom is also not received; if the perfection of wisdom is not received, it is not the perfection of wisdom, because its nature is empty.
Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is empty.
To thus observe that the mind has no place of activity is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of Non-Appropriation.
Its vast function is not shared with Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

This wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) is also not apprehended, because of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārthaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyantaśūnyatā*), beginningless emptiness (*anavarāgraśūnyatā*), dispersed emptiness (*anavakāraśūnyatā*), essential emptiness (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*), the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambhaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāvaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of existence (*bhāvaśūnyatā*), and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence (*abhāvabhāvaśūnyatā*).
Why is this? This sarvajñā (all-knowledge) cannot be attained through the practice of signs, for the practice of signs is defiled.
What are these defiled signs?
The characteristics of form, up to and including the characteristics of dhāraṇīs and the gates of samādhi—these are called defiled characteristics.
If one could attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) by receiving or cultivating these characteristics, then the brahmin Śreṇika would never have given rise to faith in omniscience.

What is faith? It is to have faith in the prajñāpāramitā by means of discernment, understanding, weighing, and reflection, neither by way of phenomena with marks nor by way of phenomena without marks.

In this way, the brahmin Śreṇika did not grasp at signs while abiding in the stage of practice through faith; employing the wisdom of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, he entered into the characteristics of all phenomena, neither grasping at form, nor grasping at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they cannot be apprehended.

This Brahmin Śreṇika does not see this wisdom because it is obtained through internal contemplation; he does not see this wisdom because it is obtained through external contemplation; he does not see this wisdom because it is obtained through both internal and external contemplation; nor does he see this wisdom by means of a contemplation that is devoid of wisdom.
Why is this? Because the brahmin does not perceive these dharmas; it is because the wise know the dharmas and know their locus.

This brahmin does not perceive this wisdom within internal form (*rūpa*), nor does he perceive this wisdom within internal feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*). He does not perceive this wisdom within external form, nor does he perceive this wisdom within external feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive this wisdom within both internal and external form, nor does he perceive this wisdom within both internal and external feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Furthermore, he does not perceive this wisdom apart from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, for both the internal and external are empty (*śūnya*).
Śreṇika, the brahmin, has attained faith and understanding in omniscience within this very mind.
For this reason, O brahmin, he has faith in the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), because all phenomena are unattainable.
Having thus attained such faith and understanding, there is no dharma to be grasped.
All dharmas are signless because they are beyond recollection.
This brahmin likewise finds nothing to be attained among all dharmas; he neither grasps nor abandons, for grasping and abandoning are themselves unattainable.
This brahmin also does not conceive of wisdom, because the characteristics of all dharmas are without conception.
World-Honored One!
This is called the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Because this shore and the other shore are not crossed over, this bodhisattva does not grasp at form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Because all dharmas are not grasped, they do not even grasp at the various dhāraṇīs or the gates of samādhi.

Because all dharmas are not grasped, this bodhisattva does not likewise take up nirvāṇa within them, as long as they have not yet fulfilled the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, nor the ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

Why is this? These four foundations of mindfulness are not four foundations of mindfulness, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are not eighteen unique qualities. All these dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas; this is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, wherein form is not grasped, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities which are not grasped.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the prajñāpāramitā should reflect in this way: 'What is this prajñāpāramitā?'"
"For what reason is it called 'prajñāpāramitā'? Whose prajñāpāramitā is it?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā reflects in this way:
“If dharmas are non-existent and unobtainable, this is the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“Which dharmas are non-existent and unobtainable?”
Subhūti said: “The perfection of wisdom is a dharma that does not exist and cannot be apprehended;

the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity—these dharmas do not exist and cannot be apprehended.”

Because of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence.

Śāriputra! The dharma of form is non-existent and unattainable; the dharmas of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent and unattainable; the dharma of internal emptiness is non-existent and unattainable; and so on, up to the dharma of the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is non-existent and unattainable.
Śāriputra! The dharmas of the four foundations of mindfulness are non-existent and unobtainable; even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are non-existent and unobtainable.

Śāriputra! All dharmas of the supernormal powers are non-existent and unapprehendable; as with the *tathatā* (suchness), dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable. The dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the dharma-characteristic (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the dharma-position (*dharmasthiti*), the dharma-abiding (*dharmaniyāmatā*), and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)—these dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable.

Śāriputra! The Buddha is non-existent and unattainable; the dharma of sarvajñatā is non-existent and unattainable; the dharma of sarvākārajñatā is non-existent and unattainable, because of the emptiness of the internal and so forth, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates and observes in this manner, and his mind does not sink, does not regret, is not startled, is not afraid, and is not terrified, you should know that this bodhisattva is not separated from the practice of the prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "By what causes and conditions should it be known that a bodhisattva does not depart from the practice of the prajñāpāramitā? Subhūti replied:

“Form is detached from the nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached from the nature of consciousness; the six perfections are detached from the nature of the six perfections; and so on, up to the limit of reality, which is detached from the nature of the limit of reality.”
Śāriputra again asked Subhūti: "What is the nature of form?
What is the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
“What is the nature of the limit of reality?
Subhūti replied, “Non-existence is the nature of form;
non-existence is the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to non-existence being the nature of the limit of reality.”

Śāriputra! For these reasons, you should know that form is detached from the nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached from the nature of consciousness; and so on, up to the limit of reality, which is detached from the nature of the limit of reality.

Śāriputra! Form is also detached from the characteristic of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also detached from the characteristic of consciousness; even the limit of reality is detached from the characteristic of the limit of reality.
Characteristics are also detached from characteristics, and nature is also detached from nature.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: “If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, will they attain the realization of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, so it is! Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they will achieve the realization of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are neither produced nor accomplished. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason are all phenomena neither produced nor accomplished?
Subhūti replied, "Form is empty of form;
thus, the production or accomplishment of form cannot be apprehended."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of consciousness; thus, the arising and the accomplishment of this consciousness cannot be apprehended.
This extends even to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), which is empty of the limit of reality; thus, the arising and the accomplishment of this limit of reality cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they gradually approach omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and gradually attain purity of body, purity of mind, and purity of marks.

Because they gradually attain purity of body, purity of mind, and purity of marks, these bodhisattvas do not give rise to a mind of attachment, do not give rise to a mind of anger, do not give rise to a mind of delusion, do not give rise to a mind of arrogance, do not give rise to a mind of stinginess and greed, and do not give rise to a mind of wrong views.
Because this bodhisattva does not give rise to defiled thoughts, nor even thoughts of wrong views, they never again enter a mother’s womb, but always attains birth by transformation.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields, never being separated from the Buddhas until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way; they should study the perfection of wisdom in this way.
Chapter Ten: On Characteristics and Practice (*Lakṣaṇa-caryā-parivarta*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, lacking skillful means, wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, yet practices with form as a mental object, or practices with feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness as a mental object;”

If one practices with the notion that form is permanent, this constitutes the characteristic of practice; if one practices with the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent, this constitutes the characteristic of practice.

If one practices with the notion that form is impermanent, this constitutes the characteristic of practice; if one practices with the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, this constitutes the characteristic of practice.
If one takes form as being pleasant as the mode of practice, or if one takes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being pleasant as the mode of practice;
or if one takes form as being painful as the mode of practice, or if one takes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being painful as the mode of practice.
If form is characterized by the activity of existence, or if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are characterized by the activity of existence;
if form is characterized by the activity of emptiness, or if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are characterized by the activity of emptiness.

If one practices with the thought that form is self, this is a mode of practice; if one practices with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is self, this is a mode of practice.

If one practices with the thought that form is non-self, this is a mode of practice; if one practices with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is non-self, this is a mode of practice.

If form is characterized by the practice of detachment, it is a mode of practice; if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are characterized by the practice of detachment, they are modes of practice.

If form is characterized by the practice of tranquility, it is a mode of practice; if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are characterized by the practice of tranquility, they are modes of practice.
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the four foundations of mindfulness without skillful means as their mode of practice, up to and including practicing the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha as their mode of practice.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, forms this thought:
‘I am practicing the perfection of wisdom.’”
"Even the practice of 'attaining something' is itself a characteristic of practice.
World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought:"
"To be able to practice in this way is to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
This, too, is a mode of practice.
One should know that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means (upāya).
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the prajñāpāramitā, falsely conceptualizes form, sensation, and mindfulness.”

If one falsely understands form through mindfulness of sensation and thus performs karmic formations for the sake of form, and if one performs karmic formations for the sake of form, one will be unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, as well as the suffering of future lives.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, lacks skillful means, they will falsely conceptualize the perception of the eye up to the mind; false conceptualize forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); false conceptualize the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; false conceptualize eye-contact up to mind-contact; false conceptualize the feelings produced by conditions of eye-contact up to the feelings produced by conditions of mind-contact; and they will falsely conceptualize the perception of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), performing practices for the sake of those eighteen unique qualities.

If one acts with such [dualistic] conduct, this bodhisattva will be unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, as well as the sufferings of future lives.
Such a bodhisattva cannot even attain the realization of the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, let alone attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; such a thing is impossible.
“Śāriputra, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"How should one know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom possesses skillful means?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice form, nor does he practice feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; he does not practice the marks of form, nor does he practice the marks of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness."

One does not practice with respect to the permanence of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not practice with respect to the impermanence of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. One does not practice with respect to the pleasure of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not practice with respect to the suffering of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. One does not practice with respect to the self of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not practice with respect to the non-self of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. One does not practice with respect to the emptiness of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not practice with respect to the signlessness of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not practice with respect to the wishlessness of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not practice with respect to the detachment from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not practice with respect to the cessation of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
This form is empty, and thus it is not form; apart from emptiness there is no form, and apart from form there is no emptiness. Form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
The emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness; apart from emptiness there is no consciousness, and apart from consciousness there is no emptiness.

Emptiness is itself consciousness, and consciousness is itself emptiness. This extends even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*): the emptiness of the eighteen unique qualities is not the eighteen unique qualities; apart from emptiness there are no eighteen unique qualities, and apart from the eighteen unique qualities there is no emptiness. Emptiness is itself the eighteen unique qualities, and the eighteen unique qualities are themselves emptiness.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom with skillful means.
By practicing the perfection of wisdom in this way, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not grasp at practicing, nor does he grasp at not practicing, nor does he grasp at both practicing and not practicing, nor does he grasp at neither practicing nor not practicing; he does not even grasp at non-grasping itself.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“For what reason and by what causal conditions does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not grasp when practicing the perfection of wisdom?”
Subhūti said: "This Prajñāpāramitā is not accepted because its intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended. Why is this?"
The dharma of non-existence is the perfection of wisdom.

Śāriputra, for this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not grasp at practicing, nor does he grasp at not practicing, nor does he grasp at both practicing and not practicing, nor does he grasp at neither practicing nor not practicing; he does not even grasp at non-grasping.
Why is this? Because the nature of all dharmas is non-existent; they do not follow the course of any dharmas, nor do they grasp at the characteristics of any dharmas.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s samādhi of non-appropriation of all dharmas, which possesses vast efficacy and is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by practicing this samādhi without departing from it, will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Śāriputra said,
"Is it only by not departing from this samādhi that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva swiftly attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"Are there further samādhis?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "There are further samādhis;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these samādhis, he will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Śāriputra asked: "What is the samādhi by practicing which a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Subhūti said: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess a samādhi called 'Courageous Progress' (śūraṅgama-vikrāmin); this samādhi enables bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
There are the samādhis known as the Renowned Jewel Seal, the Lion’s Play, the Wondrous Moon, the Moon Banner Mark,
the Emergence of the Seal of All Dharmas, the Contemplation of the Summit, the Culmination of the Nature of Dharmas,
the Culmination of the Banner Mark, the Vajra, and the Entry into the Seal of Dharmas.
The Samādhi King Firmly Established Samādhi, the Royal Seal Samādhi, the Radiating Light Samādhi,
the Power and Progress Samādhi, the Birth Samādhi, the Entering Eloquence Samādhi, the Entering Names Samādhi,
the Contemplation of Directions Samādhi, the Dhāraṇī Seal Samādhi, the Non-Forgetfulness Samādhi, and the Gathering of All... [Samādhi].
The Dharma-seal Samādhi, the Pervasive-Encompassment-of-Space Samādhi, the Vajra-Wheel Samādhi, the Jewel-Severance Samādhi,
the Able-to-Illuminate Samādhi, the Non-Seeking Samādhi, the Non-Abiding-in-Any-Place Samādhi,
the Mindless Samādhi, the Pure-Lamp Samādhi, the Boundless-Light Samādhi, and the Able...
The Samādhi of Illumination, the Samādhi of Universal Illumination, the Samādhi of Firm Purity of All Samādhis, the Samādhi of Stainless Illumination,
the Samādhi of Creating Bliss, the Samādhi of Lightning Flash, the Samādhi of Exhaustlessness, the Samādhi of Majestic Virtue,
the Samādhi of Transcending Exhaustion, the Samādhi of Immovability, and the Samādhi of Adornment.
The Sunlight Samādhi, the Moon-Purity Samādhi, the Pure-Light Samādhi, the Light-Producer Samādhi,
the Active-Conduct Samādhi, the Knowledge-of-Marks Samādhi, the Vajra-like Samādhi, the Mind-Abiding Samādhi, the Universal-Illumination Samādhi,
the Secure-Establishment Samādhi, the Jewel-Summit Samādhi, and the Seal of the Sublime Dharma.
The samādhi of equality, the samādhi of equality of dharmas, the samādhi that gives rise to joy, the samādhi that reaches the pinnacle of dharmas, the samādhi capable of dispersing,
the samādhi that destroys the locus of all dharmas, the samādhi of the equal characteristics of letters, the samādhi of departing from letters,
the samādhi of severing conditions, the indestructible samādhi, the samādhi of the characteristic of seedlessness, and the samādhi of no location.
The Samādhi of Practice, the Samādhi of Departing from Darkness, the Samādhi of Non-Departure, the Samādhi of Immovability,
the Samādhi of Transcending Conditions, the Samādhi of Accumulating All Virtues, the Samādhi of Abiding in Mindlessness, the Samādhi of the Wondrous Pure Flower,
the Samādhi of Awakening the Mind, the Samādhi of Immeasurable Eloquence, the Samādhi of the Peerless, and the Samādhi of Deliverance.
The samādhi of all dharmas, the samādhi of discerning all dharmas, the samādhi of dispelling doubt, the samādhi of non-abiding, the samādhi of the single characteristic,
the samādhi of the arising of practice, the samādhi of the single practice, the samādhi of the non-single practice, the samādhi of wondrous practice,
the samādhi of penetrating the bottom of all existence and dispersing [delusion], and the entry into words.
The samādhi of speech; the samādhi of being detached from sounds, syllables, and words; the samādhi of the blazing torch; the samādhi of pure marks; the samādhi of destroying marks;
the samādhi of the excellence of all aspects; the samādhi of taking no delight in suffering or pleasure;
the samādhi of inexhaustible practice; the samādhi of many dhāraṇīs; and the samādhi of grasping the characteristics of both the heterodox and the orthodox.
The samādhi of tranquility, the samādhi of extinguishing hatred and love, the samādhi of the inverse and the conformable, the samādhi of pure light, the samādhi of firmness,
the samādhi of the pure light of the full moon, the samādhi of great adornment, the samādhi that can illumine all worlds,
the samādhi of equanimity, the samādhi of non-contentious conduct, and the samādhi of the bliss of no-abiding-place.
The samādhi of non-obscuration, the samādhi of abiding as it is, the samādhi of destroying the body, the samādhi of destroying speech like space,
and the samādhi of detachment like space and being unstained.
Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice these samādhis, they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable asaṃkhyeya gates of samādhi and gates of dhāraṇī; when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study these gates of samādhi and gates of dhāraṇī, they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Venerable Subhūti, following the Buddha’s intention, said:

“It should be known that those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice this samādhi have already received a prediction from the Buddhas of the past; the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions likewise bestow predictions upon these bodhisattvas.”
This bodhisattva does not perceive these samādhis, nor does he dwell upon them; nor does he think:
"I shall enter this samādhi," "I am now entering this samādhi," or "I have entered this samādhi."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva has no conceptualization or thought at all. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has dwelled in these samādhis, does he receive a prediction from the Buddhas of the past?"
Subhūti replied: "No, Śāriputra! Why is that?"
The perfection of wisdom is not different from the various samādhis, and the various samādhis are not different from the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva is not different from the perfection of wisdom and the samādhis, and the perfection of wisdom and the samādhis are not different from the bodhisattva.
The perfection of wisdom is itself samādhi, and samādhi is itself the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva is himself the perfection of wisdom and samādhi, and the perfection of wisdom and samādhi are themselves the bodhisattva.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If the samādhi is not different from the bodhisattva, and the bodhisattva is not different from the samādhi;
if the samādhi is itself the bodhisattva, and the bodhisattva is himself the samādhi."
"How does a bodhisattva know the samādhi 'All dharmas are equal'?
Subhūti replied, "When a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, at that time he does not form such a thought:"
"I enter this samādhi by means of this dharma. For this reason, Śāriputra,
this bodhisattva neither knows nor recollects these samādhis.
Śāriputra asked: "For what reason is there neither knowing nor recollecting? Subhūti replied:
"Because all samādhis are non-existent, this bodhisattva neither knows nor recollects them.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! It is in accordance with this meaning that I have declared you to be foremost among those who practice the samādhi of non-contention.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity in this manner; they should likewise train in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha in this same way.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, is he training in the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are training in the perfection of wisdom, because these dharmas are unapprehendable.”
This extends even to training in the *dānapāramitā*, because these dharmas are unattainable;
and training in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikadharma*), because these dharmas are unattainable.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus studies the prajñāpāramitā, is this dharma unobtainable?”
The Buddha said:
"In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the prajñāpāramitā, these dharmas are unobtainable. Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
What dharmas are unobtainable?
The Buddha said:
“The self cannot be apprehended, nor can the knower or the seer, because they are ultimately pure.
The five aggregates cannot be apprehended, the twelve bases cannot be apprehended, and the eighteen elements cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.”
Ignorance is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure;
even up to old age and death, they are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;
the Truth of Suffering is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
The truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.
The desire realm cannot be apprehended, because it is ultimately pure.
The form realm and the formless realm cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.
The four foundations of mindfulness are unattainable because they are ultimately pure.
This extends up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are unattainable because they are ultimately pure.
The six perfections are unattainable because they are ultimately pure.
The stream-enterer is unattainable because of ultimate purity;
the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha are unattainable because of ultimate purity.
“The Bodhisattva cannot be apprehended, because he is ultimately pure.
The Buddha cannot be apprehended, because he is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is ultimate purity?
The Buddha said:
“Non-emergence and non-arising, no attainment and no action—this is called ultimate purity.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, in what dharma is he training?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he does not train in any dharma.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, the characteristics of all dharmas are not as ordinary people are attached to them.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does the true mark of all dharmas exist?”
The Buddha said:
"All phenomena exist in such a way that they have no existence; they are thus non-existent.
Not knowing this fact is called ignorance."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is it that does not exist, such that not knowing this matter is called ignorance?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, because of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not exist, because of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.”
In this regard, ordinary persons, through the power of ignorance and the thirst of craving, engage in false views and conceptual discrimination; this is what is called "ignorance.

These ordinary persons are bound by the two extremes; they neither know nor see that all phenomena are non-existent, yet they engage in recollection, thought, and discrimination, becoming attached to form and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Because this person is attached, they form a cognition, knowledge, and view regarding dharmas that do not exist; such is the ordinary person who neither knows nor sees.
What is it that they do not know and do not see?
Not knowing and not seeing form, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they likewise do not know and do not see them.
For this reason, they fall into the category of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) like children; such people do not emerge [from saṃsāra].
Where does it not emerge?

It does not emerge from the desire realm, it does not emerge from the form realm, it does not emerge from the formless realm; it does not emerge from among the teachings of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
This person likewise does not have faith.
What do they not believe?
They do not believe that form is empty, and so on, up to not believing that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty.
This person does not abide.
In what do they not abide?
They do not abide in the dānapāramitā, nor indeed do they abide in the prajñāpāramitā.
They do not abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage, nor in the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
For these reasons, they are called ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), like small children, and are also termed "those who cling."

What constitutes attachment? It is attachment to form up to consciousness; attachment to the eye-base up to the mind-base; attachment to the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; attachment to lust, anger, and delusion; attachment to various false views; and attachment to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the path of the Buddha.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, does he not train in the *prajñāpāramitā* and fail to attain *sarvajñatā*?”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not train in the prajñāpāramitā and shall not attain sarvajñatā."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva neither study the prajñāpāramitā nor attain sarvajñatā?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas lack skillful means, they conceive of, discriminate, and become attached to the perfection of wisdom; they become attached to the perfection of dhyāna, the perfection of vīrya, the perfection of kṣānti, the perfection of śīla, and the perfection of dāna, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities and all-knowledge, conceiving of, discriminating, and becoming attached to them.”
For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not train in the prajñāpāramitā, nor do they attain sarvajñatā.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, does he not train in the prajñāpāramitā and fail to attain sarvajñatā?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, yet does not train in the prajñāpāramitā, they will not attain sarvajñatā."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva now train in the prajñāpāramitā so as to attain sarvajñatā?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he does not perceive the prajñāpāramitā."
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the prajñāpāramitā in this way, they attain sarvajñā because it is unattainable.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘unobtainable’?
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are empty internally, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 3; *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 4.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on the Study of Illusion (In the Dan edition, this is titled "The Chapter on Human Beings").
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If someone were to ask:
‘If an illusory person studies the Prajñāpāramitā, will they attain sarvajñatā?’”

If an illusory person were to study the dhyāna-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, and dāna-pāramitā; if they were to study the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the knowledge of all modes—would they attain omniscience (sarvajñatā)?
"How should I answer? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I shall question you in return; answer me according to your own understanding."
Subhūti, what do you think? Is form different from an illusion?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"What do you think? Is the eye different from an illusion?
And so on, up to: is the mind different from an illusion?
Are forms, and so on, up to mental phenomena, different from an illusion?"
Is the eye-element, up to and including the mind-consciousness-element, different from an illusion?

Are eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, and the feelings produced by the conditions of eye-contact, up to and including the feelings produced by the conditions of mind-contact, different from an illusion?
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One. [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think? Are the four foundations of mindfulness different from an illusion?”
"Is there any difference between the eightfold noble path and an illusion?
"No, World-Honored One. "What do you think?
Is there any difference between emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness and an illusion?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, what do you think? Is the perfection of giving different from an illusion?"
"Is there any difference between the eighteen unique qualities and an illusion? "No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti!"
"What do you think? Is there any difference between anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and an illusion?
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?"
Form is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from form; form itself is illusion, and illusion itself is form.
World-Honored One!

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; consciousness itself is illusion, and illusion itself is consciousness.
World-Honored One!
The eye is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the eye; the eye is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the eye.
It is the same for the feelings produced by the conditions of eye-contact, up to and including the feelings produced by the conditions of mind-contact.
World-Honored One!

The four foundations of mindfulness are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness are themselves illusion, and illusion is itself the four foundations of mindfulness.

Up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is itself illusion, and illusion is itself *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Does an illusion have defilement or purity?
“No, World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does an illusion have arising or cessation?
“No, World-Honored One.”
“If an illusion is neither born nor extinguished, can this dharma study the *prajñāpāramitā* and attain *sarvajñatā*?
“No, World-Honored One!”
“What do you think: is the conventional designation ‘the five aggregates of clinging’ the bodhisattva?
“It is so, World-Honored One. “What do you think:
does the conventional designation ‘the five aggregates of clinging’ have arising and ceasing, or defilement and purity?”
"No, World-Honored One. "What do you think?

If a dharma exists as a mere name—neither body nor bodily action, neither speech nor vocal action, neither mind nor mental action; neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure—could such a dharma study the *prajñāpāramitā* and attain *sarvajñatā*?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in the prajñāpāramitā in this way, they shall attain sarvajñā (all-knowledge), because of non-apprehension."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the prajñāpāramitā in this manner, so as to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just as a phantom person trains.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
You should know that the five aggregates are themselves the illusory person, and the illusory person is itself the five aggregates.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? If these five aggregates study the prajñāpāramitā, will they attain sarvajñatā?”
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
The nature of these five aggregates is non-existent, and even this non-existence cannot be apprehended."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? If one practices the prajñāpāramitā while regarding the five aggregates as like a dream, will one attain sarvajñatā?"
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
The nature of a dream is non-existent, and that which is non-existent cannot be apprehended."
"What do you think? If one practices the perfection of wisdom with the five aggregates being like an echo, like a shadow, like a flame, and like a magical creation, will one attain all-knowledge?"
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
Because the nature of echoes, shadows, flames, and transformations is non-existent, and that which is non-existent cannot be apprehended."
The six sense-faculties are also like this,
World-Honored One!
The five aggregates are the six sense-faculties, and the six sense-faculties are the five aggregates.
"Such dharmas are all unattainable because they are internally empty, and so on, up to being unattainable because they are empty of non-existence and existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Will a bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon the Mahāyāna not experience fear upon hearing the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon the Mahāyāna lacks skillful means regarding the Prajñāpāramitā and does not encounter a good spiritual friend, that bodhisattva may become startled, terrified, or afraid.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are these skillful means?”
"When a bodhisattva practices these skillful means, he is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom and, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), contemplate the mark of impermanence in form; yet even this [mark] is unapprehendable."
To contemplate the marks of impermanence in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, yet to find that these too are ungraspable— Subhūti,
this is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), contemplates the characteristic of suffering in form; yet even this is unobtainable. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

In accordance with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one contemplates that form (*rūpa*) has the characteristic of non-self (*anātman*), yet even this [characteristic] is unapprehendable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of sarvajñā, contemplates the mark of emptiness of form; even this [mark] is unobtainable. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One contemplates form as being without the mark of marks, yet even this cannot be apprehended; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
One contemplates form as being without the mark of activity, yet even this cannot be apprehended; up to and including consciousness, it is also like this.
One contemplates the mark of the cessation of form, yet even this cannot be apprehended; it is the same for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness.
One contemplates the mark of the detachment from form, yet even this cannot be apprehended; it is the same for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom with skillful means.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the mark of impermanence in form, yet even that cannot be apprehended.

One contemplates the characteristic of suffering, the characteristic of non-self, the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of signlessness, the characteristic of wishlessness, the characteristic of cessation, and the characteristic of detachment regarding form; yet even these are unattainable. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva formed this thought:
"I shall preach this dharma of impermanence for the sake of all sentient beings, yet even this is unattainable.

I shall preach the characteristic of suffering for all sentient beings, and preach the characteristics of non-self, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, cessation, and detachment; yet even these are unattainable."
"This is called the dānapāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not,
with the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, contemplate form as impermanent, nor is it apprehended."
One does not, with the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, perceive that consciousness is impermanent, for it is likewise unattainable.

One does not, with the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, perceive that form is suffering, non-self, empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, or detached, for these are likewise unattainable; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is called the śīla-pāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñā-pāramitā, they endure and take delight in the mark of impermanence of all these dharmas, up to and including their mark of detachment.
This is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), they contemplate that the characteristic of impermanence in form (rūpa) is also unapprehendable, and even its characteristic of detachment is unapprehendable; it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
To accord with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) without abandoning or ceasing it—
this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s vīryapāramitā (perfection of vigor). "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or any other unwholesome thoughts.
This is called the dhyānapāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they reflect in this way:
'Form is not empty because of emptiness; rather, form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.'"

It is not because of emptiness that the eye is empty; the eye itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is the eye. This extends up to the feeling born from the condition of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa-pratyaya-utpanna-vedanā*).
It is not because of emptiness that feeling is empty; feeling itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is feeling.

It is not because of emptiness that the four foundations of mindfulness are empty; rather, the four foundations of mindfulness are themselves emptiness, and emptiness itself is the four foundations of mindfulness.

This continues up to: it is not because of emptiness that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty; rather, the eighteen unique qualities are themselves emptiness, and emptiness itself is the eighteen unique qualities.
"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What is it that, by being protected by good spiritual friends, causes a bodhisattva mahāsattva not to be startled, not to be afraid, and not to be terrified upon hearing this teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Regarding the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they teach that form is impermanent and also unapprehendable; they cause these roots of goodness not to be directed toward the path of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge.”
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

They teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent and also unapprehendable; they maintain these roots of goodness and do not direct them toward the paths of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only toward omniscience (sarvajñatā).

These are called the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, furthermore, there are other good spiritual friends for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who teach that form is suffering, yet it is ungraspable;

they teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering, yet they are ungraspable. They teach that form is selfless, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are selfless, yet these are ungraspable. They teach that form is empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, and detached, yet these are ungraspable; they teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, and detached, yet these are ungraspable. Possessing these roots of goodness, they do not direct them toward the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
Subhūti! These are called the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have spiritual friends who teach that the eye is impermanent, and so on, up to its separation being unapprehendable; likewise, they teach that everything from the feelings born of the conditions of mental contact is impermanent, and so on, up to their separation being unapprehendable. Taking these roots of goodness, they do not direct them toward the paths of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
These are called the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Subhūti, furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has other good spiritual friends who teach the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the point that even detachment cannot be apprehended; they take these roots of goodness and do not direct them toward the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge.
Subhūti! These are called the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Even when it is taught that the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities and the cultivation of all-knowledge are unapprehendable, one should take these roots of goodness and not direct them toward the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge.
"This is called the good spiritual friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā without skillful means follows an evil spiritual friend and, upon hearing this prajñāpāramitā being taught, becomes startled, terrified, and afraid?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva, separated from the mind of omniscience, practices the perfection of wisdom; having attained this perfection of wisdom, he contemplates this perfection of wisdom. He likewise attains and contemplates the perfection of dhyāna, the perfection of vīrya, the perfection of kṣānti, the perfection of śīla, and the perfection of dāna.”

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having departed from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), contemplates form as empty internally up to emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty internally up to emptiness of non-existence and existence; contemplates the eye as empty internally up to emptiness of non-existence and existence; and so on, up to contemplating feeling produced through the condition of mental contact as empty internally up to emptiness of non-existence and existence—if they still harbor thoughts regarding these dharmas or apprehend them as real entities, [they do not practice the perfection of wisdom].
Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom while remaining detached from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they cultivate and both attend to and attain the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to cultivating and both attending to and attaining the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, because they lack skillful means, they will be startled, terrified, and afraid upon hearing this perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva follows an evil friend and, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, becomes startled, fearful, and terrified?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The evil friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are those who teach them to distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom, and to distance themselves from the perfection of dhyāna, the perfection of vīrya, the perfection of kṣānti, the perfection of śīla, and the perfection of dāna.”
Subhūti! These are called the evil friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may have evil friends who do not speak of the deeds of Māra nor of the transgressions of Māra, and who do not say:
"An evil Māra may come in the form of a Buddha and instruct the Bodhisattva to abandon the six pāramitās."
He said to the Bodhisattva:
"Good son! What is the use of practicing the Prajñāpāramitā?"
For what purpose does one practice the dhyāna-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, and dāna-pāramitā?
"You should know that this is an evil friend (pāpamitra) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an evil Māra may again assume the form of a Buddha and go to where the bodhisattva is, preaching the sūtras of the śrāvakas—from the *sūtra* (sūtra) down to the *upadeśa*—instructing, analyzing, and expounding such scriptures, yet failing to explain the works of Māra or the transgressions of Māra. You should know that this is an evil friend of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One,
may take the form of a Buddha and approach the bodhisattva, saying: 'Good son!'"
"You lack the true mind of a bodhisattva, nor do you abide on the stage of avaivartika; furthermore, you shall not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"If one does not explain such demonic activities and demonic offenses to them, you should know that this person is a bad friend (pāpamitra) to the bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
a wicked Māra may assume the form of a Buddha, go to where the bodhisattva is, and say to the bodhisattva:"
"Good son! Form is empty, without self and without what belongs to a self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, without self and without what belongs to a self.
The eye is empty, without self and without what belongs to a self."
Even the feeling born of the condition of mental contact is empty, being without self and without what belongs to a self.
The perfection of giving is empty, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, which is empty.
"The four foundations of mindfulness are empty, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty.
What use have you for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
If one neither speaks of nor teaches such demonic deeds and demonic offenses, one should know that this person is a bad friend to the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One,
may manifest in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and approach the Bodhisattva,
saying to him: 'Good son!'"
"The ten directions are all empty; within them there is no Buddha, no bodhisattva, and no śrāvaka.
If one neither speaks of nor teaches such demonic activities and demonic offenses, one should know that this is a bad friend (pāpamitra) to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One, may come to the bodhisattva in the form of a preceptor or an ācārya, instructing them to abandon the bodhisattva path; instructing them to abandon all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā); instructing them to abandon the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; instructing them to abandon the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma); and instructing them to enter into emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, saying:
'O son of good family!'"
"You practice mindfulness of these dharmas to attain the realization of a śrāvaka; what use is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to you?
If one neither speaks of nor teaches such demonic deeds and demonic offenses, one should know that this person is a bad friend to the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One,
may take the form of a father or mother and approach the bodhisattva, saying to him: 'Son!'"
"You exert yourself with diligent effort for the sake of realizing the fruit of a stream-enterer, even up to exerting yourself with diligent effort for the sake of realizing the fruit of an arhat.
What use have you for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
In seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one must undergo birth and death for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, enduring various agonies such as having one's hands and feet cut off.
"If one does not speak of nor instruct regarding such deeds of Māra and such offenses of Māra, you should know that this person is a bad friend to the bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
a wicked Māra may take the form of a bhikṣu and go to where the bodhisattva is, saying to the bodhisattva:"

"The eye is a dharma that can be apprehended as impermanent, and so on up to the mind being a dharma that can be apprehended as impermanent; the eye is suffering, the eye is non-self, the eye is empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, and detached—these are dharmas that can be apprehended—and so it is for the mind as well."

"To teach the four foundations of mindfulness by means of a dharma that is apprehended as having existence, and even to teach the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha by means of a dharma that is apprehended as having existence—Subhūti, such things are the work of Māra and the transgressions of Māra;
they are neither spoken of nor taught [as such]. You should know that these are a bodhisattva’s bad friends. Having recognized them, you should keep far away from them."
Chapter Twelve: On the Meaning of the Words. From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter Twelve: On the Meaning of the Words. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The absence of a term is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'."
Why is this? Because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* has no referential object and no self; for this reason, the absence of a referential meaning is the meaning of the term "Bodhisattva."
Subhūti! Just as a bird flying through the void leaves no trace, so too is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" non-existent. Subhūti!
For example, just as that which is seen in a dream has no location, so too the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent. Subhūti!

For example, just as a magical illusion has no real substance, and just as a mirage, an echo, a shadow, and a transformation created by a Buddha have no real substance, so too the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as suchness, the dharma-nature, the dharma-characteristic, the dharma-position, and the limit of reality have no referential meaning, so too the referential meaning of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist.

Subhūti! For example, just as a phantom person has no referent for "form," and a phantom person has no referent for "feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent.
Subhūti! Just as a phantom person’s eye has no objective referent, and so on up to the mind having no objective referent; Subhūti!
Just as the form of an illusory person has no referent, and so on up to phenomena having no referent;

and just as the feeling produced by the condition of eye-contact, and so on up to the feeling produced by the condition of mind-contact, have no referent—so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as there is no referent when an illusory person practices inner emptiness, and so on up to practicing the emptiness of non-existence and existence, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as a phantom person practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities has no referential meaning, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referential meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the term "form" has no referent because form does not exist, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, there is no referential meaning in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—because this consciousness does not exist—so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referential meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as the Buddha-eye has no locus, and so on up to the mind having no locus; just as form, and so on up to mental phenomena, have no locus; and just as the feeling produced by the condition of eye-contact, and so on up to mind-contact, has no locus—so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as the Buddha’s internal emptiness has no location, and so on up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence which has no location, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as the four foundations of mindfulness of a Buddha have no locus, and even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) have no locus, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the referential meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as within the nature of the conditioned there is no meaning of the unconditioned nature, and within the nature of the unconditioned there is no meaning of the conditioned nature, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent.

Subhūti! Just as the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing has no location, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
Subhūti! Just as that which is unproduced, unarisen, unattained, neither defiled nor pure, and without location has no objective reality, so too the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By virtue of what dharma being neither born nor extinguished is there no location?
By virtue of what dharma not being created, not emerging, not being attained, and being neither defiled nor pure is there no location?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Because form is neither arising nor ceasing, it has no location; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither arising nor ceasing, they have no location; even up to being neither defiled nor pure, it is likewise.”
Because the elements (*dhātu*) are neither arising nor ceasing, they have no location; even up to being neither defiled nor pure, it is likewise.

Because the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are neither arising nor ceasing, they have no location; even up to being neither defiled nor pure, it is likewise. Even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), because they are neither arising nor ceasing, they have no location; even up to being neither defiled nor pure, it is likewise.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Subhūti!
Subhūti, just as the meaning of purity in the four foundations of mindfulness is ultimately unattainable,
so too is the referent of the term "bodhisattva" non-existent when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti! Just as the meaning of purity for the four right efforts, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, is ultimately unattainable, so too is the referent of the term "bodhisattva" non-existent when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti! Just as within purity the self cannot be apprehended, because the self does not exist;
even so, within purity the knower and the seer cannot be apprehended, because the knower and the seer do not exist.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Subhūti!
Just as there is no darkness when the sun rises, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist.

Subhūti! Just as there is no substance whatsoever during the conflagration at the end of a kalpa, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
Subhūti! Within the Buddha’s precepts, there is no breaking of the precepts. Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Subhūti,

it is as when there is no distracted mind within the Buddha’s concentration, no delusion within the Buddha’s wisdom, no lack of liberation within the Buddha’s liberation, and no lack of the knowledge and vision of liberation within the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of liberation.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Subhūti!

For example, within the light of the Buddha, the light of the sun and moon does not appear; likewise, within the light of the Buddha, the light of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmakāyika Heaven, up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, does not appear.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Why is this?

This unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the bodhisattva, and the meaning of the term "bodhisattva"—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance; they have a single mark, which is the so-called "markless."
