"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in and should also know the characteristic of non-obstruction regarding all dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are all phenomena? How should one understand the training in unimpeded correspondence regarding all phenomena?”

The Buddha told Subhūti: “All dharmas are: wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas; determinate dharmas and indeterminate dharmas; mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas; outflowing dharmas and non-outflowing dharmas; conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas; shared dharmas and unshared dharmas.”
Subhūti! These are called all dharmas.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in and understand the characteristic of non-obstruction regarding all dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are called the wholesome dharmas of the world?”

The Buddha told Subhūti: “Worldly wholesome dharmas are: filial piety toward one’s parents; making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; reverently serving elders and superiors; the bases of merit consisting of giving, the bases of merit consisting of ethical discipline, and the bases of merit consisting of meditative cultivation; exhorting others toward meritorious deeds; generating merit through skillful means; the ten worldly paths of wholesome action; the nine contemplations on the corpse—namely, the bloated appearance, the bloody appearance, the disintegrating appearance, the festering appearance, the bluish appearance, the gnawed appearance, the scattered appearance, the skeletal appearance, and the burned appearance; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments; and mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of wholesomeness, mindfulness of ānāpāna, mindfulness of the body, and mindfulness of death. These are called worldly wholesome dharmas.”
What are unwholesome dharmas?

Taking the life of another, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view—these ten unwholesome paths of action and so forth are called unwholesome dharmas.
What are determinate dharmas?
Whether they be wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, these are called determinate dharmas.
What are indeterminate dharmas?

Neutral bodily action, verbal action, and mental action; neutral four great elements; neutral five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements; and neutral retribution—these are called neutral phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*).
What are called mundane dharmas?

Mundane dharmas are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments; these are called mundane dharmas.

What are called supramundane dharmas? They are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path; the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; the three untainted faculties—the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known"; the three samādhis—samādhi with directed thought and sustained thought, samādhi without directed thought and with sustained thought, and samādhi without directed thought and without sustained thought; clarity, liberation, mindfulness, wisdom, right recollection, and the eight liberations.
What are the eight?
Contemplating forms while possessing form is the first liberation (vimokṣa).
Being internally without the perception of form, one contemplates external forms; this is the second liberation.
Realizing the purity of the liberation with the body as a witness is the third liberation.

Because one transcends all signs of form, because one extinguishes all signs of resistance, and because one does not attend to any signs of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation (vimokṣa).
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation.
The nine successive attainments.
What are the nine?
Detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one enters the first dhyāna.

With the cessation of applied and sustained thought through internal purity, one enters the second dhyāna, which is characterized by concentration free from applied and sustained thought, born of rapture and joy.

Through the fading away of rapture, one dwells in equanimity, experiences pleasure with the body, and—of whom the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in pleasure who possesses mindfulness and equanimity"—enters the third dhyāna.

By abandoning pleasure and pain, and by the prior cessation of sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
By transcending all perceptions of form, by the cessation of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Transcending all stages up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception.

Furthermore, there are supramundane dharmas: internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and omniscience; these are called supramundane dharmas.
What are the phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*)?

They are the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), the six classes [of objects], the six contacts (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*), the six feelings (*ṣaḍ-vedanā*), the four dhyānas, and up to the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*). These are called phenomena with outflows.
What are the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*)?
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) and all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); these are called untainted dharmas.
What are the conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)?

If a phenomenon arises, abides, and ceases—whether it be the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; the five aggregates up to the feeling produced by the condition of mental contact; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and omniscience—these are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?

They are that which is neither born, nor abides, nor ceases; they are the exhaustion of passion, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion; they are suchness (*tathatā*), non-alteration (*ananyathā*), the mark of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), the nature of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*), the fixed position of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). These are called unconditioned phenomena.
What are the shared dharmas?
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments—such as these are called the shared dharmas.
What are called the unshared dharmas?
From the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), these are called the unique qualities.

Within these phenomena that are empty of their own marks (svalakṣaṇa-śūnya), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be attached, because they are immovable; furthermore, a bodhisattva should know that all phenomena are non-dual in character and immovable—this is the meaning of "bodhisattva."

Chapter 13: The Diamond Chapter (*Vajraparivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. (The Dan-ben [Dunhuang manuscript] refers to this as the "Mahāsattva Chapter. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is he called a Mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva is the foremost among the assembly of those who are fixed in certainty; for this reason, he is called a Mahāsattva."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the assembly of those fixed in certainty, of whom these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas serve as leaders?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Those of the fixed group consist of persons of the lineage-ground (gotrabhūmi), the eight types of noble ones, the stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the non-returner (anāgāmin), the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattvas from those who have first resolved for awakening up to those on the stage of the irreversible (avaivartika).”
Subhūti! These are the bodhisattvas who are the leaders of the assembly of those destined for certainty.
Within this, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to the great mind that is indestructible like a vajra; they shall serve as the leaders of the assembly of those destined for certainty.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is the great mind generated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva that is indestructible like a vajra?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought:

‘I shall don the great armor amidst immeasurable births and deaths; I should relinquish all that I possess; I should maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings; and I should deliver all sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to enter nirvana without remainder.’”
"Once I have delivered all sentient beings, there shall not be even a single person who has entered nirvāṇa.

I should understand that all dharmas possess the characteristic of non-arising; I should practice the six pāramitās solely with the mind of *sarvajñatā*; I should study wisdom so as to thoroughly comprehend all dharmas; I should master the gate of wisdom regarding the single characteristic of all dharmas; and I should master the gates of wisdom regarding even infinite characteristics."
"Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s generation of the great mind, which is indestructible like a vajra.
Abiding in this mind, this bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes the foremost among those in the assembly of the certain (niyata-rāśi), because these dharmas are practiced through non-apprehension."
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought:

"I shall take upon myself, on behalf of all sentient beings of the ten directions—whether they be beings in the hells, beings among the animals, or beings among the hungry ghosts—to undergo their suffering and pain. For each and every sentient being, I shall undergo the sufferings within the hells for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, until that sentient being enters nirvana without remainder."
For this reason, on account of these dharmas, I undergo all manner of hardships for the sake of these sentient beings.

Only after these sentient beings have entered nirvana without remainder shall I myself cultivate roots of goodness and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the great mind that is indestructible like a vajra; abiding in this mind, he acts as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty."
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to a mind of great joy; dwelling within this mind of great joy, he acts as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the great joyful mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha said:

"From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not give rise to thoughts of passion, thoughts of malice, or thoughts of delusion; he does not give rise to thoughts of pride, nor thoughts of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. This is called the great joyful mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Abiding in this mind, he acts as the leader for the assembly of those who are certain, yet he does not even think that such a mind exists. Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to an unshakable mind.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is meant by ‘unshakable mind’?
The Buddha said:

“Constantly recollecting the mind of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā-citta), yet not recollecting that there is such a mind—this is called the immovable mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti:”
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should give rise to a mind of benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings.
What is meant by a "mind of benefit and happiness"?

It is to rescue and protect all sentient beings and never abandon them, yet without even thinking that one possesses such a mind; this is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva giving rise to a mind of benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings.
Thus it is, Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, is the most preeminent among those in the assembly of the certain.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the mind that delights in the Dharma, rejoices in the Dharma, and finds joy in the Dharma. What is this Dharma?
That which is called "Dharma" refers to the non-subversion of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
What is meant by "desiring the Dharma and rejoicing in the Dharma"?
It is faith in the Dharma, patience toward the Dharma, and acceptance of the Dharma; this is called desiring the Dharma and rejoicing in the Dharma.
What is called "delighting in the Dharma"?
Constantly practicing this Dharma is what is called "delighting in the Dharma. Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to act as the foremost among the assembly of those destined for certainty, because this dharma is practiced through non-apprehension.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, abiding in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, they are able to act as the leader for a group of those destined for certainty; this is because these dharmas are used through non-apprehension."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, dwelling in the four foundations of mindfulness up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they are able to act as the leader for the assembly of those destined for enlightenment, because these dharmas are practiced through non-apprehension."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the vajra-like samādhi and so forth, up to the space-like non-attachment and unstained samādhi; therein they act as the leader among the assembly of those destined for enlightenment, because these dharmas are practiced through non-apprehension."
Thus it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling within these dharmas, is able to act as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty.
For this reason, he is called a mahāsattva.

Chapter 14: On Eloquence (Pratibhāna) In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen, "On Eloquence" (in the Danzang edition, this is titled "On the Severance of Views"), at that time the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I also wish to explain why one is called a mahāsattva.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Speak then."

Śāriputra said: “I see the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, the view of a soul; the view of birth, the view of nourishment; the view of a multitude, the view of a person; the view of acting, the view of causing to act; the view of arising, the view of causing to arise; the view of experiencing, the view of causing to experience; the view of a knower, the view of a seer; the view of annihilation, the view of permanence; the view of existence, the view of non-existence; the view of the aggregates, the view of the sense-bases, the view of the elements; the view of the truths, the view of dependent origination; the view of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the view of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the view of the Buddha-way, the view of maturing sentient beings, the view of purifying Buddha-lands, the view of a Buddha, and the view of turning the wheel of Dharma. It is for the sake of severing all such views that he preaches the Dharma; this is called a Mahāsattva.”
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "By what causes and conditions is the view of form considered a false view?
By what causes and conditions are the views of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the view of turning the wheel of Dharma, called false views?"
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, because they lack skillful means, they give rise to views regarding form, due to their grasping at something obtainable;
they give rise to views regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the turning of the wheel of Dharma, due to their grasping at something obtainable.”

In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they preach the Dharma by means of skillful power to sever the net of all views, doing so through the principle of non-apprehension.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, wish to explain why one is called a mahāsattva.”
The Buddha said, "Speak then. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
This mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is the unequaled mind; it is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

Why is this? Because this mind of omniscience is untainted and unconditioned; furthermore, within that which is untainted and unconditioned, it does not cling. For these reasons, it is called a Mahāsattva.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"What is the unequaled mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the mind that is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?"

Subhūti said: “From the first moment of generating the mind of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva never perceives any dharma as having arising or ceasing, increasing or decreasing, being defiled or purified.”

Śāriputra! If a dharma is without arising and without cessation, and so forth, up to being without defilement and without purity, within it there is no mind of a śrāvaka, no mind of a pratyekabuddha, no mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and no mind of a Buddha.
“Śāriputra! This is called the unequaled mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a mind not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"As Subhūti has said, one does not even cling to the mind of omniscience, the untainted mind, or the unconditioned mind. Subhūti!

One does not cling to form, nor does one cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
"Why do you say that this mind alone is unattached? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is!"
“Śāriputra! One does not cling even to form, nor even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"The minds of ordinary worldlings are also untainted and unconditioned because their nature is empty; the minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the minds of all buddhas, are also untainted and unconditioned because their nature is empty."
Subhūti said: “So it is, Śāriputra! Śāriputra then said to Subhūti:
"If form is also untainted and unconditioned, because its nature is empty;
and if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also untainted and unconditioned, because their natures are empty;
and even if feeling produced with mind-contact as a condition is also untainted and unconditioned, because its nature is empty?"
Subhūti said, "So it is. Śāriputra said:
"The four foundations of mindfulness are also untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty.
This extends even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are also untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty."
Subhūti said: "It is so.
As Śāriputra has said, the minds of ordinary persons are also untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty."
"Even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they are likewise untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃbaddha*), because their nature is empty.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "As Subhūti has explained, because emptiness is without mind, one does not cling to this mind."

Subhūti! Because form (*rūpa*) does not exist, one does not cling to form; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even up to the feeling born from the condition of mind-contact (*manas-saṃsparśa-pratyaya-utpanna-vedanā*)—do not exist, one does not cling to feeling.

Because the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) do not exist, one does not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness; even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), because they do not exist, one does not cling to the eighteen unique qualities.
Subhūti said: “It is so, Śāriputra!

Because form does not exist, one does not cling to form; likewise, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because they do not exist, one does not cling to the eighteen unique qualities.”

In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do so with the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the unequaled mind, the mind not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; yet they do not think of having such a mind, nor do they become attached to it, because all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, he is called a Mahāsattva. Chapter Fifteen:

Eloquence (*Pratibhāna*) In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen, “Eloquence,” which in the Danben (Dunhuang) edition is titled the “Pūrṇa” Chapter, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I, too, would like to explain why one is called a mahāsattva.
The Buddha said, "Speak then."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said: "This bodhisattva is adorned with great vows;
this bodhisattva has set out upon the Great Vehicle; this bodhisattva rides upon the Great Vehicle. For these reasons, this bodhisattva is called a mahāsattva."
Śāriputra said to Pūrṇa: "What is meant by the 'great vow-adornment' of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Pūrṇa replied to Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell in or practice the perfection of giving for the sake of such-and-such a number of persons.
Rather, he dwells in and practices the perfection of giving for the sake of all sentient beings."

It is not for the sake of such persons that one dwells in the perfection of ethical discipline, practices the perfection of ethical discipline, nor the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they abide in the *prajñāpāramitā* and practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is adorned with great vows and does not set limits upon sentient beings, thinking: "I shall deliver so many people, but not others."
He does not say:
"I have caused so many people to reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, while others have not.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has made a great vow and is adorned with its armor for the sake of all sentient beings without exception.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I shall personally fulfill the dānapāramitā, and I shall also cause all sentient beings to practice the dānapāramitā."

Having personally fulfilled the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), and the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), and having personally fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they also cause all sentient beings to practice the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), all his acts of giving are in accord with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā) and he dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)."
Śāriputra! This is called the great vow-adornment of the perfection of giving when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, he should give with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā), not toward the levels of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Śāriputra! This is called the great vow-adornment of the śīla-pāramitā when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dāna-pāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), he gives with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā). This faith, patience, and aspiration regarding all these acts of giving is called the great vow-adornment of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) when practicing the perfection of giving.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), he gives with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā) and diligently cultivates this without ceasing; this is called the adornment of the great vow of the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) while practicing the perfection of giving.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā),
he should practice giving with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā).
To gather the mind so as not to give rise to the thoughts of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha is called the great vow-adornment of the dhyānapāramitā when practicing the dānapāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), he gives with a mind directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). He contemplates all phenomena as being like an illusion, perceiving neither the giver, nor the object given, nor the recipient. This is called the great vow-adornment of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) when practicing the perfection of giving.
In this way, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accords with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā) and neither grasps nor apprehends the marks of the various pāramitās, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is adorned with the great vow.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives gifts with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā) and dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi). This is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), his faith, patience, and aspiration toward all these dharmas is called the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) for that bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he cultivates it with diligence without ceasing; this is called the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *śīlapāramitā*, he does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; this is called the *dhyānapāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the *śīlapāramitā*.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he contemplates all phenomena as being like an illusion; moreover, he does not even think that this precept exists, because he employs the principle of non-apprehension. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline.

In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they encompass all the perfections; for this reason, it is called the "adornment of the great vow."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he gives gifts with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta) and dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This is the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of patience."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he does not adopt the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but adopts only the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta). This is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he accords with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta) and exerts himself in body and mind without rest; this is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they collect the mind in a single point; although there may be painful circumstances, the mind does not become distracted. This is called the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), he accords with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā) and contemplates all phenomena as empty, being without an agent and without an experiencer. If there are those who revile him or cut his body, his mind is like an illusion or a dream; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *vīryapāramitā*, they practice giving with a mind directed toward *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), such that they do not allow body or mind to become indolent. This is called the *dānapāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the *vīryapāramitā*."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), he maintains the precepts with complete purity from beginning to end in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta). This is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), he practices patience (kṣānti) in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā); this is called the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *vīryapāramitā*, he accords with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), collects his mind, becomes detached from desire, and enters the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). This is called the *dhyānapāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the *vīryapāramitā*.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *vīryapāramitā*, he acts in accordance with the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and does not grasp at the characteristics (*nimitta*) of any phenomena; even regarding this non-grasping of characteristics, he does not [cling to it]. At that time, he subsumes all the *pāramitās*.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, he acts in accordance with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge); with a concentrated mind, he practices giving without allowing the mind to become distracted. This is called the dānapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyānapāramitā."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, by means of the power of his morality and meditative concentration in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), he prevents any phenomena of broken precepts from entering; this is called the śīlapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyānapāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, he endures all afflictions and harms because his mind accords with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and is established in the concentration of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-samādhi*). This is called the kṣāntipāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyānapāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, he accords with the mind of sarvajñatā; he does not relish or become attached to dhyāna, but constantly seeks progress, proceeding from one dhyāna to another. This is called the vīryapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyānapāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, he accords with the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), does not rely upon any phenomena, and is not reborn according to the stages of dhyāna; this is called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyānapāramitā.
In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, they encompass all the pāramitās. Furthermore, Śāriputra:

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice giving in accordance with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), without cherishing anything internal or external. They do not perceive a giver, a recipient, or the gift itself; this is called the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he accords with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge); because he does not perceive the two things of observing precepts and breaking precepts, this is called the śīlapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), he does not perceive one who reviles, one who scolds, one who strikes, or one who kills; nor does he perceive that it is by means of this emptiness that he is able to practice patience. This is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he accords with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and contemplates all phenomena as ultimately empty; yet, out of great compassion, he practices all wholesome dharmas. This is called the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in accordance with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), contemplating all meditations as having the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of signlessness, and the characteristic of wishlessness. This is called the *dhyānapāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they encompass all the perfections. Śāriputra!
This is called the great vow-adornment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
When a bodhisattva is thus adorned with this great vow, the Buddhas of the ten directions rejoice and, amidst the great assemblies, proclaim their names and praise them, saying:
"In such-and-such a land, such-and-such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is adorned with the great vow; he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies Buddha-lands."
The Venerable Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out upon the Great Vehicle?”
Pūrṇa said to Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he is detached from all desires and detached from all evil and unwholesome states. With directed thought and sustained thought, born of detachment, joy and bliss, he enters the first dhyāna, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna. With a mind that is vast, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from malice, he dwells pervading one direction, two, three, and four directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, throughout the entire world.
He does the same with the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.”

When this bodhisattva enters into or emerges from dhyāna, he dedicates all meditative absorptions, immeasurable minds, and their constituent factors, together with all sentient beings, toward sarvajñā (omniscience); this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Great Vehicle through the dhyānapāramitā.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the meditative concentrations and the immeasurable minds, forms this thought:
"I shall attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and shall preach the Dharma for the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings."
This is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), cultivates and dwells in the first dhyāna—and likewise in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas—without accepting any other mind, namely the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), enters the various dhyānas and forms this thought:
"I shall preach the Dharma for the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings."

These various mental desires, inclinations, and forbearances are called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the various dhyānas with a mind corresponding to omniscience (sarvajñatā), dedicates all roots of goodness toward omniscience, and practices diligently without ceasing, this is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), enters the four dhyānas and their constituent factors, contemplates the mark of impermanence, the mark of suffering, the mark of non-self, the mark of emptiness, the mark of signlessness, and the mark of wishlessness, and dedicates this together with all sentient beings toward sarvajñā—this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of dhyāna.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Mahāyāna, they practice the mind of loving-kindness and form this thought:

"I shall bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings and enter the mind of compassion; I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings and enter the mind of sympathetic joy; I shall ferry across all sentient beings and enter the mind of equanimity; I shall cause all sentient beings to attain the exhaustion of all outflows."
"This is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the immeasurable minds.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva directs these meditative absorptions and immeasurable minds neither toward the stage of a śrāvaka nor that of a pratyekabuddha, but solely toward omniscience (sarvajñatā), this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the immeasurable minds."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), he does not covet the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but instead patiently delights in and desires omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the immeasurable minds.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā), practices the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa) and practices only pure conduct, this is called the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the immeasurable minds.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters meditative absorption (dhyāna) and the immeasurable states of mind (apramāṇa), he does not arise following after those absorptions or immeasurable states; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful means and perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) when practicing the immeasurable states of mind.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle, they cultivate all aspects of the four foundations of mindfulness up to all aspects of the eightfold noble path; they cultivate all aspects of the three doors of liberation up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because the wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva functions through non-apprehension in the emptiness of the internal, and so on up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Great Vehicle."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that is neither distracted nor fixed amidst all dharmas is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle, they possess the wisdom that [things] are neither permanent nor impermanent; the wisdom that they are neither pleasant nor painful, neither real nor empty, and neither self nor non-self. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle by means of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the wisdom of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not operate in the past, does not operate in the future, and does not operate in the present; yet it is not that he is ignorant of the three periods of time. This is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle, because he employs the principle of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle, their wisdom does not function within the desire realm, does not function within the form realm, and does not function within the formless realm; yet it is not that they are unaware of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, because they employ the principle of non-apprehension. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle, their wisdom does not engage with worldly dharmas, nor does it engage with supramundane dharmas; it does not engage with conditioned dharmas, nor does it engage with unconditioned dharmas; it does not engage with tainted dharmas, nor does it engage with untainted dharmas. Yet, it is not that they are ignorant of worldly and supramundane dharmas, or conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, or tainted and untainted dharmas, for they employ the principle of non-apprehension.
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Great Vehicle.
Chapter Sixteen: The Vehicle of Vehicles From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Pūrṇa:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva ‘riding upon the Great Vehicle’? Pūrṇa replied to Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he rides upon the *dānapāramitā*. Yet he does not apprehend the *dānapāramitā*, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend the recipient. Because these dharmas are used through non-apprehension, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the *dānapāramitā*.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they mount the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration; they mount the perfection of wisdom as well, yet they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor do they apprehend the bodhisattva. Because these dharmas are used through non-apprehension, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva mounting the perfection of wisdom.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
This is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, Śāriputra:

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with the Great Vehicle and a single-mindedness corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness because dharmas are subject to disintegration; likewise, up to a single-mindedness corresponding to sarvajñā, he cultivates the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha because dharmas are subject to disintegration—and even this [cultivation] is unapprehendable.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"The 'bodhisattva' exists as a mere name, for sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Great Vehicle.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
'Form exists as a mere name, because form is unapprehendable. "
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness exist as mere names, for consciousness cannot be apprehended.
The eye exists as a mere name, for the eye cannot be apprehended;
and so it is, up to and including the mind.
The four foundations of mindfulness exist only as names, because the four foundations of mindfulness are unattainable.
This extends even to the eightfold noble path, which exists only as names, because the eightfold noble path is unattainable.
Internal emptiness exists as a mere name, because internal emptiness cannot be apprehended.
This continues up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which exists as a mere name, because the emptiness of non-existence and existence cannot be apprehended.
Even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), there are only names, because the eighteen unique qualities are unattainable.
All phenomena (*dharma*) are merely names, because suchness (*tathatā*) is unattainable.

The characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the fixed position of phenomena (dharmasthiti), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) exist only as names, because the limit of reality is unattainable.
Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi and the Buddha exist only as names, because the Buddha is unattainable.
"In this way, Śāriputra, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who rides upon the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, Śāriputra..."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment, fulfills the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers to bring sentient beings to maturity, travels from one buddha-field to another, reverently makes offerings to, honors, and praises the Buddhas, and receives the teachings of the Dharma from those Buddhas—namely, what is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattvas.

This Bodhisattva Vehicle is the Great Vehicle; it travels from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, purifying Buddha-fields and bringing sentient beings to maturity, yet from the very beginning it is devoid of the notion of a Buddha-field and the notion of sentient beings.

This person dwells within the dharma of non-duality and takes on a body for the sake of sentient beings; according to what is appropriate for them, they transform their own form to teach and transform them, never departing from the Bodhisattva Vehicle until the attainment of all-knowledge.
This is called the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas.
Having attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they turn the wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, or the people of the world.
At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, joyfully called his name and praised him, saying:
"In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, a certain Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, riding upon the Great Vehicle, has attained all-knowledge and turns the wheel of Dharma."
“Śāriputra! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Great Vehicle.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Five, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter Seventeen:
The Chapter on Adornment (Vyūha-parivarta). Chapter Seventeen: The Chapter on Adornment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva—what is this ‘great adornment’?”
“What kind of bodhisattva is able to achieve great adornment? The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“The Great Vehicle’s great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the adornment of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); the adornment of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path; the adornment of inner emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); the adornment of the ten powers (*daśabala*) up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) and all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); and the adornment of manifesting a body like that of a Buddha.”

The light shines universally throughout the trichiliocosm, and likewise illuminates lands in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; it is the same for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

The three thousandfold world-system shook in six ways; likewise, it shook the lands in the eastern direction equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River, and so too did it shake the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the great adornment of the Mahāyāna, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

This trichiliocosm is transformed into lapis lazuli, and he manifests as a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin rājā*), providing food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, clothing, bedding, flowers, incense, garlands, powdered incense, perfumes, dwellings, lamps, and medicines—granting all manner of necessities to them.
Having given [these things], he preaches the Dharma for them, namely that which accords with the six pāramitās.
Those sentient beings who hear this Dharma shall never depart from the six pāramitās until they reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus it is, Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!

Suppose, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to manifest a great multitude at a crossroads and provide them with whatever they required—giving food to those who needed food and drink to those who needed drink, and so on, until all their various needs were fully supplied?
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does that illusionist truly have any sentient beings to whom he gives anything?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."

“Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who manifests as a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), fully endowed with all things: he gives food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, and provides everything else that is required.
Although there is giving, in reality there is nothing given.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because the characteristics of all dharmas are like an illusion.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) manifests birth in the family of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), and teaches and transforms sentient beings through the ten paths of wholesome action; there are also those who teach and transform sentient beings through the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).
Sentient beings who hear this Dharma will never be separated from it until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

It is like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, at a crossroads, conjures a great multitude of people and teaches them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action; furthermore, he teaches and leads them to practice the four *dhyānas*, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Subhūti, what do you think? Does that illusionist truly have any sentient beings whom he instructs to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One. “Subhūti!”

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: by means of the ten paths of wholesome action, they teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to practice up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; yet, in reality, there are no sentient beings who practice the ten paths of wholesome action up to the eighteen unique qualities.
Why is this? Because the characteristics of all dharmas are like an illusion, Subhūti!
This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the perfection of patience teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to practice the perfection of patience.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), teach and transform sentient beings so that they practice the perfection of patience?

Subhūti! From the moment they first resolve their minds toward enlightenment, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess such great adornment that even if all sentient beings should revile them or harm them with swords and staves, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not give rise to a single thought of malice therein, and furthermore, they teach all sentient beings to practice this patience.
It is, for example, like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, at a crossroads, conjures a great multitude of people and causes them to practice patience; the rest is as described above.
Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of vigor, teaches all sentient beings to practice the perfection of vigor. Subhūti!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), teach all sentient beings to practice the perfection of vigor? Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), applies physical and mental diligence to teach and transform sentient beings.
It is like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, at a crossroads, conjures a great multitude and instructs them to practice physical and mental diligence; the rest is as explained above.
This is called the great adornment of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the dhyānapāramitā, teaches all sentient beings to practice the dhyānapāramitā.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the dhyānapāramitā, teach all sentient beings to practice the dhyānapāramitā?
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the equality of all dharmas, they do not perceive any dharma as either distracted or concentrated. It is thus, Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the dhyānapāramitā, teaches all sentient beings to practice the dhyānapāramitā, so that until they reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they never depart from the dhyānapāramitā.

For example, suppose a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great multitude of people at a crossroads and instruct them to practice the dhyāna-pāramitā; the rest is as explained above.
Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom and teaches all sentient beings to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in the perfection of wisdom and teach all sentient beings to practice the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that attains this shore or the other shore.
Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the prajñāpāramitā, teaches all sentient beings to practice the prajñāpāramitā.
It is, for example, like a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice who,
at a crossroads, conjures a great multitude of people and instructs them to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Great Adornment consists of transforming his own body according to the needs of sentient beings within as many lands in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, abiding in the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, and likewise instructing sentient beings to practice the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
These sentient beings practice this Dharma, and until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they never depart from this Dharma. Subhūti,
it is as if a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to conjure up sentient beings at a crossroads and instruct them to practice the six *pāramitās*, as described above.
Thus it is, Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The great adornment of the bodhisattva mahāsattva accords with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), such that he does not give rise to this thought:
"I have established so many people in the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), and I have not established so many people in the perfection of giving."
This applies even up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One does not give rise to the thought:
"I instruct so many people to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, but I do not instruct so many people to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness."
This applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Furthermore, he does not give rise to this thought:

"I have taught so many people to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva*), the path of a pratyekabuddha, or all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*"; nor does he think: "I have not taught so many people to attain the fruit of stream-entry up to all-knowledge."

I shall cause immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings to abide in the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; I shall establish sentient beings in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and I shall cause immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings to attain the fruit of stream-entry up to all-knowledge.

"It is, for example, like a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice who, at a crossroads, conjures a great multitude of people and instructs them to practice the six pāramitās up to the attainment of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā); the rest is as explained above."
“Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

According to the meaning I have heard from the Buddha, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the absence of great adornment constitutes great adornment, because the self-characteristics of all dharmas are empty.”

That which is called form is empty of the characteristic of form; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristics of consciousness. The eye is empty of the characteristic of the eye, and so on up to the mind being empty of the characteristic of the mind. Form is empty of the characteristic of form, and so on up to phenomena being empty of the characteristic of phenomena. Eye-consciousness is empty of the characteristic of eye-consciousness, and so on up to mind-consciousness being empty of the characteristic of mind-consciousness. Eye-contact is empty of the characteristic of eye-contact, and so on up to mind-contact being empty of the characteristic of mind-contact.

The feeling born of the condition of eye-contact is empty of the characteristic of feeling, and so on up to the feeling born of the condition of mind-contact, which is empty of the characteristic of feeling.
World-Honored One!

The *dānapāramitā* is empty of the characteristic of the *dānapāramitā*, and so on up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is empty of the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Internal emptiness is empty of the characteristic of internal emptiness, and so on up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is empty of the characteristic of the emptiness of non-existence and existence. The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are empty of the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. The Bodhisattva is empty of the characteristic of the Bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!
For these reasons, it should be known that for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the absence of great adornment constitutes great adornment.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said, Subhūti."
"All dharmas are not conditioned phenomena, and sentient beings are also not conditioned phenomena; for these sentient beings, the Bodhisattva undertakes the great adornment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

For what reason is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and why are these sentient beings also not conditioned phenomena, such that the bodhisattva undertakes this great adornment for the sake of these sentient beings?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Because an agent cannot be apprehended, sarvajñatā is neither a created nor an originated dharma; these sentient beings, likewise, are neither created nor originated dharmas."
Why is this? Subhūti!

Form is neither made nor unmade; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither made nor unmade; the eye is neither made nor unmade, and so on up to the mind, which is neither made nor unmade.

From form up to mental phenomena; from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; from eye-contact up to mind-contact; and from the feeling born of the causal condition of eye-contact up to the feeling born of the causal condition of mind-contact—these are neither created nor uncreated.
Subhūti! I am neither an agent nor a non-agent; even the knower and the seer are neither agents nor non-agents. Why is this?
Because these dharmas are ultimately unattainable. Subhūti,
a dream is neither an act nor a non-act.
Why is this? Because they are ultimately unattainable.
An illusion, an echo, a shadow, a mirage, and a transformation are neither created nor uncreated.
Why is this? Because it is ultimately unattainable, Subhūti!
Internal emptiness is neither created nor uncreated, because it is ultimately unapprehendable.
This extends up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is neither created nor uncreated, because it is ultimately unapprehendable.
Subhūti! The four foundations of mindfulness are neither created nor uncreated, because they are ultimately unattainable.
This extends even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are neither created nor uncreated.
Why is this? Because these dharmas are ultimately unattainable. Subhūti!

The suchness, the characteristic of phenomena, the nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the fixed position of phenomena, and the limit of reality of all phenomena are neither created nor uncreated, because they are ultimately unapprehendable.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva neither acts nor does not act, because they are ultimately unapprehendable.
Omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) neither act nor do not act, because they are ultimately unapprehendable.

For this reason, Subhūti, all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is neither a created nor an arisen dharma, and these sentient beings are likewise neither created nor arisen dharmas; it is for the sake of these sentient beings that the bodhisattva undertakes the great adornment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As I perceive the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, World-Honored One:
form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.”
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Subhūti: "Form is neither bound nor liberated;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated."
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is!
Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.”
Pūrṇa asked Subhūti: "What is form that is neither bound nor liberated?
What are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are neither bound nor liberated?"

Subhūti said: "Just as form in a dream is neither bound nor liberated, so too feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness in a dream are neither bound nor liberated. Just as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like an echo, like a shadow, like a magical illusion, like a mirage, and like a transformation, they are neither bound nor liberated."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra! Past form is neither bound nor liberated;
past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Future form is neither bound nor liberated;
future feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
In the present, form is neither bound nor liberated; in the present, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Why are they neither bound nor liberated?

Because this form is non-existent, it is neither bound nor liberated; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent, they are neither bound nor liberated. They are neither bound nor liberated because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen.

Pūrṇa! Wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated; unwholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated; neutral form is neither bound nor liberated, and neutral feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated; mundane and supramundane, as well as tainted and untainted form, are neither bound nor liberated, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because they are non-existent, detached, quiescent, and unarisen, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Pūrṇa!
All dharmas are likewise neither bound nor liberated; because they are non-existent, detached, quiescent, and unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated. Pūrṇa!

The perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) is neither bound nor liberated; the perfections of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), diligence (vīrya-pāramitā), meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) are neither bound nor liberated. Because they are non-existent, because they are detached, and because they are quiescent and unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.

Pūrṇa! Internal emptiness is neither bound nor liberated, and so on up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is also neither bound nor liberated. The four foundations of mindfulness are neither bound nor liberated, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are neither bound nor liberated. Because they are non-existent, because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.

Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is neither bound nor liberated; all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) are neither bound nor liberated; the bodhisattva is neither bound nor liberated; and the Buddha, too, is neither bound nor liberated. Because they are non-existent, because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.

Pūrṇa! The suchness of all dharmas, their characteristics, their nature, their stability, their fixed position, the limit of reality, and unconditioned dharmas are neither bound nor liberated. Because they are non-existent, because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Pūrṇa! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s being neither bound nor liberated.

From the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and from the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are neither bound nor liberated.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) that is neither bound nor liberated, up to dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that is neither bound nor liberated; they dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) that are neither bound nor liberated, up to dwelling in the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) that is neither bound nor liberated. They bring sentient beings to maturity that is neither bound nor liberated, purify buddha-fields that is neither bound nor liberated, shall make offerings to all Buddhas that is neither bound nor liberated, shall listen to the Dharma that is neither bound nor liberated, and shall never be separated from the Buddhas that is neither bound nor liberated.

Without bondage and without liberation, they never depart from the various supernormal powers; without bondage and without liberation, they never depart from the five eyes; without bondage and without liberation, they never depart from the gateways of dhāraṇī; without bondage and without liberation, they never depart from the gateways of samādhi. Without bondage and without liberation, they shall give rise to the knowledge of the modes of the path; without bondage and without liberation, they shall attain all-knowledge. Without bondage and without liberation, they turn the wheel of Dharma; without bondage and without liberation, they establish sentient beings in the three vehicles.

In this way, Pūrṇa! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās that are neither bound nor liberated, one should know that all dharmas are neither bound nor liberated, because they are non-existent, detached, quiescent, and unarisen.
"Pūrṇa! This is called the Great Adornment of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which is neither bound nor liberated.
Chapter 18: Inquiry into the Vehicle (*Yāna-pṛcchā-parivarta*) At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
How should one know that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has set out upon the Mahāyāna?”
"What is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? Subhūti,
the six pāramitās are the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
What are the six?

They are the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
What is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*)?

Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), dedicates all internal and external things they possess toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*) together with all sentient beings, by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
Subhūti! This is called the dānapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What is called the śīlapāramitā?

Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), personally practices the ten paths of wholesome action and also teaches others to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, because they do so by way of non-apprehension.
This is called the śīla-pāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
What is called the kṣānti-pāramitā? Subhūti!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), personally fulfills patience and also teaches others to practice patience, by way of non-apprehension.
This is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā)? Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), practices the five pāramitās with unremitting diligence and also establishes all sentient beings in the five pāramitās, by way of non-apprehension.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
What is called the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā)? Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), personally enters the various dhyānas through skillful means without being reborn according to those dhyānas; he also teaches others to enter the various dhyānas, because of non-apprehension.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s dhyānapāramitā. What is called prajñāpāramitā? Subhūti!

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), does not cling to any phenomena and contemplates the nature of all phenomena; because they are unapprehendable, they also teach others not to cling to any phenomena and to contemplate the nature of all phenomena, because they are unapprehendable.
This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there is another Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely:

internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of the conditioned, emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristics, emptiness of all dharmas, emptiness of the non-apprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of existence, and emptiness of both non-existence and existence."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is internal emptiness?
The Buddha said:
“Internal dharmas are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The eye is empty of the eye, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Its nature is thus:

the ear is empty of the ear, the nose is empty of the nose, the tongue is empty of the tongue, the body is empty of the body, and the mind is empty of the mind, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
What is external emptiness?
External phenomena are defined as form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects.
Form is empty of form, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because their nature is such.

Sound is empty of sound; fragrance is empty of fragrance; taste is empty of taste; touch is empty of touch; phenomena are empty of phenomena, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called external emptiness.
What is internal-and-external emptiness?
Internal-and-external phenomena refer to the six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases.
Internal phenomena are empty of internal phenomena, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because such is their nature.
External phenomena are empty of external phenomena, for they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).
