What is the emptiness of emptiness?
All dharmas are empty, and this very emptiness is also empty, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this so?
Its nature is thus of itself;
this is called the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). What is the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*)?
The eastern direction is empty of the characteristics of the eastern direction, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Because its nature is inherently so.
The south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir are empty, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because such is their inherent nature.
This is called the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārthaśūnyatā*)?
The ultimate truth is named nirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is empty of nirvāṇa, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
What is emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?
Conditioned phenomena refer to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

The desire realm is empty of the desire realm; the form realm is empty of the form realm; the formless realm is empty of the formless realm, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this so?
Its nature is thus;
this is called the emptiness of the conditioned.
What is the emptiness of the unconditioned?
Unconditioned phenomena are defined as those that possess no characteristic of arising, no characteristic of abiding, and no characteristic of cessation.
Unconditioned phenomena are empty of unconditioned phenomena because they are neither eternal nor subject to extinction. Why is this?
Its nature is thus of itself;
this is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). What is the emptiness of the ultimate (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)?
Ultimate means that all dharmas are ultimately unobtainable, because they are neither permanent nor subject to extinction.
Why is this? Because their nature is inherently so.
This is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
What is beginningless emptiness (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*)?
It is when the initial point of origin of any phenomenon cannot be found, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of that which has no beginning.
What is the emptiness of dispersion?
"Dispersion" refers to the non-extinction of all phenomena,
because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of dispersion.
What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*)?

The intrinsic nature of all phenomena—whether the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena or the intrinsic nature of unconditioned phenomena—is a nature that is not created by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or buddhas, nor is it created by anyone else. This nature is empty of intrinsic nature because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of nature.
What is the emptiness of self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?

Self-characteristic refers to the characteristic of disintegration in form (*rūpa*), the characteristic of experiencing in feeling (*vedanā*), the characteristic of grasping in perception (*saṃjñā*), the characteristic of conditioning in formations (*saṃskāra*), and the characteristic of cognizing in consciousness (*vijñāna*). In this way, each of these conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is empty of its own self-characteristic, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)?

All phenomena refer to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; the eye-element, form-element, and eye-consciousness-element, up to the mind-element, mental-object-element, and mind-consciousness-element.
These dharmas are empty of these dharmas, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because their nature is inherently so.
This is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*)?
Seeking all phenomena and finding them unapprehendable—this is the emptiness of the unapprehendable.
Because it is neither eternal nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of the unobtainable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*)?
If a phenomenon does not exist, that too is empty, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because such is its inherent nature.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*)?

"Existing phenomena" refers to the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) within the combination of all phenomena; this is the emptiness of existing phenomena, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

Among all phenomena there is non-existence; within the combination of all phenomena there is the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). This is the emptiness of non-existence and existence, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because such is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Phenomena are empty of the characteristic of phenomena;

non-phenomena are empty of the characteristic of non-phenomena; self-phenomena are empty of the characteristic of self-phenomena; and other-phenomena are empty of the characteristic of other-phenomena."
What is meant by "the emptiness of phenomena in their own nature" (*dharmadharmatā-śūnyatā*)?
"Phenomena" refers to the five aggregates; that the five aggregates are empty is what is called "the emptiness of phenomena in their own nature.
What is meant by "the emptiness of non-phenomena in their own nature" (*abhāvābhāva-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?
The non-existence of dharmas is called the unconditioned dharma; this is termed the emptiness of the non-existence of dharmas as non-existent dharmas.
What is termed the emptiness of self-dharmas as self-dharmas?
All dharmas are empty of their own nature; this emptiness is not produced by knowledge nor produced by vision. This is termed the emptiness of self-dharmas as self-dharmas.
What is meant by "other dharmas being empty of other dharmas"?

Whether a Buddha has appeared or a Buddha has not appeared, the dharma-abiding, the dharma-characteristic, the dharma-position, the dharma-nature, suchness, and the limit of reality—these dharmas transcend [subject and object] and are empty; this is called "other dharmas being empty of other dharmas."
This is called the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva consists of what are known as the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Ratnamudrā [Samādhi], and so forth.

"What is called the śūraṅgama-samādhi?"
To know the spheres of activity of all samādhis is called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Why is it called the Ratnamudrā Samādhi?
Because by abiding in this samādhi one can seal all samādhis; therefore, it is called the Ratnamudrā Samādhi.
What is called the Lion’s Play Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to play among all samādhis like a lion; therefore, it is named the Lion’s Play Samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of the Wondrous Moon?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to illuminate all samādhis like the pure moon; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Wondrous Moon.
What is called the Samādhi of the Lunar Banner Mark?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to maintain the characteristics of all samādhis; this is called the Moon Banner Mark Samādhi (*candradhvajaketu-samādhi*).
What is called the Emergence from All Dharmas Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to give birth to all samādhis; this is called the Emergence from All Dharmas Samādhi (*sarvadharmotthāpana-samādhi*).
What is called the Samādhi of Contemplating the Summit?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to contemplate the summit of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Contemplating the Summit.
What is called the Samādhi of the Ultimate Nature of Phenomena (Dharmatā)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one definitively knows the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); this is called the samādhi of the ultimate nature of phenomena.
What is called the samādhi of the ultimate banner-mark?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to uphold the banners of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of the ultimate banner-mark.
What is called the Vajra Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to shatter all other samādhis; therefore, it is named the Vajra Samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of Entering the Seal of the Dharma (Dharmamudrā)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one enters the seals of all dharmas; this is called the "Samādhi of Entering the Seals of Dharmas" (*dharmamudrā-praveśa-samādhi*).
What is called the "Samādhi of the King’s Firm Establishment" (*samādhirāja-vyavasthāna-samādhi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is firmly established among all samādhis like a king; this is called the "Samādhi of the King’s Firm Establishment."
What is called the *raśmipramokṣa* samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to emit light that illuminates all samādhis; this is called the *raśmipramokṣa* samādhi.
What is called the *balavikrāmin* samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to exercise power over all samādhis; this is called the *balavikrāmin* (Powerful Progress) samādhi.
What is called the *udgata* (Exalted) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to increase all samādhis; this is called the *udgata* samādhi.
What is called the samādhi of "certain entry into eloquence"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to eloquently expound upon all samādhis; therefore, it is named the samādhi of certain entry into eloquence.
What is called the Samādhi of Explaining Names?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to explain the names of all samādhis; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Explaining Names.
What is called the Samādhi of Contemplating Directions?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to contemplate the directions of all samādhis; this is called the "Contemplation of Directions" (diśām-avalokana) samādhi.
What is called the "Dhāraṇī Seal" (dhāraṇī-mudrā) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one maintains the seals of all samādhis; this is called the "Dhāraṇī Seal" samādhi.
What is called the "Non-deceptive Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not deceive regarding any samādhis; thus it is named the Non-deceptive Samādhi.
What is called the "Samādhi that Encompasses the Ocean of All Dharmas"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to encompass all samādhis like the waters of the great ocean; this is called the "Samādhi that Encompasses the Ocean of All Dharmas.
What is called the "Samādhi that Pervasively Covers Space"?
Abiding in this samādhi, it universally covers all samādhis like space; therefore, it is called the "Samādhi that Universally Covers Space.
What is called the "Vajra-Wheel Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to maintain the constituent parts of all samādhis; this is called the Vajracakra Samādhi.
What is called the Ratnavicheda Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one cuts off the defilements of all samādhis; this is called the Ratnavicheda Samādhi.
What is called the "Able-to-Illuminate Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to manifest and illuminate all samādhis with light; this is called the Able-to-Illuminate Samādhi.
What is called the "non-seeking samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, there is no dharma to be sought; thus it is named the non-seeking samādhi.
Abiding in this samādhi, the mind and mental factors do not function; thus it is named the mindless samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of the Pure Lamp?
Abiding in this samādhi, one acts as a light among all samādhis like a lamp; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Pure Lamp.
What is called the "Infinite Radiance Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one provides infinite radiance for all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Infinite Radiance Samādhi.
What is called the samādhi capable of producing illumination?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is immediately able to produce illumination for all samādhis; this is named the samādhi capable of producing illumination.
What is called the Samādhi of Universal Illumination?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to illuminate all gates of samādhi; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Universal Illumination.
What is called the Samādhi of Firmly Purifying All Samādhis?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to firmly purify the characteristics of all samādhis; therefore, it is called the "Samādhi that Firmly Purifies All Samādhis.
What is called the "Stainless Radiance Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to remove the defilements of all samādhis and can also illuminate all samādhis; this is called the stainless light samādhi (*vimalaprabhā-samādhi*).
What is called the joyous samādhi (*prāmodya-samādhi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to receive the joy of all samādhis; this is called the *pramuditā* (Joyful) Samādhi.
What is called the *vidyut-pradīpa* (Lightning-flash) Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one illuminates all samādhis like a flash of lightning; this is called the *vidyut-pradīpa* Samādhi.
What is called the "Inexhaustible Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the exhaustion of any samādhis; this is called the Inexhaustible Samādhi.
What is called the "Majestic Virtue Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one’s majestic power illuminates all other samādhis; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Majestic Power (*vīryaprabhāsa*).
What is called the Samādhi of Freedom from Exhaustion?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the exhaustion of any samādhis; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Freedom from Exhaustion (*akṣaya-vimukti*).
What is called the "immovable samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one causes all samādhis to be immovable and free from frivolous distraction; this is called the immovable samādhi.
What is called the "non-retrogressive samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able not to see the regression of any samādhis; this is called the "Non-regressing Samādhi" (Avinivartanīya-samādhi).
What is called the "Sun-lamp Samādhi" (Sūryapradīpa-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one emits light that illuminates all gates of samādhi; this is called the "Sun-lamp Samādhi."
What is called the Moon-Purity Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to remove the darkness of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Moon-Purity Samādhi.
What is called the Pure-Luminosity Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the four kinds of unobscured knowledge regarding all samādhis; this is called the *viśuddhaprabhāsa* (Pure Radiance) samādhi.
What is called the *prabhākara* (Able to Produce Radiance) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to produce illumination regarding all doors of samādhi; this is called the "Able-to-Produce-Illumination" (Prabhākara) samādhi.
What is called the "Performing-Activity" (Kāraka) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one enables each of the various samādhis to perform their respective functions; this is called the samādhi of performing actions (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-samādhi).
What is called the samādhi of knowing characteristics (lakṣaṇajñāna-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one perceives the characteristics of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of knowing characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñāna-samādhi*).
What is called the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to penetrate through all dharmas, yet does not even perceive that penetration; this is called the diamond-like samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of the Abiding Mind?
Abiding in this samādhi, the mind is unmoving, non-turning, and unafflicted; furthermore, one does not even conceive the thought that "this is the mind. This is named the Samādhi of the Abiding Mind.
What is called the Samādhi of Universal Radiance?
Abiding in this samādhi, one universally perceives the radiance of all samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of Universal Radiance.
What is called the Samādhi of Stable Establishment?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is firmly established and immovable among all samādhis; this is called the "Firmly Established" (Pratiṣṭhita) samādhi.
What is called the "Jewel Heap" (Ratnakoṭi) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one perceives all samādhis universally as if seeing a heap of jewels; this is called the Jewel Heap samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to seal all samādhis; because it seals with the seal of non-sealing, it is called the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma.
What is called the samādhi of the equality of dharmas?
Abiding in this samādhi, one contemplates that all dharmas are equal and that there are no dharmas that are not equal; this is called the samādhi of the equality of dharmas.
What is called the samādhi of severing joy?
Abiding in this samādhi, one cuts off all joy within all dharmas; this is called the "samādhi of cutting off joy.
What is called the "samādhi of reaching the summit of dharmas"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one extinguishes the darkness of all dharmas and also stands above all other samādhis; this is called the "samādhi of reaching the summit of dharmas."
What is called the samādhi capable of dispersing?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to break apart and disperse all phenomena; therefore, it is named the samādhi capable of dispersing.
What is called the samādhi of discerning the phrases of all phenomena?
Abiding in this samādhi, one discerns the various phrases of all dharmas within all samādhis; this is called the "Samādhi of Discerning the Phrases of All Dharmas.
What is the "Samādhi of the Equal Characteristics of Names"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the equality of the names of all samādhis; this is the samādhi of the equality of names and signs.
What is called the "samādhi of detachment from letters"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive even a single letter within all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of detachment from letters.
What is called the samādhi of severing conditions?
Abiding in this samādhi, one severs the conditions of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of severing conditions.
What is called the indestructible samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the transformation of any phenomena; this is called the "indestructible samādhi" (akṣaya-samādhi).
What is called the "samādhi of the signless nature" (animitta-lakṣaṇa-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not see the various characteristics of any phenomena; this is called the "samādhi of the signless nature."
What is called the "Samādhi of Moving Without Abode"?
Dwelling in this samādhi, one does not perceive the abodes of any samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of Moving Without Abode.
What is called the "Samādhi of Departing from Obscurity"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is free from the subtle darkness of all samādhis; this is called the "samādhi free from obscurity.
What is called the "samādhi of no departure"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristic of departure in any samādhi; this is called the "samādhi of no departure."
What is called the samādhi of non-alteration?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the marks of alteration in any samādhis; this is called the samādhi of non-alteration.
What is called the samādhi of transcending conditions?
Abiding in this samādhi, one transcends all conditions and objects of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of transcending conditions.
What is called the samādhi of gathering all merits?
Abiding in this samādhi, one gathers the merits of all samādhis; this is called the "samādhi that gathers all merits.
What is called the "samādhi of abiding in mindlessness"?
Abiding in this samādhi, the mind does not enter into any other samādhis; this is called the "samādhi of abiding in mindlessness."
What is called the Samādhi of Pure and Wondrous Flowers?
Abiding in this samādhi causes all samādhis to become pure and wondrous like flowers; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Pure and Wondrous Flowers.
What is called the *bodhyaṅga* (awakening-factor) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the seven factors of awakening among all samādhis; this is called the *bodhyaṅga* samādhi.
What is called the *apramāṇapratibhāna* (immeasurable eloquence) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains immeasurable eloquence regarding all phenomena; this is called the "Immeasurable Eloquence Samādhi.
What is called the "Unequaled Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the mark of "unequaled equality" among all samādhis; this is called the "Unequaled Equality Samādhi.
What is called the "Samādhi that Transcends All Dharmas"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one transcends all three realms; this is called the samādhi of transcending all dharmas (*sarvadharma-samatikrānta*).
What is called the samādhi of discerning all dharmas (*sarvadharma-vibhakti*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one discerns and perceives all samādhis and all dharmas; this is called the samādhi of discerning all dharmas.
What is called the Samādhi of Dispelling Doubt?
Abiding in this samādhi, one dispels all doubts regarding phenomena; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Dispelling Doubt.
What is called the Samādhi of Non-Abiding?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive a dwelling place for any phenomena; this is called the "samādhi of non-dwelling.
What is called the "samādhi of single adornment"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one ultimately does not perceive the dual characteristics of any phenomena; this is called the "samādhi of single adornment."
What is called the samādhi of the arising of formations?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the arising of any formations; this is called the samādhi of the arising of formations.
What is called the samādhi of a single practice?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the near shore or the far shore of any samādhis; this is called the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.
What is called the *anekavyūha-samādhi*?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any single characteristic among all samādhis; this is called the *anekatīrthika-samādhi*.
What is called the *sucarita-samādhi*?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any dual characteristics among all samādhis; this is called the *sucarita-samādhi*.
What is called the samādhi of penetrating the bottom of all existence?

Abiding in this samādhi, one enters into all existence and all samādhis; wisdom penetrates them, yet there is nothing to be penetrated. This is called the samādhi of penetrating the bottom of all existence.
What is called the samādhi of entering names and words?
Abiding in this samādhi, one enters the names and words of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of entering names and words.
What is called the samādhi of being free from sounds, syllables, and speech?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the sounds, syllables, or speech of any samādhis; this is called the samādhi of being free from sounds, syllables, and speech.
What is called the "Blazing Torch Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, its majestic power illuminates like a torch; therefore, it is named the Blazing Torch Samādhi.
What is called the "Pure Characteristic Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one purifies the characteristics of all samādhis; this is called the "Purifying Characteristics Samādhi" (śubhalakṣaṇa-samādhi).
What is called the "Destroying Characteristics Samādhi" (lakṣaṇavibheda-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristics of any samādhis; this is called the "Destroying Characteristics Samādhi."
What is called the Samādhi of the Perfect Endowment of All Aspects?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is fully endowed with all varieties of samādhis; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Perfect Endowment of All Aspects.
What is called the samādhi of not delighting in suffering or pleasure?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the suffering or pleasure of any samādhis; this is called the samādhi of not delighting in suffering or pleasure.
What is called the "Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Mark"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the exhaustion of any samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Mark.
What is called the "Tathā-dhāraṇī Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to uphold all samādhis; this is called the *tathā-dhāraṇī* samādhi.
What is called the samādhi that gathers all marks of the heterodox and the orthodox?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the marks of either the heterodox or the orthodox among all samādhis; this is called the "samādhi that subsumes all heterodox and orthodox marks.
What is called the "samādhi that extinguishes hatred and love"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive hatred or affection toward any samādhis; this is called the "extinguishing hatred and affection" (dveṣānunaya-nirodha) samādhi.
What is called the "contrary and conforming" (pratiloma-anuloma) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the contrariety or conformity of any dharmas or any samādhis; this is called the "contrary and conforming" samādhi.
What is called the "Pure Light Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the defilements of the light of any samādhis; this is called the Pure Light Samādhi.
What is called the "Firm Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any other samādhis as being unstable; this is called the "Firm Samādhi" (Dṛḍha-samādhi).
What is called the "Pure Light of the Full Moon Samādhi" (Pūrṇacandra-vimala-prabhā-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, all samādhis are fulfilled like the moon on the fifteenth day; this is called the Samādhi of Full Moon Pure Radiance.
What is called the Samādhi of Great Adornment?
Abiding in this samādhi, one accomplishes all samādhis through great adornment; this is called the Great Adornment Samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi Able to Illuminate All Worlds?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to illuminate all samādhis and all dharmas; therefore, it is called the "Samādhi that Illuminates All Worlds.
What is called the "Samādhi Equal to Samādhis"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristics of concentration or distraction within any samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of Equality of Samādhis.
What is called the Samādhi that Encompasses All Contested and Uncontested States?

Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to cause all samādhis to be without discrimination regarding whether they are contentious or non-contentious; this is called the "samādhi that encompasses all contentious and non-contentious states."
What is called the samādhi of not delighting in any dwelling place?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any basis for the various samādhis; this is called the samādhi of not delighting in any dwelling place.
What is called the samādhi of abiding in suchness?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not transcend the suchness-characteristic (tathatā-lakṣaṇa) of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of abiding in suchness.
What is called the samādhi of destroying the decay of the body?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the marks of the body; this is called the "samādhi that destroys the decay of the body.
What is called the "samādhi that destroys speech so that it is like space"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not see the verbal activity of any samādhis as being like space; this is called the "samādhi that destroys speech so that it is like space."
What is called the "Samādhi of Non-attachment and Non-staining like Space"?

Abiding in this samādhi, one perceives all phenomena as being unobstructed like space, and yet one is not stained by this samādhi either; this is called the "Samādhi of Non-attachment and Non-staining like Space."
"Subhūti! This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Chapter 19:
The Chapter on the Vast Vehicle (*Mahāyāna-parivarta*). In the Danben (Dunhuang manuscript), this is titled "The Chapter on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four? Subhūti!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body, yet has no perception of a body, because it cannot be apprehended;
he contemplates the body within the external body and within both the internal and external bodies, yet has no perception of a body, because it cannot be apprehended.
With diligent effort and single-mindedness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow.

One contemplates internal feelings, internal mind, and internal phenomena; external feelings, external mind, and external phenomena; and both internal and external feelings, internal and external mind, and internal and external phenomena. Thus one observes according to the Dharma, yet there is no perception of a dharma, because nothing can be apprehended.
With diligent effort and single-mindedness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow. Subhūti,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the contemplation of the body within the internal body?

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when walking, knows that he is walking; when standing, knows that he is standing; when sitting, knows that he is sitting; and when lying down, knows that he is lying down—thus does he know the movements of his body.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus gazes upon his internal body with single-mindedness—whether bending or stretching, looking down or up, wearing the saṃghāṭī robe, holding the robes and bowl, eating, drinking, lying down, resting, sitting, standing, waking, sleeping, speaking, remaining silent, or entering and emerging from meditative concentration—he is likewise always single-minded.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates the body within the internal body, because it is ungraspable.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body with single-minded mindfulness, he knows the inhalation when inhaling and the exhalation when exhaling; he knows the long inhalation when inhaling for a long duration and the long exhalation when exhaling for a long duration; he knows the short inhalation when inhaling for a short duration and the short exhalation when exhaling for a short duration.
For example, just as a turner or a turner’s apprentice knows when the cord is long that it is long, and knows when the cord is short that it is short;

so too, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with single-minded mindfulness, knows when inhaling that he is inhaling, and knows when exhaling that he is exhaling. When the inhalation is long, he knows the inhalation is long; when the exhalation is long, he knows the exhalation is long; when the inhalation is short, he knows the inhalation is short; and when the exhalation is short, he knows the exhalation is short.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly covetousness and grief, because [the body] is ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the four great elements of the body and forms this thought:

'Within the body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element, just as a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice slaughters an ox with a knife and divides it into four parts.'"
"Having divided [the body] into four parts, whether standing or sitting, one contemplates these four parts.

In the same way, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they contemplate the various elements of the body—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
Thus it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body, because [the body] is unapprehendable. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the internal body from the feet to the crown of the head, encompassed by a thin skin, filled within with various kinds of impurities.

He forms this thought: "Within the body there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, muscle, sinew, bone, and marrow; spleen, kidneys, heart, and gallbladder; liver, lungs, small intestine, large intestine, stomach, and bladder; feces, urine, filth, sweat, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, spittle, pus, and blood; as well as yellow phlegm, white phlegm, watery phlegm, fat, grease, brain, and membranes."

"It is, for example, like a farmer’s granary filled to the brim with various grains—rice, hemp, millet, sorghum, beans, and wheat, each kept in separate compartments. So too, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, this body is surrounded by a thin skin, yet its interior is filled with all manner of impurities: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, and even the brain and membranes."
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body with diligence, vigor, and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow because [the self] is unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a discarded human corpse—one day, two days, or up to five days after death—swollen, livid, and oozing with pus, he reflects:
'My own body is likewise of such a nature and such a character; it has not escaped this condition.'"
"In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the body, with diligent effort and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow because they are unobtainable."

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a discarded human corpse that has been dead for six or seven days, being torn apart and eaten by various birds and beasts such as crows, ravens, vultures, eagles, jackals, wolves, foxes, and dogs, he reflects:
"My own body is of such a nature and such a character; it has not escaped this condition."
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the body, with diligent vigor and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow because they are unobtainable."
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a discarded human corpse that has been eaten by various birds and beasts until it is impure, putrid, and foul-smelling, he reflects:
"My own body has such characteristics and such a nature; it has not yet escaped this condition."
"…and so on, until he removes worldly greed and sorrow. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a discarded human corpse, its skeleton smeared with blood and flesh, with tendons and bones still connected, he reflects to himself:"
"My body has such characteristics and such qualities; it is not yet liberated from these dharmas.
Thus, he eliminates worldly greed and sorrow. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a discarded human corpse whose bones and flesh have already separated but whose tendons and sinews remain connected, he reflects:
"My body is of such a nature and such a character; it has not yet escaped this condition."
"…up to the point where he removes worldly greed and sorrow. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a discarded human corpse whose skeletal remains are already scattered upon the ground, he reflects to himself:"
"My body has such characteristics and such qualities; it is not yet free from these qualities.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body, and so on, until he removes worldly greed and sorrow.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a discarded dead human body with its bones scattered upon the ground—the foot-bones in one place, the shin-bones, thigh-bones, hip-bones, rib-bones, vertebrae, hand-bones, neck-bones, and skull each in a different place—he reflects:
"My own body has such characteristics and such a nature; it has not yet escaped this condition."
"In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body, even unto the removal of worldly greed and sorrow. Furthermore, Subhūti,"
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees the bones of a discarded dead person lying on the ground for many years, bleached white like a conch shell by the wind and sun, he reflects:
"My own body has such characteristics and such a nature; it has not yet escaped this condition."
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body, up until the removal of worldly greed and sorrow, because they are unapprehendable."

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the bones of a discarded dead person lying on the ground for many years, their color like that of a pigeon, decayed and rotted away, fused together with the earth, he reflects:
"My own body has such characteristics and such a nature; it has not escaped this condition."

"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body within the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly covetousness and grief, because [the body] is unapprehendable."

The same applies to the external body and the internal-external body; the application of mindfulness to feelings, the application of mindfulness to the mind, and the application of mindfulness to phenomena should also be explained in detail in this way, Subhūti.
This is called the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is what is known as the four right efforts."
What are the four? Subhūti,

for the sake of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, and takes hold of the mind to practice the path;
For the sake of abandoning unwholesome and unvirtuous states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies energy, and disciplines the mind to practice the path;
for the sake of giving rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies energy, and disciplines the mind to practice the path;

and for the sake of maintaining, preventing the loss of, cultivating to fulfillment, and increasing wholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies energy, and disciplines the mind to practice the path.
Because they cannot be apprehended, Subhūti,
this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
What are the four?

The base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment; the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment; the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of vigor accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment; and the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by the formative forces of abandonment—these are cultivated because they are non-apprehendable.
Subhūti! This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
What are these five?

They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. These are termed the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva because they are non-apprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the five powers.
What are these five?

The power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom—these are called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because they are ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
What are the seven?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness—which relies on detachment, relies on dispassion, and leads toward nirvāṇa—and likewise the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, diligence, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—which rely on detachment, rely on dispassion, and lead toward nirvāṇa—by way of non-apprehensibility, this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is what is called the eightfold noble path.
What are the eight? "

Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these are called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because they are non-apprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the three samādhis.
What are the three?
The samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Emptiness-samādhi refers to the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness.
Signlessness refers to the destruction of the characteristics of all phenomena, such that one neither recollects nor attends to them; this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness.
"Non-action" (anabhisaṃskāra) means not aspiring to act among all phenomena; this is called the gate of liberation of non-action.
This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because it is ungraspable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of phenomena, inferential knowledge, worldly knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of things as they truly are."
What is called the knowledge of suffering?
To know that suffering does not arise is called the knowledge of suffering.
What is called the knowledge of the origin?
Knowing that the origin [of suffering] should be abandoned is called the knowledge of the origin.
What is called the knowledge of cessation?
Knowing the cessation of suffering is called the knowledge of cessation.
What is called the knowledge of the path?
Knowing the eight factors of the noble path is called the knowledge of the path.
What is called the knowledge of exhaustion?
To know that all lust, hatred, and delusion are exhausted is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
What is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?
To know that there is no further arising within any state of existence is called the knowledge of non-arising.
What is called "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna)?
To know the fundamental nature of the five aggregates is called knowledge of phenomena.
What is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna)?
To know that the eye is impermanent, up to and including that the feeling born of the causal condition of mind-contact is impermanent, is called inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
What is called worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*)?
To know the names of causes and conditions is called worldly knowledge.
What is called the knowledge of others' minds?
To know the minds of other sentient beings is called the knowledge of others' minds.
What is called the knowledge of things as they truly are?
The all-encompassing wisdom of all Buddhas is called "knowledge as it truly is.
Subhūti, this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because it is non-apprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the three faculties:
the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,' the faculty of knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known."
What is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?

It refers to the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom belonging to those in training who have not yet attained the fruit; these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is called the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*)?
The faculties ranging from faith to wisdom attained by those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have realized the fruits [of the path]—this is called the faculty of knowing.
What is called the faculty of one who has known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)?
The faculties of all those beyond training—whether Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, or Buddhas—from the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom, are called the faculties of the wise.
Subhūti! This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because it is non-apprehendable. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva consists of what are called the three samādhis.
What are the three?
They are the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, the samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra, and the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is called the samādhi with directed thought and sustained evaluation?

Detached from all desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, one enters the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by directed thought and sustained evaluation, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion; this is called the samādhi with directed thought and sustained evaluation.
What is called the samādhi without vitarka and with vicāra?
That which lies between the first and second dhyānas is called the samādhi without vitarka and with vicāra.
What is called the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra?
From the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the ten recollections.
What are these ten?

Mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of virtue, mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, mindfulness of the body, and mindfulness of death.
Subhūti! This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because it is non-apprehendable. Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva consists of what are known as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive concentrations.
Subhūti! This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because it is non-apprehendable. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to the ten powers of a Buddha.
What are these ten?
First, the Buddha knows, in accordance with reality, the characteristics of what is possible and what is impossible regarding all phenomena; this is the first power.

To know, as they truly are, the past, future, and present karmas and the various dharmas of experience of other sentient beings; to know the locus where karma is created, to know its causes and conditions, and to know its retribution—this is the second power.
To know, as they truly are, the characteristics of the distinctions between the defilement and purification of the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and concentrations is the third power.
To know, as they truly are, the superior and inferior characteristics of the faculties of other sentient beings is the fourth power.
To know, as they truly are, the various inclinations and understandings of other sentient beings is the fifth power.
To know, as they truly are, the various and innumerable natures of the world is the sixth power.
To know, as it truly is, the path leading to all destinations is the seventh power.

To know various past lives together with their characteristics and causal conditions—from one birth, two births, up to hundreds of thousands of kalpas—knowing that at the end of such a kalpa I was born among those sentient beings, having such a clan, such a name, such food and drink, such suffering and pleasure, and such a length of life.
Dying there, one is born here; dying here, one is born again there.
Birth in this world—whether in terms of name and clan, food and drink, pleasure and pain, or the length of one's lifespan—is likewise [to be known]. This is the eighth power.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of all other beings, the Buddha sees sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—whether they are handsome or ugly, great or small, whether they fall into evil realms or good realms—and how they receive retribution according to the causes and conditions of their karma. He sees those sentient beings who have accomplished evil physical karma, accomplished evil verbal karma, and accomplished evil mental karma; who have slandered and reviled the noble ones; and who, due to the causes and conditions of their karma of wrong views, at the dissolution of the body after death, enter the evil realms and are born in hell.

These sentient beings, having accomplished wholesome karma of body, accomplished wholesome karma of speech, and accomplished wholesome karma of mind, do not slander or revile the noble ones; by virtue of the causes and conditions of right view, at the time of death when the body perishes, they enter a good destination and are reborn in the heavens.
This is the ninth power.

Because the Buddha knows, as it truly is, that all taints (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, he possesses the liberation of mind through the absence of taints and the liberation of wisdom through the absence of taints. Within the present phenomena, he realizes for himself and enters into this state, namely: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; and from this world, there will be no further seeing of a future existence."
The ten powers, Subhūti!
This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because it is non-apprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of what are called the four fearlessnesses.
What are the four?
The Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"I am one who possesses all-encompassing right knowledge.
If there should be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, or any deva, māra, or brahmā, or indeed any other being, who should challenge this according to reality, saying:
"I do not know this Dharma," and so forth, nor do I perceive even the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and I dwell securely in the station of the Noble Lord; amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion’s roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
No śramaṇas, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings can truly turn it back;
this is the first fearlessness.
The Buddha made this truthful declaration:
"I have exhausted all outflows.
Should there be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, or any deva, māra, or Brahmā, or any other being, who might challenge this according to reality, saying:
"These outflows are not yet exhausted," and so on,
until he does not perceive even the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, I abide securely in the station of the Holy Lord, and amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion's roar and can turn the Brahma-wheel.
"None among the śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings can truly turn it back.
This is the second fearlessness."
The Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"I have taught the obstructing dharmas.
Should any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or any other being challenge this according to reality, saying:
"Receiving this Dharma does not obstruct the Path.

Even down to not perceiving the slightest sign of fear—for this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and I dwell securely in the station of the Noble Lord. Amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion’s roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
No śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, brahmās, or any other beings can truly turn it back.
This is the third fearlessness.
The Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"The noble path I have taught is able to transcend the world; by practicing it accordingly, one can bring an end to suffering.
Should there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, whether gods, Māras, Brahmas, or any other beings, who might truthfully challenge this by saying:
"Practicing this path cannot transcend the world, nor can it bring an end to suffering"—
even down to not perceiving the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and dwelling securely in the station of the Holy Lord, I roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
Neither any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, nor any other beings can truly overturn these four fearlessnesses.
Subhūti! This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because it is non-apprehendable. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva consists of what are called the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
What are the four? They are:

unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
Subhūti! This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because it is non-apprehendable. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva consists of what are called the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
What are these eighteen?
First, the Buddhas have no failure of body; second, no failure of speech; third, no failure of mindfulness.
4. No dissimilarity in physical marks; 5. No lack of concentration; 6. No lack of awareness when relinquishing the mind;
7. No decrease in aspiration; 8. No decrease in diligence; 9. No decrease in mindfulness; 10. No decrease in wisdom; 11.
No decrease in liberation; 12. No decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
13. His knowledge and vision do not diminish; 14. all his bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; 15.
all his verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; 16. all his mental actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; 17.
with wisdom he knows and sees the past without obstruction or hindrance. 18. Wisdom...
Wisdom knows and sees the future world without hindrance or obstruction; eighteen, wisdom knows and sees the present world without hindrance or obstruction. Subhūti!
This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, because it is ungraspable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to the equality of letters, the equality of speech, and the gateways of all syllables.
What are the gateways of the equality of syllables and the equality of speech?
The gateway of the syllable *A* is because all phenomena are originally unarisen.
The gateway of the syllable *Ra* is because all phenomena are free from defilement.
The syllable *pa* is a gateway because all phenomena are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The syllable *ca* is a gateway because all phenomena are ultimately unattainable, for all phenomena neither cease nor arise.
The letter-gateway *Na*: all phenomena are free from names, because their intrinsic nature and characteristics are neither gained nor lost.
The letter-gateway *La*: all phenomena transcend the world, and because the causes and conditions of craving and its branches are extinguished.
The gateway of the letter *ḍa*: because all phenomena arise from a wholesome mind, and because they possess the characteristic of giving.
The gateway of the letter *ba*: because all phenomena are free from the letter *ba*.
The gateway of the letter *ṭa*: because all phenomena are pure through the letter *ṭa*.
The gateway of the letter *ṣa*: because the nature of all phenomena is the purity of the six sovereign kings.
The gateway of the letter *ha*: because one enters into all phenomena where the path of speech is severed.
The gateway of the letter *ta*: because one enters into all phenomena as they are, being immovable.
The gateway of the syllable *ya* leads into all phenomena because they are non-arising in accordance with reality.
The gateway of the syllable *ṭha* leads into all phenomena because their subjugation is unattainable.
The gateway of the syllable *ka* leads into all phenomena because an agent is unattainable.
The gateway of the letter *sa*: one enters all phenomena because time is unobtainable, for all phenomena arise and transform through time.
The gateway of the letter *ma*: one enters all phenomena because the "mine" (*mamakāra*) is unobtainable.
The letter-gate *ga*: one enters all phenomena because a goer cannot be apprehended.
The letter-gate *tha*: one enters all phenomena because a locus cannot be apprehended.
The letter-gate *ja*: one enters all phenomena because arising cannot be apprehended.
The gateway of the syllable *ḍha*: one enters all phenomena because the syllable *ḍha* is unapprehendable.
The gateway of the syllable *ṭa*: one enters all phenomena because their nature is unapprehendable.
The gateway of the syllable *śa*: one enters all phenomena because their fixedness is unapprehendable.
The gateway of the syllable Kha: one enters all phenomena because emptiness is unapprehendable.
The gateway of the syllable Cha: one enters all phenomena because exhaustion is unapprehendable.
The gateway of the syllable Ta: one enters all phenomena because existence is unapprehendable.
The letter-gateway *ja*: entry into all dharmas because wisdom is unapprehendable.
The letter-gateway *ṭha*: entry into all dharmas because the letter *ṭha* is unapprehendable.
The letter-gateway *ba*: entry into all dharmas because destruction is unapprehendable.
The gateway of the letter *cha*: one enters all phenomena because desire is unattainable, and because the five aggregates are like a shadow and likewise unattainable.
The gateway of the letter *ma*: one enters all phenomena because the letter *ma* itself is unattainable.
The gateway of the syllable *hu*: one enters all phenomena because a "caller" (*hvan*) is unapprehendable.
The gateway of the syllable *ca*: one enters all phenomena because the syllable *ca* is unapprehendable.
The gateway of the syllable *ga*: one enters all phenomena because "thickness" (*gāu*) is unapprehendable.
The letter-da gate: because one enters all phenomena as being unobtainable in their locus.
The letter-na gate: because one enters all phenomena as neither coming nor going, neither standing nor sitting nor reclining.
The letter-gateway PHA: it enters all dharmas because they are everywhere unobtainable.
The letter-gateway GA: it enters all dharmas because their accumulation is unobtainable.
The letter-gateway CA: it enters all dharmas because the letter CA is unobtainable within them.
The letter *cha* is a gateway, for one enters all phenomena through the non-apprehensibility of their activity.
The letter *ṭha* is a gateway, for one enters all phenomena through the non-apprehensibility of their hunchbackedness (*vaṅka*).
The letter *ṭa* is a gateway, for one enters all phenomena at the limit of their boundary; they neither end nor arise, and beyond *ṭa*, there is no word to be spoken.
Why is this? Because there are no further characters.
All characters are unimpeded; names also cease to exist. They cannot be spoken, they cannot be shown, they cannot be seen, and they cannot be written.
Subhūti! You should know that all dharmas are like space. Subhūti!
This is called the gateway of dhāraṇīs, namely the meaning of the syllable *a*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva seals all these gateways of syllables with the seal of the syllable *a*, whether by hearing, receiving, reciting, reading, upholding, or explaining them to others, they should know that by doing so they will obtain twenty merits.

What are these twenty? They are: attaining powerful mindfulness and recollection; attaining a sense of shame and dread of blame; attaining a firm and resolute mind; attaining the essential purport of the sūtras;
attaining wisdom; attaining unimpeded eloquence; easily attaining all other *dhāraṇī* gates; and attaining non-... [text continues]

With a mind free from doubt and regret, one hears good things without joy and hears evil things without anger; one attains a state of mind that dwells neither high nor low, being without increase or decrease;
one attains skillful knowledge of the languages of sentient beings;
and one attains skillful discernment of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four conditions, and the four noble truths.

He attained skillful discernment of the sharpness and dullness of the faculties of sentient beings; he attained skillful knowledge of the minds of others; he attained skillful discernment of days, months, years, and seasons;
he attained skillful discernment of the supernormal power of the divine ear; he attained skillful discernment of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives;
he attained skillful discernment of the supernormal power of knowing death and rebirth; and he attained the ability to skillfully explain what is possible and what is impossible.
They skillfully understand the bodily postures of coming and going, sitting and rising, and so forth. Subhūti!
These gateways of dhāraṇī, such as the gateway of the letter A and others, are called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Five;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty: On Setting Out The Buddha addressed Subhūti: “You asked:”
"What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s setting out in the Great Vehicle?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing the six pāramitās, proceeds from one stage to the next stage, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s setting out in the Great Vehicle."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva proceed from one stage to the next?”
The Buddha said:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all dharmas have no characteristic of coming or going; furthermore, there is no dharma that comes or goes, arrives or does not arrive, because the characteristics of all dharmas are non-extinguished.”
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not recollect or contemplate the various stages (*bhūmi*), yet cultivates the karmic activities for purifying those stages, nor does he perceive the stages themselves.
What are the karmic activities for purifying the stages of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the first stage, they practice ten matters:
first, their profound resolve is firm because they employ the principle of non-apprehension;
second, they maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings because sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Third, practicing generosity, because neither the giver nor the recipient can be apprehended.
Fourth, associating with virtuous friends, while remaining free from self-exaltation.
Fifth, seeking the Dharma, because all dharmas are unattainable.
Sixth, constantly leaving the household life, because the household is unattainable.
Seventh, loving and delighting in the Buddha’s body, because the primary and secondary marks are unattainable.
Eighth, the exposition of the Dharma teachings, because the differentiation of all phenomena is unattainable.
Ninth, the destruction of pride, because the wisdom arising from the Dharma is unattainable.
Tenth is truthful speech, because all words are unattainable.
Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this first stage, they cultivate and purify these ten matters as the karmic activities for purifying the stage.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the second stage, they constantly keep eight dharmas in mind.
What are these eight?
First, purity of precepts;
second, knowing gratitude and repaying kindness;
third, abiding in the power of patience.
Fourth, experiencing joy;
fifth, not abandoning any sentient beings;
sixth, entering the mind of great compassion.
Seventh, they have faith in their teacher and respectfully receive instruction from them.
Eighth, they diligently seek all the pāramitās. Subhūti!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the second stage and fulfilling eight dharmas. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the third stage practices five dharmas."
What are the five?
First, to have great learning without ever being satisfied.
Second, to give the gift of the Dharma purely, and likewise not to exalt oneself.
Third, purifying buddha-fields without becoming self-exalting.
Fourth, undergoing immeasurable hardships and toil in the world without becoming weary of them.
Fifth, abiding in a state of shame and remorse.
Subhūti! These are called the five dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the third bhūmi should fulfill. Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the fourth stage should practice and not abandon ten dharmas.
What are these ten?
First, not abandoning the dwelling place of an araṇya.
Second, having few desires;
third, being content;
fourth, not abandoning the merits of the dhūta practices.
Fifth, not forsaking the precepts;
sixth, loathing all sensual desires;
seventh, possessing a mind weary of the world and conforming to the mind of nirvana.
Eighth, relinquishing all that one possesses.
Ninth, the mind does not sink into despondency.
Tenth, not begrudging any material thing.
Subhūti! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the fourth stage who does not abandon these ten dharmas. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the fifth stage, they remain far removed from twelve things.
What are these twelve?
First, they remain far removed from associating with laypeople.
Second, staying far away from bhikṣuṇīs;
third, staying far away from stinginess regarding other families;
fourth, staying far away from useless talk.
Fifth, to remain far removed from ill will;
sixth, to remain far removed from self-conceit;
seventh, to remain far removed from disparaging others.
Eighth, to stay far removed from the ten unwholesome paths of action.
Ninth, to stay far removed from great arrogance.
Tenth, to stay far removed from self-willedness.
Eleventh, they are far removed from perversions.
Twelfth, they are far removed from lust, anger, and delusion. Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the fifth stage remains far removed from twelve matters. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the sixth stage should fulfill six dharmas."
What are these six?
They are the so-called six pāramitās.
Furthermore, there are six things that one should not do.
What are the six?
First, not to give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Second, not to give rise to a mind of anxiety when practicing giving.
Third, when seeing those who seek something, one’s mind does not sink.
Fourth, one gives away all that one possesses.
Fifth, after having given, one’s mind feels no regret.
Sixth, not doubting the profound Dharma.
Subhūti, these are called the six dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the sixth stage should fulfill and the six dharmas from which they should remain far removed.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the seventh stage should distance himself from twenty things that he ought not to be attached to.
What are these twenty?
First, non-attachment to a self;
second, non-attachment to sentient beings;
third, non-attachment to a life-span.
Fourth, not being attached to the categories of beings, up to and including the knower and the seer.
Fifth, not being attached to the view of annihilationism.
Sixth, not being attached to the view of eternalism.
Seventh, one should not form signs.
Eighth, one should not form views regarding causes.
Ninth, one should not be attached to name-and-form.
Tenth, non-attachment to the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Eleventh, non-attachment to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Twelfth, non-attachment to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Thirteenth, not being attached to the three realms.
Fourteenth, not forming views of attachment.
Nineteenth, not being attached to views that rely upon the Sangha.
Twentieth, not being attached to views based on the precepts.
These are the twenty things to which one should not be attached.
Furthermore, there are twenty other things that should be fully perfected.
What are the twenty?
First, the fulfillment of emptiness.
Second, the realization of signlessness.
Third, knowing the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Fourth, the threefold purity.
Fifth, being fully endowed with the wisdom of compassion toward all sentient beings.
Sixth, not to dwell upon any sentient beings.
Seventh, to contemplate all dharmas as equal, yet without attachment even to this.
Eighth, to know the true mark of all dharmas, yet not to dwell upon this matter either.
Ninth, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Tenth, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpatti-jñāna*).
Eleventh, the teaching that all phenomena have a single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*).
Twelfth, the destruction of the marks of conceptual discrimination;
thirteenth, the transformation of mental recollection and ideation;
fourteenth, the transformation of views.
Fifteenth, the transformation of afflictions;
sixteenth, the stage of the equality of concentration and wisdom;
seventeenth, the disciplining of the mind.
Eighteenth, the tranquility of the mind.
Nineteenth, unimpeded wisdom.
Twentieth, non-attachment to craving.
Subhūti! These are called the twenty dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the seventh stage should fulfill. Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the eighth stage should be fully endowed with five dharmas.
What are these five? They are:
entering in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
They sport with the various supernormal powers and behold the buddha-fields;
according to the buddha-fields they have seen, they themselves adorn their own lands.
One contemplates the Buddha’s body as it truly is and thus adorns the Buddha’s body oneself.
These five dharmas are fully perfected. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the eighth stage, they further fulfill five dharmas.
What are these five? They are:
knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings.
They purify buddha-fields,
enter the illusion-like samādhi,
and constantly abide in samādhi.
Subhūti, taking on a body in accordance with the roots of goodness appropriate for sentient beings—
this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the eighth stage fulfills five dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the ninth stage should fulfill twelve dharmas.
What are these twelve?
He receives his portion of those to be delivered throughout boundless worlds.
The Bodhisattva attains that which he has vowed;
he understands the languages of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, and expounds the Dharma for them.
Accomplishment in the womb,
accomplishment of family,
and accomplishment of birth.
Accomplishment of lineage,
accomplishment of retinue,
and accomplishment of birth.
The perfection of renunciation;
the perfection of adorning the Bodhi tree;
and the complete fulfillment and sufficiency of all virtuous merits.
Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva who, dwelling in the ninth stage, should fulfill twelve dharmas. Subhūti!
"A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage should be known as being like a Buddha.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s cultivation of the ground through the profound mind?
The Buddha said:

"The bodhisattva-mahāsattva gathers all roots of goodness in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta); this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s cultivation of the ground through the profound mind."
“How does a bodhisattva maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings?
The Buddha said:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā), gives rise to the four immeasurable minds—namely, loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā)—this is called maintaining an impartial mind toward all sentient beings.”
“How does a bodhisattva cultivate the practice of giving?
The Buddha said,
“When a bodhisattva bestows gifts upon all sentient beings without making any distinctions, this is called cultivating the practice of giving.”
“How does a bodhisattva associate with spiritual friends?
The Buddha said:
“One who can teach others to enter into and abide within sarvajñā.”
"To thus approach, consult, revere, and make offerings to such spiritual friends is called 'approaching spiritual friends.
What is a bodhisattva’s seeking of the Dharma?"
The Buddha said:
“When a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā), and does not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, this is called seeking the Dharma.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s practice of the stage of cultivation consisting in constant renunciation?
The Buddha said:

“The bodhisattva, in life after life, renounces the world with an undistracted mind, renouncing within the Buddha-dharma without anyone being able to create obstacles; this is called the practice of the stage of cultivation consisting in constant renunciation.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s practice of purifying the ground through delighting in the Buddha’s body?
The Buddha said:

“If a bodhisattva, upon seeing the marks of the Buddha’s body, never ceases to mindfully recollect the Buddha until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is called the practice of purifying the ground through delighting in the Buddha’s body.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s practice of purifying the stages by expounding the teachings?
The Buddha said:

“Whether the Buddha is present or has passed into parinirvāṇa, the bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings—good in the beginning, middle, and end; excellent in meaning and phrasing; pure, complete, and perfect. That is to say, from the sūtras up to the upadeśas. This is called the practice of purifying the stages by expounding the teachings.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s practice for purifying the ground by destroying arrogance?
The Buddha said:
“Because the bodhisattva destroys this arrogance, he is never born into a lowly family; this is called the practice for purifying the ground by destroying arrogance.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s practice of truthful speech as a purifying activity for the stages?
The Buddha said:
“When a bodhisattva acts in accordance with what they have spoken, this is called the practice of truthful speech as a purifying activity for the stages.”
"These are the ten matters for cultivating the ground that constitute the practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva while dwelling in the first stage.
"What is the purity of a bodhisattva’s precepts?

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor any thoughts of breaking the precepts or obstructing the dharmas of the Buddha-way, this is called the purity of precepts."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva knowing gratitude and repaying kindness?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing the bodhisattva path, does not forget even a small kindness, let alone a great one, this is called knowing gratitude and repaying kindness."
“How does a bodhisattva abide in the power of patience?
“If a bodhisattva is without anger and without malice toward all sentient beings, this is called abiding in the power of patience.”
“How does a bodhisattva experience joy?
“It is said that taking the maturation of sentient beings as one’s joy is what is called experiencing joy.
“How does a bodhisattva not abandon any sentient being?”
“If a bodhisattva maintains the thought of wishing to rescue all sentient beings, this is called not abandoning any sentient being.
How does a bodhisattva enter into the mind of great compassion?”
“If a bodhisattva reflects thus:

‘For the sake of each and every sentient being, I shall undergo arduous suffering within the hells for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River, until that person attains the Buddha-way and enters nirvana.’”
"This is what is called enduring suffering for the sake of all sentient beings in the ten directions; this is called entering the mind of great compassion.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s faith in the teacher, and their respectful inquiry and reception of instruction?"
“If a bodhisattva regards all teachers as the World-Honored One, this is called having faith in the teacher and respectfully receiving their instruction.
How does a bodhisattva diligently seek the various pāramitās?”
“If a bodhisattva single-mindedly seeks the perfections without engaging in other matters, this is called diligently seeking the perfections.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the second stage fulfills eight dharmas.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s insatiability in extensive learning?

It means that one desires to hear and retain all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas—whether those spoken by the Buddhas in this world-system or in the world-systems of the ten directions. This is called being insatiable in extensive learning.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s pure gift of Dharma?
To give the gift of Dharma even without seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, let alone any other matter—this is called the gift of Dharma that seeks neither fame nor profit.”
“How does a bodhisattva purify a buddha-field?
“By dedicating all roots of goodness toward the purification of a buddha-field; this is called purifying a buddha-field.”
“How does a bodhisattva undergo immeasurable worldly toil and suffering without becoming weary?
