Because they are fully endowed with all roots of goodness, they are able to bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn the buddha-fields, even until they are fully possessed of sarvajñā; never tiring or wearying, this is called undergoing immeasurable toil and suffering without becoming weary.”
“How does a bodhisattva abide in a state of shame and modesty?
“To feel shame regarding the mentalities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—this is called abiding in a state of shame and modesty.”
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the third stage, fulfills five dharmas.
"How does a bodhisattva not abandon a forest hermitage?"
"To be able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called not abandoning the forest hermitage.
What is the bodhisattva’s fewness of desires?"
“Even regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one does not desire it, let alone other desires; this is called having few desires (*alpecchatā*).
What is the bodhisattva’s contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*)?”
"To attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is called 'contentment.
How does a bodhisattva not abandon the merit of the dhūta practices?
To contemplate the patience regarding all profound dharmas is called 'not abandoning the merit of the dhūta practices.'"
“How does a bodhisattva not abandon the precepts?
“Not grasping at the characteristics of the precepts is called not abandoning the precepts.
“How does a bodhisattva loathe all desires?”
“Because the mind of desire does not arise, this is called loathing all desires.
“What is the bodhisattva’s mind of world-weariness and the mind that accords with nirvāṇa?”
“Because one knows that all phenomena are uncreated, this is called the mind of world-weariness and the mind that accords with nirvāṇa.
How does a bodhisattva relinquish all that they possess?”
“Because one does not begrudge any phenomena, whether internal or external, this is called relinquishing all that one possesses.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s mind not sinking?
“Because the mind does not give rise to the two types of spheres of consciousness, this is called the mind not sinking.”
"What is meant by a bodhisattva not begrudging any object?
Not being attached to or dwelling upon any object—this is called not begrudging any object."
"These are the ten dharmas that a bodhisattva does not abandon while in the fourth stage.
"How does a bodhisattva distance himself from intimacy with laypeople?

"A bodhisattva is born into the life of a renunciant; traveling from one buddha-field to another, he always leaves the household life, shaves his head, and wears dyed robes. This is called distancing oneself from intimacy with laypeople."
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from bhikṣuṇīs?
“He does not dwell together with bhikṣuṇīs; he does not even give rise to a thought toward them for as long as a finger-snap. This is called remaining far removed from bhikṣuṇīs.”
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from stinginess regarding the households of others?
“The bodhisattva reflects thus:
‘I should bring peace and happiness to sentient beings; since these others now assist me in bringing peace and happiness, why should I give rise to stinginess?’”
"This is called being far removed from stinginess regarding other households.
"How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from places of unprofitable discourse?

"If there is a place of discourse where the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha might arise, I shall remain far removed from it; this is called being far removed from places of unprofitable discourse."
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from ill will?
Not allowing thoughts of anger, vexation, or contention to enter is called remaining far removed from ill will.”
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from self-conceit?
“It is by not perceiving internal phenomena; this is called remaining far removed from self-conceit.
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from disparaging others?”
"It is said that because one does not perceive external phenomena, this is called 'being far removed from disparaging others.
How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from the ten unwholesome paths?"
"These ten unwholesome paths can obstruct the Eightfold Noble Path; how much more so can they obstruct *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? This is called 'staying far away from the ten unwholesome paths.'"
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from great pride?
“It is when this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma that could serve as a basis for great pride; this is called remaining far removed from great pride.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s distancing from self-will?
It is when this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma that can be used for self-will; this is called distancing from self-will.”
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from inversion?
“Because the locus of inversion cannot be apprehended, this is called being far removed from inversion.
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from lust, anger, and delusion?”
"Because the locus of lust, anger, and delusion cannot be perceived, this is called being far removed from lust, anger, and delusion.
This is how a bodhisattva dwelling in the fifth stage remains far removed from these twelve things."
“How does a bodhisattva dwelling in the sixth stage fulfill six dharmas?
“They are the so-called six pāramitās.
That all Buddhas, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, dwell within the six pāramitās and are able to cross to the other shore—this is called fulfilling the six dharmas.”
“How does a bodhisattva not give rise to the mindset of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha?
[The Buddha replied: “They form this thought:
‘The mindset of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha is not the path to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
"How does a bodhisattva give gifts without giving rise to a mind of distress?
[The Buddha replied: "He forms this thought:
'This is not the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.'"
“How does a bodhisattva’s mind not sink when seeing someone who asks for something?
[The Buddha replied: “He forms this thought:
‘This is not the path to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
"What is the bodhisattva’s giving of all possessions?
When the bodhisattva first resolves upon the mind [of awakening], they practice giving without saying:
'This may be given;'"
"This cannot be given.
"How is it that a bodhisattva has no regret in their heart after giving?
"Because of the power of compassion."
“How does a bodhisattva not doubt the profound Dharma?
“Because of the power of faith in its merits.
This is how a bodhisattva dwelling in the sixth stage remains far removed from these six things.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to a self?
“Because ultimately there is no self.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to sentient beings, not cling to a life-span, not cling to a multitude of persons, and so on, up to a knower or a viewer?”
“Because these dharmas are ultimately unattainable.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to the view of annihilationism?
“Because there is no dharma that is annihilated; all dharmas are ultimately unborn.”
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to the view of eternalism?
“If a phenomenon is unarisen, it cannot be made eternal.
“How should a bodhisattva not grasp at signs?”
“Because they are free from all afflictions.
“How is it that a bodhisattva should not form views regarding causes?
“Because all views are themselves unobservable.”
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to name-and-form?
“Because the characteristics of the sphere of name-and-form do not exist.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to the five aggregates, not cling to the eighteen elements, and not cling to the twelve bases?”
“Because the intrinsic nature of these dharmas does not exist.
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not cling to the three realms?
“Because the intrinsic nature of the three realms does not exist.”
“How should a bodhisattva not form a mind of attachment?
How should a bodhisattva not form a vow?
How should a bodhisattva not form a basis?”
“Because the intrinsic nature of these dharmas does not exist.
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not cling to the view of relying on the Buddha?
“Because one who forms a view of reliance does not see the Buddha.”
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to views based on the Dharma?
“Because the Dharma cannot be seen.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to views based on the Saṅgha?”
“Because the characteristics of the Saṃgha are unconditioned and thus cannot be relied upon.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to reliance on views regarding the precepts?
“Because they do not cling to [the concepts of] transgression or non-transgression.”
"These are the twenty things to which a bodhisattva dwelling in the seventh stage should not become attached.
"How should a bodhisattva fulfill emptiness?
"By fulfilling the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena."
“What is the bodhisattva’s realization of signlessness?
“Because they do not attend to any signs.
“What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the unconditioned?”
“Because one does not create [karma] within the three realms.
“What is the bodhisattva’s purity of the three spheres?
“Because of the fulfillment of the ten paths of wholesome action.”
“How does a bodhisattva become fully endowed with the wisdom of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings?
“Because they have attained great compassion.
“How does a bodhisattva not dwell upon [the concept of] all sentient beings?”
“Because of the perfection of the pure land.
“What is the bodhisattva’s equal contemplation of all dharmas?
“Because of neither diminishing nor augmenting any dharmas.”
“How does a bodhisattva know the true nature of all phenomena?
“Because the true nature of all phenomena is without cognition.
“What is a bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena?”
“It is because one practices patience regarding the fact that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished.
“What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of non-arising?
“It is knowing that name-and-form do not arise.”
“How does a bodhisattva teach that all phenomena have a single characteristic?
“Because the mind does not engage with dual characteristics.
“How does a bodhisattva destroy the characteristic of conceptual differentiation?”
“Because all dharmas are non-discriminative.
“How does a bodhisattva transform conceptualization?
“By transforming perceptions of the small, the great, and the immeasurable.”
“How does a bodhisattva transform views?
“By transforming the views regarding the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“How does a bodhisattva transform afflictions?”
“Because of severing all afflictions.
“What is the bodhisattva’s stage of equalizing concentration and wisdom?
“It is the attainment of the knowledge of all modes.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s disciplining of the mind?
“Because it is unmoving within the three realms.
“What is the bodhisattva’s tranquility of mind?”
“Because they restrain the six sense faculties.
“What is the unimpeded wisdom of a bodhisattva?
“Because they have attained the Buddha-eye.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being unstained by craving?
It is because of having abandoned the six sense objects.
This is the twentyfold dharma that a bodhisattva fulfills while dwelling in the seventh stage.”
“How does a bodhisattva enter into accordance with the minds of sentient beings?
“The bodhisattva, by means of a single mind, knows the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings.”
“How does a bodhisattva sport in the various supernormal powers?
“By means of these supernormal powers, they go from one buddha-field to another buddha-field, yet they do not form the notion of a 'buddha-field.'”
“How does a bodhisattva contemplate the buddha-fields?
“Abiding in their own field, they see immeasurable buddha-fields, yet they have no conception of them as ‘buddha-fields.’”
“How does a bodhisattva adorn his own land just as he has seen the Buddha-lands?
By abiding in the stage of a universal monarch (cakravartin), he travels throughout the trichiliocosm to adorn it.”
“How does a bodhisattva contemplate the Buddha’s body as it truly is?
“By contemplating the Dharma-body as it truly is.
This is how a bodhisattva dwelling in the eighth stage fulfills five dharmas.”
“How does a bodhisattva know the superior and inferior faculties?
A bodhisattva, abiding in the ten powers of a Buddha, knows the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings.”
“How does a bodhisattva purify a buddha-field?
“By purifying sentient beings.
“What is a bodhisattva’s illusion-like samādhi?”
“Because by abiding in this samādhi, one can accomplish all tasks while also not giving rise to mental characteristics.
“How does a bodhisattva constantly enter samādhi?”
“Because the bodhisattva has attained the samādhi of birth by retribution.
“How does the bodhisattva receive a body according to the roots of goodness appropriate for sentient beings?
“The bodhisattva knows the roots of goodness that should arise in sentient beings and receives a body accordingly, in order to bring sentient beings to maturity.”
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva dwelling in the eighth stage to be fully endowed with these five dharmas.
"How does a bodhisattva receive their portion of those to be saved in infinite worlds?
"They deliver and liberate the sentient beings in the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions who are to be saved according to the teachings of all Buddhas."
“How does a bodhisattva attain that which accords with their vows?
“By attaining the fulfillment of the six pāramitās.
“How does a bodhisattva know the languages of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas?”
“Because of the power of eloquence.
“How does a bodhisattva achieve perfection of birth from a womb?
“Because a bodhisattva is always born by transformation in every lifetime.”
"What is the perfection of the bodhisattva’s family?
It is because they are always born into great families.
What is the perfection of the bodhisattva’s birth?"
“Because he is born into a kṣatriya family or born into a brāhmaṇa family.
“What is the accomplishment of a bodhisattva’s lineage?
“It is because he is born from within the same lineage as that from which past bodhisattvas were born.”
“What is the perfection of a bodhisattva’s retinue?
It is having exclusively bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as one’s retinue.
What is the perfection of a bodhisattva’s birth?”
“At the time of birth, light universally illumines immeasurable and boundless worlds, yet this is because he does not grasp at signs.
How does a bodhisattva achieve success in leaving the household life?”
“At the time of his renunciation, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of devas attended him as he left the home life; all these sentient beings will certainly attain the three vehicles.
“How does a bodhisattva accomplish the adornment of the Bodhi tree?”

"This Bodhi tree has roots of gold, and its trunk, nodes, branches, and leaves are made of the seven treasures; the radiance from its trunk, nodes, branches, and leaves shines universally throughout incalculable trichiliocosms in the ten directions."
“How does a bodhisattva bring all virtuous merits to fulfillment and perfection?
“A bodhisattva attains the purity of sentient beings, and the buddha-field is likewise purified.”
"This is how a bodhisattva dwelling in the ninth stage fulfills twelve dharmas.
"How should it be known that a bodhisattva dwelling in the tenth stage is like a Buddha?

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the six pāramitās and the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities and the omniscience of all modes, and has severed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the tenth stage who should be known as being like a Buddha."

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within these ten stages, by means of the power of skillful means, they practice the six pāramitās and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha. They transcend the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the stage of the bodhisattva. Having transcended these nine stages, they abide in the stage of the Buddha; these are called the ten stages of a bodhisattva.
"In this way, Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Great Vehicle.
Chapter 21: Departure. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-one: Departure. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"As for what you asked:
'From where does this vehicle depart? Where does it abide? "
The Buddha said: "This vehicle emerges from within the triple world and dwells within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), because it is by means of the dharma of non-duality."

Why is this? The Mahāyāna and sarvajñatā are two dharmas that are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance, having a single characteristic, which is to say, the characteristic of no-characteristic.
If a person wishes to cause the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma (*animitta-dharma*) to emerge.
If a person wishes to cause suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), or the inconceivable nature (*acintyatā*) to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge.
If a person wishes to cause the emptiness of form to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge.
If a person wishes to cause the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The mark of the emptiness of form neither emerges from the triple world nor abides in omniscience (sarvajñā).
The emptiness of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*).

Why is this? Because the characteristic of form is empty of the characteristic of form, and the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If a person wishes to cause the emptiness of the eye to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge.
If a person wishes to cause the emptiness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge.
If a person wishes to cause even the feeling born from the condition of mental contact to emerge as empty, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to emerge.
Why is this? Subhūti!

The emptiness of the eye does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*); likewise, even up to the emptiness of sensation born of the causal condition of mental contact does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience.

Why is this? Because the eye is empty of the characteristic of an eye, and so on, up to the feeling produced by the condition of mind-contact being empty of the characteristic of the feeling produced by the condition of mind-contact.
If someone wishes to cause a dream to emerge, that person wishes to cause a dharma without characteristics to emerge.
If a person wishes to cause an illusion, a mirage, an echo, a shadow, or a transformation to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge.
Why is this? Subhūti!

The characteristics of a dream neither emerge from the triple world nor abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*); likewise, the characteristics of an illusion, a mirage, an echo, a reflection, and a transformation neither emerge from the triple world nor abide in omniscience.
Subhūti! If anyone wishes to bring forth the dānapāramitā, that person wishes to bring forth the signless dharma.
If anyone wishes to bring forth the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, or prajñāpāramitā, that person wishes to bring forth the signless dharma.

Why is this? Because the characteristic of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) neither emerges from the triple world nor abides in omniscience (sarvajñatā); likewise, the perfections from ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) up to wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) neither emerge from the triple world nor abide in omniscience.

Why is this so? Because the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is empty of the characteristic of the perfection of giving; and because the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are each empty of the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom.
If a person wishes to cause inner emptiness to emerge, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge. Why is this?

Subhūti! The characteristics of inner emptiness, up to the characteristics of the emptiness of non-existence and existence, neither emerge from the triple world nor abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Why is this?

Because internal emptiness is empty of the nature of internal emptiness, and so on up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence being empty of the nature of the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
if a person wishes to cause the four foundations of mindfulness to emerge, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to emerge.
Why is this? The nature of the four foundations of mindfulness neither exits from the triple world nor abides in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
Because the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is empty of the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness.

If anyone wishes to cause the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path to emerge, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to emerge.
Why is this? Because the nature of the eightfold noble path does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
Because the nature of the eightfold noble path is empty of the nature of the eightfold noble path;
and so it is, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, Subhūti!
If a person wishes to cause an Arhat to arise, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to arise.
If a person wishes to cause a Pratyekabuddha to arise, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to arise.
If a person wishes to cause the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha to arise, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to arise.
Why is this? The nature of an Arhat, the nature of a Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-nature do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (sarvajñā). Why is that?

Because the nature of an arhat is empty of the nature of an arhat, the nature of a pratyekabuddha is empty of the nature of a pratyekabuddha, and the nature of a buddha is empty of the nature of a buddha.

If a person wishes to cause the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the fruit of an arhat, the path of a pratyekabuddha, the path of a buddha, or all-knowledge to emerge, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to emerge.
As stated above:
if a person wishes to cause names, conventional designations, and conceptual characteristics to emerge as mere verbal expressions, that person is wishing to cause the signless dharma to emerge.
Why is this? Names are empty; they do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
Because the characteristic of names is empty of the characteristic of names;
this applies likewise up to conventional designations.
This person wishes to cause the unarisen and undestroyed dharmas, the neither-defiled nor-pure, and the unconditioned dharmas to emerge; this person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge.
Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena—from non-arising up to the unconditioned—neither exits the triple world nor dwells in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
Because the nature of non-arising, up to the nature of non-activity, is empty of intrinsic nature.
Subhūti, for this reason, the Mahāyāna emerges from the triple world and reaches all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), abiding there immovably.
“Subhūti! As for what you asked:
‘Where does this vehicle go to abide?’”
"Subhūti, this Great Vehicle has no place of abiding. Why is that?"
Because all dharmas have the characteristic of non-abiding, this vehicle—if it were to abide—would abide in the dharma of non-abiding.
Subhūti, it is as with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, without marks and without activity; it neither abides nor does not abide.
Subhūti! This vehicle is also like this: it neither abides nor does it not abide. Why is that?
The characteristic of the dharma-nature neither abides nor does not abide.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of the dharma-nature is empty, and so on, up to the fact that the nature of non-action is itself empty of the nature of non-action.
All other dharmas are likewise so,
Subhūti! For this reason, this vehicle has no abiding place.
Because of the dharma of non-abiding and the dharma of immovability. “Subhūti!
As for what you have asked:”
As for the question, "Who shall set out by means of this vehicle?
there is no person who sets out by means of this vehicle. Why is this?
This vehicle, the one who departs by means of it, the dharmas employed, and the time of departure—all these dharmas are non-existent.
If all dharmas are non-existent, by what dharma should one depart?
Why is this? Because the self is unapprehendable, up to and including the knower and the seer, because they are ultimately pure.
The inconceivable nature is unapprehendable, because it is ultimately pure.
The aggregates, bases, and elements are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
The perfection of giving is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
This continues up to the perfection of wisdom, which is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
Internal emptiness is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
This extends up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
The four foundations of mindfulness are unapprehendable, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
The stream-enterer is unattainable, and so on up to the arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and buddha, because they are ultimately pure.
The fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the Buddha, and all-knowledge are unattainable, because they are ultimately pure.
Non-arising and non-ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, without origination and without activity, they are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
In the past, future, and present, arising, abiding, and ceasing are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
Increase and decrease cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure. Why are phenomena unapprehendable?
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unapprehendable, they are unapprehendable;

because suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable nature, the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the fixed position of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), and the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) are unapprehendable, they are unapprehendable; and so on, up to the fact that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is unapprehendable, and thus unapprehendable.
Because internal emptiness cannot be apprehended, it is unapprehendable; up to and including because the emptiness of non-existence and existence cannot be apprehended, it is unapprehendable.

Because the four foundations of mindfulness cannot be apprehended, they are unapprehendable; up to and including because the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha cannot be apprehended, they are unapprehendable.
Because the stream-enterer is unattainable, he is unattainable; up to and including because the Buddha is unattainable, he is unattainable.
Because the fruit of stream-entry is unattainable, it is unattainable; up to and including because the path of a Buddha is unattainable, it is unattainable.
Because they are unarisen and undying, and because they are neither produced nor created, they cannot be apprehended;

thus they are "unapprehendable. Furthermore, Subhūti, because the first stage cannot be apprehended, it is "unapprehendable," and so on up to the tenth stage, which because it cannot be apprehended is "unapprehendable," due to its ultimate purity.
What are the stages from the first to the tenth? They are:

the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of attenuation, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Buddha.
Within internal emptiness, the first stage cannot be apprehended; likewise, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the first stage cannot be apprehended.
Within internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Subhūti,
the first stage is neither attained nor not attained, and so on up to the tenth stage, which is neither attained nor not attained, because it is ultimately pure.
Within the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the maturing of sentient beings cannot be apprehended, because it is ultimately pure.
Within the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the purification of Buddha-fields cannot be apprehended, because it is ultimately pure.
Within inner emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the five eyes cannot be apprehended,
because they are ultimately pure. Thus, Subhūti,
because all dharmas cannot be apprehended, the bodhisattva mahāsattva mounts this Mahāyāna, exits the triple world, and dwells in sarvajñā (omniscience).
Chapter 22: The Chapter on Superiority. From the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the twenty-second chapter, "The Chapter on Superiority. The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Mahāyāna, Mahāyāna! It surpasses all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras. World-Honored One, this Mahāyāna is equal to space;
just as space accommodates immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings, so too does the Mahāyāna accommodate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.
World-Honored One!

This Mahāyāna is not seen to have a place from which it comes, a place to which it goes, or a place in which it abides. This Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended at its prior limit, cannot be apprehended at its posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended at its middle limit; the equality of the three periods of time is this Mahāyāna.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, this vehicle is called the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So it is, so it is! The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva consists of what are called the six pāramitās: the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā. This is termed the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of all the doors of dhāraṇī and all the doors of samādhi—namely, from the Śūraṅgama-samādhi up to the Non-attachment to Space and Untainted Samādhi. This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
As Subhūti has said, this Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras. Subhūti!

If the realm of desire were to possess reality, were not false, were not different from the truth, were not inverted, possessed permanence, possessed an indestructible nature, and were not a non-existent dharma, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti! Because all notions of impermanence and non-existent dharmas are merely the conjunction of names and so forth,
arising from the false conceptualizations and discriminations of the desire realm, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the realm of form and the formless realm were truly existent—not false, not different from reality, not inverted, permanent, possessing an indestructible nature, and not non-existent—then this Mahāyāna would not be able to transcend all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! Because the realms of form and the formless realm are merely false conceptualizations, discriminations, and the combination of names and so forth, they possess the characteristic of all things being impermanent, subject to destruction, and non-existent dharmas.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras. Subhūti,

if form were to exist as a reality— not illusory, not different from truth, not inverted, permanent, possessing an indestructible nature, and not a non-existent thing— then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! Because form is a mere false conceptualization, discrimination, and a combination of names and so forth, it is characterized by all that is impermanent, subject to destruction, and non-existent.
For this reason, this Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

Subhūti, if the eye up to the mind; forms up to phenomena; eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; eye-contact up to mind-contact; and the feelings produced by the conditions of eye-contact up to the feelings produced by the conditions of mind-contact were truly existent, not false, not different from reality, not inverted, permanent, possessing an indestructible nature, and not non-existent, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! From the eye up to the contact of the mind, feelings arise through causes and conditions; these are a combination of false recollections, conceptualizations, and designations. They possess the characteristic of being entirely impermanent, subject to destruction, and non-existent as phenomena.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti,
if the nature of phenomena were a thing that exists rather than a non-thing, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti! Because the nature of phenomena is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon, for this reason the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature were existent dharmas rather than non-existent dharmas, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! Because suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, for this reason the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti! If the dānapāramitā were an existent phenomenon and not a non-phenomenon, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Because the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma, for this reason the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

If the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom were existent dharmas rather than non-existent dharmas, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Because the perfections from śīlapāramitā up to prajñāpāramitā are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, were a dharma that exists rather than a dharma that does not exist, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Because of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and because of the non-existence of both phenomena and non-phenomena, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, for this reason, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the dharmas of the nature of persons were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Because the nature of persons and dharmas is neither existent nor non-existent, for this reason, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the dharma of the person on the eightfold path, the dharma of the srotāpanna, the dharma of the sakṛdāgāmin, the dharma of the anāgāmin, the dharma of the arhat, the dharma of the pratyekabuddha, and the dharma of the Buddha were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Because the dharma of the eight persons, up to the Buddha-dharma, is neither a non-existent dharma nor a dharma, for this reason, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti! If the person of the stage of nature were a real dharma and not a non-dharma, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Because those of the stage of nature (gotrabhūmi) do not perceive dharmas or non-dharmas, for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the dharmas of the eight types of persons, from the srotāpanna up to the Buddha, were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras.
Because for the eight types of persons up to the Buddha, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma; for this reason, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras, were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Because all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras, lack both dharma and non-dharma, for this reason the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, all the mental states of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the interim were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Because from the initial generation of the mind of awakening until reaching the site of enlightenment, all minds in the interval between them are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas; for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the diamond-like wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva were a dharma that exists rather than a non-dharma, that bodhisattva mahāsattva would be unable to know all fetters and habitual tendencies; lacking both dharma and non-dharma, they could not attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

Subhūti! Because the vajra-like wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma, the bodhisattva knows that all fetters and their residual impressions are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, and thereby attains all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
For this reason, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras. Subhūti,

if the thirty-two marks of the Buddhas were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, the majestic power and virtue of the Buddhas would not be able to shine forth and excel all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! Because the thirty-two marks of the Buddhas are neither phenomena nor non-phenomena, for this reason the majestic virtue of the Buddhas shines forth, surpassing all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the radiance of the Buddhas were an existent dharma and not a non-existent dharma, the radiance of the Buddhas would be unable to universally illumine lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

Subhūti! Because the light of the Buddhas is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma, for this reason the Buddhas are able to universally illuminate lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with their light.

Subhūti! If the sixty kinds of adorned voices of the Buddhas were existent dharmas rather than non-existent dharmas, the Buddhas would not be able to reach immeasurable asaṃkhyeya lands in the ten directions by means of those sixty kinds of adorned voices.

Subhūti! Because the sixty kinds of adorned vocal sounds of the Buddhas are neither phenomena nor non-phenomena, for this reason, the Buddhas are able to reach immeasurable asaṃkhyeya lands throughout the ten directions with their sixty kinds of adorned vocal sounds.

Subhūti! If the Dharma-wheel of the Buddhas were a dharma that exists and not a dharma that does not exist, the Buddhas would be unable to turn the Dharma-wheel—that wheel which no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings in the world can turn according to the Dharma.

Subhūti! Because the Dharma-wheel of all Buddhas is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma, for this reason the Buddhas turn the Dharma-wheel, which no śramaṇas, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings in the world can turn in accordance with the Dharma.

Subhūti! When the Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, if these sentient beings possessed any real dharma rather than being without dharma, they would not be able to lead these sentient beings to parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.

Subhūti! Because the Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, these sentient beings have neither dharmas nor non-dharmas. For this reason, they are able to cause sentient beings to have already extinguished, are now extinguishing, and will in the future extinguish [all afflictions] within *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What you have said regarding the Great Vehicle being equal to emptiness is so, it is so!
Subhūti! The Mahāyāna is equal to space. Subhūti!
Just as space has no eastern direction, no southern, western, or northern directions, nor the four intermediate points, nor above or below;
so too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna: it has no eastern direction, no southern, western, or northern directions, nor the four intermediate points, nor above or below.
Subhūti! Just as space is neither long nor short, neither square nor round. Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither long nor short, neither square nor round. Subhūti!
It is like space, which is neither blue, nor yellow, nor red, nor white, nor black.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither blue, nor yellow, nor red, nor white, nor black.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti! Just as space is neither past, nor future, nor present, so too is the Mahāyāna: it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti, just as space neither increases nor decreases, so too is the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it neither increases nor decreases.
Subhūti, it is just as space is neither defiled nor pure.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither defiled nor pure.
Subhūti, it is just as space has no arising and no cessation, no abiding and no alteration.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is without arising and without cessation, without abiding and without change.
Subhūti, it is just as space is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, neither determinate nor indeterminate.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, neither determinate nor indeterminate.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Just as space is without seeing, without hearing, without cognition, and without consciousness, so too is the Mahāyāna:
without seeing, without hearing, without cognition, and without consciousness.
Just as space cannot be known, cannot be cognized, cannot be seen, cannot be severed, cannot be realized, and cannot be cultivated, so too is the Mahāyāna:
it cannot be known, cannot be cognized, cannot be seen, cannot be severed, cannot be realized, and cannot be cultivated.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Just as empty space is neither characterized by defilement nor characterized by separation, so too is the Mahāyāna: it is neither characterized by defilement nor characterized by separation.
Just as space is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm, so too is the Mahāyāna:
it is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm.
Just as space has no initial resolve for enlightenment, nor does it have a second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth resolve;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it has no initial resolve, up to and including no tenth resolve.

Just as in space there is no stage of dry wisdom, no stage of the nature-person, no stage of the eight persons, no stage of seeing, no stage of refinement, no stage of freedom from desire, and no stage of having completed what was to be done.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it has no stage of dry wisdom, nor even up to the stage of those who have already accomplished their task.
Just as space has no fruit of stream-entry, no fruit of once-returning, no fruit of non-returning, and no fruit of arhatship.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it has no fruit of the srotāpanna, up to and including no fruit of the arhat.
It is like space, which has no stage of the śrāvaka, no stage of the pratyekabuddha, and no stage of the Buddha.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it has no stage of the śrāvaka up to the stage of the Buddha.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Just as space is neither form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant, and neither joined nor dispersed; so too is the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither with resistance nor without resistance, neither joined nor dispersed.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti, just as space is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self; so too is the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti! Just as space is neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, and neither conditioned nor unconditioned, so too is the Mahāyāna:
it is neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, and neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti, just as space is neither quiescent nor non-quiescent, neither detached nor non-detached; so too is the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither quiescent nor non-quiescent, neither detached nor non-detached.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti! Just as space is neither darkness nor light,
so too is the Mahāyāna neither darkness nor light.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness. Subhūti,
just as space is neither obtainable nor unobtainable.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither obtainable nor unobtainable.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness. Subhūti!
Just as space is neither expressible nor inexpressible, so too is the Mahāyāna; it is neither expressible nor inexpressible.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Subhūti, for these reasons and conditions,
it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti! As you have said:
"Just as space accommodates immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings, so too does the Mahāyāna accommodate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings."
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that space does not exist."
Because space does not exist, one should know that the Mahāyāna also does not exist.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings.
Why is this? Because these dharmas—the sentient beings, space, and the Mahāyāna—are all unattainable. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) is non-existent.
Because the incalculable is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable (*aprameya*) is non-existent.
Because the immeasurable is non-existent, one should know that the boundless is non-existent.
There are no boundless or finite sentient beings. Why is this?
These sentient beings, space, the Mahāyāna, the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the boundless (*ananta*)—all these dharmas are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because the self does not exist, and so on up to the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that suchness, the dharma-nature, and the reality-limit do not exist."

Because suchness, the nature of phenomena, and the limit of reality are non-existent, one should know that even up to the immeasurable, the boundless, and the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) are non-existent.
Because the immeasurable, the boundless, and the incalculable are non-existent, one should know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti, this Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings. Why is that?

This is because all these dharmas—from sentient beings up to the knower and the seer, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and even the immeasurable, the boundless, and the incalculable (asaṃkhyeya)—are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because the self does not exist, and so on up to the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that inconceivable nature does not exist."
Because inconceivability itself is non-existent, one should know that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent.
Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) is non-existent.
Because the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) is non-existent.
Because the immeasurable is non-existent, one should know that the boundless (*ananta*) is non-existent.
Because it is boundless and non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent. For this reason, Subhūti,
you should know that the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.
Why is this? Subhūti,
it is because all dharmas, from "I" up to "knower" and "seer," are entirely unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because the self does not exist, and so on up to the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that the eye does not exist, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not exist."
Because the eye and so forth, up to the mind, are non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) is non-existent.
Because the incalculable is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) is non-existent.
Because the immeasurable is non-existent, one should know that the boundless is non-existent.
Because the boundless is non-existent, one should know that all phenomena are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
Subhūti! This is because everything from "I" up to all dharmas is ultimately unattainable. Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because "I" do not exist, and even up to "the knower" and "the seer" do not exist, you should know that the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) does not exist, and the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), diligence (*vīryapāramitā*), meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) do not exist.
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable, the boundless, and the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) are non-existent.
Because the immeasurable, the boundless, and the incalculable are non-existent, one should know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti, this Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
Because the self, sentient beings, and indeed all dharmas are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because the self does not exist,
and so on up to the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that internal emptiness does not exist, and so on up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence does not exist."
Because the emptiness of non-existence and existence is itself non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the asaṃkhyeya, the immeasurable, and the boundless are non-existent.
Because the asaṃkhyeya, the immeasurable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti, this Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
Because the self, sentient beings, and indeed all dharmas are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because the self, sentient beings,
and even the knower and the seer do not exist, one should know that the four foundations of mindfulness do not exist."
Because the four foundations of mindfulness are non-existent, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are non-existent.
Because the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the incalculable, the immeasurable, and the boundless are non-existent.
Because the asaṃkhyeya, the immeasurable, the boundless, and the non-existent do not exist, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent. For this reason, Subhūti!
This Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is this?
Because the self, sentient beings, and even all phenomena (*dharma*) are ultimately unattainable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because the self and sentient beings do not exist, up to and including the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that the stage of the nature of phenomena does not exist, up to and including the stage of having already accomplished it does not exist."
Because the ground already established is non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*aprameya*), and the boundless (*anantya*) are non-existent.
Because the incalculable, the immeasurable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, this Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
Because the self, sentient beings, and even all dharmas are ultimately unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because the self, sentient beings, and so forth, up to the knower and the seer, do not exist, one should know that the srotāpanna does not exist."
Because the srotāpanna is non-existent, one should know that the sakṛdāgāmin is non-existent.
Because the sakṛdāgāmin is non-existent, one should know that the anāgāmin is non-existent.
Because the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is non-existent, one should know that the arhat is non-existent.
Because the arhat is non-existent, one should know that even all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
"Subhūti! This is because everything from 'I' up to all dharmas is ultimately unapprehendable. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because the self, up to and including the knower and the seer, do not exist, one should know that the Śrāvaka vehicle does not exist.
Because the Śrāvaka vehicle does not exist, one should know that the Pratyekabuddha vehicle does not exist.
Because the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas is non-existent, one should know that the vehicle of the buddhas is non-existent.
Because the vehicle of the buddhas is non-existent, one should know that the śrāvaka is non-existent.
Because the śrāvaka is non-existent, one should know that the srotāpanna is non-existent.
Because the srotāpanna is non-existent, up to and including the Buddha, all are non-existent.
Because the Buddha is non-existent, one should know that all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is non-existent.
Because all-knowledge is non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that even all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, this Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
Because from "self" up to all dharmas, none are to be apprehended.

Subhūti! For example, just as within the nature of nirvāṇa immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings are accommodated, so too this Mahāyāna accommodates immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.
For this reason, Subhūti, just as space accommodates immeasurable,
boundless, and incalculable sentient beings, so too does this Mahāyāna accommodate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.
“Subhūti! As for what you have said:
‘This Mahāyāna is not seen to come from anywhere, not seen to go anywhere, and not seen to abide anywhere.’”
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! This Mahāyāna is not seen to have a place from which it comes, nor is it seen to have a place to which it goes, nor is it seen to have a place where it dwells."
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because all dharmas have the characteristic of immovability.
This dharma has no place of coming, no place of going, and no place of abiding.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! The dharma of form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere; the dharmas of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! The suchness of form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere; the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere.

Subhūti! The nature of form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere; the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! The characteristic of form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere; the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! The eye, the phenomena of the eye, the suchness of the eye, the nature of the eye, and the characteristics of the eye come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the phenomena of the mind, the suchness of the mind, the nature of the mind, and the characteristics of the mind also come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are also like this. Subhūti!

The earth element, the dharma of the earth element, the suchness of the earth element, the nature of the earth element, and the characteristics of the earth element come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere. The water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements; the dharmas of the consciousness element; the suchness of the consciousness element; the nature of the consciousness element; and the characteristics of the consciousness element are also like this.
Subhūti! Suchness, the nature of suchness, such-as-it-is-ness, the essence of suchness, and the characteristic of suchness come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! The reality limit (bhūtakoṭi), the dharma of the reality limit, the suchness of the reality limit, the nature of the reality limit, and the characteristics of the reality limit come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Subhūti! The inconceivable, the inconceivable dharma, inconceivable suchness, inconceivable nature, and inconceivable characteristic come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the dharma of the perfection of giving, the suchness (*tathatā*) of the perfection of giving, the nature (*svabhāva*) of the perfection of giving, and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the perfection of giving come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere. The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), as well as the dharma of the perfection of wisdom, the suchness of the perfection of wisdom, the nature of the perfection of wisdom, and the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom, come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! The four foundations of mindfulness, the dharmas of the four foundations of mindfulness, the suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness, the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness, and the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere, nor do they abide anywhere.
This applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). Subhūti!

A bodhisattva, the qualities of a bodhisattva, the suchness of a bodhisattva, the nature of a bodhisattva, and the characteristics of a bodhisattva do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere, nor do they abide anywhere.
The Buddha, the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-tathatā, the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-characteristics come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, its tathatā, its nature, and its characteristics come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! Conditioned phenomena, the dharmas of conditioned phenomena, the suchness of conditioned phenomena, the nature of conditioned phenomena, and the characteristics of conditioned phenomena come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

Subhūti! Unconditioned phenomena, the dharma of unconditioned phenomena, the suchness of unconditioned phenomena, the nature of unconditioned phenomena, and the characteristics of unconditioned phenomena come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
For this reason, Subhūti, this Mahāyāna is not seen to have a place from which it comes, a place to which it goes, or a place in which it abides. Subhūti!
As for what you said:

"This Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended at its prior limit, cannot be apprehended at its posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended in its middle; this vehicle is called 'the equality of the three periods of time.'"
"For this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna. "So it is, so it is! Subhūti!"

This Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended at its prior limit, cannot be apprehended at its posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended in its middle; this vehicle is called the equality of the three periods of time.
For this reason, it is named Mahāyāna.

Why is this? Subhūti! The past world is empty of the past world; the future world is empty of the future world; the present world is empty of the present world; the equality of the three times is empty of the equality of the three times; the Mahāyāna is empty of the Mahāyāna; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti!
This emptiness is not one, not two, not three, not four, not five, and not different.
For this reason, it is called the "equality of the three times," which is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Within this Mahāyāna, because neither the characteristic of equality nor inequality can be apprehended, defilement and non-defilement cannot be apprehended; hatred and non-hatred cannot be apprehended; delusion and non-delusion cannot be apprehended; pride and non-pride cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, which cannot be apprehended.

Within this Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), permanence is unapprehendable and impermanence is unapprehendable; pleasure is unapprehendable and suffering is unapprehendable; reality is unapprehendable and emptiness is unapprehendable; self is unapprehendable and non-self is unapprehendable; the desire realm is unapprehendable, the form realm is unapprehendable, and the formless realm is unapprehendable; the transcendence of the desire realm is unapprehendable, the transcendence of the form realm is unapprehendable, and the transcendence of the formless realm is unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of this Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended.

Past form is empty of past form; future and present form are empty of future and present form. Past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; future and present feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of future and present feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Within this emptiness, past form cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can past form be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, future and present form cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can future or present form be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, future and present feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended.

Why is this? Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can future, present, or past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended within emptiness? Subhūti!
The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) of the past is unapprehendable; the perfection of giving of the future is unapprehendable; the perfection of giving of the present is unapprehendable.
Within the equality of the three times, even the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
Within that equality, the past time cannot be apprehended, the future time cannot be apprehended, and the present time cannot be apprehended.
Even within equality, equality itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can the past, future, and present worlds be apprehended within equality?

It is the same for the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti! In the past, the four foundations of mindfulness are unobtainable, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha which are unobtainable in the past."
The same applies to the future world and the present world.

Furthermore, Subhūti, within the equality of the three times, the four foundations of mindfulness are unattainable; within the equality of the three times, even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are unattainable.

Why is this? Within equality, the four foundations of mindfulness of the past cannot be apprehended; within equality, the four foundations of mindfulness of the future cannot be apprehended; and within equality, the four foundations of mindfulness of the present cannot be apprehended.
This applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Within equality, equality itself cannot be apprehended; how much less could the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) of the past, future, or present be apprehended within equality?
Even equality within equality cannot be apprehended; how much less can the past, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), be apprehended within it?
The same applies to the future and present worlds, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities.
Furthermore, Subhūti! An ordinary person (pṛthagjana) of the past cannot be apprehended; an ordinary person in the future or the present cannot be apprehended.
Within the equality of the three periods of time, even ordinary persons cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, and so on, up to the knower and the seer, who cannot be apprehended.
In past ages, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas cannot be apprehended; in future and present ages, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas cannot be apprehended.
Within the equality of the three periods of time, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, up to and including the knower and the seer.

In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the study of the equality of the three periods of time within the perfection of wisdom, they shall fulfill all-knowledge; this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Regarding what is called the mark of the equality of the three periods of time, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within this vehicle, they surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras, and accomplish sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!”
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also study within this Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) and shall attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
World-Honored One!
Now, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya lands of the ten directions likewise study within this Great Vehicle and attain all-knowledge.
"For this reason, World-Honored One,
this vehicle is truly the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! The Buddhas of the past, future, and present have studied within this Mahāyāna; they have attained, will attain, and are now attaining all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Six. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"Regarding what you asked:
'From where does this vehicle depart?'"
To the question, "Where does it abide?
the Buddha said: "This vehicle emerges from within the three realms and abides within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), because it is by way of the non-dual dharma."

Why is this? The Mahāyāna and sarvajñatā are two dharmas that are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without form, without shape, and without resistance, having but a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless."
If a person wishes to emerge from the dharma of signlessness, they wish to emerge from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If they wish to emerge from the dharma of signlessness, they wish to emerge from suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the inconceivable nature.

If one wishes to emerge from the dharma of signlessness, it is because one wishes to emerge from the emptiness of form, or because one wishes to emerge from the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this so? Subhūti!

The mark of the emptiness of form does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*); the marks of the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience.
Why is this? Because form is empty of the characteristic of form, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristic of consciousness.

If one wishes to emerge from signless dharmas, it is because one wishes to emerge from the emptiness of the eye, the emptiness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and even the emptiness of the feeling produced by conditions such as eye-contact, and the emptiness of the feelings produced by conditions such as contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Why is this? Subhūti!

The eye is empty; it does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This extends even to the feeling produced by the condition of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa-pratyaya-utpanna-vedanā*), which is empty; it does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience.

Why is this? Because the eye is empty of the characteristic of an eye, and so on, up to feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition, which is empty of the characteristic of feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition.
If one wishes to emerge from signless dharmas, it is as if one wished to emerge from a dream, or from an illusion, a mirage, an echo, a reflection, or a transformation created by a Buddha.
Why is this? Subhūti!

The characteristics of a dream do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Likewise, the characteristics of an illusion, a mirage, an echo, a reflection, and a transformation do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? The characteristic of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) neither emerges from the triple world nor abides in omniscience (sarvajñatā); likewise, the perfections from ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) up to wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) neither emerge from the triple world nor abide in omniscience.

Why is this? Because the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving; the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are each empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom.
If one wishes to emerge from the dharma of signlessness, it is because one wishes to emerge from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
The emptiness of the internal, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, neither issues forth from the triple world nor abides in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is this?

Because the emptiness of the internal is empty of the emptiness of the internal, and so on, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence being empty of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
If one wishes to emerge from the dharma of signlessness, it is for the sake of wishing to emerge from the four foundations of mindfulness. Why is this?
Because the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness neither emerges from the triple world nor dwells in omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
Why is this? Because the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is empty of the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness.

If one wishes to emerge from signless phenomena, it is for the sake of emerging from the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
Why is this? Because the nature of the eightfold noble path does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Why is that?
