Because the nature of the eightfold noble path is empty of the nature of the eightfold noble path, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, it is likewise. Subhūti!

If one wishes to emerge from signless dharmas, it is for the sake of wishing to emerge from the place of birth of an arhat, for the sake of wishing to emerge from the place of birth of a pratyekabuddha, and for the sake of wishing to emerge from the place of birth of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Why is this? The nature of an Arhat, the nature of a Pratyekabuddha, and the nature of a Buddha do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
The nature of an arhat is empty of the nature of an arhat; the nature of a pratyekabuddha is empty of the nature of a pratyekabuddha; the nature of a buddha is empty of the nature of a buddha.

If one wishes to emerge from signless dharmas, it is because one wishes to emerge from the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of a pratyekabuddha, the path of a buddha, and all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

Why is this? Because the nature of the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including the knowledge of all modes, does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Why is that?
From the fruit of stream-entry up to all-knowledge, because all-knowledge is empty of the nature of all-knowledge;
if one wishes to emerge from signless dharmas, it is for the sake of emerging from names, from the signs of provisional designations, which are merely words.
Why is this? Because names do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
The characteristic of names is empty because of the emptiness of the characteristic of names.
This applies even up to conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

If one wishes to emerge from the dharma of signlessness, it is because one wishes to emerge from that which is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, and without production or activity.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Reconciling with the Source At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“The Buddha has commissioned Subhūti to expound the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; why then does he now speak of the Mahāyāna?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"When I speak of the Mahāyāna, would it not be apart from the Prajñāpāramitā? The Buddha said, "No, Subhūti."
What you have spoken of as the Mahāyāna follows the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and is not separate from it. Why is this?

Because all existing wholesome dharmas that assist the path—whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas—all these dharmas are subsumed within the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What are those various wholesome dharmas, the factors conducive to enlightenment, the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the buddhas that are all subsumed within the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"What are called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities—these are characterized by the absence of error and are always practiced with relinquishment."

Subhūti! All these other wholesome dharmas that assist the path—whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas—are all subsumed within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s Mahāyāna consists of the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of dhyāna,
the perfection of vīrya, the perfection of kṣānti, and the perfection of śīla...
The perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
eye, forms, and eye-consciousness; eye-contact and the various feelings arising with eye-contact as a condition; and so on, up to mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness;
mind-contact and the various feelings arising with mind-contact as a condition; the earth element up to the consciousness element; and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight [fold path].
The factors of the noble path, the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and all wholesome dharmas, whether with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned;
whether the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, or the truth of the path; whether belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Whether it be internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the various gates of samādhi, the various gates of dhāraṇī,
the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities, or whether it be the Buddha-dharmas,
the nature of the Buddha-dharmas, suchness, the limit of reality, the inconceivable nature, or nirvāṇa— all these phenomena are [empty].
All are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, without resistance, without obstruction, and without equal—a single mark, which is called "marklessness. Subhūti!
For this reason, what you have spoken regarding the Mahāyāna accords with the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is that? Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna is not different from the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā is not different from the Mahāyāna; the Prajñāpāramitā and the Mahāyāna are non-dual and without distinction.

The perfection of giving is not different from the Mahāyāna, and the Mahāyāna is not different from the perfection of giving; the perfection of giving and the Mahāyāna are non-dual and without distinction.
It is the same for the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as well.

Subhūti, the four foundations of mindfulness are not different from the Mahāyāna, and the Mahāyāna is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness and the Mahāyāna are non-dual and without distinction.

Even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they are not different from the Mahāyāna; the Mahāyāna is not different from the eighteen unique qualities. The eighteen unique qualities and the Mahāyāna are non-dual and without distinction.
"For this reason, Subhūti, when you speak of the Mahāyāna, you are speaking of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Chapter 25: The Ten Non-existences (*Daśābhāva*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The prior limit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be apprehended, the posterior limit cannot be apprehended, and the middle limit cannot be apprehended; because form is boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise boundless.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also boundless.
That form is the bodhisattva mahāsattva—this, too, is unapprehendable.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva mahāsattva, yet these too are unapprehendable.
Thus it is, Blessed One!
In every way and in every place, a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
"Bhagavān! Which bodhisattva mahāsattvas should I instruct in the perfection of wisdom? Bhagavān!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva exists as a mere name.
Just as when one speaks of the "name" of a self, that self is ultimately unarisen,
so too are all phenomena likewise without intrinsic nature.
What is form that is ultimately non-arising?
What are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are ultimately non-arising?
World-Honored One!
That which is ultimately unborn is not called form; that which is ultimately unborn is not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
World-Honored One, if dharmas are ultimately unborn, should one teach them this *prajñāpāramitā*?
Apart from that which is ultimately unborn, there is also no bodhisattva practice of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If, upon hearing this teaching, a bodhisattva’s mind does not sink, does not regret, is not startled, is not terrified, and is not afraid, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason do you say that the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s prior limit is unapprehendable, the subsequent limit is unapprehendable, and the middle limit is unapprehendable?"
Subhūti! For what reason is it said that because form (*rūpa*) is boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also boundless;
and because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also boundless?

Subhūti! For what reason do you say that form is the bodhisattva, yet this too cannot be apprehended; and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva, yet these too cannot be apprehended?
Subhūti! For what reason do you say that a bodhisattva is unapprehendable in every respect and in every place; toward what kind of bodhisattva, then, should one teach the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti! For what reason do you say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists as nothing more than a mere name? Subhūti!
For what reason do you say that just as my name is spoken, I am ultimately unarisen?
Just as I am, so too are all phenomena without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
What kind of form is ultimately unarisen?
What is this feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are ultimately non-arising? Subhūti,
for what reason do you say that what is ultimately non-arising is not called form, and what is ultimately non-arising is not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
Subhūti! For what reason is it said that if dharmas are ultimately non-arising, one should teach them this *prajñāpāramitā*? Subhūti!
For what reason do you say that, apart from ultimate non-arising, there is also no bodhisattva practicing for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Subhūti!

For what reason is it said that if a bodhisattva, upon hearing such a teaching, does not sink in heart, does not regret, is not startled, is not terrified, and is not afraid, and if they can practice in this way, they are called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*?
At that time, Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Because sentient beings do not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because sentient beings are empty, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended."
Because sentient beings are non-existent, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra, because form does not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; [and so on for the other aggregates].
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because form is empty, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because form is detached, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended. Śāriputra!
Because the nature of form does not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended. Śāriputra!
Because the perfection of giving does not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom do not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Śāriputra, within emptiness,
a prior limit cannot be apprehended, a posterior limit cannot be apprehended, and a middle limit cannot be apprehended.
Emptiness is not different from the bodhisattva, and the bodhisattva is not different from the prior limit.
Śāriputra, emptiness,
the bodhisattva, and the prior limit— these dharmas are non-dual and without distinction.
For this reason, Śāriputra, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended. Śāriputra!

Because the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is empty, because the perfection of giving is detached, and because the perfection of giving lacks intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;

because the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are empty, because the perfection of wisdom is detached, and because the perfection of wisdom lacks intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Śāriputra, within emptiness,
a prior limit cannot be apprehended, a subsequent limit cannot be apprehended, and a middle limit cannot be apprehended.
Emptiness is not different from the bodhisattva, nor is it different from the prior limit.
Śāriputra, emptiness,
the bodhisattva, and the prior limit are non-dual and without distinction.
For this reason, Śāriputra, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended. Furthermore, Śāriputra:

Because internal emptiness is non-existent, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to because the emptiness of non-existence and existence is non-existent, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.

Because internal emptiness is empty, because internal emptiness is detached, and because internal emptiness lacks intrinsic nature—and so on, up to because the emptiness of non-existence and existence is empty, detached, and lacks intrinsic nature—the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the four foundations of mindfulness are non-existent, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;..."
Because the four foundations of mindfulness are empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because they are non-existent, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because the eighteen unique qualities are empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
The rest is as explained above.
For these reasons, Śāriputra, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because all gates of samādhi and all gates of dhāraṇī do not exist, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because the gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī are empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended."
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; [the same applies to] the future limit and the present."
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Because they do not exist, because they are empty, because they are detached, and because they lack intrinsic nature; because the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) does not exist, because it is empty, because it is detached, and because it lacks intrinsic nature; and because the inconceivable nature does not exist, because it is empty, because it is detached, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the śrāvaka does not exist,
the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;..."
Because the śrāvaka is empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because the pratyekabuddha does not exist, is empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because the Buddha does not exist, because he is empty, because he is detached, and because his intrinsic nature does not exist, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not exist, and so on up to its intrinsic nature not existing, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.

Furthermore, because all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not exist, and so on up to its lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Śūnyatā cannot be apprehended in the past, it cannot be apprehended in the future, and it cannot be apprehended in the middle; likewise, the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended. Śāriputra!
Emptiness is not different from the bodhisattva, nor is it different from the prior limit.
Emptiness, the bodhisattva, and the prior limit—these dharmas are non-dual and without distinction. For this reason, Śāriputra!
The prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; the same is true for the posterior limit and the middle limit.

As Śāriputra has said: "Because form is limitless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also limitless; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also limitless."
Śāriputra! Form is like space; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like space. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Just as with space, its limits cannot be found and its center cannot be found.
Because it is neither bounded nor centered, it is merely designated by the name "space."
In this way, Śāriputra, form has no limit that can be apprehended and no middle that can be apprehended; because form is empty, within emptiness there is neither limit nor middle.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—neither an extreme nor a middle can be apprehended therein. Because consciousness is empty, and within emptiness there is neither extreme nor middle.
For these reasons, Śāriputra!
Because form is boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also boundless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also boundless.
This applies likewise even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
"As Śāriputra has said, form is the bodhisattva, yet this too is unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva, yet these too are unapprehendable."
Śāriputra! Form is empty of the characteristic of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristic of consciousness.
The perfection of generosity is empty of the characteristic of the perfection of generosity, and so it is for all others up to the perfection of wisdom.

Internal emptiness is empty of the characteristic of internal emptiness; up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is empty of the characteristic of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.

The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness; up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are empty of the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Suchness, the dharma-nature, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature are empty of the characteristic of the inconceivable nature.

The gateways of samādhi are empty of the characteristic of the gateways of samādhi; the gateways of dhāraṇī are empty of the characteristic of the gateways of dhāraṇī; all-knowledge is empty of the characteristic of all-knowledge; the knowledge of the path is empty of the characteristic of the knowledge of the path; and the knowledge of all modes is empty of the characteristic of the knowledge of all modes.

The Śrāvaka vehicle is empty of the characteristics of the Śrāvaka vehicle; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is empty of the characteristics of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; the Buddha vehicle is empty of the characteristics of the Buddha vehicle.

The person of the Śrāvaka is empty of the characteristics of the person of the Śrāvaka; the person of the Pratyekabuddha is empty of the characteristics of the person of the Pratyekabuddha; the Buddha is empty of the characteristics of the Buddha.
In space, form cannot be apprehended; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended.
For this reason, Śāriputra, that which is form is the bodhisattva, yet even that cannot be apprehended.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva, yet these too cannot be apprehended.
As Śāriputra has asked: "For what reason is the bodhisattva unapprehendable in every respect and in all places? To which bodhisattva should one teach the perfection of wisdom?"
Śāriputra! Form cannot be apprehended within form; form cannot be apprehended within sensation.
Sensation cannot be apprehended within sensation; sensation cannot be apprehended within form; sensation cannot be apprehended within perception.
One cannot find [the self] within perception; one cannot find it within perception of form, feeling, or formations; one cannot find it within formations.
One cannot find it within the formations of form, feeling, or perception; one cannot find it within perception of consciousness. One cannot find [the self] within consciousness;
one cannot find it within consciousness of form, feeling, perception, or formations.
Śāriputra! The eye cannot be apprehended within the eye, nor can it be apprehended within the ear;
the ear cannot be apprehended within the ear, nor can it be apprehended within the eye, nor can it be apprehended within the nose; the nose and ear cannot be apprehended within one another.

The nose cannot be apprehended within the nose; the nose cannot be apprehended within the eye or the ear; the nose cannot be apprehended within the tongue. The tongue cannot be apprehended within the tongue;
the tongue cannot be apprehended within the eye, ear, or nose; the tongue cannot be apprehended within the body. The body cannot be apprehended within the body;
the body cannot be apprehended within the eye, ear, nose, or tongue; the body cannot be apprehended within the mind.
The mind cannot be apprehended within the mind; it cannot be apprehended within the eye, ear, nose, tongue, or body.
It is likewise with the six sense bases, the six consciousnesses, and the six contacts; the feelings produced through the conditions of the six contacts are also thus.

The *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*; from internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); all gateways of samādhi and all gateways of dhāraṇī; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) up to the *pratyekabuddha*-dharma; the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage; and likewise, the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is likewise for those from the *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*, the *pratyekabuddha*, the *bodhisattva*, and the Buddha.
A bodhisattva cannot be apprehended within a bodhisattva, nor can a bodhisattva be apprehended within the *prajñāpāramitā*.

The *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be apprehended within the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can the *prajñāpāramitā* be apprehended within a bodhisattva; within the *prajñāpāramitā*, even the non-existence of that which is to be transformed cannot be apprehended.

Within the act of teaching and transforming others, there is nothing that exists or can be apprehended; within the act of teaching and transforming others, neither the bodhisattva nor the prajñāpāramitā exists or can be apprehended.
Śāriputra! Thus, all dharmas are non-existent and unobtainable.
For this reason, in every respect and in every place, a bodhisattva is unobtainable; toward what bodhisattva, then, should one teach the perfection of wisdom?
“As Śāriputra has said, for what reason do you say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists only as a mere designation?
Śāriputra! Form is a mere designation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are mere designations.”
Form is called non-form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called non-consciousness.
Why is this? Because names are empty of the characteristic of naming; if they are empty, they are not the bodhisattva.
For these reasons, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva exists only as a provisional designation. Furthermore, Śāriputra:
The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) exists only as a name; within the name there is no perfection of giving, and within the perfection of giving there is no name.
For these reasons, a bodhisattva exists only as a conventional designation.

The perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) exist only as names. Within these names there is no perfection of wisdom, and within the perfection of wisdom there are no names.
For these reasons, a bodhisattva exists only as a provisional designation.
Śāriputra, inner emptiness exists only as a name, and so on, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which exists only as a name.
Within names there is no internal emptiness; within internal emptiness there are no names.
Why is this? Because both names and internal emptiness are unapprehendable.
This applies even up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence. For this reason, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva exists only as a mere designation.
Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness exist only as names; even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha exist only as names.
It is the same for all gateways of samādhi, all gateways of dhāraṇī, and even up to the knowledge of all modes.
For these reasons, Śāriputra, I say that a bodhisattva exists only as a provisional designation.
As you have asked, Śāriputra, for what reason do I say that my own name is ultimately unarisen?
Śāriputra! Since the self is ultimately unapprehendable, how could there be birth?
Even up to the knower and the seer, since they are ultimately unapprehendable, how could there be birth?
Śāriputra! Since form is ultimately unattainable, how could it have arising?
Since feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately unattainable, how could they have arising?
The eye is ultimately unattainable, and even the feeling produced through the causal condition of mental contact is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be arising?
The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is ultimately unattainable, and even the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be arising!
Since internal emptiness is ultimately unapprehendable, and even the emptiness of non-existence and existence is ultimately unapprehendable, how could there be arising?
Since the four foundations of mindfulness are ultimately unapprehendable, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ultimately unapprehendable, how could there be arising?
Since the various gates of samādhi and the various gates of dhāraṇī are ultimately unobtainable, how could they ever arise?
Since the śrāvakas up to the Buddhas are ultimately unobtainable, how could they ever arise?
For this reason, Śāriputra, I say that just as my name is, so too am I ultimately unarisen.
As you have said, Śāriputra, all dharmas are likewise without intrinsic nature.
Śāriputra! Because all dharmas arise through combination, they lack intrinsic nature. Śāriputra!
What is the lack of intrinsic nature in that which arises through combination?
Śāriputra, form arises through combination and lacks intrinsic nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise through combination and lack intrinsic nature.
The eye arises through a combination of conditions and lacks intrinsic nature; likewise, up to the mind, it arises through a combination of conditions and lacks intrinsic nature.

From forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); from the eye-element up to the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*); from the earth element up to the consciousness element; from eye-contact up to mind-contact; and from the feeling produced by the condition of eye-contact up to the feeling produced by the condition of mind-contact—all arise through a combination of conditions and lack intrinsic nature.
From the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, they arise through combination and lack intrinsic nature.
From the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they arise through combination and lack intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all dharmas are impermanent and yet they do not perish. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“What dharmas are impermanent yet do not perish? Subhūti replied: “Form is impermanent yet does not perish;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent yet do not perish.”
For what reason?
If dharmas were impermanent, they would possess the characteristic of movement and the characteristic of emptiness.
For this cause and condition, Śāriputra!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and yet do not perish.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, whether they be contaminated or uncontaminated phenomena, or whether they be determinate or indeterminate phenomena.
Why is this? If a dharma is impermanent, it is a characteristic of movement and a characteristic of emptiness. For these reasons, Śāriputra!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent yet do not perish.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, all dharmas are neither permanent nor subject to extinction.
Śāriputra asked: "What dharmas are neither permanent nor subject to cessation? Subhūti replied:
"Form is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Because its nature is such."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why?
Because their nature is inherently so.
Even up to feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why?
Because such is its very nature.
For these reasons, Śāriputra, all dharmas arise through combination and lack intrinsic nature.
As you have asked, Śāriputra, for what reason is form ultimately unarisen?
"Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ultimately non-arisen?
Subhūti replied, "Form is not a conditioned phenomenon;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not conditioned phenomena."
Why is this? Because an agent cannot be apprehended, Śāriputra.
The eye is not a conditioned phenomenon. Why?
Because an agent cannot be apprehended.
It is the same for the mind as well.
It is the same for the eye-element up to the feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All dharmas neither arise nor are produced.
Why? Because an agent cannot be apprehended.
For these reasons, Śāriputra, form is ultimately unarisen;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately unarisen.

As you have asked, Śāriputra: for what reason is that which is ultimately unarisen not called "form," and why is that which is ultimately unarisen not called "feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness"?
Subhūti said: "The nature of form is empty;
this emptiness is without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or changing.
The nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty; this emptiness is without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or changing."
From the eye up to all conditioned phenomena, their nature is empty; this emptiness is without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or changing. For these reasons, Śāriputra!
That which is ultimately unarisen is not called form; that which is ultimately unarisen is not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
"As Śāriputra has said, for what reason and by what causal conditions should one teach this *prajñāpāramitā* regarding dharmas that are ultimately unarisen?"
Subhūti said: "Ultimate non-arising is itself the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom is itself ultimate non-arising."
The perfection of wisdom and ultimate non-arising are non-dual and without distinction.
For this reason, Śāriputra, when I say that ultimate non-arising should be taught as this perfection of wisdom, is it not so?
"As Śāriputra has said, for what reason is it that, apart from ultimate non-arising, there is no bodhisattva practice of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

Subhūti said: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive ultimate non-arising as distinct from the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ultimate non-arising as distinct from the bodhisattva."
Ultimate non-arising and the bodhisattva are non-dual and without distinction.
One does not perceive ultimate non-arising as being different from form. Why is this?
This ultimate non-arising and form are non-dual and without distinction.
One does not perceive ultimate non-arising as being different from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is this?
Ultimately unborn, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual and without distinction.
This applies even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). For this reason, Śāriputra!
"Apart from that which is ultimately unborn, there is no bodhisattva practice of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Śāriputra, for what reason does a bodhisattva, upon hearing such a teaching, have a mind that does not sink, does not regret, is not startled, is not terrified, and is not afraid? This is called a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*."

Subhūti said: “A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any phenomenon as having the notion of cognition; he perceives all phenomena as being like a dream, like an echo, like an illusion, like a mirage, like a shadow, and like a transformation.”
“Śāriputra! For these reasons, when a bodhisattva hears such a teaching, their mind does not sink, they feel no regret, and they are not startled, terrified, or afraid.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates all dharmas in this manner, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp form, does not indicate form, does not abide in form, does not cling to form, nor does he say, ‘This is form.’”

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also not received, not indicated, not dwelt upon, and not clung to; nor are they spoken of as "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The eye is also not received, not indicated, not dwelt upon, and not clung to; nor is it spoken of as "the eye."
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not received, not indicated, not dwelt upon, and not clung to; nor is it said that "this is the mind.
The dānapāramitā is not received, not indicated, not dwelt upon, and not clung to; nor is it said that "this is the dānapāramitā."

The perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom—these are not received, not shown, not dwelled upon, and not clung to; nor does one say, "This is the perfection of wisdom."
Internal emptiness is not received, not shown, not abided in, and not clung to; nor is it said to be "internal emptiness.
This applies likewise up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not accept, do not indicate, do not dwell in, and do not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness, nor do they say, "These are the four foundations of mindfulness."

Even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), he does not accept them, does not demonstrate them, does not dwell in them, and does not cling to them; nor does he say, "These are the eighteen unique qualities.

Regarding all gateways of samādhi, all gateways of dhāraṇī, and even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he does not accept them, does not demonstrate them, does not dwell in them, and does not cling to them; nor does he say, "This is all-knowledge."
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive form, nor do they perceive anything up to and including all-knowledge.
Why is this? Because the non-arising of form is not form; the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness.
The non-arising of the eye is not the eye; the non-arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is not the mind.

The perfection of giving does not arise; it is not that this is not the perfection of giving. This continues up to the perfection of wisdom, which does not arise; it is not that this is not the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Form and non-arising are not two and are not distinct.
This extends up to the perfection of wisdom and non-arising, which are not two and are not distinct.

The emptiness of the internal is non-arising; this is not the emptiness of the internal. This extends up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is non-arising; this is not the emptiness of non-existence and existence. Why is this?
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, they are unborn, non-dual, and undifferentiated.
World-Honored One, the four foundations of mindfulness are unborn; they are not the four foundations of mindfulness.
Why is this? The four foundations of mindfulness are non-arising, non-dual, and undifferentiated. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This dharma of non-arising is neither one, nor two, nor three, nor different.
For this reason, the four foundations of mindfulness are non-arising, non-dual, and undifferentiated.
Even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they are neither produced nor are they not the eighteen unique qualities. Why is this?
Because the eighteen unique qualities are non-arising, non-dual, and without distinction.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
This dharma of non-arising is neither one, nor two, nor three, nor different.
For this reason, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are not produced, nor are they non-eighteen-unique-qualities.
World-Honored One!
Just as that which is non-arising is not "suchness," so too, up to the point of the nature of the inconceivable, that which is non-arising is not "the inconceivable nature."
"Blessed One!
This *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is non-arising; omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are non-arising, and this is not [merely] the knowledge of all aspects."
Why is this? This *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), is non-arising, non-dual, and undifferentiated. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This non-arising is neither one, nor two, nor three, nor different.
For this reason, even up to omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), it is non-arising and not omniscience.
World-Honored One!
The characteristic of the non-extinction of form is non-form. Why is this?
Form and the characteristic of non-extinction are non-dual and not distinct. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This dharma of non-extinction is not one, not two, not three, and not different.
For this reason, the mark of non-extinction of form is not form; the marks of non-extinction of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not consciousness.
Why is this? Consciousness and non-extinction are neither two nor distinct. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This dharma of non-extinction is not one, not two, not three, and not different.
For this reason, the non-extinction of consciousness is not consciousness.

The same applies to the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; and likewise for the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
World-Honored One!

For this reason, form enters into the category of non-dual dharmas; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness enter into the category of non-dual dharmas; and so on, up to all-knowledge entering into the category of non-dual dharmas.
Chapter 26: On Non-Arising The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Six: On Non-Arising At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he contemplates all dharmas."
What is a bodhisattva?
What is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
What is contemplation?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“Regarding your question, ‘What is a bodhisattva?’—it is one who has set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; because this person has generated the great mind, they are therefore called a bodhisattva.”
He also knows all dharmas and all their various characteristics, yet he does not cling even to them.
He knows the characteristics of form and does not cling to them, and so on, up to knowing the characteristics of the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) and not clinging to them either.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti, “What is the characteristic of all phenomena? Subhūti replied:

"If one knows all phenomena through the conjunction of causes and conditions such as names—knowing that 'this is form, this is sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomenon,' 'this is internal, this is external,' or 'this is a conditioned phenomenon, this is an unconditioned phenomenon'—and knows all phenomena through these characteristics of names and verbal expressions, this is called knowing the characteristics of all phenomena."
As Śāriputra has asked: "What is this prajñāpāramitā?
It is called prajñāpāramitā because of its detachment.
From what phenomena is it detached?

It is far removed from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; it is far removed from the perfection of giving up to the perfection of meditation; and it is far removed from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
For this reason, detachment is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, it is detachment from the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including detachment from the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and detachment from all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
For these reasons, it is called "far removed" as the *prajñāpāramitā*.
As Śāriputra asked: "What is this contemplation? Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate form as neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither quiescent nor non-quiescent, and neither detached nor non-detached; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

From the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); from internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); all gateways of samādhi, all gateways of dhāraṇī, and even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—one contemplates these as neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with marks nor markless, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither cessation nor non-cessation, and neither detached nor non-detached.
“Śāriputra! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of all dharmas when practicing the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"For what reason is it that the non-arising of form is not form, the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness, and so on, up to the non-arising of all-knowledge is not all-knowledge?"
Subhūti said: "Form is empty of the characteristic of form; within the emptiness of form, there is no form and no arising.
For this reason, the non-arising of form is not form."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristics of consciousness; within the emptiness of consciousness, there is no consciousness and no arising.
For these reasons, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not arise, and they are not [identical to] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Śāriputra! The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is empty of the characteristic of the perfection of giving; within the emptiness of the perfection of giving, there is no perfection of giving and no arising.

The perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are empty of the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom; within the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom, there is no perfection of wisdom and no arising.
For this reason, Śāriputra, the *prajñāpāramitā* does not give rise to the notion that "this is not the *prajñāpāramitā*.

It is the same for internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), as well as for the four applications of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

For this reason, internal emptiness does not arise, and that which is not internal emptiness is also not internal emptiness; likewise, up to and including all-knowledge, all-knowledge does not arise, and that which is not all-knowledge is also not all-knowledge.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"For what reason do you say that form is non-dual and is not non-form; that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual and are not non-consciousness; and so on, up to omniscience being non-dual and not non-omniscience?"
Subhūti replied: "Whatever form there is, whatever non-duality there is;

whatever feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there are, whatever non-duality there is—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed, colorless, formless, and non-resistant; they have a single characteristic, which is the so-called 'characteristic-less'."
It is the same for the eye up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For this reason, Śāriputra, form (*rūpa*) is non-dual and is not non-form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are non-dual and are not non-consciousness; and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes, which is non-dual and is not non-knowledge of all modes.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"By what cause and condition do you say that this form enters into the category of non-dual dharmas, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness enter into the category of non-dual dharmas, even up to the knowledge of all modes entering into the category of non-dual dharmas?"
Subhūti replied: "Form is not different from non-arising, and non-arising is not different from form; form itself is non-arising, and non-arising itself is form."

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not different from non-arising; non-arising is not different from consciousness. Consciousness itself is non-arising, and non-arising itself is consciousness. For this reason, Śāriputra!

"The form aggregate enters into the category of non-dual dharmas; the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness aggregates enter into the category of non-dual dharmas; and so it is even for up to all-knowledge.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates all phenomena in this way, at that time they see that form is unarisen because it is ultimately pure;
they see that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unarisen because they are ultimately pure.
One sees that the self is unarisen, up to and including the knower and the seer, because they are ultimately pure.
One sees that the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is unarisen, up to and including the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because they are ultimately pure.
One perceives that from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence there is no arising, because they are ultimately pure.
One perceives that from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha there is no arising, because they are ultimately pure.
One sees that all samādhis and all dhāraṇīs are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
even up to seeing that all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is non-arising, because it is ultimately pure.
One sees that ordinary persons and the dharmas of ordinary persons are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.

One sees that the srotāpanna and the dharma of the srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin and the dharma of the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin and the dharma of the anāgāmin, the arhat and the dharma of the arhat, the pratyekabuddha and the dharma of the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva and the dharma of the bodhisattva, and the Buddha and the dharma of the Buddha are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.

Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "According to the meaning I have heard from what Subhūti has said, form is unarisen; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unarisen; and even up to the Buddha and the Buddha-dharmas, they are unarisen."

If that were so, one would now be unable to attain the stage of a srotāpanna or the fruit of srotāpanna; the stage of a sakṛdāgāmin or the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin; the stage of an anāgāmin or the fruit of anāgāmin; the stage of an arhat or the fruit of arhat; nor could one attain the path of a pratyekabuddha or the state of a pratyekabuddha. One would also be unable to attain the all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there would be no distinction between the six realms of existence, and one could not attain the five kinds of enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti! If all dharmas have the characteristic of non-arising, for what reason does the srotāpanna cultivate the path to sever the three fetters?
And why does the sakṛdāgāmin cultivate the path to attenuate lust, anger, and delusion?
Does the non-returner (anāgāmin) cultivate the path for the sake of severing the five lower fetters?
Does the arhat cultivate the path for the sake of severing the five upper fetters?
Does the pratyekabuddha cultivate the path for the sake of the pratyekabuddha-dharma?
For what reason do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform difficult practices and undergo various sufferings for the sake of sentient beings?
For what reason does the Buddha attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"For what reason does the Buddha turn the wheel of Dharma? Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"I do not wish for there to be anything attained within the dharma of non-arising; nor do I wish for one to attain the stage of a stream-enterer or the fruit of stream-entry within the dharma of non-arising, up to and including not wishing for one to attain the stage of an arhat or the fruit of arhatship, or the path of a pratyekabuddha or the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood within the dharma of non-arising."

I also do not wish to cause bodhisattvas to perform difficult practices for the sake of sentient beings by making them undergo various sufferings; nor does a bodhisattva practice the path with a mind that regards it as difficult. Why is this?
Śāriputra! One who gives rise to a mind of difficulty and a mind of suffering cannot benefit immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings. Śāriputra!
Now, the Bodhisattva out of compassion for sentient beings regards them as his parents and brothers, and as his children and even as his own self.
In this way, he is able to benefit immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, because he employs the principle of non-apprehension.
Why is this? A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to such a thought:
"Just as I am unapprehendable in all places and in all ways, so too are internal and external phenomena."
If one gives rise to such a conception, then there will be no mind of difficulty or suffering. Why is this?
It is because this bodhisattva does not accept any phenomena in any manner, at any place, or in any respect.

Śāriputra! I do not wish for a Buddha to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the state of non-arising; nor do I wish for the turning of the wheel of Dharma within the state of non-arising; nor do I wish for the attainment of the Way by means of the dharma of non-arising.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti, "Do you now intend that one attains the Way by means of dharmas that arise, or that one attains the Way by means of dharmas that do not arise?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"I do not wish for one to attain the Way by means of dharmas that arise. Śāriputra said:
"Does Subhūti now wish for one to attain the Way by means of dharmas that do not arise?"
Subhūti said: "I, too, do not wish for one to attain the Way by means of a dharma that is unarisen. Śāriputra said:
“As Subhūti has said, there is neither knowing nor attaining. Subhūti replied,
“There is knowing and there is attaining, yet not by means of dualistic dharmas.”

Now, it is by means of worldly designations that there is knowing and attaining; it is by means of worldly designations that there are those from the Stream-enterer up to the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddhas.
"In the ultimate reality, there is neither knowledge nor attainment; there is no stream-enterer, up to and including no Buddha.
"Subhūti! If it is by way of worldly designations that there is knowledge and attainment, then the distinctions among the six realms of existence also exist by way of worldly designations."
“Is it not by means of the foremost ultimate truth? Subhūti replied, “So it is, so it is!”
Śāriputra! Just as there is knowing and attaining due to worldly designations, so too the distinctions between the six realms of existence exist due to worldly designations;
they do not exist by way of the ultimate, true meaning.
Why is this? Śāriputra, within the ultimate reality,
there is neither karma nor retribution, neither arising nor ceasing, and neither purity nor defilement.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: “Does a non-arisen dharma arise?
Or does an arisen dharma arise?”
Subhūti said: "I do not wish to cause unarisen dharmas to arise, nor do I wish to cause arisen dharmas to arise. Śāriputra said:
“What are those non-arising phenomena that one does not wish to cause to arise?
Subhūti replied, “Form is a non-arising phenomenon; because its intrinsic nature is empty, one does not wish for it to arise.”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-arising phenomena; being empty of intrinsic nature, they do not desire to arise.
This extends even to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is a non-arising phenomenon; being empty of intrinsic nature, it does not desire to arise.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "Is it that which has already arisen? Or is it that which has not yet arisen?"
Subhūti said: “It is neither that which arises from arising, nor that which arises from non-arising. Why is this?”

Śāriputra! Arising and non-arising—these two dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance. They have but a single characteristic, which is called "characteristiclessness."
"Śāriputra! For this reason, it is neither that which arises from arising, nor that which arises from non-arising.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“Subhūti delights in speaking of non-arising dharmas and the characteristics of non-arising.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: “I delight in speaking of non-arising dharmas and I also delight in speaking of the characteristics of non-arising.”

Why is this? All dharmas—those dharmas that are unarisen, the characteristics of non-arising, and the eloquent discourse on them—are all neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are formless, shapeless, and without resistance; they have but a single characteristic, which is called "characteristiclessness."

Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "If you delight in speaking of non-arising dharmas and also delight in speaking of the characteristics of non-arising, is this speech that delights in speaking also non-arising?"
Subhūti said: "So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!"
Why is this? Śāriputra! Form does not arise;
sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not arise.

The eye does not arise, up to and including the mind; the earth element does not arise, up to and including the consciousness element; bodily formations do not arise, vocal formations do not arise, and mental formations do not arise; the perfection of giving does not arise, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) does not arise.

For these reasons, Śāriputra, I delight in speaking of non-arising dharmas and I also delight in speaking of the characteristics of non-arising; even this speech of delight in speaking is itself non-arising.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“Subhūti should be foremost among those who preach the Dharma. Why is this?”
"Subhūti is able to answer whatever is asked. Subhūti said:
"Because all dharmas have nothing upon which they rely."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "In what way are all dharmas without support? Subhūti replied:
"The nature of form is eternally empty; it does not depend on the internal, it does not depend on the external, nor does it depend on that which is between the two.

The natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are eternally empty; they do not depend on the internal, they do not depend on the external, nor do they depend on that which is between the two."
The nature of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is eternally empty; it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two.

The nature of form is eternally empty, and so on up to the nature of phenomena (dharma), which is eternally empty; it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two.

The nature of the perfection of giving is eternally empty, up to and including the nature of the perfection of wisdom, which is eternally empty; it does not rely on the internal, it does not rely on the external, nor does it rely on that which is between the two.

The emptiness of the internal is eternally empty, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence; it does not rely on the internal, it does not rely on the external, and it does not rely on that which is between the two.

Śāriputra! The nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is eternally empty, up to and including the nature of the knowledge of all modes, which is eternally empty; it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two.
For this reason, Śāriputra, all dharmas have no basis, because their nature is eternally empty. Thus it is, Śāriputra!
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, they should purify form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including purifying all-knowledge.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the bodhisattva path while practicing the six pāramitās?"
Subhūti said: "There is the mundane perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), and there is the supramundane perfection of giving.

There are also mundane and supramundane perfections of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), diligence (vīrya-pāramitā), meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā)."
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "What is the mundane perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?
What is the supramundane perfection of giving?"

Subhūti said: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva acts as a donor, able to give to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and impoverished beggars—giving food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, clothing to those who need clothing, bedding, couches, dwellings, incense, flowers, garlands, and medicines, as well as all kinds of necessary articles for livelihood; or even internal and external things such as wife, children, kingdom, head, eyes, hands, feet, limbs, and joints—if he gives these all away in charity."
At the time of giving, one forms this thought:
"I give and he receives; I am not stingy or greedy.
I am the donor; I am able to relinquish everything."
"I give in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; I practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Having made this offering, he employs the Dharma thus obtained in common with all sentient beings, dedicating it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and reflects:
"By the causal conditions of this giving, may sentient beings obtain happiness in the present life, and hereafter may they attain the bliss of nirvāṇa."
This person’s giving is characterized by three obstacles.
What are the three?
The mark of self, the mark of other, and the mark of giving.
To practice this threefold mark of giving is called the mundane *dānapāramitā*.
For what reason is it called mundane?
Because it neither moves nor emerges from within the world, it is called the mundane *dānapāramitā*.
What is called the supramundane dānapāramitā?
It is that which is pure in three aspects.
What are these three?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving, they do not apprehend a self, they do not perceive a recipient, they do not apprehend the gift, and they do not expect a reward; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) with the threefold purity.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, he bestows gifts upon all sentient beings, yet even these sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Dedicating this generosity toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one does not perceive even the subtlest marks of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*).
Śāriputra, this is called the supramundane *dāna-pāramitā*.
For what reason is it called "supramundane"?
Because it can move within and transcend the world, it is therefore called the supramundane dānapāramitā.
When the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) has a basis, it is called mundane śīlapāramitā; when it is without a basis, it is supramundane śīlapāramitā.
The rest is as explained in the *Dānapāramitā*.
Regarding the *Kṣāntipāramitā*, *Vīryapāramitā*, *Dhyānapāramitā*, and *Prajñāpāramitā*, that which has a basis is called mundane; that which is without a basis is called supramundane.
The rest is also as explained in the *Dānapāramitā*. Thus, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he purifies the bodhisattva path.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the path to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Subhūti replied:

“The four foundations of mindfulness are the path for a bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment; and so on, up to the eightfold noble path; the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; all gates of samādhi and all gates of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.”
“Śāriputra! This is called the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! By the power of which pāramitā? Subhūti replied:
"This is the power of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Why is this so? Because the Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all wholesome dharmas—whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas."
Śāriputra! The prajñāpāramitā is able to receive all wholesome dharmas: the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of buddhas.

Śāriputra! The Buddhas of the past practiced the prajñāpāramitā and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; the Buddhas of the future will also practice the prajñāpāramitā and shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! Now, in all the lands of the ten directions at present, the Buddhas likewise practice this Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears the teaching of the prajñāpāramitā and neither doubts nor objects to it, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the bodhisattva path.
One who practices the bodhisattva path, for the sake of rescuing all sentient beings, does not abandon any sentient being in mind.
Because of non-apprehension, this bodhisattva should always remain inseparable from this thought, namely, the thought of great compassion.
Śāriputra asked again:
"If one wishes to cause a bodhisattva mahāsattva to never be separated from this mindfulness— namely, the mindfulness of great compassion—
and if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is always not separated from the mindfulness of great compassion, then all sentient beings would now become bodhisattvas."
Why is this? Subhūti!
It is because all sentient beings are likewise not apart from various thoughts.
Subhūti said: "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!"
You wish to challenge me in order to establish my thesis. Why is this?

Because sentient beings do not exist, mindfulness does not exist; because the nature of sentient beings does not exist, the nature of mindfulness does not exist; because the phenomena of sentient beings do not exist, the phenomena of mindfulness do not exist; because sentient beings are detached, mindfulness is also detached; because sentient beings are empty, mindfulness is also empty; and because sentient beings are unknowable, mindfulness is also unknowable.

Śāriputra! Because form (*rūpa*) does not exist, mindfulness (*smṛti*) also does not exist; because the nature of form does not exist, the nature of mindfulness also does not exist; because the phenomenon of form does not exist, the phenomenon of mindfulness also does not exist; because form is detached, mindfulness is also detached; because form is empty, mindfulness is also empty; because form is unknowable, mindfulness is also unknowable.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

From the eye up to the mind, from forms up to mental phenomena, from the earth element up to the consciousness element; from the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all gates of samādhi, all gates of dhāraṇī, and from all-knowledge and all-aspect knowledge up to unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment—because these do not exist, mindfulness also does not exist. Up to unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment being unknowable, mindfulness is also unknowable.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this path, I desire that they never be separated from this mindfulness—namely, the mindfulness of great compassion.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
This Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas should be explained by whoever speaks of it in this very manner.
All that you have said regarding the Prajñāpāramitā is because you have received the Buddha’s intention.”
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom should train as you have described.
When Subhūti spoke this chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways:

it rose in the east and sank in the west; it rose in the west and sank in the east; it rose in the south and sank in the north; it rose in the north and sank in the south; it rose in the center and sank at the edges; and it rose at the edges and sank in the center.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what cause and condition do you smile?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Just as I am teaching the Prajñāpāramitā in this land, so too do the Buddhas in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya lands to the east teach the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, they also teach this Prajñāpāramitā.”
When this chapter on the *Prajñāpāramitā* was being taught, twelve *nayutas* of devas and humans attained the realization of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the Buddhas of the ten directions teach this *Prajñāpāramitā*, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings likewise resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Chapter 27: Inquiry on Abiding (*Vihāra-parivarta*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, this is the twenty-seventh chapter, "Inquiry on Abiding" (the Danzang edition titles it "The Chapter on the Heavenly Lord"). At that time, the Four Great Kings of the Trichiliocosm, each accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of billions of devas, came together to join the assembly.

The Śakras of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, the kings of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the kings of the Suyāma heaven, the kings of the Yāma heaven, the kings of the Tuṣita heaven, the kings of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, the kings of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, and the gods of the Vaśavartin heaven—all came to the assembly together with countless hundreds of thousands of billions of devas.

The Brahma Kings of the three thousand great thousandfold world systems, up to and including the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, each accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of billions of devas, came together to the assembly.

The light from the bodies born of karmic retribution belonging to these gods, from the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, does not shine nor manifest when compared to even a hundredth or a thousandth part of the Buddha’s constant radiance; it is like a charred pillar compared to Jambūnada gold.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
"All the gods from the Four Great Kings of this trichiliocosm up to those of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens have assembled together, desiring to hear Subhūti explain the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā."
Subhūti! How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell within the perfection of wisdom?
What is this perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Kauśika!..."
I shall now, following the Buddha’s intention and sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, expound the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
O sons of the gods! As to how a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should abide within the Prajñāpāramitā—[listen].
Those who have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should now resolve their minds toward it.
However, O sons of the gods, those who have entered the fixed stage of the śrāvaka cannot resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because it creates a barrier between them and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
If such a person should resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I too shall rejoice in it.
Why is this? A superior person should seek even higher dharmas; I shall never obstruct their merit. Kausika!
What is the perfection of wisdom?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), contemplates form as impermanent, contemplates form as suffering, contemplates form as empty, and contemplates form as non-self; he contemplates form as being like a disease, like a festering ulcer, like an arrow piercing the body—painful, afflictive, decaying, fearful, and unstable—because of the principle of non-apprehension.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

Regarding the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—one contemplates them as impermanent, up to being sorrowful, fearful, and unstable, because these too are non-apprehendable.
One contemplates that form is quiescent and detached, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.

One contemplates that the element of earth, up to the element of consciousness, is quiescent and detached, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, because nothing can be apprehended therein.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā), contemplates that ignorance conditions the formative forces (saṃskāra), and so on, up to the mass of great suffering conditioned by old age and death; yet, because there is nothing to be apprehended therein, he does not perceive them."

One contemplates that because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; and so on, until because birth ceases, old age and death cease; and because old age and death cease, the entire mass of suffering—sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair—ceases, for there is nothing to be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā), cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness by way of non-apprehension."
...up to the cultivation of the Buddha’s ten powers and eighteen unique qualities, because they are non-apprehendable.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
corresponding with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), because it is non-apprehendable."
They practice the perfection of śīla, the perfection of kṣānti, the perfection of vīrya, and the perfection of dhyāna, because they do so by way of non-apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he contemplates in this way:

'It is merely that all phenomena (dharmas) mutually act as causes and conditions for one another, providing moisture, benefit, growth, and conceptual calculation; herein there is no self and nothing belonging to a self. The mind of dedication does not exist within the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not exist within the mind of dedication. The mind of dedication cannot be apprehended within the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be apprehended within the mind of dedication.'"
"Although a bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas, there is no dharma that can be apprehended; this is called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"In what way does the mind of dedication not reside within the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
How is it that the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not abide within the mind of dedication?
How is it that the mind of dedication cannot be apprehended within the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"How is it that the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be apprehended within the mind of dedication?
Subhūti said to Śakra-devānām-indra: "Kauśika!..."
The mind of dedication and the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are not minds; they are the characteristic of non-mind. Within the characteristic of non-mind, there can be no dedication.

This non-characteristic of mind is eternally a non-characteristic of mind; this inconceivable characteristic is eternally an inconceivable characteristic. This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"You have expounded the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and you have brought comfort to the minds of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I ought to repay their kindness; I should not fail to repay it.

In the past, the Buddhas and their disciples taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened the Bodhisattvas by expounding the six pāramitās. At that time, the World-Honored One was also among them, training therein and attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I shall now likewise expound the six pāramitās for the sake of all bodhisattvas, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them, so that they may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām-indra:
"Kauśika, you should now listen to how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide and how they should not abide within the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Kauśika! Form is empty of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
A bodhisattva is empty of being a bodhisattva.

This emptiness of form and the emptiness of the bodhisattva are non-dual and not distinct; the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and the emptiness of the bodhisattva are non-dual and not distinct. Kausika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
