Furthermore, the eye is empty of the eye, and so on up to the mind being empty of the mind; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
The emptiness of the eye and the emptiness of the bodhisattva are non-dual and not distinct.
The same applies to the six sense objects.
The earth element is empty of the earth element, and so on, up to the consciousness element being empty of the consciousness element.
A bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.
Kausika! The element of earth is empty, up to and including the element of consciousness; the emptiness of the bodhisattva is non-dual and not distinct from them.
Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in this manner within the perfection of wisdom:
ignorance is empty of ignorance, and so on, up to old age and death being empty of old age and death.
The cessation of ignorance is the emptiness of the cessation of ignorance; and so on, up to the cessation of old age and death is the emptiness of the cessation of old age and death.
A bodhisattva is the emptiness of a bodhisattva. Kausika!

The emptiness of ignorance up to the emptiness of old age and death, and the emptiness of the cessation of ignorance up to the emptiness of the cessation of old age and death—the emptiness of the bodhisattva is non-dual and undifferentiated from these. Kausika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in this manner within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). This applies to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom;

from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); all gateways of samādhi and all gateways of dhāraṇī; the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the buddhas; likewise for the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the buddha; and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is empty of the knowledge of all modes.
The bodhisattva is empty;
omniscience is empty. The emptiness of the bodhisattva and the emptiness of omniscience are non-dual and not distinct, Kauśika!
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell thus within the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra asked Subhūti:
“In what way should one not dwell within the perfection of wisdom?”
Subhūti said: "Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell within form."
Because of apprehending something,
one should not dwell within feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness; because of apprehending something.
One should not abide in the eye, nor even in the mind; one should not abide in forms, nor even in mental phenomena (*dharma*).

One should not abide in visual consciousness up to mental consciousness, in visual contact up to mental contact, or in the feelings produced by conditions of visual contact up to the feelings produced by conditions of mental contact.
Because they involve apprehension,
one should not dwell upon the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness.
Because they involve apprehension.
One should not dwell in the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, nor in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
because these involve the apprehension of something obtainable.
One should not dwell in the fruit of stream-entry,
because it involves apprehension of an object. Likewise,
one should not dwell in the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, the path of the Buddha, or in omniscience.
Because there is something to be apprehended.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell on the notion that form is permanent, nor should they dwell on the notion that form is impermanent; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One should not dwell on form as being either pleasant or painful, pure or impure, self or non-self, empty or non-empty, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached.
Because there is something apprehended.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Furthermore, Kausika!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell upon the unconditioned mark of the fruit of stream-entry, the unconditioned mark of the fruit of once-returning, the unconditioned mark of the fruit of non-returning, or the unconditioned mark of the fruit of arhatship.
One should not dwell on the unconditioned mark of the path of the pratyekabuddha, nor on the unconditioned mark of the path of the Buddha.
One should not dwell on the field of merit of the srotāpanna; one should not dwell on the fields of merit of the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell in the first stage because of the apprehension of something to be attained."
One should not dwell even in the ten stages because they involve the apprehension of something to be attained.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the initial resolve should not dwell on the thought, "I shall fulfill the dāna-pāramitā."
Even up to: "I shall fulfill the perfection of wisdom"—one should not dwell therein.
"Having fulfilled the six perfections, I shall enter the stage of a bodhisattva"—one should not dwell therein.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, one should not dwell on the thought that "I shall abide in the stage of non-retrogression.
A bodhisattva should fulfill the five supernormal powers, yet should not dwell therein,
because they involve apprehension of an object.

Once the bodhisattva has established himself in the five supernormal powers, he shall travel to immeasurable asaṃkhyeya buddha-fields to pay homage to, revere, and make offerings to all Buddhas and listen to the Dharma; having listened to the Dharma, he shall explain it for the sake of others.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell in such a manner, because it involves apprehending something as an object.
Nor should they dwell thinking, "Just as the buddha-fields of all the Buddhas are adorned and purified, so shall I also adorn and purify a buddha-field."
Because there is something to be attained, one should not dwell on the thought that one should bring sentient beings to maturity and cause them to enter the Buddha-way.

One should not dwell on the thought that one should go to the abodes of the Buddhas in immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* lands to honor, revere, and make offerings to them, using incense, flowers, necklaces, fragrant unguents, powdered incense, banners, flags, canopies, and hundreds of thousands of billions of kinds of precious robes to make offerings to those Buddhas.
Because of the notion of attainment, one should not abide in the thought:
"I shall cause immeasurable, incalculable sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Thus, a bodhisattva should not dwell therein.
"I shall produce the five eyes—the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye"—he should not dwell upon this.
"I shall produce all gateways to samādhi"—he should not dwell upon this.
One should not dwell on the thought, "I shall sport at will in all the samādhis";
one should not dwell on the thought, "I shall give birth to all the doors of dhāraṇī";
one should not dwell on the thought, "I shall attain the ten powers of a Buddha."
"I shall attain the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique dharmas"—one should not dwell upon this.
"I shall be fully endowed with great loving-kindness and great compassion"—one should not dwell upon this.
I should not dwell on the thought, "I shall be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks," nor should I dwell on the thought,
"I shall be fully endowed with the eighty secondary characteristics," because these involve the apprehension of something as an object.

One should not dwell on the thought that "these eight persons are followers by faith" or "these are followers of the Dharma," nor should one dwell on the thought that "a stream-enterer will be reborn at most seven more times."
One should not dwell on the idea that [a stream-enterer] will go from family to family; one should not dwell on the idea that a stream-enterer’s life will end with the exhaustion of defilements;
one should not dwell on the idea that a stream-enterer will enter nirvana in the intermediate state.
One should not dwell on the thought that this person is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin;
one should not dwell on the thought that this person, as a Sakṛdāgāmin, will enter nirvāṇa after returning once more to this world;
one should not dwell on the thought that this person is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of Anāgāmin.
One should not dwell on the thought that "this person is a sakṛdāgāmin of one remaining birth";
nor should one dwell on the thought that "this person is an anāgāmin who will enter nirvāṇa in that very realm";
nor should one dwell on the thought that "this person is one who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of arhatship."
One should not dwell on the thought: "I am an Arhat who shall enter nirvana without remainder in this very life.
One should not dwell on the thought: "I am a Pratyekabuddha.
One should not dwell on the thought: "Having transcended the stages of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, I shall abide in the stage of a Bodhisattva."
One should not dwell in the knowledge of the aspects of the path,
because it involves apprehension.
Having known all aspects and all phenomena, one should not dwell in the abandonment of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies.
One should not dwell on the thought that the Buddha, having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, should turn the wheel of Dharma;
nor should one dwell on the thought that he should perform the work of a Buddha by delivering immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings and leading them into *nirvāṇa*.
One should not dwell in the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
One should not dwell in entering this samādhi and remaining for a lifespan as long as the sands of the Ganges River.
One should not dwell in the thought, "I shall attain a lifespan of incalculable eons."
One should not dwell on the thirty-two marks, each adorned with a hundred merits;
nor should one dwell on the thought that "my single world is like worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions."
"I should not dwell in the thought that my trichiliocosm is composed entirely of vajra.

My Bodhi tree shall emit such fragrance that any sentient beings who smell it will be free from lust, anger, and ignorance; they will have no thoughts of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and all these people will surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

If sentient beings were to hear this fragrance, and if in my world there were not even the name of the *dānapāramitā*, up to and including the name of the *prajñāpāramitā*; if in my world there were not even the names of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the names of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and if there were also no name for the *srotāpanna*, up to and including the name of a Buddha—then one should not dwell [in such a state].
Because there is something to be attained. Why is this?
When the Buddhas attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they find that all dharmas are unattainable.
"In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva should not dwell upon the perfection of wisdom because of the apprehension of something to be attained.
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"How, then, should a bodhisattva now dwell within the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti, knowing what was in Śāriputra’s mind, said to him:
"What do you think? Where do the Buddhas dwell?"
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: “The dharmas of all Buddhas have no place of abiding. All Buddhas do not abide in form;

they do not abide in sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not abide in the conditioned nature, nor do they abide in the unconditioned nature; they do not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they do not abide in the knowledge of all modes.”
“Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in this way within the perfection of wisdom.
Just as the Buddhas dwell— in all phenomena neither dwelling nor not dwelling— so should they.”
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom in this way:
"I shall abide by means of the dharma of non-abiding."
At that time, there were among those in the assembly certain sons of the gods who thought to themselves:

“The speech, words, and phrases spoken by the yakṣas can still be understood; however, the speech, discourse, and explanations concerning the *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by Subhūti are utterly impossible to comprehend.”
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them:
"Do you not understand? Do you not know?
The sons of the gods replied:
"Venerable sirs!
I do not understand; I do not know.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"You should naturally not know that I have nothing to discourse upon; indeed, I do not speak even a single word, nor is there anyone who listens.

Why is this? All syllables are not the *prajñāpāramitā*, and within the *prajñāpāramitā* there is no listener. The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas is without syllables and without discourse."
"O sons of the gods!

It is as if a Buddha were to manifest a transformed being, and that transformed being were further to manifest the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—and this transformed being were then to preach the Dharma within that fourfold assembly."
"What do you think? In this matter, is there a speaker, a listener, or a knower?
The devaputras replied, "No, Great Virtue!"
Subhūti said: "All dharmas are like transformations; herein there is no speaker, no listener, and no knower.
O sons of the gods!"
Suppose, for example, that a person sees a Buddha preaching the Dharma in a dream. What do you think: in this situation, is there a speaker, a listener, or a knower?
The devaputras replied,
“No, Venerable One! Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"All dharmas are like dreams; there is no speaker, no listener, and no knower.
O sons of the gods!
It is as if two people were on opposite sides of a vast, deep ravine, each praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and two echoes emerged."
"What do you think, sons of the gods? Do these two echoes understand one another?
The sons of the gods replied, "No, Venerable One!"
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"All dharmas are likewise: there is no speaker, no listener, and no knower. O devaputras!"
For example, suppose a skilled illusionist were to manifest at a crossroads a Buddha and the fourfold assembly, and therein preach the Dharma.
What do you think, O sons of gods: in this, is there anyone who speaks, anyone who listens, or anyone who understands?
At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"What Subhūti has spoken is intended to be easy to understand, yet it becomes ever more profound and ever more subtle.
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, addressed them, saying:
“Form is neither profound nor subtle; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither profound nor subtle.
The nature of form is neither profound nor subtle; the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither profound nor subtle.”

The nature of the eye up to the nature of the mind; the nature of forms up to the nature of phenomena; the nature of the eye-element up to the nature of the mind-element; eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; eye-contact up to mind-contact; and feeling born of conditions consisting of eye-contact up to feeling born of conditions consisting of mind-contact.

From the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all gateways of samādhi and all gateways of dhāraṇī; up to all-knowledge and the nature of all-knowledge—none of these are deep or subtle.

The sons of the gods again had this thought: "In this teaching of the Dharma, form is not spoken of; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not spoken of; from eye-contact up to mind-contact, and the feelings born of their conditions, these are not spoken of; the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom are not spoken of; inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence are not spoken of; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not spoken of; the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi up to all-knowledge are not spoken of; the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship are not spoken of; the path of the pratyekabuddha is not spoken of; and the path of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is not spoken of."
"In this Dharma, names and speech are not spoken.
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them: "So it is, so it is!"
"O sons of the gods!
Within this Dharma, the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is an ineffable characteristic; therein is no speaker, no listener, and no knower."
For this reason, O sons of the gods!

A son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer and wishes to realize the fruit of a stream-enterer, that person does not depart from this patience.
Whether one wishes to abide in or realize the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, the path of a Pratyekabuddha, or the path of a Buddha, one cannot do so apart from this patience.
Thus it is, O sons of the gods!
From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in this manner within the perfection of wisdom, because there is neither speaker nor listener.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Seven;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 28: On Hearing Like an Illusion (The "On People Hearing Like an Illusion" version in the Dan edition is titled "On Illusory People Hearing the Dharma").
At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"By what kind of people should the Dharma taught by Subhūti be heard?"
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them:
"I should employ people who are like illusory transformations to listen to the Dharma."
"Why is this? Because such a person has neither heard nor listened, neither known nor realized.
The devaputras said to Subhūti:
“Are these sentient beings like illusions, and those who hear the Dharma also like illusions?
Are sentient beings like magical transformations, and those who hear the Dharma also like magical transformations? “It is so, it is so!”
O sons of the gods!
Sentient beings are like illusions, and those who hear the Dharma are also like illusions;
sentient beings are like transformations, and those who hear the Dharma are also like transformations.
O sons of the gods!
I am like an illusion and like a dream; sentient beings, up to and including those who know and those who see, are also like illusions and like dreams.
O sons of the gods!

Form is like an illusion, like a dream; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like illusions, like dreams. From the eye up to the feelings produced by the conditions of contact with the mind, they are like illusions, like dreams.
Internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, are like illusions, like dreams.
O sons of the gods!

The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are like an illusion and like a dream; the fruit of a stream-enterer is like an illusion and like a dream; the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha are like an illusion and like a dream.
"O sons of the gods!
The Buddha-way is like an illusion and like a dream.
At that time, the sons of the gods asked Subhūti:
“You have said that the Buddha-way is like an illusion and like a dream; do you also say that nirvāṇa is likewise like an illusion and like a dream?
Subhūti addressed the devaputras:
“I say that the Buddha-way is like an illusion and like a dream; I say that nirvāṇa is also like an illusion and like a dream.”
If there were any phenomenon superior to nirvāṇa, I would say that it, too, is like an illusion and like a dream. Why is this?
O sons of the gods!
"Thus, illusion and dreams, and nirvāṇa, are neither two nor distinct.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākāśyapa, and countless thousands of bodhisattvas asked Subhūti:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is thus exceedingly profound; it is difficult to see, difficult to understand, and difficult to know—tranquil, subtle, and wondrous."
“Who, then, shall receive it?
At that time, Ānanda spoke to the great disciples and the bodhisattvas:

“The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) are able to receive this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is difficult to see, difficult to understand, difficult to know, and which is quiescent and subtle.”
Those who have achieved right view, the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted and whose aspirations are fulfilled, are likewise able to believe and accept it.

Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family who have frequently seen the Buddhas, made many offerings at the abodes of the Buddhas, planted roots of goodness, associated with spiritual friends, and possess sharp faculties—such persons are able to receive it and do not say that this is the Dharma or that it is not the Dharma.

Subhūti said: “One does not differentiate form by means of emptiness, nor does one differentiate emptiness by means of form; it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

One does not differentiate form by means of signlessness or wishlessness, nor does one differentiate signlessness or wishlessness by means of form; it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”

One does not, by means of non-arising, non-ceasing, quiescence, or the departure from conceptualization, take form as the basis for distinguishing non-arising, non-ceasing, quiescence, or departure; and it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It is the same for the feelings produced by conditions such as eye-contact, up to mind-contact. It is the same for the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*;

for internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); for the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); for all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī; and for the stream-enterer up to the arhat, pratyekabuddha, Buddha, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). One does not differentiate omniscience by means of emptiness, nor does one differentiate emptiness by means of omniscience. One does not differentiate the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) by means of emptiness, nor does one differentiate emptiness by means of the knowledge of all modes. It is the same for signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-arising, non-ceasing, quiescence, and detachment.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profound; who is able to receive it?
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can be shown, and no dharma that can be spoken."
"If there is no dharma that can be shown and no dharma that can be spoken, then even the recipient cannot be apprehended.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Within the Prajñāpāramitā, the teachings of the three vehicles are extensively expounded, as well as the teachings for protecting and sustaining bodhisattvas."

From the stage of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment up to the tenth stage, from the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and from the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities—these protect the teaching of the Bodhisattvas.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they are always born through transformation (*upapāduka*), do not lose their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and travel through various buddha-fields fully endowed with roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Whatever they desire to offer to the Buddhas, they obtain according to their wish; from those Buddhas, they hear and receive the teachings of the Dharma, such that until they reach *sarvajñā*, it is never interrupted, and they are never apart from samādhi.
One shall attain swift eloquence, sharp eloquence, inexhaustible eloquence, unassailable eloquence, appropriate eloquence, eloquence regarding meaning, and the supreme eloquence of all the world.
Subhūti said: "So it is, so it is! It is as Śāriputra has said:

the Prajñāpāramitā extensively expounds the teachings of the three vehicles and the teachings for the protection and sustenance of bodhisattvas, up to and including the fact that even the attainment by a bodhisattva mahāsattva of the most supreme eloquence in all the world is ultimately unattainable."

This is because the self, up to and including the knower and the seer, cannot be apprehended; form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, cannot be apprehended; internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, cannot be apprehended; and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-knowledge, likewise cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"By what causes and conditions is it that within the Prajñāpāramitā the three vehicles are extensively explained, yet cannot be apprehended?"
For what cause and condition does the Prajñāpāramitā protect and sustain the bodhisattva?
For what cause and condition do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain swift eloquence, up to the supreme eloquence of all the world?
"Because they are unattainable. Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Because of internal emptiness, the three vehicles cannot be attained as extensively explained in the Prajñāpāramitā."
Because of the emptiness of the external, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the three vehicles are extensively explained as being unattainable.
Because of the emptiness of the internal, one protects and maintains the bodhisattva, up to the supreme eloquence of all the world.
Because they are ungraspable;
because of the emptiness of the external up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, one protects and maintains the bodhisattva and even the supreme eloquence of all the world.
"Because it is unattainable. 29.

Chapter on Scattering Flowers, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Nine. At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra and all the devas from the Four Great Kings in the trichiliocosm up to those in the Akaniṣṭha heaven had this thought:
"The Venerable Subhūti is raining down the rain of Dharma."
"We would rather transform ourselves into flowers and scatter them over the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the community of bhikṣus, Subhūti, and the Prajñāpāramitā."

Immediately, Śakra-devānām-indra and all the devas within the trichiliocosm manifested flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the community of bhikṣus, and Subhūti, thereby making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā as well.
At that time, flowers completely filled the void of the trichiliocosm, transforming into flower pedestals that were exquisite and sublime.
Subhūti thought to himself:
"These flowers scattered by the devaputras are unlike any flowers I have ever seen in the heavens; these flowers are conjured flowers, not flowers grown from trees."
"These flowers scattered by the sons of the gods are born from the wish-fulfilling trees; they are not flowers born from ordinary trees.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing what Subhūti was thinking in his mind, said to Subhūti:
"Venerable One!"
"These flowers are not born from plants, nor are they produced by mind-born trees.
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra, "Kauśika!..."
You say that these flowers are not born from seeds nor produced by a mental tree.
Kausika! If these flowers were not phenomena that arise, they could not be called flowers.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"Venerable One!
It is not only these flowers that are unarisen; form is also unarisen, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise unarisen."
Subhūti said: “Kauśika!
It is not only these flowers that are unarisen; form, too, is unarisen.”
If they do not arise, they are not called form (*rūpa*).
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise do not arise; if they do not arise, they are not called consciousness.
The same applies to the six sense bases, the six consciousnesses, and the six contacts, as well as the various feelings produced through the conditions of the six contacts.
The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is non-arising; if it is non-arising, it is not called the perfection of giving.
This continues up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is non-arising; if it is non-arising, it is not called the perfection of wisdom.
Internal emptiness is non-arising; if it were not arising, it would not be called internal emptiness.
This extends up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is non-arising; if it were not arising, it would not be called the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
The four foundations of mindfulness do not arise; if they do not arise, they are not called the four foundations of mindfulness.
This extends up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which do not arise; if they do not arise, they are not called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), if it does not arise, then it is not called 'all-knowledge.
At that time, Śakra Devendra thought to himself:
"This Venerable Subhūti possesses profound wisdom; he explains the characteristics of all phenomena without destroying conventional designations."
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the mind of Śakra Devānām Indra, said to him: "So it is, so it is! Kausika!"
"Subhūti’s wisdom is profoundly deep; he speaks of the characteristics of all dharmas without destroying conventional designations.
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Venerable Subhūti, how is it that he explains the characteristics of all dharmas without destroying conventional designations?
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
“Form is merely a conventional designation; Subhūti explains the characteristics of all dharmas without destroying conventional designations.”

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are merely provisional designations; Subhūti also speaks of the characteristics of all phenomena without destroying these provisional designations. Why is this?
Because these characteristics of all phenomena are neither destroyed nor not destroyed, and what Subhūti speaks of is likewise neither destroyed nor not destroyed.
The same applies to the various feelings arising from the conditions of contact through the eye up to the mind.

The same applies to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), to inner emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*), and to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).

It is the same for the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, the path of the Buddha, all-knowledge, and the knowledge of all aspects.

From the stream-enterer up to the arhat and the pratyekabuddha, "Buddha" is merely a provisional designation; Subhūti, without destroying these provisional designations, explains the characteristics of all dharmas.
Why is this? Because these characteristics of all phenomena are neither destroyed nor indestructible; what Subhūti has spoken is likewise neither destroyed nor indestructible. Thus it is, Kauśika!
“Subhūti does not destroy conventional designations while he speaks of the characteristics of all dharmas.
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: “So it is, so it is!”
Kauśika! As the Buddha has taught, all dharmas are merely provisional names.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand in this way: all dharmas are merely provisional names.
One should train in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way.
Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not train in form, nor do they train in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive form as something that can be learned, nor does one perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as something that can be learned.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they are training in the non-training of the dāna-pāramitā.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) as something that should be learned;
and so on, up to not learning the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this? Because one does not perceive a *prajñāpāramitā* that should be studied.
To study in such a manner is to not study anything from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, as something that can be studied.
To study in this manner is to not study the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as something that can be learned.
To train in this manner is to not train for the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Why is this? Because one does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including all-knowledge, as something that can be learned.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
“For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not see form, nor even see the knowledge of all modes?
Subhūti replied, “Form is empty of form,
and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes being empty of the knowledge of all modes.”
Kauśika! Form is empty and does not train in the emptiness of form; likewise, up to and including all-knowledge, it is empty and does not train in the emptiness of all-knowledge. Kauśika!
If one does not train in emptiness in such a manner, this is called training in emptiness, because of non-duality.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the emptiness of form because of non-duality, and so on, up to training in the emptiness of all-knowledge because of non-duality.

If they train because form and emptiness are non-dual, up to training because the emptiness of all-knowledge is non-dual, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to train in the dānapāramitā because of its non-duality.
Up to and including the ability to study the *prajñāpāramitā*, because of non-duality;
the ability to study the four foundations of mindfulness, because of non-duality;
up to and including the ability to study the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), because of non-duality.
One can study the fruit of srotāpanna because of non-duality;
up to and including one can study all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) because of non-duality.

This bodhisattva can study immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddha-dharmas; if they can study immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddha-dharmas, this bodhisattva does not train for the increase of form (*rūpa*), nor do they train for the decrease of form.
He does not train for the increase of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor does he train for its decrease.

If he does not train for the increase or decrease of form (*rūpa*), and so on up to the increase or decrease of all-knowledge, then this bodhisattva does not train for the apprehension of form, nor does he train for its cessation; likewise, he does not train for the apprehension of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he train for their cessation.
"Even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not train for the sake of grasping it, nor does one train for the sake of extinguishing it. Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he does not train for the sake of grasping form (*rūpa*), nor does he train for the sake of extinguishing form."
"Even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not train for the sake of grasping it, nor does one train for the sake of extinguishing it. Subhūti said:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he does not train for the sake of grasping form (*rūpa*), nor does he train for the sake of extinguishing form."
Even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not train for its acquisition, nor does one train for its cessation. Subhūti,
for what reason and by what causal conditions does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not train for the acquisition of form, nor train for the cessation of form?
“...up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), is it not for the sake of grasping that one trains, nor for the sake of extinguishing that one trains? Subhūti replied:

“This form (*rūpa*) cannot be grasped, nor is there anyone who grasps form; up to and including all-knowledge, it cannot be grasped, nor is there anyone who grasps it, because of internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).”
"In this way, Śāriputra,
because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any phenomena, they are able to reach all-knowledge.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“By training in the perfection of wisdom in this way, can a bodhisattva mahāsattva reach all-knowledge? Subhūti replied,
“By training in the perfection of wisdom in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can reach all-knowledge, because they do not grasp at any dharma.”
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains by neither grasping nor extinguishing any phenomena, how can that bodhisattva mahāsattva reach all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)?"

Subhūti said: “When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising of form, nor does he perceive the cessation of form; he does not perceive the acceptance of form, nor does he perceive the non-acceptance of form; he does not perceive the defilement of form, nor does he perceive the purification of form; he does not perceive the increase of form, nor does he perceive the decrease of form.”

Why is this? Śāriputra, because the nature of form is empty, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither seen to arise nor seen to cease; they are neither seen to be grasped nor seen to be ungrasped; they are neither seen to be defiled nor seen to be pure; and they are neither seen to increase nor seen to decrease.
Why is this? Because the nature of consciousness is empty.

This extends even to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*): one neither perceives its arising nor its cessation; one neither perceives its acceptance nor its non-acceptance; one neither perceives its defilement nor its purity; and one neither perceives its increase nor its decrease.
Why is this? Because all-knowledge is empty of the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge. Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Because all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither accepted nor rejected, neither defiled nor pure, neither conjoined nor dispersed, and neither increasing nor decreasing, the bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the prajñāpāramitā and is thus able to reach all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
"Because there is nothing to be learned and nothing to be reached.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Śāriputra:
"Where should one seek the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?"
Śāriputra said: "The Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should be sought within the 'Subhūti Chapter'.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra spoke to Subhūti:
"It is by your spiritual power that you caused Śāriputra to say:
'The Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should be sought within the "Subhūti Chapter."'"
Subhūti said to Śakra-devānām-indra: "It is not through my supernatural power."
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti,
"By whose spiritual power is this? Subhūti replied:
"This is the Buddha's supernatural power.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"All dharmas are without a place of reception; why, then, do you say this?"
"This is the Buddha's spiritual power.
Apart from the mark of the state of non-apprehension, the Tathāgata cannot be found.
"Apart from suchness, a Tathāgata also cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "So it is, so it is!"
Kauśika! Apart from the characteristic of the signless state of non-apprehension, the Tathāgata cannot be found;
apart from suchness, the Tathāgata likewise cannot be found.
In the characteristic of the absence of a locus for sensation, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended; in suchness, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended.
Within the suchness of form, the suchness of the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended; within the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of form cannot be apprehended.

Within the characteristics of form-dharmas, the characteristic of the Tathāgata-dharma cannot be apprehended; within the characteristic of the Tathāgata-dharma, the characteristic of form-dharmas cannot be apprehended.
This applies likewise to the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), in accordance with the Dharma.

Kauśika! The Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined within the suchness of form; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined within the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The Tathāgata is apart from the suchness of form, neither conjoined nor disjoined; he is apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, neither conjoined nor disjoined.
This applies even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined from the characteristic of form (*rūpadharma-lakṣaṇa*); he is neither conjoined nor disjoined from the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna-dharma-lakṣaṇa*).

The Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined from the characteristic marks of the dharma of form; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined from the characteristic marks of the dharmas of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This applies even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Kauśika! Within all such dharmas as these, there is neither conjunction nor dispersion; this is due to the Buddha’s spiritual power, which employs the dharma of non-apprehension.
As Kauśika has said:
“Where should one seek the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva? “Kauśika!
One should not seek the Prajñāpāramitā within form (rūpa), nor should one seek the Prajñāpāramitā apart from form.”
One should not seek it within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor should one seek it apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā, as well as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance; they have but a single characteristic, which is called "characteristiclessness."
One should not seek the perfection of wisdom within all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor should one seek the perfection of wisdom apart from all-knowledge.

Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā and all-knowledge—these are all dharmas that are neither conjoined nor dispersed, without form, without shape, and without resistance; they have but one mark, which is the so-called "markless."

Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither form nor separate from form; it is neither feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to: it is neither the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) nor is it separate from the knowledge of all modes.

The *prajñāpāramitā* is neither the suchness (*tathatā*) of form nor is it apart from the suchness of form; it is neither the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

The *prajñāpāramitā* is neither the dharma of form nor is it apart from the dharma of form; it is neither the dharma of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it apart from the dharma of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to: it is neither the suchness of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) nor is it apart from the suchness of the knowledge of all modes.
The perfection of wisdom is neither the dharma of omniscience nor is it apart from the dharma of omniscience.
Why is this, Kauśika?
All these dharmas are non-existent and unattainable. Because they are non-existent and unattainable, the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither form nor apart from form;

it is neither the suchness of form nor apart from the suchness of form; it is neither the dharma of form nor apart from the dharma of form. This extends up to: it is neither the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) nor apart from the knowledge of all modes; it is neither the suchness of the knowledge of all modes nor apart from the suchness of the knowledge of all modes; it is neither the dharma of the knowledge of all modes nor apart from the dharma of the knowledge of all modes.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"This great pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
this immeasurable pāramitā, this boundless pāramitā, is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
All stream-enterers and the fruit of stream-entry are accomplished through training in this perfection of wisdom.

Likewise, all arhats and the fruit of arhatship, all pratyekabuddhas and the path of the pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are accomplished through training in this perfection of wisdom.
"One is able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-lands;
the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is all accomplished through learning from this.
Subhūti then said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"So it is, so it is! Kauśika, this great pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
The immeasurable pāramitā, the boundless pāramitā—this is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Within this, one trains to achieve the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; within this prajñāpāramitā, they train and achieve perfection.
They are able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—having attained it, now attaining it, or about to attain it.
Kauśika! Because form is great, the Prajñāpāramitā is also great. Why is this?
This form (rūpa) cannot be apprehended at its prior limit, cannot be apprehended at its posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended in its middle.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna) are great, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is also great.
Why is this? Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended in the past, cannot be apprehended in the future, and cannot be apprehended in the present.
This applies even unto the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For these reasons, Kauśika, this great pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Kauśika!
Because form is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Why is this? Because the measure of form cannot be apprehended.
Kauśika! Just as the measure of space cannot be apprehended, so too is form; its measure cannot be apprehended.
Because space is immeasurable, form is immeasurable.
Because form is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so forth, up to all-knowledge, are immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Why is this? Because the measure of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended.
Just as the measure of space cannot be apprehended, so too is all-knowledge; its measure cannot be apprehended.
Because space is immeasurable, all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is immeasurable.
Because all-knowledge is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is immeasurable. For these reasons, Kauśika!
This prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is immeasurable.
Kausika! Because form (rūpa) is boundless, the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is boundless.
Why is this? Kauśika!
This form cannot be apprehended at its prior limit, cannot be apprehended at its posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended in its middle limit.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, the perfection of wisdom is boundless.
Why is this? Because the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable.
Furthermore, because all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is boundless, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is boundless.
Why is this? Because the prior, posterior, and middle limits of all-knowledge are all unapprehendable.
For this reason, Kauśika, this prajñāpāramitā is boundless;
form is boundless, and so on, up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) being boundless.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, because its object is boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
"Subhūti! [Kauśika said:]
"How is it that because conditions are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless? Subhūti replied,
"Because it takes all boundless dharmas as its conditions, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless."
“How is it that the perfection of wisdom is limitless because it takes all limitless phenomena as its object?
Subhūti replied, “The perfection of wisdom is limitless because it takes the limitless nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as its object.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika, because suchness is boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“How is it that because the *tathatā* (suchness) is boundless, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless?
Subhūti replied: “Because *tathatā* is boundless, its object-condition (*ālambana*) is also boundless.”
Because conditions are boundless, suchness is also boundless.
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is boundless.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, because sentient beings are infinite, the Prajñāpāramitā is infinite.
Śakra Devendra asked Subhūti:
“How is it that because sentient beings are infinite, the *prajñāpāramitā* is infinite?
Subhūti replied, “What do you think? What dharma is designated as ‘sentient being’?”
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"There is no dharma that is called 'sentient being'; it is only by way of a provisional name that there are sentient beings.
This name originally has no dharma and has no objective referent; it is merely a name applied by force."
“Kauśika! What do you think? Is it said in this Prajñāpāramitā that sentient beings exist as real entities?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“There is not. “Kauśika!
If the Prajñāpāramitā truly does not speak of sentient beings, then even ‘the limitless’ cannot be apprehended.”
Kauśika! What do you think?
If a Buddha were to speak of the names of sentient beings for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River, would there be any dharma among those sentient beings that has arising or cessation?
Śakra Devānām Indra said, “No. “For what reason?”
Because sentient beings have been eternally pure from the very beginning. For this reason, Kauśika,
you should know that because sentient beings are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.

Chapter 30: The Triple Exclamation. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Thirty: The Triple Exclamation (in the Dan edition, this is titled "The Chapter on Looking Back"). At that time, the various heavenly kings and their gods, the various Brahma kings and their Brahma gods, the Īśāna gods and all the immortals (*ṛṣi*), along with the various goddesses, simultaneously exclaimed three times:
"How wonderful! How wonderful!"
The Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti is entirely the teaching spread through the power and grace of the causal conditions for the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices this prajñāpāramitā without departing from it, we regard such a person as a Buddha.

Why is this? Although within this Prajñāpāramitā no dharma can be apprehended—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)—there nevertheless exist the teachings of the three vehicles:
namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras: "So it is, so it is! O devaputras!"

As you have said, although within this Prajñāpāramitā no dharma can be apprehended—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge—there nevertheless exist the teachings of the three vehicles, namely:
the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle.
O sons of the gods!
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices this prajñāpāramitā without departing from it, one should regard such a person as a Buddha.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended. Why is this?
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the teachings of the three vehicles are extensively expounded—namely, the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddhayāna.
Within the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), a Buddha cannot be found; apart from the perfection of giving, a Buddha likewise cannot be found.
This extends even to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā): within the perfection of wisdom, a Buddha cannot be found; apart from the perfection of wisdom, a Buddha likewise cannot be found.

"From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even the knowledge of all modes—it is likewise so.
The Buddha said to the devaputras:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in all these dharmas—namely, from the perfection of giving up to the knowledge of all modes—for this reason, one should regard this bodhisattva mahāsattva as a Buddha."
"O sons of the gods!
In the past, at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I practiced the perfection of generosity, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom."
They are not separate from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, nor from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
They are not separate from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, all doors of samādhi, and all doors of dhāraṇī.

They do not depart from the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and other immeasurable practices of the Buddhas' Dharma.

Because there was nothing to be attained, at that time the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction: "In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa has passed, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."
At that time, the sons of the gods addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Prajñāpāramitā is most rare, for it enables all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) by neither grasping nor abandoning form; by neither grasping nor abandoning feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to neither grasping nor abandoning the knowledge of all modes.”

At that time, the Buddha surveyed the fourfold assembly—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all the devas from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, who were all seated together in the assembly.
Having observed this universally, the Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying: “Kauśika!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, an upāsikā, or any sons of gods or daughters of gods—whoever hears, receives, maintains, draws near to, reads, recites, correctly reflects upon, and explains this Prajñāpāramitā to others, and does not depart from the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)—O sons of gods!”
Such a person cannot be taken advantage of by Māra or the followers of Māra. Why is this?

Because these good sons and good daughters have clearly understood that form is empty; emptiness cannot take advantage of emptiness, signlessness cannot take advantage of signlessness, and wishlessness cannot take advantage of wishlessness.

One clearly and thoroughly understands that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; emptiness cannot find an opportunity against emptiness, and even non-action cannot find an opportunity against non-action.

This continues until one clearly and thoroughly understands that the knowledge of all modes is empty; emptiness cannot find an opportunity against emptiness, and even non-action cannot find an opportunity against non-action.
Why is this? Because the self-characteristic nature of these dharmas cannot be apprehended; since no objective basis can be found, who is there to experience affliction? "Furthermore, Kauśika!
These good sons and good daughters cannot be harmed by humans or non-humans. Why is this?

Because these good sons and good daughters have well-cultivated the mind of loving-kindness, as well as the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings, by way of non-apprehension.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family shall never meet with an untimely death. Why is this?
This is because these good sons and good daughters practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) by providing for all sentient beings with an impartial mind. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

Among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and the Bṛhatphala Heaven within this trichiliocosm, there are those who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* but have not yet heard, nor have they received, upheld, or drawn near to this *prajñāpāramitā*. These sons of the gods should now hear, receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, and correctly contemplate it, never departing from the mind of *sarvajñatā*.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If any sons or daughters of good family hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, draw near to it, read and recite it, maintain right mindfulness of it, and do not depart from the mind of *sarvajñatā*, then these sons and daughters of good family—whether in an empty house, in the wilderness, or in a human habitation—will never be afraid."
Why is this? Because these good sons and good daughters are clear regarding internal emptiness, because they have nothing to apprehend;
they are clear regarding external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, because they have nothing to apprehend.

At that time, the Cāturmahārājika devas, Trāyastriṃśa devas, Yāma devas, Tuṣita devas, Nirmāṇarati devas, Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, and all the devas up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens in this trichiliocosm addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"We shall always protect those sons and daughters of good family who are able to receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, who draw near to it, read and recite it, maintain right mindfulness of it, and do not depart from the mind of sarvajñatā."
For what reason?
World-Honored One!

It is because of the causes and conditions of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that the three evil realms are severed, the poverty of gods and humans is severed, and all calamities, afflictions, diseases, and famines are severed.

Because of the Bodhisattva’s causes and conditions, there appear in the world the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the perfection of giving, emptiness, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to all-knowledge.

It is because of the causes and conditions of bodhisattvas that there exist in the world the great clans of kṣatriyas, the great clans of brahmins, the great households of householders, as well as various kings and wheel-turning sage-kings (cakravartin), from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

It is because of the bodhisattva as a causal condition that there exist the srotāpanna and the fruit of srotāpanna, up to the arhat and the fruit of arhat, as well as the pratyekabuddha and the path of the pratyekabuddha.

Because of the causes and conditions of bodhisattvas, there is the accomplishment of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields; thus, there is the appearance of Buddhas in the world, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the knowledge of the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Sangha of Bhikṣus.
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world should protect this bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "So it is,
so it is, Kauśika!"
It is because of the causes and conditions of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that the three evil realms are severed and even the Three Jewels appear in the world.
For this reason, the devas, humans, and asuras should always protect, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Kauśika! To offer worship, honor, respect, and praise to these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is to offer worship to me.
For this reason, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always be protected, worshipped, honored, respected, and praised by devas, humans, and asuras.
Kauśika! Suppose this trichiliocosm were filled with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as dense as a forest of bamboo, reeds, rice, or hemp.
If some son or daughter of good family were to provide them with offerings, respect, honor, and praise;

It is not equal to the merit obtained by making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has first resolved on awakening and does not depart from the six pāramitās. Why is this?
It is not because of the causes and conditions of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all buddhas appear in the world.
It is because of the causes and conditions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas appear in the world.
For this reason, Kauśika,
all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world should constantly protect, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise these bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Chapter 31: The Chapter on the Settling of Disputes (*Vivāda-vyupaśama-parivarta*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, this is the thirty-first chapter; in the Dan-ben (Dharmarakṣa) edition, it is titled "The Chapter on Manifesting Merit. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How truly marvelous and rare!
These bodhisattvas also bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn and purify buddha-fields.
Traveling from one buddha-field to another, they provide offerings to all Buddhas, obtaining whatever requisites they desire for making offerings, exactly as they wish.
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, they shall never forget it until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

They will also achieve the perfection of family, the perfection of mother, the perfection of birth, the perfection of retinue, the perfection of marks, the perfection of radiance, the perfection of eyes, the perfection of ears, the perfection of samādhis, and the perfection of dhāraṇīs.

By the power of skillful means, this bodhisattva transforms his body to appear like a Buddha and travels from one land to another to reach places where no Buddha resides. There, he praises the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); he praises the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; and he praises the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Using the power of skillful means, he preaches the Dharma for them and delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles—namely, the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-vehicle.
World-Honored One!
How wonderful and rare!

To uphold the Prajñāpāramitā is to have already encompassed all five pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it also encompasses the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the Buddha, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra: “So it is, so it is! Kausika!”
By upholding the Prajñāpāramitā, one has already comprehensively encompassed the five pāramitās up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Furthermore, Kauśika,

listen with single-minded attention to the merits attained in this present life by those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, explain to others, and correctly contemplate this Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“So be it, World-Honored One! I shall receive your instruction.”
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:

"Kauśika! If there are heterodox practitioners, brahmins, Māras or their followers, or those with overweening pride who wish to cause discord, error, or destruction regarding the bodhisattva’s mind of prajñāpāramitā."
As soon as these people give rise to such thoughts, they immediately vanish, and their wishes are never fulfilled.
Why is this? Kausika!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have for a long night practiced the perfection of giving, and they have practiced the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Because sentient beings have long been attached to and contentious over worldly things, the Bodhisattva completely relinquishes all internal and external possessions to establish sentient beings within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Because sentient beings have long violated the precepts, the Bodhisattva completely relinquishes all internal and external phenomena to establish sentient beings in ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Because sentient beings have engaged in strife and contention throughout the long night, the Bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and establishes sentient beings in patience (*kṣānti*).
Because sentient beings have been indolent throughout the long night, the Bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and establishes sentient beings in diligence (*vīrya*).
Because sentient beings have long been distracted in mind throughout the night of saṃsāra, the bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and establishes sentient beings in dhyāna.
Because sentient beings have long been deluded throughout the night of saṃsāra, the bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and establishes sentient beings in the prajñāpāramitā.

Because sentient beings have for a long night been bound by the fetter of craving and thus wander through birth and death, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through the power of skillful means, sever the fetter of craving in sentient beings and establish them in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They establish sentient beings in the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat, in the path of a pratyekabuddha, and in the path of a buddha. Kausika!

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom attains merit in the present life and merit in future lives; they attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, turn the wheel of Dharma, fulfill their vows, and enter nirvana without remainder.
Kauśika! These are the merits of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in future lives.

Furthermore, whether it be Māra, the subjects of Māra, non-Buddhist brahmins, or those with overweening pride who wish to disparage, challenge, or destroy the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will ultimately never succeed.

That person’s evil intentions will gradually diminish and their merit will increasingly grow; because they have heard this Prajñāpāramitā, they will gradually attain the exhaustion of all suffering through the path of the Three Vehicles.
For example, Kauśika, there is a medicine called Maghi. Suppose there is a snake that,
being hungry, wanders about seeking food and sees an insect it wishes to devour.
When the insect went to the place where the medicine was, because of the power of the medicine's fragrance, the snake could not advance and immediately retreated on its own. Why was this?
It was because the power of this medicine was able to overcome the poison.
Kauśika! The medicinal herb *maghī* possesses such power.

If these sons and daughters of good family hear, receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, explain to others, and correctly attend to this *prajñāpāramitā*, then should various conflicts arise that seek to cause destruction, by the majestic power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they shall be swiftly extinguished at the very place where they arise.
That person will immediately give rise to a wholesome mind and increase their merit. Why is this?
Because this Prajñāpāramitā is able to extinguish all disputes and disturbances regarding dharmas.
What are these phenomena? They are namely: lust, anger, and delusion; ignorance up to the great mass of suffering; the various hindrances, fetters, and entanglements;

the view of a self, the view of a person, and the view of a sentient being; the view of annihilationism and eternalism; the view of impurity as pure and the view of purity as impure; and the view of existence and non-existence.

All such views as these—stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distraction, and lack of wisdom; the notions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self; and such modes of craving as attachment to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; attachment to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); attachment to internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); attachment to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); attachment to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and attachment to nirvana.
All these disputes and disturbances regarding all dharmas can be completely extinguished and prevented from increasing. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

All the Cāturmahārājika devas, Śakras, Brahmās, and even those up to the Akaniṣṭha devas within the trichiliocosm will constantly protect those good men and good women who are able to hear, receive, and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, and who honor, recite, explain it to others, and correctly attend to the Prajñāpāramitā."

The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions also collectively protect these good men and good women who are able to hear, receive, uphold, make offerings to, recite, explain to others, and correctly contemplate this Prajñāpāramitā.
For these sons and daughters of good family, unwholesome dharmas are extinguished and wholesome dharmas increase further.
That is to say, the dāna-pāramitā increases further, because of non-apprehension.
Even up to the perfection of wisdom, it increases further because of non-apprehensibility.
Inner emptiness increases further, even up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, because of non-apprehensibility.
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha increase further because they are non-apprehendable.
The various gates of samādhi, the various gates of dhāraṇī, all-knowledge, and the knowledge of all modes increase further because they are non-apprehendable.
What these good men and good women speak is believed and accepted by all.
Their friends and relatives are steadfast.
They do not utter useless words; they are not overwhelmed by anger, nor are they overcome by arrogance, stinginess, greed, or envy.
This person does not kill living beings themselves, teaches others not to kill living beings, praises the dharma of non-killing, and also joyfully praises those who do not kill.

He himself abstains from taking what is not given, and he also teaches others to abstain from taking what is not given; he praises the practice of abstaining from taking what is not given, and he also joyfully commends those who abstain from taking what is not given.

He himself abstains from sexual misconduct, teaches others to abstain from sexual misconduct, praises the practice of abstaining from sexual misconduct, and also joyfully commends those who abstain from sexual misconduct.

He himself abstains from false speech, teaches others to abstain from false speech, praises the practice of abstaining from false speech, and also joyfully commends those who abstain from false speech.
It is the same for double-tongued speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
One does not covet oneself, teaches others not to covet, praises the dharma of non-covetousness, and also joyfully commends those who do not covet.
It is the same for non-ill will and non-wrong views.
One practices the *dānapāramitā* oneself, teaches others to practice the *dānapāramitā*, praises the dharma of the *dānapāramitā*, and also joyfully commends those who practice the *dānapāramitā*.

They personally practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), teach others to practice the perfection of ethical discipline, praise the dharma of the perfection of ethical discipline, and also joyfully extol those who practice the perfection of ethical discipline.

They personally practice the perfection of patience, teach others to practice the perfection of patience, praise the dharma of the perfection of patience, and also joyfully commend those who practice the perfection of patience.

One practices the perfection of vigor oneself, teaches others to practice the perfection of vigor, praises the dharma of the perfection of vigor, and also joyfully commends those who practice the perfection of vigor.
They personally practice the dhyāna-pāramitā, teach others to practice the dhyāna-pāramitā, praise the dharma of the dhyāna-pāramitā, and also joyfully extol those who practice the dhyāna-pāramitā.

They practice the perfection of wisdom themselves, teach others to practice the perfection of wisdom, praise the dharma of the perfection of wisdom, and also joyfully praise those who practice the perfection of wisdom.

They personally cultivate internal emptiness, teach others to cultivate internal emptiness, praise the dharma of internal emptiness, and also joyfully praise those who cultivate internal emptiness. This continues up to:

they personally cultivate the emptiness of non-existence and existence, teach others to cultivate the emptiness of non-existence and existence, praise the dharma of the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and also joyfully praise those who cultivate the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Having entered all samādhis oneself, one teaches others to enter all samādhis, praises the dharma of all samādhis, and also joyfully extols those who practice all samādhis.
They themselves attain dhāraṇīs, teach others to attain dhāraṇīs, praise the methods for attaining dhāraṇīs, and also joyfully extol those who have attained dhāraṇīs.
Having entered the first dhyāna oneself, one teaches others to enter the first dhyāna, praises the method of the first dhyāna, and also joyfully extols those who have entered the first dhyāna.
It is the same for the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

Having entered the mind of loving-kindness oneself, one teaches others to enter the mind of loving-kindness, praises the dharma of loving-kindness, and also joyfully extols those who have entered the mind of loving-kindness.
It is the same for the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Having entered the sphere of infinite space oneself, one teaches others to enter the sphere of infinite space, praises the dharma of the sphere of infinite space, and also joyfully extols those who have entered the sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness oneself, teaches others to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, praises the dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness, and also joyfully commends those who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are also like this.
