Non-dual dharma-characteristics are the prajñāpāramitā; non-dual dharma-characteristics are the dhyānapāramitā, and so on, up to the dānapāramitā.
Kauśika! If a person wishes to obtain two characteristics of the dharma-nature, that person wishes to obtain two characteristics of the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?

Kauśika! The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are non-dual and without distinction; this is likewise true for all perfections up to the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).

If a person wishes to perceive two distinct characteristics in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the inconceivable nature, that person wishes to perceive two distinct characteristics in the perfection of wisdom.
"Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā and the inconceivable nature are non-dual and without distinction.
Śakra Devendra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All people of the world, as well as devas and asuras, should pay homage to and make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this so?
It is by training in the Prajñāpāramitā that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

World-Honored One, I am always seated upon the Hall of Good Dharma; when I am not present on my seat, the sons of the gods come to make offerings to me, pay homage to my seat, circumambulate it, and then depart.
The sons of the gods had this thought:
"Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is seated in this place in order to preach the Dharma to the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!

Wherever this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra scroll is written down, upheld, recited, and explained to others, there all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas from the worlds of the ten directions will come to pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā, and having made offerings, they will depart.
Why is this? It is because within this Prajñāpāramitā all Buddhas are born, as well as all the requisites for the happiness of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the relics of the Buddhas are also the causal conditions for the abiding of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
For this reason, World-Honored One,
of these two portions, I choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, World-Honored One:
If I uphold, receive, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, my mind will enter deeply into the Dharma.
At that time, I shall not perceive any signs of fear. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is without marks and without appearance; it is without speech and without explanation.
World-Honored One!
It is without marks and without form, without speech and without discourse; this is the *prajñāpāramitā*, and even so is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

World-Honored One, if the *prajñāpāramitā* were to possess marks rather than being markless, the Buddhas would not have been able to realize that all phenomena are without marks and without form, without speech and without discourse, thereby attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For the sake of his disciples, he teaches that all dharmas are likewise without marks and without form, beyond words and beyond description.
World-Honored One,
it is because the *prajñāpāramitā* is in truth without marks, without form, beyond words, and beyond description.

The Buddhas, knowing that all dharmas are without marks, without appearance, without words, and without speech, have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and, for the sake of their disciples, teach that all dharmas are likewise without marks, without appearance, without words, and without speech.
For this reason, World-Honored One,
this Prajñāpāramitā should be revered, made offerings to, honored, and praised by all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world, with incense, flowers, necklaces, and even banners and canopies.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there is a person who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, and who draws near to it, recites it, explains it, correctly contemplates it, and transcribes it, making offerings of flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies—this person shall not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; nor shall they fall into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. Until they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they will constantly behold all Buddhas, traveling from one Buddha-field to another to make offerings to those Buddhas, honoring, respecting, and praising them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Suppose one portion consists of the relics of the Buddha filling a trichiliocosm, and another portion consists of a written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Which of these two would you take?"
Between these two portions, I would therefore choose the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this,
World-Honored One?
It is from within this Prajñāpāramitā that the śarīras of all Buddhas arise.
For this reason, the śarīras receive offerings, honor, respect, and praise.

Because these good sons and good daughters offer worship and honor to the śarīras, they enjoy the blissful merits among devas and humans, never falling into the three evil realms; and according to their aspirations, they gradually enter nirvāṇa by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
Whether one sees the Buddha of the present or sees a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, they are equal and no different. Why is this?
"Bhagavān! This prajñāpāramitā is non-dual and indistinguishable from the Buddha.
Furthermore, Bhagavān!"
Just as when the Buddha, abiding in the three modes of manifestation, teaches the twelve divisions of the sūtras— from the *sūtra*, the *geya*, up to the *upadeśa*—
if there are other sons or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, recite, and explain this *prajñāpāramitā*, it is equal and no different.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, the manifestation of the three categories and the twelve divisions of the scriptures—from the Sūtra up to the Upadeśa—are produced.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
The Buddhas of the ten directions, abiding in the three modes of manifestation, preach the twelve divisions of the scriptures—from the Sūtras up to the Upadeśas."
Furthermore, there may be someone who receives the Prajñāpāramitā and explains it to others; this is equal to and no different [from the former].
Why is this? It is because within the Prajñāpāramitā all Buddhas are born, as well as the twelve divisions of the scriptures—from the Sūtras up to the Upadeśas.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If there were someone who made offerings to all the Buddhas in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
honoring, respecting, and praising them;
With flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies;
furthermore, there are those who transcribe the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scrolls,
and treat them with reverence, respect, and praise!
Flowers and incense, up to banners and canopies—
their merit is exactly equal. Why is this?
All Buddhas of the ten directions are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if good sons and good daughters hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive, uphold, read, recite, and correctly contemplate it, and also explain it to others."
Such a person does not fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts, nor do they fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Why is this?
You should know that because these sons and daughters of good family dwell correctly within the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*),
this Prajñāpāramitā distances them from all suffering, affliction, and decline.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If there are good sons or good daughters who write out this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, receive and uphold it, draw near to it, make offerings to it, and honor, respect, and praise it."
"Such a person is free from all terrors, World-Honored One!
It is like a debtor who approaches a king and serves his attendants; the creditors, in turn, come to honor and respect this person, and he no longer stands in fear."
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
It is because this person relies upon and stays close to the king, depending on his power and influence.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Because the relics of the Buddhas have been cultivated and perfumed by the Prajñāpāramitā, they receive offerings and veneration.
World-Honored One!"
One should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is like a king, while the *śarīra* relics are like a debtor.
Just as a debtor receives offerings by relying on the king, so too do the *śarīra* relics receive offerings by relying on the cultivation and perfuming of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
World-Honored One!
You should know that the all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas is also accomplished through cultivation by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
For this reason, World-Honored One!
Of these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this,
World-Honored One?

Within the Prajñāpāramitā are born the śarīra relics of the Buddhas and the thirty-two marks; within the Prajñāpāramitā are also born the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
World-Honored One!
Within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the five perfections arise and thereby receive the name "perfection.
Within the perfection of wisdom, the all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) of all Buddhas arises.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In whatever place within this trichiliocosm where one receives, maintains, makes offerings to, reveres, honors, and praises the Prajñāpāramitā, neither humans nor non-humans shall be able to find an opportunity to harm them; such a person will gradually enter into nirvāṇa."
"Bhagavān! The Prajñāpāramitā is of such great benefit that it is able to perform the work of a Buddha within the trichiliocosm. Bhagavān!"
"World-Honored One, wherever the Prajñāpāramitā resides, there is a Buddha.
It is like a priceless mani-jewel; wherever it dwells, non-human beings cannot find an opportunity to cause harm."
If any man or woman suffers from fever, by placing this jewel upon their body, the fever shall be immediately cured.
Whether they suffer from wind-related ailments, cold-related ailments, or a combination of heat, wind, and cold, by placing the jewel upon their body, all such conditions shall be entirely healed.
In the darkness, this jewel can bring forth light;
in the heat, it can bring coolness, and in the cold, it can bring warmth.
Wherever the jewel dwells, the ground there is neither cold nor hot, and the seasons are harmonious and temperate.
Furthermore, that place is free from all other venomous stings.
Should a man or woman be bitten by a poisonous snake, if one shows them this jewel, the poison will be immediately eliminated.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a man or woman suffers from eye pain, cataracts, or blindness, by bringing this jewel near them, it will be immediately cured."
If there is a leprous sore or a malignant swelling, by placing this jewel upon the body, the disease is immediately cured.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
wherever this maṇi-jewel is in water, the water takes on a single color accordingly."
“World-Honored One!
If this jewel is wrapped in a blue object and placed in water, the color of the water becomes blue.
If it is wrapped in a yellow, red, white, crimson, or pale green object and placed in water, the water accordingly takes on those yellow, red, white, crimson, or pale green colors.”
If various such colored objects are wrapped and placed within water, the water will accordingly take on those various colors.
World-Honored One!
If the water is turbid, by placing a jewel within it, the water immediately becomes clear.
"Such are the virtues of this jewel.
At that time, Ānanda asked Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!..."
"Is this maṇi jewel a celestial treasure,
or is it a treasure of Jambudvīpa?
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Ānanda:
"This is a treasure of the heavens.
People of Jambudvīpa also possess such treasures, but their meritorious characteristics are slight and incomplete.
The treasures of the heavens are pure, light, and sublime; they cannot be compared by means of worldly analogies."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If this maṇi jewel is placed inside a casket and then taken out, because its merit has perfumed the casket, all people will love and respect it."
"So it is, World-Honored One!

Wherever the written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra is located, that place shall be free from the afflictions of various troubles, just as wherever a maṇi jewel is placed, there shall be no various calamities."
"Bhagavān! That the relics receive offerings after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is entirely due to the power of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). It is due to the power of these merits:

from the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) down to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*); from internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) down to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) down to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); and all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the fixedness of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable nature (*acintyatā*), and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
Good sons and good daughters form this thought:

"These relics of the Buddha are the abode of all the merits of the Buddhas, including all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñā*), great loving-kindness and great compassion, the severing of all fetters and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), constant equanimity, and the practice of the Dharma without error."
"For this reason, the relics receive offerings. World-Honored One!

These relics are the abode of the perfection of all jewels of merit; they are the abode of the perfection of neither defilement nor purity; the perfection of neither arising nor ceasing; the perfection of neither entering nor exiting; the perfection of neither increasing nor decreasing; and the perfection of neither coming, nor going, nor staying."

These relics of the Buddha are the dwelling place of the *pāramitā* of the characteristics of all phenomena; because they have been cultivated and perfumed by this *pāramitā* of the characteristics of all phenomena, the relics receive offerings.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Let us set aside the relics filling a trichiliocosm.

Suppose there were one portion consisting of the relics filling as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and another portion consisting of a written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra."
Of these two portions, I would take the Prajñāpāramitā. Why?
Because it is from within this Prajñāpāramitā that the śarīra of all Buddhas is born; and because they have been cultivated and perfumed by this Prajñāpāramitā, the śarīra receives offerings.
“World-Honored One!
If there are good sons or good daughters who make offerings to the śarīra, honoring, respecting, and praising it, the karmic reward of their merit shall be beyond measure.”

One receives the bliss and happiness of humans and devas, namely among the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and the great households of householders, as well as receiving bliss and happiness from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations.
Furthermore, by virtue of these causes and conditions of merit, they shall attain the end of suffering.

If one receives this Prajñāpāramitā, recites it, explains it, and maintains right mindfulness of it, that person will be able to fulfill the Dhyānapāramitā and even fulfill the Dānapāramitā; they will be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness and even fulfill the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they will transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and abide in the rank of a Bodhisattva.
Having established themselves in the bodhisattva stage, they attain the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva and travel from one buddha-field to another.

For the sake of sentient beings, these bodhisattvas assume bodies and bring them to maturity according to what is appropriate: they may become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), or members of the great kṣatriya clans, or members of the great brāhmaṇa clans, thereby maturing sentient beings.

For this reason, World-Honored One, it is not out of disrespect or lack of reverence that I do not accept the relics; rather, it is because when good men and good women make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, they are thereby making offerings to the relics.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there are people who wish to see the present Dharma-body and form-body of the Buddhas within the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, those people should hear, receive, and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā; they should read and recite it, correctly contemplate it, and expound it for others."
In this way, these good sons and good daughters shall behold the Dharma-body and form-body of all Buddhas throughout the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions.
These sons and daughters of good family who practice the *prajñāpāramitā* should also cultivate the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* by means of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family who wish to see the Buddhas of the present should receive this *prajñāpāramitā* and even maintain right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) of it.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
there are two kinds of dharma-characteristics:
the characteristics of conditioned dharmas and the characteristics of unconditioned dharmas."

What are the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)? They are the wisdom within the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), up to the wisdom within the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); the wisdom within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), up to the wisdom within the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); the wisdom within the ten powers of a Buddha (*buddhabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); the wisdom within wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) and unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*), within contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), and within mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*) and supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*). These are called the characteristics of conditioned phenomena.
What is called the dharma-characteristic of unconditioned phenomena?

It is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, which is without arising and without cessation, without abiding and without change, without defilement and without purity, and without increase and without decrease.
What is called the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena?
The non-existent nature of all phenomena is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
This is called the characteristic of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "So it is, so it is! Kauśika!"

The Buddhas of the past attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*; the disciples of the Buddhas of the past also attained the path of the *srotāpanna* up to the paths of the *arhat* and *pratyekabuddha* by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*. The immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas of the future and present throughout the ten directions will likewise attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*.
The disciples of all Buddhas of the future and the present will likewise attain the path of the srotāpanna up to the path of the pratyekabuddha by means of this Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, the meaning of the three vehicles is explained in detail; this is because they are dharmas without marks,
dharmas without arising or ceasing,
and dharmas without defilement or purity.
Because it is a dharma that is unconditioned and unarisen, neither entering nor exiting, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither grasping nor abandoning.
This is according to conventional truth, not according to the ultimate truth.

Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā is neither this nor that; it is neither high nor low; it is neither equal nor unequal; it is neither with marks nor without marks; it is neither mundane nor supramundane; it is neither with outflows nor without outflows; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Why is this? Kausika!
The Prajñāpāramitā does not grasp at the dharmas of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor does it abandon the dharmas of ordinary persons.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the minds of all sentient beings, yet they do not apprehend a ‘sentient being,’ nor do they apprehend even a ‘knower’ or a ‘seer.’”

This bodhisattva does not apprehend form, nor does he apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he does not apprehend the eye up to the mind; he does not apprehend forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); he does not apprehend the feelings produced by the condition of eye-contact up to the feelings produced by the condition of mind-contact; he does not apprehend the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; he does not apprehend unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); he does not apprehend the dharmas of a buddha; and he does not apprehend a buddha.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā does not arise for the sake of attaining dharmas. Why is this?
"The nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent and unobtainable.
The dharmas employed are unobtainable, and their locus is likewise unobtainable.
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
"So it is, so it is, Kauśika! As you have said,

for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has practiced the perfection of wisdom throughout the long night, even *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be apprehended, let alone the bodhisattva or the qualities of a bodhisattva."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice only the perfection of wisdom and not the other perfections?”
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:

“Kauśika! A bodhisattva practices all six pāramitās by way of non-apprehension: when practicing dānapāramitā, he does not apprehend a giver, a recipient, or material wealth; when practicing śīlapāramitā, he does not apprehend the precepts, one who maintains the precepts, or one who breaks the precepts; and so on, up to practicing prajñāpāramitā, he does not apprehend wisdom, one who possesses wisdom, or one who lacks wisdom.”
Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, the perfection of wisdom acts as his guiding light, enabling him to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the precepts, the perfection of wisdom acts as their guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the śīla-pāramitā.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, the perfection of wisdom acts as their guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the kṣānti-pāramitā.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence, the perfection of wisdom acts as a guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the perfection of vigor.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices dhyāna, the perfection of wisdom acts as their guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas, the perfection of wisdom acts as their guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the prajñā-pāramitā.
All dharmas are non-apprehendable, namely from form (*rūpa*) up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Kausika!
It is like the various trees in Jambudvīpa, with their various leaves, various flowers, various fruits, and various colors—their shade makes no distinction.
"The various pāramitās enter into the prajñāpāramitā; it is likewise that they reach omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) without distinction, because nothing is apprehended.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The perfection of wisdom accomplishes great merit.
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom accomplishes all merit.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the accomplishment of immeasurable merit, the accomplishment of boundless merit, and the accomplishment of incomparable merit.
World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who write out this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, and with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies, respectfully offer, revere, honor, and praise it, while maintaining right mindfulness as taught in the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, if there are good men or good women who transcribe a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others,
which of these produces more merit?
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra:
“Kauśika! I shall now question you; answer me according to your own understanding.

Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who made offerings to the relics of the Buddhas, honoring, respecting, and praising them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.”

Furthermore, if there is someone who divides the relics into portions the size of a mustard seed and gives them to others, causing them to offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.
"Of what kind would that merit be most abundant?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
According to the meaning of the Dharma as I have heard it from the Buddha: if a son or daughter of good family makes offerings to the relics themselves, even with banners and canopies;
yet if another person were to divide the relics into portions the size of a mustard seed and give them to others to make offerings of, the latter’s merit would be far greater.
World-Honored One!
Because the Buddha perceives this benefit for sentient beings, he enters the Vajra Samādhi and shatters his vajra-body into powdered śarīra.
For what reason?

"If there is someone who, after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, makes offerings to the Buddha’s relics even as small as a mustard seed, their meritorious reward will be boundless, continuing until the end of suffering.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "So it is, so it is!"

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and makes offerings to it with reverence, using incense, flowers, and even banners and canopies;
Furthermore, if there is someone who copies a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to another person to study, the merit of that son or daughter of good family will be exceedingly great.
Furthermore, Kauśika,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family explains the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā to others, revealing, demonstrating, and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand;

These sons and daughters of good family surpass the merit of the former sons and daughters of good family; those from whom they hear the Prajñāpāramitā should be regarded as Buddhas and also as sublime practitioners of the holy life.
Why is this? One should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is itself the Buddha; the *prajñāpāramitā* is not different from the Buddha, and the Buddha is not different from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present have studied within the Prajñāpāramitā, thereby attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becoming sublime practitioners of the Brahma-faring.
Those who practice the sublime holy life—namely, the *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattvas—also study this *prajñāpāramitā*, and they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śrāvakas who study this Prajñāpāramitā attain the path of an Arhat.
Those seeking the path of a Pratyekabuddha who study this Prajñāpāramitā attain the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
When a bodhisattva studies this Prajñāpāramitā, they attain entry into the bodhisattva stage. For this reason, Kauśika,

a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to make offerings to the Buddhas of the present— honoring, respecting, and praising them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies— should make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Seeing this benefit, when I first attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I had this thought:
"Who is there that can be provided with offerings, honored, revered, praised, and relied upon as a basis for dwelling?"
"Kauśika! Within all the worlds—whether among devas, Māras, or Brahmās, or among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—I do not see anyone who is my equal, let alone anyone who is superior."
I further reflected to myself:
"The Dharma that I have attained shall lead me to become a Buddha.
I shall make offerings to this Dharma, honoring, respecting, and praising it, and I shall dwell in reliance upon it."
"What is this Dharma?
It is what is called the Prajñāpāramitā. "Kauśika! [he said.]
I myself have made offerings to this Prajñāpāramitā, and having honored, respected, and praised it, I dwell in reliance upon it.

How much more so should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi not offer to, honor, respect, and praise the Prajñāpāramitā with flowers, incense, garlands, and even banners and canopies?
Why is this? Because it is from within the perfection of wisdom that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born, and it is from within all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that all buddhas are born.
For this reason, Kauśika!

Good sons and good daughters, whether seeking the path of the Buddha, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, or the path of the Śrāvaka, all should make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, honoring, respecting, and praising it with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.

Chapter 38: The Gift of Dharma. From the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-Eight, "The Gift of Dharma" (in the Dan-zang edition, Chapter Ten, "The Ten Wholesome Deeds"). The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying: "Kauśika!
If there were a son or daughter of good family who taught the people of a single Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, what do you think:
would they, by reason of this cause, obtain much merit?
He replied, “Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to merely write out this Prajñāpāramitā sūtra and uphold it; rather, they gain far greater merit by giving it to others so that they may read, recite, and explain it."

Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, all untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are extensively expounded; from it, sons and daughters of good family have studied, are studying, and will study. They have entered, are entering, and will enter the stage of the true dharma (*samyaktva-niyāma*). They have attained, are attaining, and will attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*), up to and including the fruit of an arhat (*arhat-phala*).
The seeking of the path of a pratyekabuddha is also like this.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they enter the stage of the true dharma—having entered, currently entering, or about to enter—and they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—having attained, currently attaining, or about to attain it.
Kauśika! What are the outflow-free dharmas?

They are the so-called four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; the four noble truths; internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; and the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities.
Sons and daughters of good family who study this Dharma will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they have attained it, they are attaining it now, and they shall attain it in the future. Kausika!

If there is a son or daughter of good family who instructs a single person to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the merit obtained by this person surpasses that of one who instructs all the people of Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
Why is this? Kausika!
Even if one were to teach the people of a single Jambudvipa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, they would still not escape the sufferings of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Kauśika! To instruct a single person so that they attain the fruit of srotāpanna is to cause them to leave the three evil destinies.
This applies likewise up to the fruit of arhatship and the path of the pratyekabuddha.

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct the people of a single Jambudvīpa so that they attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha;
It is not as meritorious as when a son or daughter of good family instructs a single person to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Kauśika! It is because of the bodhisattva that there arise those from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat and pratyekabuddha.
It is because of the bodhisattva that the Buddhas arise.

For this reason, Kauśika, you should know that a good man or a good woman who writes out a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to others so that they may write it, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it, will obtain much merit.
Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā all wholesome dharmas are extensively explained.

By training in these wholesome dharmas, there arise the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and the great families of householders; from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; and there arise the four foundations of mindfulness up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); there arise those from the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddhas.
Kauśika! Setting aside the people of a single Jambudvīpa,
suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught the sentient beings within the lands of the four continents to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
"What do you think? Would that person, by reason of these causes and conditions, acquire much merit?
He replied, "Very much, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious as for a good man or a good woman to write out a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others, causing them to write it down, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it; the latter gains far more merit."
The rest is as explained above.
Kausika! Let alone the sentient beings within the lands of the four continents.
It is the same if one were to teach the sentient beings within a small thousandfold world system to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
Kausika! Let alone the sentient beings within a small thousandfold world system.
If one were to instruct the sentient beings within two thousand worlds of the central land to practice the ten paths of wholesome action,

and if there were a son or daughter of good family who were to write out this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others so that they might copy, uphold, read, recite, and explain it, this person would obtain far more merit.
The rest is as explained above.
Kausika! Let alone the sentient beings within two thousand intermediate world-systems.
If one were to instruct all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm to practice the ten paths of wholesome action,

and another person were to write out a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others so that they might copy, uphold, read, recite, and explain it, the latter would generate far greater merit.
Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings within the trichiliocosm,
suppose one were to teach all the sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
If, moreover, there is someone who writes out a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to another person to write, uphold, read, recite, and explain, their merit is greater.
The rest is as explained above.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! Suppose there were someone who taught the sentient beings of one Jambudvīpa, causing them to establish themselves in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers."
"What do you think, Śakra Devānām Indra? Is the merit of this son or daughter of good family great or not?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "It is very great, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious as for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to write out a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others, causing them to write it down, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it; the latter gains far more merit."
Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, all wholesome dharmas are explained in detail.
The rest is as stated above.
Kauśika! Let alone the sentient beings within Jambudvīpa.

Furthermore, let alone the sentient beings within the lands of the four continents, the sentient beings within a small thousandfold world system, the sentient beings within a medium two-thousandfold world system, and the sentient beings within a great trichiliocosm.

Kauśika! Suppose there were someone who taught the sentient beings in as many lands in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, causing them to establish themselves in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges.
"What do you think?
Is the merit of this person great or not? He replied:
“Very much, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“It is not as great as the merit obtained by a son or daughter of good family who writes out a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to others, causing them to write it, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it.”
Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, all wholesome dharmas are explained in detail.
The rest is as stated above.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who receive this Prajñāpāramitā, uphold, read, recite, explain, and correctly bring it to mind."

The merit of this person surpasses that of those who teach the people of Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, establish themselves in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.
One who practices right mindfulness upholds and draws near to the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including right mindfulness, neither by way of dualistic dharmas nor by way of non-dualistic dharmas;

one upholds and draws near to the *dhyānapāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, and *dānapāramitā*, up to and including right mindfulness, neither by way of dualistic dharmas nor by way of non-dualistic dharmas;

for the sake of *anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*, one practices right mindfulness of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), neither by way of dualistic dharmas nor by way of non-dualistic dharmas.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for the sake of others, expound the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* through various causes and conditions, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand;
Kauśika! What is the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā? Kauśika!

The meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā should not be viewed through the characteristic of duality, nor should it be viewed through the characteristic of non-duality; it is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics. It does not enter or exit, it neither increases nor decreases, it is neither defiled nor pure, it neither arises nor ceases, it neither grasps nor abandons. It neither abides nor does not abide; it is neither real nor unreal, neither joined nor dispersed, neither attached nor unattached, neither caused nor uncaused, neither dharmic nor non-dharmic, neither suchness nor non-suchness, and neither the limit of reality nor non-limit-of-reality.

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can, for the sake of others, expound the meaning of this Prajñāpāramitā through various causes and conditions, revealing, clarifying, and analyzing it so that it is easily understood, the merit obtained by that son or daughter of good family will be far greater than that of one who merely upholds the Prajñāpāramitā themselves, or who approaches, recites, explains, and correctly contemplates it.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family personally upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, draws near to it, reads and recites it, explains it, and correctly contemplates it; and furthermore, for the sake of others, they expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā through various causes and conditions, revealing, clarifying, and analyzing it so that it may be easily understood."
"The merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters is exceedingly great.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Good sons and good daughters should expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in this way, revealing, clarifying, and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: “So it is, Kauśika!”
These sons and daughters of good family should expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in this way, revealing, clarifying, and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand. Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in this way—elucidating, analyzing, and making it easy to understand—they will obtain immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merit.

If there are good sons or good daughters who make offerings to the immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions throughout their entire lifespans, providing whatever they require, honoring, respecting, and praising them with offerings of flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.

Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who, through various causes and conditions, extensively expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā to others, revealing, demonstrating, and analyzing it so that it may be easily understood.
The merit of these sons and daughters of good family is exceedingly great. Why is this?
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present have studied within this Prajñāpāramitā, thereby attaining, currently attaining, and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices the perfection of giving for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable eons.

It is not as meritorious for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā to others, revealing, demonstrating, and analyzing it so that it is easily understood; their merit is far greater, because they do so by way of non-apprehension.
What is meant by "having something to apprehend"? Kausika!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving with something to apprehend, at the time of giving he forms this thought:
"To think, 'I am giving this object to that recipient,' is called attaining *dāna*, but not the *pāramitā*. To think, 'I am observing the precepts;
this is morality' [is called attaining *śīla*, but not the *pāramitā*]."
"This is called attaining precepts, but not the pāramitā;
'I practice patience, I practice patience for the sake of this person'—
this is called attaining patience, but not the pāramitā."
"I am diligent; I exert myself with diligence for this purpose"—this is called attaining diligence, but not the perfection (pāramitā) of diligence.
"I cultivate dhyāna; this is the dhyāna I cultivate."
"This is called attaining dhyāna, but not the pāramitā;
'I cultivate wisdom, and this is the wisdom I cultivate'—
this is called attaining wisdom, but not the pāramitā."

Kauśika! A son or daughter of good family who practices in this manner will not attain the fulfillment of the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, or prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice so as to fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?”
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, if they do not apprehend the giver, do not apprehend the recipient, and do not apprehend the object given, this person fulfills the perfection of dāna."
Even when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not apprehend wisdom, nor does one apprehend the wisdom being practiced; such a person attains the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom.
Kauśika! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā.
Sons and daughters of good family who practice the prajñā-pāramitā in this way should expound its meaning for others, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand.
He expounded upon the meaning of the dhyāna-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, and dāna-pāramitā, elucidating and analyzing them so that they might be easily understood.
Why is this? Kauśika!
In future ages there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who, wishing to speak of the *prajñāpāramitā*, will instead speak of a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
There may be sons or daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet upon hearing this counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, they lose the true path.
Good sons and good daughters should fully expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā for such persons, revealing and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is this counterfeit prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who speak of the prajñāpāramitā as something to be attained, this is a counterfeit prajñāpāramitā."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that when good sons and good daughters speak of the prajñāpāramitā as something to be attained, this is called a counterfeit prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said:
"Good sons and good daughters who speak of the prajñāpāramitā as something to be attained are practicing a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā."
Regarding that which resembles the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it explains that form (rūpa) is impermanent.
It makes this statement:
"One who can practice in this way is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
If a practitioner seeks the impermanence of form, this is practicing a semblance of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
To speak of the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and to say:
"One who can practice in this way is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*," [is likewise a semblance].
When a practitioner seeks the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is practicing a semblance of the Prajñāpāramitā.
It consists of teaching that the eye is impermanent up to teaching that the mind is impermanent, and teaching that forms are impermanent up to teaching that phenomena are impermanent.

It is taught that the eye-element is impermanent, the form-element and the eye-consciousness-element are impermanent, and so on, up to the teaching that the mind-element, the phenomena-element, and the mind-consciousness-element are impermanent.
He taught that the earth element is impermanent, up to and including the teaching that the consciousness element is impermanent;
he taught that the eye-consciousness element is impermanent, up to and including the teaching that the mind-consciousness element is impermanent;
he taught that eye-contact is impermanent, up to and including the teaching that mind-contact is impermanent.

He taught that the feeling born of eye-contact conditioned by causes and conditions is impermanent, and so on, up to the teaching that the feeling born of mind-contact conditioned by causes and conditions is impermanent,
as explained in detail in the section on the five aggregates.
He taught that form is suffering, and so on, up to the teaching that the feeling born of mind-contact conditioned by causes and conditions is suffering.
He teaches that form is non-self, and so on, up to teaching that feeling produced by the condition of mind-contact is non-self;
all of this is as explained regarding the five aggregates.

When a practitioner practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), [the teacher] teaches them that form is impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and so on, up to teaching that feeling produced by the condition of mind-contact is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
It is the same for the *śīlapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, he teaches them that these are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
When practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, they teach impermanence, suffering, and non-self;
even when practicing up to the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they teach impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
He gives such instruction as this:
"One who can practice in this way is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), Kauśika!"
This is called a counterfeit perfection of wisdom. "Furthermore, Kauśika,
if in a future age these sons of good family or daughters of good family should preach a counterfeit perfection of wisdom, saying:
"O son of good family, O daughter of good family, as you practice the Prajñāpāramitā, while practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, you shall attain the first bhūmi, and so on, up to the tenth bhūmi."
The same applies to the dhyāna-pāramitā up to the dāna-pāramitā.
The practitioner cultivates this prajñā-pāramitā by means of a semblance of attainment and by way of general characteristics.
Kauśika! This is called the counterfeit prajñāpāramitā. "Furthermore, Kauśika!"
Good sons and good daughters who wish to expound the Prajñāpāramitā should speak thus:
"O good sons and good daughters, once you have practiced the Prajñāpāramitā, you shall transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
This is called the counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā. "Furthermore, Kauśika,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family speaks thus to those who seek the path of the Buddha:

“O son of good family, O daughter of good family, having practiced the *prajñāpāramitā*, you shall enter the stage of a bodhisattva and attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Having attained this patience regarding non-arising, you shall abide in the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, traveling from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to the Buddhas, and honoring, respecting, and praising them.”
To speak in such a manner is called a semblance of the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Furthermore, Kauśika,
if a son or daughter of good family speaks thus to those who seek the path of the Buddha:

"O son of good family, O daughter of good family, if you study this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it, and maintain right mindfulness of it, you shall attain immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merit."
To speak in such a manner is called a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, good sons and good daughters who seek the Buddha-way may speak thus:

"Just as the roots of merit and the foundations of goodness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—from their first resolution until they attained Buddhahood—are entirely gathered together and dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"To speak in such a manner is called a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that good sons and good daughters do not speak of a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* to those who seek the path of the Buddha?
The Buddha said:
"If good sons and good daughters speak the *prajñāpāramitā* to those who seek the path of the Buddha:"
“Good son! As you practice the Prajñāpāramitā, do not contemplate form as impermanent. Why is this?
Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form.
This nature of form is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma; this is what is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within the perfection of wisdom, form is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Why is this? Because within this, even form cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence. Kausika!
Good sons and good daughters who speak in this manner are said not to be speaking of a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! A son of good family or a daughter of good family speaks to one who seeks the path of the Buddha, saying:
'You, son of good family!'"
When practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one should neither transcend nor abide in any phenomena.
Why is this? Because within the perfection of wisdom, there is no phenomenon that can be transcended or abided in.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is empty of intrinsic nature is not a phenomenon; that which is not a phenomenon is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"In the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can enter or exit, arise or cease. Kauśika!
When a son of good family or a daughter of good family speaks in this way, it is called not speaking a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā.
The detailed explanation is as above.
To be similar yet contradictory is called "not speaking of the similar Prajñāpāramitā. Thus it is, Kausika!
Good sons and good daughters should expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner.
If they expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in this way, the merit they obtain will surpass that of the former.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were instructed and led to attain the stage of Srotāpanna.
What do you think? Would that person acquire much merit?"
He replied, “Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as this: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of others, explains its meaning through various causes and conditions, revealing, demonstrating, and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand, saying:
'Sons of good family, daughters of good family!'"
Come, receive this Prajñāpāramitā; diligently recite, read, and explain it, maintain right mindfulness of it, and practice according to what is taught within the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, all srotāpannas are born. Kausika!

Setting aside the sentient beings within Jambudvīpa, and further setting aside the sentient beings of the four continents, the small thousandfold world system, the medium two-thousandfold world system, and the great trichiliocosm world system.

If there were someone who taught the sentient beings within as many lands in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, instructing them all until they attained the stage of Srotāpanna—what do you think? Would this person acquire much merit?
He replied, "Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as this: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of others, were to expound its meaning through various causes and conditions, revealing, clarifying, and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand, saying:
'O son of good family!'"
Come, receive this Prajñāpāramitā; diligently recite, read, and explain it, maintain right mindfulness of it, and practice according to what is taught within the Prajñāpāramitā?
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, all srotāpannas are born. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught the people of Jambudvīpa and caused them to attain the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat—what do you think? Would that person gain much merit?
He replied, “Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as this: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of others, expounds its meaning through various causes and conditions, elucidates, analyzes, and makes it easy to understand, saying:
'Son of good family!'"
Come, receive this Prajñāpāramitā; diligently recite, read, and explain it, maintain right mindfulness of it, and practice according to what is taught within the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, all Srotāpannas, Sakṛdāgāmins, Anāgāmins, and Arhats are born.
This applies likewise even to the sentient beings in lands throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach the sentient beings within one Jambudvīpa so that they attain the path of a Pratyekabuddha."
"What do you think, would that person gain much merit? He replied,
"Very much, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as when a son of good family or a daughter of good family uses the *prajñāpāramitā* to expound its meaning to others through various causes and conditions, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand, saying:
'O son of good family!'"
Come, receive this Prajñāpāramitā; diligently read, recite, explain, and correctly contemplate it, and practice according to what is taught within the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the path of all Pratyekabuddhas is born.
It is the same for the sentient beings in the four continents, and even throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! Suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings within a single Jambudvīpa, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"What do you think? Would that person gain much merit?
He replied, "Very much, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as this son or daughter of good family who, for the sake of others, explains the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā through various causes and conditions, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand, and further says:
'You should train according to the Prajñāpāramitā; you shall thereby attain the dharma of omniscience.'"
If you attain the dharma of all-knowledge, you will then attain the cultivation, increase, and fulfillment of the prajñāpāramitā.
If you attain the cultivation, increase, and fulfillment of the prajñāpāramitā, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Kauśika! It is because within the Prajñāpāramitā all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved upon awakening are born.
This applies even to as many lands in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River. Furthermore, Kauśika,
if a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa and cause them to abide in the stage of *avaivartika*.
"What do you think, would that person’s merit be great?
He replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as this son or daughter of good family who, for the sake of others, explains its meaning through various causes and conditions, revealing and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand, and speaks thus:
'Come, son of good family!'"
If you receive this Prajñāpāramitā and practice even as it is taught therein, you will then attain the dharma of omniscience.
Having attained the dharma of omniscience, you will eventually attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) for all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is produced.
This is likewise true even for lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.

"Furthermore, Kausika! Suppose all the sentient beings within a single Jambudvipa resolve their minds to seek anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for the sake of these people, extensively expounds the Prajñāpāramitā along with its interpretations, revealing and analyzing it, saying:
'Come, son of good family!'"
Having received this Prajñāpāramitā and practicing even according to what is taught within it, once you have completed your training, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, suppose there is another person who expounds the *prajñāpāramitā* and its interpretations for a single *avaivartika* bodhisattva, revealing and analyzing it, saying:
"Come and receive this *prajñāpāramitā*, and practice according to what is taught within the *prajñāpāramitā*; having trained, you shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"The merit obtained by this son of good family is exceedingly great.
It is likewise so throughout as many lands in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges.
Furthermore, Kauśika!..."
Suppose all sentient beings within a single Jambudvīpa were to attain the state of non-retrogression and unexcelled, perfect, complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Furthermore, suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who expounded the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā for these beings. Within this assembly, there was a bodhisattva who desired to swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect, complete enlightenment.
If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of this bodhisattva, expound the Prajñāpāramitā and its interpretive meaning, the merit of such persons is the greatest.
"Even so it is for as many lands in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River.
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws ever closer to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so too should they be progressively taught to practice the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā; they should be taught inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities. Furthermore, they should be provided with offerings of clothing, bedding, food, and medicine, according to whatever is required.
If these sons or daughters of good family provide offerings of Dharma-giving and material gifts to this bodhisattva, the merit they obtain will surpass that of the former. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Kauśika! For you,

as a noble disciple, to comfort those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are dedicated to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, benefiting them through the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth— this is indeed how it ought to be."
Why is this? Because within the bodhisattvas, the assembly of all Buddhas and noble ones is born.
If a bodhisattva does not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that bodhisattva would be unable to train in the six *pāramitās* up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharmas*).
If one does not study the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then there would be no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, Kauśika,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
When they study the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they sever the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; thereupon, the world comes to possess great clans of Kṣatriyas, great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and great households of householders; from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; and even the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*; from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) appear in the world; and the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the Buddhas all manifest in the world.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Ten. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
Chapter 39: Rejoicing (The Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication) At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
“There are bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who rejoice in merit and share it with all sentient beings, dedicating it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by way of non-apprehension.”

Whether it be the merit of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or the merit of all sentient beings—whether through giving, observing precepts, practicing meditative concentration, or sympathetic joy—that merit of sympathetic joy belonging to this bodhisattva mahāsattva is shared with all sentient beings and dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; that merit is supreme, foremost, most wondrous, unsurpassed, and peerless.

Why is this? The giving, upholding of precepts, cultivation of concentration, and sympathetic joy of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings arise for the sake of self-discipline, self-purification, and self-deliverance; that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

The Bodhisattva rejoices in merit and dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he maintains these merits for the sake of disciplining all sentient beings, purifying all sentient beings, and delivering all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:

"The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas bring to mind the immeasurable, boundless, and asaṃkhyeya Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa within the immeasurable, boundless, and asaṃkhyeya lands of the ten directions—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, entered nirvana without remainder, and even until the exhaustion of the Dharma."

Within this interval, there are all roots of goodness corresponding to the six pāramitās and the roots of goodness of the śrāvakas— namely, the merit of giving, the merit of maintaining the precepts, and the merit of practicing meditative concentration— as well as the untainted roots of goodness of those in training (śaikṣa), the untainted roots of goodness of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), the Buddha’s aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration,

the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; the omniscience, the great loving-kindness and great compassion, and all other immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) qualities of a Buddha, as well as all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas.
Within this Dharma, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and enters the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
as do other sentient beings who plant various roots of goodness.

All these roots of goodness, combined together, are dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as merit arising from sympathetic joy; they are supreme, foremost, most wondrous, unsurpassed, and peerless.
Having thus rejoiced, one takes this merit of rejoicing and dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If there is a son of good family who practices the Bodhisattva vehicle and thinks:
"It is my mind that dedicates [this] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"This is the arising of a mind that takes an object as its condition.
If a son of good family were to grasp at signs and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, could he obtain it in accordance with what he has conceived?"
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:
“When these sons of good family who practice the bodhisattva vehicle dedicate toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, their minds take that as an object.”
"If a son of good family grasps at signs, he will not attain what was intended.
Subhūti said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"If all conditions and all things are non-existent, then this son of good family who practices the Bodhisattva vehicle grasps at signs regarding the roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the ten directions—from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until the exhaustion of the Dharma—as well as the roots of goodness of the Śrāvakas, both those in training and those beyond training. He unites all these merits of sympathetic joy and dedicates them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Because they are signless, these bodhisattvas will be free from inversion.

To regard the impermanent as permanent is an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view; to regard the impure as pure, suffering as pleasure, and non-self as self is an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view.

If it is as the Suchness of conditions and as the Suchness of things, so it is for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; so it is for the mind of dedication, and so it is for the pāramitās of dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, and prajñā, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
If that is so, what is the condition?
What is the objective entity?
And what is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"What are these roots of goodness?
What is this mind of sympathetic joy that dedicates [merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:

"If Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have long practiced the six pāramitās, made extensive offerings to the Buddhas and planted roots of goodness, associated with virtuous friends, and have well studied the dharma of the emptiness of self-characteristics."

These bodhisattvas take these things as their objects; they rejoice in the merit of all Buddhas and all roots of goodness, and dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without grasping at signs. By means of the non-dual dharma—which is neither dual nor non-dual, neither characterized by signs nor signless, neither an attainable dharma nor an unattainable dharma, neither pure nor defiled, and a dharma that is neither arising nor ceasing—this is called dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If bodhisattvas have not practiced the six perfections for long, have not made extensive offerings to the Buddhas, have not planted roots of goodness, have not associated with spiritual friends, and have not skillfully studied the dharma of the emptiness of self-characteristics.

If these bodhisattvas, regarding these conditions and these matters, take signs with their minds as they rejoice in the merit of the various Buddhas' roots of goodness, and dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is not called dedication.

Subhūti! The meaning of this prajñāpāramitā, up to the meaning of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)—namely, from internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā)—should not be taught to a newly initiated bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because all the slight faith, joy, reverence, and pure mind that this bodhisattva possesses will be lost.
This should be spoken in the presence of an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If there are those who are protected by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), or who have long made offerings to the Buddhas and planted various roots of goodness (kuśalamūla), for such persons one should explain the meaning of this Prajñāpāramitā, up to the meaning of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)—that is to say, from internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā).
When such a person hears this Dharma, they do not sink, are not startled, are not terrified, and are not afraid. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva’s merit of sympathetic joy should be dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this manner.

When a bodhisattva applies their mind to rejoice in merit and dedicate it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, that mind is exhausted, ceases, transforms, and departs from those conditions and those objects; likewise, all those roots of goodness are also exhausted, cease, transform, and depart.
Among these, what is the mind of sympathetic joy?
What are the various conditions?
And what are the various matters?
What are these roots of goodness that are rejoiced in and dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Two minds do not coexist; furthermore, this nature of mind cannot be apprehended for dedication.
How does a bodhisattva dedicate the mind of sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they know that this *prajñāpāramitā* has no dharma; even the *dānapāramitā* has no dharma. Form has no dharma; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no dharma; and even up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is no dharma.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus rejoice in merit and dedicate it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one can dedicate in this manner, it is called the dedication of the merit of rejoicing toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti: “Subhūti,
will bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds not be startled, terrified, or afraid upon hearing this matter?”
How does a bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind dedicate all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Furthermore, how do they dedicate the merit of sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not grasp this perfection of wisdom, because it is non-apprehendable and signless.”
This applies even up to the *dānapāramitā*.

One extensively believes in and understands internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), and so on, up to extensively believing in and understanding the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); one extensively believes in and understands the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and always associates with virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
These spiritual friends explain the meaning of the six pāramitās, revealing and analyzing them.

Teaching in this way, they cause [the practitioner] to never be separated from the prajñāpāramitā until they enter the stage of the bodhisattva-dharmas; until the end, they are never separated from the prajñāpāramitā, nor from the dānapāramitā, nor from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
He also teaches them regarding the works of Māra.
Having heard these various works of Māra, they neither increase nor decrease. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not grasp at any phenomena,
this bodhisattva is also never separated from the Buddhas until they attain the rank of a bodhisattva.

Within this, they plant roots of goodness; by virtue of these roots of goodness, they are born into the family of Bodhisattvas, and until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they never depart from these roots of goodness.

"Furthermore, a newly resolved bodhisattva mahāsattva [should reflect upon] the Buddhas of the past in the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable lands of the ten directions—those who have severed the path of birth and death, severed the path of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), completely cast off the heavy burden, extinguished the thorns of the village, severed the fetters of existence, and attained liberation through right knowledge.

And as for the merit performed by their disciples—whether it be the roots of goodness planted among the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, or the great families of householders, or those planted by the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven—one should combine and weigh all of this together and, with a heart of sympathetic joy, rejoice in it as the most supreme, foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless.
"Having rejoiced, one dedicates [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:

"If a newly resolved bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the roots of goodness of all Buddhas and their disciples, the merit of such rejoicing is supreme, foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless."
Having rejoiced, one should dedicate [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How does a bodhisattva avoid falling into inversion of perception, inversion of mind, and inversion of view?

Subhūti said: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings to mind the Buddhas and the Saṃgha, yet within this does not give rise to the notion of 'Buddha' nor the notion of 'Saṃgha,' and has no notion of 'roots of goodness,' and employs this mind to dedicate [the merit] toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet within this mind also does not give rise to the notion of 'mind.'"
When a bodhisattva thus dedicates [merit], their perception is non-perverted, their mind is non-perverted, and their view is non-perverted.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, however, recollects the roots of goodness of the Buddhas and the Saṃgha while grasping at signs, and having grasped these signs, dedicates them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
In this way, the bodhisattva is said to have an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva uses such a mind to contemplate the Buddhas, the Saṅgha, and all roots of goodness, at the very moment he contemplates them with that mind, he knows they are utterly extinguished. If these phenomena are utterly extinguished and cannot be apprehended, then the dedicating mind used for the dedication is likewise characterized by utter extinction; the place of dedication and the phenomena dedicated are also of this same nature.
