If one dedicates in such a manner, it is called right dedication and not wrong dedication.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should dedicate toward unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment in this way.
"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva [dedicates] the roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the past and the roots of goodness of their disciples,
as well as the roots of goodness planted by ordinary persons who heard the Dharma therein,
or those of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas..."
Rāga, having heard the Dharma, planted roots of goodness; likewise, whether they be of great Kṣatriya clans, great Brāhmaṇa clans, or great householder families,
or from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, having heard the Dharma,
they planted roots of goodness and gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi— all such merit as this...
Having weighed and assessed these virtues through their harmonious union, one rejoices in this merit which is supreme, foremost, most wondrous,
unsurpassed, and peerless, dedicating it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, if a bodhisattva understands that all these phenomena are utterly extinguished, and that both the destination to which one dedicates [merit] and the phenomena themselves are empty of intrinsic nature, and is able to dedicate in this manner, this is called the true dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva understands in this way, there is no dharma that can be dedicated to another dharma.
Why? Because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature."
If one dedicates in this manner, it is called the correct dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, they do not fall into inversion of perception, inversion of mind, or inversion of view.

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva does not cling to this dedication, nor does he perceive a place where these roots of goodness are dedicated toward the mind of enlightenment; this is called the unsurpassed dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that the merit they have performed is detached from the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); and if they also know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is characterized by detachment, and likewise that the *dānapāramitā* is characterized by detachment; and that from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is characterized by detachment; and that from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) is characterized by detachment."
In this way, the merit arising from the mind of sympathetic joy of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called dedication toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva rejoices in merit, they know that the self-nature of the rejoicing in merit is detached; they also know that the Buddhas are detached from the nature of Buddhahood, that all roots of goodness are detached from the nature of roots of goodness, that the mind of awakening is detached from the nature of the mind of awakening, that the dedication is detached from the nature of dedication, that the bodhisattva is detached from the nature of a bodhisattva, that the *prajñāpāramitā* is detached from the nature of *prajñāpāramitā*, and that the *dhyānapāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, and *dānapāramitā* are detached from the nature of *dānapāramitā*, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), which are detached from the nature of the eighteen unique qualities."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom that is free from signs in this manner; this is called the merit of rejoicing produced within the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to dedicate the roots of goodness of all the Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa, they should dedicate them in this way."
He forms this thought:

"As is the mark of the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, so too is the mark of all roots of goodness; as is the mark of the dharma of parinirvāṇa, so too is the mark of this mind with which I dedicate [these roots]. The mark of this mind is likewise such."
If one can dedicate in this manner, it should be known that this dedication is for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such a dedication does not fall into the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, or the inversion of view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, grasps at the marks of the roots of goodness of the Buddhas and dedicates them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is not called dedication.
Why is this? The past Buddhas and their roots of goodness are neither conditioned by signs nor unconditioned by signs.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva grasps them in such a way as to take them as signs, this is not called the dedication of roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva falls into perversion of perception, perversion of mind, and perversion of view.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not grasp at the signs of the Buddhas, their roots of goodness, or their mental states, this is called dedicating those roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; in this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not fall into inversion of perception, inversion of mind, or inversion of view.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva asked Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, without grasping at signs regarding any roots of goodness, succeed in dedicating them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

Subhūti said: "For this reason, it should be known that within the Prajñāpāramitā in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains, there must be the power of skillful means (upāyakauśalya) of the Prajñāpāramitā."
If merit were divorced from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it could not be dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Why is this?

Because within the perfection of wisdom, the Buddhas cannot be apprehended, the roots of goodness cannot be apprehended, and the mind that dedicates [merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment also cannot be apprehended.
In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should reflect in this way:
"The bodies of the past buddhas and their disciples have all ceased, and their roots of goodness have also ceased."

If I now grasp at signs and differentiate the various Buddhas, their roots of goodness, and their minds, and then dedicate [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of such grasping at signs, this is not permitted by the Buddhas.
Why is this? Because they grasp at signs and perceive something to be attained;
that is to say, they grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the Buddhas of the past.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to dedicate all roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should not have the notion of attainment, nor should they take up signs; in this manner should they perform dedication.
If one performs dedication while grasping at attainment or signs, the Buddhas do not say that there is great benefit. Why is this?
Because such dedication is mixed with poison.
It is like fine food mixed with poison; although it possesses an attractive appearance and a pleasant fragrance, people crave it because of its flavor, yet it is infused within with poison.
A foolish person eats it with joy, coveting its fine color, fragrance, and delicious taste.
When the food one has eaten begins to digest, one experiences suffering such as death or that which is equal to death.

This is because the good man or good woman has not received it with clarity, has not grasped its characteristics with clarity, has not recited it with clarity, and does not understand its inner meaning.
He instructs others in this way:
"O son of good family!
All Buddhas of the ten directions—past, future, and present—from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained [Buddhahood]..."
From the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* until entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and the exhaustion of all phenomena,
during that interval while practicing the *prajñā-pāramitā*, one performs various roots of goodness;
likewise while practicing the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, the *vīrya-pāramitā*, the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, and the *śīla-pāramitā*.
...when practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one cultivates all roots of goodness;

when practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), and the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśa tathāgatabalāni*) up to the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharmāḥ*), one cultivates all roots of goodness; and when purifying the buddha-fields and bringing them to fulfillment...
The roots of goodness planted by sentient beings; the multitudes of precepts, concentrations, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all Buddhas;
their constant practice of equanimity regarding all-knowledge and the non-erroneous Dharma;
the roots of goodness planted therein by their disciples; and those whom the Buddhas have prophesied shall become [Buddhas].
Regarding the pratyekabuddhas, it is therein that the various devas, nāgas, asuras,
garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others plant roots of goodness.
One should weigh, harmonize, and rejoice in all these merits, dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
However, because this dedication involves grasping at signs and acquiring dharmas, it is like food mixed with poison; one who acquires dharmas can never achieve a correct dedication.
Why is this? Because such an attainment of the Dharma is mixed with poison; it possesses signs, movement, and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one dedicates [merit] in such a manner, one slanders the Buddha, does not follow the Buddha’s teaching, and does not accord with the exposition of the Dharma.
These sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way should train themselves in this way:

regarding all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until the exhaustion of the Dharma—as well as their disciples, during the time they practiced the *prajñāpāramitā* and performed roots of goodness up to the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The rest is as explained above.
What is the correct dedication of all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Any son of good family or daughter of good family seeking the Buddha-way who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* and does not wish to slander the Buddhas should dedicate all merits in this manner.
Just as the Buddhas know with unsurpassed wisdom, so too do I rejoice in these characteristics of the roots of goodness and the nature of these roots of goodness.
Just as the Buddhas know, so too do I dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path should dedicate [their merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this manner.
If they dedicate in this way, they do not slander the Buddha; it is as the Buddha has taught and as the Buddha-dharma declares.
The dedication of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is free from mixed poison.
Furthermore, when sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way practice the prajñāpāramitā, they should dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner.
Just as form is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm,
so too unbound phenomena (asaṃyukta-dharma) are not called past, not called future, and not called present.
Just as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm;
so too, that which is unbound is not designated as past, future, or present.
The twelve bases and eighteen elements are also like this.
Just as the Prajñāpāramitā is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm.
Dharmas that are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are not designated as past, future, or present.

It is the same for the perfection of dhyāna up to the perfection of dāna; it is likewise for inner emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā).
Just as the four foundations of mindfulness are not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm;
that which is unbound is not designated as past, future, or present.
It is the same for the eightfold noble path; it is the same for the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities.

It is the same for suchness, the dharma-nature, the dharma-characteristic, the stability of dharmas, the fixed position of dharmas, the reality-limit, and the inconceivable nature. It is the same for the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; for all-knowledge; and for the practice of constant relinquishment, which is the non-erroneous dharma that is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm.
As for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they are not designated as past, future, or present.
This dedication, the object to which it is dedicated, and the practitioner who performs it are likewise all unconditioned.
These Buddhas are also unconditioned; these roots of goodness are also unconditioned; and the roots of goodness of these śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are also unconditioned.
That which is an unconditioned dharma is not designated as past, future, or present.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know in this way that form is not bound to the three realms; that which is not bound to dharmas is not designated as past, future, or present.
If dharmas are past, future, or present, one cannot take their marks or grasp them as attainable phenomena and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because this form is unarisen.
If a dharma is unarisen, it is no dharma; and within that which is no dharma, there can be no dedication.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

From the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the dharma of non-delusion, they are always practiced with equanimity and are not bound to the three realms.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are likewise neither past, future, nor present.
If they are not past, future, or present phenomena, one cannot take their marks or grasp them as attainable phenomena and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because these dharmas are unarisen.
If they are unarisen, they are non-existent; and within that which is non-existent, there can be no dedication.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, there is no admixture of poison.

If a son or daughter of good family seeking the Buddha-way dedicates their roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of grasping at signs or apprehending dharmas, this is called wrong dedication.
If one performs a wrong dedication, it is not praised by the Buddhas.

By means of such a wrong dedication, one cannot fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); one cannot fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path; one cannot fulfill inner emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); one cannot fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśabala*) up to the practice of constant relinquishment free from error; and one cannot fulfill the purification of buddha-fields or the maturation of sentient beings.
If one cannot purify the Buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity, then one cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
This is because such dedication is mixed with poison.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought:
"As the Buddhas know it, the dedication of all roots of goodness is true dedication."
"I, too, should dedicate by means of these characteristics of dharmas.
This is called right dedication.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti:
“Excellent, excellent! What you have done is to perform the work of a Buddha.

You have taught the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma that should be dedicated, because it is without marks, without attainment, and without emergence; because it is without defilement and without purity; because it is the nature of non-dharmas; because its own-characteristics are empty and its constant self-nature is empty; and because it is like the nature of dharmas and like the limit of reality.”

Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm were to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would those beings acquire much merit?
"Very much, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"It is not as good as this: that a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a mind unattached to any roots of goodness, dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Subhūti! The merit of these good sons and good daughters is supreme, foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Suppose that all sentient beings within the three thousandfold world-system were to attain the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhatship or Pratyekabuddhahood.

If there were a son or daughter of good family who, for as long as they lived, provided them with offerings, respect, reverence, and praise, and supplied them with their necessities—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.
"What do you think, Subhūti? On account of this cause and condition, would that son or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
"Very much, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

“It is not equal to when these sons and daughters of good family, with minds unattached to any roots of goodness, dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the most supreme, the foremost, the most wonderful, the unsurpassed, and the peerless.”
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose all sentient beings within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to each give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If every single sentient being in as many lands throughout the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges were, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, to reverently honor, respect, praise, and make offerings to this bodhisattva, providing them with all necessities such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine;
"What do you think, Subhūti? By reason of this, would that son of good family or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
"Very much, World-Honored One!"
"Immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), it cannot be compared by means of analogy, World-Honored One!
If this merit were to have a physical form, the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, would not be able to contain it."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.”

Nevertheless, it is not equal to when a son or daughter of good family, with a mind unattached to any roots of goodness, dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the most supreme, the foremost, the most wondrous, the unsurpassed, and the peerless.

This merit of dedication free from attachment, compared to the previous merit, is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold, and even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy.

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family grasp at signs and acquire dharmas as they practice the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.

They grasp at signs and receive the Dharma-offering of a stream-enterer, honoring, respecting, praising, and providing them with whatever is required— robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites—
even to the extent that they grasp at signs while making offerings to a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, together with twenty thousand devas, joined their palms in homage to the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!

This is the greatest dedication of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: by means of the power of skillful means, by means of non-apprehension, by means of the dharma of signlessness, and by means of the dharma of non-awakening, they dedicate all roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"By dedicating in this manner, one does not fall into dualistic dharmas.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, together with countless hundreds of thousands of billions of gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and other sons of gods, took celestial flowers, necklaces, powdered incense, liquid perfumes, celestial robes, banners, canopies, and drums, and performed divine music as offerings to the Buddha, saying these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s supreme dedication is performed through the power of skillful means, by way of non-apprehension, by way of signless dharmas, and by way of unawakened dharmas, dedicating all roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Dedication in this manner does not fall into dualistic dharmas.

Then the Deva-king Suyāma, together with a thousand devaputras, and the Deva-kings of Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin, each accompanied by a thousand devaputras, having made offerings to the Buddha, spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s supreme dedication of merit is performed through the power of skillful means, by way of non-apprehension, by way of signless dharmas, and by way of dharmas without conceptualization, dedicating all roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"By dedicating in this way, one does not fall into dualistic dharmas.

At that time, the Brahmā devas, together with countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of devas, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, and raised their voices in great sound, saying:
"It is unprecedented!
World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, being protected by the perfection of wisdom and through the power of skillful means, surpasses those aforementioned sons and daughters of good family who grasp at signs and have something to be attained.

The Ābhāsvara devas up to the Akaniṣṭha devas, together with hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of devas, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and raised their voices in great sound, saying:
"It is unprecedented! It is marvelous!"
“World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, being protected by the perfection of wisdom and through the power of skillful means, surpasses those aforementioned sons and daughters of good family who grasp at signs and have something to be attained.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras from the Four Great Kings up to those of Akaniṣṭha:

“Suppose all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. These bodhisattvas would then contemplate the roots of goodness of all Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present—from their initial generation of the mind until the duration of the Dharma—including all the roots of goodness therein, as well as all the roots of goodness of all other sentient beings, namely: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom; the pāramitās from dāna-pāramitā up to prajñā-pāramitā; and the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.”

In this way, one rejoices in all these other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas in their entirety; having rejoiced, one dedicates [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of grasping at signs and with the notion of something to be attained.
Furthermore, there may be sons or daughters of good family who resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and reflect upon all Buddhas,
śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present—
from their first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment until the duration of the Dharma— including all the roots of goodness therein, as well as all others.
All the roots of goodness possessed by sentient beings—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom;
from the *dānapāramitā* up to the immeasurable qualities of the Buddhas—all these are combined and weighed together.
Because they are non-apprehendable, because they are non-dual, and because they do not exist...
Because it is the dharma of signs, because it is non-attachment to dharmas, and because it is the dharma of non-conceptualization,
this is the supreme sympathetic joy— the foremost, most wondrous, unsurpassed, and peerless sympathetic joy.
Having rejoiced, they dedicate [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The merit of these sons and daughters of good family surpasses the merit of the former sons and daughters of good family by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold, even to the extent that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The World-Honored One has said that when good sons and good daughters gather all roots of goodness, weigh them, rejoice in them, and dedicate them, this is the most supreme, the foremost, the most wonderful, the unsurpassed, and the peerless.”
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘rejoicing that is supreme, even unto being peerless’?
The Buddha said:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, neither grasps nor rejects them; neither contemplates nor does not contemplate them; neither attains nor does not attain them—within these phenomena, there is no phenomenon that arises or ceases, whether it be defiled or pure."

All dharmas neither increase nor decrease; they neither come nor go; they neither unite nor disperse; they neither enter nor exit. Just as the characteristics of all dharmas of the past, future, and present—namely, the suchness-characteristic, the dharma-nature, the stability of dharmas, and the fixed position of dharmas—I likewise rejoice in accordance with them.
Having rejoiced, one dedicates [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such dedication is supreme, foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless.

Subhūti! This dharma of sympathetic joy, compared to other forms of sympathetic joy, exceeds them a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold, even to the point that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

A son of good family or daughter of good family seeking the Buddha-way who wishes to rejoice in all the roots of goodness—from giving up to wisdom, from the *dānapāramitā* up to the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha—belonging to the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present, from their first generation of the mind until the duration of the Dharma; as well as all the roots of goodness belonging to all other sentient beings during that interval—they should rejoice in them in this manner.
He forms this thought:
"Generosity is equal to liberation; ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are equal to liberation;
form is equal to liberation, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise equal to liberation."
Inner emptiness is equal to liberation, and so on up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is also equal to liberation;
the four foundations of mindfulness are equal to liberation, and so on up to the eightfold noble path, which is also equal to liberation;

the ten powers of a Buddha are equal to liberation, and so on up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is also equal to liberation; and the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation are also equal to liberation.
Rejoicing is equal to liberation;
all dharmas of the past, future, and present are equal to liberation;
and the Buddhas of the ten directions are equal to liberation.
The dedications of all Buddhas are equal to liberation;
all Buddhas are equal to liberation;
the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas is equal to liberation.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who are disciples of the Buddhas are equal to liberation;
the parinirvāṇa of the disciples of the Buddhas is equal to liberation;

the dharma-characteristics of the Buddhas are equal to liberation, the dharma-characteristics of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are equal to liberation, and the characteristics of all dharmas are likewise equal to liberation.
By means of these roots of goodness and the merit of sympathetic joy, I dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is also equal to liberation.
“Because it is neither born nor extinguished.
Subhūti, this is called the merit of the rejoicing of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is the most supreme, the foremost, the most wondrous, the unsurpassed, and the peerless.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva accomplishes this merit of sympathetic joy, they shall swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Suppose there were good sons and good daughters currently seeking the Buddha-way who, throughout their entire lives, provided all that was required for the Buddhas and their disciples of the ten directions—numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges River—who are presently existing, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.

After these Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, they diligently practice offerings, reverence, respect, and praise day and night—with flowers, incense, and even banners, canopies, and music—because they grasp at signs and hold to the notion of attainment.
They maintain ethical discipline, practice patience, exert diligence, cultivate meditative concentration, and develop wisdom, all because they grasp at signs and believe in something to be attained.

Furthermore, there may be sons or daughters of good family who resolve to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practice the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*. By means of the skillful power of non-apprehension and the dharma of non-attainment, they dedicate all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This merit is supreme, foremost, most wondrous, unsurpassed, and peerless; it exceeds the previous merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-millionfold, and even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy.

In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, and when practicing the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they should, by means of skillful power, dedicate all roots of goodness toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Because of the non-apprehension of signs and the dharma of non-attainment.

Chapter 40: Illumination (*Āloka*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Forty, "Illumination"—in the Dan edition, titled "Great Crossing"—at that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is this the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said,
"This is the perfection of wisdom."
“World-Honored One!
The prajñāpāramitā can illuminate all dharmas because it is ultimately pure.
World-Honored One!”
One should pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā does not cling to the triple world.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā dispels all darkness, because it eliminates all afflictions and all views.
World-Honored One!
“O Bhagavat, the Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme among all dharmas that assist the path. O Bhagavat,
the Prajñāpāramitā is secure, for it is able to sever all fear, dread, and suffering.”
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā can bestow illumination, for it is the adornment of the five eyes.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā can guide sentient beings who have fallen onto wrong paths, because it is free from the two extremes.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), because it has severed all afflictions along with their residual tendencies (vāsanā).
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for it is able to give birth to all Buddha-dharmas.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is neither born nor extinguished, because its own-characteristic is empty.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is far removed from birth and death, because it is neither permanent nor subject to extinction.
World-Honored One!
The *prajñāpāramitā* provides protection for those who have no protector, because it bestows all precious jewels.
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is endowed with power, for nothing can destroy it.
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is able to turn the wheel of Dharma of three revolutions and twelve aspects, because all dharmas neither revolve nor return.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the nature of all dharmas, because of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
World-Honored One!
"How should one make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
"One should do so as one would make offerings to the World-Honored One."
One should pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā as one pays homage to the World-Honored One. Why is this?
Because the World-Honored One is not different from the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā is not different from the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One is indeed the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā is indeed the World-Honored One.
From within this Prajñāpāramitā are born all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Srotāpannas.

Within the Prajñāpāramitā are produced the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
"It is from within this Prajñāpāramitā that the ten powers of a Buddha, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the knowledge of all modes arise.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra thought to himself:
"For what cause and condition does Śāriputra ask about this matter?"
Having reflected thus, he said to Śāriputra:
"For what reason and by what causal conditions do you ask about this matter?
Śāriputra then spoke to Śakra, the Lord of the Devas:
“Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are protected by the prajñāpāramitā through the power of upāyakauśalya.

Regarding all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until the duration of the Dharma—they combine all the roots of goodness cultivated during that interval, rejoice in them with sympathetic joy, and dedicate them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
For this reason, I ask about this matter. Kausika!
The prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses the dānapāramitā, as well as the śīla-, kṣānti-, vīrya-, and dhyānapāramitās.

For example, Kausika, suppose there were a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand people born blind; lacking a guide, they would be unable to proceed upon the road or enter the city. Kausika!
The other five perfections are also like this:
separated from the perfection of wisdom, they are like blind people without a guide; they cannot proceed upon the path, nor can they attain all-knowledge.
Kauśika! If the five pāramitās are led and guided by the prajñāpāramitā, at that time the five pāramitās are said to possess eyes.
Led and guided by the prajñāpāramitā, they obtain the name of "pāramitās."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Śāriputra:
"As you have said, it is because the five perfections are led by the perfection of wisdom that they receive the name 'perfection'."
Śāriputra! Without the assistance of the dānapāramitā, the other five pāramitās do not receive the name "pāramitā.
Likewise, without the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, and dhyānapāramitā, the five pāramitās do not receive the name "pāramitā."
“If that is so, for what reason do you alone praise the Prajñāpāramitā?
Śāriputra replied, “It is so, it is so!”
Kauśika! Without the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), the other five perfections cannot obtain the name "perfection.

Without the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), the five perfections cannot obtain the name "perfection."

However, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom, they are able to fulfill the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
For this reason, Kauśika, among the five pāramitās,
the prajñāpāramitā is supreme, foremost, most excellent, unsurpassed, and without equal.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How should one generate the prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Because form is non-arising, the perfection of wisdom arises;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-arising, the perfection of wisdom arises."
Because the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) is non-arising, the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) arises;
and so on, up to: because the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) is non-arising, the perfection of wisdom arises.

Because internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes do not arise, the perfection of wisdom arises.
"Because all these dharmas are non-arising, the Prajñāpāramitā should be brought forth. Śāriputra said,
"World-Honored One!"
How is it that because form (*rūpa*) is non-arising, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) arises?
And so on, up to: how is it that because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are non-arising, the perfection of wisdom should arise?
The Buddha said:
"Because form does not arise, does not originate, cannot be obtained, and cannot be lost.
Because all dharmas, up to and including all phenomena, do not arise, do not originate, cannot be obtained, and cannot be lost, the Prajñāpāramitā arises."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When this kind of prajñāpāramitā arises, with what dharma does it accord?
The Buddha said:
"It is because there is nothing with which it can be conjoined that it is named Prajñāpāramitā.
"World-Honored One!"
"With what kind of phenomena is it not associated? The Buddha said:

"It is not associated with unwholesome phenomena, nor is it associated with wholesome phenomena; it is not associated with mundane phenomena, nor is it associated with supramundane phenomena; it is not associated with tainted phenomena, nor is it associated with untainted phenomena; it is not associated with blameworthy phenomena, nor is it associated with blameless phenomena; it is not associated with conditioned phenomena, nor is it associated with unconditioned phenomena."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā does not arise for the sake of attaining any dharma.
For this reason, it does not conjoin with any dharmas.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is likewise not conjoined with sarvajñatā.”
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Kauśika! The prajñāpāramitā likewise does not unite with sarvajñā, because it cannot be apprehended."
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that the prajñāpāramitā neither joins with sarvajñatā nor attains it?”
The Buddha said,
"The Prajñāpāramitā does not correspond to names, nor to marks, nor to the synthesis of conditioned phenomena.
Śakra-devānām-indra said:
"How, then, is there union?
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not grasp, does not receive, does not dwell, does not cling, and does not sever, then in such a way there is union, yet there is nothing to which one is united."
"Thus it is, Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom is conjoined with all dharmas, yet there is nothing to which it is conjoined.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!
This power of the *prajñāpāramitā* arises because it causes all dharmas to be without arising or birth, and without gain or loss.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, forms this thought:”
"If the Prajñāpāramitā is either conjoined with or not conjoined with all dharmas," then that bodhisattva-mahāsattva abandons the Prajñāpāramitā and remains far removed from the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Furthermore, there are causes and conditions by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva abandons the prajñāpāramitā and distances himself from the prajñāpāramitā.”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"This prajñāpāramitā is non-existent, empty, and not solid," that bodhisattva mahāsattva then abandons the prajñāpāramitā and distances himself from the prajñāpāramitā.
“Subhūti, it is for these reasons that one abandons the prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When one has faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*, what dharmas does one not believe in?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"One who has faith in the *prajñāpāramitā* does not believe in form (*rūpa*), nor does he believe in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*).

He does not believe in the eye up to the mind (*cakṣus*... *manas*); he does not believe in forms up to phenomena (*dharma*); he does not believe in the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*...
*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*); he does not believe in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)..."
They do not believe in the dāna-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, or dhyāna-pāramitā;
they do not believe in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; they do not believe in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they do not believe in the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities; and they do not believe in the srotāpanna.
They do not believe in the fruit of the Stream-enterer, the fruit of the Once-returner, the fruit of the Non-returner, the fruit of Arhatship,
the path of the Pratyekabuddha, nor do they believe in the path of the Bodhisattva, nor in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that when one has faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not have faith in form (*rūpa*) up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because form cannot be apprehended, one has faith in the perfection of wisdom and does not have faith in form.
Up to and including because all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) cannot be apprehended, one has faith in the perfection of wisdom and does not have faith in all-knowledge.”
"For this reason, Subhūti,
when one has faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not have faith in form, nor even in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is called the mahāpāramitā. “Subhūti!
"For what reason is this perfection of wisdom called the 'great perfection' (mahāpāramitā)? Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
This Prajñāpāramitā does not make form great, nor does it make form small; it does not make feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness great, nor does it make them small.
From the eye up to the mind, from forms up to phenomena, and from the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, it does not make them great, nor does it make them small.
From the perfection of giving up to the perfection of meditative concentration, one does not conceive them as great or small.
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, one does not conceive them as great or small.
From the four foundations of mindfulness up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one does not conceive them as great nor as small.
The dharmas of all Buddhas are not conceived as great nor as small.
The Buddhas do not make things great, nor do they make them small.

This Prajñāpāramitā does not effect the conjunction of form, nor does it effect its dispersion; it does not effect the conjunction or dispersion of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to the Buddhas themselves, whom it neither effects as conjoined nor as dispersed.

One does not conceive of form as infinite, nor does one conceive of form as non-infinite; this extends up to the Buddhas, whom one does not conceive as infinite, nor does one conceive of them as non-infinite.
One does not conceive of form as vast, nor does one conceive of form as narrow; this extends up to the Buddhas, whom one does not conceive as vast, nor does one conceive of them as narrow.
One does not conceive of form as having power, nor does one conceive of form as lacking power; this extends even to the Buddhas, whom one does not conceive as having power, nor as lacking power.
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, this Prajñāpāramitā is called the Mahāpāramitā.

"Bhagavān! If a newly resolved bodhisattva mahāsattva does not distance himself from the prajñāpāramitā, does not distance himself from the dhyānapāramitā, does not distance himself from the vīryapāramitā, does not distance himself from the kṣāntipāramitā, does not distance himself from the śīlapāramitā, and does not distance himself from the dānapāramitā, and thus reflects:
'This prajñāpāramitā does not make form great, nor does it make form small; and so on, up to: it does not make the Buddhas great, nor does it make them small.'"

One does not construct the conjunction of form, nor the dispersion of form; one does not construct form as infinite, nor form as non-infinite; one does not construct form as having power, nor form as lacking power; and so on, up to the Buddhas, whom one does not construct as having power, nor as lacking power.
"World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva understands in this way, this constitutes not practicing the prajñāpāramitā. Why is that?"
These are not the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
That is to say, [the notion that] form is large or small, up to all Buddhas being large or small; or that form has power or lacks power, up to all Buddhas having power or lacking power.
“World-Honored One!
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva operates with the notion of ‘attainment,’ there is a great fault.
That is to say, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, they conceptualize form as large or small, and so on, up to conceptualizing the Buddhas as having power or lacking power.”
Why is this? For one who possesses the mark of apprehension, there is no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is that?
Because sentient beings are non-arising, the Prajñāpāramitā is non-arising;
because form is non-arising, the Prajñāpāramitā is non-arising;
and so on, up to: because the Buddha is non-arising, the Prajñāpāramitā is non-arising.
Because the nature of sentient beings is non-existent, the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent;
because the nature of form is non-existent, the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent;
and so on, up to: because the nature of a Buddha is non-existent, the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent.
Because sentient beings are not dharmas, the Prajñāpāramitā is not a dharma;
because form is not a dharma, the Prajñāpāramitā is not a dharma;
and so on, up to: because the Buddha is not a dharma, the Prajñāpāramitā is not a dharma.
Because sentient beings are empty, the prajñāpāramitā is empty;
because form is empty, the prajñāpāramitā is empty;
and so on, up to because the Buddha is empty, the prajñāpāramitā is empty.
Because sentient beings are detached, the Prajñāpāramitā is detached;
because form is detached, the Prajñāpāramitā is detached;
and so on, up to: because the Buddha is detached, the Prajñāpāramitā is detached.
Because sentient beings do not exist, the perfection of wisdom does not exist;
because form does not exist, the perfection of wisdom does not exist;
and so on, up to: because a Buddha does not exist, the perfection of wisdom does not exist.
Because sentient beings are inconceivable, the Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable;
because form is inconceivable, the Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable;
and so on, up to: because the Buddha is inconceivable, the Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable.
Because sentient beings are not extinguished, the perfection of wisdom is not extinguished;
because form is not extinguished, the perfection of wisdom is not extinguished;
and so on, up to: because the Buddha is not extinguished, the perfection of wisdom is not extinguished.
Because sentient beings are unknowable, the Prajñāpāramitā is unknowable;
because form is unknowable, the Prajñāpāramitā is unknowable;
and so on, up to: because the Buddha is unknowable, the Prajñāpāramitā is unknowable.
Because the power of sentient beings is not accomplished, the power of the prajñāpāramitā is not accomplished;
because the power of form is not accomplished, the power of the prajñāpāramitā is not accomplished;
and so on, up to: because the power of the Buddha is not accomplished, the power of the prajñāpāramitā is not accomplished.
“World-Honored One!
For these reasons, the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is called the mahāpāramitā.

Chapter 41: On Faith and Slander (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter 41, titled "Faith and Slander" or "Hell" in the Dharmarakṣa translation). At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Where did those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have faith and resolve in this prajñāpāramitā pass away before coming to be born here?”
"How long has it been since you first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
How many Buddhas have you made offerings to?

For how long and in making offerings to how many Buddhas have you practiced the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*, such that you are now able to accord with and understand the profound meaning of the *prajñā-pāramitā*?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva has made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions and has come to be born here.
Since this bodhisattva first resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, immeasurable, boundless, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas have passed.”

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment, have constantly practiced the six pāramitās, made offerings to immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and asaṃkhyeya Buddhas, and have come to be born in this world.
Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva sees or hears the Prajñāpāramitā, he forms this thought:
"I see the Buddha; I hear the Dharma from the Buddha."
“Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accord with and understand the meaning of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, because it is signless, non-dual, and non-apprehendable.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
can this Prajñāpāramitā be heard or seen?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This prajñāpāramitā has no hearer and no seer. Prajñāpāramitā is neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient."
The dhyāna-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, and dāna-pāramitā are neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient.
Internal emptiness is neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient.
This extends even to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient.
The four foundations of mindfulness are neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient.
Up to and including the eightfold noble path, there is neither hearing nor seeing, because all phenomena are insentient.
From the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities, there is neither hearing nor seeing, because all phenomena are insentient.
“Subhūti! The Buddha and the Buddha-way are neither heard nor seen, for all dharmas are insentient.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For how long has this bodhisattva practiced the Buddha-way to be able to study and practice such profound prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In this regard, it should be explained through further analysis.

Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having first resolved their minds, practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, and *dānapāramitā*."

By the power of skillful means, they do not destroy or disrupt any phenomena; they do not perceive any phenomenon as being without benefit, nor do they ever abandon the practice of the six pāramitās, nor do they distance themselves from the Buddhas.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, if they wish to make offerings to all buddhas through the power of their roots of goodness, they shall obtain it at will.

They shall never again be born from a mother’s womb; they shall never be separated from the various supernormal powers; and they shall never give rise to afflictions or the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields.
Subhūti, it is such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these who are able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have seen many Buddhas—perhaps immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis—and from those Buddhas they have practiced giving, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, all of which was done with the notion of something to be attained.
When this bodhisattva hears the profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they immediately rise from the assembly and depart, showing no reverence for the profound *prajñāpāramitā* nor for the Buddhas.
This bodhisattva is now sitting among this assembly; having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, because he does not delight in it, he abandons it and departs. Why is this?

These sons and daughters of good family, having abandoned [this teaching] when they heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, now likewise abandon it when they hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this life.

When body and mind are in disharmony, this person plants the causal conditions for ignorance and the seeds of karma; because of the offenses resulting from these causal conditions of ignorance, they revile and disparage the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* when it is heard.
Because they revile the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they revile the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Because this person slanders the omniscience of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they give rise to the karma of destroying the Dharma.

Due to the accumulation of the causes and conditions of this karma of destroying the Dharma, they shall fall into the great hells for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years.
These people who destroy the Dharma pass from one great hell to another; when the fire calamity arises, they go to a great hell in another direction and are born there.
From one great hell to another great hell, when the fire calamity arises in between, they again go to other great hells in other directions and are born there.
From one great hell to another great hell, they thus traverse the ten directions; when the fire-kalpa arises in those places, they die there.

Because the karmic causes and conditions for their destruction of the Dharma are not yet exhausted, they return to this world and are born within the great hells here, where they likewise pass from one great hell to another, undergoing immeasurable suffering.

When the kalpa-ending fire arises here, they will again be reborn in other lands throughout the ten directions among the animal realm, where they will undergo the suffering of the karmic retribution for destroying the Dharma, as described in the section on the hells.

Their heavy sins are transformed and thinned, or they may obtain a human body, yet they are born into the families of the congenitally blind, into the families of caṇḍālas, or into various lowly and base families such as those who clean latrines or carry out the dead.
Whether they lack eyes, have only one eye, or are blind; whether they lack a tongue, lack ears, or lack hands;
or whether they are born in places where there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no disciples of the Buddha.
"Why is this? Because they have fully accumulated and perfected the heavy and thick karma of destroying the Dharma, they undergo this retribution.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are the five heinous crimes similar to the crime of destroying the Dharma?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"One should not say they are similar. Why is that?
If there is someone who, when this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being preached, disparages it and does not believe in the *prajñāpāramitā*, saying: "
"One should not study this Dharma; it is not the Dharma, it is not good, and it is not the Buddha's teaching.
The Buddhas do not speak such words.

This person thus disparages the *prajñāpāramitā* themselves and teaches others to disparage the *prajñāpāramitā*; they destroy their own bodies and destroy the bodies of others; they drink poison to kill themselves and give poison to others to drink; they lose their own lives and cause others to lose their lives; being themselves ignorant and lacking faith, they disparage the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and teach others to likewise lack faith and remain ignorant.
Śāriputra, such people possess a nature that is decayed, turbid, and dark.
If anyone listens to their words or places trust in their speech, they too shall undergo such suffering. Śāriputra!
"If a person destroys the Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that such a person is called one who destroys the Dharma.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The World-Honored One has spoken of the grave offenses incurred by those who destroy the Dharma, yet you have not mentioned the size of the bodies such persons receive.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There is no need to mention the size of the bodies received by such persons.”
Why is this? If those who destroy the Dharma hear of the size of their own bodies as they have received them, they will immediately vomit hot blood, or die, or suffer near-death agony.

When those who have destroyed the Dharma hear that such a body incurs such grave offenses, they become greatly afflicted by sorrow and poison, as if an arrow had entered their hearts, and they gradually wither away.
He reflects thus:
"Because of the sin of destroying the Dharma, I have obtained such a hideous body and undergo such immeasurable suffering.
For this reason, the Buddha did not permit Śāriputra to ask about the size of the physical body received by such a person.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that the Buddha will explain this, to serve as an illumination for future generations, so that they may know how, by the accumulation of the karma of destroying the Dharma, one obtains such a body of great deformity and undergoes such suffering."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“In future generations, if people hear of this accumulation of the karma of destroying the Dharma—its weightiness and fullness—they will undergo immeasurable suffering for a long, long time within the great hells.”
"Hearing of this suffering for such a long and immeasurable time will serve as a clear warning for future generations.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

If a son or daughter of good family who possesses a pure and bright nature hears this Dharma, they shall take it as sufficient basis for reliance; rather than losing their body or life, they will not destroy the Dharma.
They will think to themselves:
"If I were to destroy the Dharma, I would have to undergo such suffering."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A son of good family or a daughter of good family should properly restrain the actions of body, speech, and mind, so as not to undergo such various sufferings.”

Either they do not see the Buddha, or they do not hear the Dharma, or they do not associate with the Sangha; or they are born in a land where there is no Buddha, or they are born among humans in a family of poverty, or people do not believe or accept their words.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it because of the accumulation of verbal karma that there is such a grave offense of destroying the Dharma?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“It is because of the accumulation of verbal karma that there is this grave offense of destroying the Dharma. Subhūti!”
Such a foolish person, having left the household life and received the precepts within the Buddha-dharma, violates the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and, disparaging it, refuses to accept it. Subhūti!
If one destroys the Prajñāpāramitā or slanders the Prajñāpāramitā, one thereby destroys the omniscience (sarvajñatā) of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Because omniscience is destroyed, the Jewel of the Buddha is destroyed.
Because one destroys the Buddha-jewel, one destroys the Dharma-jewel.
Because one destroys the Dharma-jewel, one destroys the Saṃgha-jewel.
Because one destroys the Three Jewels, one destroys right view in the world.
Because one destroys the right view of the world, one then destroys the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to destroying the dharma of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because one destroys the dharma of all-knowledge, one incurs immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sins.
"Having incurred immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) offenses, one will then experience immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sorrow and suffering.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“By how many causes and conditions do these foolish people revile and destroy this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“There are four causes and conditions by which these foolish people revile and destroy this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
what are these four?”
The Buddha said:
"Because these deluded persons are incited by Māra, they wish to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
this is called the first causal condition."
This foolish person does not believe in the profound Dharma; lacking faith and understanding, their mind fails to attain purity—this is the second cause and condition.

This foolish person wishes to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; this foolish person associates with evil friends, sinks into indolence, and remains stubbornly attached to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).
This is due to the third cause and condition.
Furthermore, these foolish people wish to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; these foolish people frequently practice anger, exalting themselves and disparaging others.
This is due to the fourth cause and condition.
These deluded persons wish to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti, it is for these four reasons that deluded persons wish to destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult for those who do not apply diligent effort, who have planted unwholesome roots, and who associate with evil friends to believe in or understand.”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
"This profound Prajñāpāramitā is difficult for those who do not apply diligent effort, who have planted unwholesome roots, and who associate with evil friends to believe in or understand.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that this Prajñāpāramitā is so profound, difficult to believe in,
and difficult to understand? "Subhūti,
form is neither bound nor liberated."
Why is this? The nature of non-existence is form (*rūpa*).
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is precisely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
The perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? The nature of non-existence is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
The perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
The perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the dhyāna-pāramitā.
The prajñā-pāramitā is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Subhūti, the nature of non-existence is the perfection of wisdom.
Inner emptiness is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the nature of non-existence is inner emptiness.
Even the emptiness of non-existence and existence is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the nature of non-existence is the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
The four foundations of mindfulness are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the four foundations of mindfulness.
Even all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti! The original limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The ultimate limit of form has the nature of non-existence; that is form.
The ultimate limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even up to all-knowledge is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Subhūti, the nature of the non-existence of the prior limit is omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Form is neither bound nor liberated at its posterior limit.
Why is this? Because the nature of the future limit is non-existence; it is form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge, are neither bound nor liberated at the future limit.
Why is this? Subhūti, the non-existence of a future limit is omniscience. Subhūti!
Present form is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of present form is non-existence; that is form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge in the present, are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence in the present is all-knowledge.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Prajñāpāramitā is truly difficult to believe and difficult to understand for those who do not exert diligent effort, who have not planted roots of goodness, who associate with evil friends, who are indolent and lack progress, who are prone to forgetfulness, and who lack skillful wisdom.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"

This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult for those who do not exert diligent effort, who have not planted roots of goodness, who associate with evil friends, who are bound by Māra, who are indolent and lack progress while being prone to forgetfulness, and who lack skillful wisdom; such persons truly find it difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Why is this? Because the purity of form is the purity of its fruit; the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also the purity of their fruits.
This extends even to the purity of the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure; because the perfection of wisdom is pure, form is pure.

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure; because the perfection of wisdom is pure, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure."

The purity of even the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the purity of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of the knowledge of all modes.
The purity of form (*rūpa*) and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, without distinction, uninterrupted, and indestructible.
"Up to and including the purity of all-knowledge and the purity of the perfection of wisdom, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, uninterrupted, and indestructible. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because non-duality is pure, form is pure;
because non-duality is pure, even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure. Why is this?
This is because the purity of non-duality and the purity of form, up to the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are without duality and without distinction;
it is because the purity of the self, the purity of sentient beings, up to the purity of the knower and the seer, are likewise so.
Form is pure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) being pure.
Because form is pure up to and including all-knowledge being pure, the self is pure, and sentient beings up to and including the knower and the seer are pure.

Why is this? Because the purity of the self, of sentient beings, and even of the knower and the viewer, is identical to the purity of form, and so on, up to the purity of all-knowledge; these are non-dual and undifferentiated, without interruption and without destruction.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because desire is pure, form is pure, and so on up to the purity of all-knowledge. Why is that? "
The purity of desire, the purity of form, and so on up to the purity of all-knowledge are non-dual and undifferentiated.
Because hatred and delusion are pure, form is pure, and so on up to all-knowledge being pure.
Why is this? Because the purification of hatred and delusion, the purification of form, and so forth, up to the purification of all-knowledge, are non-dual and not distinct.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

Because ignorance is pure, volitional formations are pure; because volitional formations are pure, consciousness is pure; because consciousness is pure, name-and-form is pure; because name-and-form is pure, the six sense bases are pure; because the six sense bases are pure, contact is pure; because contact is pure, feeling is pure; because feeling is pure, craving is pure; because craving is pure, clinging is pure; because clinging is pure, becoming is pure; because becoming is pure, birth is pure; and because birth is pure, old age and death are pure.
Because old age and death are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
Because the perfection of wisdom is pure, even up to the perfection of generosity is pure.
Because the perfection of generosity is pure, internal emptiness is pure; because internal emptiness is pure, even up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence is pure.

Because the emptiness of non-existence and existence is pure, the four foundations of mindfulness are pure; because the four foundations of mindfulness are pure, everything up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is pure.
Because all-knowledge is pure, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure.

Why is this? Because this purity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and this purity of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are non-dual and undifferentiated, without interruption and without destruction.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
Because the perfection of wisdom is pure, form is pure; and so on, up to: because the perfection of wisdom is pure, all-knowledge is pure.
This purity of the perfection of wisdom and this purity of all-knowledge are non-dual and not distinct.

Subhūti! Because the dhyānapāramitā is pure, up to and including the purification of all-knowledge; because the vīryapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, śīlapāramitā, and dānapāramitā are pure, up to and including the purification of all-knowledge.

Because inner emptiness is pure, up to and including the purity of all-knowledge; because the four foundations of mindfulness are pure, up to and including the purity of all-knowledge. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because all-knowledge is pure, even up to the purity of the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, each one is as previously explained. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the conditioned is pure, the unconditioned is pure.
Why is this? Because the purity of the conditioned and the purity of the unconditioned are non-dual and undifferentiated, neither severed nor destroyed.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because the past is pure, the future and the present are pure; because the future is pure, the past and the present are pure; because the present is pure, the past and the future are pure."
Why is this? Because the purity of the present, the past, and the future are non-dual and undifferentiated, neither severed nor destroyed.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 11.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twelve, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Forty-Two: Praising Purity (Praising Purity, Chapter Forty-Two).
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This purity is most profound.”
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“Through the purification of what dharma is this purity so profound?
The Buddha said:
“Through the purification of form (rūpa), this purity is profound.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure;
because the four foundations of mindfulness are pure, up to and including the eightfold noble path being pure;
because the ten powers of a Buddha are pure, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha being pure.
“Because the bodhisattva is pure and the Buddha is pure, omniscience and the knowledge of all modes are pure.
This purity is profound.
“World-Honored One! [he said.]
"This is pure clarity.
The Buddha said,
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked: "By the purification of what dharma is this purity and clarity attained?
The Buddha said:
"Because the perfection of wisdom is pure, it is luminous purity; up to and including because the perfection of generosity is pure, it is luminous purity.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge are pure, they are luminous purity."
“World-Honored One!
This purity is non-continuous.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
“By the non-continuation of what dharma is this purity non-continuous?”
The Buddha said:
"Because form does not depart and is not continuous, this purity is non-continuous.
This extends up to: because all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not depart and is not continuous, this purity is non-continuous."
“World-Honored One!
This purity is stainless.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
“By virtue of what dharma being without stain is this purity without stain?”
The Buddha said:
"Because the nature of form is eternally pure, this purity is stainless.
This extends even to the nature of all-knowledge, which is eternally pure; therefore, this purity is stainless."
“World-Honored One!
This purity is without attainment and without attachment.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
“By virtue of what dharma being without attainment and without attachment is this purity without attainment and without attachment?”
The Buddha said:
"Because form is without attainment and without attachment, this purity is without attainment and without attachment.
Up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), because it is without attainment and without attachment, this purity is without attainment and without attachment."
“World-Honored One!
This purity is non-arising.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
“By the non-arising of what dharma is this purity non-arising?”
The Buddha said:
"Because form is non-arising, this purity is non-arising.
Up to and including: because all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is non-arising, this purity is non-arising."
“World-Honored One!
This purity does not arise within the desire realm.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra asked: "In what way is this purity such that it does not arise within the desire realm?"
The Buddha said,
“Because the nature of the desire realm cannot be apprehended, this purity is not born within the desire realm.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"This purity does not arise within the form realm.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked: "In what way is this purity not born within the form realm?
The Buddha said:
“Because the nature of the form realm cannot be apprehended, this purity does not arise within the form realm.
“World-Honored One!
This purity does not arise within the formless realm.”
The Buddha said:
