"Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“How is it that this purity does not arise in the formless realm?
The Buddha said:
“Because the nature of the formless realm cannot be apprehended, this purity does not arise in the formless realm.”
“World-Honored One!
This purity is non-cognition.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
"In what way is this purity non-cognition?"
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are dull, this purity is without cognition.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"Form is without cognition; this is purity within purity.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked: "In what sense is form without cognition, and how is it 'pure purity'?
The Buddha said:
“Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty, form is without cognition; this is the purity of purity.
“World-Honored One!
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without cognition; this is the purity of purity.”
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
"What is meant by 'feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without cognition; this is pure purity'?
The Buddha said:
"Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of intrinsic nature, they are without cognition; this is pure purity."
“World-Honored One!
Because all dharmas are pure, this purity is purity.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
“In what way are all dharmas pure such that this purity is itself pure?”
The Buddha said:
“Because all dharmas are unobtainable, all dharmas are pure; this purity is the purity of purity.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"This Prajñāpāramitā neither benefits nor harms sarvajñatā.
The Buddha said, "Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
"How is it that the prajñāpāramitā neither benefits nor harms sarvajñatā?
The Buddha said:
"Because phenomena abide in their constant nature, the prajñāpāramitā neither benefits nor harms sarvajñatā."
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is pure; regarding all dharmas, it has nothing that can be grasped.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
"In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure, such that it does not apprehend any phenomena?"
The Buddha said:
"Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is immovable, this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) purifies all phenomena such that there is nothing to be grasped.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because the self is pure, form is pure.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti asked:
"By what cause and condition is form pure because the self is pure, being ultimately pure?"
The Buddha said:
"Because I have nothing, form has nothing; it is ultimately pure.
[The Venerable One asked: "World-Honored One!"
"Because the self is pure, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure.
The Buddha said,
"Because they are ultimately pure."
Subhūti said: "By what causes and conditions are self-purity, the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and their ultimate purity [attained]?
The Buddha said:
“Because the self does not exist, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist and are ultimately pure.

“World-Honored One! Because the self is pure, the perfection of giving is pure; because the self is pure, the perfection of ethical discipline is pure; because the self is pure, the perfection of patience is pure; because the self is pure, the perfection of vigor is pure; because the self is pure, the perfection of meditative concentration is pure.”
“World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
World-Honored One!”
"World-Honored One! Because the self is pure, the four foundations of mindfulness are pure.
World-Honored One!
Because the self is pure, even up to the eightfold noble path is pure."
World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, the ten powers of the Buddha are pure.
World-Honored One!
"Because the self is pure, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are pure.
The Buddha said:
"Because they are ultimately pure."
Subhūti said: "By what causes and conditions is my purity the purity of the perfection of giving, and why is my purity [the purity] of everything up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?"
The Buddha said:
"Because I am non-existent, the perfection of giving is pure through non-existence; likewise, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are pure through non-existence."

“World-Honored One! Because the self is pure, the fruit of the stream-enterer is pure; because the self is pure, the fruit of the once-returner is pure; because the self is pure, the fruit of the non-returner is pure; because the self is pure, the fruit of the arhat is pure; because the self is pure, the path of the pratyekabuddha is pure; and because the self is pure, the path of the Buddha is pure.”
The Buddha said, “Ultimately pure. Subhūti said:

"For what reason are the purity of the fruit of stream-entry, the purity of the fruit of once-returning, the purity of the fruit of non-returning, the purity of the fruit of arhatship, the purity of the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the purity of the path of the Buddha [attained]?"
The Buddha said:
"Because their own-characteristics are empty.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"Because I am pure, all-knowledge is pure.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Subhūti said: "By what cause and condition is it that because I am pure, all-knowledge is pure?
The Buddha said:
“Because it is signless and without conceptualization.
“World-Honored One!
Because of the purity of these two, there is neither attainment nor attachment.”
The Buddha said, “Ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
“For what reason is it that, because of the purity of both, there is neither attainment nor attachment, which is ultimate purity?
The Buddha said:
“Because there is neither defilement nor purity.”
“World-Honored One!
Because I am boundless, form is pure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure.
The Buddha said:
"Ultimately pure. Subhūti asked:
"By what cause and condition is it that because the self is boundless, form is pure, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure?"
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately empty and beginninglessly empty.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can understand in this way, this is called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti asked:
“By what causes and conditions is a bodhisattva mahāsattva able to know in this way? Is this called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha said,
“Because they know the seeds of the Path.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means, they form this thought:

"Form does not know form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not know consciousness. Past phenomena do not know past phenomena; future phenomena do not know future phenomena; present phenomena do not know present phenomena."
The Buddha said: “When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, by the power of skillful means (*upāya*), he does not form such thoughts as:

‘I give to that person; I maintain the precepts in this way; I cultivate patience in this way; I exert diligence in this way; I enter meditative concentration in this way; I cultivate wisdom in this way; I obtain merit in this way; I shall enter the stage of the bodhisattva-dharmas; I shall purify the buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; I shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).’”
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, by virtue of skillful means, is free from all recollections, conceptions, and discriminations."

Because of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, and the emptiness of self-characteristics.
“Subhūti! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom; by the power of skillful means, they are without any hindrance.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra asked Subhūti:
“What are the obstructing dharmas for a son of good family who seeks the bodhisattva path?
Subhūti replied to Śakra, Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!

There are sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path and grasp at the characteristics of the mind; that is to say, they grasp at the characteristic of the dāna-pāramitā, the characteristic of the śīla-pāramitā, the characteristic of the kṣānti-pāramitā, the characteristic of the vīrya-pāramitā, the characteristic of the dhyāna-pāramitā, and the characteristic of the prajñā-pāramitā;
they grasp at the characteristic of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the characteristic of the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
and they grasp at the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the characteristic of the eightfold noble path.
They grasp the marks of the ten powers of the Buddha up to the marks of the eighteen unique qualities;
they grasp the marks of all Buddhas;
and they grasp the marks of planting roots of goodness in all Buddhas.
Kauśika, to combine all these merits, grasp their marks, and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*— this, O Kauśika,
is called the obstructing dharma for a son or daughter of good family who seeks the bodhisattva path.
Because of these dharmas, one cannot practice the prajñāpāramitā without hindrance.
Why is this so, Kauśika?

The characteristic of form cannot be dedicated; the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be dedicated; and so on, up to the characteristic of all-knowledge, which cannot be dedicated.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva instructs, exhorts, benefits, and gladdens others regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden them regarding the true mark of all dharmas.
If good sons or good daughters seeking the bodhisattva path practice the dānapāramitā, they should not engage in such discrimination as saying:
"I am giving; I am observing the precepts; I am practicing patience; I am exerting vigor; I am entering meditative concentration; I am cultivating wisdom."
I practice inner emptiness, outer emptiness, and inner-and-outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
I cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including my practice for unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment.

“Good sons and good daughters should thus instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden others regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If they thus instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden them regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they will themselves be free from error and will likewise instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden others according to the Dharma taught by the Buddha, causing these good sons and good daughters to remain far removed from all obstructing dharmas.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti:
"Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have explained the dharmas of obstruction for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
Subhūti! Listen now further as I speak of the subtle characteristics of obstruction. Subhūti!
"Listen attentively with a single mind.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are sons of good family and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet they conceive of and dwell upon the Buddhas by grasping at their marks (*nimitta*)."
Subhūti! Whatever possesses marks is entirely a mark of obstruction.

Furthermore, regarding all the Buddhas—from their first resolution for enlightenment until the endurance of the Dharma—if one grasps at marks and recollects all the roots of goodness within that interval, [one does not see them].
Having grasped the signs and brought them to mind, one dedicates [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, whatever has signs is entirely a sign of obstruction.

Furthermore, one takes up the marks of all roots of goodness belonging to the Buddhas and their disciples, as well as the roots of goodness of other sentient beings, and dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! Whatever possesses marks is entirely a mark of obstruction. Why is this?
"One should not take up signs when recollecting the Buddhas, nor should one take up signs when recollecting the roots of goodness of the Buddhas. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep.
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are eternally detached."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
I shall pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because this prajñāpāramitā is without arising and without activity, there is no one who can attain it. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are likewise unknowable and unobtainable.
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas have a single nature and not a dual nature.
Subhūti, this single dharma-nature is itself a non-nature; this non-nature is itself the nature, and this nature neither arises nor ceases."

In this way, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all dharmas have a single nature— that is to say, they are without nature, without arising, and without activity— then they remain far removed from all signs of obstruction.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to know and difficult to understand.”
The Buddha said:
"As you have said, this Prajñāpāramitā has no seer, no hearer, no knower, no cognizer, and no attainer."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable.
The Buddha said:

"As it has been said, this Prajñāpāramitā does not arise from the mind, nor does it arise from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it does not even arise from the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."

Chapter 43: The Chapter on Non-Action, from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Chapter on Non-Action, the Forty-third; [also known as] the Chapter on the Thousand Buddhas of Each Face. Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“This *prajñāpāramitā* performs no action.”
The Buddha said:
"Because an agent cannot be apprehended, form cannot be apprehended, and so on, up to all dharmas being unapprehendable.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, how should they practice? The Buddha told Subhūti:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom does not practice by way of form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. They do not practice by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. This extends even to not practicing by way of the knowledge of all modes; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing [the notion that] form is permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing [the notion that] anything up to all-knowledge is permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing whether form is suffering or pleasure is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing whether up to all-knowledge is suffering or pleasure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with the thought that form is self or that it is not-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, up to and including not practicing with the thought that all-knowledge is self or that it is not-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to the purity or impurity of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing with regard to the purity or impurity of anything up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because this form has the nature of non-existence; how could it have permanence or impermanence, suffering or pleasure, self or non-self, purity or impurity?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have the nature of non-existence; how could they have permanence or impermanence, up to and including purity or impurity?
Since even the non-existence of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is itself non-existent, how could there be permanence or impermanence, up to and including purity or impurity?
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not practicing that form is incomplete is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are incomplete is practicing the perfection of wisdom; and so on, up to not practicing that the knowledge of all modes is incomplete is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? That which is not complete in form is not called "form.
To practice in this manner is to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
That which is incomplete in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not called consciousness.
Likewise, to practice in such a manner is to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

This extends even to the point where that which is incomplete in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is not called the knowledge of all modes. To practice in such a manner is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
"To practice in this manner is also to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"It is unprecedented!"
“World-Honored One, you have well explained the characteristics of obstruction and non-obstruction for sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is!”
Subhūti! The Buddha has well explained the characteristics of obstruction and non-obstruction for sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path. Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not practice by way of non-obstruction regarding form, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not practice by way of non-obstruction regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with the eye and being unimpeded is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with the ear, nose, tongue, or body and being unimpeded is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with the mind and being unimpeded is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing the perfection of giving without obstruction is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing the perfection of ethical discipline without obstruction is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing the perfection of patience without obstruction is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
To practice the perfection of vigor without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice the perfection of meditation without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice the perfection of wisdom without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Even to the point of not practicing non-obstruction regarding all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they know that form (*rūpa*) is unobstructed; they know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are unobstructed; and even up to knowing that all-knowledge is unobstructed.

He knows that the fruit of srotāpanna is unobstructed; he knows that the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin is unobstructed; he knows that the fruit of anāgāmin is unobstructed; he knows that the fruit of arhatship is unobstructed; he knows that the path of the pratyekabuddha is unobstructed; and he knows that the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is unobstructed.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!”
"This profound Dharma neither increases nor decreases when it is taught, nor does it increase nor decrease when it is not taught.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
This profound Dharma neither increases nor decreases when it is taught, nor does it increase or decrease when it is not taught.

It is like space: even if a Buddha were to praise or disparage it for the remainder of his life, it would neither increase nor decrease when praised, nor would it increase or decrease when disparaged.
Subhūti! It is like an illusory person: when praised, they neither increase nor decrease; when reviled, they likewise neither increase nor decrease.
When praised, they feel no joy; when reviled, they feel no sorrow.
Subhūti! The dharma-characteristic of all dharmas is also like this:
whether they are spoken of, they remain as they were originally and do not differ; whether they are not spoken of, they remain as they were originally and do not differ.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is most difficult for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to accomplish; when they practice this prajñāpāramitā, they are neither sorrowful nor joyful, yet they are able to train in the prajñāpāramitā and do not turn back from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Cultivating the perfection of wisdom is like cultivating empty space; just as in empty space there is no perfection of wisdom, so too there is no dhyāna, no vīrya, no kṣānti, no śīla, and no dānapāramitā.

Just as in space there is no form, no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and likewise no internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
There are no four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including no eightfold noble path;
there are no ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including no eighteen unique qualities;
and there are no fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship.
There is no path of the pratyekabuddha, and there is no anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā is also like this,
World-Honored One.
One should pay homage to these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to adorn themselves with great vows.
World-Honored One!

These people, for the sake of sentient beings, adorn themselves with great vows and exert diligent vigor, just as if they were adorning themselves with great vows and exerting diligent vigor for the sake of empty space.
World-Honored One!
This person wishes to deliver sentient beings as if wishing to deliver empty space.
World-Honored One!
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are adorned with great vows, just as one would adorn the vastness of space for the sake of all sentient beings.
World-Honored One, when these people, adorned with great vows, desire to deliver sentient beings, it is as if they were attempting to lift up space itself.
World-Honored One!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having attained the power of great diligence, resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, adorned with great vows and desiring to deliver sentient beings, give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"World-Honored One!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, possessing great courage and valor, resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of delivering sentient beings who are as vast as space."
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
Suppose the great trichiliocosm were filled with Buddhas, as dense as a forest of bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, hemp, and flax.

If all Buddhas were to constantly preach the Dharma for an eon, or even slightly less than an eon, each and every Buddha would deliver immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings, causing them to enter *nirvāṇa*.
World-Honored One!
This nature of sentient beings neither decreases nor increases. Why is this?
Because sentient beings do not exist and because sentient beings are detached [from inherent existence].
This applies even to all the sentient beings being delivered by the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
World-Honored One!
For this reason, I have said this:
"This person, desiring to deliver sentient beings, has resolved their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as if they wished to deliver empty space."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who spoke as follows:
"I pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā.

Although within the Prajñāpāramitā there is no dharma that arises and no dharma that ceases, there exist the aggregate of precepts, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; and there exist all the srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas."
"When there are Buddhas, there is the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus, and there is the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, what dharma is he practicing?"
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“Kauśika! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are practicing the dharma of emptiness.”
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, draws near to, reads, recites, explains, and correctly contemplates this Prajñāpāramitā;”
"What kind of protection should I provide?
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!..."
"Do you see any such dharma that can be protected?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "No, Subhūti."
"I do not see any dharma that ought to be protected. Subhūti said: "Kauśika!..."
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices as it is taught in the Prajñāpāramitā, that itself constitutes protection.

That is to say, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family never departs from practicing the Prajñāpāramitā as it has been taught, then neither humans nor non-humans shall find an opportunity to harm them.
You should know that these sons and daughters of good family do not distance themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kauśika! If anyone wishes to protect a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, they wish to protect empty space.
“Kauśika! What do you think?
Are you able to protect a dream, a mirage, a reflection, an echo, an illusion, or a magical creation?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"One cannot protect them.
"If a person wishes to protect bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā, it is likewise; they will only exhaust themselves in suffering."
"Kauśika! What do you think?
Is it possible to protect that which has been conjured by the Buddha?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"One cannot protect them.
"Kauśika, it is the same for anyone who wishes to protect bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom."
"What do you think? Can one protect the nature of dharmas, the reality limit (bhūtakoṭi), suchness (tathatā), and the inconceivable nature?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "One cannot protect them."
“If one wishes to protect the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, it is also like this.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra asked Subhūti:

“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom know and see all dharmas as being like a dream, like a mirage, like a shadow, like an echo, like an illusion, and like a magical transformation?”

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perceive things as they truly are, they do not conceive of a dream, do not conceive of "this is a dream," do not conceive of using a dream, and do not conceive of "I am dreaming. It is the same for a mirage, a reflection, an echo, an illusion, and a magical creation.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not conceive of form, does not conceive 'this is form,' does not conceive 'the use of form,' and does not conceive 'my form. This bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise able not to conceive of a dream, not to conceive 'this is a dream,' not to conceive 'the use of a dream,' and not to conceive 'my dream.'"

Even regarding transformations, one does not think of them as transformations, does not think "this is a transformation," does not think of using transformations, and does not think "I am a transformation.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they do not think of omniscience, do not think "this is omniscience," do not think of using omniscience, and do not think "I am omniscient. In this same way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also able not to think of dreams, not to think "this is a dream," not to think of using dreams, and not to think "I am dreaming."
This applies even to emanations as well. Thus it is, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are like a dream, like a mirage, like a shadow, like an echo, like a magical illusion, and like an emanation.

At that time, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, all the devas of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Brahmakāyika-parṣad Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, and so on up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven within the trichiliocosm, all these devas scattered celestial *candana* flowers from afar upon the Buddha. They approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the gods of the Four Great Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, and the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens—down from Brahmā-devānām-indra to all the gods of the Pure Abodes—by the spiritual power of the Buddha, saw a thousand Buddhas preaching the Dharma in the eastern direction; they were of such appearance and such names, and they were preaching this chapter on the Prajñāpāramitā in the same manner.
All the bhikṣus were named Subhūti, and all those who questioned and debated the "Chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom" were named Śakra-devānām-indra.
It was the same in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir; in each direction, a thousand Buddhas appeared.
At that time, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he too shall preach the Prajñāpāramitā at this very place."
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of this Bhadrakalpa attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, they too shall preach the Prajñāpāramitā at this very place.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, by what marks, by what causes, and by what meanings will he explain this meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he shall teach the Dharma in this way: ‘Form is neither permanent nor impermanent.’”
"One should teach the Dharma thus: 'Form is neither suffering nor pleasure; form is neither self nor non-self;
form is neither pure nor impure. One should teach the Dharma thus: 'Form is neither bound nor liberated.'"
"One should teach the Dharma thus: 'Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor impermanent,' up to 'neither bound nor liberated.
One should teach the Dharma thus: 'Form is not of the past; form is not of the future; form is not of the present.'"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Form is ultimately pure; one should teach the Dharma in this way.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately pure"—one should teach the Dharma in this way.
"Up to 'the ultimate purity of all-knowledge,' one should preach the Dharma in this manner.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This Prajñāpāramitā is pure.
The Buddha said:
"Because form is pure, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure."
“Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“World-Honored One,
how is it that because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?”
“How is it that because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha said:
“If form is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, this is called the purity of form.”

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure; this is called the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
“Because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“World-Honored One,
in what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because space is pure?”
The Buddha said:
“Because space is neither born nor extinguished, it is pure.
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.”
Furthermore, Subhūti, because form is unstained,
the perfection of wisdom is pure; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“World-Honored One!
In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because form is unstained?
In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unstained?”
The Buddha said:
"Just as space cannot be defiled, space is pure. [He asked:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that space is pure because it cannot be defiled?
The Buddha said,
"Space is pure because it cannot be grasped."
Because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure. Furthermore, Subhūti,
because space can be described, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“World-Honored One!
How is it that because space can be described, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha said:
“Because two sounds have issued from the midst of space, the Prajñāpāramitā is also like space; it is pure because it can be spoken of. Subhūti!
“Because space is ineffable, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“World-Honored One,
why is it that because space is ineffable, the perfection of wisdom is pure?”
The Buddha said:
"Because space is ineffable, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
Furthermore, because space is ungraspable, the perfection of wisdom is pure."
“World-Honored One!
In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because it is as unobtainable as space?
The Buddha said:
"Just as space has the characteristic of being unapprehendable, so too is the perfection of wisdom like space;
because it is unapprehendable, it is pure. Furthermore, Subhūti!
“Because all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure.
“World-Honored One,
in what way is the Prajñāpāramitā pure because all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure?”
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are ultimately pure, the prajñāpāramitā is pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, draws near to, and correctly contemplates this Prajñāpāramitā, they shall never suffer from eye disease; nor shall their ears, nose, tongue, or body ever suffer from disease. Their bodies shall remain free from physical deformity, they shall not grow old or decay, and they shall never meet with an untimely death.”

On countless days—on the twenty-ninth, the fifteenth, and the thirtieth—the assemblies of devas, as well as good sons and good daughters who serve as Dharma-preachers, all gather wherever the Prajñāpāramitā is being taught.
These sons and daughters of good family who teach this Prajñāpāramitā amidst the great assembly shall obtain immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, and incalculable merit.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!

If these sons or daughters of good family, on the six fast days—the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of the month—expound the meaning of this Prajñāpāramitā before the assembly of devas, those sons or daughters of good family will obtain immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, inconceivable, and incomparable merit.”
Why is this? Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā is a great and precious treasure.
What is this great treasure?

It is the Prajñāpāramitā, which can extract beings from the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and human poverty; it can bestow [birth in] the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and the great households of householders; it can bestow the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and it can bestow the fruit of a Srotāpanna, the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an Anāgāmin, the fruit of an Arhat, the path of a Pratyekabuddha, and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, there is an extensive exposition of the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; it extensively expounds the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom;
and it extensively expounds inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
He extensively explains the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
By training in this, one gives birth to great clans of Kṣatriyas, great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and great families of householders;
one gives birth to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, and the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Yāma Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven,
the Brahmakāyika-parṣadya Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābhā Heaven, the Apramāṇābhā Heaven,
the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubha Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
The devas, the Anābhaka devas, the Puṇyaprasava devas, the Bṛhatphala devas,
the Asaṃjñisattva devas, the Avṛha devas, the Atapa devas, the Sudṛśa devas, the Sudarśana devas,
the Akaniṣṭha devas, the Ākāśānantyāyatana devas, the Vijñānānantyāyatana devas, and the Ākiṃcanyāyatana devas.

In the heavens of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one trains in these dharmas and attains the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship; one attains the path of the pratyekabuddha, and attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Subhūti,
the perfection of wisdom is called a great treasure.
Within this treasure-perfection, there is no dharma to be found— neither arising nor ceasing, neither defilement nor purity, neither grasping nor relinquishing.
In the Jewel Perfection as well, there is no dharma whatsoever—whether wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned.
For this reason, Subhūti, this is called the precious perfection of non-apprehension. Subhūti!
This precious perfection of pāramitā cannot be defiled by any dharma.
Why is this? Because the dharmas that could cause defilement are unattainable.
Subhūti! For this reason, it is called the "Stainless Jewel Pāramitā," Subhūti.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they likewise do not know, likewise do not differentiate, likewise cannot apprehend, and likewise do not engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). This is what is meant by being able to practice the prajñāpāramitā, and being able to pay homage to and visit all Buddhas, traveling from one buddha-field to another, making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising those Buddhas, wandering through the buddha-fields, maturing sentient beings, and purifying the buddha-lands.

Subhūti! This prajñāpāramitā has neither power nor lack of power regarding all phenomena; it neither receives nor gives; it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

This Prajñāpāramitā is neither past, nor future, nor present; it does not abandon the realm of desire nor abide in the realm of desire, it does not abandon the realm of form nor abide in the realm of form, and it does not abandon the formless realm nor abide in the formless realm.

This Prajñāpāramitā does not associate with the Dānapāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Śīlapāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Kṣāntipāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Vīryapāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Dhyānapāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Prajñāpāramitā, nor does it abandon it.
One neither associates with nor abandons internal emptiness, and so on, up to neither associating with nor abandoning the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
One neither associates with nor abandons the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to neither associating with nor abandoning the eightfold noble path.
He neither bestows nor relinquishes the ten powers of a Buddha, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which he neither bestows nor relinquishes.
He neither bestows nor relinquishes the fruit of a stream-enterer, and so on, up to the fruit of an arhat, which he neither bestows nor relinquishes.
It does not bestow the path of the pratyekabuddha nor does it abandon it, and so on, up to not bestowing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) nor abandoning it.

This Prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the dharmas of an arhat nor does it abandon the dharmas of an ordinary person; it does not bestow the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha nor does it abandon the dharmas of an arhat; it does not bestow the dharmas of a Buddha nor does it abandon the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha.
This Prajñāpāramitā neither joins with unconditioned phenomena nor abandons conditioned phenomena.
Why is this? Whether there are Buddhas or no Buddhas, the characteristics of these dharmas remain eternally present and do not change.

"The characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), the abiding of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), and the fixed course of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā) are eternally present, for they are neither erroneous nor lost.
At that time, the sons of the gods stood in the midst of the sky, raising a great sound and leaping with joy, scattering *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers over the Buddha.
They spoke these words:
"We see the second turning of the Wheel of Dharma in Jambudvīpa.
Within this assembly, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This turning of the wheel of Dharma is neither a first turning nor a second turning.
This Prajñāpāramitā emerges neither for the sake of turning nor for the sake of returning, because of the emptiness of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it that because of the emptiness of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas, the Prajñāpāramitā does not proceed nor does it return?”
The Buddha said:
“Prajñāpāramitā is empty of the characteristic of prajñāpāramitā; even up to dānapāramitā, dānapāramitā is empty of the characteristic of dānapāramitā.”

Internal emptiness is empty of the characteristic of internal emptiness; up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is empty of the characteristic of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.

The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness; up to and including the eightfold noble path, which is empty of the characteristic of the eightfold noble path.
The ten powers of the Buddha are empty of the characteristic of the ten powers of the Buddha; even so, the eighteen unique qualities are empty of the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities.

The fruit of stream-entry is empty of the characteristic of the fruit of stream-entry; the fruit of once-returning is empty of the characteristic of the fruit of once-returning; the fruit of non-returning is empty of the characteristic of the fruit of non-returning; the fruit of arhatship is empty of the characteristic of the fruit of arhatship; the path of the pratyekabuddha is empty of the characteristic of the path of the pratyekabuddha; and the knowledge of all modes is empty of the characteristic of the knowledge of all modes.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The prajñāpāramitā of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the mahāpāramitā.”

Why is this? Although all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, it is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; yet there is no dharma that can be attained, no wheel of Dharma that can be turned, and no dharma that can be returned.
Within this Mahāpāramitā, there is likewise no dharma to be perceived. Why is this?
Because these dharmas cannot be found, whether in their progression or their return, for all dharmas are ultimately unarisen.

Why is this? Because this mark of emptiness cannot be turned back nor returned; the mark of signlessness cannot be turned back nor returned; the mark of wishlessness cannot be turned back nor returned.

If one can thus speak of the Prajñāpāramitā—teaching, illuminating, revealing, analyzing, manifesting, and explaining it in a simple and accessible manner—then such a teacher is said to be teaching the Prajñāpāramitā with purity; yet therein is neither a speaker, nor a recipient, nor one who realizes.
"If there were no teaching, no receiving, no realization, and no cessation, then within this Dharma there would likewise be no definitive field of merit.

Chapter 44: Universal Praise (Sarva-stuti-parivarta) of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra; Chapter 44 of the "Hundred Perfections" (Bhāṣya) version. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The boundless *pāramitā* is this *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is like space, which is boundless."
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of equality is this perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because all dharmas are equal.
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is free from extremes.”
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately empty.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"The perfection of non-destruction is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said,
"Because all dharmas are unattainable."
“World-Honored One!
The perfection that has no further shore is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is without name and without body.
"World-Honored One!
The perfection of the element of emptiness is the perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha said:
“Because inhalation and exhalation are unattainable.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"The perfection that is inexpressible is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said,
"Because both vitarka and vicāra are unattainable."
“World-Honored One!
The nameless perfection is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended.
“World-Honored One!
The non-going perfection is the perfection of wisdom.”
The Buddha said,
“Because all dharmas do not come.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"The perfection that is without shifting is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said,
"Because all dharmas cannot be overcome."
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of exhaustion is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are ultimately exhausted.
"World-Honored One!
The non-arising perfection is the perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are non-extinguished.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"The perfection of non-extinction is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said,
"Because all phenomena are unarisen."
“World-Honored One!
The non-activity perfection is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Because an agent cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!
The perfection of non-knowledge is the perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha said:
“Because that which knows cannot be apprehended.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"The non-arrival at the other shore is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Because birth and death cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of non-loss is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because all dharmas are non-forfeiting.
“World-Honored One!
The dream-pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said:
"Because even that which is seen within a dream cannot be apprehended.
[Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!"
"The echo-perfection is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Because that which hears the sound cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of reflection is the perfection of wisdom. The Buddha said:
“Because a mirror surface cannot be apprehended.”
“World-Honored One!
The fire-pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:
“Because the flow of water cannot be apprehended.
“World-Honored One!
The illusion-perfection is the prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said:
"Because the matter of magical arts cannot be attained.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"The non-defiled perfection is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Because all afflictions are unapprehendable."
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of non-purity is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because afflictions are false and deceptive.
“World-Honored One!
This untainted perfection is the perfection of wisdom.”
The Buddha said:
"Because a location cannot be apprehended.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
“The perfection that is free from conceptual proliferation is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because all conceptual proliferations have been destroyed.”
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of non-recollection is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because all conceptualizations are shattered.
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of immovability is the perfection of wisdom.”
The Buddha said:

Chapter 45: On Hearing and Retaining (The "Ear Chapter" in the Danzang edition).
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra had this thought:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with their ears, such a person has performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and has been accompanied by virtuous friends."

How much more so for those who receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and practice according to the teaching—know that such sons and daughters of good family have drawn near to many Buddhas.

Those who are able to hear, receive, draw near to, read, and recite [this teaching], and even maintain right mindfulness of it, practicing according to the instructions, and being able to ask questions and provide answers—know that these good sons and good daughters have, in previous lives, extensively made offerings to and drawn near to many Buddhas.

If one hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid, you should know that this person has also practiced the *dānapāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā* for immeasurable billions of kalpas.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are not startled, not terrified, and do not fear it; and having heard it, they receive, uphold, draw near to, and practice it as taught—then one should know that these good sons and good daughters are like *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Why is this? World-Honored One!

This Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound; if one has not practiced the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā for a long time in previous lives, one will ultimately be unable to believe in or understand the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
"Bhagavān! If there are good sons or good daughters who revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that these persons also reviled the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their previous lives."
Why is this? This good man does not ask the Buddhas and their disciples:
"How should one practice the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā?"
How should one cultivate internal emptiness, up to and including how should one cultivate the emptiness of non-existence and existence?
How should one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including how should one cultivate the eightfold noble path?
"How should one cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, and so on, up to how should one cultivate the eighteen unique qualities? Śakra Devānām Indra said to Śāriputra:

"Regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who have not for long practiced the *dānapāramitā*, the *śīlapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *dhyānapāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā*; who do not practice inner emptiness, outer emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; who do not practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; and who do not practice the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eightfold noble path; nor who do not practice the ten powers of a Buddha, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities."
That such a person does not have faith or understanding in this Prajñāpāramitā—what is there to be surprised about?
Venerable Śāriputra!
I pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā; to pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: “So it is, so it is! Kauśika!”
To pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
Why is this so, Kauśika?
The all-knowledge of all Buddhas arises from the perfection of wisdom; all-knowledge is itself the perfection of wisdom.
For this reason, Kauśika!
Sons and daughters of good family who wish to abide in all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) should abide in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Sons and daughters of good family who wish to give rise to the knowledge of the modes of the path (mārgākārajñatā) should practice and cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
Those who wish to sever all fetters along with their residual tendencies should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Sons and daughters of good family who wish to turn the wheel of Dharma should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Good sons and good daughters who wish to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, and the fruit of arhat should practice the prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha, one should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If one wishes to teach sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin), the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha, one should practice the perfection of wisdom.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to instruct sentient beings so that they may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, or wishes to gather and sustain the saṅgha of bhikṣus, they should practice the prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to practice the *dāna-pāramitā* and the *śīla-pāramitā*?”
How does one dwell in internal emptiness, external emptiness, and so forth, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence?
How does one dwell in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers?
How does one abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How does one abide in the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities?
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom, up to the perfection of generosity, and the emptiness of the internal, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha?
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!"
That you are able to joyfully inquire about this matter is entirely due to the Buddha’s spiritual power, Kauśika!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the prajñāpāramitā, does not dwell within form, they are practicing the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
If one does not dwell within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one is practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
It is the same for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena; and likewise for the eye-element up to the consciousness-element.
Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide within the perfection of wisdom, it is for the sake of practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not abide within the perfection of dhyāna, it is for the sake of practicing the perfection of dhyāna.
Not abiding in the perfection of vigor is the practice of the perfection of vigor;
not abiding in the perfection of patience is the practice of the perfection of patience.
Not dwelling within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline;
not dwelling within the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is the practice of the perfection of generosity.
Thus it is, Kauśika! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom by not dwelling within the perfection of wisdom.

Kauśika! Not abiding in internal emptiness is the practice of internal emptiness; likewise, not abiding in the emptiness of non-existence and existence is the practice of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.

Not dwelling within the four dhyānas is the practice of the four dhyānas; not dwelling within the four immeasurables is the practice of the four immeasurables; not dwelling within the four formless attainments is the practice of the four formless attainments; and not dwelling within the five supernormal powers is the practice of the five supernormal powers.

Not abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness is the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness; likewise, not abiding in the eight factors of the noble path is the practice of the eight factors of the noble path.
Not abiding in the ten powers of a Buddha is the practice of the ten powers of a Buddha; likewise, not abiding in the eighteen unique qualities is the practice of the eighteen unique qualities.
Why is this? Kauśika!

This bodhisattva does not apprehend form as a place where one can dwell or practice; likewise, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they do not apprehend those eighteen unique qualities as places where one can dwell or practice.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice with regard to form; if one does not practice with regard to form, this is called practicing with regard to form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

Why is this? Because for this bodhisattva mahāsattva, the prior limit of form cannot be apprehended, its middle limit cannot be apprehended, and its posterior limit cannot be apprehended; and so it is for all things up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep.”
The Buddha said:
"Because the suchness of form is profound, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound.
Because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is profound, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound."
"Even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), it is likewise so. Śāriputra said:
"World-Honored One!"
"This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to measure.
The Buddha said,
"Because form is difficult to measure, the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to measure."

“Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are difficult to measure, the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to measure.
“World-Honored One! [he said.]
"This Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable.
The Buddha said,
"Because form (rūpa) is immeasurable, the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable."
"Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are immeasurable, the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, does not practice with the thought that form is profound, he is practicing the Prajñāpāramitā."

Not practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor even practicing with regard to the profound eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, is to practice the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?

The profound characteristic of form is non-form; the profound characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are non-unique qualities.
Not practicing in this way is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not practicing the notion that form is difficult to fathom is to practice the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including not practicing with regard to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha which are difficult to fathom—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?

The characteristic of form that is difficult to measure is non-form; the characteristics of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, that are difficult to measure are non-unique qualities.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not practice the infinitude of form, he is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on up to not practicing with regard to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha in their immeasurable aspects, is to practice the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?

Form has immeasurable characteristics and is therefore not form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, have immeasurable characteristics and are therefore not those eighteen unique qualities.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā has an extremely profound nature; it is difficult to see, difficult to understand, and inconceivable.”
This should not be spoken before bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds. Why?

Because when bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they may become startled and terrified, giving rise to doubt and regret, failing to believe it, and failing to practice it.
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be taught before irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
When these bodhisattvas hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will not be startled, terrified, or fearful, nor will their minds harbor doubt or regret; thus they are able to practice with faith.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"If one were to preach this profound Prajñāpāramitā in the presence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly resolved their minds, what fault would there be?"
Śāriputra replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: “Kauśika!

If this profound Prajñāpāramitā were preached before bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, they might become startled and terrified, or disparage it and lack faith; such a possibility exists for these bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.”
If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and, disparaging it, does not believe in it, they plant the karma for the three evil realms.
Due to the causal conditions of this karma, it will be difficult for them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for a long time.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"Is there any bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet received a prediction [of enlightenment] who, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, is neither startled nor terrified?"
Śāriputra said: “So it is, Kauśika!

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, is neither startled nor terrified, you should know that this bodhisattva will receive the prediction of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment before long—not more than after one or two Buddhas.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "So it is, so it is!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has long since resolved his mind to practice the six pāramitās and has made extensive offerings to many Buddhas. Upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, he is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; upon hearing it, he immediately receives and upholds it, practicing according to what is taught within the prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I wish to speak a parable."

If a son or daughter of good family who seeks the bodhisattva path practices the perfection of wisdom even in their dreams, entering meditative concentration, exerting diligent effort, being fully endowed with patience, guarding their ethical discipline, and practicing generosity.
When one practices inner emptiness, outer emptiness, and so forth, up until sitting at the site of enlightenment,
you should know that these sons and daughters of good family are close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

How much more so for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, desiring to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practices the prajñāpāramitā while awake, enters meditative concentration, exerts diligent effort, fulfills patience, guards the precepts, and practices giving—how could such a one not swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and sit at the site of enlightenment?
“World-Honored One!
When good sons and good daughters have perfected their roots of goodness, they will hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, and even practice it according to the teaching.”

It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has long since resolved his mind [on awakening] and planted roots of goodness; he has made offerings to many Buddhas and associated with spiritual friends. Such a person is able to receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect the *prajñāpāramitā*. It should be known that this person is close to receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

It should be known that these good men and good women are like bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive); they are immovable and irreversible from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they are able to attain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and having attained it, they are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and even correctly contemplate it.
World-Honored One!

It is as if a person wishing to cross a wilderness or a perilous path of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, or four hundred yojanas first sees various signs, such as herdsmen, boundary markers, or groves and gardens.
By means of such signs as these, one knows that a city or village is nearby.
Having seen these signs, the person forms this thought:
"According to the signs I see, it should be known that the city or village is not far away."
"Their minds attain peace and security; they do not fear the perils of bandits, evil insects, hunger, or thirst.
World-Honored One!
It is the same for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

If one attains this profound Prajñāpāramitā and upholds, recites, and even correctly contemplates it, you should know that they are close to receiving the prediction of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi before long; you should know that such a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva need not fear falling into the stages of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.
"These are the preceding signs, namely, that one has heard, seen, received, and maintained this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including its correct recollection.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "So it is, so it is!"
"If you wish to speak further, then speak.
"World-Honored One!
It is like a person who, wishing to see the great ocean, resolves to go there."
If one does not see the appearance of trees nor the appearance of mountains, although such a person has not yet seen the great ocean, they know that the great ocean is not far away.
Why is this? Because the location of the great ocean is level, being devoid of the appearance of trees and the appearance of mountains.
"So it is, World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receives, upholds, and even correctly recollects it, although they have not yet received a prediction of their kalpa-count before the Buddha—whether for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas—that bodhisattva knows for themselves that they will soon receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Why is this? "Because I have heard this profound Prajñāpāramitā, and have received, upheld, read, recited, and even correctly contemplated it," [he says].
World-Honored One!
For example, in early spring, when the old leaves of all the trees have fallen, one should know that new leaves, flowers, and fruits will appear before long. Why is this?
Because one perceives these prior signs of the trees, one knows that flowers, leaves, and fruits will soon emerge.
At that time, the people of Jambudvīpa, seeing these preliminary signs of the tree, were all filled with joy.
World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this profound prajñāpāramitā, receives, upholds, reads, recites, and even correctly contemplates it, and practices according to its teaching, one should know that this bodhisattva has perfected their roots of goodness and has made extensive offerings to many buddhas.
This bodhisattva should form this thought:
"Pursued by the roots of goodness from previous lives, I am heading toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

By these causes and conditions, I have been able to see and hear this profound prajñāpāramitā, and I receive, uphold, read, recite, and even correctly contemplate it, practicing in accordance with what is taught."
Among them, those devaputras who had previously seen the Buddha were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking to themselves:

"The former bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also had such preliminary signs when they received their prediction; now it will not be long before this bodhisattva-mahāsattva receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"World-Honored One!

It is like a woman who is pregnant; her body becomes heavy and painful, her gait is unsteady, she is uneasy when sitting or rising, and her sleep and appetite diminish. She takes no pleasure in speech and grows weary of her former habits because she suffers from pain."
Just as there are women who, seeing certain preliminary signs, know that childbirth will occur before long;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Having planted roots of goodness, made extensive offerings to the Buddhas, practiced the six pāramitās for a long time, and associated with spiritual friends, his roots of goodness reach fulfillment. He then hears this profound Prajñāpāramitā, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and even more, correctly contemplates it and practices according to its teaching.
"These people also know that it will not be long before this bodhisattva mahāsattva receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Whatever you delight in expounding is entirely through the power of the Buddha.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has well entrusted the affairs of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi bring peace and security to many sentient beings, cause immeasurable sentient beings to attain happiness, and out of compassion benefit all devas and humans.”

When these bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path, they gather immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings through the four means of attraction: namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.

He also brings sentient beings to maturity through the ten paths of wholesome action; he himself practices the first dhyāna and also teaches others to practice the first dhyāna, and so on, up to practicing the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception himself and also teaching others to practice up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One practices the dāna-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the dāna-pāramitā; one practices the śīla-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the śīla-pāramitā; one practices the kṣānti-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the kṣānti-pāramitā; one practices the vīrya-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the vīrya-pāramitā; one practices the dhyāna-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the dhyāna-pāramitā; one practices the prajñā-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the prajñā-pāramitā.

This bodhisattva, having attained the perfection of wisdom, uses the power of skillful means to teach sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, while he himself does not realize it within.
He teaches sentient beings to attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and the fruit of *arhat*, yet he himself does not realize them within.
He teaches sentient beings to attain the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, yet he himself does not realize it within.
They practice the six pāramitās themselves and also instruct immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas to practice the six pāramitās.
They abide themselves on the stage of avaivartika and also instruct others to abide on the stage of avaivartika.
They themselves purify Buddha-fields and also teach others to purify Buddha-fields;
they themselves bring sentient beings to maturity and also teach others to bring sentient beings to maturity;
they themselves attain the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva and also teach others to cause them to attain the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva.
They themselves purify the gateway of dhāraṇīs and also teach others to purify the gateway of dhāraṇīs;
they themselves possess the eloquence of joyful speech and also teach others to possess the eloquence of joyful speech.
They themselves accomplish the attainment of the marks of physical beauty and also teach others to accomplish the attainment of the marks of physical beauty;
they themselves accomplish the thirty-two major marks and also teach others to accomplish the thirty-two major marks.
One personally accomplishes the stage of youthful purity and also teaches others to accomplish the stage of youthful purity.
One personally accomplishes the ten powers of a Buddha and also teaches others to accomplish the ten powers of a Buddha.
They themselves practice the four fearlessnesses and also teach others to practice the four fearlessnesses;
they themselves practice the eighteen unique qualities and also teach others to practice the eighteen unique qualities.
They personally practice great loving-kindness and great compassion, and they also teach others to practice great loving-kindness and great compassion.
They themselves attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), and they also teach others to cause them to attain all-knowledge.
Having personally become free from all fetters, latencies, and habitual tendencies, they also teach others to become free from all fetters, latencies, and habitual tendencies;
having personally turned the wheel of Dharma, they also teach others to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished great merit, in that they practice the prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all sentient beings, desiring to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“World-Honored One!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive an increase in form nor do they perceive a decrease in form; they do not perceive an increase in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they perceive a decrease in them; and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes, which they do not perceive as increasing nor do they perceive as decreasing."
At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive this as dharma or non-dharma; they do not perceive these as past dharmas, future, or present dharmas; they do not perceive them as wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, or as determinate or indeterminate dharmas; they do not perceive them as conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas; they do not perceive the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they do not perceive the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), or the perfection of wisdom; and so on, up to not perceiving the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva fully practices the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without marks.
"All dharmas are empty, deceptive, and lacking solidity; they have no self and no life-principle. Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
