By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows the great minds of these sentient beings as they truly are, as great minds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows the immeasurable minds of sentient beings as they truly are, as immeasurable minds."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that the Buddha,
by means of the prajñāpāramitā, knows the immeasurable minds of sentient beings as they truly are— namely, as immeasurable minds?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"By means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha knows that the minds of these sentient beings neither see abiding nor see non-abiding. Why is this?"
Because these immeasurable states of mind have no basis of dependence, who could abide in them or not abide in them?
In this way, Subhūti, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows immeasurable minds as they truly are— immeasurable minds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! By means of the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha knows the invisible mind of sentient beings as it truly is—that it is an invisible mind."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does the Buddha, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, truly know the invisible mind of sentient beings as an invisible mind?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The minds of sentient beings are signless; the Buddha knows them as they truly are to be signless, because their own-characteristics are empty.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
The Buddha knows the minds of sentient beings, which cannot be seen by the five eyes. Thus, Subhūti,
it is through the *prajñāpāramitā* that the Buddha knows, as it truly is, the invisible mind of sentient beings as an invisible mind.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows, in accordance with reality, the emergence and submergence, the contraction and extension of the mental activities of sentient beings.
[Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!"
"How does the Buddha, by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are the arising and ceasing, the contraction and expansion, of the mental activities of sentient beings?
The Buddha said:

"The arising and ceasing, the contraction and expansion, and so forth, of all sentient beings' mental activities, all arise in dependence upon form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."

Subhūti! Within this, the Buddha knows the arising and ceasing, the contraction and expansion of the mental states of sentient beings—namely, views such as "the self and the world are eternal," or "this alone is the truth and all else is false"—all of which are based upon form.
"The self and the world are impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on form.
"The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on form.
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view relies on form (*rūpa*).
"The self and the world are eternal; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view relies on feeling (*vedanā*).
"The self and the world are impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this is a view based on clinging.
"The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this is a view based on clinging.
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view relies upon feeling.
"The self and the world are eternal; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view relies upon perception.
"The self and the world are impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on perception.
"The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on perception.
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on perception.
"The self and the world are eternal; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on volitional formations.
"The self and the world are impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this is a view based on conduct.
"The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this is a view based on conduct.
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on conduct.
"The self and the world are eternal; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on consciousness.
"The self and the world are impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view relies upon consciousness.
"The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view relies upon consciousness.
"That the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite—this is the truth, all else is falsehood"—this view relies upon consciousness.
"That the world is finite—this is the truth, all else is falsehood"—this view relies upon form.
"The world is infinite; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on form.
"The world is both finite and infinite; this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is based on form.
"The world is neither finite nor infinite; this is the truth, all else is false. This view is based on form (*rūpa*).
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra, vijñāna*).
"The self is identical to the body"—this view relies on form (*rūpa*).
"The self is distinct from the body"—this view also relies on form.
It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"The Tathāgata exists after death; this is the truth, all else is falsehood"—this view is dependent upon form.
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death; this is the truth, all else is falsehood"—this view is dependent upon form.
"Whether the Tathāgata exists after death or does not exist after death—this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is dependent on form.
"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—this is the truth, all else is false"—this view is dependent on form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness. Thus, Subhūti,
it is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* that the Buddha knows, as they truly are, the arising and ceasing, the bending and extending, of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Buddha knows the characteristics of form (*rūpa*).
How does he know the characteristics of form?

One knows that the suchness-characteristic (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) of form is indestructible; it is without conceptual differentiation, without marks, without recollection, without proliferation, and without attainment.
The characteristic of form is likewise so.
Subhūti! The Buddha knows the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
How does he know the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
The suchness-characteristic of consciousness is indestructible; it is without discrimination, without marks, without recollection, without conceptual proliferation, and without attainment.
The characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus.
Thus it is, Subhūti! The Buddha knows the suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of the arising, ceasing, bending, and extending of the mental factors of sentient beings.
This suchness of the five aggregates and this suchness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is precisely the suchness of all dharmas.
What is the suchness of all dharmas?
It is the suchness of the six pāramitās.

The suchness of the six *pāramitās* is the very same as the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the very same as the suchness of the eighteen kinds of emptiness; the suchness of the eighteen kinds of emptiness is the very same as the suchness of the eight liberations; the suchness of the eight liberations is the very same as the suchness of the nine successive attainments; the suchness of the nine successive attainments is the very same as the suchness of the Buddha’s ten powers; the suchness of the Buddha’s ten powers is the very same as the suchness of the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities is the very same as the suchness of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); and the suchness of all-knowledge is the very same as the suchness of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, mundane and supramundane dharmas, and out-flowing and non-out-flowing dharmas.
The suchness of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena is itself the suchness of all phenomena of the past, future, and present.
The suchness of all phenomena of the past, future, and present is itself the suchness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
The suchness of conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena is itself the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry.
The suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is itself the suchness of the fruit of once-returning.
The suchness of the fruit of once-returning is itself the suchness of the fruit of non-returning.
The suchness of the fruit of non-returning is itself the suchness of the fruit of arhatship.
The suchness of the fruit of arhatship is the suchness of the path of the pratyekabuddha.
The suchness of the path of the pratyekabuddha is the suchness of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The suchness of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the very suchness of all Buddhas.
The suchness of all Buddhas is a single suchness.
It is non-dual and undifferentiated, inexhaustible and indestructible; this is called the suchness of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
The Buddha attains this mark of suchness by means of the perfection of wisdom; for this reason, the perfection of wisdom can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the marks of the world.
Thus it is, Subhūti! The Buddha knows all dharmas as they truly are (tathatā): they are not otherwise than their true nature, nor do they differ from it.
Because he has realized this true nature, the Buddha is called the Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This suchness of all dharmas is profound; it is not a state of non-suchness, nor is it a state of difference.”
World-Honored One!
It is by means of this suchness that all Buddhas preach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
Who is able to believe and understand this?
Only irreversible bodhisattvas, persons endowed with right view, and arhats whose outflows are exhausted. Why is this so?
“The Buddha has attained this profound suchness and teaches it to others in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This suchness is profound because its characteristic is inexhaustible.”
Subhūti asked: "By virtue of what dharma being characterized by inexhaustibility is it profound?
The Buddha said:
“Because all dharmas are inexhaustible.
Thus, Subhūti, having realized the suchness of all these dharmas, the Buddha teaches them for the sake of sentient beings.”

Chapter 49: Inquiry into Characteristics *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Forty-nine: Inquiry into Characteristics At that time, all the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm within the trichiliocosm scattered flowers and incense from afar and came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, the *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by you is profound. What are the characteristics of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha addressed the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm: "Devaputras!
The mark of emptiness is the mark of this profound prajñāpāramitā; it is signless, unconditioned, unarisen, neither born nor extinguished, and neither defiled nor pure."
The state of non-existence, signlessness, lack of dependence, and the characteristic of emptiness— these are the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
O sons of the gods!

Such characteristics as these are the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; the Buddha has taught them for the sake of sentient beings by employing worldly conventions, but they are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
O sons of the gods!
These various marks cannot be destroyed by any in the world—gods, humans, or asuras. Why is this?
Because these gods, humans, and asuras of the entire world are themselves also marks.
O sons of the gods!

Characteristics cannot destroy characteristics; characteristics cannot know characteristics; characteristics cannot know the absence of characteristics; and the absence of characteristics cannot know characteristics.
These marks and these marklessness—both marks and marklessness are non-existent.
This is because the mark that is known, the knower, and the dharma that is known are all unattainable. Why is this so?
O sons of the gods!
These marks are not produced by form; they are not produced by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

They are not produced by the perfection of generosity; nor are they produced by the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom.

It is not produced by internal emptiness, nor produced by external emptiness, nor produced by internal-and-external emptiness; it is not produced by the emptiness of non-existence, nor produced by the emptiness of existence, nor produced by the emptiness of both non-existence and existence.
It is not produced by the four foundations of mindfulness, nor even by the knowledge of all modes.
O sons of the gods!
This mark does not belong to humans, nor does it belong to non-humans; it is neither mundane nor supramundane, neither with outflows nor without outflows, neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputras:
"Suppose, for example, someone were to ask:
'What is the characteristic of empty space?'"
"Is this person asking correctly?
The sons of the gods replied,
"World-Honored One!"
This is an improper question. Why is that?
World-Honored One!
"This space has no characteristic that can be described, for space is unconditioned and without arising.
The Buddha addressed the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm:
"Whether a Buddha appears or not, the characteristics and nature [of phenomena] abide eternally."
"Because the Buddha has attained the nature of the suchness of reality, he is called the Tathāgata.
The devaputras addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
The nature of the various marks attained by the World-Honored One is profoundly deep.
Because he has attained these marks, he has attained unimpeded wisdom.
Abiding within these marks, he gathers the specific characteristics of all phenomena through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The devaputras said: "It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
This profound prajñāpāramitā is the path constantly traversed by all Buddhas; by practicing this path, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Having attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, one thoroughly penetrates the characteristics of all dharmas—whether the characteristic of form, or the characteristics of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the characteristic of the knowledge of all modes.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is!
O sons of the gods!"
The characteristic of affliction and decay is the characteristic of form (*rūpa*); the attainment of Buddhahood is signless (*animitta*).

The perceiver is the characteristic of sensation (*vedanā*), the grasper is the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*), the initiator of action is the characteristic of formations (*saṃskāra*), and the one who discerns is the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*); the attainment of Buddhahood is signless.

The characteristic of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is the ability to relinquish; the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is the absence of feverish affliction; the characteristic of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is immutability; the characteristic of the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) is invincibility; the characteristic of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) is the gathering of the mind; and the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is renunciation. The Buddha has attained this signlessness (*animitta*).
That which is without mental affliction or distress is the characteristic of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; the Buddha has attained this signlessness.
That which is supramundane is the characteristic of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the Buddha has attained this signlessness.

Suffering has the characteristic of the liberation door of non-action; its origination has the characteristic of the liberation door of emptiness; and its cessation has the characteristic of the liberation door of signlessness. The Buddha has attained this signlessness.

The Victor possesses the mark of the ten powers; the Fearless One possesses the mark of the four fearlessnesses; the All-Knowing One possesses the mark of the four unhindered knowledges; and that which others cannot attain possesses the mark of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—thus, the Buddha has attained these signless marks.

Compassionately regarding sentient beings is the mark of great kindness and great compassion; reality is the mark of being free from error; having nothing to grasp is the mark of constant relinquishment; manifest thorough knowledge is the mark of the wisdom of all modes. The Buddha has attained these signless states.
"In this way, O sons of the gods!
The Buddha has attained the signlessness of all dharmas; for this reason, the Buddha is named 'Unobstructed Wisdom'.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Subhūti:

“The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas; the Prajñāpāramitā is able to reveal the characteristics of the world. For this reason, the Buddha relies upon and practices this Dharma, and he makes offerings to, reveres, honors, and praises this Dharma.”
What is this Dharma?
It is the Prajñāpāramitā. All Buddhas abide by relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā; they revere, make offerings to, honor, and praise this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all Buddhas;
the Buddha knows how to act as a person.
If someone were to ask correctly about one who knows how to act, there would be no answer more correct than that of the Buddha.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Subhūti, because the Buddha knows how to act as a person,
he has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the Dharma upon which he rides and the path from whence he comes.
This vehicle and this path are those which the Buddha himself reveres, honors, respects, praises, upholds, and protects.
Subhūti, this is called the Buddha’s knowledge of those who act as persons.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Buddha knows that all dharmas have the characteristic of non-action, because an agent does not exist.
All dharmas have the characteristic of non-arising, because any formal activity cannot be apprehended."
Subhūti! By means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha knows that all dharmas have the characteristic of non-action.
For this reason, the Buddha knows the person who acts.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* that the Buddha realizes the non-arising of all phenomena, because there is nothing to be apprehended.
For this reason, the *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the characteristics of the world."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If all dharmas have no knower and no seer, how can the prajñāpāramitā give birth to the Buddhas and reveal the characteristics of the world?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
All dharmas truly have no knower and no seer.”
What is meant by "no knower" and "no seer"?
All dharmas are empty, deceptive, and lacking in solidity; therefore, all dharmas have no knower and no seer.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! How is it that all dharmas have no knower and no seer?
All dharmas are without support and without attachment."
For this reason, all dharmas have no knower and no seer. Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the characteristics of the world.

Because one does not perceive form, one demonstrates the characteristics of the world; because one does not perceive feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness, one demonstrates the characteristics of the world; and so on, up to because one does not perceive the knowledge of all modes, one demonstrates the characteristics of the world.
"In this way, Subhūti, the prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the characteristics of the world. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that by not seeing form, the *prajñāpāramitā* reveals the characteristics of the world?
How is it that by not seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so forth, up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), it reveals the characteristics of the world?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If consciousness does not arise conditioned by form, this is called teaching by way of not seeing the marks of form.

If consciousness does not arise conditioned by feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and so on up to if consciousness does not arise conditioned by the knowledge of all modes, this is called teaching by way of not seeing the marks of the knowledge of all modes.”
Thus it is, Subhūti! This profound prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the characteristics of the world. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
"How is it that the Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas and reveal the characteristics of the world? Subhūti,
the Prajñāpāramitā reveals the emptiness of the world."

How does one demonstrate that the world is empty? One demonstrates that the world of the five aggregates is empty; one demonstrates that the world of the twelve bases is empty; one demonstrates that the world of the eighteen elements is empty; one demonstrates that the world of the twelve links of dependent origination is empty; and one demonstrates that the world of the view of self and the sixty-two fundamental views is empty. One demonstrates that the world of the ten paths of wholesome action is empty;

one demonstrates that the world of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments is empty; and one demonstrates that the world of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is empty.
He demonstrates that the six *pāramitās* are empty of the world;

he demonstrates that internal emptiness is empty of the world, external emptiness is empty of the world, internal-and-external emptiness is empty of the world, the emptiness of non-existence is empty of the world, the emptiness of existence is empty of the world, the emptiness of both non-existence and existence is empty of the world, conditioned emptiness is empty of the world, and unconditioned emptiness is empty of the world.

He demonstrates that the ten powers of a Buddha are empty of the world, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are empty of the world, and so on, up to demonstrating that all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is empty of the world.
Thus it is, Subhūti! The perfection of wisdom can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the characteristics of the world. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

By means of this prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha demonstrates the emptiness of the world, knows the emptiness of the world, awakens to the emptiness of the world, contemplates the emptiness of the world, and discerns the emptiness of the world.
Thus it is, Subhūti! The perfection of wisdom can give birth to all Buddhas and can demonstrate to the world the emptiness of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the characteristics of the world. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the Prajñāpāramitā reveals to the Buddha that the world is inconceivable."
How does he demonstrate that the world is inconceivable?
He demonstrates that the world of the five aggregates is inconceivable, and so on, up to demonstrating that the world of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is inconceivable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā demonstrates that the Buddha is detached from the world.
How does it demonstrate detachment from the world?
It demonstrates the detachment from the world of the five aggregates, up to and including the demonstration of the detachment from the world of all-knowledge. In this way, Subhūti,
the Prajñāpāramitā demonstrates the detachment of the Buddha from the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals to the Buddha the tranquility of the world.
How does it reveal the tranquility of the world?
It demonstrates the quiescence of the world of the five aggregates, up to and including the demonstration of the quiescence of the world of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the Prajñāpāramitā demonstrates that the world of the Buddhas is ultimately empty."
How does one demonstrate that the world is ultimately empty?
One demonstrates that the world of the five aggregates is ultimately empty, and so on, up to demonstrating that the world of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is ultimately empty.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals to the Buddha that the nature of the world is empty.
How does it reveal that the nature of the world is empty?
It demonstrates that the world of the five aggregates is empty of intrinsic nature, and so on, up to demonstrating that the world of all-knowledge is empty of intrinsic nature. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the Prajñāpāramitā demonstrates that the world of the Buddhas is the emptiness of non-existence."
How does it demonstrate that the world is empty of non-existent phenomena?

It demonstrates that the world of the five aggregates is empty of non-existent phenomena, and so on, up to demonstrating that the world of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is empty of non-existent phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals that the phenomena of the world are empty.
How does it reveal that the phenomena of the world are empty?
He demonstrates that the dharmas of the world of the five aggregates are empty, and so on, up to demonstrating that the dharmas of the world of all-knowledge are empty. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Prajñāpāramitā demonstrates to the Buddha that the world is empty of both non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas.
How does it demonstrate that the world is empty of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas?

It demonstrates that the world of the five aggregates is empty of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas, and so on, up to demonstrating that the world of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is empty of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals that the world is uniquely empty for the Buddha.
How does it reveal that the world is uniquely empty?
"It demonstrates that the world of the five aggregates is uniquely empty, and so on, up to demonstrating that the world of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is uniquely empty. 'In this way, Subhūti,
the Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to the Buddhas and can demonstrate the characteristics of the Buddha-world.'"
Subhūti! This profound Prajñāpāramitā reveals the characteristic of the world, namely, the characteristic of neither arising in this world nor in future worlds. Why is this?
"Because all dharmas have no characteristics that can be used to produce this world or future worlds.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This perfection of wisdom arises for the sake of a great task,
World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom arises for the sake of an inconceivable task.
World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā arises for the sake of an immeasurable matter.
World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom arises for the sake of immeasurable matters,
World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom arises for the sake of matters that are unequaled.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
The perfection of wisdom arises for the sake of a great matter;
it arises for the sake of an inconceivable matter;
it arises for the sake of an incomparable matter.
It arises for the sake of immeasurable matters;
it arises for the sake of matters that are unequaled. Subhūti!
In what way does this perfection of wisdom arise for the sake of a great task?
Subhūti, the "great tasks" of the Buddhas are as follows: namely, to rescue all sentient beings and never to abandon any sentient being.
Subhūti! In what way does this prajñāpāramitā arise for the sake of inconceivable matters? Subhūti!
"Inconceivable matters" refer to the dharmas of all Buddhas, the dharmas of Tathāgatas, the dharmas of self-enlightened ones, and the dharmas of those with all-knowledge.
For this reason, Subhūti!
The Prajñāpāramitā of all Buddhas arises for the sake of the inconceivable matters of all Buddhas.
Subhūti, how is it that the Prajñāpāramitā arises for the sake of the immeasurable matters?
Subhūti! Among all sentient beings, there is none who is able to conceive of or describe the Buddha-dharma, the Tathāgata-dharma, the self-awakened one’s dharma, or the dharma of the omniscient one.
For this reason, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom arises for the sake of an immeasurable matter. Subhūti!
In what way does the perfection of wisdom arise for the sake of immeasurable matters?

Subhūti, it arises for the sake of all sentient beings—there being none among them who can measure the Buddha-dharma, the Tathāgata-dharma, the self-realized dharma, or all things that are peerless. It arises for the sake of these matters.
Subhūti! Among all sentient beings, there is none who can equal the Buddha, let alone surpass him. For this reason, Subhūti!
"The perfection of wisdom arises for the sake of the task that is equal to the unequaled.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

Is it that the phenomena of the Buddha-dharma, the Tathāgata-dharma, the self-enlightened one’s dharma, and the all-knowing one’s dharma—these inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled matters—arise?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
The Dharma of the Buddhas, the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, the Dharma of the Self-Existent Ones, and the Dharma of the Omniscient Ones are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled.”

Form is also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled; even up to all-knowledge, the nature of phenomena, and the characteristics of phenomena, they are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled.
Within this, the mind and mental factors are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, form is inconceivable, and that too is unapprehendable; even up to 'form is unequaled,' that too is unapprehendable."
“Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge, are unequaled; yet even these are unapprehendable.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
For what reason are form, up to and including the unequaled, inconceivable, and likewise unattainable?
Why are feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge, the unequaled, and likewise unattainable?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Because the measure of form cannot be apprehended; because the measures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to the measure of all-knowledge, which cannot be apprehended.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason and by what conditions is the measure of form unobtainable?"
"...up to the point that the measure of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because form (*rūpa*) is inconceivable, and so on up to because form is unequaled-with-the-equal (*asamasama*), its measure cannot be apprehended."
Subhūti, because all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is inconceivable, and because all-knowledge is unequaled with the unequaled, its measure cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!
What do you think? Can that which is inconceivable, up to and including the unequaled, be apprehended?
Can form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge, be apprehended?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
it cannot be apprehended.”
"For this reason, Subhūti, all dharmas are inconceivable; even 'the unequaled' is likewise so, Subhūti."
The dharmas of all Buddhas are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable,
and unequaled. Subhūti,
these are called the dharmas of all Buddhas that are inconceivable, and so forth, up to unequaled.
Subhūti! These dharmas of the Buddhas are inconceivable, because they transcend the characteristics of the conceivable;
they are incomparable, because they transcend comparison.
It is immeasurable because it transcends all measure;
it is unequaled because it transcends all that can be equaled. Subhūti!
For this reason, all dharmas are also inconceivable, up to and including unequaled. Subhūti,
"inconceivable" means that their meaning is inconceivable.
"Inconceivable" means that its meaning cannot be conceived;
"immeasurable" means that its meaning cannot be measured;
"unequaled" means that its meaning is without equal.
Subhūti! These dharmas of the Buddhas are inconceivable, even unto the unequaled.
They are inconceivable, just as space is inconceivable.
It is incalculable, like space which is incalculable;
it is immeasurable, like space which is immeasurable;
it is unequaled, like space which is unequaled.
Subhūti! This is also called the inconceivable nature of the Buddhas' dharmas, up to and including the unequaled.
The Buddha-dharmas are thus immeasurable; no one among all the worlds—whether devas, humans, or asuras—is able to conceive of or calculate them.

When this chapter on the inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled nature of the Buddhas' dharmas was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus, through non-acceptance of all dharmas, exhausted their outflows, attained liberation of mind, and realized arhatship.
Twenty thousand bhikṣuṇīs, because they did not grasp at any dharmas, exhausted their outflows and attained arhatship.
Sixty thousand upāsakas and thirty thousand upāsikās became free from dust and defilement regarding all dharmas, and the Dharma-eye arose within them regarding all dharmas.

Twenty thousand koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and shall receive their prediction [of enlightenment] within this Bhadrakalpa.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Fourteen: "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because form (*rūpa*) is unapprehendable, it is inconceivable.
Up to and including: because form is unapprehendable, it is unequaled.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are unapprehendable, they are inconceivable.
Because consciousness is unapprehendable, it is unequaled;
because everything up to all-knowledge is unapprehendable, it is inconceivable;
because everything up to all-knowledge is unapprehendable, it is unequaled.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is form unattainable, and thus inconceivable, up to and including unequaled-with-the-equal?”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable, they are inconceivable, up to and including "unequaled with the unequaled"?
And because even the knowledge of all modes is unapprehendable, it is inconceivable, up to and including "unequaled with the unequaled"?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because form has no measure, it cannot be apprehended.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no measure, they cannot be apprehended.”
"Up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), because they cannot be measured, they are unattainable.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason, Subhūti, is form unapprehendable because it cannot be measured?
And so on, up to why is the knowledge of all modes unapprehendable because it cannot be measured?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) are inconceivable, they cannot be measured.
... up to ... because the characteristics of form are unequaled with the unequaled (*asamasama*), they cannot be measured.
... up to ... because the characteristics of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) are inconceivable, they cannot be measured."
"Up to and including the fact that the marks of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) are equal to the unequaled,
there is no measure. — *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 15.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Fifty: Accomplishment (The "Great Events Arise" Chapter in the Dan Edition).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* arises for the sake of a great matter; it arises for the sake of an inconceivable matter; it arises for the sake of an incomparable matter; it arises for the sake of an immeasurable matter.”
“World-Honored One!
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* arises for the sake of that which is unequaled.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! This profound Prajñāpāramitā arises for the sake of a great task, even unto the task of that which is unequaled. Why is this?

The perfection of wisdom contains and encompasses the five perfections; the perfection of wisdom contains and encompasses inner emptiness, outer emptiness, and so forth up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; it contains and encompasses the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* contains and encompasses the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is like a consecrated king who is honored within his kingdom; he entrusts all matters of state to his great ministers, while the king remains at ease, free from affairs, and acts as he pleases.

Thus it is, Subhūti! All the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, whether they be the dharmas of bodhisattvas or the dharmas of buddhas, all reside within the prajñāpāramitā; it is the prajñāpāramitā that is able to accomplish their tasks.
For this reason, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom arises for the sake of a great task, even unto the task of that which is unequaled. Furthermore, Subhūti:
This perfection of wisdom is accomplished because it does not grasp at form and does not cling to form;
it is accomplished because it does not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and does not cling to them.
Because they do not grasp at or cling to anything up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to accomplish it.

Because they do not grasp at or cling to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) up to and including the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*), they are able to accomplish them.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way does the perfection of wisdom accomplish its task by not grasping and not clinging to form?

In what way does the perfection of wisdom accomplish its task by not grasping and not clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do you perceive this form as something that can be grasped or clung to? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, what do you think?
Do you perceive anything—from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—that can be grasped or clung to?"
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! I, too, do not perceive this form as something that can be grasped or clung to.”
Because they are not seen, they are not grasped; because they are not grasped, they are not clung to.
I likewise do not see anything—from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and all-knowledge—that can be grasped or clung to.
Because they do not see them, they do not grasp them; because they do not grasp them, they do not cling to them. Subhūti!
I likewise do not see any Buddha-dharma, Tathāgata-dharma, self-realized dharma, or all-knower dharma that can be grasped or clung to.
Because they do not see them, they do not grasp; because they do not grasp, they do not cling.

For this reason, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should neither grasp nor cling to form, nor should they grasp or cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and likewise, they should neither grasp nor cling to anything from the dharmas of the Buddha, the dharmas of the Tathāgata, the dharmas of the self-existent one, and the dharmas of the omniscient one.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to see and difficult to understand; it cannot be known through thought or analogy. It can be known only by those with subtle, skillful wisdom and who have attained tranquility.”

One who is able to have faith in this Prajñāpāramitā should be known as a bodhisattva who has made offerings to many Buddhas, planted many roots of goodness, and associated with virtuous friends, such that they are able to believe in and understand the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
"World-Honored One!

If all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were to become practitioners of faith, practitioners of the Dharma, those on the eighth stage, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas—whether in terms of their wisdom or their abandonments—it would not equal a bodhisattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a single day with patient endurance, contemplation, and deliberation."

Why is this? Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to those who practice through faith, those who practice through the Dharma, the eight types of persons, the srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, the arhat, or the pratyekabuddha—that is itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Buddha addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms: "So it is, so it is! O devaputras!"

Whether they be those who practice through faith, those who practice through Dharma, those of the eight stages, stream-enterers, up to arhats, or pratyekabuddhas—these are themselves the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
O sons of the gods!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, writes it down, upholds it, receives it, reads it, recites it, explains it, and correctly brings it to mind, that son or daughter of good family will swiftly attain *nirvāṇa*. They surpass those sons and daughters of good family who seek the vehicle of the *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, yet remain far removed from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and practice other sūtras for an eon, or even less than an eon.
Why is this? Because within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the supreme and wondrous Dharma is extensively expounded.

This is what those who practice through faith, those who practice through the Dharma, the *aṣṭamaka*, the *srotāpanna*, the *sakṛdāgāmin*, the *anāgāmin*, the *arhat*, and the *pratyekabuddha* should study; it is also what the *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas* should study. Having studied it, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm all raised their voices and said:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is called the Mahāpāramitā.”
World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is called the inconceivable, the incomparable, the immeasurable, and the unequaled pāramitā.

Those who practice through faith and those who practice through the Dharma, as well as the eight types of persons in training, study this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and thereby attain the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*, or become *pratyekabuddhas*. By studying this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they become *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas*; within the study of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Yet, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* neither increases nor decreases.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
Not far from there, they suddenly vanished and each returned to their own abode.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, immediately believes and understands it, from where did they pass away to come and be born here?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, immediately believes and understands it, without sinking, retreating, finding it difficult, doubting, or regretting; if they joyfully delight in hearing it, and having heard it, they keep it in mind and do not distance themselves from this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they never abandon or forget it, and always follow the Dharma teacher."
Just as a newborn calf does not leave its mother, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
for the sake of hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they never remain far removed from the Dharma teacher.
"Up until they attain this profound Prajñāpāramitā, reciting it with their mouths and understanding it with their minds, and attaining penetration through right view.
Subhūti! You should know that these bodhisattvas have passed away from among human beings and are reborn here again among human beings."

Why is this? Because those who seek the Buddha-way in their previous lives heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, copied it, upheld it, revered, honored, and praised it, and made offerings to it with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.

"By reason of these causes and conditions, having passed away from among humans, they will be reborn again among humans and, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, will immediately believe and understand it.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Are there any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having accomplished such meritorious qualities and having made offerings to the Buddhas in other lands, pass away from there and are reborn here, hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and immediately believing and understanding it, copying, upholding, reciting, and correctly contemplating it?
"Is there such a person?

The Buddha said, "There are bodhisattvas who have accomplished such merit and virtue; having made offerings to the Buddhas in other lands, they pass away there and are reborn in this world. Upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they immediately believe and understand it, copying, upholding, reciting, and correctly contemplating it."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Buddhas of other directions; having believed, understood, written down, maintained, recited, explained, and correctly recollected it, they have passed away there and been born here. One should know that such persons have accomplished the merits of their previous lives.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas who,
having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya,
have been born here in this world by virtue of those roots of goodness."
Subhūti! Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although they heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in a previous life, did not inquire about its meaning;
having been reborn among humans, when they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds harbor doubt and regret, making it difficult for them to realize it.

Subhūti! You should know that such a bodhisattva, although they heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, failed to inquire about it; therefore, they continue to harbor doubts and regrets, making it difficult for them to awaken.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, although having heard of the dhyāna-pāramitā in previous lives, did not inquire about its essential points;
and now, upon hearing the prajñā-pāramitā in this life, does not inquire for that same reason, they will continue to give rise to doubt and regret.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, although having heard the *vīryapāramitā* in previous lives, did not inquire into its essential meaning;
and now in this life, upon hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, does not inquire because of that former neglect, they will continue to harbor doubt and regret.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, although having heard of the pāramitā of patience in previous lives, did not inquire into its essential meaning;
and in this present life, having heard of the prajñāpāramitā, does not inquire into it for that same reason, they will continue to harbor doubts and regrets.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, although having heard the śīlapāramitā in previous lives, did not inquire about its inner details;
and in this present life, upon hearing the prajñāpāramitā, does not inquire—because of this failure to inquire, they will continue to harbor doubt and regret.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva may have heard of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence in previous lives, they did not inquire into its essential meaning. Having been reborn among humans,
because they do not inquire upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they continue to harbor doubts and regrets, making it difficult for them to realize it."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva may have heard in previous lives of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, the ten powers of a buddha, and even up to all-knowledge, they did not inquire about the meaning therein.
Having been reborn among humans, because they do not inquire upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they continue to harbor doubts and regrets, making it difficult for them to realize it."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva previously heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in a former life but questioned its contents without putting them into practice, at the time of his rebirth, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* for one day, two days, three days, four days, or five days, his mind becomes firm and nothing can destroy it."
If one departs from what has been heard, one will then fall away and lose it. Why is this?
When in previous lives they heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, although they inquired about its central matters, they did not practice in accordance with what was taught.
Such a person may at times wish to hear [the Dharma] and at other times not wish to hear it; their mind is frivolous and unstable, and their will is disordered and unsettled.
They are like light feathers that drift east and west with the wind.
Subhūti!

It should be known that this bodhisattva has not long since resolved [upon enlightenment]; they have not associated with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), nor have they made extensive offerings to the Buddhas. In previous lives, they did not write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor did they read, recite, or correctly contemplate it. They did not study the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor did they study the *dhyānapāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *śīlapāramitā*, or the *dānapāramitā*. They did not study the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). They did not study the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). They did not study the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), or the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśabala*), up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Thus it is, Subhūti! You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has newly resolved upon the Great Vehicle; because his faith is slight and his joy is slight, he is unable to write down this profound prajñāpāramitā, nor is he able to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or correctly attend to it.

Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family seeking the Buddha-way does not write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, does not receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or correctly attend to it, and is neither protected by the profound *prajñāpāramitā* nor even protected by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), such a person likewise does not practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as taught, nor do they practice the knowledge of all modes as taught.
Such a person may fall into one of two stages: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha. Why is this?

It is because these sons or daughters of good family do not write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they read, recite, explain, or correctly attend to it; such persons are neither protected by the profound *prajñāpāramitā* nor do they practice according to its teaching.
For this reason, these sons and daughters of good family shall fall into one of two stages.
Chapter 51: The Parable The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Fifty-one: The Parable The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Subhūti, it is as if a ship were wrecked in the great ocean. If the people on board do not take hold of wood, nor take hold of vessels, nor take hold of a life-preserver, nor take hold of a corpse—Subhūti!”
You should know that such a person will not reach the other shore, but will perish by drowning in the sea. Subhūti, if the boat is wrecked,

those among them who take hold of wood, or take hold of a vessel, a float, or a corpse— know that these people will ultimately not drown, but will arrive safely and without hindrance at the other shore.
Subhūti! It is the same for sons and daughters of good family who seek the path of the Buddha.

If they possess only faith and delight, yet do not rely on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and neither write it down, read it, recite it, nor correctly attend to it; if they do not rely on the *dhyānapāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, or *dānapāramitā*, and neither write them down, read them, recite them, nor correctly attend to them; and so on, up to not relying on the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience), and neither writing it down, reading it, reciting it, nor correctly attending to it.

Subhūti! You should know that such a son of good family will suffer a decline midway; before reaching all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), this person will attain realization at the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family seeking the Buddha-way who, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, possess faith and patience, a pure mind and a profound mind, aspiration and understanding, renunciation and diligence.
These persons rely on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, copying, upholding, reading, reciting, explaining, and correctly reflecting upon it.

For the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these sons and daughters of good family possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a deep mind, aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence; they are protected by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and even protected by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Because they are protected by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and even protected by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), they will never suffer decline or exhaustion along the way; they will transcend the stages of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*, purify buddha-fields, bring sentient beings to maturity, and shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! It is as if a man or a woman were to take water in an unbaked clay jar; you should know that this jar will soon rot and break. Why is this?
Because this jar has not yet been fired, it returns to earth.

In the same way, Subhūti, although a son of good family or a daughter of good family may have set their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and may possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a profound mind, aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence; yet, if they are not protected by the power of skillful means of the *prajñā-pāramitā*, nor protected by the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, and *dāna-pāramitā*; nor protected by the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); nor protected by the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); nor protected by the ten powers of a Buddha (*buddha-bala*) up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Subhūti! You should know that such a person will suffer decline midway and fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti!
For example, if a man or a woman takes a well-baked jar to fetch water from a river, a well, a pond, or a spring, you should know that this jar will hold the water securely and safely.
Why is that? Because this jar has reached maturity. Thus it is, Subhūti!

"Good sons and good daughters who seek anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi possess various forms of faith and patience, a pure mind and a profound mind, as well as aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence. Because they are protected by the power of skillful means of the prajñā-pāramitā, and because they are protected by dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, dāna, and even up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), Subhūti!"

You should know that such a person does not suffer decline midway; they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, are able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Subhūti! It is as if, for example, on the shore of the great ocean, one were to place goods and wealth upon a ship that has not yet been prepared or repaired. Subhūti!"

You should know that this ship was wrecked midway and sank; the people, the ship, and the goods were each left in a different place. Because these merchants lacked the power of skillful means, they lost their precious treasures.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Although these sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way possess the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and have faith, patience, a pure mind, a profound mind, aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence, because they are not protected by the power of skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth, because they are not protected by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), you should know that such persons will decline midway and lose their great treasure.
The great treasure is what is called the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Wastage is falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Subhūti!

It is, for example, like a person who, possessing wisdom and skillful means, repairs a large ship by the seashore, then pushes it into the water, loads it with goods and wealth, boards it, and departs.
"You should know that this ship will not sink or be destroyed midway; it will certainly reach its destination in safety.

In the same way, Subhūti, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, possesses faith, patience, a pure mind, a profound mind, aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence; and because they are protected by the power of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) of the prajñā-pāramitā, and protected by dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, dāna, and even up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), you should know that such a bodhisattva will attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi and will not fall midway into the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."

“Subhūti! Suppose there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, aged and with matured faculties, who was further afflicted by wind-disorders, cold-disorders, heat-disorders, or various combined disorders.”
"Subhūti, what do you think? Would this person be able to rise from his bed? Subhūti replied:
"No," [the interlocutor] replied. The Buddha said:
"There might be some among these people who are able to rise; how so?"
Subhūti said: "Although this person is able to rise, they cannot travel far—whether ten li or twenty li—because of their old age and illness."

“Thus it is, Subhūti! Although a son of good family or a daughter of good family may have set their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a profound mind, aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence, if they are not protected by the power of skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth, until they are not protected by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), you should know that such a person will fall midway into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.”
Why is this? Because they are not protected by the power of skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Subhūti!
Suppose there were an old man, one hundred and twenty years of age, whose faculties were matured by his advanced years, and who was further afflicted by wind, cold, heat, or various other diseases.
If this man wished to rise and walk, and two strong men each supported one of his armpits, saying to the old man:
"Do not be distressed; go wherever you wish, for we two shall never abandon you."

"In this way, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, possesses faith, patience, a pure mind, a profound mind, aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence; and if they are protected by the power of skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and even protected by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), you should know that such a person will not fall midway into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but will be able to reach that place, namely, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, the Buddha again praised Subhūti, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
It is well that you have asked the Buddha about this matter for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Subhūti,

if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who seek the path of the Buddha, from the time they first resolve their minds until now, they practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom with a mind of "I" and "mine."
When these good sons and good daughters practice giving, they form this thought:
"I am the donor; I give to this person; I give this object."
"I observe the precepts; I cultivate patience; I exert diligence; I enter meditative concentration; I cultivate wisdom.
Thus, these good sons and good daughters conceive thoughts such as: "There is this giving; this is my giving," and so on, up to: "There is this wisdom; this is my wisdom."
Why is this? Within the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), there is no such discrimination; being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of giving.

Within the perfections of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), patience (kṣāntipāramitā), diligence (vīryapāramitā), meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there is likewise no such discrimination.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā* is the transcendence of both this shore and the other shore.

Such a person does not know this shore and does not know the other shore; because they are not protected by the *dānapāramitā* up to and including the *sarvākārajñatā*, they fall into the stage of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha and cannot reach *sarvajñā*.
Subhūti! What is it for a person seeking the path of Buddhahood to lack skillful means? Subhūti!

When a person seeking the path of the Buddha, from the time they first resolve their mind [on enlightenment], practices giving, maintains precepts, practices patience, exerts diligence, cultivates meditative concentration, and develops wisdom without skillful means.
This person forms such a thought:
"I am practicing giving; I give to this person, giving with these things.
I maintain the precepts, cultivate patience, exert diligence, enter meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom—thus I cultivate wisdom."
"This person thinks, 'I have this gift,' and 'This is my gift,' and because of this gift, he exalts himself.
He thinks, 'I have this precept,' and 'This is my precept,' and because of this precept, he exalts himself."
One thinks, "I have this patience; this is my patience," and thus exalts oneself because of this patience.
One thinks, "I have this diligence; this is my diligence," and thus exalts oneself because of this diligence.
One thinks, "I possess this meditative concentration; this is my meditative concentration," and thus exalts oneself on account of that concentration.
One thinks, "I possess this wisdom; this is my wisdom," and thus exalts oneself on account of that wisdom.

Why is this? Within the *dānapāramitā*, there is no such discrimination; being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the *dānapāramitā*. Being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the *śīlapāramitā*;

being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the *kṣāntipāramitā*; being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the *vīryapāramitā*; being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the *dhyānapāramitā*; and being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā there is no such recollection or discrimination.

These sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way do not know this shore, nor do they know the other shore. Such persons are not protected by the dānapāramitā; they are not protected by the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, or prajñāpāramitā; and because they are not protected even by the sarvākārajñatā, they may fall into the path of the śrāvaka or fall into the path of the pratyekabuddha, and are unable to attain sarvajñā.

Thus it is, Subhūti! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not protected by the power of skillful means in the perfection of wisdom, they may fall to the level of a śrāvaka or fall to the level of a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being protected by the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), does not fall into the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

Subhūti! From the very beginning, a bodhisattva practices giving through the power of skillful means, giving with a mind free from the notions of self and what belongs to self, and so on, up to cultivating wisdom with a mind free from the notions of self and what belongs to self.
This person does not form such thoughts as:
"I have this gift; this is my gift. They do not exalt themselves on account of this gift, and it is the same even up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This bodhisattva does not think:
"I am practicing giving," nor does he think:
"I give to this person; I give using these things.
He does not think:
"I uphold the precepts; I possess these precepts."
He does not think:
"I am practicing patience; I possess this patience.
He does not think:
"I am diligent; I possess this diligence.
He does not think:
"I am in meditative concentration; I possess this meditative concentration."
He does not think:
"I cultivate wisdom; I possess this wisdom. Why is that?
Within this perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), there is no such discrimination; being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of giving.

Being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*); being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*); being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*); being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*); being free from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Why is this? Because within this *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no such recollection or conceptual discrimination.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows this shore and knows the other shore. Because this person is protected by the *dānapāramitā*, protected by the *śīlapāramitā*, protected by the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *dhyānapāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā*, and even protected by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but attain *sarvajñā*.

In this way, Subhūti, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are protected by the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Chapter 52: On Knowledge. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Fifty-Two: On Knowledge. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

How should a newly initiated bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a newly initiated bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to study the perfection of wisdom, as well as the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, he should first draw near to and make offerings to a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who is able to expound this profound perfection of wisdom.”
This person gives this instruction:
"O son of good family!
Whatever giving you perform, dedicate it all toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Good son! All precept-keeping, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are entirely dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Do not regard form as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; do not regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Do not regard the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; do not regard the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Do not regard anything from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Do not regard the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
do not regard the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, or the five supernormal powers as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
do not regard the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? Because by not grasping at form, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; by not grasping at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and by not grasping at the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Without grasping at anything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one then attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! When practicing this profound prajñāpāramitā, do not crave form. Why is that?"
"Good son! This form is not something to be craved.
Do not crave feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not objects of craving. Good son!
Do not crave the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom;
do not crave inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
do not crave the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Do not covet the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless absorptions, or the five supernormal powers;
do not covet the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Why is this? Because omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) is not something to be craved.
Son of good family!
Do not covet the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; do not covet the path of the pratyekabuddha; do not covet the stage of the bodhisattva; do not covet anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not something to be craved. Why is that so?
"Because all dharmas are empty by nature.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform what is difficult: they seek anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi within all phenomena that are empty of intrinsic nature, desiring to attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform what is difficult: they seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within all dharmas that are empty of intrinsic nature, desiring to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! It is for the sake of bringing peace and security to the world that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;

it is for the sake of bringing happiness to the world, for the sake of rescuing the world, for the sake of being a refuge for the world, for the sake of being a place of reliance for the world, for the sake of being an island for the world, for the sake of being the ultimate path for the world, for the sake of being a guide for the world, and for the sake of being a destination for the world, that they resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolve their mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of bringing peace and security to the world?

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they pull sentient beings from the six realms of existence and establish them on the shore of fearlessness, the state of nirvāṇa.
Subhūti! It is for the sake of bringing peace and security to the world that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of bringing happiness to the world, resolve their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they uproot the various sorrows, sufferings, griefs, and anxieties of sentient beings, and establish them on the shore of fearlessness, in the state of nirvāṇa.
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the mind set on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of bringing happiness to the world.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the mind set on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of rescuing the world?

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they rescue sentient beings from the various sufferings within birth and death, and they also preach the Dharma for the sake of severing these sufferings.
Sentient beings, hearing the Dharma, gradually attain liberation through the three vehicles. Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of rescuing the world, gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolve their mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of being a refuge for the world?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they uproot sentient beings from the states of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, sorrow, and despair, and establish them on the shore of fearlessness, in the state of *nirvāṇa*.
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves their mind on unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment for the sake of being a refuge for the world.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolve their mind on unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment for the sake of being a place of reliance for the world?
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, they teach all dharmas to sentient beings as being without a basis.
Subhūti! It is for the sake of being a refuge for the world that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it that all dharmas have no place of reliance?”
The Buddha said:
"That form does not continue is itself the non-arising of form; that form does not arise is itself the non-extinction of form; that form does not extinguish is itself the absence of a basis for form.
This is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even up to all-knowledge."
Subhūti! It is for the sake of being a refuge for the world that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolve their mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of being the ultimate path for the world? Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings in this way:

"The ultimate characteristic of form is not form; the ultimate characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), are not all-knowledge."
"Subhūti! Just as the characteristic of ultimate reality is, so too are the characteristics of all phenomena. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
