If the characteristics of all dharmas are identical to their ultimate characteristics, how is it that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Within the ultimate characteristic of form (*rūpa*), there is no discrimination; within the ultimate characteristics of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is no discrimination; and so on, up to the ultimate characteristic of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is no discrimination—namely, that "this is form," "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," and so on, up to "this is all-knowledge."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!

Within the ultimate characteristic of form there is no discrimination; within the ultimate characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the knowledge of all modes, there is no discrimination—namely, that ‘this is form’ up to and including ‘this is the knowledge of all modes.’”
Subhūti! This is a difficult task for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: to contemplate the mark of the cessation of all dharmas in this way, yet their mind neither sinks nor retreats. Why is that?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms this thought:
"I should understand these profound dharmas in this way, so as to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Such a subtle and wondrous Dharma of quiescent extinction should be preached for the sake of sentient beings.
This is how a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, for the sake of the ultimate path of the world, resolves their mind upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolve their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of being an island for the world?
Subhūti, it is like this:
for example, when the waters on all four sides of a river, a stream, or the great ocean are cut off, that is called an island.

Subhūti! Form is likewise severed at its prior and posterior limits; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are severed at their prior and posterior limits; even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is severed at its prior and posterior limits.
Because the past and future limits are severed, all dharmas are also severed. Subhūti!

Because all these dharmas have their past and future limits severed, they are quiescent extinction; they are the wondrous jewel, namely emptiness, non-apprehension, the exhaustion of craving, the remainderless, the departure from desire, and nirvāṇa.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma of cessation for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of being an island for the world.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of being a guide for the world?

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he teaches sentient beings that form is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure; he teaches that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure. He teaches that the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure. He teaches that the fruit of a srotāpanna, up to the fruit of an arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure. He teaches that the ten powers of a buddha, up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure.
Subhūti! It is for the sake of being a guide for the world that a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves their mind upon anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi.
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of the world’s destiny?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he teaches sentient beings that form (*rūpa*) has the destiny of emptiness; he teaches that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) have the destiny of emptiness; and so on, up to teaching that all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) has the destiny of emptiness."
For the sake of sentient beings, he teaches that form is neither a destination nor a non-destination.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of this form is emptiness; it is neither a destination nor a non-destination.
It is said that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither going nor not going.
Why is this? Because these—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are characterized by emptiness; they are neither going nor not going.
Even up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), it neither approaches nor departs. Why is this?
Because the mark of emptiness of all-knowledge neither approaches nor departs.
Thus it is, Subhūti! For the sake of the world’s welfare, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? All dharmas tend toward emptiness; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is this?
Because in space, going and not-going cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward signlessness; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because within the signless, neither "going" nor "not going" can be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward non-action; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because within non-action, neither "tending" nor "not tending" can be apprehended.
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward non-arising; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is that?
Because within non-arising, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward non-existence, being neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because within that which is non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither going nor not going cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward the dream; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why? Because within a dream, neither "tending" nor "not tending" can be apprehended.
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward illusion, toward echoes, toward shadows, and toward transformations; they do not transcend these tendencies. Why is this?
Because within these transformations and so forth, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward the immeasurable and boundless; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because within the immeasurable and boundless, neither coming nor going can be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward neither giving nor taking; this tendency does not transcend [the nature of reality]. Why is this?
Because within neither-giving-nor-taking, both "tendency" and "non-tendency" are unapprehendable.
Subhūti! All things do not enter nor exit, are neither joined nor dispersed, and are neither attached to nor severed; this is the way that does not transcend. Why is this?
Because neither attachment nor abandonment can be apprehended within the middle, nor going nor not-going, Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward the self, sentient beings, life-span, persons, those who cause arising, those who cause action, agents, knowers, and seers; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because from "self" up to "knower" and "seer," these are ultimately unfindable; how, then, could there be going or not going? Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward permanence; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Since permanence is ultimately unattainable, how could there be any tending or non-tending?
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward bliss, purity, and self; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is that?
Pleasure, purity, and self are ultimately unobtainable; how, then, could there be going or not going?
Subhūti, all dharmas tend toward impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self are ultimately unapprehendable; how, then, could there be going or not going? Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward the matter of desire; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because the matter of desire is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be tending or not tending?
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward the matter of hatred, the matter of delusion, and the matter of views; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is that?
The objects of anger, the objects of delusion, and the objects of views are ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be going or not-going?
Subhūti, all dharmas go toward suchness, and they do not transcend this going.
Why is this? Because, Subhūti, in suchness there is neither coming nor going. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the inconceivable nature;
they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because within the nature of dharmas, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature, there is neither coming nor going.
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward equality; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is that?
Because within equality, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward the mark of immovability; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because within the mark of immovability, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward form; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because form is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be tending or not tending?
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is that?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately unapprehendable; how, then, could there be going or not going?
It is the same for the twelve bases and the eighteen elements, Subhūti.
All dharmas tend toward the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), yet they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because giving is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be a tendency or a non-tendency?
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward the śīlapāramitā; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is that?
Since ethical discipline (*śīla*) is ultimately unattainable, how could there be going or not going?
Subhūti, all dharmas go toward the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*); they do not transcend this going.
Why is this? Because patience (kṣānti) is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be going or not going? Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward the *vīrya-pāramitā*; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why? Because *vīrya* is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be tending or not tending?
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward the dhyāna-pāramitā; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is this?
Since dhyāna is ultimately unattainable, how could there be going or not going?
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward the prajñāpāramitā; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because the perfection of wisdom is ultimately unattainable, how could there be going or not going? Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward internal emptiness; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is this?
Because internal emptiness is ultimately unattainable, how could there be any tending or non-tending?
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward external emptiness; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is that?
Since external emptiness is ultimately unattainable, how could there be going or not going?
Subhūti, all dharmas tend toward internal and external emptiness; they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) is ultimately unattainable, how could there be going or not going?
This applies even to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*), which go toward the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); they do not transcend this going.
Why is this? Because the emptiness of non-existence and existence is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be going or not-going? Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, up to the eightfold noble path;
they do not transcend this tendency.
Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, are ultimately unobtainable; how, then, could there be a tending or a non-tending?
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including all-knowledge; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is that?
Subhūti, because within the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) neither "approaching" nor "not approaching" can be apprehended,

all dharmas approach the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), the fruit of an arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha; they do not transcend this approach.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because within the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the path of a pratyekabuddha, neither "progressing" nor "not progressing" can be apprehended. Subhūti!
All dharmas tend toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is this?
Because within anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, neither "tending" nor "not tending" can be apprehended.
Subhūti! All dharmas tend toward the stage of a srotāpanna up to that of a Buddha; they do not transcend this tendency. Why is this?
“Because, from the stage of a stream-enterer up to that of a Buddha, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Who among them will be able to believe and understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā*? The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have long practiced the six *pāramitās* in the presence of various Buddhas; whose roots of goodness are fully matured; who have made offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; and who have associated with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Such persons as these will be able to believe and understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā*."

"Subhūti, when one has severed and abandoned the nature and characteristics of desire, hatred, and delusion, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is then able to believe in and understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
Chapter 53: On the Course of Wisdom. From the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Fifty-Three, "On the Course of Wisdom. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"To where will these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* proceed?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* shall proceed toward all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to advance toward all-knowledge does so because they cultivate the perfection of wisdom as a place of refuge for all sentient beings.”
World-Honored One!
To cultivate the perfection of wisdom is to cultivate all dharmas.
World-Honored One!
"To practice nothing is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice neither acceptance nor destruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Through the destruction of what dharma is the perfection of wisdom cultivated as a cultivation of destruction?
“World-Honored One!
Through the destruction of form, the perfection of wisdom is cultivated as a cultivation of destruction;”

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the twelve bases and the eighteen elements, are subject to disintegration, the perfection of wisdom is cultivated as a practice of disintegration;
because the self, up to the knower and the seer, are subject to disintegration, the perfection of wisdom is cultivated as a practice of disintegration.
“World-Honored One!
Because the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is subject to destruction, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is a cultivation of destruction;
and so on, up to: because the perfection of wisdom is subject to destruction, the perfection of wisdom is a cultivation of destruction.”

Because internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the fruit of stream-entry up to all-knowledge are subject to destruction, the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of destruction.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
Because form is subject to destruction, the perfection of wisdom is a cultivation of destruction;
and so on, up to: because all-knowledge is subject to destruction, the perfection of wisdom is a cultivation of destruction.
At that time, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"Within this profound Prajñāpāramitā, one should verify and know the irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become attached to this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that these are the marks of an *avaivartika*.

If they do not become attached to the *dhyānapāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, and do not become attached to the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one should know that they are an *avaivartika*.

When an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not take the words of others as authoritative, nor do they act according to the instructions of others.
An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva is not led astray by thoughts of desire, anger, or delusion.
Furthermore, if an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva does not distance themselves from the six pāramitās.

If an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is not startled, does not sink into despondency, is not terrified, does not fear, and has no regrets, but instead listens with joy, receives, upholds, recites, correctly contemplates, and practices according to the teaching.

Subhūti! You should know that this bodhisattva has already in previous lives inquired about these matters within this profound Prajñāpāramitā, and has already received, upheld, recited, explained, and correctly recollected it.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess great majestic power; upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds are not startled, not terrified, not afraid, not submerged, and have no regrets; they joyfully delight in hearing it, receiving and upholding it, reciting it, and correctly contemplating it.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, is not startled, not terrified, and even maintains right mindfulness;”
“World-Honored One!
How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva practice this prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
“Conforming to the mind of omniscience, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'a mind that accords with all-knowledge,' such that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way?
The Buddha said,
"To accord with emptiness is for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice the profound perfection of wisdom."

By conforming to the signless, the unconditioned, the non-existent, and that which is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner.

"To practice in accordance with [the understanding that things are like] a dream, an illusion, a mirage, an echo, and a transformation is to practice the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Buddha,

"The Buddha has taught that practicing in accordance with emptiness, and so forth, up to practicing in accordance with being like a dream and like an illusion, is to practice the perfection of wisdom."
“World-Honored One!
What dharma does this bodhisattva mahāsattva practice—whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in form, does not course in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to not coursing in all-knowledge. Why is this?

This is the sphere of practice of the bodhisattva: it is a dharma that is unconditioned and indestructible; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it has no place of abiding; this dharma is incalculable and immeasurable.

If it is incalculable and immeasurable, this dharma cannot be apprehended; it cannot be apprehended by means of form, nor can it be apprehended even by means of the knowledge of all modes. Why is this?
Form is itself omniscience (*sarvajñā*), and omniscience is itself form.
This extends up to: all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is itself omniscience, and omniscience is itself all-knowledge.
If the suchness of form, up to and including the suchness of all-knowledge, are all one suchness, without duality or distinction;
if the suchness of form and the suchness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) are one suchness, without duality or distinction.
"Even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is likewise so.

In the eleventh year of the Tianjian era, the year of Renchen, the Imperial Commissioner, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Commandant, General of the South for the Various Armies of Jiangzhou, Grand Master with the Rank of the State Councilor, Governor of Jiangzhou, Prince Jian'an, Xiao Wei, reverently commissioned the production and circulation of one thousand scrolls of various scriptures. May the divine majesty behold the six realms; may his pure legacy [be preserved]; may the numinous spirits provide assistance; may all auspicious blessings arrive; may his profound faith be firm and clear; may his great compassion increase; may he illuminate the profound principles within the basket of teachings and attain the essence of the Great Image.

With a mind that relinquishes body, life, and wealth, they uphold the correct cultivation of the bodhisattva path; single-mindedly directed toward the One Vehicle, they encompass all sentient beings and guide their physical forms [to liberation], [revealing] the true nature of reality so that all may rest together at the site of enlightenment.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Fifty-Four: On Greatness (Mahatvavarga). [In the Dan edition: Chapter on the Characteristics of Greatness (Mahatvalakṣaṇavarga).]

At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the devaputras of the form realm took celestial powdered sandalwood incense and celestial blue lotuses, red lotuses, pink lotuses, and white lotuses, scattering them from afar over the Buddha. They approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas is profound, difficult to see and difficult to understand, and cannot be known through discursive thought.
It is subtle and tranquil; it can be known by those with wisdom, but it is something that the entire world cannot believe.
Why is this? Because it is thus taught in this profound Prajñāpāramitā:
"Form is itself omniscience (sarvajñatā), and omniscience is itself form."
Even so, all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is itself omniscience (sarvajñatā), and omniscience is itself all-knowledge.
The suchness of form and the suchness of omniscience are one single suchness; they are non-dual and without distinction.
"Even up to the suchness of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the suchness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they are a single suchness, without duality and without distinction.
The Buddha told the devaputras of the desire and form realms: "So it is, so it is!"
O sons of the gods!
Form is itself omniscience (sarvajñā), and omniscience is itself form.
This extends even to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñā), which is itself omniscience, and omniscience is itself the knowledge of all modes.
The suchness of form, up to and including the suchness of all-knowledge, is a single suchness, without duality or distinction.
O sons of the gods!
For this reason, when the Buddha first attained the Way, his mind delighted in silence and did not delight in preaching the Dharma.
Why is this? Because this Dharma of the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is profound, difficult to see and difficult to understand, and cannot be known through discursive thought.
This subtle and tranquil extinction can be known by the wise, but it cannot be believed by anyone in the world.

Why is this? In *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is no one who attains, no place of attainment, and no time of attainment; this is called the profound characteristic of all phenomena, namely, that there are no two distinct dharmas.
"O sons of the gods!
Because space is profound, this Dharma is profound.
Because it is profound, this Dharma is profound."

Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profoundly deep, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is profoundly deep, and because they are inconceivable and boundlessly profound, this Dharma is profound.
Because it is profoundly deep in being neither coming nor going, this Dharma is profound.
Because it is profound—being neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither known nor attained—this Dharma is profound.
O sons of the gods!
Because I am profound, even unto the knower and the seer being profound, this Dharma is profound.
O sons of the gods!
Because form is profound, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are profound, this Dharma is profound.
Because the perfection of giving is profound, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, this Dharma is profound.
Because internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence is profound, this dharma is profound.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) are profound, this dharma is profound.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma that has been taught cannot be believed by anyone in the entire world.”
World-Honored One!
This profound Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping form, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning form.

It is not taught for the sake of grasping feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It is not taught for the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning the fruit of stream-entry.
This extends even to not being taught for the sake of attaining all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor for the sake of abandoning all-knowledge.

It is said that all worldly beings experience and cling to conditioned formations, namely: "Form is my self, it belongs to my self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are my self, they belong to my self," and so on, up to: "The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are my self, they belong to my self."
"The fruit of the stream-enterer is my self, it is mine; even up to all-knowledge is my self, it is mine.
The Buddha told the devaputras: "So it is, so it is!"
O sons of the gods!

This Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping form, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning form; and so on, up to: it is not taught for the sake of grasping all-knowledge, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning all-knowledge.
"O sons of the gods!

If a bodhisattva practices for the sake of grasping form, and so on, up to practicing for the sake of grasping all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), that bodhisattva cannot cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); cannot cultivate the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), or the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*); cannot cultivate the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*); and so on, up to being unable to cultivate all-knowledge."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma accords with all dharmas.”
"What is this dharma that accords with all dharmas?
"This dharma accords with the prajñāpāramitā, and so on, up to and including the dānapāramitā."
This dharma accords with inner emptiness, and so on, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
This dharma accords with the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to and including all-knowledge.
This Dharma is unimpeded; it is not impeded by form, nor is it impeded by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to being unimpeded by the knowledge of all modes.
O sons of the gods!

This dharma is called the characteristic of non-obstruction because it is equal to space; because it is the suchness, the dharma-nature, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature; and because it is emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and so forth.

This dharma has the characteristic of non-arising, because the non-arising of form cannot be apprehended; because the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to the non-arising of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) which cannot be apprehended.

This dharma has no location, because a location for form cannot be apprehended, because locations for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, and so on, up to the point that a location for all-knowledge cannot be apprehended.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Subhūti is a son of the Buddha; he was born from the Buddha’s own mouth.”
"Why is this? Because all that Subhūti has spoken accords with emptiness.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the devaputras:
"You have said: 'Subhūti is a son of the Buddha; he was born after the Buddha.
In what way is he born after the Buddha?"
O sons of the gods!
Because he accords with the mark of reality (dharmatā), Subhūti is born after the Buddha. Why is this?
The Tathāgata’s mark of suchness neither comes nor goes; Subhūti’s mark of suchness likewise neither comes nor goes. Therefore, Subhūti is born after the Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti has been born after the Buddha from the very beginning.
Why is this? The suchness of the Tathāgata is precisely the suchness of all dharmas; the suchness of all dharmas is precisely the suchness of the Tathāgata.
Within this suchness, there is also no suchness. For this reason, Subhūti is said to be "born after the Buddha."
Furthermore, just as the Tathāgata has the characteristic of being eternally abiding, so too does the *tathatā* (suchness) of Subhūti have the characteristic of being eternally abiding.
There is no difference and no distinction between the *tathatā*-characteristic of the Tathāgata; the *tathatā*-characteristic of Subhūti is likewise without difference and without distinction.
Therefore, Subhūti is born after the Buddha.
The Tathāgata’s suchness has no place of obstruction, and the suchness of all dharmas likewise has no place of obstruction.
This suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of all dharmas are a single suchness; they are non-dual and without distinction.

This mark of suchness is without fabrication and never fails to be as it is; therefore, this mark of suchness is a single suchness, without duality or distinction. For this reason, Subhūti is said to be born after the Buddha.

The Tathāgata’s mark of suchness is, in all places, without thought and without distinction; Subhūti, the mark of suchness is likewise thus: it is in all places without thought and without distinction.
The Tathāgata’s mark of suchness is neither different nor distinct and cannot be apprehended; Subhūti, the mark of suchness is also like this.
For this reason, Subhūti is said to be born after the Buddha.

The Tathāgata’s suchness does not depart from the suchness of all dharmas; that suchness never fails to be suchness. Therefore, because Subhūti’s suchness is not different [from it], he is said to be born after the Buddha, yet there is nothing to which he conforms.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s mark of suchness does not belong to the past, the future, or the present; the mark of suchness of all dharmas likewise does not belong to the past, the future, or the present. For this reason, Subhūti is said to be born after the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s suchness does not exist within the suchness of the past, nor does the suchness of the past exist within the Tathāgata’s suchness.
The Tathāgata’s suchness does not exist within the suchness of the future, nor does the suchness of the future exist within the Tathāgata’s suchness.
The suchness of the Tathāgata does not exist within the suchness of the present, and the suchness of the present does not exist within the suchness of the Tathāgata.
The suchness of the past, future, and present, and the suchness of the Tathāgata, are a single suchness; they are non-dual and without distinction.

The suchness of form is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the suchness of the Tathāgata. This suchness of form, the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and the suchness of the Tathāgata are a single suchness, without duality and without distinction.
The suchness of the self, up to the suchness of the knower and the seer, and the suchness of the Tathāgata, are a single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

The suchness of the perfection of giving, up to the suchness of the perfection of wisdom; the suchness of internal emptiness, up to the suchness of the emptiness of non-existence and existence; the suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the suchness of all-knowledge, and the suchness of the Tathāgata—these are a single suchness, without duality and without distinction.
“Subhūti! Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have attained this Suchness (tathatā), they are called Tathāgatas.
When this Chapter on the Characteristics of Suchness was being spoken, the great earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

It surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east; it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the four sides; it surged at the four sides and subsided in the center.

At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the devaputras of the form realm scattered celestial powdered sandalwood incense over the Buddha and over Subhūti, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is unprecedented!
“World-Honored One!
Subhūti has been born after the Tathāgata, following the Buddha.
Subhūti then spoke again to the devaputras, saying:
“O sons of the gods!
Subhūti does not follow the Buddha’s birth through form, nor does he follow the Buddha’s birth through the suchness of form;
he does not follow the Buddha’s birth apart from form, nor does he follow the Buddha’s birth apart from the suchness of form.”

Subhūti does not follow the Buddha’s birth from within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does he follow the Buddha’s birth from within the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

He does not follow the Buddha’s birth apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does he follow the Buddha’s birth apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Nor does he follow the Buddha from within omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor does he follow the Buddha from within the suchness (*tathatā*) of omniscience;
nor does he follow the Buddha apart from omniscience, nor does he follow the Buddha apart from the suchness of omniscience.
Subhūti does not follow the Buddha’s birth from within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor does he follow the Buddha’s birth from within the suchness (*tathatā*) of the unconditioned;
yet he does not follow the Buddha’s birth apart from the unconditioned, nor does he follow the Buddha’s birth apart from the suchness of the unconditioned.
"Why is this? Because all these dharmas are non-existent and unobtainable; there is neither that which arises in succession nor any dharma that arises in succession.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This is as it truly is and not false; the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthiti), and the fixed position of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā) are profoundly deep. Within them, form cannot be apprehended, and the suchness of form (rūpatathatā) cannot be apprehended.”
Why is this? Since form (*rūpa*) itself cannot be apprehended, how much less could the suchness (*tathatā*) of form be apprehended?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, nor can the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended.

Why is this? Since feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, how much less can the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended?
Even up to the point that all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, the suchness of all-knowledge cannot be apprehended.
"Why is this? Even all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended; how much less could the suchness (*tathatā*) of all-knowledge be apprehended?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"So it is, so it is! Śāriputra! This is true and not false; the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), and the fixed position of phenomena (dharmasthititā) are profoundly deep. Within this, form (rūpa) cannot be apprehended, and the suchness of form (rūpatathatā) cannot be apprehended."
Why is this? Since even form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, how much less could the suchness (*tathatā*) of form be apprehended?
This extends up to the point that even all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, and the suchness of all-knowledge cannot be apprehended.
"Why is this? Even all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended; how much less can the suchness (*tathatā*) of all-knowledge be apprehended?
When Śāriputra spoke these words regarding the characteristic of suchness, two hundred bhikṣus, through non-attachment to all dharmas, exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*) and attained arhatship.
Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena and being reborn among gods and humans.
Five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because these sixty bodhisattvas did not grasp at any dharmas, their outflows were exhausted, their minds attained liberation, and they became arhats.

"Śāriputra, in previous lives these sixty bodhisattvas encountered five hundred buddhas, drawing near to and making offerings to them. Under the teachings of those five hundred buddhas, they practiced giving, morality, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration; yet, because they lacked the perfection of wisdom and the power of skillful means, they practiced with distinct and divergent characteristics, forming this thought:"
"This is giving, this is morality, this is patience, this is diligence, this is meditative concentration.

Because they lack the perfection of wisdom and the power of skillful means, their practices of giving, morality, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration manifest as distinct and separate characteristics.
Because the practices have distinct characteristics, one cannot be without distinct characteristics.
Because one cannot be without distinct characteristics, one cannot enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Because one cannot enter the stage of a bodhisattva, one attains the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat.

Śāriputra! Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the path—whether it be emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness—if they are far removed from the perfection of wisdom and lack the power of skillful means, they will then realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and take up the vehicle of the śrāvaka.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what reason do those who practice emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet lack the power of skillful means, realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and take up the vehicle of the śrāvaka?”
Do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas also cultivate the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and by virtue of their skillful means, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There are bodhisattvas who distance themselves from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) and cultivate the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; because they lack the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they take up the vehicle of the śrāvaka."

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who do not distance themselves from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), yet cultivate the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; by virtue of their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they enter the stage of a bodhisattva and attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Śāriputra! It is as if there were a bird, a hundred yojanas tall, or perhaps two or three hundred yojanas tall, yet lacking wings, which would cast itself down from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven toward Jambudvīpa.
"Śāriputra, what do you think? Would this bird, while midway, think to itself:
'I wish to return to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above'?"
“Can they be recovered? “They cannot, World-Honored One. “Śāriputra!”
This bird further made this vow:
"Upon reaching Jambudvīpa, I wish that my body shall be neither pained nor afflicted. Śāriputra!
"What do you think? Would that bird suffer pain or distress?
Śāriputra replied, "It would not, World-Honored One."
When this bird reaches the ground, it will experience pain, distress, death, or suffering equal to death. Why is this,
World-Honored One?
“Śāriputra, it is because this bird’s body is large but it has no wings. Śāriputra,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this.”

Although one may practice giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River, and though one may initiate great undertakings and give rise to the great mind, making immeasurable vows for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, [this alone is not sufficient].
Because this bodhisattva is far removed from the power of skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā, they may fall into the state of an arhat or fall into the path of a pratyekabuddha. Why is this?

If this bodhisattva practices giving, morality, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration while remaining far removed from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and because they lack the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they will fall into the stage of a śrāvaka or onto the path of a pratyekabuddha.

Śāriputra! Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva recollects the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and takes up these marks for retention, such a person does not truly know or understand the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas. Rather, having merely heard the sounds of the names "emptiness," "signlessness," and "wishlessness," they take up those names and sounds and dedicate them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates [merit] in this way, they will remain within the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and will be unable to transcend them. Why is this?
Because they lack the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā* while maintaining various roots of goodness and dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Śāriputra!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from the time they first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], do not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) as they practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.

Because they do not distance themselves from the power of skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not grasp at the signs of the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; they do not grasp at the sign of the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor do they grasp at the signs of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
Śāriputra! You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall into the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but proceeds directly to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? Because since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have practiced giving without grasping at signs; they have practiced morality, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration without grasping at signs; and they have [regarded] the morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation of all buddhas of the past, future, and present without grasping at signs.

Śāriputra! This is called the power of a bodhisattva’s skillful means: with a mind free from signs, they practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, up to practicing the knowledge of all modes with a mind free from signs.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not distance himself from the power of skillful means associated with the prajñāpāramitā, one should know that this bodhisattva is close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Why is this? Because from the time this bodhisattva-mahāsattva first resolved on enlightenment, there has been no dharma that can be apprehended—whether it be form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
“World-Honored One!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path but remain far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā* and the power of skillful means, you should know that such persons may or may not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!

All the acts of giving performed by these sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path are characterized by grasping at signs; all their observance of precepts, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration are likewise characterized by grasping at signs.
For this reason, World-Honored One, these sons and daughters of good family are not fixed in their progress toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

For this cause and condition, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should not distance themselves from the power of skillful means (*upāya*) within the *prajñāpāramitā*.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling within the power of skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā, should practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration with a mind that is non-apprehending and signless; even up to cultivating all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) with a mind that is non-apprehending and signless.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain.”
"Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva should know all dharmas, yet these dharmas are also unobtainable.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! O sons of the gods!
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain; I do not apprehend any dharma whatsoever."
Even omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) is unapprehendable;
there is no one who knows, nothing that can be known, and no knower. Why is this?
"Because all dharmas are ultimately pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain.
Yet, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, my mind reflects that this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is easy to attain.
Why is this? There is no one who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any dharma that can be attained.
All dharmas and all characteristics of dharmas are empty; there is no dharma to be attained, and no one capable of attaining it.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are empty.
Furthermore, there is no dharma that can be increased, nor any dharma that can be diminished.

That which is called generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and even the knowledge of all modes—these dharmas are all unobtainable, and there is no one who can obtain them.
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, I believe that Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is easy to attain. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!

Form is empty of the characteristic of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristic of consciousness; and so on, up to all-knowledge, which is empty of the characteristic of all-knowledge. Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If all dharmas are empty like space, space does not form this thought:
'I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"

"If it were easy to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has faith and understanding that all dharmas are empty like space, then why would these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who now seek unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, turn back?"
"Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is not easily attained.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think? Does form regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied, "No."
“Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied, “No.”
“...up to and including the knowledge of all modes— does one ever fall back from unexcelled, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, “No.”
“Is there any dharma apart from form that regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, “No.”
“Is there any dharma apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, “No.”
“Is there any dharma, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), that regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, “No.”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Does the mark of the suchness of form regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Śāriputra replied:

"No. "Does the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the suchness of all-knowledge, ever regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said, “No. [The Buddha asked:
“Apart from the mark of the suchness of form, is there any dharma that regresses from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
Śāriputra said: "No. [The Buddha asked:

"Apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to apart from the suchness of all-knowledge, is there any dharma that regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said, “No. “Śāriputra!
"What do you think? Would one ever fall back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied, "No."

“Does the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the fixed position of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the reality limit (bhūtakoṭi), and the inconceivable nature (acintyadharmatā) ever regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra replied, “No. [The Buddha said,] “Śāriputra!
"What do you think? Apart from suchness, is there any dharma that regresses from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Śāriputra replied, "No."

"Apart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti), the fixed position of phenomena (dharma-vyavasthāna), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and the inconceivable nature (acintyatā), is there any phenomenon that regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said, "No. Subhūti spoke to Śāriputra:
"If all dharmas are ultimately unobtainable, what dharma could regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "According to what Subhūti has said, within this *dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*, there is no bodhisattva who regresses from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor one who does not regress."
The Buddha taught that there are three kinds of seekers of the Way:
the path of the Arhat, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha.
These three are non-differentiated.
"As Subhūti has said, there is only a single bodhisattva-mahāsattva who seeks the Buddha-way.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra,
"One should ask Subhūti whether there is indeed one who belongs to the bodhisattva vehicle."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“Subhūti! Do you wish to say that there is but one vehicle for bodhisattvas?”
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Within the suchness of all dharmas, do you wish for there to be three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the vehicle of the Buddha?"
Śāriputra said, “No. [The Buddha said,] “Śāriputra!”
"Can one distinguish three vehicles within that middle? Śāriputra replied, "No."
“Śāriputra! Does this *tathatā* have one mark, two marks, or three marks? Śāriputra replied:
"No. "Śāriputra, do you perceive even a single bodhisattva within suchness?"
Śāriputra said, “No. [The Buddha continued,] “In this way,
among these four kinds, persons of the three vehicles cannot be found.”
Śāriputra, why do you have this thought:
"This person seeks the vehicle of the śrāvaka;..."
"These are people who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
these are people who seek the vehicle of the buddhas. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas, their mind is not startled, does not sink, does not regret, and does not doubt; this is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva being able to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
"What you have said is entirely through the power of the Buddha. Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing it explained that suchness is without the differentiation of any dharmas, does not become startled, does not become terrified, does not become afraid, does not find it difficult, does not sink in despair, and does not feel regret, you should know that this bodhisattva is able to achieve anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what kind of bodhi is accomplished?”
The Buddha said:
"One accomplishes the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of a Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should they practice?
The Buddha said:
"One should give rise to an impartial mind toward all sentient beings and likewise speak with an impartial mind, without partiality or favoritism.
One should give rise to a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings and likewise speak with a mind of great compassion."
One should maintain a humble attitude toward all sentient beings and speak with a humble mind.
One should give rise to a mind of peace and security toward all sentient beings and speak with a mind of peace and security.
One should give rise to a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings, and one should also speak with a mind free from obstruction.
One should give rise to a mind free from affliction toward all sentient beings, and one should also speak with a mind free from affliction.

One should give rise to a heart of love and respect toward all sentient beings, regarding them as one's father or mother, elder brother or younger brother, sister, son, kinsman, or friend; furthermore, one should address them with a heart of love and respect.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should personally refrain from taking life, instruct others to refrain from taking life, praise the dharma of refraining from taking life, and joyfully extol those who do not take life.
Thus it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi should practice in this manner.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should personally practice the first *dhyāna*, and also teach others to practice the first *dhyāna*, praise the method of practicing the first *dhyāna*, and rejoice in and praise those who practice the first *dhyāna*;
it is the same for the second, third, and fourth *dhyānas*.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should personally practice a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), teach others to practice a mind of loving-kindness, praise the dharma of practicing a mind of loving-kindness, and rejoice in and praise those who practice a mind of loving-kindness; it is the same for the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*),
sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)."

One practices the sphere of infinite space oneself, teaches others to practice the sphere of infinite space, praises the dharma of practicing the sphere of infinite space, and joyfully extols those who practice the sphere of infinite space;
it is the same for the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

He himself fulfills the dāna-pāramitā, and also teaches others to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā; he praises the practice of fulfilling the dāna-pāramitā, and rejoices in praising those who fulfill the dāna-pāramitā.
It is the same for śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, and prajñā-pāramitā.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* personally practices the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), teaches others to practice the emptiness of the internal, praises the dharma of practicing the emptiness of the internal, and joyfully commends those who practice the emptiness of the internal;
this applies likewise up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

One practices the four foundations of mindfulness oneself, teaches others to practice the four foundations of mindfulness, praises the Dharma of practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, and joyfully commends those who practice the four foundations of mindfulness;
this applies likewise up to the eightfold noble path.

He personally cultivates the samādhi of emptiness, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi; he also teaches others to cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he praises the dharmas of cultivating the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and he joyfully commends those who cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

They personally practice the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) and also teach others to practice the eight liberations; they praise the dharma of practicing the eight liberations and rejoice in praising those who practice the eight liberations.

They personally practice the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*) and also teach others to practice the nine successive attainments; they praise the dharma of practicing the nine successive attainments and rejoice in praising those who practice the nine successive attainments.

They themselves fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha and also teach others to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha; they praise the dharma of fulfilling the ten powers of a Buddha and joyfully extol those who fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha.

They themselves practice the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion, and they also teach others to practice the four fearlessnesses up to great loving-kindness and great compassion; they praise the dharma of practicing the four fearlessnesses up to great loving-kindness and great compassion, and joyfully extol those who practice the four fearlessnesses up to great loving-kindness and great compassion.

They personally contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, teach others to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, praise the dharma of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, and joyfully extol those who contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should practice in this way. Furthermore, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should personally know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path; they should also teach others to know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path; they should praise the dharma of knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing its cessation, and cultivating the path; and they should joyfully praise those who know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path.

They themselves give rise to the realization-wisdom of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), yet they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); furthermore, they teach others to be attached to the fruit of stream-entry, praise the dharmas of the fruit of stream-entry, and joyfully extol those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry;
it is the same for the fruits of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship (*arhat*).

He personally realizes the path of knowledge and wisdom of a pratyekabuddha, yet he does not himself realize the path of a pratyekabuddha; he also teaches others to enter the path of a pratyekabuddha, praises the dharma for attaining the path of a pratyekabuddha, and joyfully extols those who have attained the path of a pratyekabuddha.

Having entered the bodhisattva stage themselves, they also teach others to enter the bodhisattva stage; they praise the dharma of entering the bodhisattva stage and joyfully extol those who have entered it.

They themselves purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; they also teach others to purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; they praise the dharmas of purifying Buddha-fields and bringing sentient beings to maturity; and they rejoice in and praise those who purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.

He himself gives rise to the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva, teaches others to give rise to the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva, praises the practice of giving rise to the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva, and joyfully commends those who give rise to the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva.

He himself gives rise to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), teaches others to give rise to all-knowledge, praises the dharma that gives rise to all-knowledge, and joyfully extols those who have given rise to all-knowledge.

He himself severs all fetters, habitual tendencies, and latent proclivities; he also teaches others to sever all fetters, habitual tendencies, and latent proclivities; he praises the dharma of severing all fetters, habitual tendencies, and latent proclivities; and he joyfully extols those who have severed all fetters, habitual tendencies, and latent proclivities.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should practice in this manner. Furthermore, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment should personally accomplish the attainment of longevity, teach others to accomplish the attainment of longevity, praise the method for accomplishing the attainment of longevity, and joyfully praise those who have accomplished the attainment of longevity.

One personally abides in the dwelling of the dharma of accomplishment, teaches others to abide in the dwelling of the dharma of accomplishment, praises the dharma of the dwelling of the dharma of accomplishment, and joyfully commends those who abide in the dwelling of the dharma of accomplishment.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should practice in this way and should likewise train in the power of skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā.

When this bodhisattva trains in this way and practices in this way, they shall attain unimpeded form, attain unimpeded feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and even attain the dwelling in unimpeded phenomena.

Why is this? Because from the very beginning, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not apprehended form, nor have they apprehended feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including the knowledge of all modes.
"Why is this? That which does not grasp form is not form; and so on, up to that which does not grasp all-knowledge is not all-knowledge.
When this "Chapter on the Practice of Bodhisattvas" was being taught, two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Chapter 55: Non-Retrogression From the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Fifty-Five: Non-Retrogression. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"By what conduct, by what category, and by what characteristics can one know that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to know that the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, and the stage of buddhas—these various stages—are non-dual and undifferentiated within the suchness (*tathatā*) of all things, and neither conceives of them nor discriminates between them, then entering into this suchness, upon hearing these matters, they pass directly through them without doubt."
Why is this? Because within suchness there is neither the mark of oneness nor the mark of duality.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not engage in useless speech, but speaks only words that accord with benefit, and does not look upon the long or the short in others.
“Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one knows this to be an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, by what conduct, categories, or characteristics can one know that this is an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to contemplate all dharmas as being without activity, without category, and without characteristics, one should know that such a person is called an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are without activity, without category, and without characteristics, in what dharma does a bodhisattva turn so that it is called ‘non-turning’?”
The Buddha said:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns away from form, and turns away from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is called a bodhisattva who does not turn away. Furthermore, Subhūti!”
The bodhisattva mahāsattva turns within the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), up to and including turning within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);
he turns within inner emptiness (adhyātmaśūnyatā), up to and including turning within the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā);
and he turns within the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), up to and including turning within the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma).
Whether they turn back from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or even turn back from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should know that such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not truly turn back.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Since the nature of form does not exist, in what could such a bodhisattva abide?
"Even up to the point where the nature of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* itself does not exist,
in what would this bodhisattva abide? Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not observe the facial features or speech of non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, nor does he form such thoughts:"
"Among these non-Buddhists—whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—it is impossible for them to truly know or truly see, or to speak of right view.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva does not give rise to doubt, does not cling to attachment to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and does not fall into false views; nor does he seek worldly auspiciousness as a means to purification, nor does he worship other deities with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, music, prostrations, or offerings.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that he is named an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva is never born into a lowly family, nor is he ever born in any of the eight difficult conditions; he never again receives a female body.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly practice the ten paths of wholesome action: they themselves refrain from taking life, do not instruct others to take life, praise the dharma of refraining from taking life, and joyfully praise those who refrain from taking life;
and so on, until they themselves refrain from wrong views, do not instruct others in wrong views, do not praise the dharma of wrong views, and do not joyfully praise those who practice wrong views.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is named an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
Even in their dreams, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not practice the ten unwholesome paths of action.
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that they are called irreversible Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving for the benefit of all sentient beings; and so on,
up to practicing the perfection of wisdom for the benefit of all sentient beings."
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is named an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
All the dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva receives, reads, recites, explains, and correctly contemplates—namely, from the sūtras up to the upadeśas.
When this bodhisattva practices the gift of Dharma, they form this thought:
"By means of these causes and conditions of the gift of Dharma, may the vows of all sentient beings be fulfilled.
Through the merit of this gift of Dharma, I share it with all sentient beings and dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is named an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!”
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva has no doubt and no regret regarding the profound Dharma. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!”
“By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva have no doubt and no regret regarding the profound Dharma?
The Buddha said:

“This irreversible bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma as a basis for giving rise to doubt—whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment; he perceives no such dharma that could serve as a basis for doubt or regret.”
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that he is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The physical, verbal, and mental actions of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are supple.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the compassionate actions of body, speech, and mind. Subhūti!"
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell together with the five hindrances: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. Subhūti!
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva has no attachment whatsoever in any place.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters or exits, goes or comes, sits or lies down, walks or stands, he is constantly mindful with a single mind.

Whether entering or exiting, going or coming, sitting or lying down, walking or standing, lifting or lowering his feet, he moves with stability and deliberation, always mindful with a single mind, looking at the ground as he walks."
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
Subhūti, the clothing and bedding used by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are not loathsome or foul to others; they delight in purity and cleanliness, and suffer little from illness. Subhūti!
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

In the bodies of ordinary persons, there are eighty thousand families of worms that consume their flesh; however, in the body of an Avaivartika Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, these worms do not exist. Why is this?
The merit of this bodhisattva transcends the world; for this reason, this bodhisattva has no such intestinal worms.
As the merit of this bodhisattva increases, they attain purity of body and purity of mind in accordance with that merit.
"Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, you should know that he is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain purity of body and purity of mind?
The Buddha said:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in accordance with the increase of their acquired roots of goodness, eliminate mental crookedness and mental perversity. Subhūti,
this is called the purity of body and the purity of mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
Because of this purity of body and mind, he is able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the rank of the bodhisattvas.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, you should know that such a person is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not prize gain and offerings; although he practices the twelve dhūtas, he does not prize the dharma of the araṇya, nor even the dharma of possessing only the three robes."
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never give rise to a mind of stinginess or greed; they do not give rise to a mind that breaks the precepts, a mind of agitation through anger, a mind of indolence, a mind of distraction, a mind of delusion, or a mind of jealousy.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is named an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mind abides immovably and his wisdom penetrates deeply; with single-minded attention, he listens to and receives the Dharma from which he hears it, and all worldly affairs are brought into accord with the prajñāpāramitā.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any worldly affairs that do not enter into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); he perceives all such things as being in union with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
For these reasons, Subhūti, this is called an irreversible bodhisattva and the marks of irreversibility. Furthermore, Subhūti:

If a wicked Māra, before an avaivartika bodhisattva, conjures up eight great hells, and within each of these hells there are ten trillion bodhisattvas, all of whom are being burned and boiled, undergoing various bitter, acrid, and poisonous sufferings.
He said to the bodhisattva:
"All these bodhisattvas are indeed *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), having been granted the prediction by the Buddha, yet they have fallen into the great hell.
If you are one who has been granted the prediction of *avaivartika* by the Buddha, you too shall enter this great hell."
"The Buddha has conferred upon you the prediction of rebirth in hell.
It would be better for you to renounce the bodhicitta; by doing so, you may avoid falling into hell and instead attain birth in the heavens. Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva, upon seeing or hearing such things, their mind remains unmoved, without doubt or alarm, and reflects:
"It is utterly impossible for an avaivartika bodhisattva to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts."
"Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Māra transformed himself into a bhikṣu, wearing the robes and approaching the Bodhisattva, and said to him:
"You have previously heard that you should thus purely cultivate the six pāramitās, and so on, up to: you should thus purely cultivate them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
