Regarding this matter, you should quickly repent and abandon it.

You should now rejoice in and dedicate toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all the roots of goodness you previously cultivated among the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—from their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the duration of the Dharma—and throughout that entire interval.
"You must also quickly relinquish this matter.
If you relinquish it quickly, I shall speak to you of the true Buddha-dharma.
What you have previously heard is none of the Buddha-dharma and none of the Buddha's teaching; it is all merely a compilation of literary embellishments."
"What I have spoken is the true Dharma of the Buddha.

If, upon hearing these words, a bodhisattva’s mind is startled, doubtful, or regretful, it should be known that this bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas, nor is he firmly established within the nature of *avaivartika*.

If a bodhisattva’s mind is unmoving, unstartled, free from doubt, and free from regret; if they accord with and rely upon the dharma of non-action and non-arising; if they do not believe the words of others nor follow the conduct of others; and when practicing the six pāramitās they do not follow the words of others, and even when practicing toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi they likewise do not follow the words of others.

Subhūti! For example, it is like an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted; he does not rely on the words of others nor follow the conduct of others, for he directly perceives the true reality of all dharmas, such that even Māra, the Evil One, cannot turn him away from it.
In this way, Subhūti, it is also thus for an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva: those who seek the path of śrāvakas or the path of pratyekabuddhas are unable to break or subdue their mind.
Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly abide in the stage of *avaivartika*.

He does not follow the words of others—even the words of a Buddha—nor does he accept them through mere faith; how much less so the words of those seeking the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, or the words of evil Māras, non-Buddhists, or brahmins; such a thing is absolutely impossible.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma that can be followed with faith—whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; whether it be the suchness of form up to the suchness of consciousness; and even up to not perceiving either unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment or the suchness of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
Māra, having assumed the form of a bhikṣu, came to where the Bodhisattva was and said to him:
"That which you practice is the dharma of birth and death; it is not the path to sarvajñatā."
"You shall now personally realize the exhaustion of suffering.

At that time, Māra the Evil One, for the sake of the Bodhisattva, taught a counterfeit path using worldly practices. These counterfeit paths are bound to the three realms, namely: the perception of bones, or the first dhyāna, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He said:
"Good son! By means of this path and by means of this practice, you shall attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, up to and including the fruit of an arhat."
"You practice this path; the suffering of this present life is now exhausted. Why do you continue to undergo the various afflictions within birth and death?
If even this body composed of the four great elements is no longer to be accepted, how much less should one accept a future body?"
"Subhūti! If the mind of this bodhisattva mahāsattva is not startled, does not doubt, and feels no regret, and he thinks:
'This bhikṣu has benefited me not a little, for he has taught me a dharma that resembles the Path.'"

Practicing these dharmas that resemble the Path, one will not reach the realization of the fruit of Srotāpanna, nor will one attain the realization of the path of Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, let alone attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva becomes even more joyful and thinks:
"This bhikṣu has benefited me no small amount, for he has taught me the dharmas that obstruct the path."
"I know that these are dharmas that obstruct the path; they do not obstruct the training in the paths of the three vehicles.
At that time, the evil Māra, knowing that the bodhisattva was filled with joy, spoke these words:
"O son of good family!

Do you wish to see this bodhisattva mahāsattva making offerings to as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges—providing them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life;

and likewise practicing the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) under as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges; and furthermore, attending upon as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges and inquiring about the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?

How does he practice the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā)? And how does he practice the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) up to great loving-kindness and great compassion (mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā)?

"If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells, practices, and cultivates in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, and if this bodhisattva-mahāsattva teaches and trains in this manner, they still do not attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, nor do they attain omniscience (sarvajñā); how much less, then, could you possibly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment?"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this matter and their mind is neither altered nor startled, but instead becomes even more joyful, they should think:
"This bhikṣu has benefited me no small amount, for he has taught me the dharmas that obstruct the Path."

These dharmas that obstruct the path prevent one from attaining the stage of *srotāpanna*, up to and including the stages of *arhat* and *pratyekabuddha*; how much less could one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
At that time, the evil Māra, knowing that this bodhisattva’s mind was neither discouraged nor alarmed, immediately manifested many bhikṣus at that very spot and said to the bodhisattva:
“All of these are bodhisattvas who have resolved to seek the Buddha-way, yet they all now abide in the stage of arhatship.”
"Even these people cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how could you possibly attain it?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva then thinks: "This is Māra, the Evil One, speaking of what resembles the practice of the Path."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not turn back from the mind set on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor should they fall into the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
He further reflects:

"It is impossible that one who practices the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of wisdom, and so forth up to all-knowledge, should not attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment."
"Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought:

"If a bodhisattva can, as the Buddha has taught, not depart from the mind of the perfection of wisdom up to and including all-knowledge, that bodhisattva will never regress from anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If a bodhisattva recognizes these as the deeds of Māra, they shall not lose their *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By such conduct, categories, and characteristics, one should know that these are the marks of an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by turning away from what dharma is one said to be ‘not turning’?”

The Buddha said: “It is by turning away from the marks of form; by turning away from the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; by turning away from the marks of the twelve bases and the eighteen elements; by turning away from the marks of lust, hatred, and delusion; by turning away from the mark of false views; by turning away from the marks of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the marks of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and even the mark of a buddha—it is for this reason that it is called the mark of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

Why is this? Because this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of these dharmas that are empty of self-characteristics, enters the stage of a bodhisattva and attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Why is it called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?

Because herein not even the slightest phenomenon can be apprehended; because it cannot be apprehended, there is no volitional formation (*anabhisaṃskāra*); because there is no volitional formation, there is no arising. This is called the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 16; *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 17.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Fifty-Six: On Firmness (in the Danben [Zhu] edition:
On Turning and Not Turning). "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Māra approaches the Bodhisattva to corrupt his mind and says:
"Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is equal to space; it is empty and characterized by non-existence.
All dharmas are also equal to space; they are empty and characterized by non-existence."
Within these dharmas such as space, which are empty and devoid of any marks, there is no one who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there anyone who does not attain it.
"All these dharmas are like space; they are empty and devoid of any marks.
Your diligent toil is in vain.
That which you have heard regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is entirely the work of Māra, not what was taught by the Buddha."
"You should relinquish this vow; do not undergo such instability, anxiety, and suffering for a long night, nor fall into the evil realms.
When these sons and daughters of good family hear these words, they should reflect thus:
"This is the work of Māra, seeking to destroy my resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Although all dharmas are like empty space—non-existent and empty of intrinsic characteristics—sentient beings do not know, see, or understand this.

I, too, through the great vow adorned with the realization that they are like empty space, non-existent, and empty of intrinsic characteristics, have attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). For the sake of sentient beings, I preach the Dharma so that they may attain liberation, reaching the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), the path of the pratyekabuddha, and unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Subhūti! From the moment they first resolve their minds [on awakening], Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, upon hearing such a Dharma as this, should make their minds firm, unshakable, and irreversible."
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the six pāramitās with this firm mind, an unshakable and irreversible mind, shall enter the rank of bodhisattvas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
“Is one called *avaivartika* because of not turning back,
or is one called *avaivartika* because of turning back?
The Buddha said:
“Because they do not turn back, they are called *avaivartika*;
because they do turn [toward awakening], they are also called *avaivartika*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that by not turning back one is called *avaivartika*,
and by turning back one is also called *avaivartika*?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not turn back toward the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha, for this reason they are called 'one who does not turn back.'"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns away from the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha, for this reason they are also said to be "non-retrogressive.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, one should know that these are the marks of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
By virtue of these practices, categories, and characteristics, evil Māras will be unable to corrupt their minds and cause them to turn away from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

If an avaivartika bodhisattva wishes to enter the first dhyāna, the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, up to the dhyāna of the cessation of perception and feeling, they are able to enter them immediately.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, or the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, up to the five supernormal powers, he shall immediately attain their cultivation."
Although this bodhisattva cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the five supernormal powers, he does not receive the fruit of the four foundations of mindfulness;
although he cultivates the various dhyānas, he does not receive the fruits of those dhyānas, nor does he receive the fruit of the dhyāna of the meditative absorption of cessation.
They do not realize the fruit of a srotāpanna, nor do they realize anything up to the path of a pratyekabuddha.
Because these bodhisattvas intentionally take on bodies for the sake of sentient beings, they benefit them according to what is appropriate for each.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly recollects anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and never departs from the mind of sarvajñā.

Because they do not distance themselves from the mind of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they do not prize form, nor do they prize marks; they do not prize the *śrāvaka* or the *pratyekabuddha*; they do not prize the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); they do not prize the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, or the four formless attainments; they do not prize the five supernormal powers; they do not prize the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they do not prize the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*); they do not prize the purification of Buddha-fields; they do not prize the maturing of sentient beings; they do not prize the seeing of Buddhas; and they do not prize the planting of roots of goodness.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*).
One does not perceive any phenomenon that is worthy of esteem, nor anything that can give rise to a mind of esteem.
Why is this? Because all these dharmas are equal to space; they are non-existent and empty of their own characteristics. Subhūti!

This irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva accomplishes this mind, such that within the four modes of physical deportment—coming and going, sitting and lying down, walking and standing—he remains single-minded and undistracted.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

If an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva lives as a householder, by the power of skillful means and for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he accepts the five desires; he practices giving to sentient beings, providing food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, clothing, bedding, and even all other necessities of life, giving them all completely.
This bodhisattva personally practices the dāna-pāramitā, teaches others to practice dāna, praises the method of practicing dāna, and joyfully extols those who practice the dāna-pāramitā;
it is the same for the śīla-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā.

Subhūti! When an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva is living at home, he is able to give away to sentient beings precious jewels filling Jambudvīpa, even up to giving away to sentient beings precious jewels filling the entire trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, he does not practice the holy life for his own sake, nor does he treat others with contempt or plunder them to cause them distress and affliction. Subhūti!
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Vajrapāṇi spirit-king constantly follows the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, making this vow:

'When this bodhisattva mahāsattva shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I will constantly follow him, and even until the five classes of Vajrapāṇi spirits are constantly following and protecting him.'"
For this reason, neither gods, nor Māras, nor Brahmās, nor any other powerful beings in the world can destroy it.
This is called the *sarvajñatā-citta* (mind of omniscience) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, which persists until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! This is called the mark of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is constantly endowed with the five bodhisattva faculties—the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom—this is called the mark of an avaivartika.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is a superior person, not an inferior person.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What constitutes a superior person?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with a single-minded focus, their mind undistracted, they constantly keep the Buddha-way in mind; for the sake of a pure livelihood, they do not perform incantations or compound medicines, nor do they invoke spirits or deities to possess men or women to inquire about their fortune or misfortune, or the destiny, fortune, or length of life of men and women."
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics and do not perceive the characteristics of dharmas, they do not engage in wrong livelihoods but practice pure livelihood.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called the mark of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
"I shall now further explain the conduct, categories, and characteristics of the irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
Listen attentively with a single-minded focus.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is never separated from the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do not speak of the phenomena of the five aggregates, do not speak of the phenomena of the twelve bases, and do not speak of the phenomena of the eighteen elements.”

Why is this? Because they constantly and mindfully contemplate the empty nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the empty nature of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).
Such Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not take pleasure in speaking of official affairs.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva dwells within the mark of emptiness of all dharmas and does not perceive any dharma as noble or base;
he does not delight in speaking of matters concerning thieves.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa-śūnya*), one perceives neither gain nor loss.
One does not take pleasure in speaking of military affairs.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa-śūnya*), one perceives neither much nor little.
One does not delight in speaking of contentious matters.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the suchness of all phenomena (dharmatā) and does not perceive any phenomenon as having either aversion or affection.
He does not delight in speaking of matters concerning women.
Why is this? Because while abiding in the emptiness of all phenomena, one perceives neither the beautiful nor the ugly;
therefore, one does not speak of matters concerning villages.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics, one does not perceive any phenomenon as either joining together or dispersing.
One does not take pleasure in speaking of matters concerning cities and towns.
Why is this? Because abiding within the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena, one perceives neither victory nor defeat.
One does not take pleasure in discussing matters of state.
Why is this? Because abiding within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one does not perceive any phenomenon as belonging to oneself or not belonging to oneself.
One does not delight in speaking of matters concerning the self.
Why is this? Because they abide within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they do not perceive a self or a non-self in phenomena, nor do they perceive a knower or a seer.

Thus, they do not speak of various worldly matters, but rather delight in speaking of the *prajñāpāramitā* without departing from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). When practicing the *dānapāramitā*, they do not engage in acts of stinginess or greed.
When practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), one does not engage in acts that violate the precepts.
When practicing the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), one does not engage in acts of anger or contention.
When practicing the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), one does not engage in acts of indolence.
When practicing the dhyāna-pāramitā, one does not engage in distracted activities;
when practicing the prajñā-pāramitā, one does not engage in ignorant activities.
Although this bodhisattva practices the emptiness of all phenomena, they still cherish and delight in the Dharma.

Although this bodhisattva practices the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they constantly praise the indestructible Dharma and cherish spiritual friends—namely, the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—who are able to provide instruction and cause others to joyfully abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This person constantly aspires to see all Buddhas and hear them wherever they reside.
In whichever Buddha-land there is a currently dwelling Buddha, they will be reborn there in accordance with their vow.
Such a mind is constantly active day and night; it is what is called the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, by the power of skillful means, gives rise to a mind belonging to the desire realm and is reborn among those sentient beings who are able to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, or in places where a Buddha currently resides.
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

When an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, and so forth, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; they abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Within their own stage, they understand clearly and have no doubt as to whether they are an avaivartika or not an avaivartika.
Why is this? Because, Subhūti, one does not perceive even the slightest dharma that either turns toward or turns away from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti!

For example, just as a person who has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and dwells within the stage of a *srotāpanna* clearly understands for themselves and never doubts or regrets, so too is it with an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva; dwelling within the stage of non-retrogression, they never doubt.
Abiding in this stage, they purify Buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity.
When various demonic activities arise, they immediately perceive them; they neither follow after such demonic activities nor allow them to cause destruction.

Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who commits the five heinous crimes; the mind of those five heinous crimes follows that person constantly until the moment of death and does not abandon them, such that even the arising of other thoughts cannot obstruct or separate it.
Subhūti! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is irreversible (avaivartika): he abides in his own stage, and his mind is always immovable.
No one among the devas, humans, or asuras in all the worlds can cause him to waver.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have transcended all worlds of devas, humans, and asuras; they have entered the stage of the true dharma and abide in the stage of self-realization; they are fully endowed with the supernormal powers of bodhisattvas, and are able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they plant various roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions, drawing near to and inquiring of those Buddhas.

Abiding in this manner, the bodhisattva recognizes and does not follow the various demonic activities that arise; through the power of skillful means, they remain amidst demonic activities while dwelling within the sphere of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Within the stage of self-realization, there is neither doubt nor regret.
Why is this? Because within the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no characteristic of doubt.

Knowing that this reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is neither one nor two, for this reason, such a person—even when they change bodies—will ultimately never turn toward the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti, for this bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, they do not perceive any phenomenon as arising or ceasing, nor as defiled or pure. Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, even when undergoing a change of existence, does not doubt whether he will attain anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi or not.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all dharmas is itself anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the stage of self-realization, does not follow the words of others, and none are able to destroy him. Why is this?
Subhūti, because this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished immovable wisdom,
one should know by these practices, categories, and characteristics that he is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if an evil Māra should come in the form of a Buddha and say to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: 'You should now, in this very place, take up the path of an arhat;

you have not received a prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor have you attained the dharma of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); you do not possess these practices, categories, or characteristics of an avaivartika [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva, nor do you possess the marks by which one receives the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing these words, does not change in mind, and neither sinks, nor is startled, nor terrified, nor afraid,
that bodhisattva should know for themselves:”
"I shall certainly receive from all Buddhas the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
"The Bodhisattvas receive their predictions by means of these dharmas; I too possess these dharmas and shall thus receive my prediction."
"Subhūti! If an evil Māra, or one sent by Māra, should come in the form of a Buddha and bestow upon a bodhisattva the prediction of becoming a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."
Subhūti! This bodhisattva forms this thought:
"This is an evil Māra, or one sent by Māra, who has come in the form of a Buddha."
"The Buddhas should not instruct bodhisattvas to distance themselves from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and instead instruct them to abide in the paths of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti!
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called the mark of an avaivartika.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One may again manifest in the form of a Buddha, come to where the bodhisattva is, and say these words:"
"Subhūti, if [an opponent] says, 'The sūtras you study were not spoken by the Buddha, nor were they spoken by the śrāvakas; they were spoken by Māra,' then,
Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand it thus:"
"This is an evil Māra, or one sent by Māra, who teaches me to distance myself from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva has already received a prediction from the Buddhas of the past and dwells on the stage of avaivartika.

Why is this? Whatever practices, categories, and characteristics belong to those who are irreversible (avaivartika), these same practices, categories, and characteristics are also found in this bodhisattva; this is called the mark of an irreversible bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, for the sake of protecting and upholding all dharmas, he does not begrudge even his own body or life, let alone other things."
Because this bodhisattva upholds and protects the Dharma, they form this thought:
"I do not uphold the Dharma of a single Buddha; I uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ten directions."
"Subhūti! How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of upholding the Dharma, does not begrudge his own body or life? Subhūti!"
When the Buddha taught that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, there were at that time foolish people who rejected and destroyed it, saying:
"This is not the Dharma, it is not good, and it is not the teaching of the World-Honored One."
"Subhūti! Because Bodhisattvas uphold and protect such Dharma as this, they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives.
A Bodhisattva should also form this thought:"
"I shall also be among the number of Buddhas in future ages; I shall receive my prediction of enlightenment therein, and this Dharma shall also be my Dharma.
For this reason, he does not begrudge his body or life.
Subhūti! Because the bodhisattva perceives these benefits, he upholds and protects the Dharma, not begrudging even his own body or life. Subhūti!
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one knows these to be the marks of an *avaivartika* [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
when an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva hears the Buddha preaching the Dharma, they have no doubt and no regret."
Having heard it, they receive and uphold it, never forgetting or losing it. Why is this?
Because they have attained dhāraṇī.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
what kind of dhāraṇī must one obtain so that, upon hearing the various sūtras spoken by the Buddha, one does not forget them?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because a bodhisattva has attained dhāraṇīs such as 'hearing and retaining,' when the Buddhas preach various sūtras, they do not forget them, do not lose them, do not doubt them, and do not regret them."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
do those who merely hear the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma not forget it, not lose it, not doubt it, and not regret it?”

Are the teachings spoken by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those spoken by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, likewise neither forgotten nor lost, and free from doubt or regret?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Regarding all spoken words and various matters, a bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī neither forgets nor loses them, and neither doubts nor regrets them.”
"Subhūti! When one is thus accomplished in such conduct, categories, and characteristics, you should know that this is an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Chapter 57: The Profound (The Lamp-Wick Chapter in the Dan-ben [Dunhuang] edition). Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is irreversible has accomplished great merit.
World-Honored One!”
"This irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished immeasurable merit and accomplished boundless merit.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
This irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished great merit; this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished immeasurable and boundless merit.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained immeasurable and boundless wisdom, which is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The avaivartika bodhisattva, dwelling within this wisdom, gives rise to the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Because he has attained these unimpeded knowledges, no one among the gods or humans of all the worlds is able to exhaust them.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha is able, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to praise and describe the practices, categories, and characteristics of the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!

What profound state is it, wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible dwells while practicing the six pāramitās, thereby fulfilling the four foundations of mindfulness up to and including the fulfillment of all-knowledge?”
The Buddha praised Subhūti: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
It is because you, as an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva, have asked about this profound matter.
Subhūti, that which is called "the profound matter" has emptiness as its meaning.
Subhūti, [these are] signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-birth, non-defilement, cessation, detachment, suchness, the nature of phenomena, the limit of reality, and nirvāṇa.
“Such dharmas as these constitute the profound meaning.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
“Is it only emptiness up to nirvāṇa that is profound, and not all dharmas?
The Buddha said,
“All dharmas are also of profound meaning.”
Subhūti! Form is also profound; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also profound.
The eye is also profound, and so on up to the mind; form up to mental phenomena; the eye-element up to the mind-consciousness element.
The perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom;
and from the four foundations of mindfulness up to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment are likewise profound.
“World-Honored One!
Why is form profound, and so on, up to why even *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is profound?
The Buddha said:
“Because the suchness of form is profound, form is profound.

Because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the suchness of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, is profound, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is profound.”
“World-Honored One!
Why is the suchness of form profound, and so on, up to why is the suchness of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment profound? “Subhūti!
This suchness of form is neither form nor apart from form.
This extends up to the suchness of consciousness, which is neither consciousness nor apart from consciousness.

It extends even to the suchness of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is neither unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment nor apart from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

By the power of subtle and wondrous skillful means, you cause the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive (avaivartika) to attain nirvāṇa by departing from the sphere of form; you also cause them to attain nirvāṇa by departing from the spheres of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and you cause them to attain nirvāṇa by departing from all dharmas—whether worldly or supramundane, contentious or non-contentious, outflowing or non-outflowing.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"

By means of his subtle and wondrous power of skillful means, the Buddha causes the avaivartika bodhisattva to attain nirvāṇa apart from the sphere of form, and even to attain nirvāṇa apart from the spheres of both out-flowing (sāsrava) and non-out-flowing (anāsrava) dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus contemplates, evaluates, and reflects upon this profound dharma in conjunction with the prajñāpāramitā, they should form this thought:
'I should practice in this way, as taught in the prajñāpāramitā.'"
"I should train in this way, as it is taught in the Prajñāpāramitā.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice as taught and train as taught, observing according to the Prajñāpāramitā, and if they possess diligent vigor such that even at the arising of a single thought-moment, they shall obtain immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merit.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends immeasurable kalpas and draws near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How much more so when they constantly practice the prajñāpāramitā and maintain mindfulness directed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Subhūti! Suppose, for example, there is a man of great lust who makes an appointment with a beautiful and pure woman.
This woman, however, is obstructed and unable to go at the appointed time. Subhūti, what do you think? Where does that man’s thought abide?
“World-Honored One!
This person is constantly with that woman in every thought-moment, always forming this thought, recollecting and imagining future times when they will sit and lie together in joy.”
“Subhūti! How many thoughts arise in such a person in one day and one night? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
In one day and one night, this person’s thoughts are exceedingly many, exceedingly many.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the prajñāpāramitā and practices this path as it is taught within the prajñāpāramitā, they transcend the number of kalpas in a single thought-moment, just as that person [in the analogy] counts the thoughts in a single day and night.”
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they remain far removed from all offenses, namely, those offenses that are contrary to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the roots of goodness and merit attained in a single day—even if the merit filling as many trichiliocosms as there are sands in the Ganges were gathered together—would still not equal even a fraction of the remaining merit; it would not reach a hundredth part, nor a thousandth, nor a ten-thousandth, nor a billionth, nor even that which can be reached by calculation or metaphor.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being far removed from the perfection of wisdom, were to practice giving to the Three Jewels—the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus—for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges River."
"Subhūti, what do you think? By reason of this, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so—immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is not as much as the merit gained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, for a single day, practices according to the teaching within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this?
The *prajñāpāramitā* is the path of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas; riding upon this path, they swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to distance themselves from the prajñāpāramitā and, for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges River, make offerings to srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Based on these causes and conditions, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One!"
"Very much, very much.
The Buddha said:
"It is not as much as the merit gained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as taught for even a single day."

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this prajñāpāramitā, they transcend all stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the rank of a bodhisattva, and gradually attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is far removed from the perfection of wisdom may practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One!..."
"Very much, very much.
The Buddha said:

"It is not as great as the merit obtained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom as taught, practicing for a single day through giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
Why is this? Subhūti,
it is because the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
This Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; for when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide within the Prajñāpāramitā, they are able to fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being far removed from the perfection of wisdom, were to practice the gift of Dharma for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. Subhūti!
If you practice the perfections as they have been taught, even practicing the gift of Dharma for a single day will bring greater merit.
Why is this? Subhūti!
If this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not distance himself from the prajñāpāramitā, then he does not distance himself from all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā);
if he does not distance himself from all-knowledge, then he does not distance himself from the prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should not remain far removed from the prajñāpāramitā.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to remain far removed from the perfection of wisdom for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River, yet practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and [the meditations on] internal emptiness up to all-knowledge;
"Subhūti, what do you think? Would these sons of good family or daughters of good family acquire much merit? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so, it is very much so!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as much as the merit obtained by a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the four foundations of mindfulness up to the knowledge of all modes for a single day, in accordance with the teaching of this profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not remain far removed from the prajñāpāramitā, it is impossible that they would turn away from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Subhūti! It is possible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having become distant from the prajñāpāramitā, might turn away from sarvajñatā. Subhūti!
For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should never be separated from the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were separated from the perfection of wisdom, even if they were to give away their life, wealth, and Dharma-teachings, as well as the merit of meditative concentration, for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges River, and dedicate them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would that person acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One! [He would acquire much merit]."
"Very much, very much!
The Buddha said:

"It is not equal to the merit gained by a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught, even for a single day, through the merit of material giving, the gift of Dharma, and meditative concentration, dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The latter gains far more merit."
Why is this? Because this is the foremost dedication, namely, the dedication of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one is divorced from the dedication of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it cannot be called a dedication.
Subhūti! For this reason, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should skillfully train in the dedication of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, being far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*, should, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, rejoice in the roots of goodness of all Buddhas and their disciples of the past, future, and present, and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Would that person gain much merit? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so, it is very much so!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as much as the merit obtained by a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the teaching, even for a single day, rejoicing in its roots of goodness and dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The latter obtains far more merit."

Subhūti! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should train in the skillful means within the prajñāpāramitā and dedicate [their merit] toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the dharmas of dependent origination arise from false conceptualization and are not real.”
"How is it, World-Honored One, that a son or daughter of good family attains great merit?

By reason of these causal conditions, one should not attain right view or enter the stage of the Dharma; one should not attain the fruit of a Srotāpanna, nor even the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is, so it is! Subhūti!”
Because of these causes and conditions, one who gives rise to dharmas should not attain right view or enter the stage of the Dharma, nor should they even attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows that the dharma of dependent origination is also empty, lacks solidity, and is deceptive and unreal.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have well studied internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence; because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in these eighteen kinds of emptiness and contemplate all conditioned phenomena as empty in various ways, they do not depart from the prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus gradually does not depart from the prajñāpāramitā, they will gradually attain incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the difference between ‘incalculable,’ ‘immeasurable,’ and ‘boundless’?”
“Subhūti! ‘Incalculable’ means that it does not fall within the reckoning of either the conditioned nature or the unconditioned nature.
‘Immeasurable’ means that no measure can be found, whether in the past, the future, or the present.”
"Regarding 'boundless,' it means that the limits of all phenomena cannot be apprehended. Subhūti said,
"World-Honored One!"
“Is there any form that is also innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless?
Is there any feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that is also innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless? “Subhūti!”
"There is a reason why form is also countless, immeasurable, and boundless; and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also countless, immeasurable, and boundless.
"World-Honored One!"
By what causes and conditions are form, as well as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, also countless, immeasurable, and boundless?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because form is empty, it is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, they are incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless."
“World-Honored One!
Is it only form that is empty, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are empty, while all dharmas are not empty? “Subhūti!”
“Have I not always taught that all phenomena are empty?
Subhūti replied, “World-Honored One, [you have].”
The Buddha has taught that all phenomena are empty.
World-Honored One!
That which is the emptiness of all phenomena is inexhaustible; it is numberless, immeasurable, and boundless.
World-Honored One!
Within emptiness, number cannot be apprehended, measure cannot be apprehended, and limits cannot be apprehended.
For this reason, World-Honored One!
"This is inexhaustible; the meanings of 'innumerable,' 'immeasurable,' and 'boundless' are not different.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
The meaning of these dharmas is without distinction, Subhūti!

These dharmas are ineffable; it is by the power of skillful means that the Buddha distinguishes and explains them—namely, as inexhaustible, innumerable, immeasurable, boundless, and unattached; as empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unproduced, unceasing, unstained, and nirvāṇa.
“The Buddha has taught through various causes and conditions by means of his power of skillful means.
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”
The true reality of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*) is ineffable, yet the Buddha speaks of it by means of skillful power (*upāyakauśalyabala*).
World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, all phenomena are likewise ineffable.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Subhūti!"
"All dharmas are ineffable.
That which is the ineffable nature of all dharmas is emptiness, and this emptiness is ineffable.
"World-Honored One!"
“Is there any increase or decrease in the meaning that is ineffable? The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti.”
“The ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases.
“World-Honored One!

If the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, then the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) must also neither increase nor decrease, and so on up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which must likewise neither increase nor decrease.”

The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path shall likewise be without increase or decrease; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, as well as the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha shall likewise be without increase or decrease.

"Bhagavān! If the six pāramitās of a bodhisattva mahāsattva do not increase, and even the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) do not increase, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
The ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases.
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom with skillful means, they do not form such a thought as:
"I increase the perfection of wisdom," up to and including, "I increase the perfection of generosity."
One should form this thought:
"It is merely by way of a name that it is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, he dedicates that mind and all those roots of goodness toward the mark of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Even when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one dedicates that mind and all roots of goodness in accordance with the mark of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said,
"The suchness of all dharmas is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is this ‘suchness’ (tathatā) of all dharmas that is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The mark of the suchness of form, the mark of the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the mark of the suchness of nirvāṇa—this mark of suchness is unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it neither increases nor decreases."
Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the prajñāpāramitā, but constantly contemplates this suchness (tathatā) of dharmas, seeing neither increase nor decrease.
For this reason, Subhūti, the meaning that is ineffable neither increases nor decreases.
The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) likewise neither increases nor decreases, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharmas*), which also neither increase nor decrease.
“Subhūti! By means of this dharma that neither increases nor decreases, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the initial mind,
or does he attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the final mind?”
World-Honored One!
This initial mind does not reach the subsequent mind, and the subsequent mind does not abide in the initial mind.
World-Honored One!
If the mind and mental factors are thus incomplete, how can the roots of goodness increase?
If the roots of goodness do not increase, how will one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“I shall provide you with a simile, for when the wise obtain a simile, the meaning becomes easy to understand. Subhūti!
"Suppose a lamp is lit: is the wick consumed by the initial flame, or is it consumed by the final flame? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is not by the first flame that the wick is burned, nor is it apart from the first flame.
World-Honored One!”
"It is not by the final flame that the wick is burned, nor is it apart from the final flame.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Is the wick burned?"
“World-Honored One!
The wick is indeed scorched.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi by means of the initial mind, nor does he attain anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi apart from the initial mind;
he does not attain anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi by means of the final mind, nor does he attain anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi apart from the final mind— and yet, he attains anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi.”

Subhūti! In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, practices the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the ten stages, and attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are these ten stages, which, once fully perfected by a bodhisattva, lead to the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said:

"A bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the buddha. Having fulfilled these stages, he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has trained in these ten stages, they do not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the initial mind, nor do they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi apart from the initial mind;
they do not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the final mind, nor do they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi apart from the final mind.
"And thus one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"

This Dharma of dependent origination is profoundly deep: namely, that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* neither by means of the initial mind nor apart from the initial mind, neither by means of the final mind nor apart from the final mind, yet one does attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Once a mind has ceased, does that same mind arise again?
"No, World-Honored One."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the arising of the mind possess the characteristic of cessation?
“World-Honored One, [it does].”
"This is the characteristic of cessation.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Is the characteristic of the mind's cessation itself cessation?"
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does he also abide in this way?"
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
It abides in this very way; it abides as suchness.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? If this mind were to abide as suchness (tathatā), would it realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Is this *tathatā* (suchness) profound? [Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"Profound, indeed profound!
"Subhūti, what do you think? Is it only such a mind?"
"No, World-Honored One! "Is he free from such a mind? "No, World-Honored One!"
“Subhūti, what do you think? Is suchness seen as suchness? “No, World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? If a bodhisattva can practice in this way, is he practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they are practicing the profound perfection of wisdom.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, in what sphere does he practice? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they practice without a locus. Why is that?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the suchness of all phenomena; therein is no such thought, no object of thought, and no thinker.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, where does he practice? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are practicing within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
because two modes of practice cannot be apprehended.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? If a bodhisattva practices within the ultimate truth and in a state of non-conceptualization, is that practicing with signs?
“No, World-Honored One.”
“What do you think, Subhūti? Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva destroy signs?
“No, World-Honored One,” he replied.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What is meant by ‘the mark of non-disintegration’? Subhūti replied,
“World-Honored One!”
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form the thought:
"I shall destroy the characteristics of all phenomena.
World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, as long as they have not yet fully perfected the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and eighteen unique qualities, they do not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One!
By means of the power of skillful means, a bodhisattva mahāsattva neither grasps at the marks of phenomena nor destroys their marks. Why is this?
"Bhagavān! This bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*).

Abiding in this emptiness of own-characteristics, for the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the three samādhis and uses these three samādhis to bring sentient beings to fulfillment."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva enter the three samādhis to bring sentient beings to maturity?”
The Buddha said:

“When a bodhisattva abides in these three samādhis, he sees sentient beings practicing within the sphere of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*), and through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), he teaches them so that they may attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
He sees sentient beings practicing within the sphere of the mark of self (*ātman*), and through the power of skillful means, he teaches them to practice emptiness (*śūnyatā*).”
Seeing that sentient beings act within all marks (*nimitta*), he uses the power of skillful means to teach and lead them to act within the markless (*animitta*). In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom enters the three samādhis and brings sentient beings to fulfillment through these three samādhis.

Chapter 58: On Dreaming Practice (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter Fifty-Eight, "On Dreaming Practice"; in the old translation, "On Entering Samādhi in a Dream"). At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the three samādhis—the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness—while dreaming, would this be of benefit to the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva enters the three samādhis during the day, it is beneficial for the prajñāpāramitā;
it shall likewise be beneficial even in dreams at night."
Why is this? Because there is no difference whatsoever between day and night, or between waking and dreaming. Śāriputra!

If practicing the perfection of wisdom during the day is beneficial for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, then practicing the perfection of wisdom even in a dream should likewise be beneficial for that bodhisattva.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva performs an action within a dream, is that action accumulated?
As the Buddha has taught, all phenomena are like dreams.”
For this reason, there should be no accumulation.
Why? Because within a dream, there is no dharma that can be accumulated.
"If one were to engage in recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination while awake, there would necessarily be an accumulation [of karma]. Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Suppose a person kills a sentient being in a dream."
Having awakened, he recalled and conceptualized the signs, thinking:
"Was it not a pleasure for me to kill him? Śāriputra!
"What is the meaning of this? Śāriputra replied:
"Without conditions, karma does not arise; without conditions, volition does not arise."
“With conditions, karma arises; with conditions, volition arises. “Śāriputra, it is so, it is so!”
Without conditions, karma does not arise; without conditions, volition does not arise.
With conditions, karma arises; with conditions, volition arises.

Mind arises toward phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and known; it does not arise from phenomena that are not seen, heard, sensed, or known. Within this mind, there is both purity and defilement.
For this reason, Śāriputra, karma arises from conditions; it does not arise without conditions.
Volition arises from conditions; it does not arise without conditions.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "As the Buddha has taught, all karma and all volitions are devoid of their own characteristics.
How then can you say:"
"Because there is a condition, karma arises; without a condition, karma does not arise.
Because there is a condition, volition arises; without a condition, volition does not arise. Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Because of grasping signs, karma arises with an object; it does not arise without an object.
Because of grasping signs, volition arises with an object; it does not arise without an object."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in a dream, practices giving, upholding the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and dedicates these roots of goodness and merit toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Is this a true dedication?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"The Bodhisattva Maitreya is present here before us; the Buddha has bestowed upon him the prediction of non-retrogression, that he shall become a Buddha."
"You should ask Maitreya; Maitreya shall answer.
Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya: "Subhūti said:..."
"Maitreya Bodhisattva is now present before us; the Buddha has bestowed upon him the prediction of non-retrogression, that he shall become a Buddha.
Maitreya shall answer.
Maitreya Bodhisattva then spoke to Śāriputra:
"Should one answer by means of the name 'Maitreya'?
Or should one answer by means of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
Or should one answer by means of the emptiness of form?"
If one asks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, form cannot answer;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot answer; the emptiness of form cannot answer; and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot answer.
I do not perceive any dharma that can be answered, nor do I perceive one who can answer.
I do not perceive such a person who receives a prediction, nor do I perceive any dharma that can be predicted, nor do I perceive the locus of prediction.
"All these dharmas are without duality and without distinction.
Śāriputra said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"According to what you have said, O Noble One, is this how one attains the realization of the Dharma?"
Maitreya replied to Śāriputra:
"The Dharma as I have taught it is not realized in such a manner.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:

“Maitreya Bodhisattva’s wisdom is profoundly deep; having long practiced the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā through the principle of non-apprehension, he is able to speak in such a manner.”
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think? Do you perceive that dharma by means of which you attained arhatship?"
Śāriputra said, "I do not see them. [The Buddha said,] "Śāriputra!"
It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā):
they do not form such thoughts as,

"This dharma shall receive the prediction," "this dharma has already received the prediction," or "this dharma shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)."

"In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not doubt whether they will attain it or not; they know for themselves that they truly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"There may be a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, while practicing the perfection of dāna, sees sentient beings who are hungry, cold, and famished, their clothing tattered and worn out."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should make this vow:

"For as long as it takes me to practice the dāna-pāramitā, when I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), may the sentient beings in my buddha-field be free from such things."

Their clothing, food, drink, and requisites for sustaining life shall be like those of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the dānapāramitā and draw near to anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he sees sentient beings who—from killing up to holding wrong views—suffer short lifespans, many illnesses, and unsightly complexions; they lack majesty and virtue, are destitute of wealth and possessions, are born into low-born families, and have deformed or ugly bodies.
One should make this vow:
"For as long as it takes for me to practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), when I attain Buddhahood, may the sentient beings in my buddha-field be free from such things."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the śīla-pāramitā and draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he sees sentient beings who are mutually angry and abusive toward one another, harming each other with swords, staves, tiles, and stones, even taking one another's lives."
One should make this vow:
"For as long as it takes for me to practice the perfection of patience, when I become a Buddha, may the sentient beings in my land be free from such things."

They shall regard one another as a father or a mother, as an elder brother or a younger brother, as a sister, or as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and all shall practice loving-kindness and compassion. Subhūti!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice in this manner, they are able to fulfill the pāramitā of kṣānti and draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), he sees sentient beings who are indolent and lack diligent application, thereby abandoning the three vehicles— the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha-vehicle."
One should make this vow:
"For as long as it takes me to practice the *vīryapāramitā*, may it be such that when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the sentient beings in my buddha-field shall have no such things."
"All sentient beings who diligently cultivate vigor shall each attain liberation through the paths of the three vehicles. Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the *vīryapāramitā* and draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, he sees sentient beings covered by the five hindrances—sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt—and thus deprived of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; deprived of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and deprived of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
One should make this vow:
"For as long as it takes me to practice the dhyānapāramitā, may the sentient beings in my buddha-field have no such things when I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the dhyānapāramitā and draw near to anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he sees sentient beings who are deluded and have lost the right view of both the mundane and the supramundane; some say there is no karma and no causes and conditions for karma, some say the self (ātman) is eternal, some say there is annihilation, and some say nothing exists at all."
One should make this vow:

"For as long as I practice the Prajñāpāramitā, I shall purify the Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the sentient beings in my land shall have no such things."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the prajñāpāramitā and swiftly draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he sees sentient beings abiding in three categories: first, those of the fixed category of the right;
second, those of the fixed category of the wrong; and third, those of the indeterminate category."
One should make this vow:

"For as long as it takes me to practice the six pāramitās, purify the buddha-field, and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I attain buddhahood, may there be no group of those with wrong views among the sentient beings of my land, nor even the name for such a thing."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and swiftly draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he sees sentient beings in the hells, as well as sentient beings among the animals and the hungry ghosts."
One should make this vow:

"For as long as it takes me to practice the six pāramitās, purify the Buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I attain Buddhahood, may even the names of the three evil realms not exist within my land."
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Furthermore, Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, they see this great earth as a place filled with stumps, thorns, mountains, hills, ravines, pits, and impurities.
One should make this vow:

"May I practice the six pāramitās for as long as it takes to purify the buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; when I become a Buddha, may my land be free from such evils, and may its ground be as level as the palm of a hand."
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Furthermore, Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see this great earth as consisting purely of soil, devoid of gold, silver, or precious jewels, they should make this vow:
"For as long as it takes me to practice the six pāramitās, purify the buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I become a buddha, may my own land be strewn with golden sand."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, seeing that sentient beings have attachments, they should form this aspiration:

"For as long as it takes me to practice the six pāramitās, purify the buddha-field, and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I become a buddha, may the sentient beings in my land be free from all attachment."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he sees sentient beings of the four castes: kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras."
One should make this vow:

"For as long as it takes me to practice the six pāramitās, purify the buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I become a Buddha, may there be no names of the four castes among the sentient beings in my land."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he perceives that sentient beings have inferior, middling, and superior [capacities], as well as inferior, middling, and superior families."
One should make this vow:

"For as long as it takes me to practice the six pāramitās, purify the buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I become a Buddha, may the sentient beings in my land have no such distinctions of superiority or inferiority."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, seeing that sentient beings have various different complexions, he should form this aspiration:

"May I practice the six pāramitās for as long as it takes to purify the Buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity; when I become a Buddha, may the sentient beings in my land have no various different complexions, and may all sentient beings be endowed with upright, pure, and wondrous forms."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, seeing that sentient beings have owners, they should form this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six pāramitās for as long as it takes to purify the buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity; when I become a buddha, let there not even be the name 'owner' among the sentient beings of my land, nor even the appearance of such a thing."
"Except for the Buddha, the King of Dharma. Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he sees that sentient beings have the distinctions of the six realms of existence.
He should then form this aspiration:

"For as long as it takes me to practice the six pāramitās, purify the buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I become a Buddha, may there be no names for the six realms of existence in my land—namely, 'this is hell,' 'this is the animal realm,' 'this is the realm of hungry ghosts,' 'this is the realm of gods,' 'this is the realm of humans,' or 'this is the realm of asuras. May all sentient beings therein have a single karma, practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and swiftly draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
