"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he sees that sentient beings have four modes of birth: birth from eggs, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation."
One should make this vow:

"For as long as it takes me to practice the six pāramitās, purify the buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I become a Buddha, may the sentient beings in my land not have three modes of birth, but be born exclusively through transformation."
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Furthermore, Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, seeing that sentient beings lack the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā), they should form this aspiration:

"May I practice the six pāramitās for as long as it takes to purify the buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity; when I become a buddha, may all the sentient beings in my land attain the five supernormal powers."
"...and thus they will swiftly draw near to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections, he sees sentient beings afflicted by the ailments of excrement and urine."
One should make this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field take joy as their food, and may they be free from the affliction of excrement and urine."
"Thus, [he] approaches all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he sees that sentient beings lack radiance."
One should make this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field possess radiance," and so on,
until they draw near to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he perceives the existence of days, months, seasons, and years.
He should then form this aspiration: "
"When I become a Buddha, may there be no names for sun, moon, seasons, or years within my land," and so on,
up to "approaching all-knowledge."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, if he sees sentient beings who are short-lived, he should form this aspiration: [I shall practice the six pāramitās so that all sentient beings may attain long life]."
"When I become a Buddha, may the lifespan of the sentient beings within my land be immeasurable kalpas," up to "approaching all-knowledge. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see that sentient beings lack the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence,
they should form this aspiration:
"When I become a buddha, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks."
...up to: "They draw near to all-knowledge.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he sees sentient beings who are devoid of all roots of goodness.
One should make this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, may the sentient beings within my land achieve all roots of goodness; by virtue of these roots of goodness, may they be able to make offerings to all Buddhas."
"Thus, [he] approaches all-knowledge. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he sees that sentient beings possess the three poisons and the four diseases."
One should make this vow:

"When I become a Buddha, may the sentient beings in my land be free from the four kinds of illnesses: illnesses of cold, heat, and wind; the three kinds of combined illnesses; and the illness of the three poisons."
...up to approaching all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), he sees that sentient beings possess the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*)."
One should make this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, may there be no mention of the two vehicles among the sentient beings in my land, but only the single Great Vehicle," and so on,
until they draw near to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, if he sees sentient beings possessing overweening pride (adhimāna),
he should form this aspiration: [text continues]"
"When I become a Buddha, may there not even be the name 'arrogance' among the sentient beings in my land," up to "approaching all-knowledge. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, they should make this vow:
"If my radiance and lifespan are limited, and the number of my monks is restricted, I shall make this vow:

'As I practice the six pāramitās to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, when I become a Buddha, may my radiance and lifespan be immeasurable, and the number of my monks be limitless.'"
"…and so on, up to: 'approaching all-knowledge.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he should make this vow:"
"If my buddha-field were limited, I should make this vow:

'I shall practice the six pāramitās for as long as it takes to purify a buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity; when I become a Buddha, may my single buddha-field be equal to the buddha-fields of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.'"
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he should form this thought:
'Although the path of birth and death is long and the nature of sentient beings is manifold, at that time he should maintain correct mindfulness in this way:'"

"The limits of birth and death are like space; the nature of sentient beings is also like space. Within this, there is truly no coming or going in birth and death, nor is there anyone who attains liberation."
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and draw near to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

Chapter Fifty-nine: The River Goddess. Chapter Fifty-nine: The River Goddess.
At that time, there was a woman named Gaṅgadevā who was seated among the assembly.
The woman rose from her seat, bared her right shoulder, knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I shall practice the six pāramitās and take hold of a pure buddha-field."
"As it is taught in the Buddha’s Prajñāpāramitā, I shall practice it all.

At that time, the woman took various ornaments for making offerings, including flowers of gold and silver as well as flowers grown on land and in water, and two pieces of cotton cloth woven with golden threads, and scattered them over the Buddha.
Once it was scattered, it transformed in the space above the Buddha’s crown into a four-pillared jeweled terrace, upright, magnificent, and beautiful.
This woman took this merit and shared it with all sentient beings, dedicating it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the causes and conditions of this woman’s profound mind, immediately smiled.

According to the dharmas of all Buddhas, various colored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple—issued from his mouth, universally illuminating the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-lands of the ten directions. They then circled the Buddha three times and re-entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"For what cause and condition does the Buddha smile?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not smile without a cause or condition."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This elder sister Gaṅgadevā shall become a buddha in a future age; the kalpa will be named Nakṣatra, and the buddha’s name will be Suvarṇapuṣpa.”
Ānanda! This woman will exhaust this female body and receive a male form; she shall be born in the land of Abhirati of the Buddha Akṣobhya, where she will purely cultivate the brahma-faring.
Ānanda! This bodhisattva is also named Suvarṇapuṣpa in that land.
When this Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa reaches the end of his life there, he will again go to a buddha-land in another direction.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they never depart from the presence of the Buddhas.
It is like a wheel-turning sage king who, from one palace to another palace, from birth until his end, never sets foot upon the ground.
Ānanda! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvarṇapuṣpa is also like this: from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, until he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he has never failed to see a Buddha.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought:
"When this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvarṇapuṣpa later becomes a Buddha, the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas at that time should be known as being like an assembly of Buddhas."
The Buddha, knowing what Ānanda was thinking, addressed him, saying:
“So it is, so it is! You should know that the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas during the time of the Buddha Suvarṇapuṣpa is like an assembly of Buddhas.”
Ānanda! The bhikṣu-saṃgha of this Buddha Suvarṇapuṣpa is immeasurable and boundless, beyond all description and calculation, numbering many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
“Ānanda! When this Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa becomes a Buddha, his land will be free from all evils, just as has been described above.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From where did this woman plant the foundations of merit and sow the roots of goodness?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This woman planted roots of goodness under Dīpaṃkara Buddha and first resolved her mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. She dedicated these merits toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and she also scattered golden flowers over Dīpaṃkara Buddha, seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Ānanda! Just as I at that time scattered five flowers upon the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
knowing that my roots of goodness were perfected, conferred upon me the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Upon hearing my prediction, this woman resolved her mind and said:
"May I, in a future age, likewise receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as this bodhisattva has."
"Ānanda! You should know that this woman first resolved her mind toward enlightenment under Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This woman has long practiced for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! This woman has long practiced for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Chapter Sixty:
On Non-Realization (*Aprativedha*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. (In the Dan-xue edition, this is Chapter Sixty: On Emptiness and Non-Realization. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the prajñāpāramitā, how should they train in the emptiness samādhi?
How should they enter the emptiness samādhi?”
What is training in the signless and wishless samādhi?
How does one enter the signless and wishless samādhi?
What is training in the four foundations of mindfulness?
How does one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?
... up to ... how does one train in the eightfold noble path?
How does one cultivate the eightfold noble path?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate that form is empty, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; that the twelve bases and eighteen elements are empty, and so on, up to contemplating that the realms of desire, form, and formlessness are empty."
When practicing this contemplation, one must not allow the mind to become distracted.
If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mind is not distracted, he does not perceive these dharmas; if he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not realize them.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have well studied the emptiness of self-characteristics; there is no remainder and no parts, for neither the realization of the dharma nor the realizer can be perceived.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not realize the emptiness of dharmas.”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva dwells within the dharma of emptiness without realizing it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, fully contemplating emptiness, first makes this vow:
'I should not now realize the dharma of emptiness; this is my time for training, not my time for realization.'"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not exclusively concentrate the mind by binding it to a single object; for this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor does he realize the exhaustion of outflows.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus accomplished in such great, virtuous, and sublime dharmas, why is this?
Abiding in this emptiness, they form this thought:
"Now is my time for training, not my time for realization. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect in this way:
"When I am training in the dāna-pāramitā, this is not the time for realization.

When training in the śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, and dhyāna-pāramitā; when cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the cultivation of the eightfold noble path—this is not the time for realization."
When practicing the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness, it is not the time of realization.

When practicing the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion, it is not the time of realization.

When I now train in the knowledge of all modes, it is not the time for attaining the realization of the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor even for attaining the realization of the path of a pratyekabuddha up to the fruit of an arhat.
"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they study the contemplation of emptiness and abide within emptiness;
they study the contemplations of signlessness and wishlessness, and abide within signlessness and wishlessness."

He cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness but does not realize the four foundations of mindfulness; likewise, he cultivates the factors of the eightfold noble path but does not realize the factors of the eightfold noble path.

Although this bodhisattva studies the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he does not realize the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the path of a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! It is as if there were a man of great strength, powerful and courageous, skilled in the sixty-four arts of military strategy; who holds his weapons firmly and stands immovable, proficient in all technical skills, upright and pure, loved and respected by others, and who, with little effort in his undertakings, gains many rewards and benefits.
For these reasons, he is revered, honored, and praised by the multitude; seeing others show him such respect, his joy redoubles.

On rare occasions when he must travel elsewhere, he supports the elderly and the weak as they pass through various perilous and terrifying places. He reassures his parents and instructs his wife and children, saying:
"Do not be afraid; I can pass through this, and you shall certainly suffer no hardship."

"In the midst of these perilous and difficult paths, there are many hostile bandits lying in ambush to plunder and harm; yet because that person is fully endowed with wisdom and strength, they are able to cross the evil ways and return to their original place, meeting no harm from the bandits, but remaining joyful and at ease."
Subhūti! It is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

When the mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity is fully perfected toward all sentient beings, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the four immeasurable minds, fulfills the six pāramitās, does not realize the exhaustion of outflows, and studies the knowledge of all modes, entering the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva does not follow any signs, nor does he realize the samādhi of signlessness.
Because he does not realize the samādhi of signlessness, he does not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti! It is like a winged bird that soars through the void without falling; though it is in the air, it does not dwell in the air. Subhūti!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this:
they train in the gate of liberation of emptiness, and train in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, yet they do not realize them as a final attainment.
Because they do not realize [these], they do not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Until they have fully perfected the Buddha’s ten powers, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the immeasurable qualities of all Buddhas, and the knowledge of all modes, they likewise do not realize the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Subhūti! It is like a strong man who has studied the various methods of archery and is skilled in the art of shooting; he shoots upward into the air and then shoots subsequent arrows at the preceding ones, so that each arrow supports the next and prevents it from falling, remaining under his own control as he pleases.
If one wishes to make it fall, one must stop the subsequent arrow; only then will it fall to the ground.
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of the power of skillful means, one acts for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As long as the various roots of goodness are not yet fully perfected, one does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
when the roots of goodness are accomplished, at that time one realizes the limit of reality.
For this reason, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate the characteristics of all phenomena in this manner.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do is exceedingly difficult.”

Why is this? Although they study these characteristics of all phenomena, study the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), study suchness (*tathatā*), study the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and study ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), up to and including studying the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), they never fall away midway.
“World-Honored One!
This is most rare.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not abandon all sentient beings that he makes such a vow.
Subhūti! If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva should have this thought:"
"I ought not to abandon all sentient beings; since all sentient beings are submerged within the dharma of non-existence, I should deliver them.
At that moment, he immediately enters the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness.

Subhūti! You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished the power of skillful means; although he has not yet attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he practices these gates of liberation and does not midway realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to contemplate these profound dharmas— namely, inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the three doors of liberation— [should train in the perfection of wisdom]."
At that time, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought:
"These sentient beings have for a long night practiced the notion of a self, up to the notions of a knower and a seer, and are attached to the attainment of dharmas."
‘In order to sever these various marks for the sake of sentient beings, I shall preach the Dharma when I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the Bodhisattva practices the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; yet he should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).”
Because they do not realize [these stages], they do not fall into the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including the path of a pratyekabuddha. Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to bring these roots of goodness to fulfillment with this mind, he does not realize the limit of reality midway; he does not lose the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes all factors conducive to enlightenment, which never diminish until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because this bodhisattva possesses the power of skillful means, they constantly increase wholesome dharmas and their faculties become sharp and penetrating, surpassing those of arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

'Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to the four inversions— the mark of permanence, the mark of pleasure, the mark of purity, and the mark of self— and for the sake of these sentient beings, I seek omniscience (sarvajñatā).'"
"When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall preach the Dharma of impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self.

When this bodhisattva has accomplished this resolve, he practices the *prajñāpāramitā* through the power of skillful means; yet he does not attain the Buddha-samādhi, nor is he yet fully endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor does he realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva cultivates the gate of liberation of non-action; although he has not yet attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor does he realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:

'Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to the attainment of dharmas—namely, the self, sentient beings, and so forth up to the knower and the seer; these are form, these are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these are the sense bases, these are the elements; these are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments.'"
"I shall practice in such a way that when I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), sentient beings will not have this attainment of dharmas.

With this mind thus accomplished, the bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) through the power of skillful means; yet, until the Buddha's ten powers (*daśabala*), four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), great loving-kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*), and eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are fully perfected, he does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
At that time, the bodhisattva fully cultivates the samādhi of emptiness. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"Sentient beings have long practiced various signs—namely, the sign of male, the sign of female, the sign of form, and the sign of formlessness.
I shall practice in such a way that when I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, sentient beings will be free from these faults of signs."

When this mind is accomplished, one practices the perfection of wisdom through the power of skillful means; until the Buddha’s ten powers and even the eighteen unique qualities are fully perfected, one does not realize the limit of reality.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva fully cultivates the signless samādhi.

Subhūti! If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva studies the six pāramitās; studies inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; studies the four foundations of mindfulness up to the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and studies the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
When such wisdom is perfected, it is impossible for one to compose dharmas or abide within the triple world.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva studies the factors conducive to enlightenment and practices the factors conducive to enlightenment, they should be questioned as follows:
"How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who desires to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi study these dharmas?"

"Contemplating emptiness, one does not realize emptiness or the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Because one does not realize them, one does not fall into the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the path of a pratyekabuddha.

Contemplating the signless, the wishless, the unarisen, the unborn, and non-existence, one likewise does not take the realization of the limit of reality as a goal, yet practices the *prajñāpāramitā*."
One should ask as follows:
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is questioned in this manner, and that bodhisattva answers in such a way:"
"A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should contemplate only emptiness; they should contemplate only signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-birth, and non-existence."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should not study emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-origination, and non-existence; they should not study these factors conducive to enlightenment.
"Subhūti! You should know that these bodhisattvas have not yet been granted the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the Buddhas. Why is this?"
Such a person cannot explain the characteristics of what an avaivartika bodhisattva studies, nor can they demonstrate them or provide answers.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to explain, demonstrate, and answer regarding the characteristics of what an avaivartika studies, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already practiced and studied the bodhisattva path and entered the stage of thinness (*tanubhūmi*), just like other avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have reached the avaivartika stage.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
is there any bodhisattva who has not yet attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) who is able to answer in such a manner?"
The Buddha said: “There is, Subhūti.”
Whether they have heard or not heard of the six pāramitās of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva, they are able to answer in such a manner, just like an avaivartika bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!

There are many bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha-way, but few bodhisattvas are able to answer in such a manner as this, like an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva within the path of training and the path beyond training.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
Such bodhisattvas are very few.”
Why is this? Because there are few Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have thus attained the stage of wisdom of the irreversible (avaivartika) prediction.
If one has received such a prediction, that person is able to answer in this manner.
The roots of goodness of such a person are clear and manifest, and cannot be destroyed by gods or worldlings.
Chapter 61: The Dream Vow (In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Sixty-one: The Dream Vow; in the *Dān* [Old] version, Chapter on Non-Realization in a Dream). The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, does not crave the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, nor does he crave the three realms, and contemplates all dharmas as being like a dream, like an illusion, like an echo, like a mirage, and like a transformation, yet does not realize them as such—[this is the mark of a bodhisattva].”
Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, an irreversible one. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees in a dream the Buddha preaching the Dharma to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and others, and hears the Dharma from the Buddha, they immediately understands its inner meaning and practices in accordance with that Dharma.
Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, of one who is irreversible. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees in a dream the Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, emitting great radiance and soaring into the air, preaching the Dharma amidst a great assembly of bhikṣus, and manifesting great supernormal powers by creating emanated beings; or when they see in a dream an uprising of troops, the destruction of a village, the destruction of a city, or a fire breaking out; or when they see fierce and harmful beasts such as tigers, wolves, and lions; or when they see someone coming to cut off their head; or when they see the death of their parents, brothers, sisters, or various kinsmen, friends, and acquaintances—upon seeing such various matters of sorrow and suffering, they are neither startled nor terrified, nor do they feel distress.
Having awakened from the dream, he immediately reflected:
"The three realms are illusory; they are all like dreams.
When I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I too shall preach to sentient beings that the three realms are like dreams."
"Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, an irreversible one. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
How should one know that when this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, there will be no three evil realms in his land?
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts in a dream, he should form this thought:
"I shall apply myself with diligent vigor so that, when I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, there will be no three evil paths whatsoever in my land."
Why is this? Because these dreams and all phenomena are non-dual and without distinction.
Thus spoke Subhūti.
"You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees in a dream the fires of hell burning sentient beings and makes this vow:"
"If I am truly an *avaivartika*, this fire shall be extinguished; and so the fire was immediately extinguished.
If the fires of hell are thus extinguished, this is the mark of an *avaivartika*.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees a city or town on fire during the day, he forms this thought:
"In my dream, I shall see the conduct, characteristics, and signs of an *avaivartika* [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva."
"I truly possess this now," he thought,
and made this vow to himself:
"This fire shall be extinguished."
"If the fire is extinguished, you should know that this bodhisattva has received the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and dwells on the stage of avaivartika."
If the fire does not go out, it burns one house and spares another, burning one street and sparing another.

Subhūti, you should know that the karmic causes and conditions for destroying the Dharma have been thickly accumulated by those whose houses are burned; for this reason, one house is burned while another is spared. Because these sentient beings have experienced the remaining retribution for destroying the Dharma in their present lives, they are thus burned.
"Subhūti! For these reasons, you should know that this is the mark of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, of one who is irreversible.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"I shall now further explain for you the conduct, categories, and signs of an avaivartika [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva. Subhūti!
If a man or a woman is possessed by a non-human spirit, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:"

"If I have received the prediction of future Buddhahood from the Buddhas of the past, and my mind is pure as I seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practicing the pure right path, remaining far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and far removed from the thoughts of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, then I shall surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I will certainly obtain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—it is not that I shall not obtain it."

Within the lands of the ten directions, there are currently immeasurable Buddhas who know nothing that they do not know, see nothing that they do not see, understand nothing that they do not understand, and realize nothing that they do not realize.
"The Buddhas know that my profound resolve is firm and certain, and that I shall surely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By virtue of this sincere vow, if any man or woman is possessed by non-human spirits or afflicted by non-human spirits, those non-humans shall depart from afar.

Subhūti! If a non-human being does not depart despite such a vow made by this bodhisattva mahāsattva, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddhas of the past.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes such a vow and non-human beings depart, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already received the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the buddhas of the past.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, and these are the marks of irreversibility.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva remains far removed from the six pāramitās and the power of skillful means, and does not practice the four foundations of mindfulness for long, nor practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness for long, they have not yet entered the bodhisattva stage."
This bodhisattva is harassed by an evil Māra, whereupon the bodhisattva makes this vow:
"If it is true that I have received the prediction from the Buddhas, then this non-human being shall depart."
At that time, Māra the Evil One immediately employed skillful means, commanding the non-human beings to depart.
Because Māra possessed power that surpassed all non-human beings, they departed at once.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"By the power of my vow, the non-human being has departed.
Not knowing it was the power of Māra, and relying on this realization as proof, he treated other bodhisattvas with contempt and derision, saying these words:
"I have already received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas, whereas you have not yet received it.
Because they rely on such empty vows and lack the power of skillful means, they give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Because of this matter, they distance themselves from *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and distance themselves from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment).
Subhūti, you should know that such persons fall into two stages: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
Due to these causes and conditions of their vows, demonic activities arise.

Because this person does not associate with or rely upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and does not inquire about the marks of an avaivartika [bodhisattva], they become bound by Māra even more firmly.
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas have not practiced the six pāramitās for long and lack the power of skillful means, Subhūti!
One should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Subhūti,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet practiced the six pāramitās for long, and who has not yet entered the bodhisattva stage, is harassed by evil Māras?
Subhūti! Māra, the Evil One, manifests various forms and says to the bodhisattva:

"You have received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddhas; your name is such-and-such, your father’s name is such-and-such, your mother’s name is such-and-such, your brothers and sisters’ names are such-and-such, the names of your parents for seven generations back are as follows, and you were born in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a city, in such-and-such a village."
If he sees that a bodhisattva’s nature and conduct are gentle and mild, he says to that bodhisattva:
"In your previous lives, you were likewise gentle and mild.
If he sees one who is quick-tempered and impetuous, he then says:
"You were likewise so in your previous lives.
Or, if they see a bodhisattva practicing the conduct of an araṇya-dweller, they say:
"You also practiced the conduct of an araṇya-dweller in your previous lives."

If one sees a bodhisattva who begs for food, wears rag-robes, does not drink liquids after midday, eats in a single sitting, eats from a single bowl, dwells among corpses, dwells in the open air, stays beneath trees, remains constantly seated without lying down as if on a prepared seat, and accepts only the three robes; or if one sees them possessing few desires, being content, dwelling in seclusion, not anointing their feet, or speaking little, one should say to them:
"In your previous lives, you also practiced such conduct."
"Why is this? You now possess these merits of dhūta practice; you must have certainly possessed them in previous lives as well.

When that bodhisattva hears of these matters concerning his past lives and his name and clan, and hears the present praise of his dhūta merits, he immediately feels joy and gives rise to a mind of arrogance.
At that time, Māra spoke to the bodhisattva, saying:
"Since you possess such merit and such marks, you have indeed received from the Buddhas the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Subhūti! Māra, the Evil One, may appear before a bodhisattva in the guise of a bhikṣu, or in the form of a householder, or in the body of their father or mother, and speak thus:
'You have already received the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"Why is this? Because you possess all these marks of the qualities of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) Bodhisattva. Subhūti!

"Subhūti, you should know that for such a person, the actual practices, categories, and characteristics of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva mahāsattva as I have described them do not exist at all; this bodhisattva mahāsattva is possessed by Māra."

Why is this? Because such a person lacks forever the conduct, categories, and characteristics of an avaivartika; yet, having heard these names, they give rise to a mind of arrogance, treating others with contempt, mockery, and derision.
Subhūti! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva being possessed by Māra; you should know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not long practiced the six pāramitās does not know the characteristic of names, does not know the characteristic of form, and does not know the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
The Māra comes and says:
"When you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future life, you shall have such-and-such a name.
He speaks that title according to the person's original intention.
This bodhisattva, lacking wisdom and skillful means, thinks to himself:

"I previously also had this thought regarding the name by which I shall become a Buddha; this person speaks exactly as I thought, and what he says accords with my original thought. I must certainly have received a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas."

"Subhūti! Those characteristics, categories, and signs of non-retrogression that I have described are entirely absent in this person; they merely use empty names to mock, deceive, and despise others."
Because of these matters, they become distant from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, being far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā* and lacking the power of skillful means (*upāya*), and being separated from good spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) while associating with evil associates (*pāpamitra*), fall into two stages: the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
If there are those who repent within this very body, yet continue to wander through birth and death for a long time before returning to rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā,
they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi because they encounter spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) whom they constantly follow and draw near to.
If this person does not immediately repent for this body, they shall fall into one of two stages: either the stage of an Arhat or the stage of a Pratyekabuddha. Subhūti!

For example, if a bhikṣu violates even one of the four grave prohibitions, he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya; such a person shall not attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya in his present body.

Subhūti! This bodhisattva clings to empty names; the bodhisattva’s mind is likewise, for by treating others with contempt and disparaging them, one should know that this transgression is more grave than the four pārājika offenses of a bhikṣu.

Subhūti! Setting aside these grave offenses, their sin exceeds even that of the five heinous crimes; because they have received this title, they give rise to arrogance and treat others with contempt, mockery, and disdain.
If one gives rise to such a thought, you should know that its transgression is extremely grave.
A bodhisattva must be aware of all such subtle demonic activities, including those concerning names and so forth. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva dwells in a secluded place, such as a mountain, marsh, or remote wilderness, Māra comes to where the bodhisattva is and praises the dharma of seclusion, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"What you practice is the dharma of seclusion praised by the Buddha.
Subhūti, I do not praise this kind of seclusion, which is merely being in empty, secluded places such as mountains, marshes, or remote wildernesses.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If dwelling in empty, quiet mountains, marshes, or remote wildernesses were not the dharma of seclusion, what other dharma of seclusion could there be?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva remains far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, dwelling in secluded places such as mountains, marshes, or remote wildernesses, this is the practice of seclusion permitted by the Buddha."
Subhūti! This is the practice of detachment that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate.
Practicing this practice of detachment day and night is what is called a bodhisattva who practices detachment.

Subhūti! If a Māra preaches a dharma of seclusion—such as dwelling in empty, quiet places, mountain forests, or remote wilderness—and yet the mind of this bodhisattva remains amidst clamor and distraction, namely, by not distancing himself from the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha and not diligently practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, then this bodhisattva-mahāsattva will be unable to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This bodhisattva practices the dharma of seclusion as taught by an evil Māra; his mind is not pure, yet he looks down upon other bodhisattvas who dwell near cities, whose minds are pure, who are free from the distracted minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who lack all other various defiled and evil thoughts, and who are fully endowed with meditative concentration, liberation, wisdom, and supernormal powers.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who lack skillful means and are separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, even if they dwell for one year, a hundred thousand million years, or more than ten trillion years in a desolate wilderness hundreds of *yojanas* away—a place inhabited by birds, beasts, spirits, and *rākṣasas*—they do not know that this bodhisattva is practicing the dharma of detachment.

It is said that while bodhisattvas, by means of this practice of seclusion, should with a profound mind resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and engage in unadulterated conduct, there are those bodhisattvas who, though their conduct is actually one of clamor and distraction, rely upon and become attached to this seclusion; such is their practice, which is not permitted by the Buddha.
Subhūti! Regarding the truly detached dharma that I have taught, the bodhisattva does not abide within it, nor does he perceive the characteristic of detachment. Why is this?
Because they practice this emptiness and remain detached from it,
at that time an evil Māra comes and stays in the midst of the sky, praising them,
saying: "Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! This is the Dharma of true seclusion as taught by the Buddha; if you practice this seclusion, you will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva becomes attached to this seclusion and treats other pure bhikṣus seeking the Buddha-way with contempt, regarding them as a source of clamor and distraction.
They regard what is noisy as not noisy, and what is not noisy as noisy; they show disrespect toward those who deserve respect, and show respect toward those who do not deserve respect.
This bodhisattva says:
"A non-human being has thought of me and come to praise me; that which I practice is true seclusion.
As for those who dwell near a city, who would ever praise you?"
"For this reason, they hold other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in contempt.
Subhūti, you should know that such a person is called a 'bodhisattva-cāṇḍāla' who defiles all bodhisattvas."
Such a person merely resembles a bodhisattva, but in reality is a great thief among the devas and humans, and a thief within the robes of the śramaṇas.
Those who seek the path of the Buddha should not associate with such a person, nor should they offer them offerings or show them respect.
Why is this? Subhūti,
you should know that such a person falls into overweening pride.

For this reason, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes not to abandon all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, single-mindedly seeks *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and wishes to benefit all sentient beings, they should not associate with such a person, nor should they honor or make offerings to them.

The dharma of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is that one should always diligently seek self-benefit and feel weary of the world, with a mind constantly detached from the triple realm; yet toward such persons, one should give rise to the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, thinking:
"I practice the bodhisattva path and should not produce such faults or transgressions;
if they do arise, I shall swiftly extinguish them."
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should skillfully awaken to this matter and skillfully exert himself to emerge from within it. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with a profound mind, desires to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should draw near to, revere, and make offerings to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
who are the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All Buddhas are the good spiritual friends of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise the good spiritual friends of bodhisattvas."
Subhūti! Arhats are also the spiritual friends of bodhisattvas; these are the spiritual friends of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The six perfections are also the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are also the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends.
Subhūti! Suchness, the limit of reality, and the nature of phenomena are also a bodhisattva’s spiritual friends. Subhūti!
“The six perfections are the bodhisattva. “World-Honored One! The six perfections are the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;

the six perfections are the great illumination; the six perfections are the torch; the six perfections are knowledge; the six perfections are wisdom; the six perfections are the rescue; the six perfections are the refuge; the six perfections are the island; the six perfections are the ultimate path; the six perfections are the father and the mother.”
The four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge are also like this.
Why is that? The six perfections and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are likewise the parents of the Buddhas of the past.
The six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are likewise the parents of all Buddhas of the future and present throughout the ten directions.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
Because within the six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions are born.
For this reason, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, purify Buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity should study the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the four means of attraction (saṃgraha-vastu) in order to gather in sentient beings.
What are the four?
Generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation. Subhūti!
Because of these benefits, I say:

"The six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the World-Honored Ones for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are the path, the great illumination, the torch, knowledge, wisdom, rescue, refuge, the island, the ultimate path, and the father and mother."

“Subhūti! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes not to abide according to the instructions of others, who wishes to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, and who wishes to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, should study this Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā all dharmas are extensively explained; this is the place where Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Subhūti, the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom is like the characteristic of space. Subhūti,
the perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of non-existence."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is there some causal condition such that the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā* are also the characteristics of all dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
Just as is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*, so too are the characteristics of all dharmas.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
All dharmas are devoid of marks; their intrinsic nature is the mark of emptiness.
For this reason, Subhūti, as is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*, so too are the characteristics of all phenomena; that is to say, they are characterized by detachment and emptiness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are separated from all dharmas, and all dharmas are empty of all dharmas, how can one know whether sentient beings are defiled or pure?”

"Bhagavān! Dharmas that are free from characteristics are neither defiled nor pure; dharmas that have the characteristic of emptiness are neither defiled nor pure. Dharmas that are free from characteristics and have the characteristic of emptiness cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for there is no dharma that can be attained within the state of being free from characteristics or having the characteristic of emptiness."
World-Honored One!
Within the mark of detachment and within the mark of emptiness, there is no bodhisattva who attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One!
"How should I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do these sentient beings, throughout the long night, practice with a mind of 'I' and 'mine'?"
“So it is, World-Honored One!
Sentient beings have for a long night practiced with a mind of ‘I’ and ‘mine.
What do you think: does this mind of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ possess the characteristic of detachment?”
"Is it characterized by emptiness? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"The mind of 'I' and 'mine' is characterized by detachment and emptiness.
"What do you think? Do sentient beings wander through birth and death because of this mind of 'I' and 'mine'?"
"So it is, World-Honored One!
It is because of this mind of 'I' and 'mine' that sentient beings wander through birth and death. "So it is, Subhūti!"
Because sentient beings come and go within birth and death, it is known that they possess defilements and afflictions. Subhūti!

If sentient beings were without the mind of "self" or "what belongs to self," and without a mind of attachment, these sentient beings would no longer come and go within birth and death; and if they did not come and go within birth and death, they would have no defilements or afflictions.
"In this way, Subhūti, sentient beings possess purity.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they do not practice form, nor do they practice feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they do not practice inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; and they do not practice the ten powers of a buddha up to all-knowledge.”
Why is this? Because these dharmas cannot be apprehended; there is no one who practices, no place of practice, and no dharma of practice.
World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, none among the gods, humans, or asuras of all the worlds can subdue that bodhisattva mahāsattva;
nor can any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas equal them.
Why is this? Because no one can equal the state in which they dwell, namely, the stage of a bodhisattva,
World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with a mind corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge),
such that none can equal him. Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, he swiftly approaches sarvajñā.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Suppose all the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to attain human bodies, and having attained human bodies, they were all to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If there are good men or good women who, for as long as their lives last, provide offerings, pay respect, honor, and praise [the Buddha], and dedicate these roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
"By this cause and condition, would that person obtain much merit? Subhūti replied,
"Very much, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as much as the merit of a son or daughter of good family who, amidst the great assembly, teaches this Prajñāpāramitā, displaying, analyzing, illuminating, and expounding it, while also practicing in accordance with the Prajñāpāramitā and maintaining right mindfulness; their merit is greater."
It is even so for all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm.
Subhūti, what do you think?

Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were simultaneously to attain human bodies; having attained human bodies, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless absorptions; and were to teach them to attain the stage of a srotāpanna up to the stages of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha; and were to teach them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, dedicating these roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Would these sons of good family or daughters of good family acquire much merit? Subhūti replied:
“Very much, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“It is not as great as the merit obtained by a son or daughter of good family who, for the sake of sentient beings, teaches this profound Prajñāpāramitā, revealing, analyzing, illuminating, and expounding it, while never departing from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).”
It is the same even up to the trichiliocosm.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by not being separated from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), reaches the limit of all fields of merit.
Why is this? Because, with the exception of the Buddhas, there is no other dharma that possesses power equal to that of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Why is this?

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they give rise to great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; seeing that sentient beings are heading toward the realm of death, they give rise to great compassion; while practicing this path, they experience joy and give rise to great sympathetic joy; and by not dwelling with conceptual perceptions, they attain great equanimity.
Subhūti! This is the great light of wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
That which is called the great light of wisdom refers to the six pāramitās.

Subhūti! Although these good sons and good daughters have not yet become Buddhas, they are able to serve as a great field of merit for all sentient beings. They do not turn back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and regarding the offerings they receive—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine for illness, and all necessities of life—they practice with mindfulness in accordance with the *prajñā-pāramitā*. Thus, they are able to surely repay the kindness of their donors and swiftly approach *sarvajñatā*.

For this reason, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes not to consume in vain the offerings of the land, wishes to show sentient beings the path of the three vehicles, wishes to act as a great illumination for sentient beings, wishes to pull them out from the prison of the triple world, and wishes to grant eyes to all sentient beings, they should constantly practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
When constantly practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, if one wishes to say anything, one should speak only of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Having spoken of the Prajñāpāramitā, one should always maintain mindfulness of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Having constantly recollected the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should constantly practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, not allowing other thoughts to arise; day and night, one should diligently practice the mindfulness associated with the *prajñāpāramitā* without ceasing or resting.
Subhūti! It is as if, for example, a man who had never before obtained a maṇi jewel were to obtain one at a later time; having obtained it, he would be filled with great joy and exultation.
Later, he should lose it again, whereupon he would become deeply distressed and constantly keep that maṇi jewel in mind, thinking thus:
"How could I have suddenly forgotten this great treasure? Subhūti!
It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: they constantly recollect the prajñāpāramitā and do not depart from the mind of sarvajñatā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The nature of all thoughts is inherently detached; the nature of all thoughts is inherently empty."
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom remain inseparable from the mindfulness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)?
Within this state of detachment and emptiness, there is neither a bodhisattva nor mindfulness, nor is there omniscience.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands in this way that the nature of all dharmas is inherently detached and the nature of all dharmas is inherently empty—neither made by śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas, nor made by a buddha—and that the characteristics of all dharmas are eternally abiding: the dharma-characteristic, the dharma-abiding, the dharma-position, suchness, and the limit of reality; this is called a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā without departing from the mindfulness of sarvajñatā."
"Why is this? Because the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is inherently detached and inherently empty, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is itself detached and its nature is itself empty, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being equal to the *prajñāpāramitā*, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The bodhisattva mahāsattva is equal to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), neither increasing nor decreasing. Why is this?"
Because suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality neither increase nor decrease. Why is this?
Because the perfection of wisdom is neither one nor different.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, upon hearing such characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*, is not startled, does not sink into despondency, is not afraid, is not terrified, and has no doubt, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*;
you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly abide in the stage of *avaivartika*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
if the prajñāpāramitā is empty, non-existent, and not solid, does this constitute practicing the prajñāpāramitā?”
"No, Subhūti! "World-Honored One, apart from emptiness,
is there any other dharma that practices the prajñāpāramitā?"
"No, Subhūti! "World-Honored One, does this Prajñāpāramitā practice the Prajñāpāramitā?"
"No, Subhūti. "World-Honored One, does one practice the *prajñāpāramitā* apart from the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
"No, Subhūti! "World-Honored One, is form that which practices the perfection of wisdom?"
"No, Subhūti. "World-Honored One, are feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness practicing the perfection of wisdom?"
"No, Subhūti! "World-Honored One, are the six pāramitās the practice of the prajñāpāramitā?"
"No, Subhūti. "World-Honored One!
Are the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the practice of the perfection of wisdom?"
"No, Subhūti. "World-Honored One!

Is the mark of the emptiness of form, its deceptive and unreal nature, its non-existence, its lack of solidity, the suchness of form, the dharma-mark, the stability of dharmas, the fixed position of dharmas, and the limit of reality—these practicing the perfection of wisdom?"
"No, Subhūti! "World-Honored One!

Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; emptiness; the characteristic of being deceptive and unreal; non-existence; the characteristic of lack of solidity; suchness; the dharma-characteristic; the stability of dharmas; the fixed course of dharmas; and the limit of reality—these practicing the perfection of wisdom?"
"No, Subhūti. "World-Honored One! If all these dharmas do not practice the prajñāpāramitā, how can it be called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do you perceive any dharma that practices the perfection of wisdom?
"No, World-Honored One."
“Subhūti, do you see the perfection of wisdom as a place where a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice? “No, World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti! Can that dharma which you do not perceive be apprehended?
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! If a dharma cannot be apprehended, would that dharma arise?
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s forbearance regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this forbearance, they receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).”
Subhūti! This is called the fearless and unimpeded wisdom of all Buddhas.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this Dharma with diligent vigor yet does not attain great wisdom—the knowledge of all modes, namely the knowledge of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—[it would be impossible].
If it were not so, it would be impossible. Why is this?

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and thus, up until their attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they neither diminish nor regress.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas have the characteristic of non-arising, can one receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within this?”
"No, Subhūti! World-Honored One, can one receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within this characteristic of the arising of all dharmas?"
"No, Subhūti! "World-Honored One, since all dharmas have the characteristic of neither arising nor non-arising, can they receive the prediction of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"No, Subhūti! "World-Honored One! How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know all dharmas so as to receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Do you perceive any dharma that receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti replied: “No, World-Honored One.”
"I do not perceive any dharma that receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor do I perceive any dharma that attains it, any one who attains it,
or any place where it is attained. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing to be apprehended in any dharma, they do not form this thought:
"I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;..."
"By means of this matter, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called the locus of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is that?
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are free from all recollections and conceptual discriminations. Why is this?
Because within the perfection of wisdom, there are no conceptual discriminations or recollections.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume XVIII; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume XIX.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Sixty-Two: Māra’s Grief (The Eastern [Tang] edition calls this "The Chapter on Fellow Students").
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
This Prajñāpāramitā is profound and difficult to perceive, for it is ultimately free from all recollections, conceptualizations, and discriminations.

World-Honored One, those sentient beings who, upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, are able to uphold, read, recite, and explain it; who maintain right mindfulness, draw near to it, and practice according to its teaching—remaining untainted by other thoughts or mental factors until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—have not come from small merit.
The Buddha said, “So it is,
so it is! Those who hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and maintain it without admixture of other thoughts or mental factors have not come from minor merit.”
Kauśika! What do you think?
Suppose the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa were to accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions.

Furthermore, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family upholds this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, recites it, draws near to it, correctly contemplates it, and practices according to its teaching, they will surpass all beings in Jambudvīpa who have accomplished the ten paths of wholesome action up to the four formless absorptions, by a factor of a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a million, or even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Kauśika! The merit of these sons and daughters of good family who practice the prajñāpāramitā surpasses yours."
Śakra Devānām Indra said:

"The single production of the thought of enlightenment by these sons and daughters of good family surpasses my own; how much more so when they hear this Prajñāpāramitā, write it down, uphold it, read and recite it, correctly contemplate it, and practice according to its teaching."
These sons and daughters of good family who practice the *prajñāpāramitā* not only surpass me, but also surpass all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras;
they not only surpass all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras, but also surpass the *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, *anāgāmins*, *arhats*, and *pratyekabuddhas*;
they not only surpass these *srotāpannas* up to the *pratyekabuddhas*, but also surpass bodhisattvas who practice the five *pāramitās* while remaining far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Not only does one who practices the five *pāramitās* while remaining far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā* surpass [others], but one who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* while lacking the power of skillful means also surpasses them.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught; they do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, they constantly behold all Buddhas, and they swiftly approach the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
When a bodhisattva practices in this way, it is because they desire to pull out those sentient beings who are submerged in the long-flowing stream of saṃsāra.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, it is so that they do not train in the training of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, the gods of the Four Great Kings come to the bodhisattva’s abode and speak thus: “Good son!

You should train with diligence and speed. When you sit at the site of enlightenment and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you shall likewise receive the four alms-bowls that were received by all past buddhas; we shall bring them and present them to you, O Bodhisattva.”

Furthermore, all other devas—the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and from the Brahmā Heaven up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven—shall also make offerings.
The Buddhas of the ten directions also constantly keep in mind those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught.
For such bodhisattvas, all the perils, dangers, and hardships of the world shall never again exist;
and among the four hundred and four diseases that afflict all the worlds, none shall ever arise within the bodies of these bodhisattvas.
"Because they practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they obtain these merits in the present life.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought:
"Is Śakra Devānām Indra speaking this by his own power?"
"Is this spoken through the Buddha's spiritual power?
Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing what Ānanda was thinking, said to him:
"All that I have spoken is due to the Buddha's majestic spiritual power."
The Buddha told Ānanda: “So it is, so it is!
All that Śakra Devānām Indra has spoken is due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.”
Ānanda! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice and study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the evil Māras within the trichiliocosm give rise to doubt, thinking:
"Will this bodhisattva now attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"When one realizes the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) through the Middle Way, does one fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha? Furthermore, Ānanda,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), Māra again becomes deeply distressed and poisoned, as if an arrow had entered his heart.

At that time, Māra again unleashed great fires and winds rising from all four directions, wishing to cause the Bodhisattva’s mind to sink into terror and indolence, even to the point of giving rise to a single distracted thought regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
does Māra universally harass and disturb all bodhisattvas?"
"Are there those who are not disturbed?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are those who are disturbed, and there are those who are not disturbed."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
which bodhisattvas are tormented by Māra, the Evil One?”
The Buddha said:
"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, in previous lives, heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* but did not believe or understand it in their hearts.
For such bodhisattvas, Māra gains the opportunity."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
When a bodhisattva hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their mind may harbor doubt as to whether this *prajñāpāramitā* truly exists or truly does not exist."
In this way, Māra gains an opportunity over such a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Ānanda, there are bodhisattvas who distance themselves from spiritual friends and are influenced by evil associates; consequently, they do not hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Because they have not heard it, they do not know or see it, and they do not ask:
"How should one practice the *prajñāpāramitā*? How should one cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
"In this way, Māra the Evil One gains an opportunity over that bodhisattva. Furthermore, Ānanda,
if a bodhisattva distances himself from the *prajñāpāramitā* and accepts unwholesome dharmas, that bodhisattva provides an opportunity for Māra the Evil One."
Māra thought to himself:
"These people shall have companions; they shall fulfill my wish.
These bodhisattvas will fall themselves into the two stages, and they will also cause others to fall into the two stages."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If, when a bodhisattva hears the profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they say to others:
'This *prajñāpāramitā* is so profound that I cannot even reach its bottom; what use have you for hearing or studying this *prajñāpāramitā*? "
"In this way, Māra gains an opportunity over such a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva treats another bodhisattva with contempt, saying: "
"When [the Bodhisattva] says, 'I practice the Prajñāpāramitā and practice the seclusion of emptiness;
you lack such merit,' at that time,
Māra the Evil One is filled with great joy and leaps for gladness."

If there is a bodhisattva who, relying on his own name and lineage and being well-known to many people, looks down upon other bodhisattvas who practice virtue, that person lacks the true conduct, characteristics, signs, and merits of an avaivartika.
Because they lack such merit, various afflictions arise; merely attached to empty fame, they look down upon others, saying:
"You do not abide within the Dharma as I have attained it."
At that time, Māra the Evil One thought to himself:
"Now my realm and palaces are no longer empty; the three evil paths are flourishing.
Māra the Evil One then lent him his power, causing other people to believe and accept his words.
Because they accepted his words, they received and practiced this sutra, training according to its instructions.
While training according to those instructions, their various fetters and afflictions increased.
Because these people’s minds were inverted, all the actions of their body, speech, and mind resulted in evil retribution.
For this reason, the three evil realms increase, and the palaces of Māra’s retinue become more numerous.
Ānanda! Because Māra perceives these benefits, he is filled with great joy and leaps for gladness.
Ānanda! If those who practice the bodhisattva path engage in dispute and contention with those who seek the way of the śrāvaka, Māra will think:
"These are far removed from sarvajñatā."
"Ānanda! If bodhisattvas and bodhisattvas quarrel, fight, become angry, or revile one another, at that time Māra the Evil One will rejoice greatly and leap for joy, saying:
'Both have moved far away from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).'"
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prediction of enlightenment gives rise to a malicious mind toward a bodhisattva who has received such a prediction—quarreling, fighting, or reviling them—for as many moments as those thoughts arise, for that same number of kalpas shall he remain [in the lower realms]."
"If one does not abandon all-knowledge, only then will one fulfill such great adornments over that many kalpas.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
“Ānanda, having harbored such an evil mind for as many eons as those, could one possibly escape or be freed from it during that interval?
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!”

"Ānanda, although I have said that those seeking the bodhisattva path and śrāvakas may emerge from their offenses, if a person seeking the bodhisattva path quarrels, fights, becomes angry, reviles, or harbors resentment, and does not repent or relinquish it, I do not say there is an emergence; they must certainly undergo that same number of kalpas once again."
If one does not abandon omniscience, only then is there great adornment. Ānanda!
If this bodhisattva engages in strife, anger, or abuse, they should immediately repent and reform, forming this thought:
"I have suffered a great loss!

I shall humble myself for the sake of all sentient beings, bringing about reconciliation for them in both this life and future lives. I shall endure being trampled upon by all sentient beings, acting like a bridge, like one who is deaf, and like one who is mute."
How can one repay others with harsh speech?
I ought not to destroy this profound mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I must deliver all these suffering sentient beings; how then could I give rise to anger?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should bodhisattvas dwell together with one another?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“When Bodhisattvas dwell together, they should regard one another as they would the World-Honored One. Why is this?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
"These are my true companions, traveling together on the same ship.
They train as I train, namely in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)."
If a bodhisattva practices with mixed conduct and is separated from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), I should not train in such a manner.
If a bodhisattva practices without mixed conduct and is not separated from the mind of omniscience, I should likewise train in that manner.
“When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in this manner, this is called training together.
Chapter Sixty-Three: Equal Training, from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What, Subhūti, are those dharmas equal to which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train?
“Subhūti! [the Buddha said.]
