"I shall give birth to the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique dharmas"—this is conceptual proliferation.
"I shall attain all-knowledge"—this is conceptual proliferation.
"I shall sever all afflictions and habitual tendencies"—this is conceptual proliferation. Subhūti!
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, because form—whether permanent or impermanent—is beyond frivolous conceptualization, they do not engage in such conceptualization.

Whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are permanent or impermanent, they are not subject to frivolous conceptualization; therefore, one does not frivolously conceptualize them.
This extends up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which, being beyond frivolous conceptualization, is not frivolously conceptualized.
Why is this? Nature does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding nature; non-nature does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding non-nature.
Apart from nature and non-nature, no further phenomenon can be found that is called a proliferator, a proliferated phenomenon, or a locus of proliferation.
For this reason, Subhūti, form is without conceptual proliferation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even up to all-knowledge are without conceptual proliferation. It is thus, Subhūti.
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the non-conceptualized (*niṣprapañca*) perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“How is it that form is beyond conceptual proliferation?
And so on, up to how is all-knowledge beyond conceptual proliferation?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The nature of form is non-existent, up to and including the nature of all-knowledge.
Subhūti! If the nature of a dharma is non-existent, that is the absence of conceptual proliferation.”

For this reason, form (*rūpa*) cannot be the object of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which cannot be the object of conceptual proliferation. Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus practice the non-proliferated perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), at that time they enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas have no intrinsic nature, by what path does a bodhisattva practice to enter the stage of a bodhisattva?”
Is it by means of the path of the śrāvaka?
Is it by means of the path of the pratyekabuddha?
Or is it by means of the path of the Buddha?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“One does not enter the bodhisattva stage by means of the path of the śrāvaka, nor by means of the path of the pratyekabuddha, nor by means of the path of the Buddha; rather, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the bodhisattva stage by training thoroughly in all paths.”

Subhūti! It is like an *aṣṭamaka* who first studies all the paths and then enters the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*); before attaining the fruit, he first gives rise to the path leading to that fruit.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: having first studied all paths extensively, he then enters the Bodhisattva stage; yet, even before attaining all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he first gives rise to the Vajra-like Samādhi. At that time, by means of the wisdom associated with a single thought-moment, he attains all-knowledge.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva must train thoroughly in all paths in order to enter the bodhisattva stage—namely, the path of the eight persons, the one heading toward the fruit of stream-entry and the one who has attained stream-entry; the one heading toward the fruit of once-returning and the one who has attained once-returning; the one heading toward the fruit of non-returning and the one who has attained non-returning; the one heading toward arhatship and the one who has attained arhatship; as well as the path of the pratyekabuddha and the path of the Buddha—if these various paths are each distinct from one another, [how can it be said that he enters by training in them all]?”
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva must fully train in all paths before entering the bodhisattva stage, then that bodhisattva, upon being born into the path of the eightfold [worldlings], would become an ‘eight-person’; upon being born into the path of vision, would become a srotāpanna; upon being born into the path of cultivation, would become a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat; and if born into the path of a pratyekabuddha, would become a pratyekabuddha.”
"Bhagavān! It is impossible that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should first become one of the eight persons and only thereafter enter the bodhisattva stage.
It is also impossible that one should attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) without having entered the bodhisattva stage."
It is impossible that one could become a srotāpanna, and so on up to becoming a pratyekabuddha, and only thereafter enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
It is also impossible that one could attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) without having entered the stage of a bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!
How should I understand how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully studied all paths, enters the bodhisattva stage?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It is so, it is so! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were to become one of the eight persons, attain the fruit of srotāpanna, and so on up to attaining the fruit of arhatship or the path of a pratyekabuddha, and only thereafter enter the bodhisattva stage—such a thing is impossible."
It is impossible that one who has not entered the stage of a bodhisattva should attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the six perfections and contemplates them with wisdom as they pass beyond the eight stages.
What are the eight stages?

They are the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of thinness, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having already accomplished what was to be done, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
Passing directly through, one enters the stage of a bodhisattva by means of the knowledge of the modes of the path.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, one eradicates all afflictions and their habitual tendencies by means of the knowledge of all modes.
Subhūti! Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to these eight persons, that is the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to an arhat, and whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to a pratyekabuddha—all these are the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way in the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they enter the bodhisattva stage by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).

Having entered the bodhisattva stage, they sever all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) by means of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and thereby attain the path of the Buddha.
Thus it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully trained in and perfected all the dharmas, should attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one benefits sentient beings with the fruit [of that attainment].
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The path taught by the World-Honored One is the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, and the path of the Buddhas.
What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the aspects of the path?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to the pure wisdom of all modes of the path.
Subhūti, what is this pure wisdom of the modes of the path?”
If there are any characteristics of phenomena that can be manifested, the bodhisattva should correctly know them.
Having correctly known them, he should expound and reveal them to others, so that all sentient beings may attain understanding.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand all sounds and languages, and using these sounds to preach the Dharma, he shall pervade the trichiliocosm like the nature of an echo.
For this reason, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should first fully train in all paths. Once they have perfected the knowledge of paths,

they should discern and know the deep intentions of sentient beings— namely, those in the hells, the path to hell, the causes for hell, and the fruits of hell— and they should understand these and obstruct them [from arising].
The realms of animals and hungry ghosts, the causes for animal and hungry ghost rebirths, and the fruits of animal and hungry ghost rebirths should be understood and obstructed.
The causes and fruits of the realms of nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and asuras should be understood and obstructed.
The causes and effects of the human realm should be known.

The causes and effects of the various heavenly realms should be known: those of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and the paths of the Brahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Asaṃjñisattva Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—their causes and effects should be known.

The paths of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should be understood in terms of cause and effect.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—these should be understood as cause and effect.

The gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion—their causes and effects should be understood.
By means of this path, the bodhisattva causes sentient beings to enter the path of srotāpanna, up to the paths of arhat and pratyekabuddha, and even the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s pure knowledge of the aspects of the paths.
Having trained in this knowledge of the aspects of the paths, the bodhisattva enters into the characteristics of the deep minds of sentient beings.
Having entered, he teaches the Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings as appropriate, and his words are not in vain. Why is this?

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully know the characteristics of the faculties of sentient beings, and they know the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings, as well as the destinies of their births and deaths.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner. Why is that?
All dharmas that assist the path to goodness enter into the Prajñāpāramitā; they are what all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should practice.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the four foundations of mindfulness up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—all these dharmas—are neither conjoined nor dispersed, formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive, having but one mark, which is the so-called ‘markless’.”
World-Honored One!
How can these factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) take hold of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
World-Honored One!

This is neither conjoined nor dispersed; it is without color, without form, and without resistance—the single characteristic known as the characteristicless dharma. It is without anything to be grasped and without anything to be relinquished.
It is, for example, like space, which has nothing to grasp and nothing to relinquish.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
All phenomena are empty of their own characteristics; there is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be relinquished.

Subhūti, because there are sentient beings who do not know that all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics, one manifests the factors conducive to enlightenment for the sake of these beings.
causing them to reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding all form, feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness, and all the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*..."
The perfection of giving, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom;
all forms of emptiness from internal emptiness and external emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight [liberations].
The factors of the noble path, the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive concentrations,
the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness,
great compassion, all-knowledge, and all such dharmas— within these noble dharmas, none are joined with [the self].
It is dispersed, formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive; it has but one characteristic, which is called "signlessness.
It is for the sake of worldly convention that I speak of this for sentient beings so they may understand it, and not by way of the ultimate truth.
Subhūti! Within all these dharmas, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in accordance with the Dharma through wisdom and vision.
Having so trained, they should discern which dharmas are to be applied and which are not to be applied.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
Which dharmas, having been analyzed by a bodhisattva, should be applied and which should not be applied?
The Buddha said:
“The Dharma of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should not be applied through analytical knowledge;
the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) should be applied through analytical knowledge. It is thus, Subhūti!”
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom within these noble dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason are they called 'noble dharmas' (āryadharma)?
What are these noble dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all buddhas, are neither conjoined nor disjoined with desire, hatred, and delusion; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the view of a self-identity, the grasping at precepts and rituals, or doubt; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with sensual attachment, aversion, attachment to the form realm, attachment to the formless realm, pride, or ignorance; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, or with the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with inner emptiness up to great compassion, or with the conditioned nature and the unconditioned nature.”
Why is this? Because all these dharmas are without form, without shape, and without resistance; they have but a single characteristic, which is the so-called "absence of characteristics.

A formless dharma does not conjoin with nor disperse from a formless dharma; a shapeless dharma does not conjoin with nor disperse from a shapeless dharma; an unobstructed dharma does not conjoin with nor disperse from an unobstructed dharma; a single-characteristic dharma does not conjoin with nor disperse from a single-characteristic dharma; and a dharma without characteristics does not conjoin with nor disperse from a dharma without characteristics.
Subhūti! This is formless, shapeless, and unimpeded; it is a single characteristic, namely, the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*).
The *prajñāpāramitā* is that which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study; having studied it, they do not apprehend the characteristics of any phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not train in the marks of form?”
Does one not train in the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Does one not train in the characteristics of the eye up to the mind, nor in the characteristics of forms up to phenomena;
does one not train in the characteristics of the earth element up to the consciousness element?
One does not study the characteristics of the *dānapāramitā*, nor the characteristics of the *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, or *prajñāpāramitā*;
one does not study the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*);
and one does not study the characteristics of the first dhyāna up to the characteristics of the fourth dhyāna.
One does not study the characteristics of loving-kindness up to the characteristic of equanimity;
one does not study the characteristics of infinite space up to the characteristics of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
one does not study the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the characteristics of the eightfold noble path.
One does not study the characteristics of the samādhi of emptiness, nor the characteristics of the signless and wishless samādhis;
one does not study the characteristics of the eight liberations, the nine successive concentrations;

one does not study the characteristics of the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, or the characteristics of great kindness and great compassion.
Do you not study the characteristics of the noble truth of suffering, nor those of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path?
Do you not study the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination in their direct and reverse order?
And do you not study the characteristics of conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena?
World-Honored One!

If they do not study the characteristics of all dharmas, how can Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the characteristics of all dharmas—whether conditioned or unconditioned—and having so studied, transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
If one does not transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, how can one enter the bodhisattva stage?
If one does not enter the bodhisattva stage, how can one ever attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)?
If one does not attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), how can one turn the wheel of Dharma?
If one does not turn the wheel of Dharma, how can one deliver sentient beings from birth and death by means of the three vehicles?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If all dharmas truly possessed marks, the bodhisattva should train in those marks. Subhūti!”
Because all dharmas are in reality without marks, without color, without form, and without obstruction— having but a single mark,
which is the so-called "markless. For this reason, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in marks, nor does he train in the markless.
"Why is this? Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, the single characteristic of all phenomena remains eternally present.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas have neither marks nor lack of marks, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?”
If one does not cultivate the perfection of wisdom, one cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
if one does not transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one cannot enter the rank of a bodhisattva;
and if one does not enter the rank of a bodhisattva, one will not attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
If one does not attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one cannot obtain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the bodhisattvas;
if one does not obtain the supernormal powers of the bodhisattvas, one cannot purify buddha-fields or bring sentient beings to maturity;
if one does not purify buddha-fields or bring sentient beings to maturity, one cannot attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If one does not attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one cannot turn the wheel of Dharma;

if one does not turn the wheel of Dharma, one cannot cause sentient beings to attain the fruit of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or arhatship, nor the path of a pratyekabuddha;

one cannot cause them to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), nor can one cause sentient beings to obtain the merit of giving, nor the merit of maintaining ethical discipline or cultivating meditative concentration.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
All dharmas are signless; they are neither of one mark nor of different marks.”
"If one cultivates signlessness, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said,
"World-Honored One!"
“How is it that cultivating the signless is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said,
“Cultivating the disintegration of all dharmas is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the cultivation of the disintegration of all dharmas is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said:

"To cultivate the destruction of form is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom; to cultivate the destruction of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the eye, and the destruction of the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and phenomena, is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom."
To cultivate the destruction of the dharma of form, and the destruction of sound, odor, taste, touch, and dharmas, is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
To cultivate the destruction of the contemplation of impurity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the first dhyāna, and the destruction of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To cultivate the destruction of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the destruction of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of cessation, and mindfulness of ānāpāna until they are destroyed, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

To cultivate the mark of impermanence, the mark of suffering, the mark of non-self, and the mark of emptiness; the mark of accumulation, the mark of cause, the mark of arising, and the mark of condition; the mark of cessation, the mark of extinction, the mark of excellence, and the mark of emergence; and the mark of the path, the mark of correctness, the mark of the track, and the mark of detachment—when these are brought to destruction, this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

To cultivate the destruction of the twelve links of dependent origination, to cultivate the destruction of the marks of a self, a sentient being, and a life span, and even to cultivate the destruction of the marks of a knower and a seer—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
To cultivate the destruction of the marks of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To cultivate the destruction of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the destruction of the samādhi with applied thought and sustained thought, the samādhi without applied thought but with sustained thought, and the samādhi without applied thought and without sustained thought, is the cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā.
To cultivate the destruction of the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

To cultivate the destruction of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), worldly knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
The cultivation of the destruction of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);

the cultivation of the destruction of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the destruction of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence—this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
To cultivate the destruction of the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat, as well as the path of the pratyekabuddha, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To cultivate the destruction of all-encompassing wisdom is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To cultivate the destruction of the eradication of all habitual tendencies of affliction is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

what is meant by ‘cultivating the destruction of form,’ up to and including ‘cultivating the destruction of all habitual tendencies of afflictions through their abandonment’— this being the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not to conceive of the existence of dharmas with form is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom."

Not to conceive of the existence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to not conceiving of the existence of the dharma that severs all habitual tendencies of affliction—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this? One who possesses the notion of dharmas does not cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*. Subhūti!

One who possesses the notion of dharmas does not cultivate the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti,
because such a person is attached to dharmas and does not practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to and including the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
For one who clings in this way, there is no liberation, no Path, and no Nirvana.

One who possesses the notion of dharmas does not cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path; they do not cultivate the samādhi of emptiness, nor do they cultivate up to the knowledge of all modes.
"Why is this? Because such a person is attached to dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is existence? What is non-existence?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Duality is the existence of dharmas; non-duality is the non-existence of dharmas.
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!”
"What are these two?
The Buddha said:
"The characteristic of form is duality; the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are duality."
The characteristic of the eye and so forth up to the characteristic of the mind are two; the characteristic of form and so forth up to the characteristic of phenomena are two;

the perfection of giving and so forth up to the characteristic of a Buddha and the characteristic of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, as well as the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned nature, are two.
Subhūti! All marks are dualistic;

all that is dualistic consists of existent dharmas. As soon as there are existent dharmas, there is birth and death; as soon as there is birth and death, one cannot escape from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.

For this reason, Subhūti, you should know that for one who perceives dualistic marks, there is no perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); there is no path and no fruit, up to and including no "patience in accordance with truth" (anulomikī kṣānti). How much less could there be the perception of the mark of form, up to the perception of the mark of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)?

If there were no cultivation of the path, how could one attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, the path of a pratyekabuddha, unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and the eradication of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies?
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-two; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 75: The Chapter on the Three Times (The *Dānapāramitā-sūtra* title: The Chapter on Successive Practice).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If there were any marks of dharmas, one would not even attain the patience of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti), let alone attain the Way.
World-Honored One!
If there are no marks of dharmas, will one then attain the patience of conformity?

Whether it be the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, the stage of the Buddha, or the path of cultivation—by means of this path of cultivation, should one sever the afflictions?
Because of these afflictions, one cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha to enter the rank of a bodhisattva.
If one does not enter the rank of a bodhisattva, then one cannot attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Without attaining all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one cannot attain the severance of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
World-Honored One,
if there were no characteristic of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), then these dharmas would not arise.
"If these dharmas were not produced, then one could not attain all-knowledge.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
"If there were no dharmas, then there would be the patient acceptance that accords with reality (anulomikī kṣānti), up to the severing of all habitual tendencies of affliction.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, is there any characteristic of dharmas—namely, the characteristic of form up to the characteristic of consciousness;

the characteristic of the eye up to the characteristic of the mind; the characteristic of forms up to the characteristic of phenomena; and the characteristic of the eye-element up to the characteristic of the mind-consciousness-element?
The characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the characteristics of all-knowledge;

whether it be the characteristic of form or the characteristic of the cessation of form, up to the characteristic of consciousness or the characteristic of the cessation of consciousness; the same applies to the twelve bases and the eighteen elements;

whether it be the characteristic of ignorance or the characteristic of the cessation of ignorance, up to the characteristic of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair, or the characteristic of the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.

Whether it be the mark of desire or the mark of the abandonment of desire; the mark of hatred or the mark of the abandonment of hatred; the mark of delusion or the mark of the abandonment of delusion;

the mark of suffering or the mark of the abandonment of suffering; the mark of origination or the mark of the abandonment of origination; the mark of cessation or the mark of the abandonment of cessation; the mark of the path or the mark of the abandonment of the path;
and even up to the mark of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) or the mark of the abandonment of the habitual tendencies of all afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*).
The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, there is neither the mark of a dharma nor the mark of a non-dharma; this is precisely the bodhisattva’s conformative patience.”
If there is no mark of existence and no mark of non-existence, that itself is the cultivation of the path and also the fruit of the path.
Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the existence of dharmas is the bodhisattva path, and the non-existence of dharmas is the bodhisattva fruit.
"For this reason, you should know that all dharmas have the nature of non-existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

If all phenomena have the nature of non-existence, how does the Buddha, by knowing that all phenomena have the nature of non-existence, attain buddhahood and achieve sovereign power over all phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
All dharmas have the nature of non-existence.”

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I cultivated the six pāramitās; free from all desires and free from evil, unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, I entered the first dhyāna, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna.

Thus, regarding these dhyānas and their factors, one does not grasp at signs; one does not think, "I have these dhyānas," nor does one relish the flavor of dhyāna, nor does one conceive of attaining these dhyānas. One practices the four dhyānas with undefiled purity, thinking: "In regard to these dhyānas, I do not accept their karmic retribution."

Abiding in the four dhyānas, he gives rise to the five supernormal powers—the power of the body, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, the power of recollecting past lives, and the divine eye—yet he does not grasp at the signs of these supernormal powers, does not dwell on the thought that he possesses them, does not relish the flavor of these powers, and does not conceive of them as attainments.
Subhūti, I do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding these five supernormal powers.

At that time, by means of wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, I attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—namely, the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of its Origin, the Noble Truth of its Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path. I accomplished the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion; I became a Buddha and distinguished the three categories of sentient beings:
those fixed in the right, those fixed in the wrong, and those who are undetermined.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it, World-Honored One, that within the non-existent nature of all dharmas you give rise to the four dhyānas and the six supernormal powers, and yet, although there are no sentient beings, you differentiate them into the three groups?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If those sensual desires, evil, and unwholesome states possessed any intrinsic nature—whether an intrinsic nature of their own or an extrinsic nature—then when I was formerly practicing as a bodhisattva, I would not have been able to contemplate the non-existence of those sensual desires, evil, and unwholesome states and enter the first dhyāna.”

Because all desires, evil, and unwholesome dharmas lack intrinsic nature—whether by way of self-nature or other-nature—and because they are all of the nature of non-existence, when I was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, I abandoned all desires, evils, and unwholesome dharmas, entering the first dhyāna and so on up to the fourth dhyāna.

Subhūti! If the various supernormal powers possessed an intrinsic nature—whether an intrinsic nature or an extrinsic nature—I would not have been able to know that these supernormal powers are of a non-existent nature and thereby attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! Because supernatural powers have no intrinsic nature—whether as an intrinsic nature or an extrinsic nature—they are all of the nature of non-existence.
For this reason, the Buddhas, knowing that supernatural powers are of the nature of non-existence, attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all dharmas have the nature of non-existence, yet attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the four dhyānas and the five supernormal powers.”

"Bhagavān! How do newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice in sequence, train in sequence, and follow the path in sequence within the non-existence of all phenomena? By means of this sequential practice, sequential training, and sequential path, how do they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears from the Buddhas at the outset, or hears from bodhisattvas who have made offerings to many Buddhas, or hears from arhats, or from anāgāmins, or from sakṛdāgāmins, or from srotāpannas:

‘It is because of attaining non-existence that one is a Buddha; it is because of attaining non-existence that one is an arhat, an anāgāmin, a sakṛdāgāmin, or a srotāpanna; all noble ones (ārya) receive their names because they have attained non-existence.’”
"All conditioned phenomena are of a non-existent nature; indeed, there is not even as much as a hair’s tip of anything that exists.
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this, he reflects:

"If all dharmas are without nature, it is because they have attained a state of non-existence that one is a Buddha, and so on, up to: it is because they have attained a state of non-existence that one is a srotāpanna."
Whether I should attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* or not, all dharmas are eternally without intrinsic nature.
Why then should I not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"Once I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall cause all sentient beings who course in signs to abide in that which is non-existent. Subhūti!
After the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has reflected in this way, they resolve their mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.

The sequential practice, sequential training, and sequential path undertaken by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are the same as the path traveled by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, through which they attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

A bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind should study the six pāramitās, namely: the dāna-pāramitā, the śīla-pāramitā, the kṣānti-pāramitā, the vīrya-pāramitā, the dhyāna-pāramitā, and the prajñā-pāramitā.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), he personally practices generosity, teaches others to practice generosity, praises the merit of giving, and joyfully commends those who practice generosity.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of giving, one attains great wealth.

This bodhisattva, having distanced himself from a stingy mind, bestows upon sentient beings food and drink, clothing, incense, flowers, and necklaces; houses, bedding, and lamps; and all manner of necessary articles for sustaining life, providing them all completely.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice this giving and maintain this morality, they are born among gods and humans and attain great nobility.
By virtue of this morality and giving, they obtain the aggregate of meditative concentration.

By means of this generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, one attains the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Because of these aggregates of generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, this bodhisattva transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the rank of a bodhisattva.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, one purifies buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity, attaining all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Having attained all-knowledge, one turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he delivers sentient beings from birth and death by means of the three vehicles.
Thus, Subhūti, through this giving, the bodhisattva practices in sequence, trains in sequence, and follows the path in sequence; yet all these things are unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature does not exist. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

From the first moment they resolve their minds on enlightenment, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas personally practice the precepts, teach others to uphold the precepts, praise the merit of upholding the precepts, and joyfully extol those who practice the precepts.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of observing the precepts and practicing generosity, one is born among gods and humans and attains great honor and nobility.

Seeing those who are impoverished, one bestows wealth and goods upon them; those who do not observe the precepts, one instructs to observe them; those with distracted minds, one instructs to practice meditative concentration; those who are ignorant, one instructs to cultivate wisdom; those lacking liberation, one instructs to attain liberation; and those lacking the knowledge and vision of liberation, one instructs to attain the knowledge and vision of liberation.

By means of this morality, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the rank of bodhisattvas.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, one attains the purification of buddha-fields.
Having purified the buddha-fields, one brings sentient beings to maturity.
Having brought sentient beings to maturity, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Having attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of this upholding of precepts, the bodhisattva practices in sequence, trains in sequence, and follows the path in sequence; yet all these things are unapprehendable. Why is this?
Because all dharmas lack intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, from the very beginning,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), teaches others to practice patience, praises the merit of patience, and rejoices in praising those who practice patience."

When practicing the perfection of patience, one gives to sentient beings so as to satisfy them each, and teaches them to uphold the precepts, to practice meditative concentration, and even to attain the knowledge and vision of liberation.

By virtue of these causes and conditions of giving, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, one transcends the stages of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas and enters the rank of Bodhisattvas.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, one attains a pure buddha-field.
Having attained a pure buddha-field, one brings sentient beings to maturity.
Having brought sentient beings to maturity, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Having attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he delivers sentient beings from birth and death by means of the three vehicles. Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the perfection of patience, the bodhisattva practices in sequence, trains in sequence, and follows the path in sequence; yet all these things are unapprehendable. Why is this?
Because all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

"Furthermore, Subhūti, from the very beginning, a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices vigor (*vīrya*), teaches others to practice vigor, praises the merit of practicing vigor, and joyfully commends those who practice vigor; yet even these things are ultimately unapprehendable, because they lack intrinsic nature."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, from the very beginning, a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally enters the dhyānas, the immeasurable minds, and the formless attainments; they also teach others to enter the dhyānas, the immeasurable minds, and the formless attainments; they praise the merits of entering the dhyānas, the immeasurable minds, and the formless attainments; and they joyfully praise those who practice the dhyānas, the immeasurable minds, and the formless attainments."

This bodhisattva, dwelling in the various meditative concentrations and immeasurable states of mind, bestows gifts upon sentient beings so as to satisfy each one, instructing them to uphold the precepts, and instructing them in meditative concentration and wisdom.

By means of these causes and conditions of giving, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the rank of a bodhisattva.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, one purifies the buddha-fields.
Having purified the buddha-fields, one brings sentient beings to maturity.
Having brought sentient beings to maturity, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Having attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he delivers all sentient beings by means of the three vehicles of the Dharma.
Yet even these matters are ultimately unattainable, because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, from the very beginning,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, bestowing gifts upon sentient beings so as to satisfy them each, and instructing them to uphold ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation."

When this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they personally practice the six perfections, and also teach others to practice the six perfections; they praise the merits of the six perfections and rejoice in and praise those who practice the six perfections.

By means of these causes and conditions—the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom—as well as the power of skillful means, this bodhisattva transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the rank of a bodhisattva.
Up to this point, these things are unattainable because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist. Subhūti,
this is called the sequential practice, the sequential training, and the sequential path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there is the sequential practice, the sequential training, and the sequential path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. From the very beginning, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), resolves upon the non-existent nature of all phenomena and cultivates the six recollections: namely, recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṃgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of relinquishment, and recollection of the devas."
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of the Buddha?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva recollects the Buddha not by means of form, nor by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? It is because form has no intrinsic nature, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is non-existent.
Why is this? Because there is no recollection, this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the Buddha, they do not recollect him by means of the thirty-two marks, nor do they recollect his golden body, nor his fathom-wide radiance, nor his eighty secondary characteristics.
Why is this? Because the self-nature of this Buddha-body does not exist.
If a dharma lacks self-nature, it is non-existent.
Why is this? Because there is no recollection, this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

One should not recollect the Buddha by means of the aggregate of precepts; one should not recollect the Buddha by means of the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Why is this? Because this assembly has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is non-existent.
Why is this? Because there is no recollection, this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

One should not contemplate the Buddha by means of the ten powers; one should not contemplate the Buddha by means of the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, or the eighteen unique dharmas; nor should one contemplate the Buddha by means of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Why is this? Because these dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, it is not a [real] dharma.
To be without mental recollection is to be mindful of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, one should not be mindful of the Buddha by means of the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination."
Why is this? Because the self-nature of these dharmas of dependent origination does not exist.
If a dharma lacks self-nature, it is a non-dharma.
To be without mental engagement is to recollect the Buddha.

Thus, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should recollect the Buddha in this way; this is the sequential practice, the sequential training, and the sequential path of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind upon enlightenment.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the gradual practice, the gradual training, and the gradual path, is able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; they cultivate the samādhi of emptiness, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi, up to and including all-knowledge, because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent.
This bodhisattva knows that the nature of all phenomena is non-existent; therein there is neither existence nor non-existence.
"Subhūti, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Dharma?"

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not dwell upon wholesome dharmas, nor does he dwell upon unwholesome dharmas; he does not dwell upon dharmas with definite marks, nor does he dwell upon dharmas without definite marks; he does not dwell upon mundane dharmas, nor does he dwell upon supramundane dharmas; he does not dwell upon pure dharmas, nor does he dwell upon impure dharmas; he does not dwell upon noble dharmas, nor does he dwell upon the dharmas of ordinary persons; he does not dwell upon out-flowing dharmas, nor does he dwell upon non-out-flowing dharmas; he does not dwell upon dharmas bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and he does not dwell upon conditioned dharmas or unconditioned dharmas.
Why is this? Because these dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, it is a non-dharma.
To have no mental preoccupation is to be mindful of the Dharma.
By training in this mindfulness of the Dharma, because all things are of the nature of non-existence, one shall eventually attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
When this bodhisattva attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they realize that all dharmas are of the nature of non-existence.
Within this nature of non-existence, there is neither the mark of existence nor the mark of non-existence.
Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the mindfulness of dharmas; yet within these dharmas, there is not even the slightest bit of mindfulness, let alone mindfulness of dharmas.
“Subhūti! How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate mindfulness of the Saṃgha? Subhūti!”

Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the unconditioned nature of the Saṃgha, he discerns that there is a community of the Buddha’s disciples; within this, there is not even the slightest thought [of grasping], let alone the thought of a "Saṃgha."
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the recollection of the Saṅgha. Subhūti,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of ethical discipline?

Subhūti! From the first moment they resolve their minds [on awakening], bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should be mindful of noble precepts: precepts that are unimpaired, precepts that are without fissures, precepts that are without blemish, precepts that are without turbidity, precepts that are without attachment, precepts that are sovereign, precepts praised by the wise, precepts that are complete, and precepts that accord with meditative concentration.
One should contemplate that this precept is of a non-existent nature, such that there is not even the slightest thought; how much less, then, can one think of a precept? "Subhūti!
From the first moment of generating the aspiration, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate relinquishment."

Whether one contemplates one's own relinquishment or the relinquishment of others, whether it be the relinquishment of wealth, the relinquishment of the Dharma, or the relinquishment of afflictions—one observes that this relinquishment is unattainable;
thus, there is not even the slightest thought, let alone the thought of relinquishment.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the recollection of relinquishment. Subhūti!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the devas? Subhūti,
a bodhisattva forms this thought:

"Whatever faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom the gods of the Four Great Kings possess, by virtue of which they pass away from this world and are reborn in that celestial realm—I too possess such faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom."

"Whatever faith, ethical discipline, generosity, learning, and wisdom exist even up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), and by virtue of which one passes away from this world and is reborn in that celestial realm—I too possess such faith, ethical discipline, generosity, learning, and wisdom."

"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate these devas; yet within the nature of non-existence, there is not even the slightest bit of contemplation, let alone the contemplation of devas."
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these six recollections, this is called sequential practice, sequential training, and the sequential path.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are of the nature of non-existence—namely, from mindfulness of form up to consciousness; from the eye up to the mind; from forms up to dharmas; and from the eye-element up to the mind-consciousness-element—all these are of the nature of non-existence.”

The perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-knowledge—all these are of the nature of non-existence.
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are of a non-existent nature, then there would be no path, no wisdom, and no fruit.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Do you see this nature of form as truly existent? ...
[and so on] ... up to: do you see the nature of all-knowledge as truly existent? Subhūti replied:
“I do not see them, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If you do not see that all dharmas truly exist, why do you ask such a question?”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!

I do not dare to have any doubt regarding this Dharma; however, it is for the sake of those bhikṣus in future ages who seek the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the bodhisattva.”
Such a person will speak thus:
"If all phenomena have the nature of non-existence, who is defiled and who is pure? Who is bound and who is liberated?
Because they neither know nor understand this, they violate the precepts, violate right view, violate dignified conduct, and violate pure livelihood.
Because this person has destroyed these matters, they shall fall into the three evil realms.
World-Honored One!
I fear that such things will occur in future ages; for this reason, I ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"I have faith in this Dharma; I neither doubt nor regret it. Chapter 76:

A Single Thought-Moment (*Ekacitta*) In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Seventy-Six: A Single Thought-Moment (in the "Dan" edition, this is titled "The Chapter on the Six Perfections of Untainted Practice"). Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If the nature of all dharmas is non-existent, for what benefit does the bodhisattva perceive that he should resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of sentient beings?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the nature of all dharmas is non-existent, for this reason, the bodhisattva seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of sentient beings."
Why is this? Subhūti! Those who have attainment and those who have attachment are difficult to liberate.
“Subhūti! For those who grasp at signs, there is no path, there is no fruit, and there is no anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For one who has no marks of attainment, is there a path, is there a fruit, and is there *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? “Subhūti!”
Non-attainment is itself the Path, itself the Fruit, and itself Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indestructible.
If one who seeks non-attainment wishes to attain the Path, wishes to attain the Fruit, or wishes to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they wish to destroy the nature of phenomena.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the dharma that is non-apprehensible is itself the path, itself the fruit, and itself unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), how can there be the bodhisattva’s first stage through to the tenth stage?”
What is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
What is the possession of supernormal powers obtained as a result of maturation (*vipākaja-abhijñā*)?
And what is the possession of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom obtained as a result of maturation?

Abiding within these dharmas of karmic fruition, one is able to bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, and make offerings to all Buddhas with clothing, food and drink, incense, flowers, necklaces, dwellings, bedding, lamps and candles, as well as various other requisites for life.

Until one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this merit shall not cease; even after *parinirvāṇa*, it continues until the *śarīra* relics and the disciples receive offerings, at which point it finally comes to an end?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because all dharmas have the characteristic of being unobtainable, one attains the first stage of a bodhisattva up to the tenth stage.

There are supernormal powers obtained as a result of maturation, as well as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; there is the maturing of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields. Furthermore, by virtue of the causes and conditions of these roots of goodness, one is able to benefit sentient beings, and even after parinirvāṇa, the relics and disciples receive offerings.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas have the characteristic of being unobtainable, what distinction is there between giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the various supernormal powers?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“In the dharma of non-attainment, there is no distinction between generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and supernormal powers; it is because sentient beings are attached to generosity up to supernormal powers that these are explained through differentiation.”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that there is no distinction between the dharma of non-apprehension in giving and even the supernatural powers? “Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend giving;
they practice giving while neither apprehending the giver nor the recipient.

They do not apprehend the precepts while upholding them, do not apprehend patience while practicing it, do not apprehend diligence while practicing it, and do not apprehend dhyāna while practicing it.
Having not attained dhyāna, one practices wisdom; having not attained supernormal powers, one practices supernormal powers;
having not attained the four foundations of mindfulness, one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including:
having not attained the eightfold noble path, one practices the eightfold noble path; and having not attained the samādhi of emptiness, the signless, and the wishless, one practices emptiness.
Through the samādhi of signlessness and wishlessness, one does not apprehend sentient beings yet brings them to maturity;
one does not apprehend the purification of buddha-fields yet purifies buddha-fields; and one does not apprehend the dharmas of all Buddhas yet attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the *prajñāpāramitā* of non-apprehension in this manner.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this *prajñāpāramitā* of non-apprehension, Māra or the gods of Māra cannot destroy them.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, fulfill within a single thought-moment the six *pāramitās*, the four *dhyānas*, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; the three gates of liberation; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Whatever giving a bodhisattva-mahāsattva performs is not apart from the perfection of wisdom;
whatever morality, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration they cultivate is not apart from the perfection of wisdom."

Practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, as well as the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighty minor marks of excellence, one does not depart from the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, without being separated from the prajñāpāramitā, fulfill the practice of the six pāramitās and even the eighty minor marks in a single thought-moment?”
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, all their giving does not depart from the perfection of wisdom, by way of the mark of non-duality."

When upholding the precepts, there is likewise no mark of duality; when practicing patience, exerting diligence, and entering meditative concentration, there is likewise no mark of duality; even up to the eighty secondary marks, there is likewise no mark of duality.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, there is no duality of marks?”
"...up to cultivating the eighty minor marks as a non-dual characteristic? "Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they desire to fulfill the perfection of giving."
“In the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), all the perfections, from the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) up to the eighty minor marks (*aśīty-anuvyañjanāni*),
are subsumed. “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva, when practicing giving, subsume all untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in an untainted mind while giving.
Within that untainted mind, he does not perceive any signs—namely, who gives, who receives, or what is given.”
With this markless mind and untainted mind, one severs craving and severs the mind of stinginess and greed while practicing giving.
At that time, one does not perceive the act of giving, nor even the dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This bodhisattva possesses a signless mind and an untainted mind; while observing the precepts, they do not perceive these precepts, nor do they perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
With a signless mind and an untainted mind, they practice patience and do not perceive this patience, nor do they perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas.
With a mind of signlessness and a mind free from outflows, one exerts diligence without perceiving this diligence, and so on, up to not perceiving any of the Buddha-dharmas.
With a mind of signlessness and a mind free from outflows, one enters meditative concentration without perceiving this concentration, and so on, up to not perceiving any of the Buddha-dharmas.
With a mind of signlessness and an untainted mind, one cultivates wisdom yet does not perceive this wisdom, nor even perceive all the Buddha-dharmas.

With a mind of signlessness and an untainted mind, one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness yet does not perceive these four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighty minor marks of excellence.
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are signless and unconditioned, how can one fulfill the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā?”

What is the fulfillment of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path?

How does one become fully endowed with the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness; with the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion?
"How does one become endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice giving with a mind free of marks and a mind free of outflows; they give food to those who need food, and so on, providing all manner of necessities until everything required is given."
Whether it be internal or external things—whether it be his own body dismembered, or his kingdom, city, wife, and children—he gives them as alms to sentient beings.
Suppose someone comes and says to the bodhisattva:
"What is the use of this giving?"
"This is practicing the perfection of wisdom without any benefit.
The bodhisattva then thinks:
"Although this person comes to reproach me for my giving, I shall never regret it."
I shall diligently practice giving and must not fail to give.
Having given, I shall share it with all sentient beings and dedicate it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, one does not perceive these characteristics:
who gives, who receives, what object is given, who is the one dedicating,
or what is the dharma of dedication?
What is the destination of this dedication—namely, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—the characteristics of which are all unobservable. Why is this so?

All dharmas are empty because they are empty of internal emptiness, empty of external emptiness, empty of internal-and-external emptiness, empty of the emptiness of emptiness, empty of conditioned emptiness, empty of unconditioned emptiness, empty of ultimate emptiness, empty of beginningless emptiness, empty of dispersion emptiness, empty of essential nature emptiness, empty of the emptiness of all dharmas, and empty of the emptiness of self-characteristics.
Observing in this way, one forms this thought:
"Who is it that dedicates?
To what place is it dedicated?"
"By means of what dharma is this dedication called 'right dedication'?

At that time, the Bodhisattva is able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields; he is able to fulfill the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
This bodhisattva, thus fully endowed with the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), does not receive worldly karmic retribution.
It is, for example, like the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (paranirmita-vaśavartin), who obtain whatever they require simply by their own will.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: whatever aspirations arise in the mind are obtained immediately according to one's wish.
Because of the fruit and retribution of this giving, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to make offerings to all Buddhas and is also able to satisfy all sentient beings—gods, humans, and asuras.

This bodhisattva gathers in sentient beings through the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), and by the power of skillful means, delivers them from birth and death by means of the three vehicles (triyāna).
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the dānapāramitā within all dharmas that are signless, unobtainable, and unconditioned.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the śīlapāramitā within the state that is signless, unattainable, and non-conditioned?

Subhūti! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), they maintain various kinds of precepts, namely: the noble, untainted precepts that enter into the eightfold noble path; natural precepts; precepts obtained as a result of maturation; precepts obtained through formal undertaking; and precepts arising from the mind. Such precepts as these are unimpaired and unbroken, unmixed and unpolluted, unattached and sovereign, and praised by the wise.
By means of this precept, one has nothing to grasp—whether it be form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
whether it be the thirty-two marks or the eighty secondary characteristics;
or whether it be a great clan of kṣatriyas, a great clan of brahmins, or a great household of householders.

Whether it be the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, or the Asaṃjñisattva Heaven; the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, or the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven, the Vijñānānantyāyatana Heaven, the Ākiṃcanyāyatana Heaven, or the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven;

whether it be the fruit of a Srotāpanna, the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an Anāgāmin, or the fruit of an Arhat; whether it be the path of a Pratyekabuddha, or a Cakravartin King, or a Heavenly King.
One merely shares it with all sentient beings and dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This dedication is performed through non-characteristics, non-attainment, and non-duality; however, because it is for the sake of conventional phenomena, it is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

This bodhisattva, being fully endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), gives rise to the four dhyānas through the power of skillful means; because he does not relish them, he attains the five supernormal powers (abhijñā).
By means of the four dhyānas, he obtains the divine eye (divyacakṣus); this bodhisattva abides in two kinds of divine eyes:
those acquired through cultivation and those acquired as a result of karmic retribution.
Having attained the divine eye, they see the Buddhas currently residing in the eastern direction, and until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they do not lose what they have seen;

likewise, for the Buddhas currently residing in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they do not lose what they have seen.

With this divine ear, purified and surpassing that of humans, this bodhisattva hears the Dharma preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions; retaining it exactly as heard, they are able to benefit themselves and others.

By means of the knowledge of others' minds, this bodhisattva knows the minds of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the minds of all sentient beings, and is likewise able to benefit all sentient beings.
By means of the knowledge of past lives, this bodhisattva knows the causes and conditions of all past karmas.
Because these karmic causes and conditions do not perish, he fully knows the places where these sentient beings have been born in every instance.

By means of this knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, this bodhisattva causes sentient beings to attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat and the path of pratyekabuddha; in every place and at all times, he leads sentient beings into the wholesome dharmas.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) within all phenomena that are signless, unattainable, and unconditioned.
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas are signless, unconditioned, and unattainable, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva can fulfill the perfection of patience?”

“Subhūti! From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until sitting at the site of awakening, throughout that interval, if all sentient beings were to come and strike this bodhisattva mahāsattva with tiles, stones, knives, or staves, the bodhisattva would at that time not give rise to a mind of anger, nor even produce a single thought of it.”
At that time, a bodhisattva should cultivate two kinds of patience:
first, when all sentient beings revile them with harsh words or strike them with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, they do not give rise to a mind of anger;
second, the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena, which is the realization that all phenomena are unarisen.
If a bodhisattva is encountered by someone who comes to revile him with harsh words, or strikes him with tiles, stones, knives,
or staves, at that time the bodhisattva should reflect thus:
"Who is it that reviles me?"
Who is it that reviles?
Who is it that strikes and hurls?
And who is there to receive [the blow]?
At that moment, the Bodhisattva should reflect:
"The true nature of all phenomena is what is called ultimate emptiness, the non-existence of phenomena, and the non-existence of sentient beings.
Since even phenomena themselves cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be sentient beings?"
When observing the characteristics of all phenomena in this way, one perceives neither the one who reviles nor the one who cuts and maims.
When a bodhisattva observes the characteristics of all phenomena in this manner, they immediately attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
What is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
It is knowing that the characteristics of all phenomena are eternally unarisen, and that all afflictions have also been eternally unarisen from the very beginning.
