When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in these two patiences, they are able to fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, the three gates of liberation, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Abiding in these noble, untainted, supramundane dharmas, which are not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this bodhisattva fully perfects the noble supernormal powers.

Having dwelled in the noble supernormal powers, one perceives the Buddhas of the eastern direction with the divine eye; this person attains the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), which shall never be interrupted until they reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
With the divine ear, this bodhisattva hears the Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions and explains it to sentient beings exactly as he has heard it.
This bodhisattva also knows the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions and knows the thoughts of all sentient beings; having known them, he teaches the Dharma in accordance with their minds.
By means of the knowledge of past lives, this bodhisattva knows the roots of goodness of all sentient beings in their previous existences and preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to rejoice.
By means of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, this bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, enabling them to attain the three vehicles.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, uses the power of skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity, fulfills all-knowledge, attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, and turns the wheel of Dharma.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of patience within the state that is signless, non-attainment, and unconditioned.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the *vīryapāramitā* within all dharmas that are signless, unconditioned, and unattainable?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they accomplish physical vigor and mental vigor; they enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, and experience various supernormal powers, such as being able to divide one body into many bodies, even reaching out with their hand to touch the sun and moon."

Because they have accomplished physical diligence, they fly to the eastern direction, passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-worlds, making offerings to the Buddhas of food and drink, clothing, medicine, bedding, flowers, incense, necklaces, and all manner of necessities; until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the fruit of their merit shall never be exhausted.

When this bodhisattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, all the gods and humans of the world will diligently provide offerings of clothing, food, and drink; even after he has entered nirvana without remainder, his relics and disciples shall likewise receive such offerings, all by virtue of this power of supernormal knowledge.
He goes to the abodes of the Buddhas to listen to and receive their teachings, and until he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he never violates or loses them.
While this bodhisattva cultivates the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he purifies buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom accomplishes physical diligence and is able to fulfill the perfection of vigor.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva accomplish mental diligence and thereby fulfill the *vīryapāramitā*? Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva exerts mental diligence; by means of this mental diligence that is noble and untainted, he enters the eightfold noble path and does not allow unwholesome karma of body or speech to enter.

Nor does one grasp at the characteristics of any phenomena—whether they be permanent or impermanent, suffering or happiness, self or non-self, conditioned or unconditioned; whether they belong to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; whether they are of the nature of outflows or without outflows; whether they be the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; whether they be loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity; whether they be the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; whether they be the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path; or whether they be emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; or even the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

One does not grasp at signs—whether they be permanence or impermanence, suffering or pleasure, self or non-self, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the path of a pratyekabuddha, the path of a bodhisattva, or unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Whether they be srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas.

Not grasping at signs, these beings sever the three fetters and thus attain the stage of *srotāpanna*; these beings have attenuated the three poisons and thus attain the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*; these beings sever the lower fetters and thus attain the stage of *anāgāmin*; these beings sever the upper fetters and thus attain the stage of *arhat*; these beings follow the path of a *pratyekabuddha* and thus become *pratyekabuddhas*; and these beings practice the knowledge of the modes of the path and are therefore called *bodhisattvas*.
Nor does one grasp at the characteristics of these dharmas.
Why? Because one cannot grasp at characteristics by means of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for that intrinsic nature does not exist.
Because this bodhisattva exerts diligence with such a mind, he extensively benefits sentient beings, yet he does not apprehend sentient beings.

This is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the *vīryapāramitā*, his fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas, his purification of buddha-fields, and his maturation of sentient beings—all because they are unapprehendable.
Because this bodhisattva has accomplished physical vigor and mental vigor, they embrace all wholesome dharmas, yet they do not even cling to these dharmas.

From one buddha-field to another, for the benefit of sentient beings, the supernatural powers they exercise are unimpeded according to their will: whether raining down flowers, scattering various fragrances, performing music, shaking the great earth, emitting radiance, manifesting lands adorned with the seven treasures, appearing in various bodies, or emitting the light of great wisdom to cause others to know the Noble Path and to lead them away from killing up to and including wrong views.

He benefits sentient beings either through giving, or through observing the precepts, or by offering his own limbs, or his wife and children, or his kingdom, or even his own body; he benefits sentient beings according to whatever skillful means are appropriate.

In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, within the state of all dharmas being signless, unconditioned, and unattainable, by employing physical and mental diligence, they are able to fulfill the perfection of vigor.
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, abiding in the dharmas that are signless, unconditioned, and unobtainable, manage to fulfill the perfection of dhyāna?”
“Subhūti! With the exception of the various dhyānas and samādhis of a Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fully accomplish all other dhyānas and samādhis.

This bodhisattva, free from desires and from evil, unwholesome dharmas, and possessing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, with directed thought and sustained thought, enters the first dhyāna, and so on up to entering the fourth dhyāna.”
With this mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, they pervade one direction and so on up to the ten directions, filling the entire world.

This bodhisattva, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, enters the sphere of infinite space, and so on, up to entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This bodhisattva dwells within the dhyānapāramitā, entering the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments in both forward and reverse order; he enters the samādhi of emptiness, as well as the samādhis of signlessness and wishlessness.

At times he enters the samādhi of signlessness; at times he enters the samādhi like a flash of lightning; at times he enters the noble and correct samādhi; and at times he enters the samādhi like a vajra.

This bodhisattva, dwelling within the dhyāna-pāramitā, cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and, by means of the knowledge of the modes of the path, enters all meditative concentrations. Transcending the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha, they enter the rank of a bodhisattva.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, one fulfills the stages of a Buddha.
While practicing within these stages, up until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one does not prematurely realize the fruit of the path midway.
Abiding in this dhyānapāramitā, this bodhisattva goes from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to the Buddhas.
From the presence of these Buddhas, they plant various roots of goodness and purify buddha-fields.
From one country to another, they benefit sentient beings.

They gather in sentient beings through giving, or through ethical discipline, or through meditative concentration, or through wisdom, or through liberation, or through the knowledge and vision of liberation; they teach sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, and the path of a pratyekabuddha.
All wholesome dharmas that enable sentient beings to attain the Way, he teaches them all so that they may attain them.

Abiding in this dhyānapāramitā, this bodhisattva is able to give rise to all dhāraṇī-doors, attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and obtain the various supernormal powers as a result of his retribution.
This bodhisattva never again enters a mother’s womb, nor does he ever again experience the five desires.
Being without birth, he is not born; though he appears to be born, he is not defiled by the phenomena of birth.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas perceive all conditioned phenomena as being like illusions while benefiting sentient beings, yet they do not apprehend either sentient beings or any phenomena.
To teach sentient beings so that they may attain the state of non-attainment is a conventional dharma and not the ultimate reality.
Abiding in this dhyānapāramitā, one practices all meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis, up to and including anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, never departing from the dhyānapāramitā.
When this bodhisattva practices such knowledge of the aspects of the path, they attain the knowledge of all modes and sever all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.
Having severed them, they benefit themselves and also benefit others.
Having thus benefited oneself and others, one becomes a field of merit for all the world— gods, humans, and asuras. It is in this way, Subhūti,
that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, is able to fulfill the signless perfection of dhyāna.
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide within the dharma of signlessness, wishlessness, and non-attainment, and cultivate the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom?”
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any fixed, real characteristic in any phenomena.

This bodhisattva sees that form is not fixed and is not its real characteristic, and so on up to seeing that consciousness is not fixed and is not its real characteristic; they do not see the arising of form, nor do they see the arising of consciousness.”

If one does not see the arising of form, up to and including the arising of consciousness, and if regarding all phenomena—whether with outflows or without outflows—one does not see their place of coming, nor their place of going, nor their place of accumulation.

When observing in this way, one does not apprehend the nature of form, up to and including the nature of consciousness, nor does one apprehend the nature of phenomena that are either with outflows or without outflows.
When this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they have faith and understanding that all dharmas possess the nature of non-existence.

Having thus attained such faith and understanding, one practices inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; one remains unattached to all phenomena, whether they be form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* of non-existence and is able to fulfill the bodhisattva path, namely: the six *pāramitās*, up to and including the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics.

This bodhisattva dwells within the empty and pure path of the Buddha—namely, the six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—and having attained the supernormal powers as a karmic result, benefits sentient beings through these dharmas.
Those who should be gathered through giving, he teaches and instructs them to practice giving;
those who should be gathered through ethical discipline, he teaches and instructs them to observe ethical discipline;

those who should be gathered through meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, he teaches and instructs them to cultivate meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Those who should be taught by means of the various paths of the Dharma, one should teach them so that they may attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha;
those who should be transformed by means of the Buddha-path, one should teach them so that they may attain the bodhisattva-path and become fully endowed with the Buddha-path.
In this manner, he teaches and transforms them according to their respective stages of the path, causing each to attain their proper place.
When this Bodhisattva manifests various supernormal powers, he traverses lands as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, liberating sentient beings from birth and death.
According to their needs, he provided for them all, satisfying each one.
Traveling from one land to another, he beheld pure and wondrous lands, using them to adorn his own Buddha-field.

For example, it is like the necessities of life in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, which arrive spontaneously according to one's wishes; it is also like the various pure Buddha-lands, which are free from seeking and desire.

This person, by virtue of these rewards obtained through the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), obtains as a reward the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and practices the path of the bodhisattva.
Through the accomplishment of the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), one fulfills all merits and shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, this bodhisattva does not grasp at form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*); they do not grasp at any phenomena (*dharma*), whether wholesome or unwholesome, worldly or supramundane, with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, they do not grasp at any such phenomena whatsoever.
When this bodhisattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, all the articles of livelihood and material resources in that land shall have no owners.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva practices by not grasping at any dharma, since they cannot be apprehended. Thus it is, Subhūti!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can fully perfect the *prajñāpāramitā* within the dharma of signlessness.

Chapter 77: The Six Similes. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Seventy-Seven, the Chapter on the Six Similes (in the Dan-zang edition, the Chapter on the Six Perfections), Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

How does one fully cultivate the six pāramitās—namely, the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā—amidst all dharmas that are signless, undifferentiable, and empty of intrinsic nature?
World-Honored One!
How is it that within the dharma of non-differentiation you distinguish and speak of different characteristics?
And how is it that the Prajñāpāramitā subsumes dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, and dhyāna?
"How can one practice dharmas of diverse characteristics and yet attain the fruit through a path of a single characteristic?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the five aggregates as being like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation."
Abiding therein, they practice giving, maintain the precepts, cultivate patience, exert diligence, enter meditative concentration, and develop wisdom.

They know that these five aggregates are in reality like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a flame, like an illusion, and like a transformation; the five aggregates are signless like a dream, and so on, up to being signless like a transformation.
Why is this? Dreams lack intrinsic nature; echoes, shadows, mirages, illusions, and transformations all lack intrinsic nature.
If a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, that dharma is without marks.
If dharmas are without marks, these dharmas have but one mark,
namely, the markless. For this reason, Subhūti,
you should know that when a bodhisattva practices giving, the gift is without marks, the giver is without marks, and the recipient is without marks.
To be able to know giving in this way is to be able to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā, up to and including the fulfillment of the prajñā-pāramitā;
it is to be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
and it is to be able to fulfill internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
They are able to fulfill the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness;
they are able to fulfill the eight liberations, the nine successive concentrations, the five supernormal powers, and the five hundred dharanī-doors;
they are able to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Abiding in these untainted dharmas obtained as a result of karmic retribution, this bodhisattva flies to immeasurable lands in the eastern direction, making offerings of robes, food, and drink, and providing whatever else they require to all the Buddhas.

They also benefit sentient beings by gathering those who should be gathered through generosity with generosity; teaching those who should be gathered through ethical discipline to observe ethical discipline; teaching and gathering those who should be gathered through patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom by means of patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
and even gathering those who should be gathered through various wholesome dharmas by means of those various wholesome dharmas.
This bodhisattva, having accomplished all these wholesome dharmas, assumes a worldly body yet is not defiled by worldly birth and death.
For the sake of sentient beings, he experiences noble status, wealth, and happiness among gods and humans, and through this noble status, wealth, and happiness, he gathers in sentient beings.

Because this bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are signless, he knows the fruit of srotāpanna and does not dwell therein; he knows the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat, and does not dwell therein; he knows the path of the pratyekabuddha and does not dwell therein.

Why is this? Because once this bodhisattva has known all dharmas by means of the knowledge of all modes, they shall attain the knowledge of all modes, which is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Thus it is, Subhūti! Having realized that all dharmas are signless, the bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that the six pāramitās are signless, and so on, up to realizing that all buddha-dharmas are signless.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling within the five aggregates—which are like a dream, an echo, a shadow, a mirage, an illusion, and a transformation—is able to fulfill the signless perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā). He fulfills the precepts that are unimpaired, unbroken, unmixed, unattached, praised by the noble ones, and untainted (anāsrava), thereby entering the eightfold noble path."

Abiding within this precept, one upholds all precepts—namely, the nominal precept, the natural precept, the precept of restraint, the active precept, the non-active precept, the precept of dignified conduct, and the precept of non-dignified conduct.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished all the precepts, does not form this aspiration:

"By reason of these precepts, may I be born into a great kṣatriya clan, a great brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder family; or into a minor royal family, or the family of a wheel-turning sage-king; or may I be born in the realm of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."
They do not make this vow:
"By reason of my upholding the precepts, I shall attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha."
Why is this? All dharmas are signless, which is to say they have but one single mark.

A signless dharma cannot obtain a signless dharma; a dharma with marks cannot obtain a dharma with marks; a signless dharma cannot obtain a dharma with marks; and a dharma with marks cannot obtain a signless dharma.
In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to fulfill the signless perfection of ethical discipline and enter the stage of a bodhisattva.

Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, he attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), practices the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā), and acquires the five supernormal powers obtained as a result of maturation (vipākaja).
He dwells in five hundred dharanī-doors and attains the four unhindered knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they make offerings to all buddhas, bring sentient beings to maturity, and purify buddha-fields.
Although they enter the five realms of existence, the karmic retributions of birth and death cannot defile them.

Subhūti! It is as if, for example, there were a magically conjured wheel-turning sage king who, though sitting, reclining, walking, or standing, is seen to have no place from which he comes, no place to which he goes, and no place where he stands, sits, or lies; yet he is able to benefit sentient beings, while not apprehending any sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva is also like this,
Subhūti! For example,

when the Buddha Susaṃtata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he turned the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the three vehicles, yet there was no one who received the prediction of becoming a Bodhisattva.
Having manifested as a Buddha, he relinquishes his body and life-span and enters nirvana without remainder.
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva: when practicing the perfection of wisdom, they are able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline.
Having fulfilled the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*),
one gathers all wholesome dharmas. "Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they abide in the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as being like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical transformation, thereby fulfilling the signless perfection of patience (*akṣayākāra-kṣāntipāramitā*)."
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the signless perfection of patience? “Subhūti!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in two kinds of patience, they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
What are these two kinds of patience? They are patience toward sentient beings (sattva-kṣānti) and patience toward phenomena (dharma-kṣānti).

From the first aspiration until sitting at the site of enlightenment, throughout that interval, if all sentient beings should come to revile him with harsh and abusive language, or should strike this bodhisattva with tiles, stones, swords, or staves, because this bodhisattva desires to fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he does not give rise to even a single thought of malice.
This bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"Who is it that reviles me?
Who is it that cuts me?"
"Who is it that addresses me with harsh words?
Who is it that harms me with tiles, stones, swords, or staves? Why is this so?
Since this bodhisattva has attained the patience of signlessness regarding all phenomena, how could they entertain such a thought as:
"This person is reviling me or harming me"?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Because they have fulfilled this perfection of patience, they attain the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattikadharmakṣānti).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?”
"What is severed by this patience? What is known?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"To attain the patience of dharmas (dharmanidhyānakṣānti), such that not even the slightest unwholesome dharma arises—therefore it is called 'patience of non-arising' (anutpattikadharmakṣānti).
When all afflictions to be abandoned by all bodhisattvas are exhausted, this is called 'abandonment'."
"To know through wisdom that all phenomena are unarisen— this is called knowing.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

"What is the difference between the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas of the bodhisattvas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to the srotāpannas, this is called the patience of the bodhisattva."
The wisdom and the abandonment of a Sakṛdāgāmin are called the patience of a bodhisattva;
the wisdom and the abandonment of an Anāgāmin are called the patience of a bodhisattva;
the wisdom and the abandonment of an Arhat are called the patience of a bodhisattva.
Whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of a pratyekabuddha, this is called the patience of a bodhisattva;
this is the distinction, Subhūti.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas achieve this patience, they surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Abiding in this patience of non-arising obtained as a result of retribution, they practice the Bodhisattva path and are able to fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path.

Because they are fully endowed with the knowledge of the modes of the path, they are never separated from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor from the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and they are never separated from the five supernormal powers.
Because they do not depart from the five supernormal powers, they are able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields.
Having brought sentient beings to maturity and purified the buddha-fields, they shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Thus it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the signless perfection of patience. Furthermore, Subhūti!

The bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the five aggregates that are signless—like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation—and practices physical vigor and mental vigor.
By means of physical diligence, one gives rise to supernormal powers.
By giving rise to supernormal powers, one reaches the lands of the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas and bring benefit to sentient beings.
By the power of physical diligence, they teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to abide in the three vehicles. Thus, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to fulfill the signless perfection of diligence.
This bodhisattva, through mental diligence and noble, untainted diligence, enters into the eightfold noble path and is able to fulfill the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).

This perfection of vigor encompasses all wholesome dharmas, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive concentrations; as well as the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
In this regard, the Bodhisattva practicing these dharmas should fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Having fulfilled all-knowledge, they sever all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), perfect the body endowed with the thirty-two marks, and radiate incomparable and immeasurable light.

Having emitted these rays of light, the sentient beings within the thousandfold great trichiliocosm hear the sound of the Dharma being preached and all attain liberation through the three vehicles of the Dharma. Thus it is, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of diligence, they are able to bring great benefit and can fulfill all-knowledge. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva dwells within the five aggregates as being signless—like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, and like a transformation—they are able to fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā.
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva, while abiding within the five aggregates—which are like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation—perfect the dhyāna-pāramitā?”
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna;
they enter loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, entering the four immeasurable minds.”
They enter the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

they enter the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness; they enter the samādhi like a flash of lightning, the samādhi like a vajra, and the noble right samādhi;
with the exception of the samādhis of the Buddhas, they realize and enter all other samādhis, including those shared by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, they do not experience the flavor of samādhi, nor do they experience the fruit of samādhi. Why is this?
Because these bodhisattvas know that this samādhi is signless and of a non-existent nature; how could they experience the flavor of a signless dharma within a signless dharma?
Does one who possesses no dharmas experience the flavor of the dharma of non-existence?
If one does not experience that flavor, then one will not be reborn in the realm of form or the formless realm through the power of meditative concentration.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva does not perceive these two realms, nor does he perceive this dhyāna, nor does he perceive one who enters dhyāna, nor does he perceive that which is used to enter dhyāna through this dharma, nor does he perceive the place where one enters dhyāna, because he does not apprehend any such dharma.

At that time, the bodhisattva is able to fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā of signlessness; by means of this dhyāna-pāramitā, the bodhisattva is able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva, by being fully endowed with the signless dhyāna-pāramitā, is able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva has well studied internal emptiness, well studied external emptiness, and so on, up to having well studied the emptiness of non-existence and existence.”

Thus, among all these empty dharmas there is no place where one can abide—whether it be the fruit of a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). These dharmas are empty, and that emptiness is also empty.
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices these various kinds of emptiness is able to enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
What is the non-stage? "Subhūti!..."
"Whatever is attained, that is not the stage of a bodhisattva;
whatever is unattained, that is the stage of a bodhisattva.
"World-Honored One!"
“What is that which is apprehended?
What is that which is non-apprehended? “Subhūti!

If form is apprehended as an object, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are apprehended as objects; if the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are apprehended as objects—this is not the stage of a bodhisattva.
Subhūti! As for the stage of a bodhisattva, all dharmas therein cannot be demonstrated and cannot be spoken of.
What dharmas cannot be demonstrated and cannot be spoken of?
Whether it be form, up to and including all-knowledge.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The nature of form is unindicatable and ineffable; even so, up to the nature of all-knowledge is unindicatable and ineffable. Subhūti!
This is called the stage of a bodhisattva.

When a bodhisattva enters this stage, they are fully endowed with all dhyānas and samādhis; yet they do not even arise by the power of those dhyānas and samādhis, let alone dwell in lust, anger, or delusion to give rise to sinful karma within them.

The bodhisattva dwells only within dharmas that are like illusions to benefit sentient beings; yet he neither apprehends sentient beings nor apprehends illusion, for there is nothing to be apprehended.
At such a time, he is able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the buddha-fields.

Thus it is, Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the signless dhyāna-pāramitā, culminating in the ability to turn the wheel of Dharma—namely, the wheel of Dharma that is ungraspable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he knows that all phenomena are like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical transformation."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know that all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation?”

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dream, nor does he perceive one who sees a dream; he does not perceive an echo, nor does he perceive one who hears an echo; he does not perceive a reflection, nor does he perceive one who sees a reflection; he does not perceive a mirage, nor does he perceive one who sees a mirage; he does not perceive a magical illusion, nor does he perceive one who sees a magical illusion; he does not perceive a transformation, nor does he perceive one who sees a transformation.”
Why is this? Because these things—dreams, echoes, shadows, mirages, illusions, and transformations—are all inverted phenomena belonging to foolish ordinary beings.
An Arhat does not see dreams, nor does he see one who sees dreams; likewise, he does not see transformations, nor does he see one who sees transformations.

Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all Buddhas likewise do not perceive dreams, nor do they perceive those who see dreams; they do not perceive even emanations, nor do they perceive those who see emanations.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are of a nature that does not exist, are unarisen, and are indeterminate.
If dharmas are of a nature that does not exist, are unarisen, and are indeterminate, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
In this regard, to grasp at the characteristic of arising or the characteristic of fixedness is not possible. Why is this?
If all phenomena possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature, arising, or fixedness, they could not be called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not cling to form, nor even to consciousness;
they do not cling to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm.
They do not cling to the dhyānas, liberations, or samādhis;
they do not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they do not cling to the samādhi of emptiness, nor to the signless or wishless samādhis.
He does not cling to the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom.
Because they do not cling, they are able to fulfill the first stage of a bodhisattva, yet within that first stage they do not give rise to clinging.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas do not apprehend this stage; how then could they give rise to clinging?
It is likewise for the stages up to the tenth bhūmi.
When this bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the prajñāpāramitā.

If, while practicing the prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the prajñāpāramitā, at that time they see that all dharmas enter into the prajñāpāramitā, yet they do not apprehend those dharmas either.
Why is this? Because these dharmas and the prajñāpāramitā are non-dual and without distinction. Why is this?
"Because all dharmas enter into suchness, the dharma-nature, and the reality-limit, they are without discrimination.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If all phenomena are without marks and without conceptual differentiation, how can one say that some are wholesome and others unwholesome, that some are with outflows and others without outflows, that some are mundane and others supramundane, or that some are conditioned and others unconditioned?
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, is there any dharma that can be said to be wholesome or unwholesome, or even conditioned or unconditioned;
or is there anything that is the fruit of stream-entry up to arhatship, or a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva, or unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One! It cannot be spoken of. “Subhūti!”
For this reason, Subhūti, you should know that all dharmas are signless, non-conceptual, unarisen, undetermined, and cannot be demonstrated.

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, there was likewise no dharma that could be apprehended as having an intrinsic nature—whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; or anything conditioned or unconditioned; or even the fruit of a stream-enterer up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Thus it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should skillfully study the nature of all dharmas, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thoroughly studying the nature of all dharmas is called the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By practicing this path, one can fulfill the six *pāramitās*, bring sentient beings to maturity, and purify the Buddha-fields.
Abiding within these dharmas, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, yet remains unattached even to the three vehicles.
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study the prajñāpāramitā by means of the dharma of signlessness. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 23.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-Four, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter Seventy-Eight:
The Four Means of Integration (Catuḥsaṃgrahavastu). Chapter Seventy-Eight: The Four Means of Integration.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are like dreams, like echoes, like shadows, like flames, like illusions, and like transformations—having no substantial reality, being of a non-existent nature, and empty of self-characteristics—how can one differentiate between wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas, worldly dharmas and world-transcending dharmas, out-flowing dharmas and non-out-flowing dharmas, conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas? And how can there be dharmas that enable one to attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, or the fruit of an arhat; that enable one to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha; or that enable one to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Ordinary, foolish people who experience dreams or see those who dream them, and even those who experience emanations or see those who emanate them, give rise to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate karma of body, speech, and mind; they give rise to meritorious karma, or sinful karma, and perform karma that leads to immovability.”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in two kinds of emptiness—ultimate emptiness and beginningless emptiness—and preaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying:
"O sentient beings!..."
This form is empty and non-existent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and non-existent. The twelve bases and the eighteen elements are empty and non-existent.
Form is a dream; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are dreams; the twelve bases and the eighteen elements are dreams.

Form is an echo, a shadow, a mirage, an illusion, and a transformation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus. The twelve bases and the eighteen elements are a dream, an echo, a shadow, a mirage, an illusion, and a transformation.

Within this, there are no aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), or elements (*dhātu*); there is no dream, nor is there anyone who sees a dream; there is no echo, nor is there anyone who hears an echo; there is no shadow, nor is there anyone who sees a shadow; there is no mirage, nor is there anyone who sees a mirage; there is no illusion, nor is there anyone who sees an illusion; there is no transformation, nor is there anyone who sees a transformation. All phenomena (*dharma*) lack a fundamental, real nature and are non-existent.

You perceive aggregates where there are no aggregates; you perceive sense-bases where there are no sense-bases; you perceive elements where there are no elements. All these phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they are produced by the inverted mind and belong to the retribution of karma.
"Why do you grasp at the characteristics of a fundamental basis within all phenomena, which are empty and devoid of any root?

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), by means of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), draws sentient beings out from among those who are stingy with the Dharma and teaches them to practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
By virtue of this merit from practicing generosity, one obtains great rewards of fortune; having drawn them out from these great rewards of fortune, one instructs them to uphold the precepts.
Through the merit of upholding the precepts, one is born in a noble place in the heavens; furthermore, having drawn them out from there, one causes them to abide in the first dhyāna.

The merit of the first dhyāna leads to rebirth in the Brahma heavens; the same applies to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Sentient beings practice this giving and its fruit, the observance of precepts and its fruit, and meditative concentration and its fruit; through various causes and conditions, they are extracted and established within *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and the path to nirvāṇa—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; the eight liberations, the nine successive concentrations, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities—thereby bringing peace and security to sentient beings and causing them to abide in the noble, untainted dharmas.

Within these formless, shapeless, and unimpeded dharmas, there are those who can attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*; he peacefully teaches and transforms them so that they abide in the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

There are those who can attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, the fruit of *arhat*, or the path of a *pratyekabuddha*; he causes them to abide in the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, the fruit of *arhat*, or the path of a *pratyekabuddha*.
There are those who can attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he peacefully teaches and transforms them so that they abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is most rare and difficult to equal that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to practice this profound prajñāpāramitā.”

All dharmas are of a non-existent nature; they are ultimately empty and beginningless. Yet one discriminates among these dharmas, [categorizing them as] wholesome or unwholesome, with outflows or without outflows, and so forth, even up to conditioned or unconditioned.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare and difficult to equal, for they are able to practice this profound prajñāpāramitā.”
All dharmas are of a non-existent nature; they are ultimately empty and beginninglessly empty, yet one discriminates among these dharmas. Subhūti!
If you understand that this is the rare and difficult-to-attain dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, then you will know that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot repay it, let alone others.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is this extraordinary and difficult-to-attain dharma of the bodhisattva mahāsattva that is not possessed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Listen attentively with a single mind!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā, dwelling in the six pāramitās obtained as a result of their past retribution, as well as dwelling in the five supernormal powers and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment obtained as a result of their past retribution; they dwell in all the dhāraṇīs and the various unimpeded knowledges. Reaching the lands of the ten directions, they gather in those who can be saved through giving by means of giving; they gather in those who can be saved through ethical discipline by means of ethical discipline; and for those who can be saved through patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom, they gather them in according to what is appropriate for each."

Those who can be delivered by the first dhyāna, he gathers them through the first dhyāna; those who can be delivered by the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, or by the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he gathers them according to what is appropriate for each;

those who can be delivered by the mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity, he gathers them through the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

and those who can be delivered by the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, or the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he gathers them accordingly.
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva benefit sentient beings through giving? “Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom and gives in charity, they provide whatever is required—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, horses, incense, flowers, and necklaces—granting all such necessities without exception. Whether it be for making offerings to Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, anāgāmins, sakṛdāgāmins, or srotāpannas, there is no difference; it is as if the gift were bestowed upon those who have entered the right path.
Whether it be humans, ordinary people, or even down to birds and beasts, they are all without discrimination; one bestows gifts equally upon them all. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are neither different nor discriminable; thus, for this bodhisattva, there is no distinction and no differentiation.
Having practiced giving, one shall obtain the retribution of the non-conceptual Dharma, namely, the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon seeing a beggar, should give rise to this thought:
"The Buddha is a field of merit; I should make offerings to him.
Birds and beasts are not fields of merit; they should not be offered to.
This is not the Dharma of a Bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they do not form such thoughts as:
"This sentient being should be benefited by means of giving; that sentient being should not be given to."
"By reason of these causes and conditions of giving, they are born into great kṣatriya clans, great brāhmaṇa clans, or great householder families.
Furthermore, by means of these causes and conditions of giving, they are delivered by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles and led to enter nirvana without remainder."
If sentient beings come to beg from a bodhisattva, he does not give rise to a discriminatory thought, thinking:
"I should give this to them, but I should not give that to them. Why is this?
This Bodhisattva has generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of these sentient beings.

If they engage in conceptual discrimination and selection, they will fall into a state of reproach by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as by all the gods and humans of the world, who will say:
"Who requested you to save all sentient beings?"

You are a shelter for all sentient beings, a protector for all sentient beings, and a refuge for all sentient beings; yet you engage in discrimination and selection as to what should and should not be given.
"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if a human or a non-human being comes seeking to beg for the limbs and members of the bodhisattva’s body,"
At that time, one should not give rise to two thoughts:
whether to give or not to give. Why is this?
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has taken on a body for the sake of sentient beings; when sentient beings come to take it, how could he not give it?
"I have received this body for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings; even if they do not ask, I should give it to them of my own accord."
"How much more so when one begs and is not given?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in this way.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a beggar, they should give rise to this thought:
"In this matter, who is it that gives?
Who is it that receives?"
"What is it that is given?
It is that the self-nature of all dharmas is unattainable, because they are ultimately empty.
In the dharma of the mark of emptiness, there is neither giving nor taking away.

Why is this? Because they are ultimately empty; because they are internally empty, externally empty, both internally and externally empty, great empty, emptiness of the ultimate truth, and emptiness of self-characteristic.
Dwelling in these various forms of emptiness while practicing giving, one at that time fulfills the *dānapāramitā*.
Because one has fulfilled the *dānapāramitā*, when cutting off internal or external phenomena, one forms this thought:
"Who is it that cuts me?"
"Who is it that cuts me?

Furthermore, Subhūti, with my Buddha-eye I see bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who enter the great hells and cause the fires to be extinguished and the boiling water to turn cold, teaching and transforming them through three matters: [the gift of the Dharma, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of material things]."
First is supernormal power, second is knowledge of others' minds, and third is the preaching of the Dharma.
By means of the power of supernormal faculties, this bodhisattva causes the fires of the great hells to be extinguished and the boiling water to become cold;
through knowledge of others' minds, he preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
These sentient beings, having conceived a pure mind toward the Bodhisattva, will be liberated from the hells and gradually reach the end of suffering through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
It is the same in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! With my Buddha-eye, I behold the worlds of the ten directions and see bodhisattvas in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serving as attendants to the Buddhas, providing for the Buddhas, and honoring them with devotion according to their wishes."
"If one is able to receive and uphold all that the Buddhas have taught, until reaching *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never forgetting or losing it. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

With my Buddha-eye, I behold the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in lands throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who, for the sake of animals, sacrifice their own lives and cut their bodies into pieces to distribute them in all directions.
All sentient beings who eat the flesh of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will all come to love and respect the bodhisattvas.

Because of this love and respect, they shall immediately escape the realm of animals, encounter the Buddhas, hear the Buddhas preach the Dharma, and practice according to those teachings. Gradually, by means of the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha-vehicle—they will attain parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

The benefit brought about by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly great, as they instruct and transform sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and to practice according to the teaching until they finally enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I see the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions who eliminate the suffering of hunger and thirst for all hungry ghosts; these hungry ghosts all love and revere those bodhisattvas."

By virtue of their love and reverence, they shall escape the realm of hungry ghosts, encounter the various Buddhas, hear the Buddhas preach the Dharma, and practice according to what they have heard. Gradually, through the three vehicles—the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha—they shall attain parinirvāṇa, even up to nirvāṇa without remainder.
Thus it is, Subhūti! For the sake of delivering sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the mind of great compassion. Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I see bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preaching the Dharma in the heavens of the Four Great Kings; I see them preaching the Dharma in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
When the devas hear the Bodhisattva preach the Dharma, they gradually attain parinirvāṇa through the three vehicles. Subhūti!

Among these hosts of devas, there are those who are addicted to the five desires; for their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests the breaking out of fire to burn their palaces and then preaches the Dharma for them.
He spoke these words:
"O devas! All conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent."
"Who is it that is always at peace?

"Furthermore, Subhūti, with my Buddha-eye I survey the worlds of the ten directions and see that in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there are Brahmā deities who are attached to false views; these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas instruct them to distance themselves from such false views."
He speaks thus:
"How can you give rise to false views regarding these dharmas that are empty in nature and illusory? It is thus, Subhūti!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in a mind of great loving-kindness and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. Subhūti,
this is the rare and difficult-to-attain quality of all Bodhisattvas.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! With my Buddha-eye, I behold the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in as many lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, who gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction."
What are the four?
They are generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.
How does a bodhisattva gather in sentient beings through generosity?
Subhūti! A bodhisattva gathers in sentient beings through two kinds of giving:
the gift of material wealth and the gift of the Dharma.
What is the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*) that gathers in sentient beings?

Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives various precious objects such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, conch shells, and coral; or food, drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, lamps, candles, flowers, incense, and necklaces; or sons or daughters, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, and carriages; or even his own body, providing these gifts to sentient beings.
He spoke to the sentient beings, saying:
"If you have anything you require, each of you come and take it.
Just as if you were taking your own property, do not harbor any doubt or hesitation."

After this bodhisattva has given, he teaches the three refuges—refuge in the Buddha, refuge in the Dharma, and refuge in the Sangha—or he teaches the reception of the five precepts, or he teaches the one-day precepts, or he teaches the first dhyāna, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Some were taught loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; some were taught mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, renunciation, and the devas;
some were taught the contemplation of impurity; some were taught the contemplation of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), whether by way of its signs or its contact;
and some were taught the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of psychic power.
The five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three samādhis of emptiness,
signlessness, and wishlessness, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses,
the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.
The thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics;
or teaching the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat; or teaching the path of the pratyekabuddha;
or teaching anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having used the power of skillful means to teach sentient beings through the gift of material wealth, he further teaches them so that they may attain unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa.
Subhūti! This is called the rare and difficult-to-attain dharma of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!
"How does a bodhisattva gather in sentient beings through the gift of Dharma?
Subhūti, there are two kinds of the gift of Dharma:"
There are two kinds: the mundane and the supramundane.
What is the mundane gift of Dharma?

It is the exposition and manifestation of mundane dharmas, namely: the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments.
Such worldly dharmas, as well as other dharmas practiced in common with ordinary worldlings, are called the gift of worldly dharmas.
After the Bodhisattva has thus bestowed the gift of worldly dharmas, he employs various causes and conditions to teach and transform them, leading them to distance themselves from worldly dharmas.

Having distanced themselves from worldly dharmas, they use the power of skillful means to cause them to attain the noble, untainted dharmas (*ārya-anāsrava-dharma*) and the fruits of those noble, untainted dharmas.
What are these noble, untainted dharmas?
What are the fruits of the noble, untainted dharmas?
The noble, untainted dharmas are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation.
The fruits of the noble, untainted dharmas are the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The noble, untainted dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consist of the wisdom within the fruit of srotāpanna up to the wisdom within the fruit of arhat, the wisdom within the path of the pratyekabuddha, the wisdom within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the wisdom within the six pāramitās, and even the wisdom within great loving-kindness and great compassion."

All such dharmas—whether worldly or supramundane wisdom, whether with outflows or without outflows, whether conditioned or unconditioned—the knowledge of all modes regarding these dharmas is called the noble, outflow-free dharma of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"What is the fruit of the noble, untainted dharmas?
The severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies of affliction—this is called the fruit of the noble, untainted dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain all-knowledge?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains all-knowledge."
Subhūti asked: "What is the difference between a bodhisattva and a buddha?
The Buddha said:
“There is a distinction.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is called a Buddha. Why is this so?
The bodhisattva mind and the Buddha mind are no different.
When a bodhisattva abides within this omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), there is no dharma that it does not illuminate; this is called the worldly gift of Dharma by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti! By means of the worldly gift of Dharma, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the supramundane gift of Dharma. It is thus, Subhūti!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva teaches sentient beings so that they may attain worldly dharmas, and by means of skillful power, he teaches them so that they may attain supramundane dharmas. Subhūti!
What are the supramundane dharmas of a bodhisattva?

They do not share in common with the dharmas of ordinary beings; namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive concentrations, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor signs, and the five hundred dharani-gates—these are called supramundane dharmas.
Subhūti! What are the four foundations of mindfulness?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body internally as the body, contemplates the body externally as the body, and contemplates the body both internally and externally as the body; he does so with diligent vigor, with a unified mind, and with wisdom.

One contemplates the body as arising from the collection of causes and conditions, one contemplates the cessation of the body, and one contemplates the practice of the arising and cessation of the body’s collection; this path is without dependence and has no grasping within the world.
The foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, the mind, and phenomena are also like this. Subhūti,
what are the four right endeavors?

To prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, one generates desire and exerts effort; to abandon arisen evil and unwholesome states, one generates desire and exerts effort; to give rise to unarisen wholesome states, one generates desire and exerts effort; and to increase, cultivate, and bring to fulfillment all arisen wholesome states, one generates desire and exerts effort. These are called the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).
Subhūti! What are the four bases of psychic power?

The first base of psychic power is the accomplishment of the cultivation of abandonment through the concentration of desire; likewise, there are the bases of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the cultivation of abandonment through the concentration of vigor, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation.
What are the five faculties?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
What are the five powers?
The power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
What are the seven factors of enlightenment?

The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
What are the eight factors of the noble path?
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
What are the three samādhis?
They are the gate of the emptiness samādhi, and the gates of the signless and wishless samādhis.
What is the emptiness samādhi?
To collect the mind through the practice of emptiness and the practice of non-self is called the samādhi of emptiness.
What is the samādhi of signlessness?
To collect the mind through the practice of cessation and the practice of detachment is called the samādhi of signlessness.
What is the concentration of wishlessness (*apranihita-samādhi*)?
Controlling the mind through the contemplation of impermanence and the contemplation of suffering is called the concentration of wishlessness.
What are the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*)?
Perceiving forms internally while observing forms externally is the first liberation;
not perceiving forms internally while observing forms externally is the second liberation;
the liberation of the beautiful is the third liberation.

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of all perceptions of sensory impingement, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, one contemplates infinite space and enters the sphere of infinite space;
continuing thus until, transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the liberation of the cessation of sensation and perception—these are called the eight liberations.
What are the nine successive attainments?

The practitioner, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna; then the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; and so on, up to transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. These are called the nine successive attainments.
What are the ten powers of a Buddha? They are:
knowing what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible;

knowing, as it truly is, the past, future, and present karma, dharmas, and experiences of sentient beings; knowing the place where karma is created; and knowing the causes, conditions, and retributions.
He knows, as they truly are, the distinctions between the defiled and pure aspects of all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative concentrations;
he knows the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings;
and he knows the various inclinations and understandings of other sentient beings.
He knows the various and innumerable natures of the world;
he knows the characteristics of all paths leading to their destinations;

he knows various past lives, from a single lifetime up to immeasurable eons, knowing them as they truly are; and with the divine eye, he sees sentient beings, even those born in the good and evil realms.
Because the outflows are exhausted, he knows with reality as it is that his mind is liberated from outflows; this constitutes the ten powers of a Buddha.
What are the four fearlessnesses? The Buddha makes this truthful declaration:
"I am one who possesses all-encompassing right knowledge.
If there should be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, or god, or Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else, who speaks the truth, saying:
"This dharma is not known by him," [I would acknowledge it].
"Furthermore, I do not perceive even the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I am free from all dread, and I abide securely in the station of the Noble Lord; amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion's roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel."
No śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor gods, Māras, or Brahmās, nor any other beings, can truly turn it back.
[The Buddha] is without any fear.
The Buddha makes this solemn declaration:
"I have exhausted all outflows.
If any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, or deva, or Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else should truthfully say, "These outflows are not exhausted," [I would acknowledge it].
"Even down to not perceiving the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, I abide securely in the station of the Holy Lord, and amidst the great assembly I roar the lion’s roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel."
"None among the śramaṇas or brahmins, whether gods, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings, can truly turn it back.
This is the second fearlessness.
The Buddha makes this solemn declaration:"
"I have declared these to be obstructive dharmas.
If there should be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, or any deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or any other being, who should speak according to reality, saying:
"To receive these dharmas does not obstruct the Path."
"Furthermore, I do not perceive even the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and I abide securely in the station of the Holy Lord; amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion's roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel."
No śramaṇas or brahmins, nor gods, Māras, or Brahmās, nor any other beings, can truly turn it back.
This is the third fearlessness.
The Buddha makes this solemn declaration:
"I have taught the Noble Path that can transcend the world; by practicing it accordingly, one can bring an end to suffering.
If any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, or deva, or Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else should truthfully say:
"Practicing this path cannot transcend the world, nor can it bring an end to suffering," [I would know that].
"Furthermore, I do not perceive even the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I am free from all dread, and I dwell securely in the station of the Holy Lord. Amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion's roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel."
No śramaṇas or brahmins, nor gods, Māras, or Brahmās, nor any other beings, can truly turn back these four fearlessnesses.
What are the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge?

First is the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), second is the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), third is the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and fourth is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
What is the unimpeded knowledge of meaning?
The wisdom that takes meaning as its object is the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
What is the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*)?
The wisdom that takes phenomena as its object is the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena.
What is the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*)?
Wisdom that takes expression as its object is the unimpeded knowledge of expression.
What is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)?
The wisdom based on the eloquence of joyful speech is the unimpeded knowledge of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
What are the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*)?
First, the Buddhas have no failure of body; second, no failure of speech; third, no failure of mindfulness.
4. No notion of diversity; 5. No unconcentrated mind; 6. No lack of equanimity regarding what is not known;
7. No decrease in zeal; 8. No decrease in vigor; 9. No decrease in mindfulness; 10. No decrease in wisdom; 11.
No decrease in liberation; 12. No decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
13. His knowledge and vision do not diminish; 14. all his bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; 15.
all his verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; 16. all his mental actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom;
17. with wisdom he knows the past without obstruction; 18. with wisdom he knows the future...
Unimpeded regarding future lives; eighteen, wisdom that knows the present life without impediment.
What are the thirty-two marks?
First, the soles of the feet stand level, as flat as the bottom of a cosmetic box.
Second, the soles of his feet are marked with wheels having a thousand spokes and rims, complete with all the characteristics;
third, the fingers and toes of his hands and feet are long, surpassing those of other people;
fourth, his hands and feet are soft and supple, surpassing the rest of his body.
Fifth, his heels are broad, full, and well-proportioned;
sixth, the fingers and toes of his hands and feet are joined by a web-like membrane, which is more exquisite than that of other people;
seventh, his insteps are high, level, and beautiful, being in perfect proportion with his heels.
Eighth, his calves are like those of the eneya deer, being slender and beautiful like the king of eneya deer;
ninth, standing upright, both hands reach and touch his knees;
tenth, he has the mark of the concealed organ, like that of a horse king or an elephant king.
Eleventh, his body is equal in length and breadth, like a nyagrodha tree;
twelfth, a single hair grows from each pore, blue-black in color, soft, and curling to the right;
thirteenth, the hairs on his body point upward, blue-black in color, soft, and curling to the right.
Fourteenth is the mark of golden color, its hue being subtle and exquisite, surpassing that of Jāmbūnada gold;
fifteenth, the radiance of his body extends one zhang in every direction;
sixteenth, his skin is thin, fine, and smooth, such that it does not retain dust or grime, nor do mosquitoes or gadflies alight upon it.
Seventeenth, the seven places are full:
the soles of both feet, the palms of both hands, the two shoulders, and the back of the neck; in all these places, the marks of the fullness are distinct and clear.
Eighteenth, the areas beneath both armpits are full.
Nineteenth, his upper body is like that of a lion;
twentieth, his body is broad, upright, and straight;
twenty-first, his shoulders are perfectly rounded and handsome.
Twenty-second: he has forty teeth; twenty-third:
his teeth are white, even, closely set, and deeply rooted;
twenty-fourth: his four canine teeth are the whitest and largest.
Twenty-fifth, his jawbones are square like those of a lion;
twenty-sixth, he attains the supreme flavor among all flavors, with two streams of saliva flowing from the two places in his throat;
twenty-seventh, his tongue is large, soft, and thin, capable of covering his face up to his ears and the hairline at his forehead.
Twenty-eighth, his Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching, like the call of the kalaviṅka bird;
twenty-ninth, the color of his eyes is like refined gold;
thirtieth, his eyelashes are like those of a bull king.
The thirty-first is the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, soft and white like *tūla* cotton;
the thirty-second is the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) formed of flesh and bone.
These are the thirty-two marks accomplished upon the Buddha’s body.
