The light shines universally throughout the trichiliocosm; if he wishes to shine extensively, it fills immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* lands in the ten directions, yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests a light of one *zhang*.
If he emits immeasurable rays of light, there would be no distinction between sun, moon, seasons, or years.

The Buddha’s voice fills the trichiliocosm; if he desires a great sound, it fills immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* lands throughout the ten directions, reaching everywhere according to the number of sentient beings.
What are the eighty secondary marks?
First, the crown of the head is invisible;
second, the nose is straight, high, and well-formed, with the nostrils not visible.
Third, his eyebrows are like the newly risen crescent moon, the color of deep lapis lazuli;
fourth, the lobes of his ears are perfectly formed;
fifth, his body is firm and solid, like that of Nārāyaṇa.
Sixth, the joints of the bones are like interlocking hooks;
seventh, when the body turns as a whole, it is like that of an elephant king;
eighth, when walking, the feet leave the ground four inches while the marks of the footprints appear.
Ninth, his nails are the color of red copper, thin and lustrous;
tenth, his kneecaps are firm, well-set, and perfectly rounded;
eleventh, his body is pure and clean.
Twelfth, his body is supple;
thirteenth, his body is not bent;
fourteenth, his fingers are long, slender, and rounded.
Fifteenth, his fingers are adorned with beautiful patterns;
sixteenth, his veins are deep-set;
seventeenth, his ankles do not protrude.
Eighteenth, the body is lustrous;
nineteenth, the body is self-sustaining and not crooked;
twentieth, the body is well-proportioned and full.
Twenty-first, his consciousness is fully perfected;
twenty-second, his deportment is complete and perfect;
twenty-third, he dwells in peace where no one can disturb him.
Twenty-fourth, his majesty awes all;
twenty-fifth, all delight in beholding him;
twenty-sixth, his face is neither overly large nor long.
Twenty-seventh, his facial features are upright and his expression is never distorted;
twenty-eighth, his face is perfectly full and complete;
twenty-ninth, his lips are red like the color of the *bimba* fruit.
Thirtieth, his voice is deep;
thirty-first, his navel is deep, round, and beautiful;
thirty-second, his body hairs curl to the right.
Thirty-third, his hands and feet are full;
thirty-fourth, his hands and feet are as he wishes;
thirty-fifth, the lines on his palms are clear and straight.
Thirty-sixth, the lines on the hands are long;
thirty-seventh, the lines on the hands are unbroken;
thirty-eighth, all sentient beings with malicious minds feel harmony and joy upon seeing him.
Thirty-ninth: his face is broad and beautiful; fortieth:
his face is pure and full like the moon; forty-first:
he speaks with a harmonious and joyful countenance in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
Forty-second: fragrant scents issue from his pores;
forty-third: unsurpassed fragrance issues from his mouth;
forty-fourth: his deportment is like that of a lion.
Forty-fifth, his advancing and halting are like those of an elephant king;
forty-sixth, his gait is like that of a swan king;
forty-seventh, his head is like the madana fruit.
Forty-eighth: possessing all components of perfect sound;
forty-ninth: sharp tusks;
fiftieth: a tongue of crimson color.
Fifty-first, his tongue is thin;
fifty-second, his body hair is red;
fifty-third, his body hair is pure and clean.
Fifty-fourth, his eyes are broad and long;
fifty-fifth, his orifices and features are fully formed;
fifty-sixth, his hands and feet are reddish-white, like the color of a lotus flower.
Fifty-seventh, his navel does not protrude;
fifty-eighth, his abdomen is not prominent;
fifty-ninth, his abdomen is slender.
Sixtieth, his body is not swaying;
sixty-first, his body is dignified and grave;
sixty-second, his body is large.
Sixty-third: his body is tall;
sixty-fourth: his hands and feet are clean, soft, and lustrous;
sixty-fifth: his halo extends one zhang on each side.
Sixty-sixth: walking with the body illuminated by light;
sixty-seventh: regarding all sentient beings with equanimity;
sixty-eighth: not treating sentient beings with contempt.
Sixty-ninth: following the voices of sentient beings, neither exceeding nor falling short;
seventieth: preaching the Dharma without attachment;
seventy-first: preaching the Dharma in accordance with the various languages of the multitude.
Seventy-second: A single utterance of sound responds to all sounds;
seventy-third: He preaches the Dharma according to sequential causes and conditions;
seventy-fourth: No sentient beings can fully perceive his marks.
Seventy-fifth, his contemplation is never satiated;
seventy-sixth, his hair is long and beautiful;
seventy-seventh, his hair is not disheveled.
Seventy-eighth: his hair curls beautifully;
seventy-ninth: the color of his hair is like that of a blue gem;
eightieth: his hands and feet possess the marks of virtue.
Subhūti! These are the eighty minor marks by which the Buddha-body is perfected. It is thus, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gather in sentient beings through two kinds of giving: namely, the gift of material wealth and the gift of the Dharma; this is a rare and extraordinary feat of the bodhisattvas.
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s gathering of sentient beings through loving speech?
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva preaches the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the six pāramitās, saying:
"You should practice the six pāramitās to encompass all wholesome dharmas."
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of beneficial conduct for gathering in sentient beings?
It is that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, throughout the long night, teaches sentient beings to practice the six pāramitās.
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s gathering of sentient beings through *samānārthatā* (common purpose)?

By means of the power of the five supernormal knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), the bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifests various transformations and enters the five realms of existence to engage in common activities with sentient beings, thereby gathering them through these four means.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they instruct and transform sentient beings,
saying: 'Good sons!'"
One should skillfully train in the discernment of all syllables, and likewise skillfully know the single syllable up to the forty-two syllables.
All speech enters the first letter-gateway; all speech also enters the second letter-gateway, and so on up to the forty-second letter-gateway—all speech enters within them.
"Each single character enters into all forty-two characters, and the forty-two characters likewise enter into a single character.
These sentient beings should thus skillfully study these forty-two characters; having skillfully studied the forty-two characters, they will be able to skillfully explain the dharma of characters;
having skillfully explained the dharma of characters, they will skillfully explain the dharma of no-words.

Subhūti! Just as the Buddha thoroughly knows the dharma of letters, thoroughly knows letters, and thoroughly knows the absence of letters, he teaches the dharma of letters for the sake of the dharma that is without letters. Why is this?
"Subhūti! Because it transcends all dharmas of names, it is called the Buddha-dharma.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If sentient beings are ultimately unobtainable, and dharmas are also unobtainable, and even the nature of dharmas is unobtainable—because they are ultimately empty and empty from the beginningless past.”
World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, and when practicing the *dhyānapāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, and *dānapāramitā*, how do they practice the four *dhyānas*, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighteen emptinesses; how do they practice the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics; and how do they abide in the five supernormal powers obtained as a result of their retribution to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
Sentient beings are truly unattainable.
Because sentient beings are unattainable, form is unattainable, and so on up to consciousness, which is also unattainable.
Because the five aggregates are unattainable, the six pāramitās and even the eighty minor marks are all unattainable.
Within this non-apprehensibility, there are no sentient beings, no form, and so on, up to no eighty minor marks.
World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom teach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, even the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be any bodhisattva-dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So it is, so it is! Just as you have said, because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, one should know that there is internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence."

Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, one should know that the five aggregates are empty; the twelve bases and eighteen elements are empty; the twelve links of dependent origination are empty; and the four noble truths are empty. The self is empty, as are the life-span, the individual, the being, the nourisher, the multitude, the person, the agent and the instigator of action, the originator and the instigator of arising, the experiencer and the instigator of experience, and the knower and the seer—all are empty.
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, one should know that the four dhyānas are empty, the four immeasurable minds are empty, and the four formless attainments are empty;

one should know that the four foundations of mindfulness are empty up to the eightfold noble path being empty, emptiness of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the eight liberations, and the nine successive attainments are all empty.

Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, one should know that the ten powers of a Buddha are empty, the four fearlessnesses are empty, the four unhindered knowledges are empty, and the eighteen unique qualities are empty;

one should know that the fruit of stream-entry is empty, the fruit of once-returning is empty, the fruit of non-returning is empty, the fruit of arhatship is empty, and the path of the pratyekabuddha is empty;
one should know that the bodhisattva stages are empty and unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is empty.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus perceives all dharmas as empty and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings without losing the characteristics of emptiness,
this bodhisattva, when contemplating in this way, knows that all dharmas are unimpeded.

Having realized that all phenomena are unimpeded, they do not destroy the characteristics of phenomena, nor do they engage in duality or discrimination; they simply preach the Dharma to sentient beings according to reality.
It is like a person conjured by a Buddha, who further conjures immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of people.

There are those who instruct in giving; there are those who instruct in maintaining the precepts; there are those who instruct in patience; there are those who instruct in diligence; there are those who instruct in meditative concentration; there are those who instruct in wisdom; and there are those who instruct in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless absorptions.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does a person conjured by the Buddha engage in conceptual differentiation or the destruction of dharmas?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."
“Since this emanated person has no mind and no mental factors, how could they differentiate or destroy any phenomena? “For this reason, Subhūti!”

It should be known that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs, uprooting them from the ground of perversion and causing each sentient being to attain the ground upon which they ought to abide, by means of the dharma that is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Subhūti!
This form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Form is neither bound nor liberated, and it is not form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated, and they are not consciousness.
Why is this? Because form is ultimately pure.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned—are likewise ultimately pure. Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, yet neither grasps at sentient beings nor at all phenomena, because all phenomena are ungraspable.

Because the Bodhisattva does not abide in any phenomenon, they abide within the characteristics of all phenomena—namely, that form is empty, and so on, up to the emptiness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

Why is this? Because from form (*rūpa*) up to conditioned and unconditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-asaṃskṛta-dharma*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be apprehended; therefore, they have no place of abiding.

A non-existent phenomenon does not abide in a non-existent phenomenon; a phenomenon of intrinsic nature does not abide in a phenomenon of intrinsic nature; and a phenomenon of other-nature does not abide in a phenomenon of other-nature.
Why is this? Because all these dharmas are unapprehendable.
Where, then, could an unapprehendable dharma abide?

Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of these various emptinesses, they are able to teach the Dharma in this way; practicing the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they commit no transgression against the Buddhas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.

Why is this? Because when the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats have attained this Dharma, they preach it for the sake of sentient beings, yet they do not alter the characteristics of phenomena.
Why is this? Because suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) cannot be altered. For what reason?
"Because the nature of all dharmas is non-existent.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) do not undergo transformation, is form different from the nature of phenomena?
Is form different from suchness and the limit of reality?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even up to conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, mundane and supramundane, and tainted and untainted—different [from them]?
The Buddha said: “No.

Form is not different from the dharma-nature, not different from suchness, and not different from the reality-limit; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even up to the contaminated and the uncontaminated—are likewise not different.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If form is not different from the dharma-nature, not different from suchness, and not different from the limit of reality—and if feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even all things with outflows and without outflows are likewise not different—how can one distinguish between dark dharmas that have dark retributions, namely: the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals?”
Wholesome dharmas have wholesome retribution, namely, the various devas and humans;
black-and-white dharmas have black-and-white retribution;

and neither-black-nor-white dharmas have neither-black-nor-white retribution, namely, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), the path of the pratyekabuddha, and unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is according to worldly convention that one distinguishes and speaks of the existence of karmic retribution; it is not so in the ultimate sense.
Within the ultimate sense, causes, conditions, and karmic retribution cannot be spoken of."
Why is this? Because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there are truly no marks, no conceptual differentiation, and no verbal expression.

This is because all things, from form (*rūpa*) up to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas, possess the characteristics of neither arising nor ceasing, neither defilement nor purity, being ultimately empty and empty from the beginningless past.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If it is by way of conventional truth that you distinguish and speak of the existence of karmic retribution, and not by way of the ultimate truth;”
All ordinary persons should possess the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of pratyekabuddha, and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do ordinary worldlings know that this is the conventional truth and that is the ultimate truth?"
If they were to know it, then ordinary persons would be those who have attained the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti,

because ordinary persons do not truly know the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), do not know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), do not know the Path, and do not know how to distinguish the fruits of the Path, how could there be any such fruits?
Subhūti! The noble ones know the conventional truth and know the ultimate truth; there is the path and there is the cultivation of the path.
For this reason, there are various fruits distinguished among the noble ones.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is the fruit attained by practicing the path?”
The Buddha said: "No, Subhūti!

One does not attain the fruit by practicing the path, nor does one attain the fruit by not practicing the path; nor does one attain the fruit apart from the path, nor does one attain the fruit while dwelling within the path."

In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, for the sake of sentient beings he distinguishes the fruits, yet he does not distinguish them as being either conditioned or unconditioned by nature.
“World-Honored One!

If one does not differentiate between the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to attain the various fruits, why does the World-Honored One himself say that one is called a *srotāpanna* because the three fetters are exhausted; a *sakṛdāgāmin* because lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated; an *anāgāmin* because the five lower fetters are exhausted; an *arhat* because the five higher fetters are exhausted; a *pratyekabuddha* because all phenomena that arise have the characteristic of cessation and dispersal; and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because all afflictions and habitual tendencies are severed?”
“World-Honored One!
How should I understand how one does not differentiate between the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet attains the various fruits?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Are the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the path of a pratyekabuddha, and anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi—all these fruits conditioned?”
"Is this unconditioned? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"All are unconditioned.
"Subhūti, within unconditioned dharmas, is there any discrimination?"
"No, World-Honored One!

If a good son or a good daughter penetrates all dharmas—whether conditioned or unconditioned—as having a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness, at that time, would there still be any discrimination between what is conditioned and what is unconditioned?"
“No, World-Honored One! “In this way, Subhūti,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings without discriminating among dharmas— namely, because of internal emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.”

This bodhisattva personally attains the dharma of non-attachment and also teaches others to attain the dharma of non-attachment—whether it be the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; or from the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because this bodhisattva is themselves without attachment, they also teach others to attain non-attachment.
Because they are without attachment, they are without obstruction.
It is like a person emanated by a Buddha who practices giving, yet does not receive the retribution for that giving, doing so solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Even when practicing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), they do not receive the retribution for that knowledge of all modes.

It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: although they practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) up to all dharmas—whether with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—they neither dwell in them nor receive their retribution, doing so solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have thoroughly mastered the characteristics of all dharmas.
Chapter 79: Thorough Mastery. From the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter 79, “Thorough Mastery,” Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva skillfully penetrate the characteristics of all phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Suppose, for example, a person created by transformation does not engage in lust, anger, or delusion; does not engage in form up to consciousness; does not engage in internal or external phenomena; does not engage in the various afflictions or fetters; does not engage in out-flowing phenomena or non-out-flowing phenomena, worldly phenomena or world-transcending phenomena, conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena; nor does he possess the fruits of sanctity.”
“The Bodhisattva is also like this: there is no such dharma, nor does he discriminate that there is such a dharma; this is called being well-versed in the characteristics of all dharmas.
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One!”
"How can a transformed person cultivate the Way?
The Buddha said,
"When a transformed person cultivates the Way, they are neither defiled nor pure, nor do they abide within the birth and death of the five realms."
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a person conjured by a Buddha have any fundamental reality?
Is there any defilement or purification in them?
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One.
A person conjured by the Buddha has no fundamental reality; it is neither defiled nor pure, and it does not abide within the cycle of birth and death in the five realms."
“Thus it is, Subhūti! It is likewise for the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has thoroughly mastered the characteristics of all dharmas. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Are all forms like an illusion?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness like an illusion?”
The Buddha said:
"All form is like an illusion; all feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like illusions.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
If all form is like a magical illusion, and all feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like a magical illusion, then all phenomena are like a magical illusion.

A magically created person has no form, no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they have neither defilement nor purity, neither the cycle of birth and death in the five realms nor any place of liberation.
"What kind of functional activity does a bodhisattva possess?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "What do you think?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva originally practiced the bodhisattva path, did he perceive any sentient beings who were liberated from the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, the heavens, or among humans?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Subhūti, it is likewise for the bodhisattva mahāsattva; he does not perceive any sentient being as being liberated from the three realms."
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive and know all phenomena to be like illusions and like transformations.
“World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives and knows that all dharmas are like illusions and like transformations, for what purpose do they practice the six pāramitās, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, up to and including practicing great compassion, purifying buddha-fields, and maturing sentient beings?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If sentient beings themselves knew that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would never practice the bodhisattva path for the sake of sentient beings throughout incalculable eons."

Subhūti! Because sentient beings themselves do not know that all dharmas are like illusions and like transformations, for this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the six pāramitās throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, bringing sentient beings to maturity, purifying buddha-fields, and attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation.”
"In what do sentient beings dwell, such that the Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās to extract them from it?
"Subhūti, sentient beings dwell only within names, marks, false recollections, and conceptual discriminations."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they extract sentient beings from within the false nature of names and signs.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!
"What is meant by 'name' (nāma),
and what is meant by 'characteristic' (nimitta)? The Buddha said:
"This is merely a forced construction, a mere conventional designation. That is to say:

'this is form,' 'this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness'; 'this is male,' 'this is female'; 'this is large,' 'this is small'; 'this is hell,' 'this is the animal realm,' 'this is the realm of hungry ghosts,' 'this is a human,' 'this is a deva'; 'this is conditioned' and 'this is unconditioned'; 'this is the fruit of stream-entry,' 'the fruit of once-returning,' 'the fruit of non-returning,' 'the fruit of arhatship,' 'the path of the pratyekabuddha,' and 'this is the path of the Buddha.'"
Subhūti! All phenomena that arise from the conjunction of conditions are merely provisional names; one grasps at all phenomena by means of these names, and for this reason they are called "names.
All conditioned phenomena possess only names and signs, yet foolish ordinary beings give rise to attachment within them.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by the power of skillful means, they instruct [beings] within the context of names to remain detached from them, saying:
"O sentient beings!..."
This is called a mere empty name, arising from false recollection and conceptual discrimination; you should not cling to such false recollections.
This matter is non-existent from beginning to end, for its intrinsic nature is empty; thus, it is that to which the wise do not cling.
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom uses the power of skillful means to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
Subhūti! This is what is called "name. What is "mark"?
Subhūti! There are two kinds of characteristics upon which ordinary persons become attached. What are these two?
The first is the mark of form; the second is the mark of the formless.
Subhūti, what is called the mark of form?
All forms whatsoever—whether coarse or subtle, beautiful or ugly—are empty.
Within this dharma of emptiness, to conceive through recollection and discrimination, to harbor a mind of attachment, and to grasp at signs is what is called the "sign of form."
What is the characteristic of the formless?
Regarding all formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*), the arising of afflictions due to conceptualization, discrimination, attachment, and grasping at signs is called the characteristic of the formless.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful power, teaches sentient beings to distance themselves from attachment to these signs, and causes them not to fall into dualistic dharmas within the signless dharma—namely, the distinction between "this is a sign" and "this is signless."
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom instructs sentient beings to distance themselves from signs and causes them to abide in the nature of signlessness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are merely names and signs, how is it that a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā can benefit themselves and also teach others so that they may attain wholesome benefit?”
“How does a bodhisattva fulfill the stages, proceeding from one stage to the next, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they attain the three vehicles?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If the fundamental nature of all phenomena truly existed and were not merely names and signs, then when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he would be unable to benefit himself, nor would he be able to benefit others.”
Subhūti! All dharmas have no fundamental reality; they exist only as names and signs.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he is able to fulfill the perfection of dhyāna because it is signless.
The perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity are so because they are signless.
They are fully endowed with the perfection of the four dhyānas, the perfection of the four immeasurables, and the perfection of the four formless attainments, because they are signless.
They are fully endowed with the perfection of the four foundations of mindfulness because they are signless;
and so on, up to being fully endowed with the perfection of the eightfold noble path because they are signless.
They are fully endowed with the perfection of internal emptiness because they are signless.
...up to the fulfillment of the perfection of the emptiness of non-existence and existence, because it is signless;
the fulfillment of the perfection of liberation, because it is signless;
and the fulfillment of the perfection of the nine successive attainments, because it is signless.

They fulfill the perfection of the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the fulfillment of the perfection of the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), because they are signless (*animitta*).
Because this bodhisattva is signless, they personally fulfill all these wholesome dharmas and also teach others to fulfill wholesome dharmas, because they are signless.

Subhūti! If the characteristics of all dharmas were to exist in reality even to the extent of a single hair’s breadth, then when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they would be unable to know that all dharmas are without characteristics and without recollection, and thus attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They also teach sentient beings to attain the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*). Why is this?
Because all untainted dharmas are without marks (*animitta*) and without recollection (*asmṛti*).
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom benefits sentient beings by means of untainted dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are signless and without recollection, how can one enumerate them as the Dharma of śrāvakas, the Dharma of pratyekabuddhas, the Dharma of bodhisattvas, or the Dharma of buddhas?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is the dharma of signlessness different from the dharma of the śrāvakas?
"No, World-Honored One."
“Are the dharma of signlessness different from the dharma of pratyekabuddhas, the dharma of bodhisattvas, and the dharma of buddhas?
“No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The dharma of signlessness is itself the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the dharma of pratyekabuddhas, the dharma of bodhisattvas, and the dharma of buddhas.”
Subhūti said, “So it is, World-Honored One. “Subhūti!
For this reason, Subhūti, you should know that all dharmas are signless (*animitta*).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the signlessness of all dharmas, they gain an increase in wholesome dharmas, namely: the six pāramitās, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
Why is this? Because for a bodhisattva, no other dharma is considered essential as much as the three gates of liberation, namely: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Why is that?
All wholesome dharmas enter the three gates of liberation. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics; this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness.
All phenomena are without marks; this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness.
All phenomena are without volitional activity and without the mark of arising; this is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the three gates of liberation, at that time they are able to train in the characteristics of the five aggregates, able to train in the characteristics of the twelve bases, and able to train in the characteristics of the eighteen elements; able to train in the four noble truths and the law of the twelve links of dependent origination; able to train in internal emptiness, external emptiness, and so forth up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; able to train in the six perfections, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth up to the eightfold noble path; and able to train in the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom learn the characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the characteristic of form, they know the arising and ceasing of form, and they know the suchness of form.”
How does one know the characteristic of form?
One knows that form is ultimately empty; its internal parts are distinct, void, and without reality, like foam on water which lacks solidity. This is what it means to know the characteristic of form.
How does one know the arising and ceasing of form?
When form arises, it comes from nowhere; when it passes away, it goes nowhere. If it neither comes nor goes, this is knowing the characteristic of the arising and ceasing of form.
What is knowing the suchness of form?
This suchness of form is neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure; this is called knowing the suchness of form.
Subhūti! As the name is suchness—real, not false, as it was before, so it is in the middle and at the end, always without change—this is called knowing the suchness of form.
How does one know the characteristic of feeling?
How does one know the arising and ceasing of feeling?
How does one know the suchness of feeling?
The Bodhisattva knows the characteristics of all sensations (*vedanā*) to be like bubbles on water, arising and ceasing one after another; this is knowing the characteristics of sensation.
Knowing the arising and ceasing of sensation means that these sensations come from nowhere and go nowhere; this is knowing the arising and ceasing of sensation.

To know the suchness of sensation is to know that this suchness is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither defiled nor pure; this is what is meant by knowing the suchness of sensation.
How does one know the characteristics of perception?
How does one know the arising and ceasing of perception?
How does one know the suchness of perception?

To know the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*) means that this perception is like a mirage; water cannot be found there, yet one falsely conceives the perception of water—this is knowing the characteristic of perception.
To know the arising and ceasing of perception means that this perception comes from nowhere and goes nowhere—this is knowing the arising and ceasing of perception.

To know the suchness of perception is to know that the suchness of all perceptions is neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure, and does not deviate from the true mark; this is called knowing the suchness of perception.
How does one know the characteristics of formations?
How does one know the arising and ceasing of formations?
How does one know the suchness of formations?

Regarding the characteristic of formations (*saṃskāra*): formations are like a plantain tree; when each layer is peeled away, no solid core is found. This is called knowing the characteristic of formations.
Regarding the arising and ceasing of formations: all formations arise from nowhere and go nowhere. This is called knowing the arising and ceasing of formations.

To know the suchness of all phenomena is to know that all conditioned things are neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither defiled nor pure; this is what it means to know the suchness of phenomena.
What is the characteristic of consciousness?
What is the arising and ceasing of consciousness?
What is the suchness of consciousness?
Regarding the characteristic of consciousness: consciousness is like a magician who conjures four kinds of troops, which have no reality.
The characteristic of consciousness is also like this; this is called knowing the characteristic of consciousness.
Regarding the arising and ceasing of consciousness: when consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.

This is the arising and ceasing of consciousness. Regarding the suchness of consciousness: consciousness is neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. This is the suchness of consciousness.
How does one know the sense bases (*āyatana*)?

From the eye being empty of the nature of the eye, up to the mind being empty of the nature of the mind; from forms being empty of the nature of forms, up to mental phenomena being empty of the nature of mental phenomena.
How does one know the elements (*dhātu*)?

The eye is empty of the element of the eye; visible forms are empty of the element of visible forms; and eye-consciousness is empty of the element of eye-consciousness. This applies likewise up to the element of mind-consciousness.
How, then, does one know the Four Noble Truths?
When one knows the Noble Truth of Suffering, one is detached from two things; knowing that the Truth of Suffering is neither dual nor distinct is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
It is the same for Origination, Cessation, and the Path.
How does one know the suchness of suffering?
Knowing the noble truth of suffering is itself suchness; suchness is itself the noble truth of suffering.
It is the same for the truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
"How does one know the twelve links of dependent origination?
To know that the twelve links of dependent origination have the characteristic of non-arising—this is called knowing the twelve links of dependent origination.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, discerns and knows all dharmas individually, would he not thereby destroy the nature of dharmas by means of the nature of form, and so on, up to destroying the nature of dharmas by means of the nature of all-knowledge?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there were any dharma existing apart from the nature of dharmas (dharmatā), it would destroy the nature of dharmas;
since no dharma can be found apart from the nature of dharmas, therefore it is not destroyed."
Why is this? Subhūti!

The Buddha and his disciples know that no phenomena can be found outside the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Because they cannot be found, they do not say that there are phenomena outside the nature of phenomena.
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in the dharma-nature.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the dharma-nature, there is nothing to be studied.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the dharma-nature, they study all dharmas.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are themselves the dharma-nature.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions is it that all dharmas are themselves the dharma-nature?”
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas enter into the nature of signlessness and the unconditioned; for this reason, by studying the dharma-nature, one studies all dharmas."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are themselves the dharma-nature, why do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity?”
Why do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth dhyānas?
Why do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?
Why study the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Why study the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path?
Why study the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
Why study the eight liberations, the nine successive concentrations, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities?
Why study the six supernormal powers?
Why study the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics?
Why study birth into the great clans of the Kṣatriyas, the great clans of the Brahmins, or the great households of the householders?

Why do students [aspire to] be born in the abodes of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven?
For what reason do students train in the abodes of the Brahmā-pāriṣadya gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Asaṃjñisattva gods, and the Śuddhāvāsa gods?
Why do they take birth in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Why should one study the stage of the first resolve, and the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages?
Why should one study the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhisattva-dharmatā?
Why study to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields?
Why study the various dhāraṇīs?
Why study the joy of preaching the Dharma?
Why study *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and having studied it, attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and know all phenomena?
World-Honored One,
within the *dharmatā* of all phenomena, there is no such discrimination.
"Bhagavān! Will there not be bodhisattvas who fall into non-paths?
For what reason?"
World-Honored One!

Within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is no such discrimination; within the nature of phenomena, there is no form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Furthermore, the natures of all phenomena do not depart from form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Form is itself the dharma-nature; the dharma-nature is itself form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this;
all dharmas are also like this. The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
It is as you have said.
Form is itself the dharma-nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves the dharma-nature. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they perceive any phenomenon as existing outside of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they do not seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having realized that all phenomena are themselves the dharma-nature, they employ names and signs to describe that which is without names or signs—namely, "this is form," "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," and so on, up to "this is unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment."

Subhūti! It is as if a skilled illusionist or his apprentice were to manifest illusions in a great assembly, creating various forms and colors—men, women, elephants, horses, and magnificent gardens; as well as dwellings, pavilions, flowing springs, bathing pools, clothing, bedding, perfumes, flowers, necklaces, and various delicacies and foods—and perform many kinds of music to delight the multitude;
furthermore, he would create illusory persons and cause them to practice giving, uphold the precepts, exercise patience, exert diligence, cultivate meditative concentration, and develop wisdom.

This illusionist further creates illusions of great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, and great families of householders; he creates illusions of the abodes of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three on Mount Sumeru, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven to show them to the multitude;
he further creates illusions of the Brahmakāyika Heaven up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven;
and he again creates illusions of srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas.
Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment,
practice the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā),
the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā); they practice from the first stage (bhūmi) up to the tenth stage.
Entering the stage of a bodhisattva, they sport with supernormal powers, bring sentient beings to maturity,
and purify buddha-fields; they sport in various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, practice the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses,
the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, and great kindness and great compassion, thereby becoming fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a buddha’s body.
The two marks and eighty secondary characteristics are displayed to all people.

Among them, those of little wisdom exclaim that such things have never been seen before; this person is highly skilled at performing various activities to entertain the masses, manifesting all kinds of forms and colors, even the thirty-two major marks and eighty secondary characteristics to adorn the Buddha’s body.
Among them, a wise person reflects, saying: "It is unprecedented!

There is no substantial reality herein; yet by means of dharmas that are non-existent, he entertains the multitude, causing them to perceive forms where there are no phenomena and no characteristics of phenomena, and no characteristics of existence."

"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any phenomenon apart from the dharma-nature that practices the perfection of wisdom. By means of skillful power, although they do not apprehend a sentient being, they themselves practice giving, and they also teach others to give; they praise the dharma of giving and joyfully extol those who practice giving;
they themselves maintain the precepts and also teach others to maintain the precepts."
One practices patience oneself and also teaches others to practice patience;
one practices diligence oneself and also teaches others to practice diligence;
one practices meditation oneself and also teaches others to practice meditation.
One cultivates wisdom for oneself and also teaches others to cultivate wisdom; one praises the practice of the dharma of cultivating wisdom and rejoices in those who cultivate wisdom.

One practices the ten wholesome paths of action oneself and also teaches others to practice them; one praises the practice of the dharma of the ten wholesome paths and rejoices in those who practice the ten wholesome paths.

One personally undertakes and practices the five precepts, teaches others to undertake and practice the five precepts, praises the dharma of the five precepts, and joyfully extols those who undertake and practice the five precepts.
One personally observes the eightfold precepts of the fast, teaches others to observe the eightfold precepts of the fast, praises the method of the eightfold precepts of the fast,
and joyfully commends those who practice the eightfold precepts of the fast.

One practices the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; one practices loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and one practices the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as well as teaching others to practice them.

They personally practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they personally practice the three gates of liberation and the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. They also teach others to practice the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, praise the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and joyfully praise those who practice the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Subhūti! If there were any difference in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) between the beginning, the middle, and the end, this bodhisattva mahāsattva would be unable to manifest that nature of phenomena through the power of skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity.

Subhūti! Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without difference in the beginning, middle, or end, for this reason the bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and practices the bodhisattva path for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-four; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eighty: On the Ultimate Reality (Bhūtakoṭi).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"If sentient beings are ultimately unattainable, for whose sake does the bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
Subhūti! If the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) were different from the limit of sentient beings (sattvakoṭi), the bodhisattva would not practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Subhūti!
The limit of reality!
The limit of sentient beings is not different from it.
For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they establish sentient beings within the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) by means of the non-disruption of the dharma of the reality-limit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is identical to the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*), then the bodhisattva would be establishing the limit of reality within the limit of reality."
World-Honored One!
If one were to establish the limit of reality within the limit of reality, then one would be establishing self-nature within self-nature.
World-Honored One!
"One should not establish intrinsic nature within intrinsic nature.
World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, establish sentient beings in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The limit of reality cannot be established upon the limit of reality; intrinsic nature cannot be established upon intrinsic nature. Subhūti!”

Now, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful power, they establish sentient beings in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Yet the limit of reality is not different from the limit of sentient beings; the limit of reality and the limit of sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What is the power of skillful means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? By means of this power of skillful means, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he establish sentient beings in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) without destroying the characteristic of the limit of reality?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful power establishes sentient beings in giving.”
Having established this, he explains that the beginning, end, and middle of giving are empty, saying:
"Such giving is empty at its prior limit, empty at its posterior limit, and empty in its middle;
the giver is also empty, the reward of giving is also empty, and the recipient is also empty."
"O sons of good family!
Within the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of all dharmas, nothing can be apprehended.
You should not conceive of the gift as distinct, the giver as distinct, the reward of the gift as distinct, or the recipient as distinct."

If you do not conceive of the gift as distinct from the giver, the reward for the gift as distinct, or the recipient as distinct, then at that time this giving can take up the flavor of the deathless and attain the fruit of the flavor of the deathless.
"O son of good family!
Because of this giving, do not be attached to form, and do not be attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is that?"
This giving is empty of the characteristic of giving; the giver is empty of being a giver; the reward of giving is empty of being a reward of giving;

and the recipient is empty of being a recipient. Within emptiness, giving cannot be apprehended; the giver cannot be apprehended; the reward of giving cannot be apprehended; and the recipient cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because these dharmas are ultimately empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful power, they instruct sentient beings to uphold the precepts, saying to them:
"O son of good family!
They abandon the practice of taking life, up to and including the abandonment of the practice of wrong views. Why is this?
O son of good family!
Regarding the phenomena as you have conceptualized them, these phenomena do not possess such a nature.
O son of good family!
You should reflect carefully: what is this "sentient being" that you wish to deprive of life?
"By what means does one take life?
This applies even to wrong views. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus brings sentient beings to maturity through the power of skillful means, that bodhisattva mahāsattva then explains to those sentient beings the fruits of giving and ethical discipline, saying:
"The intrinsic nature of these fruits of giving and ethical discipline is empty."
Having realized that the intrinsic nature of the fruits of generosity and ethical discipline is empty, one does not cling to them.
Because of this non-clinging, the mind is not distracted, and one is able to generate wisdom.
By means of this wisdom, one severs all fetters, afflictions, and habitual tendencies, entering nirvana without remainder.
This is a conventional dharma, not the ultimate reality.
Why is this? Within emptiness there is no cessation, nor is there anyone who causes cessation;
the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena is itself nirvāṇa. “Furthermore, Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees sentient beings with minds of anger and affliction, they instruct them, saying:
"Come, son of good family!
Practice patience and become a person of patience; you should take delight in patience."
That which you are angry at is empty of intrinsic nature.
Come, son of good family!
Reflect in this way:
"In what phenomena am I angry? Who is the one who is angry?
And who is the object of my anger?"
These dharmas are all empty; this nature of emptiness never fails to be empty.

This emptiness was not created by the Buddhas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas, nor by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. It was not created by devas, ghosts, spirits, nāga kings, asuras, kiṃnaras, or mahoragas; nor by the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven; nor by the gods from the Brahmakāyika heaven up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; nor was it created by the gods from the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
"You should reflect in this way:
'With whom is there anger?
Who is the one who is angry?'"
"What are the objects of anger?
All phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; in phenomena that are empty of intrinsic nature, there is nothing toward which one can feel anger. Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of these causes and conditions, they establish sentient beings in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, gradually and successively instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them, so that they may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is a conventional dharma, not the ultimate reality.
Why is this? Because within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no one who attains, no dharma that is attained, and no place where attainment occurs.
Subhūti! This is called the reality-limit, the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
For the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this dharma, yet even these sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are free from the mark of a sentient being. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by the power of skillful means, they see sentient beings who are indolent and instruct them to achieve physical vigor and mental vigor.
He spoke these words:
"O sons of good family!
Within the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena, there is no phenomenon of indolence, no indolent person, and no act of indolence."
The nature of all these dharmas is entirely empty; there is nothing that surpasses this emptiness of nature.
You should exert physical vigor and mental vigor, and do not be indolent for the sake of producing wholesome dharmas.
Wholesome dharmas are: whether it be generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom;
or the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis;
or the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
If there are the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—do not be indolent!
O sons of good family!

"One should know that within the emptiness of the nature of all dharmas there is the characteristic of non-obstruction; within the dharma of non-obstruction, there is neither one who is indolent nor the dharma of indolence. Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they instruct sentient beings to abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature so that they do not fall into dualistic dharmas. Why is this?
Because within this emptiness of intrinsic nature there is neither duality nor distinction.
This non-dual dharma is such that there is no place for attachment. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they instruct sentient beings to be diligent, saying:
"O sons of good family!
Diligent exertion whether it be in giving, or in ethical discipline, or in patience, or in diligence, or in meditative concentration, or in wisdom;
or in meditative concentration, liberation, and samādhi;
or in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Whether it be the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, or the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
whether it be the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, or great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Regarding these dharmas, you should not conceive of them as having dual characteristics, nor should you conceive of them as having non-dual characteristics. Why is this?
Because the nature of these dharmas is entirely empty.
"This dharma of intrinsic emptiness should not be contemplated through dualistic marks, nor should it be contemplated through non-dualistic marks. Thus, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom brings sentient beings to maturity through the power of skillful means.

Having brought sentient beings to maturity, he gradually instructs them so that they may attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of pratyekabuddha, and the stage of bodhisattva, leading them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, seeing sentient beings with distracted minds, he employs skillful means for the sake of benefiting those beings and speaks these words:
'O sons of good family!'"
"You should cultivate meditative concentration.
Do not give rise to distracted thoughts; you should give rise to a single-minded focus. Why is this?"
This dharma-nature is entirely emptiness; within emptiness, no dharma can be apprehended, whether it be distraction or single-mindedness.
You should abide in this samādhi; whatever actions you perform—whether of body, speech, or mind;
whether practicing giving, observing precepts, exercising patience, or applying diligent effort—[all should be done so].
Whether practicing meditative concentration or cultivating wisdom; whether practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
or practicing the various liberations and the successive attainments;
or practicing the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, and great compassion—
The thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics; whether it be the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, or the path of the Buddha;
or the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or all [of these].
Whether it be for the sake of maturing sentient beings or purifying Buddha-fields,
you all should act in accordance with your vows, so that you may abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through the power of skillful means for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the end, they never become weary or desist; they constantly seek wholesome dharmas to benefit sentient beings."

From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they make offerings to all buddhas and hear the Dharma from them; throughout the succession of abandoning and receiving bodies until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they never forget or lose it.
This bodhisattva constantly attains all dhāraṇī-dharmas and is endowed with all faculties—namely, the faculty of body, the faculty of speech, and the faculty of mind. Why is this?
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly cultivates the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Because they cultivate the knowledge of all modes, they cultivate all paths: whether the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers.
The Bodhisattva who practices the supernormal powers of the divine way constantly benefits sentient beings and never forgets this.
Abiding in the supernormal powers obtained as a result of retribution, this Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings and enters the five paths of birth and death without ever being diminished.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and benefits sentient beings through meditative concentration.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and abides in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they benefit sentient beings through the power of skillful means,
saying: 'You sons of good family!'"
Contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is empty.
Sons of good family!
You should perform all actions—whether bodily, verbal, or mental—to take up the flavor of ambrosia and attain the fruit of ambrosia.
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no dharma that regresses.
Why is this? Because the emptiness of intrinsic nature does not regress, nor is there anyone who regresses.
"Because emptiness by nature is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma, how could there be any falling back within these dharmas that do not exist? Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should thus instruct sentient beings so that they never become weary or negligent.

This bodhisattva personally practices the ten wholesome paths of action and also teaches others to practice them; the same applies to the accomplishment of the five precepts and the eight precepts of the upavāsa fast.
He personally practices the first dhyāna and also teaches others to practice the first dhyāna, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna.
One constantly practices the mind of loving-kindness oneself and also teaches others to practice the mind of loving-kindness; this applies likewise even to the mind of equanimity.
One practices the sphere of infinite space oneself and also teaches others to practice the sphere of infinite space; this applies likewise even to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One practices the four foundations of mindfulness oneself and also teaches others to practice the four foundations of mindfulness; this extends likewise to the eightfold noble path, the ten powers of a Buddha, and even up to the eighty minor marks of excellence.

He himself gives rise to wisdom within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) yet does not abide therein; he also teaches others to attain the fruit of stream-entry, and so on up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), which is likewise.
One generates wisdom within the path of a pratyekabuddha oneself, yet does not abide therein, and also teaches others to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha.
One generates the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi oneself, and also teaches others to generate the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path, by the power of skillful means, they never become weary or desist.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the nature of all dharmas is eternally empty, and within this eternal emptiness sentient beings cannot be apprehended, nor can dharmas or non-dharmas be apprehended,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva seek the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”
The nature of all dharmas is empty; within emptiness, sentient beings cannot be apprehended, nor can dharmas or non-dharmas be apprehended. Subhūti!

If the nature of all dharmas were not empty, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva would not rely on the emptiness of nature to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor would he preach the dharma of the emptiness of nature for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti! The nature of form is empty; the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he teaches the dharma that the five aggregates are empty by nature.
He teaches the dharma of the intrinsic emptiness of the twelve bases and the eighteen elements;
he teaches the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the dharma of the intrinsic emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
he teaches the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, and the four [fearlessnesses].
The fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion,
the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics— all these are dharmas whose nature is emptiness. [He] speaks of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning,
the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the one...
Subhūti, all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) severs the habitual tendencies of afflictions; it is the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Subhūti, if internal emptiness were not empty, or if external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā), were not empty, then one would destroy emptiness.
This emptiness of intrinsic nature is neither eternal nor discontinuous. Why is this?
This emptiness of intrinsic nature has no place of abiding; it comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere.
Subhūti! This is called the characteristic of the abiding of dharmas (*dharmasthitilakṣaṇa*).

Within this, there are no dharmas; there is no accumulation and no dispersal, no increase and no decrease, no arising and no cessation, and no defilement and no purity. This is the characteristic of all dharmas.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this, they give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet they do not perceive any dharma that is being produced; this absence of production and absence of abiding is called the characteristic of the abiding of dharmas (*dharma-sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he perceives that the nature of all phenomena is empty, and thus he does not turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma that can act as an obstacle; how, then, could doubt arise?
This is called the emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā) of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

One does not apprehend sentient beings, does not apprehend a self, does not apprehend a person, does not apprehend a life-span, and does not apprehend a life-principle; even up to, one does not apprehend a knower or a seer. Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, form is unapprehendable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable; even up to, the eighty minor marks are unapprehendable.

Subhūti! It is as if, for example, a Buddha were to manifest four assemblies—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—and constantly preach the Dharma for these assemblies for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas without ceasing.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Will these transformed beings attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, or the fruit of an arhat? Will they receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One! Why is this?"
Because these transformed beings have no fundamental reality,
all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and likewise lack any fundamental reality. What,
then, are these "beings" who attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, or who receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: though they teach the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature to sentient beings, those sentient beings are in reality unobtainable.”
Because sentient beings have fallen into perversion, one uproots them and causes them to abide in non-perversion.
Perversion is itself non-perversion; although perversion and non-perversion are of a single characteristic, there is much perversion and little non-perversion.
In the state of non-perversion and the middle way, there is no self and no sentient beings, up to and including no knower and no seer.

In the state of non-perversion and the middle way, there is also no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there are no twelve bases, up to and including no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within this and practices the perfection of wisdom, they pull sentient beings out from among the inversions of the marks of sentient beings; that is to say, they pull them out from the mark of "there are sentient beings" where there are no sentient beings, and so on, up to pulling them out from the marks of a knower and a seer.

Within the formless, they extract sentient beings from the perception of form; within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they extract them from the perceptions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. It is likewise for the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and all phenomena subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).

Subhūti! There are also various untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma), namely: the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga).
Although such dharmas as these are untainted (*anāsrava*), they do not accord with the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The characteristic of the ultimate truth is non-action (*akṛta*), unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), unborn (*ajāta*), signless (*animitta*), and ineffable (*anabhilāpya*); this is called the ultimate truth, and it is also called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and the path of all Buddhas.
Within this, no sentient being is apprehended, nor even a knower or a seer.
No form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is apprehended, nor even the eighty minor marks of physical excellence.

Why is this? It is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not seek the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of the dharmas of the path; rather, they seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of the true mark of all dharmas, which is the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
This nature is empty of intrinsic nature at the prior limit; it is also empty of intrinsic nature at the posterior limit, and it is also empty of intrinsic nature at the middle limit.
It is eternally empty of intrinsic nature; there is no time when it is not empty of intrinsic nature.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice this Prajñāpāramitā of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they seek the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgajñatā) in order to extract sentient beings from their various attachments to signs.
When seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), one traverses all paths—whether the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the bodhisattva.

This bodhisattva, having perfected all paths, extracts sentient beings from their false attachments and conceptions; once the buddha-field has been purified, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* according to their lifespan.

Subhūti! The path of the Buddhas of the ten directions in the past was what is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the paths of the Buddhas of the ten directions in the future and present are likewise empty of intrinsic nature.
Apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no path and no fruit of the path in the world.
"One must approach the Buddhas and hear that the nature of all these dharmas is emptiness; by practicing these dharmas, one does not lose sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"Most rare indeed!
