These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice this dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, yet they do not destroy the characteristic of the emptiness of intrinsic nature—namely, that form is different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and so on, up to unexcelled perfect enlightenment being different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature."
Subhūti! Form is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself form; this continues up to and including unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If form were different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and even if unsurpassed perfect enlightenment were different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not be able to attain all-knowledge."

Subhūti! Now, form is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and so on, up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, knowing that all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, resolves his mind to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because within these there is no dharma that is real or permanent; it is only because ordinary beings are attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and because ordinary beings grasp at the marks of form and grasp at the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as having a self—that their minds become attached to internal and external dharmas, thereby receiving the form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of a future body.
For these reasons, one cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, nor the wandering through the five realms of existence.

For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they do not destroy the characteristics of phenomena such as form—whether they be empty or non-empty.

Why is this? Because the nature of form is empty and does not destroy form—namely, that "this is form" and "this is emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For example, just as space does not destroy space, internal space does not destroy external space, and external space does not destroy internal space; so it is, Subhūti!
Form does not destroy the mark of emptiness of form, nor does the mark of emptiness of form destroy form. Why is this?
Because these two dharmas have no inherent nature that can effect destruction—namely, that "this is emptiness" or "this is not emptiness"—and it is the same even up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are empty and without differentiation, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the time of first generating the mind of awakening, makes this vow:”
“I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are without differentiation, how can a bodhisattva resolve their mind and say: [“I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi”]?
"I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One!
If one discriminates among dharmas, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with dualistic characteristics, there is no anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
If one discriminates by making a duality of things, there is no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one does not dualize or discriminate among all phenomena, that is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Enlightenment is characterized by non-duality and indestructibility.

Subhūti, this enlightenment does not proceed within form; it does not proceed within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; indeed, even enlightenment does not proceed within enlightenment itself.
Why is this? Form is itself awakening, and awakening is itself form; they are non-dual and without distinction. This applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"This bodhi is not practiced for the sake of grasping, nor is it practiced for the sake of abandoning.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices neither for the sake of grasping nor for the sake of abandoning awakening, where does the bodhisattva mahāsattva practice awakening?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Where does a person created by a Buddha practice?”
"If one were to grasp at the middle way,
or if one were to abandon the middle way? Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
It is neither practicing in the midst of grasping nor practicing in the midst of relinquishing.
The Buddha said:
“The awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: it does not proceed by way of grasping, nor does it proceed by way of abandoning.
Subhūti, what do you think? Where would the awakening of an arhat proceed within a dream?”
“Does one practice by grasping at the middle way, or does one practice by abandoning the middle way?
“No, World-Honored One! One does not practice by grasping at the middle way, nor does one practice by abandoning the middle way.”
“World-Honored One!
Since Arhats never sleep at all, how can there be awakening within a dream, whether by practicing through grasping or by practicing through relinquishing? “Subhūti!”

The unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: it does not proceed by way of grasping, nor does it proceed by way of relinquishing—namely, it proceeds within form, and so on, up to proceeding within all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
“World-Honored One!

Could it be that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without practicing the ten stages, without practicing the six pāramitās, without practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, without practicing the fourteen kinds of emptiness, without practicing the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, and without practicing the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighty minor marks, yet abiding in the five supernormal powers, purifying buddha-fields, and maturing sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”

Now, the Bodhisattva practices nowhere apart from bodhi; yet, if they do not fully complete the ten stages, the six pāramitās, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the ten powers of a Buddha, and even the eighty minor marks, they would be practicing constant renunciation, yet their practice would be deceptive and erroneous.
Without being fully endowed with these dharmas, one will ultimately never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, dwelling within the mark of form, dwelling within the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and even dwelling within the mark of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is able to fulfill the ten stages and eventually attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This mark is eternally quiescent; there is no dharma that can increase or decrease, arise or cease, be defiled or purified, attain the Path, or attain the fruit.

It is by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), not by way of the ultimate, true meaning (*paramārtha*). Why is this?

In the ultimate sense, there is no form, nor anything up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, there is no one who practices for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
All these dharmas are spoken of by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Subhūti,

from the time a bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolves upon enlightenment until they practice for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, neither enlightenment increases nor do sentient beings decrease, and the bodhisattva neither increases nor decreases.
Subhūti, what do you think?

When a person first attains the Way, abiding in the *anupādāya-samādhi* (uninterrupted samādhi) and obtaining the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they achieve either the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, or the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*, or the fruit of an *anāgāmin*, or the fruit of an *arhat*.
"At that time, did you have any attainment— whether it be a dream, or the mind, or the path,
or the fruit of the path? Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One!"
"It is not so," the Buddha said. "Subhūti!"
"How should one know that one has attained the path of an arhat?
"World-Honored One!
It is by way of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) that we conceptually designate it as 'the path of an arhat'."
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”

From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one speaks of a "bodhisattva," and speaks of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Within this awakening (*bodhi*), no dharma can be apprehended, whether as increasing or decreasing, because the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas is empty.

Since the intrinsic emptiness of all phenomena cannot even be apprehended, how much less could there be the apprehension of the mind of the first stage up to the mind of the tenth stage, the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhis of signlessness and wishlessness, or indeed any of the Buddha-dharmas that could be apprehended? Such a thing is impossible.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and brings benefit to sentient beings.
Chapter 81: The Chapter on Fulfillment (The Chapter on Illumination according to the *Dānzhào míngpǐn* edition). Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, yet does not fully complete the bodhisattva path, they will be unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the bodhisattva path so as to be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, practices the perfection of giving by means of skillful means—neither apprehending the gift, nor the giver, nor the recipient, yet not being separated from these dharmas while practicing the perfection of giving—this is what illuminates the bodhisattva path."
Thus it is, Subhūti! By means of the power of skillful means, a bodhisattva fulfills the bodhisattva path.
Having fulfilled it, they are able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Holding the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—even up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma)—are also like this.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means, they do not destroy form, nor do they follow after form."
Why is this? Because the nature of form does not exist, it is neither destroyed nor followed; this is likewise true for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, by the power of skillful means, they neither destroy nor follow the dānapāramitā. Why is this?
"Because the nature of the perfection of giving does not exist, it is the same for everything up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature that can be destroyed or followed, how is it that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to practice the perfection of wisdom, which is the place of training for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not study the prajñāpāramitā cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“As you have said, a bodhisattva cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without training in the prajñāpāramitā; however, it can be attained by not being separated from the power of skillful means.”
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom were able to apprehend even a single dharma-nature, they should take hold of it;
but since it cannot be apprehended, what is there to be taken?

That is to say: "This is the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), this is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), this is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), this is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical conduct (śīla-pāramitā), and the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā); this is form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)."
Śāriputra! This Prajñāpāramitā is without a mark that can be grasped; even all the dharmas of the Buddhas are without marks that can be grasped. Śāriputra!
This is called not grasping at anything from the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the Buddha-dharmas; this is what a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should study.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in this, even the characteristic of training cannot be apprehended, let alone the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Dharma of the Buddhas, the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas, the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, and the Dharma of ordinary persons?
Why is this so, Śāriputra?

Among all phenomena, not a single phenomenon possesses an intrinsic nature. Since all phenomena are thus devoid of intrinsic nature, what are they that are called ordinary persons, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas?
If these noble and holy ones did not exist, how could there be dharmas?
It is because of these dharmas that one distinguishes and speaks of ordinary persons, srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas have no nature, no reality, and no fundamental basis, how can one know that this is an ordinary person and even that this is a Buddha?”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“In the objects of attachment for ordinary people, does form have an intrinsic nature or a reality? “No, World-Honored One.”
“It is only because of the perverted mind that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— are likewise so. Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by the power of skillful means and because they see that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and lack a fundamental basis, they are able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, by means of the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), seeing that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and without a fundamental basis, is able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any fundamental basis of dharmas within which he might dwell and then fall back or become indolent.”

Śāriputra! The root of all dharmas now is truly without self, without any nature of its own, and eternally empty; it is only because of perversion and delusion that sentient beings cling to the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all dharmas have the nature of non-existence, are eternally empty, and are empty of their own characteristics, they practice the perfection of wisdom by establishing themselves therein.

Just as a magician preaches the Dharma for sentient beings—teaching the Dharma of giving to the stingy, the Dharma of maintaining precepts to those who break them, the Dharma of patience to the angry, the Dharma of diligence to the indolent, the Dharma of meditative concentration to the distracted, and the Dharma of wisdom to the ignorant.
He causes sentient beings to abide in generosity up to wisdom, and thereafter preaches for them the noble Dharma that can bring about escape from suffering.
By means of this Dharma, they attain the fruit of stream-entry, up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and even unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that these sentient beings are non-existent, they instruct them in giving, morality, and so forth, up to wisdom; only then do they preach the noble Dharma capable of bringing about deliverance from suffering.”
"By means of these dharmas, one attains the fruit of srotāpanna up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, there is no fault of 'having something to be attained' (upalambha)."

Why is this? Śāriputra, when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend a sentient being; it is only because of the continuity of empty dharmas that they are called "sentient beings."
Śāriputra! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell within the two truths and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings:
the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.

Śāriputra! Although sentient beings cannot be apprehended within the two truths, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings by means of skillful power.

When sentient beings hear this Dharma, even the "self" of the present life cannot be found; how much less could one find one who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or the dharmas used for that attainment?
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings by means of skillful power.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The mind of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is vast and expansive; there is no dharma to be apprehended—whether as a single characteristic, a different characteristic, or a distinct characteristic—and yet he is able to adorn himself with such a great vow.”

By means of this adornment, one is not born in the desire realm, not born in the form realm, and not born in the formless realm; one does not perceive the nature of the conditioned, nor does one perceive the nature of the unconditioned, yet one delivers sentient beings across the three realms while not apprehending any sentient beings.
Why is this? Because sentient beings are neither bound nor liberated.
Since sentient beings are neither bound nor liberated, they are neither defiled nor pure.
Because there is neither defilement nor purity, there is no differentiation of the five destinies.
Because there is no differentiation of the five destinies, there is no karma and no afflictions.
Because there is no karma and no afflictions, there should likewise be no retribution.
"By reason of this karmic retribution, they are born within the three realms.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "So it is, so it is!"
It is as you have said.
If sentient beings existed previously and later ceased to exist, then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be at fault;
the same would apply to all phenomena and the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
If things existed previously and later ceased to exist, then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be at fault.
Śāriputra, whether a Buddha now exists or does not exist, the characteristics of all dharmas remain eternally abiding and unchanging.

Within these characteristics of phenomena, there is not even a self, no sentient being, no life-span, nor even a knower or a seer; how much less could there be form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
If these dharmas did not exist, how could there be the coming and going of the five paths, or the place from which sentient beings are extracted? Śāriputra!

The nature of all these dharmas is eternally empty; for this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having heard these characteristics of dharmas from the Buddhas of the past, give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Within this, there is no dharma that I shall attain, nor is there any fixed place where sentient beings are attached such that they could not emerge; it is only because of the perversions of sentient beings that they are attached.
For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva makes the adornment of the great vow and never regresses from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This bodhisattva does not doubt:
"I shall not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall benefit sentient beings by means of the true Dharma, causing them to emerge from their inverted views.

Śāriputra! It is like a magician who conjures hundreds of thousands of millions of people by means of illusion, provides them with various foods and drinks until they are full, and joyfully cries out:
"I have obtained great merit!"
"What do you think? Would anyone in that place be able to eat and drink their fill?
"No, World-Honored One," he replied.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Śāriputra!

From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, the fourteen emptinesses, the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; thus fulfilling the bodhisattva path, maturing sentient beings, and purifying buddha-fields."
“There are no sentient beings to be delivered.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
By practicing this path, the bodhisattva is able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the buddha-fields.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"From the time a bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolves upon awakening, they practice the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), and they practice the perfections of ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative concentration (dhyāna), and wisdom (prajñā), up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the dānapāramitā bring sentient beings to maturity?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, when practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), give themselves as well as teach sentient beings to give, saying:
'O sons of good family!'"
"You all must not be attached to giving.
Because you are attached to giving, you will receive further bodies;
because you receive bodies, you will undergo manifold sufferings."
"O sons of good family!

Within the characteristics of all dharmas, there is no gift, no giver, and no recipient; the nature of these three factors is entirely empty. These dharmas of essential emptiness cannot be grasped, and this state of being ungraspable is itself essential emptiness."

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), he bestows gifts upon sentient beings; therein, he does not apprehend the gift, he does not apprehend the giver, and he does not apprehend the recipient."
Why is this? The perfection of non-attainment is called the *dānapāramitā*.

Because this bodhisattva does not apprehend these three dharmas, he is able to teach sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and even lead them to attain the fruits up to *arhatship*, the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they bring sentient beings to maturity.
This bodhisattva personally practices generosity, teaches others to practice generosity, praises the dharma of giving, and joyfully commends those who practice giving.

Having practiced such generosity, this bodhisattva is reborn into a great kṣatriya clan, a great brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder family; or he becomes a minor king or a universal monarch (cakravartin), at which time he gathers sentient beings through the four means of attraction.
What are these four?
They are giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.

Having gathered sentient beings through these four means, they gradually come to abide in the precepts, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the eightfold noble path; they enter the stage of certainty, attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, or attain the path of a pratyekabuddha, or are taught so that they may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He spoke these words:
"O sons of good family!
You should all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is indeed easy to obtain."
Why is this? There is no fixed dharma upon which sentient beings could become attached; it is only because of perversion that sentient beings have a place of attachment.
Therefore, you yourselves should transcend birth and death, and you should also teach others to transcend birth and death.
"You all should resolve to attain enlightenment; thus you will be able to benefit yourselves and also bring benefit to others.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) in this manner.

By virtue of these causes and conditions of practicing the dāna-pāramitā, from the first moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment until the end, he never falls into the evil realms and always becomes a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).
Why is this? Because according to what one sows, one obtains a great fruit of retribution.
When this bodhisattva acts as a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), upon seeing a beggar, he does not form such a thought:
"I have accepted the fruit of a Wheel-Turning Sage King for the sake of other matters, solely for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings.
At that time, he spoke these words:
"This is your property; take it yourself."
"Do not find it difficult; I have nothing to begrudge.
For the sake of sentient beings, I undergo birth and death; out of compassion for you all, I am fully endowed with great compassion.

Practicing this great compassion to benefit sentient beings, yet not apprehending any real or fixed characteristic of a sentient being—there are only provisional names by which one may speak of "sentient beings."
These names are also empty; they are like echoes, whose true characteristics cannot be described.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) in this way: among sentient beings, there is nothing to be begrudged, even to the point of not begrudging one's own flesh and blood, let alone external things.
By means of these dharmas, one is able to deliver sentient beings from birth and death.
What are these dharmas?

They are namely the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā, up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), which cause sentient beings to attain liberation from birth and death.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), has practiced generosity, he says:
'O sons of good family!'"
"You all have come maintaining the precepts; I shall provide for you so that you lack nothing. Clothing, food, bedding, and even all the necessities of life—I shall provide them all to you."
"It is because you lack necessities that you break the precepts; I shall provide you with whatever you require so that you have no deficiency, from food and drink up to the seven precious jewels.

Abiding within this discipline of the precepts, you shall gradually attain the end of suffering and achieve deliverance through the three vehicles: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the vehicle of the Buddha."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), if they see sentient beings who are angry and distressed, they speak these words:
'O sons of good family!'"
"For what reason are you angry and distressed?

I shall provide you with whatever you require; take from me whatever you desire, and I will supply you with everything so that you lack for nothing—not even food, clothing, or the necessities of life."
This bodhisattva, dwelling within the perfection of giving, teaches sentient beings patience, saying:
"Within all phenomena, there is nothing solid or substantial."
That which you resent—these causes and conditions—is likewise empty and lacks any solid substance; it all arises from false conceptualization and recollection.
You allow this rootless anger to corrupt your minds, leading you to use foul language and insults, to employ swords and staves against one another, even to the point of taking each other’s lives.

Do not, because of giving rise to anger toward these false and illusory phenomena, fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, nor into other evil destinies where you would undergo immeasurable suffering.
Do not, on account of these illusory and unsubstantial dharmas, commit sinful karma; for by such sinful karma, you will not even obtain a human body, let alone be born into the world of a Buddha.

"O people! A Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter, and a human body is difficult to obtain. You must not let such a favorable opportunity pass; if you let it pass, it cannot be recovered.

In this way, that bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches and transforms sentient beings. He practices patience himself, and also instructs others to practice patience; he praises the dharma of patience and joyfully extols those who practice patience.
This Bodhisattva causes sentient beings to abide in patience, so that they may gradually attain the exhaustion of all suffering through the three vehicles.
It is thus, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), causes sentient beings to abide in patience.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of giving, cause sentient beings to exert diligence? Subhūti!”
When the Bodhisattva sees sentient beings being indolent, he says to them: "Why are you indolent?
The sentient beings reply:
"Because their causes and conditions are insufficient.
When this bodhisattva practices the dānapāramitā, he says to those people:

"I shall cause your causes and conditions to be complete; whether it be through giving, or through observing the precepts, or through patience—by such causes and conditions as these, I shall cause you to be complete."
Because these sentient beings have obtained the causal conditions for the benefit of bodhisattvas, they possess physical diligence, verbal diligence, and mental diligence.
By virtue of this physical, verbal, and mental diligence, they become fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas and cultivate the noble, untainted dharmas.

By cultivating the noble, untainted dharmas, one shall attain the fruit of stream-entry, up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of a pratyekabuddha, or even unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, he dwells in the perfection of diligence to gather in sentient beings.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of giving, teach and transform sentient beings so that they cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva sees sentient beings with distracted minds, he says to them:
'You should practice meditative concentration.'"
The sentient beings said,
"It is because we lack the necessary conditions.
The Bodhisattva said:

"I shall act as a causal condition for you; by means of this causal condition, I will cause your minds not to follow discursive thought (vitarka) and investigation (vicāra), and not to wander or scatter.

Through these causal conditions, sentient beings sever discursive thought and investigation, entering the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna, and practicing the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
By reason of these causes and conditions of dhyāna and the immeasurable minds, sentient beings are able to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
While cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they gradually enter the three vehicles and attain parinirvāṇa, never losing the Way.

In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, he gathers in sentient beings through the perfection of giving and causes them to practice the perfection of meditative concentration.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of giving, gather in sentient beings by means of the perfection of wisdom?”
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva sees that sentient beings are ignorant and lack wisdom, they say this:
"For what reason do you not cultivate wisdom?"
The sentient beings say,
"Because the causes and conditions are not yet complete.
The Bodhisattva, abiding in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), speaks thus:
"Whatever wisdom you require for fulfillment, take it from me; that is to say: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and the entry into meditative concentration."
When these causal conditions are fully assembled, you should reflect in this way:
"While contemplating the Prajñāpāramitā, is there any dharma that can be apprehended?"
Can a self, a sentient being, or a life-span, up to and including a knower or a seer, be apprehended? Can form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; the six perfections; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; the path of a pratyekabuddha; or unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening be apprehended?
"When these sentient beings contemplate in this way, within the *prajñāpāramitā* there is no dharma that can be apprehended or clung to.

If they do not cling to any dharmas, at that time they do not perceive any dharma as arising or ceasing, as defiled or pure; they do not discriminate between this being hell, this the animal realm, this the realm of hungry ghosts, this the host of asuras, these gods, or these humans; nor do they discriminate between those who uphold the precepts and those who break them, or between a *srotāpanna*, a *sakṛdāgāmin*, an *anāgāmin*, an *arhat*, a *pratyekabuddha*, or a Buddha."
In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, he gathers in sentient beings by means of the perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), gather in sentient beings by means of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and even the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas)?”
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they benefit sentient beings by providing them with the necessities of life.

Through these causes and conditions of benefiting others, sentient beings are able to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
Sentient beings practice these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and thereby attain liberation from birth and death.
In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gather in sentient beings by means of untainted noble dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, he speaks thus:
'O sons of good family!'"

"From me you should take whatever things you require—whether food and drink, clothing, bedding, incense and flowers, or even the seven precious gems and various other necessities for life—and by means of these, you should gather in and sustain sentient beings."
For your long-term benefit and peace, do not harbor this thought:
"These things do not belong to me; rather, I have gathered these various objects for the sake of sentient beings over a long night."

"You should take these things as if they were your own possessions, and teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; even leading them to attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, and up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and further enabling them to attain the various untainted fruits—namely, the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), he should instruct and transform sentient beings in such a manner that they may be freed from the three evil realms and all the sufferings of wandering through birth and death."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the śīlapāramitā teaches and transforms sentient beings, saying to them:
'Sentient beings!'"

"For what reason have you broken the precepts? I shall provide for you all the necessary conditions for their fulfillment—whether it be from generosity up to wisdom, as well as various requisites for sustaining life."

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), benefits sentient beings, causing them to practice the ten wholesome paths and remain far removed from the ten unwholesome paths.
These sentient beings uphold the various precepts—precepts that are unbroken, unimpaired, unturbid, unmixed, and ungrasped—and gradually attain the end of suffering through the three vehicles.
"With the *śīlapāramitā* as the foremost, it is as explained for the *dānapāramitā*.
The remaining four *pāramitās* are also like this. — *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 25.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-Six, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eighty-Two: The Pure Land (in the Danben [Dunhuang] edition: The Chapter on Purifying the Buddha-land).
At that time, Subhūti had this thought:
"What is the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
Dwelling upon this path, the bodhisattva is able to perform such a great vow as an adornment."
The Buddha, knowing what was in Subhūti’s mind, addressed Subhūti: “The six perfections are the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;

the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; the eighteen emptinesses are the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; the eight liberations and the nine successive concentrations are the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities are the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
indeed, all dharmas are also the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that a bodhisattva does not study and yet can attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment?
Subhūti! There is no dharma that a bodhisattva should not study. Why is this?
"If a bodhisattva does not train in all dharmas, they cannot attain all-knowledge.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If all dharmas are empty, how can you say that a bodhisattva trains in all dharmas?
Would you not be engaging in conceptual proliferation within that which is free from conceptual proliferation, O Bhagavān?

That is to say: this is the Dharma and this is non-Dharma; these are worldly dharmas and these are supramundane dharmas; these are with outflows and these are without outflows; these are conditioned and these are unconditioned; these are the dharmas of ordinary persons and these are the dharmas of Arhats; these are the dharmas of Pratyekabuddhas and these are the dharmas of Buddhas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
All dharmas are truly empty.”
Subhūti! If all dharmas were not empty, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti!
Because all dharmas are in truth empty, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, as you have said:

"If all dharmas are empty, will not the Buddha be engaging in conceptual proliferation within that which is free from proliferation, making distinctions between 'this' and 'that,' such as 'these are worldly dharmas' and 'those are supramundane dharmas,' even up to 'these are the dharmas of a Buddha'?"
Subhūti! If the sentient beings of the world knew that all dharmas are empty, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would not need to train in all dharmas to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Subhūti! At present, sentient beings truly do not know that all dharmas are empty.
For this reason, after a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he discriminates among all dharmas and teaches them for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti! Regarding this bodhisattva path, from the very beginning one should reflect in this way:
"Within all dharmas, a fixed nature cannot be found; it is only because dharmas arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions that there are names for these dharmas."

I shall contemplate the true nature of all phenomena as being without attachment—whether it be the nature of the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the fruit of stream-entry, up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; emptiness does not cling to emptiness, and even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended—how much less could there be clinging within emptiness?
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way, they train in all dharmas without clinging to any dharma.
Abiding within this training, they observe the mental activities of sentient beings: 'In what state does this mind of a sentient being operate?'"
When he knows that sentient beings act within what is false and unreal, the bodhisattva then thinks:
"These sentient beings are attached to unreal and false dharmas; they are easy to deliver."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), through the power of skillful means (upāyakauśalya), instructs and transforms sentient beings, saying:
"O you sentient beings!..."
One should practice giving so as to obtain abundant wealth, yet one must not rely on the fruits of giving to become arrogant.
Why is this? Because within this there is no solid or substantial reality.
It is the same for morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
O sentient beings!

By practicing these dharmas, one may attain the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat, the path of a pratyekabuddha, or the path of a buddha; yet do not harbor the thought that there is such a dharma.
To teach and transform others in this way is called practicing the bodhisattva path, because one is unattached to all dharmas.
Why is this? All dharmas lack the characteristic of attachment, because their nature does not exist and their nature is empty.
Subhūti! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva path in this manner, they abide nowhere.

Because these bodhisattvas employ the dharma of non-abiding, they practice the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) yet do not abide therein; they practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) yet do not abide therein; they practice the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) yet do not abide therein; they practice the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) yet do not abide therein; they practice the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) yet do not abide therein; and they practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) yet do not abide therein.
One practices the first dhyāna, yet does not abide within it.
Why? Because this first dhyāna is empty of the characteristics of the first dhyāna; the practitioner of dhyāna is also empty, and the dharmas employed are also empty.
The same applies to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
It is likewise for loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the four formless attainments; the eight liberations; and the nine successive attainments.

Having attained the fruit of srotāpanna, one does not dwell therein; having attained the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, or the fruit of arhat, one likewise does not dwell therein; and having attained the path of a pratyekabuddha, one likewise does not dwell therein.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition does one not abide therein?”
The Buddha said:
"For two reasons, one does not abide therein.
What are these two? "
First, the nature of the fruits of all paths is empty; they have no place of abiding, nor is there any dharma employed, nor any one who abides.
Second, one does not consider a minor matter sufficient, but forms this thought:
"I must not fail to attain the fruit of srotāpanna; I shall certainly attain the fruit of srotāpanna, yet I should not abide therein."
"Up to and including the path of the pratyekabuddha, it is not that I shall not attain it; I must certainly attain it, yet I should not dwell therein.
Up to and including the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should not dwell [in the thought of attaining it]."
Why is this? Since I first resolved my mind [on enlightenment], I have had no other thoughts;
I have directed my single-minded attention toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva directs his single-minded attention toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and remains far removed from other thoughts, all the actions of body, speech, and mind he performs will accord with anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in this single-mindedness, is able to give rise to the path to enlightenment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are non-arising, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva give rise to the path to enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! All phenomena are unarisen. In what way are they unarisen?"
"That which is uncreated and unarisen is the non-arising of all dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Whether a Buddha appears or not, do the dharmas not have a dharma-nature that is not eternally abiding?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
Whether a Buddha appears or not, the dharma-nature of these phenomena remains eternally constant.
Because sentient beings do not know this abiding dharma-nature, for their sake the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to the path of enlightenment.
"By means of this path, one pulls sentient beings out of birth and death.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Can one attain bodhi by means of producing the path? The Buddha said, "No."
“World-Honored One!
Is bodhi attained by means of a non-arising path?
The Buddha said:
"No. "World-Honored One! Is bodhi attained through neither arising nor non-arising?"
The Buddha said, "No. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
How shall one attain bodhi?
The Buddha said:
“Enlightenment is not attained by means of the path, nor is it attained by means of what is not the path.
Subhūti! Enlightenment is itself the path, and the path is itself enlightenment.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If awakening is itself the path, and the path is itself awakening.”
If that were so, then a bodhisattva who has not yet become a Buddha should already have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why, then, do you say that the Buddhas—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—possess the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does the Buddha attain bodhi? "No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha does not attain enlightenment. Why is this?
Because the Buddha is itself enlightenment, and enlightenment is itself the Buddha.
“As Subhūti has asked, a bodhisattva should also attain awakening at that time. Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled the six pāramitās, having fulfilled the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, having fulfilled the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; having fully established himself in the vajra-like samādhi, attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment. At that time, he is called a Buddha, having attained mastery over all dharmas.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify a buddha-field?”
The Buddha said:

"There are bodhisattvas who, from the time they first resolved their minds, eliminate their own coarse karma of body, eliminate their own coarse karma of speech, and eliminate their own coarse karma of mind; they also purify the coarse karma of body, speech, and mind of others."
“World-Honored One!
What are the gross physical actions, gross verbal actions, and gross mental actions of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Unwholesome karma, from taking life up to wrong view—this is called the coarse karma of body, speech, and mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”

A mind of stinginess and greed, a mind of broken precepts, a mind of anger, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, and a mind of delusion—these are called the coarse mental actions of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, impure precepts are called the coarse karma of a bodhisattva’s body and speech.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva distances himself from the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness, this is called the coarse karma of a bodhisattva."
To be far removed from the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
and likewise, the samādhi of emptiness, the signless, and the wishless samādhis—these are also called the coarse activities of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva craves the realization of the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including craving the realization of the fruit of an arhat or the path of a pratyekabuddha, this is called the coarse karma of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva grasps the marks of form, the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the marks of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the marks of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena; the marks of male and female; the marks of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; the marks of wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas; and the marks of conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas—this is called the coarse activity of a bodhisattva."

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are all far removed from such characteristics of coarse karma; they practice giving themselves and also instruct others in giving—providing food to those who need food, clothing to those who need clothing, and even all manner of necessary articles for life, giving them all completely, while also instructing others in various forms of giving.
One holds these merits and shares them with all sentient beings for the sake of dedicating them toward the purification of Buddha-lands;
the same applies to the holding of precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva may take precious jewels filling the trichiliocosm and offer them to the Triple Gem, making this vow:
"By means of these roots of goodness, may my own land be composed entirely of the seven treasures."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva uses celestial music to make offerings to the Buddha and his stūpas, making this aspiration:
'By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, may celestial music be constantly heard within my buddha-field.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fills the trichiliocosm with celestial incense and makes offerings to the Buddhas and the stupas of the Buddhas, making this aspiration:
'By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, may my own buddha-field always possess celestial incense.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva offers food of a hundred flavors to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, making this aspiration:
'By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field obtain food of a hundred flavors.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives celestial fragrances and fine, smooth textures to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, making this aspiration:
'By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field experience celestial fragrances and fine, smooth textures.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives the five objects of sensory desire according to their wishes to the Buddha, the Saṃgha, and all sentient beings, making this vow:
'By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, may the disciples and all sentient beings within my buddha-field obtain the five objects of sensory desire according to their wishes.'"
This bodhisattva, with the five objects of desire according to their wishes, shares them with all sentient beings and dedicates them toward the purification of a Buddha-land.
They make this vow, saying:
"When I attain Buddhahood, the five celestial desires shall appear in that land at will, in accordance with one's thoughts."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he makes this vow: 'I shall personally enter the first dhyāna,

and I shall also teach all sentient beings to enter the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and even the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the same way.'"
When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall cause all sentient beings not to be separated from the four dhyānas, and even not to be separated from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to purify a buddha-field.

For as long as that bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path, they fulfill all their vows; that bodhisattva personally accomplishes all wholesome dharmas and also brings all sentient beings to accomplish wholesome dharmas."
This bodhisattva receives a handsome body, and the sentient beings they transform also attain handsomeness.
Why is this? Because the causes and conditions of their merit and virtue are profound.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should purify a buddha-field in this manner.
Within that field, there shall not even be the name of the three evil realms, nor the names of wrong views, the three poisons, or the two vehicles—the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Their ears do not hear the sounds of impermanence, suffering, or emptiness; nor is there anything belonging to a self, even to the point that the names of the fetters and afflictions do not exist, nor are there the names of various fruits of distinction.

When the wind blows through the trees made of the seven treasures, they emit sounds according to those who are to be saved—namely, the sounds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

These are like the sounds of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena: whether a Buddha exists or not, the characteristics of all phenomena are empty; within emptiness there are no signs, and within signlessness there is nothing that can be brought forth by intention.
Such sounds of the Dharma—whether by day or night, whether sitting, lying down, standing, or walking—he shall constantly hear this teaching.

When this bodhisattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddhas throughout the lands of the ten directions will praise him; and when sentient beings hear this Buddha’s name, they will certainly reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When this Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and preaches the Dharma, among those sentient beings who hear it, there shall be none who do not believe and instead give rise to doubt, saying:
"Is this the Dharma?"
"Is this not the Dharma?
Why is this? Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything is the Dharma; there is nothing that is not the Dharma.

Those people who possess little merit do not plant roots of goodness among the Buddhas and their disciples, nor do they follow virtuous friends; they are submerged in the view of a self, and even submerged in all manner of various views, falling into extreme views of either annihilationism or eternalism.
Such people, because of their false views, call what is not the Buddha "the Buddha" and call the Buddha "not the Buddha.
Such people call what is not the Dharma "the Dharma" and call the Dharma "not the Dharma."
Because such a person has destroyed the Dharma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the evil realms of hell.

When the Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they see these sentient beings wandering through the five destinies and cause them to leave the assembly of the heterodox and establish themselves within the assembly of those fixed in the right path, so that they shall never again fall into the evil realms.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Within the buddha-field purified by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, sentient beings have no defiled or impure minds regarding either worldly dharmas or supramundane dharmas, whether they be with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned; indeed, the sentient beings within that field will inevitably attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies a buddha-field.
Chapter Eighty-Three: Determination The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Eighty-Three: Determination Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is this bodhisattva mahāsattva one who is fixed in destiny,
or is he not yet fixed?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who is fixed in destiny; he is not one who is not fixed in destiny.
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!”
In what state is he definitively established?
Is it within the path of the śrāvaka,
or within the path of the pratyekabuddha?
"Is he fixed within the path of the Buddha? The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva is not fixed within the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; he is fixed within the path of the Buddha."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
are bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds fixed in their destiny?”
"Are those who are Bodhisattvas in their final existence definitively fixed?

The Buddha said, "Bodhisattvas who have first resolved on enlightenment are also definitively fixed; Bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive (avaivartika) are also definitively fixed; and Bodhisattvas in their final existence are also definitively fixed."
“World-Honored One!
Do bodhisattvas who are fixed in their destiny fall into birth within the evil realms? “No, Subhūti!”
What do you think: would an eighth-person, or a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, or pratyekabuddha ever be born within the evil realms?
“No, World-Honored One! “Thus it is, Subhūti!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment onward, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, maintains morality, practices patience, exerts diligence, cultivates meditative concentration, and develops wisdom; when they sever all unwholesome karma—such that they might fall into the evil realms, or be born among the long-lived gods, or fail to find a place to cultivate wholesome dharmas, or be born in a borderland, or be born into a family of evil and heterodox views or those with the view of non-action, where there is no mention of the Buddha, no mention of the Dharma, and no mention of the Saṅgha—it is impossible for such a thing to occur.”
Subhūti! It is impossible for a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to practice the ten unwholesome paths with a profound mind.
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has accomplished such roots of goodness and merit as you yourself have described in your own accounts of past lives where they experienced unwholesome retributions—at that time, where were those roots of goodness?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas assume bodies in accordance with their needs, and by means of these bodies, they benefit sentient beings."

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born as an animal, he possesses such power of skillful means that if an enemy or robber comes to kill him, he gives up his body through this unsurpassed patience and unsurpassed compassion, without causing any distress to the wicked thief.
"You disciples and pratyekabuddhas do not possess such power.
For this reason, Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
desiring to fulfill the mind of great compassion and for the sake of pitying and benefiting sentient beings, accept birth in the bodies of animals."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
in what roots of goodness do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide when they receive such bodies as these?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, there is not a single root of goodness that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fully perfect throughout this interval."
Having fulfilled them, one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in fulfilling all roots of goodness.
"Having cultivated the roots of goodness, one shall attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and sever all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such pure and untainted dharmas, is born among the animals in the evil destinies?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Has the Buddha not accomplished pure and untainted dharmas?"
Subhūti said: "The Buddha has accomplished all pure and untainted dharmas. [The Buddha said: "Subhūti!"
"If the Buddha himself transforms into the body of an animal to perform the work of a Buddha and deliver sentient beings,
is he actually an animal? Subhūti replied, "No."
The Buddha said:

“The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this; having accomplished pure, untainted dharmas, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he takes on the body of an animal and uses that body to teach and transform sentient beings.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Suppose an arhat were to manifest a transformation body; could he cause sentient beings to rejoice? Subhūti replied:
“Yes, he can. The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is!”

Subhūti! By means of these pure, untainted dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva assumes a body according to the needs of those to be delivered; with this body he benefits sentient beings, yet he does not undergo suffering.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Suppose a magician were to conjure various forms—such as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, women, and so forth—and display them to sentient beings.
“Subhūti! Do these elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, women, and so forth have any reality? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said, "So it is, Subhūti!"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes pure and untainted dharmas and manifests various bodies in order to instruct sentient beings.
By means of these bodies, he benefits all beings, yet he does not undergo suffering.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By the power of the great skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attained noble, untainted wisdom, they manifest in various forms according to the bodies of those sentient beings who are to be saved, thereby delivering them.”
“World-Honored One!
In what pure and white dharmas does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abide so that they can employ such skillful means without being defiled?
The Buddha said:

“By employing such skillful means through the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva benefits sentient beings in as many lands in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges, yet remains without attachment to this body.”
Why is this? The one who clings, the object of clinging, and the locus of clinging—these three dharmas are all unobtainable because their intrinsic nature is empty.
Emptiness does not cling to emptiness; within emptiness, there is neither one who clings nor a locus of clinging.
Why is this? Because within emptiness, the characteristic of emptiness cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!
"This is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
A bodhisattva dwelling within this is able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
“Does a bodhisattva attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment only by abiding in the perfection of wisdom, and not by abiding in other dharmas? “Subhūti!
“Is there any dharma that does not enter into the *prajñāpāramitā*?
“World-Honored One!
If the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty, how can all dharmas enter into the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
“World-Honored One!
In emptiness, there is no dharma that either enters or does not enter. “Subhūti!”
“Are all dharmas empty of the characteristics of all dharmas?
“World-Honored One,
they are empty.”
“Subhūti! If all dharmas are empty of the characteristics of all dharmas, why do you say that all dharmas do not enter into emptiness?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide in the emptiness of all phenomena and yet give rise to the perfection of supernormal powers?”

Abiding within this perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*), how does one travel to lands in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to make offerings to the Buddhas currently residing there, hear the Dharma taught by those Buddhas, and plant roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he contemplates that these lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all empty; the buddha-nature within those lands is also empty. It is only by way of provisional names that the buddhas manifest their bodies, and even those provisional names are empty.”
If the lands of the ten directions and the natures of all Buddhas were not empty, then emptiness would be partial.
Because emptiness is not partial, all phenomena and all characteristics of phenomena are empty.
For this reason, all dharmas and all characteristics of dharmas are empty.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they employ the power of skillful means to give rise to the abhijñāpāramitā.

Abiding within this perfection of supernatural powers (abhijñā-pāramitā), one gives rise to the divine eye, the divine ear, the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of past lives, thereby knowing the birth and death of sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva distances themselves from the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā), they will be unable to bring benefit to sentient beings, nor will they be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s perfection of supernormal powers; this is the path that brings benefit to unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Why is this so?

Using this divine eye, one personally perceives all wholesome dharmas and also teaches others to attain them; yet one does not become attached even to these wholesome dharmas, because the intrinsic nature of all wholesome dharmas is empty.
Emptiness is without attachment; if one were attached, one would experience its flavor, yet within this emptiness there is no flavor.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they are able to produce such a divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Using this eye, they contemplate all dharmas as empty. Seeing these dharmas as empty, they do not grasp at signs nor perform karmic actions. Furthermore, they explain these dharmas for others, yet they neither apprehend the mark of a sentient being nor apprehend the name of a sentient being.
In this way, by means of the dharma of non-apprehension, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the perfection of supernormal powers (ṛddhipāramitā).
By means of this perfection of supernormal powers, he is able to perform whatever is to be accomplished through supernormal powers.
This bodhisattva, using the divine eye which surpasses that of humans, beholds the lands of the ten directions.

Having seen them, he flies to the ten directions to benefit sentient beings—whether by means of generosity, or ethical discipline, or patience, or diligence, or meditative concentration, or wisdom—he benefits sentient beings.

They benefit sentient beings either by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, or by means of the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, or by means of the Dharma of the śrāvakas, or the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, or the Dharma of the bodhisattvas, or the Dharma of the Buddhas.
For those who are stingy, he preaches the Dharma in this way: "O sentient beings!
You should practice giving. Poverty is a state of suffering and affliction; if a person in poverty cannot even benefit themselves, how can they benefit others?"
For this reason, you should diligently practice giving; by doing so, you will attain happiness for yourselves and enable others to attain happiness as well.
Do not, out of poverty, devour one another, lest you fail to escape the three evil realms.
He preaches the Dharma for those who have broken the precepts, saying: "O sentient beings!
The dharma of breaking the precepts brings great suffering and affliction. A person who has broken the precepts cannot even benefit themselves; how could they possibly benefit others?"
The retribution for the suffering resulting from breaking the precepts is to be found either in hell, or among the hungry ghosts, or among the animals.
Once you have fallen into these three evil realms, you cannot save yourselves; how then can you save others?
"For this reason, you should not fall into a state of mind that violates the precepts, lest you have cause for regret at the time of death.
If there are those who are mutually angry or quarreling, he teaches the Dharma to them in this way:
"O sentient beings, do not harbor mutual anger; anger disturbs the human mind and is not in accord with wholesome dharmas."
If you now harbor mutual anger and a distracted mind, you may fall into hell, or among the hungry ghosts and animals.
For this reason, you should not give rise to even a single thought of malice, much less many.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of indolent sentient beings to enable them to attain diligence;
for those with distracted minds, he enables them to attain meditative concentration;
and for those who are ignorant, he enables them to attain wisdom—in this same manner.

For those who engage in sexual desire, he causes them to contemplate impurity; for those with anger and hatred, he causes them to contemplate loving-kindness; for sentient beings who are deluded, he causes them to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination; and for sentient beings who follow non-ways, he causes them to enter the right path—namely, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma in this way:

"The very dharmas to which you are attached are empty of intrinsic nature. Within dharmas that are empty of intrinsic nature, attachment cannot be found; the absence of attachment is the mark of emptiness."
"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide within the perfection of supernormal powers and bring about the benefit of sentient beings."
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva is far removed from the supernormal powers (abhijñā), they cannot skillfully teach the Dharma in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
For this reason, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should give rise to the supernormal powers. Subhūti,
it is like a bird that cannot soar high into the sky without wings.
Without supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), a bodhisattva cannot transform and guide sentient beings according to their wishes. For this reason, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) should give rise to the various supernormal powers.
Having aroused the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), if he wishes to benefit sentient beings, he is able to benefit them according to his will.
This bodhisattva, using the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), sees as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, as well as the sentient beings within those lands.

Having seen them, he proceeds to their location by means of his supernormal powers; knowing the minds of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each, whether it be preaching on generosity, or morality, or meditative concentration, up to and including the teaching of the Dharma of Nirvāṇa.
This bodhisattva, using the divine ear, hears two kinds of sounds: those of humans and those of non-humans.

Using the divine ear, they hear the Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions and are able to receive and uphold it all; they then preach to sentient beings according to the Dharma as they have heard it, whether teaching on generosity or even up to nirvana.

This bodhisattva purifies the knowledge of others' minds; using this knowledge of others' minds, they know the thoughts of sentient beings and preach the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate, whether it be teaching on generosity or even up to nirvana.
This bodhisattva’s knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) recollects various places of former births; they both recollect their own [lives] and those of others.
By means of this knowledge of past lives, they remember the names of the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples wherever they have been in the past.

For those sentient beings who have faith and delight in the recollection of past lives, [the Buddha] manifests past-life events for them and preaches the Dharma; he may speak of generosity, or even up to nirvana.

By means of the power of supernormal knowledges such as the power of will, they travel to various and immeasurable Buddha-lands to make offerings to the Buddhas, plant roots of goodness under those Buddhas, and then return to their own land.

This is the bodhisattva’s realization of the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows; by means of this realization of the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs, whether it be the teaching on generosity or even up to the teaching on nirvana.
Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should give rise to the various supernormal powers (abhijñā) in this manner.
By cultivating these supernormal powers, the bodhisattva assumes a body at will, remaining untainted by suffering or pleasure.
For example, a person conjured by a Buddha performs all manner of deeds yet remains unstained by suffering or pleasure.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should likewise sport with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in this way, being able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not purify buddha-fields and does not bring sentient beings to maturity cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Why is this? Because the necessary conditions are not fulfilled, one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the causal conditions of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Having fulfilled them, how does one attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All wholesome dharmas are the causes and conditions for a bodhisattva’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are these wholesome dharmas?
By means of these wholesome dharmas, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
