“From the time a bodhisattva first resolves upon awakening, the dānapāramitā is the causal condition for wholesome dharmas; herein there is no discrimination between ‘this is the giver’ and ‘this is the recipient,’ because their nature is empty.”
By means of this dānapāramitā, one is able to benefit oneself and also benefit sentient beings, drawing them out from birth and death and enabling them to attain nirvāṇa.
All these wholesome dharmas are the causes and conditions for the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
By practicing this path, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present have crossed over, are crossing over, and will cross over birth and death.

The perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā); the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti); the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; the eighteen kinds of emptiness (śūnyatā); the eight liberations (vimokṣa), the nine successive attainments (anupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti), and the doors of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a Buddha (buddha-bala), the four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (pratisaṃvid), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-dharma).
Such qualities as these are all the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, these are called wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
Once the bodhisattva mahāsattva has fulfilled these wholesome dharmas, he shall attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Having attained all-knowledge, he shall turn the wheel of Dharma.
"Having turned the wheel of Dharma, you shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“If these dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, what then are the dharmas of a Buddha?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Regarding your question as to what these dharmas that are the dharmas of a bodhisattva are, and what the dharmas of a Buddha are:”
Subhūti! The dharmas of a bodhisattva are also the dharmas of a Buddha.
If one knows all aspects, one attains all-aspect wisdom; having severed all afflictions and their habitual tendencies, the bodhisattva shall attain these dharmas.
Having known all dharmas through the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, this is the distinction between a bodhisattva and a buddha.

For example, there is a difference between one who is progressing toward the path and one who has attained the fruit; although both are noble ones (ārya), there is a distinction between those who have attained and those who are progressing.
In this same way, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices within the path of non-obstruction, they are called a bodhisattva;
when there is no longer any darkness or obscuration within the path of liberation, they are called a Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), how can there be distinctions and differences within these dharmas that are empty of their own characteristics—such as ‘this is a hell-being,’ ‘this is a hungry ghost,’ ‘this is an animal,’ ‘this is a deva,’ ‘this is a human’; or ‘this is a person on the stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*)’, ‘this is a person on the stage of the eight [liberations] (*aṣṭamaka*)’, ‘this is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)’, ‘this is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*)’, ‘this is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*)’, ‘this is an arhat’; or ‘this is a pratyekabuddha,’ ‘this is a bodhisattva,’ or ‘this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’?”
“World-Honored One!
Just as persons cannot be apprehended, so too karmic causes and conditions cannot be apprehended, and their retributive fruits cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.
Within phenomena that are empty of intrinsic characteristics, there are no sentient beings, no causes and conditions of karma, and no retributive fruits."

Subhūti! If there are sentient beings who do not know that these dharmas are empty of their own characteristics, those sentient beings will perform actions—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or immovable—as a result of causes and conditions.
Due to the causes and conditions of sinful karma, one falls into the three evil realms;
due to the causes and conditions of meritorious karma, one is born among humans and devas;
and due to the causes and conditions of immovable karma, one is born in the realm of form or the formless realm.

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they fully undertake and practice these factors conducive to enlightenment, enter the diamond-like samādhi, and attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Having attained it, one benefits sentient beings.
Because this benefit shall not be lost, one does not fall into the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, does he still undergo the cycle of birth and death within the six realms?
The Buddha said:
"No, it cannot. Subhūti said,
"World-Honored One!"
"Would one obtain karma that is black, or white, or both black and white,
or neither black nor white? The Buddha said, "No."
“World-Honored One!

If these are not attained, why do you speak of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas; of those from the stage of stream-enterer up to arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and all Buddhas?”

“Subhūti! If sentient beings knew that all phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would not seek unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, nor would they deliver sentient beings from the three evil destinies, nor even from the cycle of birth and death as they wander through the five realms of existence.”
Subhūti! Because sentient beings do not truly know that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty, they cannot escape the cycle of birth and death within the five realms.
These bodhisattvas, having heard from the Buddhas that the specific characteristics of all dharmas are empty, have resolved their minds to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti! All dharmas are not as ordinary people are attached to them. These sentient beings, within dharmas that do not exist, through inverted false imaginings and discrimination, apprehend dharmas where there are no sentient beings yet they perceive the mark of sentient beings; where there is no form yet they perceive the mark of form; where there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness yet they perceive the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

and so on, up to all conditioned dharmas which are non-existent. By means of an inverted mind of false imagination, they create the causes and conditions for the karma of body, speech, and mind, wandering through birth and death in the five destinies without attaining liberation.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they internalize all wholesome dharmas within the perfection of wisdom, practice the bodhisattva path, and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he shall preach the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering—to sentient beings; he shall reveal and analyze them, for all wholesome dharmas that assist the path are included within these Four Noble Truths.
Because these are the wholesome dharmas that assist the path, there is a distinction of the Three Jewels.
What are the three?
The Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
"Because they do not believe in and reject these Three Jewels, they cannot escape the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
Is one liberated by means of the noble truth of suffering?
Is one liberated by means of the knowledge of suffering?
Is one liberated by means of the noble truth of the origin [of suffering]?
Is one liberated by means of the knowledge of origination?
Is one liberated by means of the noble truth of cessation?
Or is one liberated by means of the knowledge of cessation?
"Is one delivered by means of the noble truth of the path,
or is one delivered by means of the knowledge of the path? The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Subhūti, it is not by means of the noble truth of suffering that one attains liberation, nor is it by means of the knowledge of suffering.
This extends up to: it is not by means of the noble truth of the path that one attains liberation, nor is it by means of the knowledge of the path.”
Because these four noble truths are equal, I say they are themselves nirvāṇa.

One does not attain nirvāṇa by means of the noble truth of suffering, nor by the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path; nor does one attain it through the knowledge of suffering, nor through the knowledge of origin, cessation, or the path.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the mark of equality of the four noble truths?”

“Subhūti! If there is no suffering and no knowledge of suffering, no origin and no knowledge of origin, no cessation and no knowledge of cessation, and no path and no knowledge of the path—this is called the mark of the equality of the Four Noble Truths.”
Furthermore, Subhūti, these Four Noble Truths— suchness, non-alteration,

the mark of phenomena, the nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the fixed position of phenomena, and the limit of reality— abide as the constant mark of phenomena whether a Buddha appears or not, because they are non-deceptive and non-failing.
"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of penetrating the ultimate truth.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of penetrating the ultimate truth? By means of penetrating the ultimate truth, how does he not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but directly enter the rank of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as they truly are, having perceived them, he attains the dharma of non-existence.

Having attained the dharma of non-existence, he perceives that all phenomena are empty—both those phenomena subsumed within the Four Noble Truths and those not subsumed within the Four Noble Truths are all empty.”

If one contemplates in this way, at that time one enters the stage of a bodhisattva; this is called the bodhisattva abiding in the stage of the nature (gotrabhūmi), from which there is no falling back from the summit.
Because of such a fall from the summit, one would fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
This bodhisattva, abiding within this stage of nature, is able to give rise to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments.

Abiding in this initial stage of concentration, the bodhisattva discriminates all dharmas and penetrates the Four Noble Truths; they know suffering but do not give rise to a mind conditioned by suffering, and so on, up to knowing the Path but not giving rise to a mind conditioned by the Path. Rather, they accord with the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, contemplating all dharmas according to their true marks.
“World-Honored One!
How does one contemplate all dharmas according to their true mark?
The Buddha said:
“Contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena.
“World-Honored One,
what is this contemplation of emptiness?”
The Buddha said: "They are empty of their own characteristics.
This bodhisattva uses such wisdom to contemplate the emptiness of all dharmas; there is no nature of dharmas to be seen, yet by abiding within this nature, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? The absence of intrinsic nature and characteristics is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is not something produced by the Buddhas, nor produced by *pratyekabuddhas*, nor produced by *arhats*, nor produced by those on the path, nor produced by those who have attained the fruit, nor produced by *bodhisattvas*.

However, because sentient beings neither know nor see the true reality of all phenomena, for this reason, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and, through the power of skillful means, preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Chapter 85: The Seven Similes. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Eighty-Five, the Seven Similes, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If the nature of all phenomena is non-existent, it is not made by Buddhas, nor made by Pratyekabuddhas, nor made by Arhats, nor made by Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, or Srotāpannas; it is not made by those on the path, nor by those who have attained the fruits, nor by Bodhisattvas.

How does one differentiate the various distinct phenomena, such as: "this is hell," "this is the animal realm," "this is the realm of hungry ghosts," "this is the human realm," "this is the deva realm," and so on, up to "this is the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"?
By reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one knows there are those born in the hells;
by reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one knows there are those born among animals or as hungry ghosts.

By reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one knows that there are those born among humans, those born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and so on, up to those born in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
Due to these causes and conditions of karma, it is known that there are those who attain the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.
By reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one knows these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
by reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one knows the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
World-Honored One!
Within dharmas that lack intrinsic nature, there is no karmic activity.

It is due to the causes and conditions of performing actions that one falls into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; or becomes a human or a deva; or even is born in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
By reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one attains the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the bodhisattva path shall attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
"Because they have attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to pull sentient beings out from within birth and death.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
Within dharmas that lack intrinsic nature, there is no karma and no retribution. Subhūti!

Ordinary persons do not enter the noble Dharma; because they do not know that all dharmas are without the characteristic of intrinsic nature, and due to their perversion and delusion, they give rise to various causes and conditions of karma.

These sentient beings receive bodies according to their karma—whether they be bodies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or devas—from the bodies of the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the bodies of the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
These dharmas are without intrinsic nature; they have no karma and no retribution, for that which lacks intrinsic nature is eternally without intrinsic nature.
As Subhūti has said: "If all dharmas lack intrinsic nature, how is it that those from the stream-enterer up to the Buddhas attain the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Path without intrinsic nature?
Are the fruit of the stream-enterer, up to and including the all-knowledge of all Buddhas, without intrinsic nature?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One! The Path has no intrinsic nature;
the fruit of a srotāpanna also has no intrinsic nature; and so on, up to the omniscience of all Buddhas, which likewise has no intrinsic nature.”
“Subhūti, can a dharma that is without intrinsic nature attain a dharma that is without intrinsic nature? “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Can a dharma that has intrinsic nature obtain a dharma that has intrinsic nature? “No, World-Honored One.”

“Subhūti! As for the dharma of non-existence and the Path—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without form, without shape, and without resistance; they have but a single characteristic, which is called ‘the absence of characteristics.’”

Subhūti! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the prajñāpāramitā, they employ skillful means to see that sentient beings, due to their inversions, are attached to the five aggregates: perceiving permanence in the impermanent, pleasure in suffering, purity in the impure, and a self in the non-self; thus they become attached to what is non-existent.
"By means of skillful power, this bodhisattva draws sentient beings out from within non-existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
Is there anything real about that which ordinary people are attached to, such that it is not different [from reality]?
Because of attachment, they give rise to karma; because of the causes and conditions of karma, they cannot escape the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In the basis for the arising of karma upon which ordinary persons are attached, there is not even as much as a hair's breadth of reality; it is merely due to perversion."
Subhūti! I shall now speak a parable for you, for the wise gain understanding through parables. Subhūti!
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there a real dwelling place for the person seen in a dream who experiences the pleasures of the five senses?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If even a dream is illusory and unattainable, how much more so is dwelling within a dream to experience the pleasures of the five senses?
"What do you think? Among all phenomena—whether with outflows or without outflows, whether conditioned or unconditioned—is there any that is not like a dream?"
“World-Honored One!
Whether dharmas are with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, there is none that is not like a dream.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is there, within a dream, the coming and going through birth and death in the five realms of existence? "No, World-Honored One."
“What do you think? In a dream, is there a path of cultivation by means of which one might become defiled or attain purity?
“No, World-Honored One.”
Why is this? Because these dream-phenomena lack any substantial reality; they cannot be described as either defiled or pure.
"What do you think: does the image in a mirror have any substantial reality?"

Can they give rise to the causes and conditions of karma? By means of these karmic causes and conditions, do they fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm; or are they born as humans or devas—from the abode of the Four Great Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception?
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One!
This image has no substantial reality; it merely deceives small children.”
"How could there be a karmic cause for this matter, by which karmic cause one would fall into hell or even reach the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
What do you think: does that reflection in a mirror cultivate the path, and by cultivating that path, become defiled or purified?"
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
"This image is empty and lacks substantial reality; it cannot be described as either defiled or pure.

"What do you think? Suppose there were an echo in a deep ravine. Does that echo have karmic causes and conditions? By means of those karmic causes and conditions, would it fall into hell or even be reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One! This matter is empty;

there is no real sound or voice. How could there be the causal conditions of karma? By means of such karmic causes and conditions, how could one fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?”
"What do you think? Does this echo have any cultivation of the path, such that by means of this cultivation of the path it would either become defiled or attain purity?
"No, World-Honored One!"
"This matter is without reality; it cannot be said to be either defiled or pure.

"What do you think? Just as a mirage is not water yet has the appearance of water, and is not a river yet has the appearance of a river—does that mirage possess any karmic causes and conditions, such that by means of those karmic causes and conditions, it would fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
"No, World-Honored One! Water in a mirage is ultimately unattainable;

it merely deceives the eyes of the ignorant. How could there be karmic causes and conditions therein? By what karma could one fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
“What do you think? Does this flame have a path of cultivation, and by means of that path of cultivation, does it become defiled or does it attain purity?
“No, World-Honored One.”
"This flame has no substantial reality; it cannot be described as either defiled or pure.

"What do you think? When the sun rises and a city of the gandharvas appears, an ignorant person perceives a city where there is no city, a palace where there is no palace, and a garden where there is no garden."

Does this city of the gandharvas have any karmic causes and conditions? By means of such karmic causes and conditions, could one fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
“No, World-Honored One! This city of the Gandharvas is ultimately unattainable;

it merely deceives the eyes of the foolish. How could there be karmic causes and conditions therein? By means of such karmic causes and conditions, how could one fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?”
"What do you think? Does this city of the gandharvas have a path of cultivation, by means of which path one might become defiled or attain purity?"
"No, World-Honored One! This city of the gandharvas has no substantial reality; it cannot be said to be either defiled or pure. "Subhūti!"
What do you think? Suppose a magician conjures various things by illusion—whether elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, or women. What do you think?

Does that illusion have karmic causes and conditions, such that by means of those karmic causes and conditions, it would fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
“No, World-Honored One! This illusory dharma is empty and lacks substantial reality;
how could there be karmic causes and conditions? How could one, by means of such karmic causes and conditions, fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?”
"What do you think? Does this illusion have a path of cultivation? By means of this path of cultivation, could it become defiled or could it attain purity?
"No, World-Honored One."
"These dharmas have no substantial reality; they cannot be described as either defiled or pure.
"Subhūti, what do you think?

If there were a person created by a Buddha through transformation, would that transformed person have karmic causes and conditions, and by virtue of those karmic causes and conditions, fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
"No, World-Honored One! This emanated person has no substantial reality;

how could there be karmic causes and conditions for such a person? By means of what karmic causes and conditions would they fall into hell, or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
“What do you think? Does this conjured person cultivate the path? By means of cultivating that path, does he become defiled or does he attain purity?
“No, World-Honored One.”
"This matter has no reality; it cannot be said to be either defiled or pure.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"What do you think? Within this mark of emptiness, is there anything that is defiled or anything that is pure?"
"No, World-Honored One! Within this there is nothing at all;
there is neither one who is defiled by attachment nor one who is pure. "Subhūti!"
Just as there is no one who possesses the defilement of attachment, nor anyone who possesses purity;
for this reason, there is likewise neither defilement nor purity. Why is this?
Sentient beings who dwell in the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self" are defiled and pure; those who see reality as it is are neither defiled nor pure.
For one who sees according to reality, there is neither defilement nor purity, and thus likewise no defilement or purity exists.
Chapter 86: On Equality. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Eighty-Six, "On Equality," Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
One who sees reality is neither defiled nor pure; one who sees unreality is likewise neither defiled nor pure.
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is non-existent.
World-Honored One!
Within that which is non-existent, there is neither defilement nor purity; within that which is existent, there is likewise neither defilement nor purity.
World-Honored One!
“World-Honored One, within both non-existence and existence, there is neither defilement nor purity.
How is it that one who speaks according to reality is neither defiled nor pure, and one who speaks what is not real is likewise neither defiled nor pure?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This mark of equality of all dharmas— I call it purity, Subhūti.”
What is the equality of all phenomena?

It refers to suchness, non-alteration, non-deception, the mark of phenomena, the nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the fixed position of phenomena, and the limit of reality. Whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature of phenomena remains eternally constant; this is called purity.
"This is spoken according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), not according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
The ultimate truth transcends all language, discourse, and sound.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are empty and ineffable, like a dream, like an echo, like a mirage, like a shadow, like an illusion, and like a transformation.”

How can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of these dharmas which are like a dream, like an echo, like a mirage, like a shadow, like an illusion, and like a transformation—dharmas that have no root and no fixed reality—be able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and make this vow:
"I shall fully complete the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the full completion of the *prajñā-pāramitā*;
I shall fully complete the *abhijñā-pāramitā* and the *jñāna-pāramitā*?"
I shall be fully endowed with the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path;
I shall be fully endowed with the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, and the nine successive attainments;
I shall be fully endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
I shall be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics; I shall be fully endowed with all the gates of dhāraṇī and all the gates of samādhi;
I shall emit great light that pervasively illuminates the ten directions, know the minds of all sentient beings, and preach the Dharma according to their needs.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Are all the dharmas you have described like a dream, like an echo, like a mirage, like a shadow, like an illusion, and like a magical transformation?"
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One.”
World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are like dreams and even like magical illusions, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
World-Honored One!
"World-Honored One, these things— from dreams up to transformations— are false and unreal. One should not,
by means of unreal and false dharmas, be able to fulfill the dānapāramitā, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma)."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
Unreal and false dharmas cannot fulfill the dānapāramitā, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities.”
Practicing these unreal and false dharmas, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! All these dharmas are merely products of recollection, imagination, and conceptual construction.
By employing such conceptualization, recollection, and mental construction, one cannot attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti!

All these dharmas can assist the path, but they cannot bring about the attainment of the fruit of benefit—namely, that all these dharmas are unarisen, unemerged, and signless. This includes the wholesome karma performed by a bodhisattva from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*) onward, whether it be the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to all-knowledge.

Why is this? Because one knows that all dharmas are like dreams and even like illusions; such dharmas do not fulfill the *dānapāramitā* up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and thus cannot bring about the maturation of sentient beings, the purification of Buddha-fields, or the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The wholesome deeds performed by this bodhisattva mahāsattva—from the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)—are like a dream, and so forth, even like a magical creation.
They also know that all sentient beings move as if in a dream, and even know that they move as if in a magical transformation.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not grasp at the perfection of wisdom as being an existent phenomenon; because of this non-grasping, they attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

One knows that all these dharmas are like dreams and are without anything to be grasped, and so on, up to the fact that all dharmas are like magical illusions and are without anything to be grasped. Why is this?

Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is a characteristic that cannot be grasped; the *dhyānapāramitā*, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), are characteristics that cannot be grasped.
Having realized that all phenomena are characterized by being ungraspable, this bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because all dharmas cannot be grasped as signs; they have no fundamental reality or substance, being like dreams and even like magical illusions.
By means of dharmas that cannot be grasped as signs, one cannot attain dharmas that cannot be grasped as signs.

However, because sentient beings do not know and do not see the true characteristics of these dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment for the sake of these sentient beings.

From the time this bodhisattva first resolved on enlightenment, all their acts of giving have been for the sake of all sentient beings; likewise, even the wisdom they cultivate is entirely for the sake of all sentient beings, not for their own person.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not seek unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment for any other purpose than for the sake of all sentient beings.

When this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they perceive that sentient beings are non-existent as sentient beings, yet they dwell within the conceptual mark of "sentient being"; even up to the point where there is no knower and no seer, they dwell within the conceptual marks of knowing and seeing, thereby causing sentient beings to distance themselves from perversion.
Having distanced himself from these, he establishes them within the nature of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Abiding therein, there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), namely, the notion of a sentient being up to the notion of a knower or a viewer.

At that time, the Bodhisattva abandons all agitated minds, conceptualizing minds, and minds of discursive proliferation, constantly practicing the unmoving mind, the non-conceptualizing mind, and the non-discursive mind.

Subhūti! By means of this power of skillful means, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they themselves remain unattached, and they also teach all sentient beings so that they may attain non-attachment.
"It is so from the perspective of worldly convention, but not from the perspective of the ultimate truth.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
When the World-Honored One attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he attained all the Buddha-dharmas.
Was this attained by way of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
or was it attained within the ultimate sense (paramārtha)?
The Buddha said: "It is according to conventional truth that it is said the Buddha attains this Dharma.
Within this Dharma, there is no dharma to be attained, nor is there any person who attains this Dharma."
Why is this? Because if such a person attains these dharmas, they have attained something great;
by employing dualistic dharmas, there is neither the Path nor the fruit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one practices by means of dualistic dharmas, there is neither the Path nor the fruit.”
"If one practices the dharma of non-duality, is there a path and is there a fruit?
The Buddha said,
"If one practices the dharma of duality, there is no path and there is no fruit."
To practice the non-dual dharma is itself neither the path nor the fruit.
If there is neither dual dharma nor non-dual dharma, that is the path and that is the fruit.
Why is this? To say that one attains the Way and the fruits through such dharmas, or that one does not attain the Way and the fruits through such dharmas—
this is frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"In all dharmas that are equal, there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); the absence of conceptual proliferation is the equality of all dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"All dharmas have the nature of non-existence; therein, what is equality?
The Buddha said:

"If there is neither the existence of dharmas nor the non-existence of dharmas, and one does not even speak of the mark of the equality of all dharmas—apart from equality there is no other dharma—and that which is the equality of the mark of equality of all dharmas is something that neither ordinary beings nor sages can practice or reach."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it that even a Buddha cannot practice and cannot arrive [at it]?”
The Buddha said:

“These dharmas are equal; all noble ones—namely, the srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all buddhas—are neither able to practice them nor able to reach them.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha possesses sovereign power and mastery in the practice of all dharmas; why, then, do you say that even the Buddha cannot practice them and cannot reach them?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If the equality of all dharmas were different from the Buddha, you should have asked in such a manner. Subhūti!"

Now, all ordinary persons are equal; all *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, *anāgāmins*, *arhats*, *pratyekabuddhas*, *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas*, and all Buddhas, as well as the noble Dharma, are all equal.
This is one, equal, and non-dual.
That is to say, among all these dharmas, neither "this is an ordinary person," nor "this is a srotāpanna," up to "this is a Buddha," can be apprehended.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If within the equality of all dharmas, none of these—ranging from ordinary persons up to Buddhas—can be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
From ordinary persons, through stream-enterers, up to Buddhas, there is no differentiation.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! Within the equality of all dharmas, there is no such discrimination as 'this is an ordinary person,' 'this is a srotāpanna,' and so on, up to 'this is a Buddha.'"
“World-Honored One!

If there is no differentiation among ordinary people, stream-enterers, and even Buddhas, how is it that one differentiates the manifestation of the Three Jewels in the world—the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel?”
The Buddha said, "What do you think? Are the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Saṃgha-jewel different from all dharmas?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As I have heard the meaning from the Buddha, the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha are no different from all dharmas.
World-Honored One!
These Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are themselves equality."
These dharmas are all neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance, having but a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless.

The Buddha possesses this power: he can distinguish the locations of these characteristicless dharmas, identifying who is an ordinary person, who is a srotāpanna, who is a sakṛdāgāmin, who is an anāgāmin, who is an arhat, who is a pratyekabuddha, who is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and who are the Buddhas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!

If the Buddhas, having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, do not differentiate among dharmas, yet one should know that 'this is hell,' 'this is the realm of hungry ghosts,' 'this is the animal realm,' 'this is the human realm,' 'this is the deva realm'—from the Cāturmahārājika devas up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, the Brahmā devas, and even up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception."

Are these the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; and from the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities?
Subhūti said: “I do not know it, World-Honored One! “For this reason, Subhūti!”
"You should know that the Buddha possesses the power of great grace; while remaining unmoved within the equality of all dharmas, he discriminates among those dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Just as the Buddha is unmoved within the equality of all phenomena, so too are ordinary persons unmoved within the equality of all phenomena, and from the stream-enterer up to the pratyekabuddha, they too are unmoved within the equality of all phenomena.
World-Honored One!

If all dharmas have the same characteristic, then that is the characteristic of ordinary persons, the characteristic of srotāpannas, and so on, up to the Buddhas—all are the characteristic of equality.
World-Honored One!

Now, all dharmas each have their own characteristics; that is to say, the characteristic of form is distinct, and the characteristics of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are distinct.

The characteristic of the eye is distinct, and the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are distinct. The characteristic of earth is distinct, and the characteristics of water, fire, wind, and space are distinct.

The characteristics of consciousness are distinct; the characteristics of desire are distinct; the characteristics of hatred and delusion are distinct; the characteristics of wrong view are distinct; the characteristics of dhyāna are distinct;
the characteristics of the immeasurable minds are distinct; the characteristics of the formless attainments are distinct;

the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness are distinct, up to and including the characteristics of the eightfold noble path; and the characteristics of the perfection of giving are distinct, up to and including the perfection of wisdom.
The characteristics of the *pāramitās* are distinct; the characteristics of the three gates of liberation are distinct; the characteristics of the eighteen kinds of emptiness are distinct;

the characteristics of the Buddha’s ten powers are distinct; the characteristics of the four fearlessnesses are distinct; the characteristics of the four unhindered knowledges are distinct; the characteristics of the eighteen unique qualities are distinct;

the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are distinct; and the characteristics of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are distinct—this is the case for ordinary beings.
The characteristics of ordinary people differ, even up to the characteristics of a Buddha.

Since all dharmas each have their own distinct characteristics, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, not engage in conceptual discrimination among these various distinct characteristics of dharmas?
If one does not engage in non-conceptualization, one cannot practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If one does not practice the perfection of wisdom, one cannot proceed from one stage (bhūmi) to the next.
If one does not proceed from stage to stage, one cannot enter the bodhisattva position.
Because one cannot enter the bodhisattva position, one cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because they cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, they cannot fulfill the perfection of supernatural powers (ṛddhipāramitā).

Because they do not fulfill the perfection of supernatural powers, they cannot fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), nor can they fulfill the perfections up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Consequently, they are unable to travel from one buddha-field to another to make offerings to the Buddhas, to plant roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas, and to use those roots of goodness to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Regarding what you have asked, these characteristics of all dharmas belong to ordinary persons as well as to those from the srotāpanna up to the Buddha."
“World-Honored One!
These various dharmas each have their own characteristics—namely, the characteristic of form is distinct, up to the characteristic of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas being distinct.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate all these characteristics without making distinctions?”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Is this mark of form empty?
And so on, up to: are the marks of all Buddhas empty?”
“World-Honored One! It is truly empty. “Subhūti!”
“Can the individual characteristics of phenomena be apprehended in space—
namely, from the characteristic of form up to the characteristics of all Buddhas? Subhūti replied:
"It cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said:

"For this reason, you should know that within the equality of all dharmas, there is neither the ordinary person nor the departure from the ordinary person; likewise, there is neither the Buddha nor the departure from the Buddha."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is this sameness a conditioned dharma?”
"Is it a conditioned dharma or an unconditioned dharma?
The Buddha said,
"It is neither a conditioned dharma nor an unconditioned dharma."
Why is this? Apart from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) cannot be found;
apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena cannot be found.

Subhūti! This conditioned nature and this unconditioned nature—these two dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without form, without shape, and without resistance; they have but a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless."
The Buddha also speaks by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why is this?

Because within the ultimate truth there is no bodily activity, no verbal activity, and no mental activity; yet, one does not attain the ultimate truth apart from bodily, verbal, and mental activities.
This mark of equality of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they perform the deeds of a bodhisattva to benefit sentient beings while remaining unmoved within that ultimate truth.
Chapter Eighty-Seven: Like an Illusion. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Eighty-Seven: Like an Illusion, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If all phenomena are equal and there is nothing that can be acted upon, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom move within the state of equality to perform the deeds of a bodhisattva—namely, through generosity, kind words, beneficial conduct, and collaborative work?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”
These dharmas are equal and unconditioned.

If sentient beings were to know for themselves that all dharmas are equal, the Buddha would not need to employ his spiritual power to extract them from the notion of a self while remaining unmoved within the equality of all dharmas, thereby delivering them through emptiness from the cycle of birth and death in the five realms, up to and including the marks of a knower and a seer.

One transcends the characteristics of form up to the characteristics of consciousness; the characteristics of the eye up to the characteristics of the mind; and the characteristics of the earth element up to the characteristics of the consciousness element. One becomes detached from the nature and characteristics of the conditioned and attains the nature and characteristics of the unconditioned; this nature and characteristics of the unconditioned is itself emptiness.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
By means of what emptiness are all dharmas empty?”
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva remains far removed from all marks of phenomena; because they employ this emptiness, all phenomena are empty. Subhūti!...”
"What do you think, Subhūti? If a conjured person were to create another conjured person, would that conjuration have any substantial reality or anything that is not empty?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."
"This emanated person has no substantial reality and is not non-empty.
"This emptiness and the emanated person—these two things are neither conjoined nor dispersed, because they are empty."
One should not make a distinction between what is empty and what is a transformation. Why?
Because these two things are equal; within emptiness, that which is called "emptiness" or "transformation" cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Subhūti! Form is itself an illusion;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves illusions; even up to all-knowledge, it is itself an illusion.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Are mundane dharmas an illusion, and are supramundane dharmas likewise an illusion?"

That is to say: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three gates of liberation; as well as the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities;

together with the fruits of all dharmas and the noble and holy ones—namely, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and all Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!
Is this Dharma also a transformation?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All dharmas are transformations.

Within these dharmas, there are transformations of the Śrāvaka-dharma, transformations of the Pratyekabuddha-dharma, transformations of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva-dharma, and transformations of the Buddha-dharma."
There is the transformation of phenomena characterized by afflictions, and there is the transformation of phenomena characterized by the causal conditions of karma. For these reasons,
Subhūti, all phenomena are transformations.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
These afflictions are severed, namely: the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the fruit of an arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha.”
“Are all the severances of the habitual tendencies of the afflictions transformations?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If there is any dharma that possesses the characteristics of arising and ceasing, it is all a transformation.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
what dharmas are not transformations?”
The Buddha said:
"If a dharma is without arising and without cessation, it is not a transformation. Subhūti said:
“What is it that is neither born nor extinguished, and is not a transformation?
The Buddha said:
“The mark of non-deception, which is nirvāṇa—this dharma is not a transformation.”
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has himself taught that all dharmas are equal—neither created by śrāvakas, nor created by pratyekabuddhas, nor created by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nor created by buddhas;
whether a buddha appears or not, the nature of all dharmas is eternally empty.”
"The emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself nirvāṇa; why then do you say that the single dharma of nirvāṇa is not like a transformation? The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
All phenomena are equal; they are not produced by Śrāvakas, and even intrinsic emptiness is itself Nirvāṇa.

If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening hears that all these phenomena are ultimately empty of intrinsic nature, and even that Nirvāṇa is like an illusion, his mind will be struck with alarm and fear.

"It is for the sake of bodhisattvas who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment that I distinguish between those subject to arising and ceasing as being like an illusion, and those beyond arising and ceasing as not being like an illusion.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"How does one instruct a bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind so that they may come to know the emptiness of intrinsic nature? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Are all dharmas something that existed originally but now no longer exist?"
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-six; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eighty-Eight: Sadāprarudita.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva seeking the prajñāpāramitā should do as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāprarudita did.”
"This Bodhisattva is now practicing the bodhisattva path in the presence of the Buddha Great Thunder Sound.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita seek the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:

"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was originally seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, he did not begrudge his own body or life, nor did he seek fame or profit. While in a secluded forest, he heard a voice in the air saying:"
"O son of good family! From here, travel eastward;
do not think of exhaustion, do not think of sleep, do not think of food or drink, do not think of day or night, do not think of cold or heat, and do not think of the internal or the external."
"Good son! When you walk, do not look to the left or right.

As you walk, do not destroy the characteristics of the body, do not destroy the characteristics of form, and do not destroy the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? If one destroys these various marks, one will encounter obstacles within the Buddha-dharma.

If one encounters obstacles within the Buddha-dharma, one will then wander through the cycle of birth and death across the five realms of existence, and will likewise be unable to attain the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita replied to the voice in the sky, saying:
"I shall follow your instructions.
For what reason?..."
I desire to act as a great illumination for all sentient beings, to gather all the teachings of the Buddhas, and to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Then, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita again heard a voice from the air saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"

You should give rise to faith in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; you should seek the Prajñāpāramitā with a mind free from signs, remaining detached from the mark of a self, and even detached from the marks of a knower and a seer.
One should distance oneself from evil associates and draw near to, and make offerings to, virtuous friends.
What constitutes a virtuous friend?

One who can explain the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and non-ceasing, as well as the knowledge of all modes, causing people’s minds to enter into joy, faith, and delight—this is a virtuous friend.
"Good son! If you practice in this way, before long you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā—whether from a written scroll or from what a bodhisattva has spoken."
"Good son! Toward the one from whom you have heard this Prajñāpāramitā, you should give rise to a mind that regards them as a Buddha. Good son!"
You should recognize this kindness and reflect thus:
"The one from whom I have heard this Prajñāpāramitā is my true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Because I have heard this Dharma, I shall swiftly attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
They shall draw near to all Buddhas, always be born within Buddha-lands, remain far removed from all hardships, and attain the perfection of a place free from difficulties. Good son!
You should contemplate and weigh these merits, and toward the place from which you hear the Dharma, give rise to the thought of it being the Buddha.
O son of good family!
Do not follow after the Dharma Master with a mind seeking worldly gain; rather, follow the Bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma solely out of love for the Dharma and reverence for the Dharma.
At that time, one should recognize this as the work of Māra.
If an evil Māra provides the conditions for the five desires to a bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma, pretending it is for the sake of the Dharma and causing them to accept them;
yet if the preaching bodhisattva enters the gateway of the true Dharma, they will accept these things through the power of their merit without being stained by them.

Furthermore, there are three reasons for accepting these five desires: by the power of skillful means; because he wishes to cause sentient beings to plant roots of goodness; and because he accepts them in order to act in common with sentient beings. You should not give rise to defiled thoughts regarding this, but should instead conceive pure perceptions.
He thought to himself:

"I have not yet attained *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means). It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings and causing them to obtain merit that the Great Master accepts these various desires through the method of skillful means."
"In the wisdom of a bodhisattva, there is no attachment and no obstruction;
it is not defiled by desire. Good son!
You should immediately contemplate the true mark of all phenomena.
What is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena?
It is that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure. Why is this so?
All phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; they are without sentient beings, without persons, and without self.
All phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like shadows, like mirages, and like transformations.
"Good son! Having contemplated the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these phenomena, you should follow the Dharma teacher; before long, you shall accomplish the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, good son!"
You should further recognize these as the deeds of Māra.
If a bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma sees someone wishing to receive the Prajñāpāramitā but does not direct their thoughts toward them, you should not give rise to a mind of resentment.
"You should simply give rise to a mind of reverence for the sake of the Dharma; do not harbor thoughts of weariness or indolence, and you should always follow after the Dharma Master.
At that time, having received this instruction from the sky, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita traveled eastward from there.
Before long, he again had this thought:
"Why did I not ask the voice in the air: 'Where shall I go?'"
"How far away is it?
From whom shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā?
At that moment, he stopped, weeping in sorrow and anxiety, and thought to himself:

"I shall dwell here for one day and night, or two, three, four, five, six, or seven days and nights; while dwelling here, I will not think of exhaustion, nor even hunger, thirst, cold, or heat, and until I have heard and received the causes and conditions of the Prajñāpāramitā, I shall never rise."
“Subhūti! It is as if a person had an only son who suddenly died; overcome by grief and the poison of suffering, he harbors nothing but anguish and gives rise to no other thought.
In the same way, Subhūti!”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had no other thought in his mind, but only reflected:
"When shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā?
Why did I not ask the voice in the sky: [when shall I hear it?]"
"Where should I go? How far or near will my destination be?
From whom shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā?"
“Subhūti! While the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita was thus grieving and reflecting, a Buddha appeared in the sky and spoke to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
‘Excellent, excellent!’”
"Good son! When the Buddhas of the past practiced the bodhisattva path, they sought the prajñāpāramitā just as you do today, good son!"
Because you possess such diligent perseverance and a love for the Dharma, proceed eastward from here; five hundred yojanas from this place, there is a city named Saṃghagandha.
The city has seven tiers, adorned with the seven treasures; its terraces, pavilions, and railings are all inlaid and decorated with the seven treasures.
There are moats made of the seven treasures, surrounded on all sides by rows of trees made of the seven treasures, forming seven concentric circles.

The city was twelve yojanas in length and breadth; it was prosperous, peaceful, and teeming with people. Its five hundred market districts and streets were aligned like a painting, and its bridges and ferries were as vast and pure as the earth itself.

Upon each of the sevenfold city walls were watchtowers made of the seven treasures, with rows of jeweled trees whose branches and leaves were fashioned from gold, silver, musaragalva, agate, coral, lapis lazuli, crystal, and red pearls. Continuous cords of jewels and nets of golden bells covered the tops of the walls; when the wind blew, the sound of the bells was harmonious and elegant.
It is like the performance of the five musical instruments, which is exceedingly delightful.
The sound of the golden nets and precious bells is likewise, bringing joy to sentient beings.
On all four sides of the city, there are flowing ponds, pure and with water of temperate temperature; within them are various boats adorned with the seven treasures.
This is brought about by the past karma of these sentient beings, who ride upon this precious ship to enjoy themselves and play.
Within the waters of the various ponds are lotuses of many kinds—blue, yellow, red, and white—and a multitude of other exquisite flowers cover the surface of the water everywhere.
All the various flowers existing within this trichiliocosm are contained therein.
On the four sides of that city are five hundred gardens and groves, adorned with the seven treasures, which are most delightful.
Within each garden there are five hundred ponds; each pond is ten li in length and breadth, all constructed of the seven treasures and adorned with various colors.

Within the waters of these various ponds, blue, yellow, red, and white lotuses also completely cover the surface; these lotuses are as large as chariot wheels, emitting a blue light from their blue hue, a yellow light from their yellow hue, a red light from their red hue, and a white light from their white hue.
Within the waters of these various ponds, fowl, wild geese, mandarin ducks, and many other species of birds harmonize their songs.

These gardens and groves belong to no one; they are the karmic retribution for the past deeds of these sentient beings. Because they have long cherished faith and delight in the profound Dharma and have practiced the causes and conditions of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they now receive this retribution.
"Good son! Within this City of Fragrant Multitude there is a great high terrace, upon which stands the palace of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
That palace is one yojana in length and breadth; it is constructed from the seven precious jewels, adorned with various colors, and is most delightful."
There were seven layers of walls, all likewise made of the seven treasures, with railings of the seven treasures and pavilions of the seven treasures.
There were seven layers of moats, all surrounded by deep trenches made of the seven treasures, constructed by piling up the seven treasures.
There are seven rows of trees with branches and leaves made of the seven treasures, surrounding [the palace] in seven tiers.
Within that palace there are four kinds of pleasure gardens:
the first is named Constant Joy, the second is named Free from Sorrow, the third is named Flower Ornament, and the fourth is named Fragrance Ornament.
Within each garden there are eight ponds:

the first is named Worthy (Bhadra), the second Worthy Superior (Subhadra), the third Joyful (Nanda), the fourth Joyful Superior (Sunanda), the fifth Peaceful (Kṣema), the sixth Abundant Peace (Bahukṣema), the seventh Remote (Viveka), and the eighth Irreversible (Avivartika).
On each of the four sides of the ponds is one kind of treasure: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
The ponds are made of ruby, and their bottoms are spread with golden sand.
On each side of every pond there are eight stairways, adorned with various exquisite jewels; between the stairways stand rows of *jambūnada* gold plantain trees.
In all the ponds, various lotuses—blue, yellow, red, and white—completely covered the surface of the water.
Along the four sides of the ponds grew beautiful flowering trees; when the wind blew, the flowers fell into the pond waters.
That pond was endowed with eight kinds of meritorious qualities; its fragrance was like that of sandalwood, and it was perfect in color and flavor, light and soft.

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, together with sixty-eight thousand court ladies, enjoyed themselves fully provided with the five desires. Likewise, the men and women of the city all entered the gardens such as Nityapramudita and the ponds such as Bhadra, where they enjoyed themselves fully provided with the five desires.
"Good son! After the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has finished sporting and enjoying himself with his ladies-in-waiting, he preaches the Prajñāpāramitā three times each day.
Within the city of Gandhavatī, men and women, both great and small, arrange a great Dharma throne in the most crowded places within the city."

The four legs of those seats were made either of gold, or silver, or lapis lazuli, or crystal; they were spread with variegated carpets and cushions, draped with curtains and ribbons, covered above with exquisite white cotton wool, and strewn with various kinds of wonderful flowers and incense.
The seat was five *li* high, draped with a white pearl canopy.

On its four sides, flowers of five colors were scattered, various famous incenses were burned, and fragrant unguents were smeared upon the ground, as an offering and mark of reverence for the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata preached the Prajñāpāramitā from this seat; those multitudes of people thus paid him respectful homage and made offerings to Dharmodgata for the sake of hearing the Prajñāpāramitā.

In this great assembly, hundreds of thousands of millions of beings—gods and humans—gathered together in one place; among them were those who listened, those who received, those who retained, those who recited, those who wrote down, those who practiced right contemplation, and those who acted according to what was taught.
At that time, by virtue of these causes and conditions, all sentient beings shall not fall into the evil realms and shall not regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"You, son of good family!
Go to the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata resides, and you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
Son of good family!"

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has been your spiritual friend throughout successive lifetimes; he is able to instruct you in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, teaching, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening you.
When the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata formerly sought the Prajñāpāramitā, he was just as you are now.
Go; do not calculate days and nights, and do not give rise to a mind of obstruction. Before long, you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was filled with joy and delight, and he thought to himself:
"When shall I be able to see this good man and hear the Prajñāpāramitā?"
“Subhūti! It is as if there were a person struck by a poisoned arrow, who has no other thought in mind but only this:
‘When shall I find a skilled physician who can pull out the poisoned arrow and remove this suffering of mine?’”
"In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāprarudita had no other thought, but made only this vow:
'When shall I behold the bodhisattva Dharmodgata, so that I may hear the Prajñāpāramitā?'"
"Having heard this Prajñāpāramitā, I have severed all thoughts of existence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita remained in that place, mindful of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata’s attainment of unimpeded wisdom and vision regarding all dharmas; immediately, immeasurable gates of samādhi appeared before him.
These are: the samādhi of contemplating the nature of all phenomena; the samādhi of the non-apprehensibility of the nature of all phenomena;

the samādhi of destroying ignorance regarding all phenomena; the samādhi of the non-differentiation of all phenomena; the samādhi of sovereign indestructibility regarding all phenomena; the samādhi of the illumination of all phenomena;
the samādhi of the departure from darkness regarding all phenomena; and the samādhi of the non-existence of all phenomena...
The samādhi of distinct continuities, the samādhi of the non-apprehensibility of all phenomena, the samādhi of scattering flowers,
the samādhi of the selflessness of all phenomena, the samādhi of illusory power, the samādhi of attaining the likeness of a mirror-image,
the samādhi of attaining the languages of all sentient beings, and the samādhi of causing all sentient beings to rejoice; [entering...]
The Samādhi of Discerning Sounds; the Samādhi of Attaining Adornments of Various Languages, Words, and Phrases;
the Samādhi of Fearlessness; the Samādhi of the Nature of Constant Silence; the Samādhi of Attaining Unhindered Liberation; the Samādhi of Freedom from Dust and Defilement;
the Samādhi of Adornments of Names, Words, and Phrases; and the Samādhi of Perceiving All Dharmas.
The Samādhi of the Unobstructed Summit of All Dharmas, the Samādhi Like Space, the Samādhi Like a Vajra,
the Samādhi of Fearlessness Toward Attachment to Form, the Samādhi of Attaining Victory, the Samādhi of Turning the Eye, the Samādhi of the Ultimate Nature of Dharmas,
the Samādhi Capable of Granting Peace, the Samādhi of the Lion’s Roar, and the Samādhi that Surpasses All Multitudes.
The Samādhi of Birth, the Samādhi of Floral Adornment, the Samādhi of Severing Doubt, the Samādhi that Follows All That is Solid,
the Samādhi of Emerging from All Dharmas to Attain Supernatural Powers and Fearlessness, the Samādhi of Being Able to Penetrate All Dharmas,
the Samādhi of the Seal of Wealth of All Dharmas, the Samādhi of Non-discriminative Vision of All Dharmas, and the Samādhi of Detachment from All...
The Samādhi of Vision, the Samādhi of Departing from All Darkness, the Samādhi of Departing from All Marks, the Samādhi of Liberation from All Attachment,
the Samādhi of Eliminating All Indolence, the Samādhi of Attaining Profound Illumination of the Dharma,
the Samādhi of the Unassailable, the Samādhi of Destroying Māra, the Samādhi of Non-attachment to the Three Realms, and the Samādhi of Arising...
The Samādhi of Radiance and the Samādhi of Beholding All Buddhas.

While the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita dwelt within these various samādhis, he immediately beheld immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions comforted the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita,
saying: "Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
"When we originally practiced the bodhisattva path, we sought the prajñāpāramitā and attained these various samādhis, just as you have now attained them.
Having attained these various samādhis, we skillfully entered the prajñāpāramitā, perfected the power of expedient means, and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression."

When we contemplate the nature of these samādhis, we do not see any dharma that emerges from or enters into samādhi; nor do we see anyone who practices the Buddha-way, nor anyone who attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! This is called the Prajñāpāramitā, which means not to be mindful of the existence of these various dharmas. Good son!"

We abide in the dharma of non-conceptualization and have attained this golden-colored body, a fathom-wide radiance, the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, and inconceivable wisdom; we are fully endowed with all merits, including unsurpassed precepts, unsurpassed samādhi, and the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
Because he is fully endowed with all merits, even a Buddha cannot grasp their characteristics and describe them exhaustively, let alone śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or any other persons.
For this reason, son of good family!
Within these Buddha-dharmas, you should redouble your reverence and affection, giving rise to a pure mind; toward spiritual friends, you should conceive the thought that they are Buddhas.
"Why is this? Because they are protected by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), Bodhisattvas quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Buddhas of the ten directions, saying:
"What are my spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) whom I should approach, serve, and make offerings to?
The Buddhas of the ten directions said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!..."
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has, throughout successive lifetimes, taught and brought you to maturity for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata protects you and instructs you in the power of skillful means regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*; he is your virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

If you were to honor and revere the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata for one eon, or two, or three, or even for more than a hundred eons—bearing him upon your head with respect and providing every kind of pleasure, including all the exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures found within the trichiliocosm—you would still not have repaid even a moment’s worth of his kindness.

Why is this? It is because of the causes and conditions provided by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata that you have attained such samādhis as these, and have acquired the power of skillful means in the Prajñāpāramitā.
After the Buddhas had thus instructed and comforted the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, causing him to rejoice, they suddenly vanished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita arose from samādhi; no longer seeing the Buddhas, he thought to himself:
"From where did these Buddhas come, and to where have they gone?"
Because he did not see the Buddhas, he was again filled with despondency and found no joy, wondering, "Who will sever my doubts? He further thought:

"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has for a very long time constantly practiced the Prajñāpāramitā; he has attained the power of skillful means and the various dhāraṇīs, has achieved mastery within the bodhisattva-dharmas, and has made extensive offerings to the Buddhas of the past."
"Life after life you have been my teacher and have constantly benefited me.
I shall now question the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata as to where all Buddhas come from and to where they go."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita conceived a heart of reverence, affection, and respect for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, and he thought:
"With what shall I make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata?"

Now I am poor and destitute; I have no flowers, incense, or necklaces; no burning incense, fragrant oils, robes, banners, or canopies; and no gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, or amber. I lack such things as these with which to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
"It is not fitting for me to go to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata empty-handed; if I were to go empty-handed, a heart of joy would not arise in me.
I should sell my body to obtain wealth, and for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā*, I shall make an offering to the Dharma-master, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."

Why is this? Throughout countless lifetimes in beginningless birth and death, I have lost my body innumerable times—whether through death, being sold, or for the sake of sensual desires—and in life after life I have endured immeasurable suffering and affliction in the hells; yet I have never sacrificed my body for the sake of the pure Dharma, nor for the sake of making offerings to a teacher of the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita entered a large city along the way and went to the marketplace, where he cried out in a loud voice:
"Who desires a person?"
"Who desires a person?
Who wishes to buy a person?
At that time, the Evil Māra thought to himself:

"Because this Sadāprarudita loves the Dharma, he wishes to sell himself for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā in order to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata; he shall rightly inquire about the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means:
'How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the Prajñāpāramitā and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?'"
They shall become endowed with great learning as vast as the waters of the great ocean.

At that time, they shall be indestructible and fully possessed of all merits, benefiting all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. For the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they shall transcend my realm and likewise teach others to transcend my realm, so that they may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"I shall now ruin this matter.

At that time, the evil Māra concealed all the brahmins and householders so that they would not hear the sound of his self-sale, with the exception of one elder’s daughter, whom Māra was unable to conceal.
At that time, Sadāprarudita was unable to sell his body; filled with grief and weeping, he stood to one side and cried out:
"I have committed a great transgression, for I cannot sell my body."
"I have sold my own body for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā* in order to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra had this thought:
"This Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita loves the Dharma so much that he has sold his own body for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā*, desiring to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."
"I shall test him to see whether this son of good family truly abandons his body out of a deep-seated love for the Dharma.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra transformed himself into the body of a brahmin, walked beside the bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, and asked:
"O son of good family!
"Why are you standing to one side, sorrowful, weeping, and with a haggard countenance? He replied, "O Brahmin!"
I cherish and revere the Dharma; I have sold my own body for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā, desiring to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

Now that I have sold my body, there is no one to buy it. I reflect upon my meager merit and lack of wealth; though I wish to sell my body to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, there is no buyer.
At that time, the brahmin said to the bodhisattva Sadāprarudita: "Good son!
I have no need for a person."
"I now wish to sacrifice to the gods; I must have human hearts, human blood, and human marrow.
Can you sell these to me?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had this thought:
"I have attained a great benefit; I have attained the supreme benefit.
I shall now say to the brāhmaṇa:
'Whatever you require, I shall give it all to you.'"
The brahmin said: "Good son! What price do you require?"
He replied, “Give it to me as you wish. Immediately,
Sadāprarudita took a sharp knife in his right hand, pierced his left arm to draw blood, cut the flesh from his right thigh, and was about to break the bone to extract the marrow.
At that time, there was the daughter of an elder on an upper terrace who saw from afar the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita cutting his own body without regard for his life, and she thought to herself:
"For what reason or cause does this son of good family afflict his body with such hardship?"
"I shall go and ask him.
The merchant's daughter then descended from the upper story and went to where Sadāprarudita was, asking him: "Noble son!..."
"For what reason do you afflict your body with such hardship?
What will you do with this heart, blood, and marrow? Sadāprarudita replied:
"I have sold myself to this Brahmin in order to provide for the *prajñāpāramitā* and to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
The daughter of the elder said, "Noble son!..."
"If one sells oneself in this way, desiring to offer one's own heart, marrow, and blood to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata,
what kind of merit and benefit will be obtained? Sadāprarudita replied,
"O virtuous woman!..."
This person has skillfully studied the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of expedient means; this person shall explain to me what a bodhisattva ought to do and the path that a bodhisattva should travel.

I shall study this Dharma and study this Path so that, when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I may serve as a refuge for sentient beings. I shall obtain a golden-colored body, the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary signs, a fathom-wide aura, immeasurable radiance, great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and the six supernormal powers.
