I shall attain inconceivable, pure morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom; I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and obtain unimpeded omniscient vision regarding all phenomena, thereby distributing the supreme treasure of the Dharma to all sentient beings.
"May I obtain such merits and benefits as these from him.

At that time, having heard this sublime Dharma of the Buddha, the daughter of the elder was filled with great joy; her heart leaped and her hair stood on end as she spoke to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!
"How most rare!
What you have spoken is subtle and difficult to encounter.
For the sake of each and every one of these meritorious qualities, one should sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Why is this? What you have spoken is most profound and subtle.
O son of good family!

Whatever you now require, I shall give it all to you: gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, amber, coral, and other such precious treasures; as well as flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, burning incense, banners, canopies, robes, musical instruments, and all other articles for making offerings—use these to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
"O son of good family!
Do not afflict your body with hardship.

I, too, wish to go to the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata dwells, so that together with you we may plant various roots of goodness for the sake of attaining such a subtle and wondrous Dharma as you have described."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra resumed his original form and praised the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
You should firmly accept this matter, with a mind that remains unshakable.
All the Buddhas of the past, when they practiced the bodhisattva path, likewise sought the prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means, thereby attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! I truly do not require human hearts, blood, or marrow; I have merely come to test you.
What is your wish? I shall grant it to you."
Sadāprarudita said, "Give me anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Śakra-devānām-indra said:
"This is not something that can be accomplished by my own power; it is the domain of all Buddhas.
I shall certainly provide you with offerings, but please seek another boon as well. Sadāprarudita said:
"If you lack the power to do this, you must certainly provide an offering that shall restore my body to its former state.
At that moment, Sadāprarudita’s body was immediately restored; it was free of any scars or blemishes, no different from how it had been originally.
After Śakra Devānām-indra had granted his vow, he suddenly vanished.
At that time, the daughter of the elder said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!..."
"Come to my home; whatever you require, ask it of my parents and they shall give it all to you.
I, too, shall take leave of my parents and go with you and your attendants to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata for the sake of seeking the Dharma."
Immediately, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the daughter of the elder went together to her house and stood outside the gate.
The daughter of the elder entered and said to her parents:

"Give me various exquisite flowers and incense, as well as necklaces, ointments, burning incense, banners, canopies, garments, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, amber, coral, and all manner of musical instruments and articles for making offerings. Furthermore, permit me and my five hundred handmaidens, who have previously served me, to go together with the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata dwells, in order to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā."
"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata shall preach the Dharma for us; we shall practice according to what he says, and we shall attain the teachings of all Buddhas.
The girl's parents said to her:
"Who is this Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita?"
The woman said: "This person is now outside the gate.
This son of good family seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi with a profound mind, desiring to deliver all sentient beings from the immeasurable suffering of birth and death."
For the sake of the Dharma, this son of good family sold his own body to make an offering to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Since the *prajñāpāramitā* is the path studied by Bodhisattvas, in order to make offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā* and to honor the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, he cried out in a loud voice at the marketplace:
"Who needs a person?"
"Who desires a person?
Who wishes to buy a person?
Unable to sell himself, he stood to one side, weeping in sorrowful distress.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra manifested as a brahmin and came to test him, asking: "Good son!..."
"Why are you standing to one side, grieving, sorrowful,
and weeping? He replied, "O Brahmin!"
"I wish to sell my body in order to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
Yet, being of meager merit, I cannot find a buyer for my body."
The brahmin said to this good man:
"I do not need a person.
I wish to perform a sacrifice to the gods, for which I require human heart, human blood, and human marrow."
"Would you be willing to sell it?
At that time, this son of good family was no longer sorrowful; his mind was harmonious and joyful, and he said to the brahmin, "Whatever you require, I shall give it all to you."
The brahmin asked, "What price do you require? He replied:
"Give it to me as you wish.

Thereupon, this son of good family took a sharp blade in his right hand, pierced his left arm to draw blood, cut the flesh from his right thigh, and further intended to break the bone to extract the marrow.
From atop my pavilion, I saw this event from afar, and at that time I thought to myself:
"For what reason does this person afflict his body with such hardship?
I shall go and ask him."
I immediately descended from the pavilion and went to ask him:
"O son of good family!
For what cause and condition do you thus afflict your own body?"
That son of good family replied to me, saying: "Sister!
For the sake of the Dharma, I wish to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, who preaches the Dharma."
I am poor and possess nothing; I have no gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, crystal, or pearls, nor do I have flowers, incense, or music.
"Sister!
For the sake of making offerings to the Dharma, I have sold my own body.
Now that I have found a buyer, they require human heart, human blood, and human marrow."
"I shall use this price to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, the teacher of the Dharma.
I then asked this good man:
"If you now offer your own body, heart, blood, and marrow to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, what merit will you obtain?"
That son of good family said:
"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata will explain for my sake the perfection of wisdom and the power of skillful means;
this is what a bodhisattva should study, what a bodhisattva should practice, and the path that a bodhisattva should travel."
I shall study this path so that, having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I may become a refuge for all sentient beings.

I shall attain a golden body, the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, a fathom-wide aura, immeasurable radiance, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the ten powers of a Buddha, the eighteen unique qualities, and the six supernormal powers; inconceivable pure morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieved unimpeded omniscient vision regarding all phenomena, I shall distribute the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma to all sentient beings.
“Such subtle and wondrous great dharmas as these, I shall obtain from him.
Having heard of these subtle, inconceivable dharmas and the merits of the Buddhas, and having heard of his great vows, my heart was filled with joy, and I thought:
“This purity, subtlety, greatness, and extreme rarity are indeed such as this; for the sake of each and every dharma, one should sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
Now, this good man, for the sake of the Dharma, is able to undergo ascetic practices and difficult tasks, namely, not sparing his own body or life.
I possess many wonderful treasures; why do you not conceive a wish to seek such a Dharma and make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata?
Having reflected thus, I said to the bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!
Do not afflict your body."

"I shall inform my parents and have them provide you with much gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, crystal, and pearls; as well as flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, robes, banners, canopies, and various musical instruments, to offer in worship to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata who preaches the Dharma."

I also request that my parents and their attendants accompany you to go together and make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata as he preaches the Dharma; we shall plant various roots of goodness together with you, so as to attain such subtle, wondrous, and pure dharmas as you have described.
“‘Father and Mother!

Now please permit me to take with me the five hundred handmaidens previously granted to me, as well as various exquisite flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, powdered perfumes, robes, banners, canopies, musical instruments, and offerings of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli; let me go together with the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Dharma-preacher Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, for the sake of attaining such pure and subtle qualities of all Buddhas.’”
At that time, the parents replied to their daughter:
"That which you have praised is rare and difficult to equal.

You have described this son of good family as one who exerts himself for the Dharma and possesses the great joy of the characteristics of the Dharma; you have also described these Buddhas and their teachings as inconceivable, the most supreme in all the world, and the cause and condition for the joy of all sentient beings."
For the sake of this Dharma, this son of good family has adorned himself with great vows.
We permit you to go and see the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, to attend upon him, and to make offerings to him.
"You have resolved upon the Great Mind and exert such diligence for the sake of all Buddhas; how could we not rejoice in this?
Thus, because that woman wished to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, she was granted permission.
She replied to her parents, saying, "We too rejoice in accordance with this mind; I shall never sever anyone's causal conditions for wholesome dharmas.

At that time, the daughter of the elder prepared five hundred carriages adorned with the seven treasures, and she and her attendants took various precious objects and articles of worship; they carried various flowers produced in water and on land, as well as gold and silver jewel-flowers, robes of many colors, fine incense, powdered incense, and fragrant unguents, along with necklaces and various delicacies and foods. Together with the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and five hundred attendants, each riding in one carriage, they respectfully surrounded him and gradually departed toward the east.

He saw the city of Saṃghāṭa adorned with the seven treasures, surrounded by sevenfold enclosures and sevenfold moats of the seven treasures; likewise, there were sevenfold rows of trees made of the seven treasures.

The city was twelve yojanas in length and breadth, prosperous, peaceful, and most delightful; its population was dense, and its five hundred market districts and streets were aligned and as magnificent as a painting, while its bridges and ferries were as level as the ground, vast and pure.

Seeing the City of Universal Fragrance from afar, he entered the city and beheld the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata seated upon a high dharma-throne on a lofty terrace, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings who paid him reverent homage as he preached the Dharma.
When the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita saw the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, his heart was immediately filled with joy,
just as a bhikṣu enters the third dhyāna, his mind collected and at peace.
Having seen this, they thought:
"It is not appropriate for us to approach the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata by carriage.
Having had this thought, they descended from their vehicles and proceeded on foot.
The daughter of the elder and her five hundred female attendants likewise alighted from their carriages.

Then, Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with the daughter of the elder and the five hundred female attendants—surrounded by and honored with various precious ornaments—went together to the place where Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata had a pavilion made of the seven precious gems, adorned with red ox-head sandalwood. It was covered above with a net of pearls, and at each of its four corners hung mani-jewels serving as lamps. Furthermore, four precious incense burners constantly burned famous incenses for the sake of making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā."
Within that terrace was a great bed made of the seven treasures, upon which a small bed made of four treasures was layered.
Upon the small bed, the Prajñāpāramitā was placed, written on sheets of gold; it was adorned with various banners and canopies hanging down to cover it.

The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the women saw this wondrous terrace, adorned with various precious jewels; they also saw Śakra-devendra and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of devas scattering celestial māndārava flowers, powdered sandalwood, and ground fragments of various jewels upon the terrace, while playing celestial music in the air to delight the terrace.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita asked Śakra Devānām Indra:

"Kauśika! For what cause and condition do you, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of devas, scatter celestial māndārava flowers, powdered sandalwood, and ground fragments of various jewels upon this terrace, and play celestial music in the void to delight this terrace?"
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"O son of good family! Do you not know?"
This is the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; it is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, capable of giving birth to all Buddhas and sustaining all bodhisattvas.
By training in this Prajñāpāramitā, bodhisattvas accomplish all meritorious qualities and attain the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience) of all Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, Sadāprarudita was filled with joy and delight, and he asked Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Kauśika! This Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; she gives birth to all Buddhas and sustains all bodhisattvas."
When a bodhisattva studies this prajñāpāramitā, they accomplish all merits and attain the omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) of all buddha-dharmas. Where is he now?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Good son! Within this pavilion there is a great bed made of the seven treasures, upon which four kinds of precious small beds are layered."

The Prajñāpāramitā was written on golden tablets and placed upon a small couch; the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has sealed it with seals of the seven precious jewels, so that we are unable to open it to show it to you.

At that time, Sadāprarudita, together with the elder’s daughter and five hundred female attendants, took the articles of offering—flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, and canopies—and divided them into two portions: one portion he offered to the Prajñāpāramitā, and the other portion he offered to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata upon the Dharma-seat.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with five hundred women, took flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, music, and various precious jewels; having made these offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, he then proceeded to the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was.

Having arrived, he saw the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata seated upon the Dharma throne; for the sake of the Dharma, he made offerings by scattering various flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, liquid perfumes, precious golden and silver flowers, banners, canopies, and jeweled robes over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

At that time, the various flowers, incense, and precious robes in the sky above the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata transformed into a flower pedestal. Fragrant sandalwood powder, precious dust, and gold and silver jeweled flowers transformed into a precious canopy. Above the precious canopy, the various precious robes scattered there transformed into a precious parasol, with various precious banners hanging down from its four sides.
When Sadāprarudita and the women saw the miraculous transformations performed by the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, they were filled with great joy and thought:
"This is unprecedented!"
The spiritual virtue of the Great Master Dharmodgata is indeed such as this.
If his supernormal powers were already like this while he was practicing the bodhisattva path, how much more so will they be when he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

At that time, the daughter of the elder and the five hundred women, with pure faith and deep reverence for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made this vow:

"Just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has attained the various profound dharmas of a bodhisattva; just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata makes offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*; just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata expounds and reveals the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* within the great assembly; and just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has attained the power of skillful means (*upāya*) through the *prajñāpāramitā*, accomplished the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and attained mastery in the bodhisattva deeds—may we also become thus."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women, having made offerings of incense, flowers, and precious objects to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.
Having stood to one side, he addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, saying:
"When I was formerly seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, I heard a voice in the air within a secluded forest, which said:
'O son of good family!'"
"You should travel east from here, and you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
Having received these words, I traveled east. After traveling for a short while, I had this thought:
"Why do I not ask the voice in the sky:"
"Where shall I go? Is the destination far or near?
From whom shall I hear [the Dharma]?"
At that time, I was filled with great sorrow and wept; I remained in that place for seven days and seven nights, so consumed by grief that I did not even think of food or drink, but thought only:
"When shall I be able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā?"
While I was thus sorrowful and single-mindedly recollecting the *prajñāpāramitā*,
I saw the body of the Buddha in the midst of the void, who spoke to me, saying:
"O son of good family!

"Do not abandon this mind of great desire and great diligence; with this mind of great desire and great diligence, travel eastward from here. Five hundred yojanas from here, there is a city named Saugandhikā."
In this assembly there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Dharmodgata; from that person you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
This Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has been your spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) throughout successive lifetimes and has constantly protected you.
"Having received the Buddha's instructions, I set out toward the east with no other thought in mind, thinking only:
'When shall I see the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata so that he may preach the Prajñāpāramitā to me?'"

At that time, as I stood upon the middle way, I attained unimpeded wisdom and vision regarding all phenomena, and various samādhis, such as the contemplation of the equality of the nature of all phenomena, became manifest before me.
Having dwelt in this samādhi, he saw immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas of the ten directions preaching this Prajñāpāramitā.
Those Buddhas praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
"Good son! When I originally sought the Prajñāpāramitā, I attained various samādhis just as you do today.
Having attained these various samādhis, I universally attained all the Buddha-dharmas."
“The Buddhas extensively expounded the Dharma for me and, having comforted me, suddenly vanished.
When I arose from samādhi, I thought:
‘From where did these Buddhas come, and to what place have they gone?’”
Because I did not see the Buddhas, I was filled with great sorrow and anxiety, and I further thought:

"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has made offerings to previous Buddhas, planted roots of goodness, long practiced the Prajñāpāramitā, and is well-versed in the power of skillful means; having attained mastery within the bodhisattva path, he is my spiritual friend who protects me."
"I shall ask the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata about this matter:
'From where do all Buddhas come, and to where do they go?
Now I ask the Great Teacher:"
"From where do these Buddhas come, and to where do they go?
Great Master, please explain to me the origins from which the Buddhas come and the destinations to which they go, so that I may understand."
"Having known this, you shall also never be separated from the sight of the Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!"
The Buddhas come from nowhere, and they go nowhere either. Why is this?
Because the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena is their immovable nature, and the suchness of all phenomena is itself the Buddha.
"Good son! The dharma of non-arising neither comes nor goes; the dharma of non-arising is itself the Buddha.
The dharma of non-extinction neither comes nor goes; the dharma of non-extinction is itself the Buddha."
The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is a dharma that neither comes nor goes; the reality-limit is itself the Buddha.
Emptiness (śūnyatā) neither comes nor goes; emptiness is itself the Buddha. Good son!
Non-defilement is without coming or going; non-defilement is itself the Buddha.
Quiescence is without coming or going; quiescence is itself the Buddha.
The nature of space is without coming or going; the nature of space is itself the Buddha.
"Good son! Apart from these dharmas, there is no further Buddha.
The suchness of all Buddhas and the suchness of all dharmas are a single suchness, without differentiation."
Good son! This Suchness is eternally one, without duality or plurality, transcending all numbers because phenomena have no inherent existence.
It is like when, at midday during the heat of the last month of spring, someone sees shimmering vapors and pursues them, hoping to obtain water.
"What do you think? From what lake, from what mountain, or from what spring does this water come?
Where does it go now?
Does it enter the eastern sea, the western sea, the southern sea, or the northern sea?"
Sadāprarudita said: "O Great Master!
If there is not even water within the mirage, how could there be a place from which it comes or a place to which it goes?"
Dharmodgata Bodhisattva said to Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva:
"Good son! Fools, lacking wisdom, are oppressed by heat and thirst; seeing the flickering of a mirage, they perceive water where there is no water."
Good son! If there are those who discriminate that the Buddhas come and go, you should know that these people are all fools. Why is this?

Good son! The Buddhas cannot be seen by means of their physical bodies; the Dharma-body of all Buddhas neither comes nor goes, and the same is true for the places from which all Buddhas come and to which they go.
Good son! It is like a magician who conjures various things through illusion—whether elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, women, or other such diverse objects.
"What do you think? From where does this illusory phenomenon come, and to where does it go?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied, "Great Master!"
"An illusion has no reality; how could it have a place from which it comes or to which it goes?
"Good son, this person’s conceptualization that the Buddha comes and goes is also like this."
"Good son! For example, suppose one sees in a dream an elephant, a horse, an ox, a sheep, a man, or a woman.
What do you think? Does that which is seen in the dream have a place from which it comes or a place to which it goes?"
Sadāprarudita said, "Great Master!
What is seen in a dream is illusory; how could there be coming or going?"
“Good son! It is just the same for this person who discriminates that the Buddha comes and goes. Good son!”
The Buddha has taught that all dharmas are like dreams.
If there are sentient beings who do not know that all dharmas are like dreams, and instead regard the name-body and form-body as the Buddha, such people discriminate that the Buddhas come and go;
because they do not know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas, they are all among the ranks of ignorant and witless fools.
These people repeatedly come and go through the five realms of existence, remaining far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā* and far removed from all Buddha-dharmas.
Son of good family!
The Buddha has taught that all dharmas are like illusions and like dreams.
If there are sentient beings who know things as they truly are, such persons do not discriminate among phenomena as coming or going, or as arising or ceasing.
If they do not discriminate among phenomena as coming or going, or as arising or ceasing, they are then able to know the true nature of all phenomena as taught by the Buddha.

This person practices the *prajñāpāramitā* and is close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they are called a true disciple of the Buddha, do not falsely consume the offerings of the faithful, and are worthy of receiving support as a field of merit for the world.

Good son! It is like the various jewels within the waters of the great ocean: they do not come from the east, nor from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below;
rather, it is due to the causes and conditions of the roots of goodness of sentient beings that these jewels arise in the sea.

This jewel also does not arise without cause or without condition; this jewel arises entirely from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and even when this jewel perishes, it does not go away to the ten directions.
They exist because various conditions converge; they cease because various conditions disperse.
Good son, the bodies of all Buddhas are likewise: they arise from the retribution of the causes and conditions of fundamental karma.
When arising, it does not come from the ten directions; when ceasing, it likewise does not go to the ten directions.
It exists merely because various conditions converge, and it ceases because those conditions disperse.
Good son! It is like the sound of a vīṇā: when it arises, it has no place from which it comes; when it ceases, it has no place to which it goes.

It is produced through the conjunction of various conditions: there is the hollow body and the neck, the skin, the strings, the pegs, and the plectrum, and there is a person who strikes it with their hand.

This sound exists through the conjunction of various conditions; yet this sound does not emerge from the hollow of the lute, nor from the neck, nor from the skin, nor from the strings, nor from the plectrum, nor does it emerge from the hands of the person playing.
Sound exists only when a multitude of conditions harmonize; yet when these causes and conditions disperse, there is no place to which it goes.
Good son, the bodies of the Buddhas are also like this: they arise from the causes and conditions of immeasurable merit, not from a single cause, a single condition, or a single merit.
Nor do they exist without causes and conditions; they exist because of the convergence of various conditions.
The bodies of the Buddhas are not produced from a single cause alone; they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
"Good son! You should understand the signs of the coming and going of all Buddhas in this way. Good son!"
Furthermore, you should know that all dharmas have no characteristic of coming or going.

If you know that all Buddhas and all dharmas possess the characteristics of neither coming nor going, and neither arising nor ceasing, you will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and you will also be able to practice the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, gave celestial māndārava flowers to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita and spoke these words:
"O son of good family!
With these flowers, you have made an offering to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; I, therefore, shall protect and honor you. Why is this?
Because by the power of your causal conditions, you today benefit hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, and thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Good son! Such virtuous people are extremely difficult to encounter; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they undergo various hardships and sufferings throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
“Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita accepted the māndārava flowers from Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and scattered them over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, saying:
‘Great Teacher!’”
"From this day forward, I entrust my body to the teacher to provide for his needs and offer him service.
Having spoken thus, she stood before the teacher with palms joined.
At that time, the daughter of the elder and her five hundred attendants said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"From this day forward, we also dedicate our bodies to the Teacher.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, may we attain such a Dharma as that which the Teacher has attained."
"Throughout our successive lives, we shall together make offerings to all Buddhas, and in every life, we shall always provide for our teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita said to the daughter of the elder and the five hundred women:
"If you entrust yourselves to me with sincere hearts, I shall accept you."
The women said, "We entrust ourselves to you with sincere hearts; we shall follow your instructions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with the daughter of the elder and five hundred women, presented to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata all their ornaments, precious objects, and exquisite offerings, as well as five hundred chariots made of the seven treasures, and addressed him, saying:
“‘Great Master! I offer these five hundred women to serve you, and these five hundred chariots for your use.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra praised the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:”
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
It is as it should be that a bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes all that they possess.”
By practicing such giving, one will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By making such offerings to those who preach the Dharma, one will certainly hear the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means.

The past Buddhas, when they originally practiced the bodhisattva path, were also like this: dwelling within generosity, they heard the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means, and thereby attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, desiring to bring the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to full completion, accepted five hundred chariots, the daughter of the elder, and five hundred female attendants.
Having received it, he returned it to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, having finished preaching the Dharma as the sun set, rose and entered his palace.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself:
"I have come for the sake of the Dharma; I should not sit or lie down. I shall wait with two postures—either walking or standing—until the Dharma Master emerges from his palace to preach the Dharma."

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata entered, with single-minded focus for seven years, immeasurable and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattva samādhis, as well as practicing the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the Prajñāpāramitā."
For seven years, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita practiced walking meditation, standing, and remaining upright; he neither sat nor lay down, and knew no sleep.
Free from desire, anger, and affliction, his mind was not attached to sensory flavors, but he thought only:
"When will the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata arise from samādhi to preach the Dharma?"
After seven years had passed, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself:
"I shall prepare a Dharma seat for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata shall preach the Dharma while seated upon it."

"I shall sprinkle and sweep this place until it is pure and clean, and scatter various kinds of flowers to adorn it, for the sake of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, who will preach the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with the daughter of the elder and her five hundred handmaidens, prepared a bed of the seven precious gems for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
The five hundred women each removed their upper garments to spread them upon the seat, thinking:
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata shall sit upon this seat and preach the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means."
After the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had spread the seats, he sought water to sprinkle upon the ground but was unable to find any.
Why was this? Because the evil Māra had concealed it, causing the water not to appear.
Māra thought to himself:

"If the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita fails to find water and, regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, gives rise to even a single thought of inferiority or a divergent mind, then his wisdom will not shine forth, his roots of goodness will not increase, and he will be delayed in reaching all-knowledge."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had this thought:
"I shall pierce my own body and sprinkle its blood upon the ground so that no dust or soil comes to defile the Great Master."
"What use have I for this body? This body must inevitably perish.
Since beginningless birth and death, I have repeatedly lost my body, yet never once for the sake of the Dharma."
Thereupon, he pierced himself with a sharp knife and shed his own blood to sprinkle upon the ground.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva, the daughter of the elder, and the five hundred female attendants all remained single-minded; even the evil Māra was unable to find an opportunity to harm them.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra had this thought: "How extraordinary!
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita loves the Dharma so much that he pierces himself with a blade and sprinkles his own blood upon the ground."
Sadāprarudita and the women’s minds remained unmoved; the evil Māra Pāpīyān could not destroy their roots of goodness.

Their resolve was firm, and they donned the great armor of magnificence, disregarding even their own bodies and lives. With a profound mind, they sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, intending to deliver all sentient beings from the immeasurable sufferings of birth and death.
Śakra-devānām-indra praised the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
Your power of diligence is great, firm, unshakable, and inconceivable.
Your love for the Dharma and your quest for the Dharma are unsurpassed.
O son of good family!

The Buddhas of the past were also like this; because they cherished the Dharma with a profound mind, prized the Dharma, and revered the Dharma, they accumulated all merits and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Then the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself:
"I have finished spreading the Dharma-seat for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata and sweeping it clean; now, where can I find fine, famous flowers to adorn this ground?"
"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata sits upon the Dharma-seat to preach the Dharma, you should likewise scatter flowers as an offering.
Śakra-devānām-indra, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, immediately gave him three thousand *droṇas* of celestial *māndārava* flowers.

Sadāprarudita received the flowers; he scattered half of them upon the ground and kept the other half to offer as an act of worship when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata sat upon the Dharma-seat to preach the Dharma.

At that time, after seven years had passed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata arose from his various samādhis. For the purpose of expounding the Prajñāpāramitā, he proceeded to the Dharma-seat, surrounded with respectful veneration by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings, and sat upon it.
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, his mind attained joy and bliss, like that of a bhikṣu entering the third dhyāna.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, together with the merchant’s daughter and her five hundred handmaidens, went to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was. They scattered celestial māndārava flowers, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and then withdrew to sit to one side.
When the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata saw that he was seated, he addressed the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Good son! Listen attentively and receive this well!"
I shall now explain for you the characteristics of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Son of good family!
Because all phenomena are equal, you should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also equal.
Because all dharmas are detached, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also detached.
Because all dharmas are immovable, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also immovable.
Because all phenomena are without thought, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also without thought.
Because all phenomena are without fear, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also without fear.
Because all phenomena are of one flavor, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also of one flavor.
Because all phenomena are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because all phenomena are unarisen, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also unarisen.
Because all phenomena are unceasing, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also unceasing.
Because space is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because the waters of the great ocean are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because Mount Sumeru is adorned, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also adorned.
Because space is without discrimination, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also without discrimination.
Because form is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because the element of earth is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because the elements of water, fire, and wind are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because the element of space is boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless.
Because it is equal to the diamond (*vajra*) and so forth, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also equal.
Because all phenomena are without discrimination, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also without discrimination.
Because the nature of all phenomena cannot be apprehended, one should know that the nature of the perfection of wisdom also cannot be apprehended.
Because all dharmas are equal in their non-existence, one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also equal in its non-existence.
Because all dharmas are without activity, one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also without activity.
“Because all dharmas are inconceivable, you should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also inconceivable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita attained various samādhis at his very seat, namely:
the samādhi of the equality of all dharmas, the samādhi of the detachment from all dharmas, and the immovable samādhi.
The samādhi of non-conceptualization, the samādhi of fearlessness regarding all phenomena, the samādhi of the single flavor of all phenomena,
the samādhi of the boundlessness of all phenomena, the samādhi of the non-arising of all phenomena, the samādhi of the non-extinction of all phenomena, the samādhi of the boundlessness of space,
the samādhi of the boundlessness of the waters of the great ocean, and the samādhi of the majesty of Mount Sumeru.
The Samādhi of Adornment, the Samādhi of Non-differentiation of Space, the Samādhi of the Boundlessness of Form,
the Samādhi of the Boundlessness of Feeling, Perception, Volition, and Consciousness, the Samādhi of the Boundlessness of the Earth Element, the Samādhi of the Boundlessness of the Water,
Fire, Wind, and Space Elements, the Samādhi Equal to a Vajra, and the Samādhi of Non-differentiation of All Dharmas.
The Samādhi of Non-Apprehension, the Samādhi of the Inconceivability of All Dharmas, and so forth; thus he attained six million gates of samādhi.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"Just as I now, within this trichiliocosm, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus, teach the Prajñāpāramitā with these signs, with these characteristics, and with these names."

Sadāprarudita attained these six million gates of samādhi and beheld, in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—throughout as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River—all the Buddhas surrounded by their bhikṣus with reverence. They were teaching this Mahāprajñāpāramitā in such a manner, with such characteristics, such appearances, and such names; it was exactly the same everywhere.
From that time forward, the bodhisattva Sadāprarudita’s vast learning and wisdom became inconceivable, like the waters of the great ocean.
He was never separated from the Buddhas, being born in lands where Buddhas reside, and even in his dreams, there was never a moment when he did not see a Buddha.
All difficulties and obstacles have been completely severed; wherever there is a Buddha-field, they will be reborn there in accordance with their vows.

Subhūti, you should know that it is through the causal conditions of this Prajñāpāramitā that a bodhisattva mahāsattva can accomplish all merits and attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

For this reason, Subhūti, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to study the six pāramitās, wish to enter deeply into the wisdom of all buddhas, and wish to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), they should receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and extensively explain to others the Prajñāpāramitā; furthermore, they should copy it into volumes and make offerings to it with respect and praise, using incense, flowers, and even music.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions, and it is that which all Buddhas of the ten directions revere.
Chapter Ninety: Entrustment. *The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Ninety: Entrustment. At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"What do you think? Is the Buddha not your Great Teacher?"
“Are you a disciple of the Buddha? Ānanda replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"The Buddha is my great teacher; the Sugata is my great teacher;
I am a disciple of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! I am your great teacher, and you are my disciple.
Whatever is to be done by a disciple, you have already completed."
Ānanda! You have served and provided for me with acts of loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind, and you have always acted according to my wishes without any transgression. Ānanda!
"While I am currently present, you have always maintained a pure heart in your love, respect, worship, and service toward me.
After my parinirvāṇa, all such acts of love, respect, worship, and service should instead be directed toward the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thus, for a second and even a third time, I entrust the Prajñāpāramitā to you."
Ānanda! Do not forget; do not become the last person to sever the lineage. Ānanda!
For as long as the Prajñāpāramitā remains in the world, one should know that for that long the Buddha remains in the world teaching the Dharma. Ānanda!

If there are those who write down the Prajñāpāramitā, receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and extensively explain it to others; and if they honor, respect, praise, and make various offerings to it with flowers, incense, banners, canopies, precious robes, lamps, and candles—one should know that such persons do not depart from seeing the Buddha and do not depart from hearing the Dharma, and thus they are constantly in close proximity to the Buddha.

When the Buddha had finished teaching the Prajñāpāramitā, Maitreya and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, Ānanda, and the rest of the entire assembly, as well as all the world with its gods, humans, gandharvas, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Twenty-Seven, The Jewel Scripture.
